# Voxeldust — The Block System and the Signal System

**Status:** design, awaiting owner decisions. Not yet binding.
**Date:** 2026-08-03 (revision 3 — detail levels).
**Scope:** everything from "what is one block" to "how does a station tell a ship to engage autopilot".
Covers roadmap phases P4 (terrain + meshing), P5 (physics/collision), P6 (block edits + persistence),
P8 (ship interiors) and P9 (functional blocks + signals).

## Revision history

- **r1 (2026-08-03)** — first full design. Ten researchers with web + repository access, then six design
  sections each drafted, attacked by an independent adversary, and revised; then one integration pass
  that merged the decision registers and reported the surviving conflicts.
- **r2** — `Addendum 1`: the owner rejected the single-planet-radius premise. Radius became per-body data
  on a 39.47 m ladder (any real body within 20 m, Earth within 0.4 m), gravity became derived from an
  authored per-body mass, and worlds became seed-**plus-configuration** with a curated starter planet.
  Also `Appendix A`: the terrain-noise benchmark was run, closing the phase-invalidation risk.
- **r3 (this revision)** — **the owner retracted the "no level-of-detail" ban outright**: *"we will need
  LODs everywhere, but in the smartest way."* `Addendum 2` designs the ladder; then all eight sections
  were swept for it, audited (25 convergence defects found — the edit-pyramid record alone had been
  specified four incompatible ways), adjudicated into one canonical resolution, re-applied, and
  re-verified. All 25 are closed, plus ten residuals found by the second audit.

## Owner rulings — answered decisions

These are settled. Where a section still argues the question, the section is stale and this table wins.

| # | Ruling | Date | Supersedes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **R1** | **The durable placement record is EIGHT bytes, not five.** "I'd rather keep slack just in case." The extra three bytes cost ≈300 MB across a hundred million edits — noise against a format migration. Fifteen bits are reserved and **rejected on decode if non-zero**, so slack cannot be spent by accident. | 2026-08-03 | Register row 2; §2's five-byte layout; §8.6 item 1's three-way disagreement — all closed |
| **R2** | **Light has a level and a colour, and both are ordinary signals where the block is functional.** An emitter publishes its level and its colour; the block lights accordingly. A non-functional emitter (a torch) carries standard values on its substance row and does not vary. | 2026-08-03 | Register row 26 (was: "is the light field coloured?" — answered YES, with the split in R3) |
| **R3** | **Colour lives where you SEE it; brightness lives where it is SIMULATED.** Emissive blocks inside the drawn radius are real renderer lights carrying full colour, at no propagation cost. The server's gameplay field stays **single-channel brightness** plus sky exposure, because the questions it answers ("can this grow", "is it dark here") have no hue. This is what makes R2 free rather than 3× the flood work and 3× the stored state. | 2026-08-03 | §2's "no coloured light" recommendation |
| **R5** | **Appearance-driving signals: BOTH lanes, narrow by default.** The common case is narrow — a block's appearance comes from its substance row and does not vary. But a functional block MAY have its appearance programmed by signals, through a **bounded** set of channels (colour, emissive level, and a small state index the renderer maps to variants). Plain terrain is never in this lane, so the streaming cost is capped at a known figure per functional block rather than being open-ended. | 2026-08-03 | §5/§7's implicit assumption that appearance is static |
| **R6** | **Provenance becomes THREE-state, not two: terrain / biome feature / player-placed.** Owner: *"terrain should not break under weight of gravity, but ideally biom and built things might."* Base terrain never collapses; **biome features** (a tree, a boulder, a rock arch, an ice shelf) collapse like built structures when cut. This spends one of R1's reserved bits — the first deliberate use of the slack, and exactly what it was reserved for. **✅ DESIGNED: `docs/investigation/block_provenance_collapse.md` (14,478 words).** Two bits at 23..22, `0 Terrain / 1 Feature / 2 Placed`, value 3 rejected on decode; reserve 15 → 14; **zero marginal bytes**, because the durable record only ever holds player-authored cells — base terrain has no record at all. Paired with a type-level validator mask so wood may never be Terrain. Fourteen sub-decisions, each with a shipping default so nothing blocks. | 2026-08-03 | §2.5.2's binary `placed` bit and its unconditional-anchor rule |
| **R7** | **Regrowth is BOTH: a player activity AND slow natural recovery, "as in the real world."** Planting is a deliberate act (so forestry is a profession the player-driven economy can price), and cleared land also recovers on its own, slowly, without anyone tending it. Consequence to design against: near settlements, harvest outpaces recovery and land stays cleared; far out, old growth persists — an emergent geography that rewards travel, which the economy design already wants. | 2026-08-03 | Feeds the provenance/collapse ruling; §2.5.2's growth mechanic gains a target field |
| **R8** | **Planted things need stored growth state; regrow-toward-baseline does not.** Owner: *"if we plant, we can plant not in the places where the original trees were… we should store something to be able to grow with time (even when the server was off)."* Correct, and it splits the mechanic in two. **Natural recovery** drifts toward the generated baseline, needs no stored target, and prunes its own delta as it succeeds. **A planted thing** is a permanent divergence from the baseline, so it is stored and it never prunes. What must be stored is only its **growth stage** (one byte, sparse) — NOT when it was planted, because growth is memoryless: a stage advances with a fixed per-tick probability, so a binomial draw over the chunk's elapsed sleep gives the exact distribution without a planting timestamp. The per-chunk last-ticked stamp already reserved for catch-up is the only other input. | 2026-08-03 | Corrects this session's claim that regrowth needs no stored state — true for natural recovery only |
| **R9** | **Reserve the terrain-instability flag now; ship it unset.** Answers R6-6. One spare bit in the per-material flag word, plus a per-realm toggle, set to "stable" on every material we ship — so mining is safe today and collapsible terrain stays a one-material change later rather than a table migration over every saved planet. | 2026-08-03 | R6-6 option (a) |
| **R10** | **The support flood is axial-free, lateral-limited.** Answers R6-5: no attenuation when a step moves toward the anchor along gravity, normal attenuation sideways; the 32-block cap keeps its role as the lateral cantilever limit and loses its role as the flood bound. Unlimited towers, limited overhangs — 7 Days to Die's shipped shape. | 2026-08-03 | §2.5.2's isotropic radius, which capped every tree, tower and mast at 32 blocks |
| **R11** | **Concealed resources: the strategic tier is never a visible block at all.** Answers register row 9 / decision 3-G. Nothing inside the client can hide anything — the secret is the function's OUTPUT, and a client that can draw the ore can enumerate it. The reframe that dissolves it: strategic materials are **what a rock assays to when broken**, not a coloured block you can see, so the client is never told and no pixel is lost. Common ore stays seed-derived, visible and free. Costs zero extra bytes on the wire and zero stored; "terrain never streams" survives with **no exception at all**. ⚠ The placement rule matters more than the key: geologically believable placement is computable from the visible terrain. **✅ `docs/investigation/concealed_resources.md`.** | 2026-08-03 | §3.8's option (C) hybrid, which needed a streaming exception |
| **R12** | **Grass and bushes are pure decoration and never collide.** Owner, accepting the ruling: *"The grass and bushes can be not collidable, pure decorational."* This also settles the one borderline the analysis left open — bushes were "collide only if they must be harvested or stood on", and they are neither. Derived, cosmetic, zero bytes stored, zero bytes sent, deliberately different per client. Grass still RESPONDS: it parts around you, it whispers, it slows you (server-side, from the soil), and it can conceal you. **Consequence to note:** a *harvestable* bush cannot be decoration — if berry-picking is ever wanted, that bush becomes a block, exactly as a stone does. Scenery and world can coexist; a given bush is one or the other. | 2026-08-03 | `docs/investigation/collidable_decoration.md` |
| **R13** | **Bushes are cells that do not collide; they slow you instead.** Owner: *"we should not collide but rather have a slow down effects."* A bush is a real cell — stored, authoritative, harvestable, identical for every player, drawn as a 3D art mesh, spanning more cells as you place more — but its shape carries an EMPTY collider, so you walk through it and are slowed. Minecraft's tall grass is the precedent: a real block with no collision box. This keeps the never-see-what-you-cannot-touch rule trivially (you touch none of it) and avoids the sub-step-height snag that is the shipped complaint against Valheim. | 2026-08-03 | `docs/investigation/collidable_decoration.md`'s "collide only if harvested or stood on" borderline |
| **R14** | **Leaves are pass-through too, like bushes.** Owner: *"leaves should be also pass through."* Canopy cells are real cells (stored, harvestable, they hold the tree's shape and its 120:1 canopy-to-trunk spread) but carry an empty collider, so you fall through a canopy rather than standing on it. This departs from Minecraft, deliberately, and makes every plant answer the collision question the same way. Trunks still collide. **⏸ DEFERRED BY THE OWNER to just before implementation:** the contained pass on what collider each shape gets, whether a pass-through cell hides faces behind it, whether it counts as solid for ambient occlusion and for building on, and the fitted-vs-cube collider for rocks. Cheap to answer then; the ruling above is what it must not contradict. | 2026-08-03 | Minecraft's standable leaves; `collidable_decoration.md`'s solid-canopy specification |
| **R15** | **A name is an address, not a key — the write-permission hole is REAL and is closed by an issued capability.** Owner: *"anybody can take over my ship simply by sending signals with the correct names."* Verified: from OUTSIDE a realm the attack already fails three ways (channels are realm-private so there is no route; no grant, no cross-boundary write; a per-bundle tamper seal). From INSIDE it is **open** — §7 asserts a write ACL three times and specifies it zero times: no owner field, no allowlist storage, no default, no enforcement site on any write path. The fix: a write capability is an **issued** compiled edge, admitted once at bind time by the realm that owns the channel, never derived from a name. Checked at bind, not per message — a per-signal check costs 3× to 37,720× the entire delivery constant. ⚠ **The blueprint attack defeats every obvious fix** and needs its own answer. **✅ `docs/investigation/signal_authority_and_relays.md`.** | 2026-08-04 | §7.5.2's "in-realm traffic is implicitly trusted" |
| **R16** | **Encryption and permission are different tools; do not swap them.** Permission (a lock on the ignition) stops people DOING. Encryption (a curtain) stops people SEEING. The takeover attack is a *doing* attack, so encryption would not stop it by an inch. Encryption stays where §7.14 already puts it — a player-built cipher block on the open radio plane, with keys as an in-game item, traffic analysis as deliberate gameplay. | 2026-08-04 | the owner's "cypher the signals" framing, answered rather than adopted |
| **R17** | **Relays become player-built functional blocks, with time as the cost.** Owner's model, and better than the engine-service relay plane §7.3 designed: a relay network is infrastructure players build, own, defend, tax and destroy, which makes long-range comms have a supply chain and makes radio jammable. Reuses §7.6's deterministic light-lag rather than inventing a second delay mechanism. Not needed now — but the message shape must admit a hop count, an arrival deadline and a dedup identity from the first slice, or it is a migration. | 2026-08-04 | §7.3.2's `Relay { net }` engine-served plane |
| **R18** | **Blueprints carry ALL wiring, and are built at a DOCK — with a connection manifest beside the bill.** Owner's mechanic, recorded here for the first time: you bring a blueprint to a dock; the dock reads it, works out the materials and sets a price; you pay; it **spins up a realm belonging to you** and the ship is fully reconstructed there, wiring intact, owned by you — optionally with a royalty to the design's author. **The manifest rule, attached:** the dock already inspects the design in order to price it, so it also lists every channel the design reaches OUTSIDE the construct, alongside the materials and the cost. Nothing is stripped and nothing is silently changed; the buyer sees `this design connects to 3 channels outside the ship` and decides. **Why the manifest is needed even though the ship is wholly yours:** the blueprint attack never relied on ownership. It relies on *your own* block being pointed at a channel a stranger can also talk on, because the design said so. Making the ship more thoroughly yours does not change what that block is listening to — informed consent does. **Three consequences worth naming:** (a) ship construction gains a place, a price and a profession, which is exactly the supply chain the player-driven economy wants; (b) the payment is the anti-abuse brake on realm spin-up, which is a real server cost and needs one; (c) author royalties require a durable author identity that survives copying — a small design in its own right, because a blueprint is data and data gets copied. | 2026-08-04 | `signal_authority_and_relays.md`'s blueprint-attack finding, and the strip-external-bindings fix I proposed and the owner rejected in favour of disclosure |
| **R19** | **✅ APPLIED to §7 — the two urgent signal fixes.** Owner: *"Fix those two urgent things now."* No signal code exists yet, so these are specification amendments, made in place with the superseded text struck rather than deleted. **(1) Channel keys are SCOPED** — `Realm` (default), `Construct`, `Net`, `Protocol` — replacing the bare-name hash that made every player's `thrust` the same channel galaxy-wide. `Protocol` names (`dock.*`, `sys.*`, `hull.*`, `chat.*`) become compiled constants **mintable by nobody**, which closes the forged-autopilot-offer phishing hole. Still computed, never allocated, so the no-global-registry argument survives; the birthday bound becomes proven per scope. **⚠ ONE-WAY DOOR — must ship in the first slice**, because it changes what a channel name resolves to and any wiring saved beforehand re-resolves to different channels. **(2) The autopilot handshake is re-ordered to verify → resolve → display**: the station's signature is checked *before* the dialog is rendered rather than after approval; the offer is resolved into the actuator set it will actually control by walking the ship's OWN subscriber list; the dialog is composed by the ship's realm, never from the station's text; and the effect set is re-resolved at mint and refused if it changed while the dialog was open. | 2026-08-04 | §7.4's bare-name `ChannelKey`; §7.12.2 steps 2 and 4 |
| **R20** | **Griefing is answered by ARMOUR-TIER MATERIALS, not by purchased protection — and the mechanism already exists.** Owner: *"Would it make sense if on foot it undestructable (for example because of material), but ships can damage?"* Yes, and it needs **no new rule**: §2.3's damage model already gives every channel a **threshold** as well as a rate, and below the threshold the result is **zero, not slow**. A steel pick's piercing force is *blocked* by granite; the same pick on a titanium hull is 346 s a block ("you do not mine a hull with a pick"); an armour-piercing round on titanium needs 5,190 rounds. So a material whose thresholds sit above hand-delivered force is genuinely immune to anyone on foot, while a ship-mounted cutter at ten times the power passes the same thresholds and cuts it in five seconds. **Why this beats insurance-as-protection** (which `construction_and_spawn.md` §5 recommends against): defence becomes a *material investment* that must be mined, hauled and paid for — finite and expensive — rather than a subscription, so the strongest defence is a position rather than a payment; it is legible from the tooltip like every other material fact; it raises griefing from "any newcomer with a pick, idly" to "someone who owns a ship, flies it there, and is seen doing it"; and **it has no failure mode when the economy is down, because nothing about it is a transaction.** **The starter spaceport is the one exception: flatly unbreakable by design**, not merely tough — about a dozen lines, what every game does, and it means the one place every new player must pass through cannot be interfered with at all. **Two consequences left open:** players can build with armour too, which makes it an *availability* question (how rare and costly is the armour tier) rather than a permissions one; and a ship at the spawn can still do damage under this rule, so whether the spawn needs a no-fire zone is a separate, still-open question. Insurance-as-PAYOUT (destroyed ship rebuilt at a dock from its plan, underwriting as a player profession) remains available later as an economy product, and is a different mechanic wearing the same word. | 2026-08-05 | `construction_and_spawn.md` §5's insurance-as-protection, recommended against and now replaced |
| **R4** | **OPEN — raised by the owner, not yet designed.** Placing several tree blocks together yields a real tree from an art pack; more blocks yield a bigger one; placing rock blocks yields a non-blocky rock. **All of it must collide.** This is NOT the decoration layer — it crosses §6's hard promotion boundary ("cosmetic scatter never collides, is never interactive, is never persisted"). It is a new subsystem: authoritative multi-block composites. See the note below and the owed design pass. | 2026-08-03 | §6's promotion boundary needs a second, authoritative lane beside it |

> **On R4, stated before anyone builds on it.** What the owner describes is a *multi-block composite*,
> not scatter: it is recognised from an authoritative block pattern, it is persisted, it collides, every
> player sees the identical one, and breaking a block under it must degrade it. Decoration remains what
> it is — derived, cosmetic, uncollidable, zero bytes on the wire. The two must not be merged, and the
> composite lane must not be built by relaxing decoration's boundary. It needs its own pass, covering at
> minimum: the pattern-recognition rule, where the collider comes from (the server has no meshes), what
> happens when the pattern is broken, the per-realm budget, and the art-direction question of stylised
> low-poly assets inside a physically-lit voxel world.

## 1. Overview

> **Amended 3 August 2026, and the amendment reverses a rule.** The owner retracted the project's
> no-detail-levels rule — *"from where do you get no LOD? Please remove it, we will need LODs
> everywhere, but in the smartest way"* — and asked for it to be built the way the best-looking
> open worlds build it. Two addenda to this document are binding alongside it: the **first** makes a
> planet's radius per-body data on a 39.47 m ladder (any real body within twenty metres, Earth within
> 0.4 m) and derives its gravity from an authored mass; the **second** builds the detail ladder that
> this section now has to introduce. Where this section previously said the opposite of what is true
> now, the old wording is **struck rather than deleted**, so a reader who remembers the old rule
> learns that it changed and why.

### What this document decides

This document fixes the complete design of the block system and the signal system: what a block *is*
and every number attached to it; how a planet, a ship, a station and a room all come to be the same
kind of object built from the same grid; how that grid is generated from a seed, saved, and changed
by players; how it becomes pixels — big textures across many blocks, materials fading into one
another, edges that are not razor-straight; how the same world is drawn from a metre away and from a
hundred kilometres up without ever becoming a different world; how grass, pebbles, bushes and leaves
appear on top of it and react when a player places or breaks something; and how every functional
block becomes a generic publisher and receiver of named values that can reach across a whole galaxy
without any part of the system holding a list of everyone who might be listening. It is written to be
*implemented* over the next five roadmap phases, so it carries the exact reserved bits, saved-record
layouts and message shapes that must be planted before the first world is written to disk, the
measured numbers each budget is held to, and — the part that matters most — a numbered register of
decisions the owner must take, ordered by how much later answers cost.
~~It does not decide the eight rendering questions already awaiting the owner elsewhere; it routes to
them and takes reserve-shaped insurance so they stay open.~~

**What the retraction changed here.** One of those eight rendering questions — how much of the world
may be simplified with distance — has been answered by the owner, in the opposite direction to the
rule this document was originally written under, and the answer is now part of the spine rather than
a routed question: **there is a detail ladder and it reaches everywhere**, with a short list of things
that never climb it. Seven of the eight remain routed rather than decided, and this document still
takes reserve-shaped insurance on those. The register moves the same way:

- The row that asked what "no detail levels" banned was the top of the register. It is **answered and
  closed**.
- The row that asks what one mesh vertex looks like **leaves the blocking set for standing on the
  ground** — an Earth-sized surface at your feet drops from about 53,000 boxes of terrain to about
  4,000, so roughly 160 MB of drawn geometry in the compact form on the conservative allowance and
  under two gigabytes even in the wasteful one — but it **remains the gate on the long view from the
  air**, where a hundred-kilometre view is about ~~270 MB~~ **120–273 MB** compact against 1.3–3.0 GB
  in today's form (in each pair the lower number is measured natural terrain and the higher one the
  conservative allowance for heavily-built ground; both are always quoted). It decides whether the
  top rungs fit in memory, not whether a planet can exist.
- **Two new rows arrive** — the saved summary that lets player changes survive coarsening, and the
  knob that trades sharpness against memory. They are the *same* two rows the second addendum asked
  for, not additional ones. ~~Both are stated at the end of this section as decisions **1-A** and
  **1-B**, and the register goes from thirty-six rows to thirty-seven open ones: one closed, two
  added.~~ **Corrected after adjudication:** only one of them is a new row. The knob that trades
  sharpness against memory is **not** new — it is folded into the register row that already asks for
  the ladder's tuning defaults, **register row 38 / [USER DECISION 8-B]**, and 1-A is struck below in
  its favour. The saved summary stays as **[USER DECISION 1-B]** below, but its *record layout* half
  is likewise folded into the row that already owned it, **register row 37 / [USER DECISION 8-A]**.
  So the register closes one row and adds one.

### The shape of the system

Read this page before any detail. Everything below it is elaboration.

**A realm is a world.** A planet is a realm. A ship is a realm. A station, a room, a floating
platform someone built in the sky — all realms. A realm owns exactly one grid of cells, one physics
world, one database file and one clock, and nothing outside it may reach in. The *only* thing that
differs between a planet and a ship is one value the realm carries: how a whole-number cell index
turns into a position in space. On a ship that is a straight lookup — cell three across is three
metres across. On a planet the same index runs through a curve that wraps a cube around a sphere, so
the cells stay aligned with which way is down no matter where you stand. Every other piece of the
system is written once and genuinely cannot tell which kind of world it is running in.

**A block is one cell of that grid.** It carries three facts: what it is made of, what shape it
occupies, and optionally what it does. Those three facts are looked up from three small tables — a
list of substances, a list of shapes, and later a list of functions — so a half-slab of granite
automatically has half the mass, half the material cost and the same toughness per cubic metre as a
full granite cube, with nobody typing a second row. Every number a block has — how heavy it is, how
much punishment it takes, how far it can span unsupported, which tools can harvest it, whether fire
can touch it — is calculated at build time from published physical facts. Hand-editing one fails the
build.

**A chunk is a box of blocks, sixty-two cells on a side.** It is the unit of everything: what the
generator produces, what the drawing code turns into triangles, what the collision code builds a
shape from, and what the database saves. A chunk that is entirely air, or entirely rock, costs
essentially nothing to store — which is what makes a planet with hundreds of billions of blocks
storable at all. What is actually saved to disk is never the terrain; it is only the cells a player
changed.

**A mesh is what one chunk looks like.** Flat faces that share a material are merged into big
rectangles, and because a merged rectangle always has exactly one material, one texture can be
stretched across dozens of blocks with no seam inside it. Where two materials meet, a one-metre strip
is peeled off the edge of the rectangle and given a two-material treatment so the ground fades from
gravel to dirt the way real ground does. Where an edge is exposed to the air, its corners are nudged
inward by up to twenty centimetres by a fixed calculation from the world seed, so dirt does not have
razor edges — but nothing ever bulges *outward* past the flat face it belongs to, so the shape you
see is always inside the shape you collide with.

**Detail is a ladder, and the world climbs most of it for free.** *(New. This is the concept the
retraction adds, and it is load-bearing everywhere below.)* One rung is one doubling of the cell size:
one-metre cells, then two, then four, ~~up to a hundred and twenty-eight~~ **and on up to the rung at
which one box covers a whole face of the world — thirteen rungs on the starter world, whose top rung
has cells four kilometres across, and nineteen rungs on an Earth-sized one** — and above the top rung
sits the drawing a world already gets when it is seen from another star, so the ladder runs
continuously from a block in your hand to a planet as a dot. That top drawing stops being an exception
to a rule and becomes simply the last rung. **How far the blocks climb before that last drawing takes
over — and therefore how many bits of a saved box's address the rung spends — is register row 1 /
one-way door 14; the recommendation is all the way, at five bits.** **A rung is a number written on a
box's address, never a second piece of code.** The generator, the tables, the mesher, the shapes and
the saved format are identical at every rung, and nothing anywhere asks which rung it is standing on.

Four things about it, in the order they matter:

- **The generated landscape coarsens itself, and it is a saving rather than a cost.** The surface is a
  sum of ripples, each half the size and half the height of the one before. A two-metre cell physically
  cannot show a one-metre ripple — adding it only produces the shimmer everyone associates with distant
  ground. So a coarse rung is made by **not adding the ripples too small to see**, which is at once the
  correct picture, the correct blur and less work: each rung up deletes one layer of ripples, measured
  at 12.19 nanoseconds per sample and 0.885 milliseconds for a whole finest-rung surface box, so a
  coarse box is strictly cheaper to make than a fine one. Caves smaller than a coarse cell simply are
  not there, which is also
  correct — you cannot see a three-metre cave from ten kilometres. This is the whole reason the ladder
  is cheap here and brutal in most voxel games: they must ship coarse data from a server, and we
  generate it.
- **Which rung is chosen by how big one cell would look on screen** — the same rule the game already
  uses to decide which distant worlds are worth drawing at all, applied one level down, so there is no
  second scheduler. At about two screen pixels per cell on a normal screen, one-metre cells are used
  out to about eight hundred metres, two-metre cells to 1.6 km, and the eighth rung reaches a hundred
  kilometres. That hundred-kilometre view costs about 6,800 boxes — roughly 120 MB of drawn geometry
  on measured terrain and 273 MB on the conservative allowance for heavily-built ground (~~270 MB~~
  alone was the conservative figure, and both are quoted from here on), and under a second of
  generation on eight cores — where drawing it all at one metre would have been 24.5 million boxes.
  **The number of boxes now grows with the logarithm of how far you can see instead
  of its square.** An earlier finding in this design's first addendum — that about one kilometre of
  drawn ground was all that could ever be afforded on any planet, and that flying above a hundred
  metres therefore could not be rendered honestly — is **dissolved**. Standing on an Earth-sized world
  costs about 4,000 boxes instead of 53,000; hovering at a hundred metres costs about 5,000 instead of
  79,000.
- **Player changes do not coarsen for free, and that is the only genuinely hard part.** The fix is a
  small running summary kept beside the saved changes: for every coarse cell that contains at least one
  changed fine cell, ~~how many of its fine cells are solid and which material dominates~~ **which of
  its eight sub-boxes contain anything, how full it is on average, and which substance dominates** —
  eight bytes, one number, and the questions still open about it are **register row 37 / [USER DECISION
  8-A]**. *Why the wording changed:* a bare count of solid cells has to be turned back into
  solid-or-empty to draw it, which is exactly what makes distant player-built things read as blobs,
  whereas knowing *which* eight sub-boxes are occupied keeps an eight-metre ramp built of eight wedges
  reading as a ramp. Every change updates **at most one entry per rung above the finest — twelve on the
  starter world's thirteen-rung ladder, and never more than the ladder is deep**; ~~a thousand-block
  tunnel produces about 1,140 entries in total, which is 1.1 times the number of changes and shrinks as
  changes cluster~~ **a thousand-block tunnel produces about 504 entries, under four kibibytes**, and
  the real cost depends on the *shape* of what was changed across a factor of fifty — a compact cluster
  0.143 entries per change, a wall a third, a one-cell-thick line about one — with about 1.1 entries
  per change as the planning figure for mixed building. A dug tunnel then becomes a partly hollow
  coarse cell instead of vanishing at two hundred metres and
  reappearing at one hundred. Ships, stations and bases have no generated landscape underneath them, so
  their coarse rungs are that summary and nothing else — which is simpler, not harder, and it fades
  continuously into the distant-object drawing.
- **Nothing ever pops.** Two rungs of the *same* terrain are both drawn for the width of a band while
  one dissolves into the other. That is a cross-fade between two versions of one thing, never a picture
  standing in for a thing. Done in the right direction — the coarse rung fading in early, the fine rung
  living exactly to its own range — the band costs about a tenth more resident boxes; done backwards it
  costs four times that, so the direction is a rule and not a preference.

And the ladder stops, hard, at four places: **collision**, which only ever sees one-metre cells;
**other players and anything that can shoot or be shot**; **anything a machine's behaviour depends
on**; and **anything whose appearance tells a player a fact they could act on**. Two players at
different distances legitimately see different *detail*. They must never see different *facts*.

**Decoration is everything sitting on top.** Grass blades, moss, pebbles, bushes, rocks, leaf
clusters. None of it is stored and none of it is sent over the network. It is worked out on demand
from the blocks, the world seed and the clock, using only whole-number arithmetic, so every machine
gets the identical result. Place a soil block and grass creeps over it; place four hundred and you
have a meadow, with no meadow rule anywhere; place a wood column and leaf blocks and the leaf cubes
stop being drawn as cubes at all — overhanging clusters are drawn instead, and they overlap enough to
dissolve the silhouette. Decoration rides the ladder by **thinning out, never by being swapped for
something else**: the number of grass blades per cell falls smoothly to zero with distance, and the
rung a box was built at hands the decoration rule its cutoff for free.

**A signal is a named value published into the world.** A functional block does not send anything to
anyone. It publishes a value under a name, and whoever asked for that name receives it. That single
property is why ninety-nine percent of the galaxy being switched off is free: with nobody listening,
publishing costs one memory write and zero bytes. A cockpit publishes "thrusters forward, one
hundred"; twelve thrusters listen for it, and each one also listens for a fuel level and a reactor
level and refuses to burn if either is zero. A station can publish an offer to an approaching ship;
if the pilot approves, the station gets a revocable permission slip and starts publishing the same
values a seat publishes — and the thrusters cannot tell the difference and are structurally unable
to look. A block cover is a transparent panel a player sticks on any block face; it names a widget
and some signals, and the server turns those into a bounded list of drawing commands the client
simply obeys.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WHAT THE PLAYER SEES                                                        │
│  a hillside · grass moving · a hull plate · a number on a panel              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
              ▲ pixels                                       ▲ pixels
┌─────────────┴───────────────────┐          ┌───────────────┴─────────────────┐
│  SURFACE APPEARANCE             │          │  DECORATION                     │
│  merge flat faces into big      │          │  grass · pebbles · bushes ·     │
│  rectangles · one texture over  │◄────────►│  leaf clusters                  │
│  many blocks · fade one material│  share   │  worked out from the blocks,    │
│  into the next · knock the      │  the     │  stored nowhere, sent nowhere   │
│  exposed edges off              │  edges   │                                 │
└─────────────┬───────────────────┘          └───────────────┬─────────────────┘
              │ asks the ladder                              │ asks the ladder
┌─────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────┐
│  THE DETAIL LADDER — one rung per doubling of the cell size                  │
│  1 m · 2 m · 4 m · … · one box per cube face · then the world seen as a dot  │
│  a rung is a NUMBER on a box's address — never a second code path            │
│  generated land coarsens for FREE: stop adding ripples too small to see      │
│  player changes coarsen by a running summary kept beside the changes         │
│  neighbouring rungs cross-fade — nothing is ever a picture of a thing        │
└─────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
              │ every rung reads the same field · COLLISION SKIPS THE LADDER:
              │ physics is only ever handed 1 m cells, wherever a player is
┌─────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  THE BLOCK FIELD — the one authoritative thing                               │
│  each cell: what it is made of · what shape it is · what it does             │
│  everything above and below is derived from it, never stored beside it       │
└─────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────┘
              │ grouped into                                 │ read and written by
┌─────────────┴───────────────────┐          ┌───────────────┴─────────────────┐
│  CHUNKS — 62 cells on a side    │          │  FUNCTIONAL BLOCKS + SIGNALS    │
│  the unit of generation,        │          │  publish a named value · anyone │
│  drawing, collision and saving  │          │  who asked for that name gets it│
│  a rung is one more number      │          │  no sender ever names a receiver│
│  on a chunk's address           │          │                                 │
│  saved = only what players wrote│          │                                 │
└─────────────┬───────────────────┘          └───────────────┬─────────────────┘
              │ live inside                                  │ leaves the realm only
              │                                              │ through one reviewed list
┌─────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────┐
│  THE REALM — a planet, a ship, a station, a room: the same object            │
│  owns one grid · one physics world · one database · one clock                │
│  the ONLY difference between kinds is how a cell index becomes a position    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

### The load-bearing commitments

~~Ten commitments~~ **Eleven commitments** hold the whole design up; the eleventh arrives with the
detail ladder and the ninth was reversed by it. Each is one sentence, with what breaks if it is
reversed.

1. **A planet, a ship, a station and a room are one kind of object, differing only in how a cell index
   becomes a position.** *Reversed:* the block system forks in two and every feature is written,
   tested and debugged twice — the exact structural failure the greenfield rebuild exists to remove.

2. **Terrain never crosses the network; only the world seed and the cells players changed travel, and
   everything else is recomputed identically on every machine.** *Reversed:* a single planet's surface
   is petabytes of traffic, and the client stops being able to generate ahead of a moving player,
   which is what makes flying possible at all.
   *Amended by the ladder:* exactly one more thing may travel, and it is **smaller** than what it
   replaces — the coarse summary of a distant world's changes, which is what a far-away viewer needs
   instead of the changes themselves. That has one consequence to plant now: a viewer must be able to
   **ask for a particular rung** of a region. The message that carries block changes between worlds
   has not been written yet, so a field for the requested rung costs nothing today and is a protocol
   migration the day after it ships. Reserve it.

3. **A block's identity is one small number naming a combination somebody approved, and every quantity
   in the game is looked up from it rather than typed.** *Reversed:* the same fact is authored once per
   material-times-shape pair, which is a drift surface that grows as the product of two catalogues and
   is the single defect this model exists to remove.

4. **Every per-block number is calculated at build time from published physical facts by a tested
   function against a short list of named constants, and a hand-edited row fails the build.**
   *Reversed:* "no magic numbers" becomes a habit somebody has to remember instead of something the
   build enforces, and the first person in a hurry breaks it invisibly. *The ladder's own knobs are
   inside this rule:* the pixels-per-cell target and the cross-fade band width are fields in one
   tuning record, never numbers typed into shader or scheduler code.

5. **Everything two machines must agree on is whole-number arithmetic, in one shared piece of code,
   behind a type that physically cannot reach the maths functions that differ between machines.**
   *Reversed:* two players see different planets, different rubble and different meadows — silently,
   only on some hardware, only sometimes, which is the most expensive class of bug this project can
   ship. *The ladder sits inside this, not beside it:* a coarse rung is the same sum with fewer terms,
   so it is identical on every machine by the same argument, and the summary of player changes is
   ~~a count and a dominant material~~ **an eight-way occupancy mask, a mean fill and a dominant
   substance** — integers.

6. **The server owns every authoritative value; the client only turns already-authoritative data into
   triangles, running the identical shared code.** *Reversed:* you rebuild the drift the floating-origin
   work already had to be redone once to remove, and the failure mode is the world visibly rewriting
   itself in front of the player.
   *The ladder does not dent this.* Which rung a client draws is a local, cosmetic choice about how
   many triangles to spend on data the server already sent; every fact still comes from the server.
   The line to hold is that **nothing may be decided from a rung** — collision and every gameplay
   question read the finest rung, which is authoritative and identical everywhere.

7. **Everything that changes lives in a compact side list, and the block field itself is a per-chunk
   lookup list with a free path for chunks that are entirely one thing.** *Reversed:* a chunk of mostly
   zeros costs more than the chunk it describes, and a planet stops fitting in memory long before it
   stops fitting on disk.

8. **Nothing crosses between two worlds except as an arm of one short reviewed list of message shapes,
   and a publisher can never name a receiver.** *Reversed:* the sealed boundary between worlds stops
   being reviewable, and the dormant-galaxy property — publishing to nobody costs nothing — is lost,
   because a sender that names a destination has already paid for one.

9. ~~**Out of range means absent: there is no half-detail version of anything.** *Reversed:* every
   subsystem grows a second representation of itself and a seam between them, and the seams are where
   the bugs live. (The exact boundary of this rule is an open owner decision; the design takes
   reserve-shaped insurance so either answer stays affordable.)~~
   **Retracted by the owner on 3 August 2026 and replaced by its opposite.** The commitment is now:
   **there is one detail ladder; every rung is the same world at a bigger cell size, produced by the
   same code from the same authoritative field; and a thing is never *substituted for* by another
   thing.** The test that keeps it honest is one question — is what I am drawing **derived from** the
   real thing, or **standing in for** it? A coarser rung of the real terrain is derived from, and is
   allowed. A sphere or a billboard where a base or a player should be is standing in for, and remains
   banned exactly as before.
   *Reversed:* if rungs are allowed to be substitutes rather than coarsenings, every subsystem grows a
   second representation of itself and a seam between them, and the seams are where the bugs live —
   which is what the old rule was trying to prevent, and what this wording prevents precisely instead
   of bluntly.
   *What the old rule cost while it stood:* it capped the drawn world near one kilometre on every
   planet at every size, which made flight above about a hundred metres impossible to render honestly
   and put the seamless law and the first playable planet demo in direct contradiction — a
   contradiction this project carried for a month before the ruling.

10. **Anything a player can build carries a declared cost, and exceeding a budget is refused loudly at
    build time rather than absorbed at run time.** *Reversed:* every limit in the system becomes a
    crash or a silent drop, and a player learns the limits by breaking the server.

11. **A change a player made is visible at every rung of the ladder.** *(New with the ladder.)*
    *Reversed:* a dug tunnel disappears at two hundred metres and comes back at one hundred, a built
    tower blinks in and out as a ship flies past, and the seamless law is broken by the very machinery
    added to serve it. This is the one genuinely hard piece of the ladder and the one that must be
    gated hardest: the acceptance run is dig a tunnel, fly away, confirm it is still there at every
    rung boundary, fly back, confirm nothing jumped.

---

### What we are not building

Stated honestly, so nobody discovers a gap late and treats it as an oversight.

- **No smooth or melted terrain.** No marching cubes, no surface nets, no dual contouring. The world is
  blocky, softened only at exposed edges. This is deliberate and it is expensive to reverse. *Extended
  by the ladder:* and no transition-cell scheme where two rungs meet either — those exist to reconcile
  two smooth surfaces that genuinely disagree along a curve, whereas ours are flat rectangles at every
  rung and simply meet in a step. A short downward apron around each box hides that step in about
  twenty lines with no case table and no dependence on what the neighbour is currently doing, which
  matters because the neighbour's rung changes as the camera moves.
- **No sub-block chisel grid** in the first release. A finer carving layer can be added later, but only
  strictly on top — the base cell is never subdividable.
- ~~**No level-of-detail meshes and no proxy geometry.** Nothing is simplified with distance. What
  exactly that bans is an open owner decision; nothing here quietly grants itself an exemption.~~
  **Retracted 3 August 2026** — *"we will need LODs everywhere, but in the smartest way."* It is
  replaced by four narrower exclusions, which are firmer than the old rule precisely because they are
  small enough to enforce:
  - **Collision never coarsens.** Physics is only ever handed one-metre cells, everywhere, always.
    This costs nothing: the finest rung is resident wherever a player is, which is exactly the region
    physics runs in.
  - **Nothing that can shoot or be shot ever becomes a picture.** No player, ship, projectile or
    vehicle is ever a billboard, a sphere or a stand-in, at any distance. This is what the old
    preference was really protecting, and it is kept in full.
  - **Behaviour never coarsens.** A beacon does not stop blinking because you flew away; a machine
    does not stop running; a published value does not stop being published. The housing may coarsen;
    what it does may not.
  - **Anything whose appearance carries a fact a player could act on stays exact** — a docking clamp's
    status light, a hull breach. Coarsen the geometry, never the state.
- **No baked or cooked detail pyramid for generated land, and no offline merge step per world.** A
  coarse rung is made by leaving out ripples, on demand, from the seed. This is the structural
  difference between us and Crimson Desert, the reference the owner named. Its makers describe their
  distance rendering as "proxy LODs" plus "hierarchical level subdivision" and have published nothing
  more technical than those two phrases; the shape those words describe is a whole region merged into
  one pre-built stand-in during an offline build step, which is only possible because their world is
  authored and frozen. One player edit invalidates such a merge, and a world that must be cooked is a
  world that cannot be edited. Only *player changes* get a stored summary, maintained as they happen.
  **Two things do transfer from them and are taken:** the loading *order* — never ask for a fine rung
  of a region whose coarse rung is not resident yet, so the world always looks complete while it fills
  in — and the finding that their distant trees are lit and shadowed by the same lighting code as the
  near ones, which is why their far field reads as solid objects rather than stickers and is the
  quality bar for our own coarse rungs.
  **On their textures specifically, since that was the second half of the question:** what reads as
  "amazingly detailed texture mapping" is high texel density plus per-pixel relief, not a residency
  system — there is no evidence of virtual texturing, sparse residency or a megatexture anywhere in
  the primary record, and the only hard sources are two patch-1.03.00 options, a *Displacement Scale*
  slider (community-identified as screen-space displacement, split out because it blurs under
  upscaling) and a *Detail Decorative Mesh* toggle, which is derived decoration and not texturing at
  all. Two things transfer and both are already taken: **256 texels per cell with parallax relief**
  rather than a streaming system, and **shipping the displacement scale as a user-facing slider from
  day one** — a tuning field with a settings entry, never a shader constant, because they had to
  retrofit exactly that in a patch. The evidence and the arithmetic are in §5.3.9.
- **No second scheduler for detail, and no per-pixel distance ladder in the shader.** Which rung to
  draw reuses the existing on-screen-size rule, and the material simplifications (dropping the fine
  surface texture, the bumps, the two-material blend) are keyed off the rung the box was built at, so
  every pixel of one box agrees with every other. A per-pixel fade and a per-box cross-fade disagree
  inside the band, which is a shimmering seam nobody can debug later.
- **No baked pictures of anything a player made or can touch.** The one place a baked picture is
  permitted is the shipped decoration catalogue — grass, tufts, small props: derived, stateless, and
  impossible to interact with — and even there it must be baked from many angles and lit by the same
  code as the real prop, so it reads as a solid object rather than a sticker. The decoration section
  carries the arithmetic (about 4.7 MB per prop archetype, so roughly 150 MB for thirty-two of them,
  which pushes props from about eighty metres out to about two hundred and fifty). Everything else —
  terrain, structures, ships, stations, players — gets a coarser **rung of the real thing** instead.
- **No client-side prediction**, of movement or of block placement. A translucent preview that vanishes
  when the server answers is offered as an option; guessing at the world is not.
- **No block-light grid sent to the client, and no coloured light.** The server keeps a single-channel
  light and sky-exposure field for gameplay questions only.
- **No full chemistry.** Rusting, weathering and a corrosive damage type; not a reacts-with web.
- **No global registry of signal names and no central message broker.** Names are content-addressed and
  routing is bounded to three explicitly-limited radii.
- **No digital signature per message.** One cheap tag per bundle per destination per tick; real
  signatures only where the rate is low and the stakes are high.
- **No player scripting language in the first release.** Logic blocks, then a bounded arithmetic
  expression; a real language only behind a written, measured gate.
- **No voice or video at launch.** The handle is reserved on the wire; the forwarding infrastructure is
  not built.
- **No order-independent transparency**, no render target per panel, no per-block screens.
- **No long chains of physics joints for machinery.** Articulation is computed, not solved.
- **No economy state anywhere near a block, a realm or the physics path.** Blocks that touch the economy
  publish and receive ordinary named values and know nothing about money.
- **No placeable decoration items** in the first release; a potted fern, if wanted, becomes a real
  block rather than a piece of scatter.
- **No monolithic door block and no per-block behaviour code**, ever — a door is an actuator, a seal and
  a controller, and adding a block adds a table row and zero code.

---

### The decisions the ladder creates

~~These are the two new register rows~~ **One of the two turned out not to be a new row at all.** What
remains here is stated here because it is cheap to take now and expensive to take late. Everything else
the ladder needs is already decided.

> ~~**[USER DECISION 1-A]** — is sharpness constant, or is memory constant?~~ **STRUCK AND FOLDED: it
> is now register row 38 / [USER DECISION 8-B]**, which asks the same question together with the
> ladder's tuning defaults and the render section's own version of it. The options, the recommendation
> (hold a fixed on-screen target, with a smoothed hysteretic governor above it) and the three
> constraints that ride with it are stated there, and nothing is decided here.

> **[USER DECISION 1-B] — is the coarse summary of player changes stored, or recomputed?**
> This is the piece that makes a dug tunnel survive being looked at from two kilometres up, and it is
> the only genuinely hard part of the ladder. It is also **permanent, change-shaped data**, so if it is
> stored, its layout joins the short list of formats that must be frozen before the first world is
> written.
>
> - **B1. Stored and maintained** *(recommended)*. The world's owner updates ~~at most eight small
>   entries on every change, one per rung~~ **at most one small entry per rung above the finest —
>   twelve of them on the starter world's thirteen-rung ladder, and never more than the ladder is
>   deep**. ~~A thousand-block tunnel produces about 1,140 entries across all rungs — 1.1 times the
>   number of changes~~ **A thousand-block tunnel produces about 504 entries, under four kibibytes**;
>   the cost per change depends on the shape of what was built, from 0.143 entries for a compact
>   cluster through a third for a wall to about one for a one-cell-thick line, with about 1.1 as the
>   planning figure for mixed building — and proportionally less as changes cluster. Storage grows
>   with edits, never with world size.
> - **B2. Recomputed when the world wakes up.** Zero stored bytes, no format to freeze, and no
>   possibility of the summary disagreeing with the truth — but the work is proportional to every change
>   ever made in that world and is paid at exactly the wrong moment, because a world must be warmed
>   *before* a player can reach it. A long-inhabited planet would make its own approach stutter, which
>   is the seamless law broken where it is most visible. No Man's Sky hit this and answered it by
>   capping terrain edits at a fixed set of 255 buffers per save and evicting the overflow, which
>   occasionally deletes players' own work — a failure mode to design out from the start rather than
>   discover.
>
> *Recommendation.* **B1, with B2 built anyway** — not as the shipping path but as a debug command and
> the test-suite oracle: recompute the summary from the changes and assert the stored one matches.
> Derived data that can silently disagree with its source needs that assertion from day one, or the
> divergence is found by a player noticing their tunnel is the wrong shape from a hilltop. One
> discipline comes free with it and should be enforced by the shape of the code rather than by
> convention: **only the finest rung is writable; every coarser rung is derived.** Space Engineers
> states exactly that as an invariant of its voxel storage, and making a write to a coarse rung
> impossible to express is what stops the two halves drifting.
>
> *One-way door?* **Half of it.** Choosing B1 or B2 is reversible. The *record layout*, if B1 is
> chosen, is not: it is permanent data beside the saved changes, so getting it wrong is a migration
> over every planet, ship and station ever saved. It must be settled with the saved-change format, not
> after it. **That half now lives in one place: register row 37 / [USER DECISION 8-A]**, which carries
> the eight-byte record and its five sub-questions — what it holds, how its fill is spent on a shape,
> how it is grouped in the file, the write rule that only the finest rung is writable, and what happens
> if it ever disagrees with the changes it was derived from. What stays here is only the
> stored-versus-recomputed choice.


---

## 2. The block model — one definition, three tables, and the mechanics they buy

This section owns the authoritative definition of what a block *is*: the static tables that describe
it, the integer parameters those tables carry, the damage model that gives every block LIFE, the
sparse side tables that hold what changes, the mechanics the parameters buy, and the bits that must
be reserved in the persisted record before the first planet is written to redb.

The whole model, stated once:

```
AUTHORED (checked in as Rust const data — no parser, no new dependency)
  physical_facts.rs  ──►  derive_material_row()  ──►  MaterialDef  (substance)
  shape_meshes/*      ──►  derive_shape_row()     ──►  ShapeDef     (form)
  function_facts.rs   ──►  derive_function_row()  ──►  FunctionDef  (function)
                                    │
GENERATED (append-only manifest, build-gated, emits Rust)
  block_types.manifest ───────────►  BlockTypeDef { material, shape, function, flags }
                                    │
RUNTIME
  BlockTypeId(u16) ──► def() ──► the three rows; every per-block number is a table lookup
  (registry_len, identity_prefix_digest) ──► handshake + store header
```

Nothing below the line is authored twice, nothing branches on a shard kind (HR3), and every number
that feeds sim math is an integer (the SPIKE-6a byte-identity gate). The client's *render* half of a
material — texture handles, warp amplitude, anti-tiling mode — lives in §5's render registry behind a
`RenderMaterialId` indirection, so no float ever enters the table the server hashes.

Two structural prerequisites this section **depends on** and does not itself provide, named here so
they are scheduled rather than discovered:

- **DEFERRED D-4 🟥** — there is no reliable client-facing `MsgClass` arm. `BulkMsg::Blob { kind:
  BulkKind::ChunkDelta }` and `EventMsg` are already declared in `crates/wire/src/channels.rs` but
  are **unroutable**. Every client-facing delivery in this section (edit deltas, damage-stage
  deltas, state-bit deltas) rides that arm. D-4 is a hard prerequisite of P6, not an optimisation.
- **A chunk-scoped delivery scope** (§2.3.4). This is *not* DEFERRED D-9's within-realm per-entity
  AoI; it is a coarser and independent mechanism, and the section states its message cost.

---

### 2.0 Amended by Addendum 2 — the detail ladder

The owner has retracted the "no level-of-detail" rule. The binding replacement is **one generic ladder**:
one rung per power of two, and **a tier is a NUMBER carried on a chunk address, never a second code
path** (HR3). For fractal terrain the coarse rung is not an approximation — tier *L* drops the *L*
highest-frequency octaves, which is simultaneously the correct anti-aliasing filter and a *saving*, so
the generated world coarsens itself for free.

Almost all of this section survives untouched, and that is the substantive finding: the block field, the
palette container, the three tables, `apply_hit`, the flood kernel and the durable placement record are
**identical at every rung**, so the ladder adds no branch anywhere in this section's code. Three things
do change, and each is marked where it lands:

> **[N10] Read every "5-byte record" in this section as "the durable placement record, provisionally
> five bytes".** Its width is **register row 2 and it is still OPEN** — §2 specifies five, §3 sizes
> eight, and §8.6 item 1 records the three-way disagreement. Five closes only if two upstream verdicts
> hold (mirroring is a shape rather than a flag; identity is one combined number rather than separate
> substance and shape fields). Nothing else in §2 depends on which way row 2 lands: the field, the
> container, the side tables and the ladder are width-agnostic. Do not read §2 as having settled it.

1. **One new persisted structure — the sparse edit pyramid (§2.4.3).** Generated terrain coarsens for
   free; player edits do not. Without it a dug tunnel vanishes at 200 m and reappears at 100 m. It is
   delta data, therefore permanent, therefore in §2.7's reservation list.
2. **A live five-bit `tier` field on `ChunkKey`, and a type-level write invariant: only tier 0 is
   writable** (§2.4.3, §2.7.1). Every coarser rung is derived. The field's width and the ladder's top
   rung are settled together as **register row 1 / one-way door 14**: five bits at `ChunkKey` bits
   60..56, and the per-body ceiling is the face-covering rung. This section's earlier "three bits at
   18..16, exactly eight rungs" wording is struck wherever it appears below.
3. **A per-observer / per-realm split the mechanics catalogue must respect** (§2.5.5). *Dormancy is a
   property of the realm and is identical for every observer; tier is a property of an observer. A
   per-observer quantity may never gate a realm-wide computation.* **Collision and every gameplay fact
   stay at tier 0, always.**

Addendum 1 §C.4's finding — *"the binding constraint is the drawn radius, not the planet radius; roughly
700 m to 1 km of fully meshed terrain is what one-metre blocks can afford"* — is **dissolved**. With the
ladder the visible chunk count grows with the *logarithm* of view distance rather than its square: a
100 km view is ≈ 3,158 chunk columns instead of 8.17 million. Neither planet size nor draw distance
binds any longer, and no statement in this section was ever load-bearing on that constraint.

---

### 2.1 Substance × form × function — three tables, one id

#### 2.1.1 The decomposition, and the id-space arithmetic that constrains it

Every shipped game that got this right separates substance from form (SE's CubeBlock vs
PhysicalMaterial vs the component bill; DF's item form vs material; Starbase's part vs the material
it is milled from). Minecraft did **not**, and the consequence is measurable: hardness, blast
resistance, luminance and flammability are re-authored per block state across 20,000+ states, and
four unrelated scalars had to be bolted on because none of them composes.

The **v1 sizes and the caps** (one set of numbers, used everywhere in this document):

| Table | v1 rows | Hard cap | Why the cap |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MaterialId` | 64 | **512** | one `u16`, but capped so the cross product stays addressable |
| `ShapeId` | 64 | **256** | SE ships 35 topologies; SE2 ships 46 per armour family |
| `FunctionId` | 0 at P6, ~64 at P9 | **256** | §8's six-kernel catalogue |
| `BlockTypeId` | ~512 | **65,536** (`u16`) | the persisted record's width |

**Canonical name for the substance row.** The cross-section name roster fixes **`SubstanceId(u16)`**
as the name of the substance-table row id, and reserves `MaterialId` for §5's *renderable* sense (the
texture-array addressing of §5.10.2). This section's `MaterialId` **is** the substance row and is
therefore `SubstanceId` under the roster; the two names denote one type, and the spelling `SubstanceId`
is used below wherever the id crosses into a shared artefact — the edit-pyramid record of §2.4.3, and
§5's dominant-substance tie-break.

The full cross product (512 × 256 × 257) is 33.7 million and is **never materialised**. This is the
allocation rule, and it is load-bearing: **`block_types.manifest` allocates a `BlockTypeId` only for
a triple the content build explicitly declares placeable.** The build fails if an already-allocated
row's triple changes. A combination nobody allocated simply does not exist: the build UI enumerates
allocated rows, so it cannot be requested, and the terrain generator can only emit ids from its own
table, so it cannot be generated. There is no "unallocated combination" failure mode to handle — the
manifest *is* the catalogue. At 512 allocated rows out of 65,536 there is 128× headroom.

**Mirroring is encoded exactly once, as a shape.** `ShapeDef.mirror_shape: [ShapeId; 3]` is
authoritative; the orientation field carries the **24 proper rotations only, 5 bits**. The reason is
physical, not aesthetic: a mirrored template needs a reversed winding order and a mirrored collider
hull, which is a different baked artefact — which is exactly why godot_voxel pre-bakes every rotated
and flipped variant and SE carries both `Mirrored: bool` and a `MirroringBlock` substitution. Making
mirroring an orientation *bit* would mean the mesher and the collider both branch on it at runtime.
Dropping the sixth orientation bit frees one bit in the 5-byte persisted record, and §2.7 spends it.
**The shape catalogue must be closed under mirroring from day one** — if it is not, symmetry mode
silently punches holes in mirrored builds, and the audit is over every shape after players have
built. A coherence test asserts closure.

The alternatives lose concretely. A flat per-block-type struct (Minecraft, Vintage Story) means
half-slab mass, integrity, airtightness and structural load are hand-maintained per
(material × shape) pair — an O(materials × shapes) drift surface. A component-bill approach (SE)
makes the row non-`Copy` and variable-size, killing cheap palette storage and wire serialisation.
**Not a one-way door for the tables themselves** (static data), but the `BlockTypeId` *numbering*
they generate is — see §2.7.

#### 2.1.2 The registry idiom: keep the proven `match`

The repo has proved the registry idiom twice — `crates/core/src/entity_kind.rs:73` and
`crates/core/src/taxonomy.rs:104/272/430`: `#[repr]` enum with explicit discriminants, `ALL`,
`from_tag()` returning `Result` (unknown tags are an error, never a Default), `def() -> &'static Def`
implemented as `match self`, guarded by a drift tripwire test. Both crates are at 100 % region+branch
because the `ALL` loop exercises every arm.

**This section mirrors that idiom exactly, including the `match`.** An earlier draft replaced it with
an array index on the grounds that a 512-arm match is 512 branch regions; that reasoning was wrong on
two counts. HR5's "generic fns are branchless shims" rule is explicitly about **generic** functions
and the per-monomorphisation trap (`CLAUDE.md`: "a branch inside a *generic* fn"); `def()` is
monomorphic. And `MATERIAL_DEFS[self as usize]` inserts a compiler-generated bounds-check panic path
that no test can reach — precisely the uncoverable region HR5 punishes, and precisely the one the
`match` avoids. rustc lowers a dense match on a `#[repr(u16)]` enum returning `&'static` references
to a jump-free load anyway. The `match` arms are **generated** by the content build alongside the
table, so a 512-arm match costs nobody's hands.

```rust
//! crates/core/src/block/material.rs — SUBSTANCE.
//! Dense, append-only tags. `def()` is a GENERATED exhaustive match (the proven
//! entity_kind.rs / taxonomy.rs idiom): no uncoverable bounds-check path, and the
//! `ALL` loop covers every arm.

/// A byte pair carried a block-registry tag this build does not know. `table` names
/// which registry so the four round-trip tests give distinct messages. (The
/// decode-to-Default ban is the CLAUDE.md persistence convention — NOT HR2, which is
/// generic transfer.)
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, thiserror::Error)]
#[error("unknown block-registry tag {table}:{tag}")]
pub struct UnknownBlockTag { pub table: &'static str, pub tag: u16 }

#[repr(u16)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum MaterialId { Air = 0, PackedSoil = 1, Sand = 2, Clay = 3, Granite = 4, Basalt = 5,
    WaterIce = 6, Oak = 7, Glass = 8, Concrete = 9, StructuralSteel = 10, TitaniumAlloy = 11,
    /* … APPEND ONLY. Never renumber, never reuse. */ }

/// The per-material static record: integers only (the SPIKE-6a byte-identity gate),
/// no `Option`, no allocation, `Copy`, **no `&'static str`** — a fat pointer would add
/// 16 bytes and force 8-byte alignment. Names live in a parallel `MATERIAL_NAMES`
/// array (debug/tooling only), which also keeps the identity digest name-free by
/// construction. 118 bytes, align 4, padded to 120.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct MaterialDef {
    pub tag: u16, pub family: MaterialFamily, pub matter_state: MatterState,
    pub render: RenderMaterialId,                  // → §5 (every float lives there)

    pub density_kg_m3: u32, pub friction_q12: u16, pub restitution_q12: u16,
    pub toughness_dp_m3: u32,                      // DERIVED from fracture work
    pub support_kg: u32,                           // DERIVED

    pub resist_gate:     [i32; DAMAGE_CHANNELS],   // DERIVED — an INTENSITY threshold
    pub resist_scale_q12:[u16; DAMAGE_CHANNELS],   // DERIVED — delivered-energy fraction
    pub shatter_frac_q12: u16,                     // family policy × K_Ic
    pub shatter_drop_q12: u16,                     // yield when shattered (§2.3.5)
    pub spall_q12: u16, pub harvest_tier: u8, pub debris_kind: u8, pub drop_table: u16,

    pub ignition_k: u16, pub melt_k: u16, pub boil_k: u16, pub fuel_mj_m3: u16,
    pub burn_rate: u8, pub k_therm_mw_mk: u16, pub heat_cap_j_kgk: u16,
    pub porosity_q12: u16, pub absorb_q12: u16,
    pub light_absorb: u8, pub emit_level: u8, pub emit_rgb: [u8; 3],
    pub conduct_class: u8, pub signal_atten: u8,
    pub oxidises_to: u16, pub oxidation_rate: u8, pub corrosion_thresh_kpa: u16,
    pub fertility: u8,
    pub pcu: u16, pub replaceable_rank: u16, pub flags: u32,
}
```

`ShapeDef` is the *form* half — everything §5 and §6 need to mesh and collide, plus the one field
that makes "no magic numbers" structurally true for mass. Note `collider: ColliderShapeId(u16)`: an
opaque index into a **project-owned** shape registry, never a foreign library's handle in a Tier-A
crate (see **[USER DECISION 2-G]**).

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]      // 28 B, align 4
pub struct ShapeDef {
    pub tag: u16,
    /// EXACT occupied volume in micro-cubic-metres; full cube = 1_000_000. DERIVED at
    /// content build from the authored mesh by a tested pure function. This single
    /// field makes mass, integrity, buoyancy and structural load derivable.
    pub volume_micro_m3: u32,
    pub solid_face_mask: u8, pub airtight_face_mask: u8, pub mount_face_mask: u8,
    pub side_pattern: [u8; 6],       // → §5/§6's deduped 32×32 occlusion-pattern table
    pub collider: ColliderShapeId,   // project-owned registry index
    pub mirror_shape: [u16; 3],      // ShapeId under mirroring in the chunk basis x/y/z
    pub walkable_slope_cdeg: u16,    // angle to the realm's local up (§2.5.3)
    pub orientation_group: u8,       // distinct placements under the 24 proper rotations
    pub legal_rotation_mask: u8,     // SE's MyBlockRotation: None|Horizontal|Vertical|Both
    pub flags: u8,                   // IS_FULL_CUBE | CONTRIBUTES_TO_AO | …
}
```

`FunctionDef` is the *function* half. §8 owns its semantics; §2 owns only its **shape as a table
row**, because the row is what the identity digest covers and what `BlockTypeId` points at. Its port
and resource lists are `(offset, len)` pairs into flat static arrays — not `&'static [T]` slices,
which are 16-byte fat pointers that would break the row's alignment and size budget.

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]      // 21 B → 24 padded
pub struct FunctionDef {
    pub tag: u16, pub kernel: Kernel, pub authority: AuthorityClass,
    pub tick: TickPolicy, pub ports_off: u16, pub ports_len: u8,
    pub port_growth: PortGrowth, pub res_off: u16, pub res_len: u8,
    pub config_schema: SchemaId, pub max_config_bytes: u16,
    pub emit_rate_limit_hz: u16, pub pcu: u16,
}

/// The generated table. One row per placeable block type; `BlockTypeId` is its index.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]      // 8 B
pub struct BlockTypeDef {
    pub material: MaterialId, pub shape: ShapeId,
    pub function: FunctionRef,   // u16; NO_FUNCTION = 0xFFFF
    pub flags: u16,              // RETIRED | NEEDS_CONFIG | TERRAIN_GENERABLE | …
}
```

#### 2.1.3 The byte budget

| Table | Row | v1 rows | v1 bytes | At cap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `MaterialDef` | 118 B → **120** padded | 64 | 7.5 KiB | 60 KiB |
| `ShapeDef` | 28 B | 64 | 1.75 KiB | 7 KiB |
| `FunctionDef` + `PortDef` table | 24 B + ~8 KiB | 0 → ~64 | 0 at P6; ~9.5 KiB at P9 | ~14 KiB |
| `BlockTypeDef` | 8 B | ~512 | 4 KiB | 512 KiB |
| **Total at P6** | | | **≈ 13 KiB** | |
| **Total at P9 (all-in)** | | | **≈ 23 KiB** | |

`MaterialDef`'s 118 bytes: identity/render 6, physical 8, structural 8, destruction **58** (the
gate+scale matrix is 48 of it), thermal 13, fluid 4, optical 5, electrical 2, chemical 5, biological
1, gameplay 8. The whole physics of the game is smaller than one texture mip, which is what makes
shipping the identity digest in the handshake (§2.8) free.

---

### 2.2 The parameter set

#### 2.2.1 What "authored" is allowed to mean

An authored row is **not** a balance opinion. The checked-in content is `physical_facts.rs` — a Rust
`const` array, deliberately **not** a TOML or JSON file, because `toml` is not a workspace dependency
and a parser would add both a dependency decision and a pile of uncoverable error branches to a
Tier-A crate. One entry per material, containing only quantities that can be looked up and cited:

```rust
PhysicalFacts { name: "granite",
    density_kg_m3: 2700, tensile_mpa_q4: 160 /* 10.0 */, flexural_mpa_q4: 240 /* 15.0 */,
    mohs_q4: 104 /* 6.5 */, vickers_mpa: 8000, work_of_fracture_j_m2: 100,
    k_ic_mpa_sqrtm_q8: 384 /* 1.5 */, elongation_pct: 0,
    melting_k: 1500, thermal_mw_mk: 2900, specific_heat_j_kgk: 790, family: Rock }
```

A tested pure function `derive_material_row(&PhysicalFacts, &GameScale) -> MaterialDef` turns that
into the integer row. `GameScale` is the ONE config struct and it holds **fourteen** named constants,
each expressible as a sentence a player would recognise:

| `GameScale` constant | Value | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| `FRAGMENT_SURFACE_M2_PER_M3` | 200 | a destroyed block breaks into roughly 3 cm fragments |
| `TOUGHNESS_BASE` | 268 | with the √ compression below, calibrates granite to 1,198 dp |
| `TOUGHNESS_COMPRESS` | ½ | real fracture energies span 10⁵; game HP must span ~10³ |
| `STRUCTURAL_FOS` | 2.8 | the factor of safety that lands "a granite beam cantilevers 12" |
| `MAX_SUPPORT_RADIUS` | 32 blocks | the support flood's bound (§2.5.2), hence the cantilever cap |
| `TOOL_DP_PER_WATT` | 4 | a 150 W hand tool delivers 600 dp/s of work |
| `BEAM_COUPLING_Q12` | 433 (10.6 %) | fraction of beam power that becomes fracture work |
| `IMPULSE_DP_PER_KJ` | 90 | a 3.4 kJ AP round breaks a granite block in 40 hits |
| `HV_REF_MPA` | 8000 | quartz: the hardness at which a blade stops cutting |
| `KTH_REF_W_MK` | 400 | copper: the conductivity at which heat is fully wicked away |
| `ELONG_REF_PCT` | 20 | the ductility at which blunt impact is fully absorbed |
| `KIC_REF_MPA_SQRTM` | 5 | the toughness above which nothing shatters |
| `SHATTER_BY_FAMILY[7]` | see §2.3.3 | the one column physics does not give us — 7 numbers |
| `FIRE_SECONDS_PER_MJ` | 1/120 | how long a fuel load burns |

That is the entire tuned surface for the whole material system. It resolves the tension the research
surfaced: Dwarf Fortress proves going "fully physical" does not eliminate tuned constants (its own
combat resolution contains `10 + 2·Qa`, `2 + 0.4·Qa`, `/50000`, a 5 %-per-layer decay and a
hand-tuned sharpness ladder). The discipline that *does* work is: **the tuned numbers are few,
global, named, and in one place; the per-material numbers are all derived from citable facts.**

Worked derivations, all integer (all intermediates in `u64` — the thermal product reaches 3.9 × 10⁹
and overflows `u32`):

```
mass_g            = density_kg_m3 × volume_micro_m3 / 1_000
fracture_work_kj  = work_of_fracture_j_m2 × FRAGMENT_SURFACE / 1_000
toughness_dp_m3   = TOUGHNESS_BASE × isqrt(fracture_work_kj × 1024) / 32      (√, integer)
integrity_dp      = toughness_dp_m3 × volume_micro_m3 / 1_000_000
cantilever_blocks = min(MAX_SUPPORT_RADIUS, isqrt(2·σ_flex/(ρ·g)) / STRUCTURAL_FOS)
support_kg        = cantilever_blocks × mass_kg                    (so the two agree by construction)
shatter_dp        = integrity_dp × shatter_frac_q12 >> 12
harvest_tier      = mohs_tier(mohs)                                (step table on the Mohs scale)
```

**Integrity is derived from work of fracture, not from strength.** This is the single most important
correction in the model. A 1 m³ block does not fail by crushing; it fails by fragmenting, and the
energy that takes is the work of fracture (J/m²) times the fragment surface. Deriving integrity from
compressive or flexural strength gives a glass cube more HP than a granite cube, which is wrong by
inspection. Because real fracture energies span 10⁵ (glass 10 J/m², granite 100, oak 10 000, steel
100 000), a square-root compression is applied — **one named exponent, stated, rather than 64
hand-tuned rows.**

The table this produces, with no per-material tuning at all:

| Material | ρ | W_frac kJ/m³ | mass kg | **integrity dp** | shatter dp | cantilever (uncapped m) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Packed soil | 1500 | 0.4 | 1500 | **169** | never | **0** (3) |
| Water ice | 917 | 0.6 | 917 | **207** | 10 | **6** (19) |
| Glass | 2500 | 2.0 | 2500 | **379** | 7 | **22** (64) |
| Granite | 2700 | 20.0 | 2700 | **1,198** | 359 | **12** (34) |
| Concrete | 2400 | 24.0 | 2400 | **1,312** | 393 | **6** (20) |
| Basalt | 2900 | 26.0 | 2900 | **1,366** | 409 | **14** (39) |
| Oak | 700 | 2,000 | 700 | **11,985** | never | **32** (171) |
| Structural steel | 7850 | 20,000 | 7850 | **37,900** | never | **32** (96) |
| Titanium alloy | 4430 | 24,000 | 4430 | **41,518** | never | **32** (201) |

Dirt cannot cantilever at all; glass is brittle but spans well; **oak has the best specific strength
of any material in the game and the worst survivability** — it cuts, burns and rots, and that is its
balance. Titanium is the endgame structural material. Not one of those numbers was typed by a
designer, and every one is reproducible from the published function.

The cantilever column is capped at `MAX_SUPPORT_RADIUS`. That is honest, not a fudge: beyond 32
blocks a span is governed by *deflection*, which we do not simulate, and 32 is also the support
flood's cost bound (§2.5.2). The uncapped physical figure is shown so the ranking is visible.

A per-material `override` column exists for the handful of cases where physics gives a bad game. It
is a **table**, `MATERIAL_OVERRIDES: &[(MaterialId, OverrideField, i64)]`, and a coherence assertion
requires it to be non-empty — otherwise the override branch in `derive_material_row` is an
uncoverable Tier-A region (HR5). The v1 entry is `WaterIce.harvest_tier`.

#### 2.2.2 The full field table
