Every row states: what it is, its integer representation, the mechanic it buys, whether it costs
per-tick simulation, and whether it is **A**uthored or **D**erived.

| Group | Field | Unit / repr | Mechanic | Per-tick | A/D |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| identity | `tag` | u16, dense | registry identity, wire discriminant | — | A |
| | `family` | u8 enum | sound/particle sets, shatter policy | — | A |
| | `matter_state` | u8 enum | which mechanics may touch it at all | — | A |
| | `render` | `RenderMaterialId` | indirection into §5's Tier-B row | — | A |
| physical | `density_kg_m3` | u32 | mass, buoyancy, inertia tensor, blast impedance | — | A (cited) |
| | `friction_q12` / `restitution_q12` | u16 Q12 | walking, sliding cargo, bounce | yes (physics) | A |
| | *mass* | grams | everything | — | **D** |
| structural | `toughness_dp_m3` | u32 | integrity | — | **D** |
| | `support_kg` | u32 | cantilever limit, collapse trigger | — | **D** |
| destruction | `resist_gate[8]` | i32, per-channel unit | the damage gate (§2.3) | — | **D** |
| | `resist_scale_q12[8]` | u16 Q12 | the damage scale (§2.3) | — | **D** |
| | `shatter_frac_q12` | u16 Q12 | one-blow catastrophic failure | — | **D** (family × K_Ic) |
| | `shatter_drop_q12` | u16 Q12 | yield when shattered | — | A |
| | `spall_q12` | u16 Q12 | overflow damage to the block behind | — | **D** |
| | `harvest_tier` | u8 0–5 | drops-or-not gate | — | **D** (Mohs) |
| | `debris_kind` / `drop_table` | u8 / u16 | what spawns, what you get | — | A |
| thermal | `ignition_k` `melt_k` `boil_k` | u16 K | the Thermal/Energy **gates** | active set | A (cited) |
| | `fuel_mj_m3` / `burn_rate` | u16 / u8 | how long and how hot it burns | active set | A / **D** |
| | `k_therm_mw_mk` / `heat_cap_j_kgk` | u16 | diffusion; the Thermal `scale` | flood kernel | A (cited) |
| fluid | `porosity_q12` / `absorb_q12` | u16 Q12 | blast absorption, leak rate, soaking | random tick | A |
| | *airtight* | `ShapeDef.airtight_face_mask` | pressurisation, decompression | O(rooms) | **D** |
| optical | `light_absorb` `emit_level` `emit_rgb` | u8 / u8 / [u8;3] | the gameplay light flood | flood kernel | A |
| electrical | `conduct_class` / `signal_atten` | u8 / u8 | §8's power and signal floods | flood kernel | A (cited) |
| chemical | `oxidises_to` `oxidation_rate` `corrosion_thresh_kpa` | u16/u8/u16 | weathering; the Corrosive gate | random tick | A |
| biological | `fertility` | u8 0–100 | can something grow on it | random tick | A |
| gameplay | `pcu` | u16 | realm sim-cost budget → demand scheduler | — | **D** |
| | `replaceable_rank` | u16 | can placement overwrite it (VS's 0–9999) | — | A |
| | `flags` | u32 | AIRTIGHT, GRAVITY_AFFECTED, CLIMBABLE, RETIRED, … | — | A |

Notes that carry design weight:

**No authored mass, no `blast_resistance`, no `deformation_ratio`.** 7DTD authors `Mass` separately
from any density and SE authors `Mass` then overwrites it from the component bill — both admissions
that the free field was a mistake. Blast resistance is column 6 of the resistance matrix; SE's
deformation ratio is our `spall_q12`. For ships this matters twice over: **ship mass, centre of mass
and inertia tensor are running incremental sums** updated by `(Δmass, Δmass·r, Δinertia)` on every
block edit — a 50,000-block ship is never re-summed on a weld.

**`drop_table` names a *game* table** (item ids and counts). Rarity, craft value, refine yield and
market price are **not** on this row and never will be: the standing law is a one-way econ→game
dependency enforced by an economy-absent CI gate, and a value field inverts it the moment any game
system reads it — and it will be read, because loot weights, tool tiers and drop tables all reach for
value. The economy keys its own table by `MaterialId`. `pcu` is the counter-example and *does* belong
here: it is a genuine server property.

**Airtightness is per-face, not per-block** — Vintage Story's independently-authored
`sideSolid`/`sideOpaque`/`sideAo` 6-bit dictionaries are the shipped proof. Our 1 m blocks make the
arithmetic clean: **1 block = 1 m³ = 1 atmosphere unit**, where SE carries 15.625 and 0.125.

**No per-block light grid ships to the client.** In vanilla Minecraft the two light nibble arrays are
4,096 bytes per 16³ section against 2,048–2,560 bytes of block ids. At 62³ one nibble plane is
116.4 KiB per chunk and two are 232.8 KiB — more than the block ids, and on a pure-renderer client
every byte is also bandwidth. The server keeps a **coarse single-channel light/sky-exposure field for
gameplay queries only**; the client uses real renderer lights inside the already-short meshed radius
plus §5's AO. See **[USER DECISION 2-A]**. Likewise thermal costs nothing at ambient — a dense
temperature field is the one genuinely forbidden design (O(all blocks) per tick), so it is a **sparse
active set** (**[USER DECISION 2-B]**) — and chemistry stops at oxidation plus a Corrosive channel
(**[USER DECISION 2-C]**).

**"Transferrable"** (the user's word) resolves into two unrelated things and neither is a new field.
A block that can be *picked up and moved* is `drop_table` + `debris_kind` + a `PORTABLE` flag bit. A
block that *transfers something* — items, fluid, power, signal — is a `FunctionDef` with the Conduit
or Converter kernel, and is §8's business entirely.

---

### 2.3 Block LIFE: the damage model

#### 2.3.1 Gate-and-scale: one formula, correct dimensions

Every destructive event — a pickaxe, a plasma cutter, a bullet, an explosion, a fire, acid rain, a
ship collision — is the same object: a **damage-channel vector** resolved against the material's
resistance row. This is Factorio's `{type, decrease, percent}` model, generalised, plus the one fix
that makes it dimensionally honest and that Starbase already ships: **the threshold and the magnitude
are different physical quantities.**

- **`resist_gate[k]`** is an **intensity threshold** in the channel's own unit. A bullet's *pressure*
  decides whether it penetrates; its *energy* decides how much it removes. Without the split, either
  a 20 kW plasma arc cannot melt anything or a rifle round destroys a hull.
- **`resist_scale_q12[k]`** is the fraction of delivered work that becomes damage.

| # | Channel | Gate unit | Gate derived from | Scale derived from |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `Blunt` | MPa (contact pressure) | tensile strength | `4096 × (1 − elong/ELONG_REF)` — ductility absorbs |
| 1 | `Cut` | MPa (edge pressure) | shear ≈ 0.6 × tensile | `4096 × (1 − HV/HV_REF)` — hard materials blunt the blade |
| 2 | `Pierce` | MPa (point pressure) | Vickers hardness | `4096` — pierce is the universal solvent |
| 3 | `Thermal` | K (source temperature) | `ignition_k` or `melt_k` | `4096 × (1 − k/KTH_REF)` — conductors wick heat away |
| 4 | `Energy` | K (beam equivalent) | `melt_k` | as Thermal |
| 5 | `Corrosive` | kPa (activity) | `corrosion_thresh_kpa` | corrosion class |
| 6 | `Blast` | MPa (overpressure) | tensile strength | `4096 × (1 − porosity_q12/4096)` |
| 7 | `Emp` | V/m | `conduct_class` shielding | **0 for matter** — see §2.3.4 |

```rust
pub const DAMAGE_CHANNELS: usize = 8;

/// A hit. `deliver` is dp (Impulse) or dp/s (Rate) BEFORE resistance, derived from the
/// source's energy; `gate` is the per-channel intensity in that channel's unit.
/// Integer throughout — byte-identical by construction, no libm, no float ordering.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct Hit {
    pub deliver: [i32; DAMAGE_CHANNELS],
    pub gate:    [i32; DAMAGE_CHANNELS],
    pub kind:    HitKind,          // Impulse | Rate
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Default)]
pub struct HitEffect { pub matter_dp: u32, pub function_dp: u32 }

/// Fixed-length const loop, branchless (the gate is an arithmetic mask, not an `if`),
/// all arithmetic in i64 so an adversarial or collision-derived input cannot overflow.
/// Monomorphic — the HR5 monomorphisation trap does not apply.
#[must_use]
pub fn apply_hit(m: &MaterialDef, hit: &Hit) -> HitEffect {
    let (mut matter, mut function) = (0i64, 0i64);
    for k in 0..DAMAGE_CHANNELS {
        // pass = 1 when hit.gate[k] >= m.resist_gate[k]; no branch, no short-circuit gap.
        let pass = i64::from(
            ((i64::from(m.resist_gate[k]) - i64::from(hit.gate[k]) - 1) >> 63) as i32 & 1);
        let dp = (i64::from(hit.deliver[k]).max(0) * i64::from(m.resist_scale_q12[k])) >> 12;
        matter   += pass * dp * i64::from(MATTER_CHANNEL[k]);
        function += pass * i64::from(hit.deliver[k]).max(0) * i64::from(FUNCTION_COUPLING[k]) >> 12;
    }
    HitEffect { matter_dp:   matter.clamp(0, i64::from(u32::MAX)) as u32,
                function_dp: function.clamp(0, i64::from(u32::MAX)) as u32 }
}

#[must_use]
pub fn resolve(m: &MaterialDef, integrity_dp: u32, state: BlockDamage, hit: &Hit) -> HitOutcome {
    let e = apply_hit(m, hit);
    // SHATTER IS CHECKED FOR IMPULSE SOURCES ONLY — a continuous sampler's per-tick
    // amount depends on the tick rate, so comparing it to a per-EVENT fracture
    // threshold would make the outcome tick-rate dependent (§2.3.2).
    if hit.kind == HitKind::Impulse && e.matter_dp >= shatter_dp(m, integrity_dp) {
        HitOutcome::Shattered
    } else if u64::from(state.damage_dp) + u64::from(e.matter_dp) >= u64::from(integrity_dp) {
        HitOutcome::Broken {
            overflow: (u64::from(state.damage_dp) + u64::from(e.matter_dp)
                       - u64::from(integrity_dp)).min(u64::from(u32::MAX)) as u32 }
    } else if e.function_dp > 0 && state.function_dp.saturating_add_frac(e.function_dp) {
        HitOutcome::Fried { damage_dp: state.damage_dp + e.matter_dp as u16 }
    } else {
        HitOutcome::Damaged { damage_dp: state.damage_dp + e.matter_dp as u16,
                              function_dp: state.function_dp + e.function_dp as u16 }
    }
}
```

Repair is **not** a negative hit — it is a separate `apply_repair(dp)` that subtracts from
`damage_dp`, so the damage path stays monotone.

#### 2.3.2 Time quantisation — the rule, stated exactly

The section commits to this because the alternative is a semantics hole, not a tuning question:

1. A **Rate** source's `deliver` vector is **dp per second**. Resistance is applied to the *per-second
   vector*, and the result is then integrated into per-tick amounts:
   `dp_tick = (apply_hit(m, rate_hit) × TICK_NUM + carry) / TICK_DEN`, with a per-(source, target)
   integer remainder accumulator so the integral is exact and **tick-rate independent**.
   The opposite order (divide the rate by the tick count, then resist) is wrong: the gate is a *rate*
   threshold, so dividing first makes a tool that clears granite in 3 s at 20 Hz do literally nothing
   at 200 Hz.
2. `TICK_NUM/TICK_DEN` is the **universe** tick, never realm-subjective time. The per-realm
   `time_multiplier` (`crates/bins/src/lib.rs:2280`, an `f64`) dilates **occupant movement only** —
   that is the exact wording of the standing law. No `f64` enters the damage path, and a test asserts
   that mining speed is identical at `time_multiplier` 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0.
3. **Shatter is checked for `HitKind::Impulse` only.** A continuous sampler never shatters; it
   ablates.

#### 2.3.3 The shatter column — the one thing physics does not give us

`shatter_dp = integrity_dp × shatter_frac_q12 >> 12`, and `shatter_frac_q12` is a **per-family
policy** modulated by K_Ic within the family. This is stated as a deliberate departure, with the
reason: at a 1 m scale the failure mode is fragmentation, not crack propagation, and every
first-principles brittleness index (K_Ic, K_Ic/σ, work of fracture, elongation) puts at least one
material class in the wrong order — K_Ic makes oak more brittle than glass. Seven numbers, in
`GameScale`, each a sentence:

| Family | `shatter_frac_q12` | Reads as |
|---|---|---|
| Ceramic / Glass | 82 (2 %) | shatters from almost anything |
| Ice | 205 (5 %) | shatters easily |
| Rock | 1229 (30 %) | shatters under a heavy single blow |
| Composite | 2458 (60 %) | delaminates under a very heavy blow |
| Metal / Organic / Granular | 4096 (100 %) | never shatters — it just breaks |

#### 2.3.4 The `Emp` channel and function damage

`Emp` has `resist_scale_q12 = 0` for every material and `MATTER_CHANNEL[Emp] = 0`, so it never
removes matter; `FUNCTION_COUPLING[Emp]` is non-zero, so it damages the block's **function** instead.
`apply_hit` therefore returns a *struct*, not a scalar, and `HitOutcome` has a `Fried` arm. Function
damage is a **third mutable per-block field**, `function_dp: u16`, in `block_state` (§2.4) and in the
§2.7 reservation list. It is sparse by construction — only a block with a `FunctionRef` can be fried.
A fried block keeps its integrity and loses its function until repaired. That asymmetry is why there
are 8 channels and not 7.

#### 2.3.5 Sources: tools, weapons and hazards are all derived

**A tool's vector is derived from (its material, its form, its power).** The forms table is the
authored content — nine rows, each with a channel split, a delivered power, a contact pressure and a
coupling factor — and `derive_tool_row(&ToolFacts, &ToolForm, &GameScale) -> Hit` is a tested pure
function under the same tripwire-5 round-trip as the material rows. There is no 128-integer table.

```
Rate source:     deliver[k] = power_w × TOOL_DP_PER_WATT × split_q12[k] >> 12
Beam source:     deliver[k] = beam_w  × TOOL_DP_PER_WATT × BEAM_COUPLING_Q12 >> 12 × split_q12[k] >> 12
Impulse source:  deliver[k] = energy_kj × IMPULSE_DP_PER_KJ × coupling_q12 >> 12 × split_q12[k] >> 12
    gate[Blunt|Cut|Pierce|Blast] = the source's contact pressure in MPa
    gate[Thermal|Energy]         = the source's temperature in K
```

**The hand-tool ladder is access and durability, not speed.** This is a decided departure from
Minecraft and it follows from the physics rather than fighting it: a flint point (HV 6000) is *harder*
than a steel one (HV 1500), so any hardness-proportional speed model makes a stone pick out-mine a
steel one. What actually differs is the tier gate and the head's survival. The **speed** ladder is
**power** — 150 W by hand, 1.5 kW powered, 20 kW ship-mounted — which is monotone, physical, and
gated by fuel, reactor output and mounting rather than by a fictional multiplier. Nothing here is a
hand-typed number.

Sample derived rows (`split` in Q12; pressure/temperature is the gate):

| Source | Power / energy | Split | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick | 150 W | Blunt 2740, Pierce 1356 | head HV (stone 6000, copper 800, steel 1500, carbide 17000) MPa |
| Axe | 150 W | Cut 3686, Blunt 410 | 2000 MPa |
| Sledgehammer | 150 W | Blunt 4096 | 2000 MPa |
| Mining drill | 1.5 kW | Pierce 3072, Blunt 1024 | carbide 17000 MPa |
| Grinder / salvage head | 1.5 kW | Cut 2048, Pierce 2048 | 2000 MPa |
| Plasma cutter (handheld / mounted) | 2 kW / 20 kW | Energy 3277, Thermal 819 | 20,000 K |
| AP rifle round | 3.4 kJ, coupling 1.0 | Pierce 3686, Blunt 410 | 2000–3000 MPa |
| HE shell (1 kg TNT) | 4.2 MJ, **coupling 0.05** | Blunt 2048, Blast 1229, Pierce 410, Thermal 410 | 8000 MPa / 3000 K |
| Wood fire | derived from `fuel_mj_m3` | Thermal 4096 | 1,100 K |
| Lava contact | derived from the lava's material | Thermal 4096 | 1,400 K |

The HE `coupling_q12` is the physically real observation that ~5 % of a blast's energy couples into a
nearby structure; without it, a kilogram of TNT deletes any block in the game.

#### 2.3.6 Six worked examples, reproducible from the published function

**Steel pick on granite.** Granite `gate = [10, 6, 8000, 1500, …]`, `scale = [4096, 0, 4096, 4066, …]`,
integrity 1,198 dp, shatter 359. The pick delivers Blunt 401 dp/s at 2,000 MPa (gate 10 → passes) and
Pierce 199 at 1,500 MPa (gate 8,000 → **blocked**; steel cannot indent quartz). Total **401 dp/s** →
`1198 / 401 = ` **2.99 s**. A **copper** pick delivers the same 401 (its Pierce is blocked too) — but
copper is Mohs 3 against granite's harvest tier 3, so the block breaks and **drops nothing**. A
**carbide** pick passes the Pierce gate (17,000 ≥ 8,000) and adds 199 → 599 dp/s → **2.00 s**. That
is the whole progression: tier gates the drop, hardness gates a channel, power gates the speed.

**Steel pick on a titanium hull plate.** Blunt 401 passes titanium's 950 MPa gate but titanium's blunt
scale is 1228 (14 % elongation absorbs impact) → 120 dp/s against 41,518 dp = **346 s**. You do not
mine a hull with a pick.

**Handheld vs mounted plasma cutter on titanium.** The 2 kW handheld delivers 829 dp/s → **50 s per
hull block**: a slow, committed breaching tool. The 20 kW ship-mounted cutter delivers 8,313 dp/s →
**5.0 s**. Boarding is a commitment; salvage needs a ship.

**Fire and lava.** Fire's gate is 1,100 K. Oak ignites at 573 K → passes → 132 dp/s against
11,985 dp = **91 s per block**. Granite's gate is 1,500 K → **fire never damages stone**; steel's is
1,800 K → **fire never damages steel** — with no rule saying so, just a temperature comparison a
player can read off the tooltip. Ice's gate is 273 K → **1.6 s**. Lava at 1,400 K burns oak in 13 s
and leaves granite and basalt untouched: basalt lava is not hot enough to melt basalt.

**AP rifle round.** 3.4 kJ × 90 = 306 dp of budget, split Pierce 275 / Blunt 30, at 2,000–3,000 MPa.
On **glass** (Pierce gate 5,500 → blocked; Blunt gate 50 → passes): 30 dp ≥ shatter 7 → **shatters on
the first round**; on a **glass pane** (a `ShapeDef` at 1/16 volume, integrity 23, shatter 0) also
first round — the *shape*, not a special case, is what makes a window fragile. **Granite**: 30 dp,
40 rounds. **Structural steel** (Blunt scale 0 — perfectly ductile; Pierce gate 1,500 → passes):
275 dp, 138 rounds. **Titanium** (Pierce gate 3,400 → blocked): **8 dp, 5,190 rounds** — small arms
are useless against a hull. A **1 kg HE shell** (18,900 dp of coupled budget) shatters granite and
takes 10,365 dp of titanium's 41,518: **four shells per hull block**, with `spall_q12` passing the
remainder to the block behind. Armour is thickness.

#### 2.3.7 Drops: the rule for all four outcomes

| Outcome | Drops |
|---|---|
| `Damaged` | none |
| `Fried` | none (the block is intact) |
| `Broken` | full `drop_table`, **if** `tool_tier ≥ harvest_tier`; otherwise nothing |
| `Shattered` | `drop_table × shatter_drop_q12`, subject to the same tier gate |

`shatter_drop_q12` is authored per material: glass 0 (shards, no pane), oak 4096 (it splits into the
same logs), granite 1024 (mostly gravel). This is what stops the perverse outcome where the most
powerful tool destroys the resource: shattering is a **legible trade** — the sledgehammer is fast and
wasteful, the drill is slower and clean — rather than an accident of a 48-dp margin nobody chose.

#### 2.3.8 Where damage lives, how it drains, and how the client learns about it

**Where.** `damage_dp: u16` and `function_dp: u16` in the per-chunk sparse side table (§2.4). Not in
the block record, not in `block_wal`. A block at full health has no entry.

**How it drains — with the bound computed, not asserted.** Constructed materials do **not**
regenerate; players repair with a welder. **Natural terrain heals on the random tick** at
`repair_dp_per_random_tick` derived from `toughness_dp_m3`. The drain is a sampling process, so the
damaged set decays exponentially with τ = `chunk_volume / samples_per_tick / tick_hz`. At 175 samples
per 62³ chunk per tick at 20 Hz, τ = **68 s**; because one heal step restores one of the 8 crack
stages, the effective time constant is **546 s**. Steady state is `fill_rate × τ_eff`, and the dense-
promotion threshold for a `u16` sparse field is 79,442 entries, so the trip point is a sustained
**146 damaged blocks per second in one chunk**. Below it the table is genuinely self-draining; above
it, and for constructed materials which never heal, the mechanism is **dense promotion, which is
lossless and hard-bounded at 465.5 KiB per chunk**. `max_dense_damage_chunks_per_realm` then bounds
the realm; exceeding it is a **loud** admission refusal on further destructive actions in that realm
(the PCU mechanism, §2.2), never a silent eviction of somebody's damage. See
**[USER DECISION 2-E]**.

**How the client learns, without a per-block stream.** The visible artefact is an 8-stage crack
overlay — eight stages is beyond visual discrimination at 1 m, and 65,536 HP steps would swamp the
snapshot budget on a no-prediction client.

```
stage = (damage_dp as u32 * 8) / integrity_dp        // u32 math; 3 bits, DERIVED, never stored
ChunkStateDelta { chunk_key: u64, entries: [(local_index: u18, stage: u3, …); N] }
```

`18 + 3 = 21` bits → **3 bytes per entry**. Four properties:

1. **Change-driven** — an entry is emitted only when a *stage* changes. A pick chipping granite for
   3 seconds emits 8 entries, not 60.
2. **Chunk-scoped, not entity-scoped, and TIER-0-scoped.** ~~The delivery scope is the set of chunks
   the subscriber has meshed, which the server already knows because the binary render rule defines
   it.~~ The binary render rule is retracted (§2.0), so "the meshed set" is no longer a bounded
   quantity — at 100 km it is ~6,800 chunks. **The replacement: the delivery scope is the
   subscriber's *tier-0* set.** An 8-stage crack overlay on a 2-metre cell is not discriminable, so
   above tier 0 the overlay is neither subscribed to nor sent (§2.5.5 rules on every per-block
   quantity this way). This is a new, coarse mechanism that this section owns; it is **not** DEFERRED
   D-9's within-realm per-entity AoI and does not depend on it.

   **The scope did not grow.** At the ladder's default two-pixels-per-cell target the tier-0 radius is
   786 m ≈ **505 chunk columns**, against the ~449 the old eye-height horizon gave — **+12 %, not
   ×100**. The ladder makes the drawn world a hundred times larger and adds **zero bytes** to this
   lane. That is not a coincidence: the ladder's whole purpose is to hold screen-space cell size
   constant, and this lane is scoped by screen-space discriminability.
3. **On the client lane, which does not exist yet** — `BulkMsg::Blob { kind: BulkKind::ChunkDelta }`
   over the **D-4** `MsgClass` arm. `InterShardFlow` is the shard↔shard taxonomy and never delivers
   to a player; the earlier claim of "no new transport class" was exactly backwards.
4. **Re-entry is one message** — a chunk entering the meshed set ships its state table once alongside
   its edit deltas.

**The message cost, in the right unit.** DEFERRED D-9's measured 1,920 msgs/tick peak is an
outbound-**message-count** baseline, not bytes. With per-tick per-subscriber batching (all changed
chunks in one message), 128 sessions in one realm cost **128 msgs/tick = 6.7 % of the measured peak**
— a real, bounded addition to a known wall, not "three orders of magnitude below it".

**The second client lane the ladder adds, and its cost.** Beyond tier 0 the client does not need
per-block state at all; it needs the **edit pyramid** (§2.4.3) so a player's tunnel and tower do not
vanish when the terrain coarsens. That rides the same D-4 arm as a new `BulkKind::ChunkPyramid`, and
the request carries a `tier: u8` — **reserve that byte now** (§2.7.2): it is free in an arm that is
not yet routable and a PROTO_MINOR bump plus a client migration afterwards. The payload is small
because coarse cells merge: a 1,000-block tunnel 500 m long produces 16 + 8 + 4 = **28 pyramid entries
at rungs 5–7 = 224 bytes** at the canonical 8-byte entry (§2.4.3; the earlier 280-byte figure was
computed against the struck 10-byte record), and those 224 bytes are what keep it visible from 25 to
100 km. There is no per-block traffic at any coarse rung, at any distance.

**The shard↔shard half.** Only *edits* cross shards, and only in the roadmap's forwarding case
(edits from ghost/overlap regions forwarded to the realm owner). They ride the reserved
`InterShardFlow::BlockEdit` arm classified as `SideEffecting { idempotency: IdempotencyKey::FencedKey
{ fence } }` — every edit carries the realm's monotone per-cell `edit_fence`, and application is
last-writer-wins by fence, which is exactly what `block_wal`'s dedup-to-final already requires. Its
`FlowDurabilityClass` is `ProducerLessReliable` (a client-originated edit has no re-driver), so its
`push_flow` site carries `Durability::Retained` and the R-6d durable outbox replays it. **Damage and
state deltas never cross a shard** — a realm's damage is the realm owner's private state (HR1).

**The pyramid does not change this.** A forwarded edit is still a tier-0 edit; the realm owner applies
it and updates its own pyramid, so the `BlockEdit` arm's payload is untouched and no shard ever ships a
coarse rung to another shard. The pyramid is derived, realm-private state served on the *client* lane.
**Zero new `InterShardFlow` arms from this section, still.**

---

### 2.4 Per-block state at scale

#### 2.4.1 The block field itself — the verdict this section owes

The memory math at the committed **62³ = 238,328-voxel chunk**:

| Representation | Per chunk | 449-chunk visible disc (server *and* client) |
|---|---|---|
| Dense `u16` block ids | 465.5 KiB | **204.1 MiB** |
| 8-bit palette index | 232.7 KiB | 102.1 MiB |
| 5-bit palette index | 145.5 KiB | 63.8 MiB |
| **4-bit palette index** | **116.4 KiB** | **51.0 MiB** |
| Single-value chunk (all air / all stone) | **0 B of index** | ~0 |

**The verdict: a per-chunk palette of `PaletteEntry`, with a bit-packed index array at
`ceil(log2(palette_len))` bits, a 4-bit floor, and a zero-bit single-value fast path.** This is
Minecraft's shipped layout, and the decisive property is the one usually undersold: **most of a
planet is a single-value chunk** — everything above the surface is `{Air}`, everything below the
regolith is `{Granite}`, both at zero index bytes. The 51.0 MiB figure is the worst case where every
visible chunk is a mixed surface chunk.

**The detail ladder does not change one number in that table, and that is the point.** A tier-*L* chunk
is the same 62³ palette container with the same `PaletteEntry` rows; only the cell size implied by its
address differs, so there is no second container, no second packing and no branch (HR3). Two
consequences worth stating explicitly, because they are what keep the ladder cheap here:

1. **The resident block field is a tier-0 quantity.** Coarse rungs are *generated transiently* for
   meshing and dropped; they are never persisted, because only tier 0 is writable (§2.4.3). So the
   51.0 MiB worst case above is the whole of the block-field budget **at any view distance**. The
   ~6,800 chunks a 100 km view needs are *meshes* in §5's budget, not palettes in this one.
2. **The tier-0 disc is 786 m ≈ 505 chunk columns** at the ladder's default pixel target, against the
   ~449 the old eye-height horizon gave — a 12 % change to a figure that was never the constraint.
   Addendum 1 §C.4's "≈ 1 km of meshed terrain is what we can afford" is dissolved (§2.0); this table
   is now a statement about the *simulated* radius, not the *drawn* one, and those have separated.

**Orientation lives inside the palette entry, not in a parallel plane** — which is the answer to the
objection that "sparse always wins" fails on ships. A dense orientation byte plane would be
232.7 KiB per chunk, larger than either mutable field, and on a player-built interior it is dense by
construction. In the palette it costs **nothing on terrain** (orientation is always 0, so it does not
widen the palette) and **only what is used** on a ship (a chunk with ~200 distinct
(type, orientation, placed) triples needs 8 bits/voxel = 232.7 KiB; a ship's empty chunks are
single-value air at zero). A 50,000-block ship spanning four occupied chunks is under 1 MiB.

```rust
/// The per-chunk palette entry. 4 bytes; the index array holds indices INTO this.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct PaletteEntry {
    pub block_type: BlockTypeId,   // u16
    pub orientation: u8,           // 5 bits used (24 proper rotations)
    pub placed: bool,              // 1 bit — generator-authored vs player-placed (§2.5.2)
}
```

#### 2.4.2 The mutable side tables

Six dense mutable fields at 62³ would be **1.705 MiB per chunk** (u16 damage + u16 function + u8
moisture + u8 growth + u8 fluid + nibble light) — almost entirely zeros.

**The design.** Per chunk, per field: two parallel sorted vectors, `keys: Vec<u32>` and
`vals: Vec<T>`, binary-searched. Two vectors rather than `Vec<(u32, T)>` because the tuple pads to
8 bytes for a `u16` payload and the split form costs 6. A sorted `Vec` beats `BTreeMap` (3–4× the
bytes) and `DetHashMap` (≈147 KiB for 10,000 entries; the default-hasher `HashMap` is banned in
sim/node anyway) and gives **deterministic iteration order for free**, which sorted-on-drain
`block_wal` already needs. **Dense promotion** is computed, not guessed: a `u16` payload costs
6 B/entry sparse against 2 B/voxel dense → dense wins above 79,442 entries = **33.3 %**; a `u8`
payload → 47,665 = **20.0 %**. `promote_at_permille` lives in the one tuning config struct (333/200).

**The complete field list, with phase and durability class:**

| Field | Type | Table | Durability class | Lands |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `damage_dp` | u16 | `block_state` | **checkpoint-carried** — see below | P6 |
| `state_bits` | u16 (§2.6) | `block_state` | checkpoint-carried, `PERSIST_MASK` subset | P6 |
| `function_dp` | u16 | `block_state` | checkpoint-carried | P9 (reserved P6) |
| `config_ref` | u32 → `config_state` | `block_config` | **durable**, write-on-change debounced | P9 (reserved P6) |
| `cover_ref` | u32 | `block_cover` | durable, debounced | P9 (reserved P6) |
| `temp_dk` | **u16, absolute deci-kelvin** | `block_thermal` | checkpoint-carried | world-sim phase (reserved P6) |
| `fluid` | u8 (4-bit kind + 4-bit level) | `block_fluid` | checkpoint-carried | world-sim phase (reserved P6) |
| `growth` | u8 | `block_state` | checkpoint-carried | world-sim phase |

`temp_dk` is **absolute** deci-kelvin, 0–6,553.5 K. A signed "delta from ambient" i16 would saturate
at ±3,276.7 K and could not represent tungsten's melting point (3,695 K), let alone a plasma arc.

**Durability, stated per class — this is the P6 crash discipline and it matters.**

- `block_wal` is durable, append-only, with P6's committed three-step fsync checkpoint. Every
  placement and break.
- `block_state`, `block_thermal`, `block_fluid` are **checkpoint-carried, not WAL-backed**. Damage
  changes on every tick for every actively-damaged block; an fsync per change is 400 fsync/s for 20
  miners at 20 Hz. They are written with the `chunk_snapshot` compaction and on realm spin-down, and
  coalesced into P7's tiered-checkpoint cadence (~1 txn/s). On `kill -9`, damage since the last
  checkpoint is lost and the block restores at its last checkpointed crack stage. That is correct:
  damage is a *recoverable* quantity; a player re-shoots. A **lost placement is not**, which is why
  placements are in the WAL and damage is not.
- **The atomicity rule for "damage reaches integrity → block removed → damage row deleted":** the
  break is written to the WAL *first*, the state row is deleted *second*. A crash between the two
  leaves a damage row for a cell the WAL says is air; recovery drops any state row whose cell the
  WAL resolves to `Air`. Idempotent, and a lost build is structurally impossible.

A **block-entity registry** — a bounded, PCU-budgeted list of genuinely per-tick machines — is the
escape hatch for the handful of blocks that need real per-tick state. It stays in the hundreds per
realm, not the millions, and the PCU budget is what enforces that.

#### 2.4.3 The edit pyramid — the one new persisted structure the detail ladder adds

The generated world coarsens itself for free (§2.0). **Player edits do not**, and that asymmetry is the
entire hard part of voxel level-of-detail: render a coarse rung from the generator alone and a dug
tunnel disappears at 200 m and reappears at 100 m, a built tower pops in and out as you fly. That is a
seamless-law violation, not a cosmetic one.

**The write invariant, made structural**

> **Only tier 0 is writable. Every coarser rung is derived.**

Space Engineers ships exactly this as an API contract on its voxel storage — *"the storage system can
only write to LOD0, with higher LODs computed based on that level"* — as a documented convention. We
make it a **type-level impossibility** instead: `BlockStore::write` takes a **`Tier0Key`**, a newtype
constructible only from a `ChunkKey` whose `tier` is 0. The one narrowing point is
`ChunkKey::as_tier0() -> Option<Tier0Key>`, which returns `None` for **every** tier 1..=31 — a real,
covered branch under HR5, and the negative test this design uses instead of a compile-fail fixture
(§2.9). ~~`Tier0Addr`, `ChunkAddr` and `Tier0Addr::try_from`~~ are struck spellings; the canonical name
roster is `ChunkKey` for the address word, `Tier0Key` for the tier-0-proven key, `CellIndex` for a cell
inside a chunk, `BlockAddr { chunk: Tier0Key, cell: CellIndex }` for a tier-0 block address and
`CoarseAddr { chunk: ChunkKey, cell: CellIndex }` for the only address admitting any rung — with **no
reverse conversion, not even a fallible one**. **Cost:** one newtype, one narrowing accessor, one
covered `None` branch. **Alternative:** a convention plus a review checklist, which is what every project
that later found a coarse-tier write in production had. **One-way door: no**, but it is free before the
write sites exist and an audit of every write site afterwards.

**The record — one canonical version, settled as register row 37 / one-way door 43**

~~An entry stores a **delta against the generated baseline**, never an absolute — `PyramidEntry {
packed: u32, solid_delta: i32, dominant: BlockTypeId }`, ten bytes, with a `lane` field and a
`DOMINANT_DIRTY` bit.~~ **The delta form is struck.** The adjudicated record is **absolute**, eight
bytes, and carries an **octant mask** and a **substance** rather than a signed count and a
`BlockTypeId`. Three reasons, each from the section that owns the ground:

- **Absolute, not delta (§3 owns persistence).** A coarse generator baseline is *binary* — one
  octave-dropped evaluation — so a signed delta needs the coarse cell's generated **solid count** at
  read time, which is 8^L tier-0 evaluations, 2,097,152 at rung 7. That is exactly the cost §4.3.2
  prices at four orders of magnitude and rejects, and it contradicts §3.5.6's whole premise.
- **An octant mask, not a count (§4 owns shape semantics).** A count thresholded to a boolean is
  precisely the "castles read as voxel-based blobs" failure this subsection exists to avoid; an
  eight-metre ramp built of eight wedges is a *feature* at rung 3, and only a mask preserves it.
- **A substance, not a `BlockTypeId` (§4).** A `BlockTypeId` carries a shape and possibly a function,
  and a coarse cell's shape must come from the mask and the fill rather than from whichever child
  dominated.

An entry exists for a coarse cell **iff** its summary differs from what the generator would produce at
that same address (see *Pruning*). That is what makes storage proportional to edits rather than to
world size, and it is the same principle as the committed "all changes saved as deltas".

```rust
// crates/core/src/block/pyramid.rs — Tier-A, 100 % region+branch. Pure integer arithmetic.
// PERSISTED, PERMANENT, ONE-WAY DOOR (register row 37 / door 43). No branch on tier.

/// The unpacked payload of one coarse-cell summary. Closed under its own update rule:
/// a parent's summary is a function of its eight children's summaries ALONE.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)]
pub struct CellSummary {
    /// Octant o (canonical order: x fastest, then z, then y) set iff child o is non-empty.
    /// At tier 0 this is the drawn variant's baked `octant_mask` (ShapeDef.octant_mask under Orient).
    pub occ_mask:  u8,
    /// Mean fill fraction of the eight children, 0..=255.
    pub fill_256:  u8,
    /// Dominant substance by SUMMED fill over non-empty children; ties -> lowest SubstanceId.
    /// When `occ_mask == 0` this MUST be the realm's declared EMPTY substance id.
    pub substance: SubstanceId,   // u16, the §2.1 substance-table row id
}

/// The persisted 8-byte word. ONE width at EVERY tier: a tier is a number, not a code path.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct PyramidEntry(u64);
```

```
Edit-pyramid entry — 8 bytes, one u64, MSB-first:
  bits 63..46  cell       (18)  CellIndex within the tier-L chunk, 0..=238_327
  bits 45..30  substance  (16)  SubstanceId — dominant by summed fill; ties -> lowest id
  bits 29..22  occ_mask    (8)  octant o set iff child octant o is non-empty
  bits 21..14  fill_256    (8)  mean fill fraction of the eight children, 0..=255
  bits 13.. 0  reserved   (14)  MUST be zero; decode REJECTS non-zero (never decode-to-Default)
```

**Keying and storage.** One table, **`chunk_pyramid`** — `ChunkKey -> PyramidRecord` — in the **same
redb file as the block deltas**, so it moves with the realm on a re-shard and flushes under the same
`BLOCK_STORE_FLUSH_STEP` fence. The **storage block is one (tier, chunk) pair** holding that chunk's
sparse entry list, in §3.9.3's two encodings (sparse `8n`, or masked-dense `29,791 + palette +
n*bits/8`; the compactor picks the smaller, same 4,256-cell crossover). `ChunkKey` orders
sector → tier → a → b → c, so one whole rung is one contiguous range scan. ~~`block_pyramid`, one row
per coarse cell~~ and ~~"beside `block_wal`"~~ are struck names.

**Composition at read time** (Addendum 2 §C.4, made exact):

```rust
fn coarse_summary(a: CoarseAddr) -> CellSummary {
    chunk_pyramid.get(a).map(PyramidEntry::summary)
                        .unwrap_or_else(|| generate_summary(a))
}
// then: representative(coarse_summary(a), &ADMITS) -> (BlockTypeId, Orient)
```

`generate_summary(a)` is THE SAME generator call the coarse mesher makes — one evaluation of
`h(dir, L)` plus one strata lookup — in `core/src/grid/gen/`, Category-A deterministic. A miss resolves
through the **generator**, never through disk and never to a `Default`.

**Keyed by the address that already exists — with a five-bit tier.** ~~§3's published `ChunkAddress`
carries `detail_tier` in bits 18..16 … three bits is exactly the eight rungs the ladder needs … a ninth
rung would take one of the 16 zero-checked reserved bits.~~ **Struck**: that layout was itself
superseded, and three bits cannot express the ladder's real top rung. The canonical word is §3.3.6's
`ChunkKey` with **`tier` at bits 60..56, five bits, 0..=31 representable** (register row 1 / one-way
door 14). The legal ceiling is the body's derived `tier_depth` — the face-covering rung plus one, which
is 13 for the starter body, 19 for an Earth-sized one and 21 for the largest addressable body — so
there is no fixed `TIER_MAX` and every "seven rungs" figure below is restated against `tier_depth`. No
second key type and no second addressing scheme (HR3). **The WAL's key always has `tier = 0` — the write
invariant expressed in the key itself.**

**The update rule: an exact recompute per rung, with an early exit**

~~`fn on_edit(…) { for tier in 1..=TIER_MAX { let e = self.entry_or_zero(at.coarsen(tier));
e.solid_delta += d; e.set_dominant_dirty(); } }` — exactly seven blind increments, reading nothing.~~
**Struck**, together with the `DOMINANT_DIRTY` bit, the deferred compaction argmax over a transient
histogram, and the `dominant_recompute_batch` tuning field. An accumulator cannot produce the absolute
record above. The canonical rule is the recursive walk-up over eight sibling summaries with a generator
fallback on a miss; §3 owns it as persistence and §4 owns the pure kernel, and it is stated here in full
because §2.9's benchmark gate is written against it.

```rust
// crates/core/src/block/coarsen.rs — Tier-A, 100 %, FOLDED INTO BlockRegistryHash.
// Branchless shim over monomorphic helpers (HR5's generic-code discipline).
pub fn coarsen(children: &[CellSummary; 8]) -> CellSummary;
```

Exact, because this is byte-identity-gated **per tier**:

```
occ_mask  = Sum_{o=0..7} ((children[o].occ_mask != 0) as u8) << o
fill_256  = ((Sum_{o=0..7} children[o].fill_256 as u16) + 4) >> 3        // round-half-up, exact
substance = argmax over distinct s of
              Sum { children[o].fill_256 as u32 : children[o].substance == s
                                               && children[o].occ_mask != 0 }
            ties broken by LOWEST SubstanceId
            if occ_mask == 0 then substance = realm.empty_substance and fill_256 = 0
```

The tier-0 leaf is the only place the block field is read:

```
summary_of_tier0_cell(a: BlockAddr) -> CellSummary {
    occ_mask  = BAKED_VARIANT[variant_index[shape][orient]].octant_mask
    fill_256  = ((volume_units as u64 * 255) + CELL_VOLUME_UNITS/2) / CELL_VOLUME_UNITS
    substance = the cell's SubstanceId
}   // CELL_VOLUME_UNITS = 196_608; full cube -> 255, half slab -> 128
```

The walk-up runs inside the WAL's own redb write transaction:

```
on commit of the edits touching tier-0 chunk C (once per batch, coarse cells deduped):
  for each touched tier-0 cell a:
      mark a.ancestor(1) dirty
  for L in 1 ..= tier_depth - 1:
      for each dirty CoarseAddr parent at rung L (deduped, ascending key order):
          siblings = [ chunk_pyramid.get(s).map(PyramidEntry::summary)
                       .unwrap_or_else(|| generate_summary(s))   // MISS -> GENERATOR, never Default
                       for s in parent.children() ]              // 8 lookups, ONE storage block
          next   = coarsen(&siblings)
          stored = chunk_pyramid.get(parent).map(PyramidEntry::summary)
          if Some(next) == stored { continue }                   // EXIT ON SUMMARY EQUALITY
          if next == generate_summary(parent) { chunk_pyramid.remove(parent) }   // PRUNE
          else { chunk_pyramid.put(parent, PyramidEntry::new(parent.cell, next)) }
          dirty_coarse_chunk(parent.chunk, L)
          mark parent.ancestor(L+1) dirty
```

The exit is on **summary** equality, not on the equality of the drawn representative: two different
summaries can share a representative, so exiting on the representative would leave an ancestor whose
stored summary is stale while the drawn pixel is right — and the recompute audit below would then fail
on visually correct data. An unchanged parent implies unchanged ancestors, so the summary test is exact.

**Cost.** `walk_up_budget_ns = (tier_depth − 1) × 8 × 5 × 12.19 ns` with *every* sibling missing —
**5.85 µs at `tier_depth` = 13, 9.75 µs at 21**, ≤ 1 % of a ~1 ms edit budget. With the early exit the
common single edit inside solid rock terminates at rung 1 or 2 (~0.5 µs). Because `CHUNK_EDGE = 62` is
even, a rung-*L* parent's eight children always lie in **one** rung-(L−1) storage block, so the eight
sibling lookups are one storage-block read; and a miss resolves through the generator, so the walk-up
never reads `block_wal` and never reads a tier-0 delta.

**Why this section's order-independence argument does not defeat that — it is answered, not ignored.**
~~"A dominant *material* cannot be maintained live: a Boyer–Moore/Misra–Gries running majority depends
on the order edits arrived, and `block_wal` is dedup-to-final, sorted-on-drain, so the live order and
the replay order differ by construction — therefore defer `dominant` to compaction."~~ The premise is
correct and the conclusion does not follow. That argument defeats a **streaming estimator**; it does not
touch an **exact recompute**. `coarsen(children)` is a pure function of the eight children's *current*
summaries with a **total** tie-break (lowest `SubstanceId`, over distinct values), so its output depends
on the tier-0 state and on nothing else. Order-independence therefore holds at every rung at every
instant — more strongly than deferral achieved, and with no compaction pass at all.

**Pruning is what makes "sublinear as edits cluster" true rather than aspirational.** An entry is
deleted **iff it equals `generate_summary` of its own address**. A player who digs a hole and fills it
back in leaves nothing behind at any rung. ~~"delete when `solid_delta` is 0 and `dominant` is
`NO_OVERRIDE`"~~ is struck along with the `NO_OVERRIDE` sentinel itself: under the canonical record an
empty coarse cell carries the realm's declared **EMPTY substance id**, not an override marker.

**The mask and the fill buy a SHAPE, not a boolean — the anti-blob rule**

Thresholding a coarse cell to solid-or-empty is precisely what makes distant player-built structures
read as lumps — the shipped failure mode Crimson Desert players describe as *"castles and buildings in
the distance look like voxel-based blobs"*, and the exact default our pure-pyramid path for ships,
stations and bases would fall into. There is deliberately **no fill threshold and no solid-or-empty
decision anywhere on this path**. The drawn geometry is:

```
bucket = (fill_256 as u16 * 9) >> 8                     // 0..=8, exact
(ShapeId, Orient) = COARSE_SHAPE[occ_mask][bucket]      // [[u16; 9]; 256], 4,608 bytes
BlockTypeId = the row for (substance, ShapeId), else the substance's `Cube` row
```

~~`fill_fraction_to_shape(frac_q12) -> ShapeId`, with the orientation taken from the gradient of the six
neighbouring cells' fill fractions~~ is struck, and so is any `solid_threshold` render-tuning field on
this decision. `COARSE_SHAPE`, the bucket function and `representative()` live in
`crates/core/src/block/coarsen.rs` (Tier-A, 100 %) and are **folded into `BlockRegistryHash`**, so a
client/owner mismatch is a **refused connection** rather than a silently wrong distant silhouette — which
is the property a client-tunable threshold would have destroyed. The one-step fallback is total by
§4.1.1's bake assertion: every substance that has any `BlockTypeDef` row has a `Cube` row. **Cost: zero
extra stored bytes**, one hashed table, and it reuses the shape catalogue rather than introducing a
second geometric representation (HR3). §4 owns the table's contents. **One-way door: no** — it is a
read-side interpretation of fields that are stored either way.

**Storage arithmetic**

A coarse cell holds 2^d fewer entries per rung than the one below it, where *d* is the effective
dimension of the edit set, so the entry count over rungs 1..`tier_depth`−1 is a geometric series and
the whole question closes in four rows. **This four-row form is the canonical treatment**: the cost per
edit depends on the *shape* of the edit set and the four cases span a factor of fifty, so any single
figure — "roughly one seventh", which is the compact-3-D row alone — is misleading for capacity
planning.

| Edit shape | Series | Entries | At 8 B |
|---|---|---|---|
| Compact 3-D cluster (a quarry, a filled-in base) | Σ 8⁻ᴸ | **0.143 n** | 1.14 B/edit |
| Surface, wall or floor (2-D) | Σ 4⁻ᴸ | **0.333 n** | 2.67 B/edit |
| Line, beam or pipe one cell thick (1-D) | Σ 2⁻ᴸ | **≈ 1.000 n** | 8.00 B/edit |
| Isolated, no two edits sharing a coarse cell | `tier_depth` − 1 per edit — the hard bound | | 8·(`tier_depth` − 1) B/edit |

Worked at `tier_depth` = 13 (the starter world, m = 4,096), so the series are not taken on faith:

- a **1,000-edit one-wide tunnel**: 250 + 125 + 63 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = **504
  entries = 4,032 B ≈ 3.9 KiB**;
- an **8,000-edit 20×20×20 tower**: 1,000 + 125 + 27 + 8 + 1×8 = **1,168 entries = 9,344 B ≈ 9.1 KiB**;
- **100 M mixed edits** at the ≈ 1.1 entries-per-edit planning figure: **≈ 880 MB of pyramid**, against
  a 500 MB WAL — so the pyramid roughly *doubles* delta storage rather than tripling it, the 10-byte
  record's 1.1 GB figure having been superseded.

Deeper ladders do not move the clustered rows — the series converge — and only the adversarial isolated
row grows, bounded by `tier_depth` − 1 by construction. That row also requires an adversary who never
edits the same coarse cell twice, and §2.5.4's `max_edits_per_second_per_session` plus the realm PCU
budget bound the input that feeds it.

**Recomputable and checked — because derived data lies quietly**

`recompute_pyramid(coarse_key) -> Vec<PyramidEntry>` rebuilds every entry beneath a coarse cell from
the **generator plus the deltas**, by the same `coarsen` fold the live path runs. It is pure,
monomorphic and Tier-A. Three uses, in ascending cost:

1. **Test suite.** Every edit fixture ends with `assert_eq!(store.pyramid(k), recompute_pyramid(k))`
   for every touched coarse cell. Equality, not `matches!` (HR5).
2. **Debug command.** `vdctl world verify-pyramid <realm>` rebuilds every entry from generator + deltas
   and asserts byte-equality; the test suite runs it after **every** edit scenario (Addendum 2 §E).
3. **Production.** Each `chunk_snapshot` compaction audits `pyramid_audit_entries_per_checkpoint`
   entries (a field in the one tuning config struct, never a literal). A mismatch **recomputes the
   entry and increments `pyramid_divergence_total`**, which the harness asserts is zero.

It does **not** refuse to open the store — deliberately, and unlike the identity digest of §2.8. The
digest guards data that *reinterprets a player's wall*; a stale pyramid entry is a cosmetic error on
data that is 100 % reconstructible from the deltas the store still holds. Refusing somebody's world over
reconstructible cosmetic data is the wrong trade. **That divergence policy is sub-question (e) of
register row 37 / [USER DECISION 8-A]**, where this section's earlier 2-I now lives.

**What the pyramid deliberately does not contain**

| Not in the pyramid | Because |
|---|---|
| `damage_dp`, `function_dp` | damage does not change solidity until the block *breaks*, and a break is an edit — so destruction reaches the pyramid through the edit path, and only when it actually removes matter |
| `state_bits` (grass, leaf, snow, wetness) | none of them changes occupancy, fill or dominant substance, so none of them changes what a coarse cell looks like (§2.6) |
| A `STATE_VISIBLE` block's runtime colour | it changes at TICK rate on data whose lifetime, key and write rate are all different; it rides the separate transient state-light lane of §7.9 (§2.6) |
| Light, `temp_dk`, `fluid` | server-side or sub-cell quantities; a fluid rung would spend some of the record's 14 reserved bits (**[USER DECISION 2-J]**) |
| The `placed` bit | structural support is tier-0 and edit-local by construction (§2.5.2) |
| Any collider data | colliders are built from `Tier0Key` only (§2.5.5), enforced by the type system |

---

### 2.5 The mechanics catalogue

#### 2.5.1 The one kernel several of them share

Block light, sky exposure, structural support, heat diffusion, radiation and signal strength are
**the same algorithm**: an attenuating flood over the 6-neighbour block graph with an increase queue
and a decrease queue. Building it once and expressing the six as data rows is HR2/HR3 applied to
field mechanics, and it makes the r³ cost budget visible in one place. Follow Starlight's algorithm,
not vanilla Minecraft's — the measured difference on the same operation is 4,089 block-state reads
versus 49,062 (place) and 181,452 (remove), **12× and 44×**, from four rules: push to neighbours
rather than pull from all six; remember the incoming direction and never re-read it (1/6 of all
reads); never enqueue a level of 1; separate the increase and decrease queues.

```rust
/// ONE monomorphic kernel. Deliberately NOT generic over the level type: the level is
/// always a u8, and a generic kernel would hit the HR5 per-monomorphisation coverage
/// trap on the hottest code in the voxel system. Variation is DATA, not types.
pub struct FloodField {
    field: FieldId,                  // Light | SkyExposure | Support | Heat | Radiation | Signal
    atten: &'static AttenTable,      // per-material cost to enter, by field
    max_level: u8,
    increase: VecDeque<FloodCell>,
    decrease: VecDeque<FloodCell>,
    budget_cells_per_tick: u32,      // the bound; carries over across ticks
}
```

Cost is exactly predictable: a level-`r` point source reaches the taxicab ball
`(2r+1)(2r² + 2r + 3)/3` cells — **4,991 at r = 15, 19,649 at r = 24, 45,825 at r = 32**. That is
9.2× the work for 2.1× the range, so the attenuation table *is* the budget and
`budget_cells_per_tick` is the backstop. Work carries over; a flood never blocks a frame.

**HR1 property, tested not assumed:** every attenuation table must reach zero at a realm boundary. A
docking interface has infinite attenuation. `flood_terminates_at_realm_boundary` is a harness
assertion, so a fire on a docked ship cannot become a distributed-systems problem. Genuinely
cross-realm propagation rides the Signal system (§8) on the already-reserved
`InterShardFlow::Signal` arm — zero new wire surface.

#### 2.5.2 The twelve mechanics

| Mechanic | Algorithm | Per-tick cost | Bound | Gravity? | Runs dormant? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Light** (gameplay only) | FloodField; `light_absorb` attenuation | O(cells touched by an edit) | `budget_cells_per_tick`; 4,991 cells at r=15 | no | yes, free |
| **Sky exposure** | FloodField, downward-biased along `gravity_dir`; per-column heightmap | per dirtied column | column-scoped | **yes** | yes, free |
| **Structural support** | FloodField from anchored blocks; `support_kg` per face | O(dirty region), **deferred budgeted job, never inline in the edit path** | `MAX_SUPPORT_RADIUS` = 32 → ≤ 45,825 cells per edit | **yes** | yes |
| **Falling blocks** | unsupported set → **merge contiguous groups into ONE rigid body** (SE grid-split) | 1 body per group | `max_falling_groups_per_tick` | **yes** | yes |
| **Fire** | sparse active set; per-second Thermal `Hit` to self and the 54-cell neighbourhood | ~54 reads/burning block/fire tick at 1 Hz — 500 fires = 27,000 reads/s | active-set cap; oxygen gate from the room graph | no | yes, capped replay |
| **Fluids** | 8-level CA with an **active frontier** | O(frontier); a settled 10,000-cell lake costs **nothing** | frontier cap | **yes** | yes, capped replay |
| **Pressure / decompression** | 3D flood over 6 cardinals (no diagonals) → room graph; a small ODE **per room** | 12 rooms on a 50,000-block ship = **12 updates/tick** | re-flood on structural change, debounced + incrementally repaired | no | yes |
| **Growth / spread** | random tick + `fertility` + sky exposure | O(loaded chunk sections), **independent of world content** | `random_tick_samples` | no | yes, closed form |
| **Weathering / oxidation** | random tick → `oxidises_to`; MC's copper rule: scan taxicab-4 (129 cells), abort if any neighbour is *less* oxidised | 129 reads on ~5.7 % of candidates | random-tick budget | no | yes, capped replay |
| **Freezing / melting** | random tick + the sparse thermal set crossing `melt_k` | active-set only | thermal active-set cap | no | yes, capped replay |
| **Explosions** | ray march (MC's shape: 1,352 rays × ~17 steps ≈ **23,000 queries per TNT-equivalent**) | 100 concurrent = 2.3 M queries — the single most expensive event | **coalesce simultaneous detonations into one march**; hard per-tick query budget; deferred queue | no | yes |
| **Radiation** | FloodField | as light | attenuation table | no | yes |
| **Sound occlusion** | **server-side portal walk over the room graph** → one attenuation scalar per (listener, source), shipped in the audio event | O(rooms on the path), single digits | rooms-visited cap | no | n/a |

**The last column now has a companion, not a replacement.** "Runs dormant?" asks whether a mechanic can
sleep and be caught up. The detail ladder introduces a *third* residency state — a realm can be resident
because somebody 40 km away needs a coarse rung of it, with nobody inside — and the answer for every row
is ruled in **§2.5.5**. The short version, stated here so the table is not read alone: **a coarse tier
changes what the owner PUBLISHES, never what it COMPUTES.** No row of this table gets cheaper because an
observer is far away.

Sound occlusion is explicitly a **server** computation. A naive air-BFS at 32 m is up to 137,258
cells per source per query; the room graph makes it free — but the room graph is server state and the
client is a pure renderer, so the server ships the scalar. The client never sees the graph.

**Bounded worst cases.** Explosions, structural collapse, mass falling-block conversion and **spall
cascades** are the four mechanics with genuinely unbounded worst cases, and all four sit behind
deferred budgeted job queues, never inline in the block-edit path. Spall is bounded by
`spall_max_depth` (default 3) in the one tuning config struct. Processing a collapse frontier at N
blocks per tick means a cathedral comes down over two seconds rather than in one frame, which also
looks better.

**Structural support must not collapse the planet.** The section's own table gives packed dirt a
cantilever of **0**, and terrain is noise-generated with overhangs and cave roofs, so a naive support
field would fail every natural overhang the instant it ran. The rule, made possible by the `placed`
bit freed in §2.1.1:

> **Generator-authored blocks (`placed = false`) are unconditionally anchored.** The support flood
> runs only in the taxicab ball of radius `MAX_SUPPORT_RADIUS` around a player edit, and within it a
> generator-authored block loses its unconditional anchor only if it has lost a generator-authored
> neighbour. A player-dug tunnel through natural rock therefore behaves *exactly* like a
> player-built one within 32 blocks of the dig, and natural terrain outside that ball is stable.

The cost is bounded: ≤ 45,825 cell visits per edit, deferred and budgeted, and zero for an edit in
undisturbed terrain.

**The random-tick scheduler is the ONLY driver for slow stochastic evolution.** Its cost is O(loaded
chunk sections) and is completely independent of world content — a player cannot slow the server down
by planting a million crops. Minecraft samples 3 positions per 4,096-block section per tick (per-block
expectation ≈ 68 s at 20 Hz); at 62³ the matching figure is 175 samples per chunk per tick, and it is
a field in the one tuning config struct, never a literal — which is also how a dormant or
low-priority realm runs at a fraction of the rate, and therefore how the dormant-world pillar gets
paid for.

**Dormant realms and catch-up (see [USER DECISION 2-D]).** Three classes, not two, and the middle one
is narrower than it looks:

- **Pure functions of the block field** (light, support, radiation, signal): recompute on spin-up,
  free. **Sky exposure is the exception** — it is not chunk-local (a chunk's exposure depends on
  every chunk above it to the top of the ±10 km build band, ≈ 323 chunks), so it needs a **persisted
  per-column heightmap**: 62² × `u16` = **7.5 KiB per chunk column**, in the §2.7 reservation list.
- **Per-block independent Bernoulli** (crop growth stage, drying): a **closed-form binomial draw**
  over the elapsed ticks per chunk — O(1) per chunk per spin-up regardless of sleep length.
- **Neighbour-coupled or history-dependent** (oxidation, fire, fluids, freezing): **capped replay.**
  Oxidation belongs here, not in the binomial class: the Minecraft copper rule aborts if any
  neighbour is *less* oxidised, and that coupling is the entire point of the mechanic — a per-chunk
  binomial destroys exactly the gradient it exists to produce. Catch-up runs at most
  `dormant_catchup_sample_budget` random-tick samples per chunk, spread over the first N live ticks,
  and then clamps. For fire and fluids the clamp is analytic — a fire either consumed the fuel within
  its reach or went out; a fluid body settled — which is only possible because `temp_dk` and `fluid`
  are **persisted** (they are in §2.7's reservation list for exactly this reason).
- Every catch-up integrator needs `last_ticked_universe_tick: u64` **per chunk**, in the chunk
  metadata row. Reserved in §2.7.

#### 2.5.3 Gravity is a capability, and HR4 binds two fixtures, not one

Four of the twelve mechanics — sky exposure, structural support, falling blocks and buoyancy —
depend on a gravity direction, and a free-flying ship has none. **So the block model does *not* have
"zero geometry dependence"**, and claiming it would be a fixture that either branches on geometry (an
HR4 violation) or silently no-ops on one side (a fixture that proves nothing). Structural support is
worse than a missing vector: on a planet the anchor is the core and the rule is a cantilever under
gravity; on a free-flying grid **nothing is anchored** and SE's answer is grid rigidity — a
categorically different model.

**The resolution.** `ShardProfile` gains one field, `gravity: Option<GravityKind>` where
`GravityKind ∈ {Radial, Uniform, Spin}`, derived in `ShardProfile::build`'s existing validated
lattice exactly like `signal_graph`. `SupportModel` is then a **data row selected by the capability
value** — `Anchored { anchor_depth }` for a gravity-bearing realm, `GridRigid { root }` for a
gravity-free one — not a `match` on a shard kind (HR3 is about kind discriminants; selecting
behaviour from a capability value is what the profile exists for). `gravity_dir` itself already sits
**above** the `FrameSpace` seam, which PLAN.md names as shared write-once, so the mechanics consume
it rather than deriving it.

**G-IDENTICAL then binds two fixtures:**

1. The **gravity-free subset** — tables, `apply_hit`, sparse side tables, light, fire, pressure,
   growth, the edit pipeline — runs the identical fixture on a Spherical planet profile and a
   Cartesian ship profile. This is P6's owed `assert_feature_anywhere` ("block edits on planet AND
   ship, one fixture forcing a reanchor") and it passes with **no branch anywhere in this section's
   code**.
2. The **gravity subset** runs its own identical fixture on two *gravity-bearing* profiles: a
   Spherical planet (`Radial`) and a Cartesian spin station (`Spin`). Same fixture, two geometries,
   two gravity kinds.

`ShapeDef.walkable_slope_cdeg` is defined as the angle between the shape's steepest walkable face
normal and the realm's local up, which is `gravity_dir` — and it is therefore meaningless, and unread,
on a gravity-free profile.

#### 2.5.4 Abuse bounds

Every one of these is a field in the one tuning config struct, never an inline literal:
`max_reach_m` (server-validated against the actor's pose — an edit outside it is refused, not
clamped); `max_edits_per_second_per_session`; server-side tool possession and `harvest_tier` check
(the client's claim is never trusted); `spall_max_depth`; `debris_merge_radius_blocks` with a per-realm
`max_debris_entities` — an HE shell breaking 500 blocks must coalesce into a handful of
`EntityKind::DroppedBlock` stacks (tag 11, Transient, already registered), because 500 transient
entities into a realm whose snapshot emit is still a whole-realm broadcast (D-9) is a self-inflicted
denial of service; and `max_dense_damage_chunks_per_realm` (§2.3.8).

#### 2.5.5 Tier, dormancy, and exactly what a coarse rung does not entitle you to skip

Everything in this subsection follows from one distinction, and getting it wrong is the way a detail
ladder turns into a correctness bug:

> **Dormancy is a property of the REALM and is identical for every observer. Tier is a property of an
> OBSERVER. A per-observer quantity may never gate a realm-wide computation.**

Let a per-observer tier decide whether a mechanic runs and two players see different *facts*: the fire
that stops consuming a forest because the only person watching is far away is not a detail difference,
it is a different world, and Addendum 2 §C.7 forbids it outright. Keep the two axes separate and they
compose cleanly with the demand scheduler that already exists: the ladder contributes a **render tier**
demand that is monotone in the *finest* rung any observer asks for, and the realm's simulation rate stays
a function of the realm's own demand — `sim_rate = f(max over observers)`, never a per-observer branch,
never a decrement.

**Three residency states, not two.**

| State | What it means | What the owner computes | What it publishes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Dormant** | no observer, no occupant | nothing; §2.5.2's three catch-up classes owe the state on spin-up | nothing |
| **Coarse-resident** | some observer needs a rung ≥ 1; nobody is inside | **one catch-up-to-now pass, then nothing** | pyramid entries at the requested tiers, from disk |
| **Fine-resident** | tier 0 is required somewhere in the realm | everything in §2.5.2, at full rate | edits, `ChunkStateDelta`, pyramid entries |

The middle row is the whole answer to *"a realm may be resident at a coarse tier with no player in it"*.
Two rulings, both exact:

1. **A coarse tier entitles the owner to skip PUBLISHING detail. It never entitles it to skip COMPUTING
   a fact.** Coarse residency asks the simulation for nothing, so there is nothing for it to skip —
   pyramid entries are *persisted* data and are served straight off disk without waking the tick loop.
   That is the strongest single argument for persisting the pyramid rather than recomputing it on
   demand, and it is why the pyramid is in §2.7's reservation list rather than being a cache.
2. **A coarse tier never entitles it to publish a STALE fact.** A dormant realm's published state must
   be current, or a player who flies toward a realm watches its terrain jump when the realm finally
   wakes and §2.5.2's catch-up runs — a pop, in view, which the seamless law forbids. So **the onset of
   coarse observation triggers exactly one thing: a catch-up-to-now pass, after which the realm returns
   to dormant if nobody is inside.** Its cost is the existing `dormant_catchup_sample_budget`, paid once
   per observation onset, and the existing demand-scheduler hysteresis is what stops a passing ship
   thrashing it. Because catch-up produces its changes *through the edit path*, it updates the pyramid
   for free — no second integration point.

**Per-block quantities, ruled one at a time.** This is the answer to "which mechanics are affected by
distance", and the pattern is uniform: a quantity gets a coarse rung only if it can change what a coarse
cell *is*.

| Per-block quantity | Coarse rung? | Ruling |
|---|---|---|
| Damage **crack stage** (§2.3.8) | **none** | Tier-0 only, and the delivery scope is tier-0 (§2.3.8). Eight crack stages on a 2 m cell are not discriminable; the overlay is a material feature that leaves on the same per-draw tier ladder as parallax and detail normals. The block's damage is a **fact** and does not change — only the overlay is a detail. |
| `Broken` (integrity reached) | **yes** | It is an edit, so it enters the pyramid like any other. A distant siege visibly eats a wall, at 8 bytes per coarse cell. |
| `function_dp` / `Fried` | **none, ever** | §C.7: signal-bearing behaviour never coarsens. A fried block stops functioning at every distance, for everybody, immediately. |
| Appearance that carries **actionable** state (a docking-clamp light, a breach indicator) | **yes, via the transient state-light lane — never via the pyramid.** Its RANGE is **[USER DECISION 7-H]** | ~~"none, ever — such a block is a functional block, and §8 already ships its state as a signal at the signal's own range"~~ is struck: the client is **not** a subscriber (§7.3.7), so there is no path by which a non-subscribing stranger three kilometres away learns a docking clamp is red, and that mechanism does not exist. The canonical mechanism is §7.9's: a separate **transient per-realm state-light lane**, one entry per coarse cell containing at least one `STATE_VISIBLE` block whose state is not its declared default, composed by the realm owner and shipped at the observer's clamped rung — so it survives to every rung including the realm proxy. It is neither persisted nor derived terrain data, and §2.6's ban on per-block state in the pyramid stands unamended. Reserve the `STATE_VISIBLE` bit in `BlockTypeDef.flags` plus `state_priority: u8` for the coalescing rule, and make it a coherence assertion that every row carrying the flag has a `FunctionRef` with an emitting port — otherwise the rule is a comment. This flag is **one** reservation covering three sections: it IS §7.9 rule 2's status-light exemption and IS §6.9's status-light exemption. |
| `state_bits` — grass, leaf, snow, wetness (§2.6) | **none** | Tier-0 only; §2.6 rules on each bit, including the one that looks like it needs a rung. |
| Gameplay **light** and sky exposure (2-A) | **none** | Server-side only and never shipped, so there is no rung to build. |
| **Rendered** emission | **derived rung** | Renderer lights are placed for tier-0 chunks; beyond it a coarse cell carries its dominant **substance**'s `emit_level` / `emit_rgb` from the same substance row. That is derived-from, not substituted-for — a lit window at 3 km is a dimmer version of the real thing, not a sprite of one. |
| `temp_dk`, `fluid` | **none in v1** | A fluid rung would spend some of the pyramid record's 14 reserved bits, so a player-flooded valley can become coarse-visible later without a record widening — **[USER DECISION 2-J]**. |
| **Collision** | **never, no exceptions** | Tier 0, always, and typed: colliders are built from `Tier0Key`. |
| Structural support, falling blocks, collapse | n/a | Edit-local at tier 0 by construction: the support flood runs inside `MAX_SUPPORT_RADIUS` = 32 blocks of an edit, and an edit only happens where a player is, which is tier-0 by definition. |
| `pcu` / `realm_pcu` | n/a | A realm property, never an observer property. The ladder adds no PCU. |

**Which of the twelve mechanics can change a coarse cell at all.** This is what §2.5.2's catch-up
classes must deliver before a realm is published, and it is a much shorter list than the catalogue —
which is why rule 2 above is affordable. A mechanic reaches a coarse cell only if it changes **which
octants are occupied**, **how full the cell is** or **which substance dominates it**, because those are
the only three things a `PyramidEntry` records.

| Mechanic | Changes solidity or family? | Coarsest rung it can reach | Catch-up class (§2.5.2) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fire | **yes** — it consumes blocks | a forest burn is 100 m+, so tier 6 | capped replay, clamped analytically (the fuel in reach was consumed or the fire went out) |
| Fluids | **yes** — a body settles and floods | a lake is 100 m+, tier 6 | capped replay, clamped analytically (the body settled) |
| Falling blocks / structural collapse | **yes** | a collapsed structure is 10–50 m, tier 4–5 | neighbour-coupled, capped replay |
| Freezing / melting | **yes** — water ↔ ice is a family change | a frozen lake is 100 m+, tier 6 | capped replay off the sparse thermal set |
| Growth / spread | **yes** — grown blocks are blocks | a tree is 1–10 m, tier 3 at most | **closed-form binomial**, O(1) per chunk per spin-up regardless of sleep length |
| Explosions | **yes** | event-driven, and an actor is always present | not a dormant mechanic |
| Weathering / oxidation | **no** — copper to patina is the same family, and it never changes solidity | none | irrelevant to the ladder |
| Light, sky exposure, radiation, signal strength | **no** — pure functions of the field, never shipped | none | recomputed on spin-up, free |
| Pressure / decompression | **no** — room state, not field state | none | irrelevant to the ladder |
| Sound occlusion | **no** | none | irrelevant to the ladder |

So five mechanics out of twelve can move a coarse cell, four of them already have an *analytic* clamp,
and the fifth is O(1). **That is the whole cost of publishing a dormant realm truthfully at any
distance** — which is the concrete reason rule 2 does not reintroduce the per-tick work rule 1 removed.

**One correction to Addendum 2 §C.7, and it matters.** §C.7 says *"tier 0 is always resident wherever a
player is, which is exactly the region physics runs in."* That is not quite the rule. **The rule is
wherever a PHYSICS BODY is** — a dropped block, a projectile, a free-flying ship, a falling-block group
— because collision is tier-0-only and a body over a coarse chunk has nothing to collide with. Without
the correction, an HE shell fired at a fort from 2 km flies through the terrain. `tier0_residency_radius_m`
is therefore a **per-body-class** field in the one tuning config struct: the projectile class wants a
short corridor ahead of the body rather than a disc, and a projectile's flight is measured in seconds.
**Cost:** a residency request per active body, which the demand loop already has machinery for.
**One-way door: no.**

**And the rule that closes the loop.** Suspending a mechanic in a dormant realm is *not* coarsening: the
realm's state genuinely is its pre-fire state while it sleeps, identically for every observer, and
catch-up advances it deterministically. Coarsening a mechanic *per observer* would be a fact difference.
The first is the dormant-world pillar (**[USER DECISION 2-D]**); the second is banned. **Two players at
different distances see different terrain detail. They never see different terrain facts, and they never
see the world at different times.**

---

### 2.6 The block-state bits the decoration layer consumes

§7's decoration layer needs to know, per block: how grassy, how leafy, how snowy, how wet. Those four
facts live in **one `BlockStateBits(u16)` field in the authoritative sparse side table** — not in a
parallel client-side channel.

| Bits | Field | Range | Why that width | Persisted? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | `grass_cover` | 0–7 | eight coverage steps drive prop-scatter density; beyond eight is not discriminable at 1 m, and it matches the damage-stage quantisation so both use one shader path | **yes** — slow state a player cultivated |
| 3 | `leaf_distance` | 0–7 | Minecraft's leaf-decay distance from the nearest log; a pure flood | no — **derived** |
| 3 | `snow_depth` | 0–7 | eighth-metre layers, matching Minecraft's 8 snow layers; the blend weight §5's material transition reads | **yes** — weather history |
| 2 | `wetness` | 0–3 | dry / damp / wet / saturated is all the shader blend and the fluid CA distinguish | no — **derived** from the region's last-rain tick |
| 5 | reserved | — | growth stage, moss, soot, algae, wear | — |

`PERSIST_MASK: u16` selects the persisted sub-fields; the derived bits are recomputed on chunk load.
One field, one mask, no parallel channels, **zero persisted bytes for the derived half**.

**Why they must be authoritative.** Three independently sufficient reasons. (1) The user's Tiny Glade
requirement is that *the surroundings react to the player adding and removing blocks* — that reaction
is a simulation, and the server does all the math (the S2/S3 floating-origin work already drifted into
client-compose once and had to be reworked). (2) Two players looking at the same hillside must see the
same meadow; a client-derived channel diverges by construction. (3) The bits are inputs to §5's
mesher-side material blend, and the mesher runs byte-identically on server and client — a state field
the server does not own cannot be an input to a byte-identical gate.

**How the four bits behave on the detail ladder.** They are **tier-0 facts and get no coarse rung**, and
each for its own reason rather than by a blanket rule:

| Bit field | Ruling | Why, and what the alternative costs |
|---|---|---|
| `grass_cover` | tier-0 only | It modulates §6's decoration *density*, and density falls smoothly to zero with distance (Addendum 2 §C.8) — so beyond the decoration range there is nothing left for the bits to modulate. The alternative, a per-coarse-cell grass summary in the pyramid, costs **+2 B per entry against an 8-byte record, a 25 % record**, to modulate a quantity that is already zero. |
| `leaf_distance` | tier-0 only | Derived, recomputed on chunk load; it never had a persisted form to coarsen. |
| `snow_depth` | tier-0 only **as a per-block field**, but the *quantity* does get a rung | This is the one that looks like a counter-example: a snow-capped mountain is a 10 km fact. It gets its rung from the **coarse weather/biome field the generator already evaluates at that tier** — derived-from, at the correct tier, exactly like the octave-dropped height. The per-block bits are the *fine-tier refinement* of that same quantity, not a different quantity. A player who shovels a path off his roof does not change the mountain's cap: a 1 m change under a 2 m cell is below the representation and correctly invisible. Different detail, same facts. |
| `wetness` | tier-0 only | Derived from the region's last-rain tick, which is itself a coarse regional field the client can evaluate at any tier. |

**No state-bit change ever enters the pyramid.** The pyramid records occupancy, fill and dominant
substance and nothing else (§2.4.3). A `STATE_VISIBLE` block's runtime colour rides the separate
transient state-light lane (§7.9), which is neither persisted nor derived terrain data; the pyramid is
permanent, derived, terrain-shape data changing at *edit* rate, and a lamp's colour changes at *tick*
rate, so the two cannot share a record. Cosmetic per-block state is therefore a tier-0 phenomenon in
exactly the way the crack overlay is. The honest consequence, stated rather than hidden: **a cleared
patch of snow or a cultivated strip of grass is invisible from a hilltop 3 km away.** If that reads as a
loss rather than as correct filtering, the fix costs 2 bytes on top of an 8-byte record — a 25 % record
and a width change on permanent data — **[USER DECISION 2-J]**.
