### 2.7 What must be reserved NOW, and the `block_wal` arithmetic

#### 2.7.1 The record, and where the chunk address lives

`roadmap.json` P6 commits to `block_wal (append-only, 5-byte dedup-to-final edits, sorted-on-drain
for determinism)`. Five bytes is 40 bits. A 62³ chunk needs 18 bits of local index
(238,328 < 2¹⁸ = 262,144; 2¹⁷ is too small, so 18 is the exact minimum). The research pool's proposal
— a 12-bit `GeometryId` **plus** a 16-bit `MaterialId` — is 28 bits of payload and does not fit.

The three-table decomposition plus the mirroring verdict resolves it exactly, with one bit to spare:

```
┌──────────────────┬──────────────────┬─────────┬───┐
│ local_index 18 b │ block_type  16 b │ orient 5│p 1│   = 40 bits = 5 bytes
└──────────────────┴──────────────────┴─────────┴───┘
```

`BlockTypeId` is a u16 index into the generated triple table, so it carries material *and* shape
*and* function in sixteen bits. Orientation is the 24 proper rotations (mirroring is a shape, §2.1.1).
`p` is `placed` — the generator-authored/player-placed bit §2.5.2 needs to keep structural support
from collapsing every natural cave roof, and the reason it exists is that the mirroring verdict freed
it.

**Orientation's reference frame, stated now because it is persisted forever.** Orientation and
`mirror_shape[x|y|z]` are expressed in the **chunk's own basis**, and a chunk's basis is fixed for
the life of the chunk: for a Cartesian realm it is the realm's basis; for a cube-sphere realm it is
the owning face's `(u, v, up)` triad. **A chunk never straddles a cube face**, so a stored orientation
is never re-interpreted; the basis change at a face seam is a *neighbour-lookup* rebasing inside the
`GridMapping` seam, not a rewrite of any record. On a realm re-parent — docking a ship to a station,
the P8 case — only the realm-to-parent transform changes; the ship's chunks keep their own basis and
not one block record is touched. `legal_rotation_mask`'s Horizontal/Vertical axes are the chunk-basis
axes, so "vertical" means "along the chunk's up", which on a planet is the local radial.

**The 5-byte record is a WAL *value* element, not a whole key.** The WAL is keyed per chunk in redb.
~~`chunk_key: u64` = face 3 | cx 12 | cz 12 | cy 8 = **35 bits** at the locked planet radius, leaving 29
bits for a realm discriminator.~~ ~~And its first replacement — sector 3 | a 14 | b 14 | c 14 |
`detail_tier` 3 at bits 18..16 | 16 reserved.~~ **Both are superseded. The canonical word is §3.3.6's
`ChunkKey`, and the tier field is FIVE bits** (register row 1 / one-way door 14):

```
crates/core/src/grid/key.rs — the ONE addressing word. PERSISTED. ONE-WAY DOOR.

pub struct ChunkKey(u64);
  bits 63..61  sector    (3)   cube face 0..=5 for a shell; 0 for an identity grid
  bits 60..56  tier      (5)   0..=31 representable; the legal ceiling is the body's `tier_depth`
  bits 55..36  a        (20)   first tangential chunk index AT THIS TIER   (m <= 1_048_575)
  bits 35..16  b        (20)   second tangential chunk index AT THIS TIER
  bits 15.. 6  c        (10)   radial / third chunk index AT THIS TIER     (V <= 1_024)
  bits  5.. 0  reserved  (6)   MUST be zero; decode REJECTS non-zero
  58 bits used, 6 spare. Ordering is sector -> tier -> a -> b -> c, so one whole rung is one
  contiguous range and one chunk column within a rung is one contiguous range.
```

- **Addendum 1 §C.2** made the radius per-body data on a 39.47 m ladder, so the tangential indices must
  hold Earth scale (161,408 chunks per face edge) — 36–37 significant bits at the committed radius, 39
  at Earth scale, which is why this section's own 14-bit tangential fields were never sufficient and why
  §3's 20-bit fields replace them. The realm discriminator moves out of the key into the table
  namespace, which the sealed-shard rule (HR1) implies anyway: a realm's tables are a realm's tables.
- **Addendum 2** makes the tier field live, and it is **five bits, not three**. Three bits give rungs
  0–7, which reaches 100 km at two pixels per cell but cannot express the ladder's real top rung — the
  data-derived rung at which one chunk covers a whole cube face, which is 12 for the 162 km starter body
  (`tier_depth` 13), 18 for an Earth-sized one and 20 for the largest addressable body. Four bits cannot
  express Earth. Five give 0..=31 with eleven values to spare, and the key still ends at 58 of 64 bits
  with six spare. The bits are free today because they are already asserted zero on decode; afterwards
  it is a key-format migration over every saved world.

The field widths are **fixed at every tier** — at tier *L* the top *L* bits of each index are simply zero
— because varying the layout per tier would make a tier a code path in the store, which HR3 forbids and
Addendum 2 §C.1 rules out by construction. Values are runs of 5-byte records, sorted on drain, and **the
WAL's key always has `tier = 0`**: the write invariant of §2.4.3, expressed in the key.

"One spare bit" is a verdict, not a shrug: everything else goes in **side tables keyed by
`(chunk_key, local_index)`**, each with its own record width and its own redb table.

| Table | Record | Why it is not in `block_wal` |
|---|---|---|
| `block_wal` | 5 B | the hot dedup-to-final placement log; fixed width is what makes sorted-on-drain determinism cheap |
| `block_state` | `(u32 local, u16 damage_dp, u16 function_dp, u16 state_bits, u8 growth)` = 11 B | changes orders of magnitude more often than placements |
| `block_thermal` | `(u32 local, u16 temp_dk)` = 6 B | the sparse thermal active set (2-B) |
| `block_fluid` | `(u32 local, u8 fluid)` = 5 B | the fluid CA's persisted cells |
| `block_config` | `(u32 local, u32 config_ref)` = 8 B → TLV blob | P9's per-instance config |
| `block_cover` | `(u32 local, u8 face, u32 cover_ref)` | the user's "HUD on any block" (§8) |
| `chunk_meta` | `(u64 chunk_key, u64 last_ticked_universe_tick, u32 registry_len, …)` | every catch-up integrator needs it |
| `column_sky` | `[u16; 62²]` = 7.5 KiB per chunk column | sky exposure is not chunk-local |
| **`chunk_pyramid`** | **one `PyramidEntry` = one `u64` = 8 B (`cell 18 \| substance 16 \| occ_mask 8 \| fill_256 8 \| reserved 14`), stored per (tier, chunk) as that chunk's sparse entry list, keyed by `ChunkKey` with `tier = L`** | **§2.4.3. It is the *derived* render truth for the coarse rungs: never written at tier 0, never read by the simulation, and the only structure in this section that is reconstructible from the data beside it. ~~`block_pyramid`, `(u32 packed, i32 solid_delta, u16 dominant)` = 10 B, one row per coarse cell~~ is struck** |

**The relief envelope is *not* a side table here, and this section reserves nothing for it.**
~~`column_relief` — `(u32 local_column, u16 min_solid, u16 max_solid)` = 8 B, sparse, edited columns
only; "§2.7 owns the name and the shape so nobody invents a second one".~~ **Struck.** The envelope has
exactly one home, §3.5.2's per-(tier, chunk column) min/max structure, and it is **derived and never
persisted** — a pure function of the seed and the edit pyramid, recomputable at any time and therefore
outside the format-freeze problem entirely. Naming §3.5.2 as the single owner discharges this section's
actual concern — that two sections would independently invent the envelope — more cheaply than a
reservation does, and it removes a second permanent format: min/max solid height is a per-**column**
quantity while a pyramid entry is a per-**cell** record, so persisting it either in its own table or
inside the entry replicates it up to 62× per column. That is also why §8 decision 37(a)'s option to put
the min/max pair inside the pyramid entry is rejected. With this row gone, §2.0's and §2.11's claim that
the ladder costs this section **exactly one** new persisted structure is accurate rather than
approximate.

#### 2.7.2 The full reservation list

| Reserve | Where | Free now / expensive later |
|---|---|---|
| `block_type: u16` at full width | the 5-byte record, wire + WAL | P4 ships < 64 types; widening later re-writes every persisted chunk |
| `orientation: u5` at full width | same | every value is 0 until §6's first slope |
| The `placed` bit | same | without it there is nowhere to put "natural vs built", and structural support has no safe rule |
| The 18\|16\|5\|1 layout, frozen and documented as FULL | same | the "no spare bits" verdict is what forces state into side tables before someone steals two for a damage stage |
| `ShapeDef.mirror_shape` + catalogue closure under mirroring | `crates/core/src/block/shape.rs` | if the catalogue is not closed, symmetry mode punches silent holes in builds |
| `MaterialId`/`ShapeId`/`FunctionId`/`BlockTypeId` numbering: **dense, append-only, never renumbered, never reused** | `crates/core/src/block/` + `block_types.manifest` | the manifest is checked in and the build FAILS if an allocated row's triple changes |
| `Retired` rows with `replaced_by: Option<BlockTypeId>` | the tables | removing a row must never free its slot |
| `(registry_len: u32, identity_prefix_digest: [u8;32])` | handshake + store header (§2.8) | the compatibility contract; retrofitting means re-stamping every store |
| `pcu: u16` per def + **`realm_pcu: u64` persisted in the realm metadata row** | `MaterialDef`, `FunctionDef`, realm store | the demand scheduler wants a realm's cost *before* spin-up; without a durable sum, every re-home and spin-up rescans the world |
| `state_bits: u16` + `PERSIST_MASK`, `function_dp: u16` | `block_state` | §2.6's five spare bits and §2.3.4's EMP outcome |
| `temp_dk: u16`, `fluid: u8` table names | `block_thermal`, `block_fluid` | a spun-down realm loses the state analytic fire/fluid catch-up needs |
| `last_ticked_universe_tick`, `column_sky` | `chunk_meta`, `column_sky` | every catch-up integrator; sky exposure spans 323 chunks vertically |
| All 8 gate + scale columns, `shatter_frac_q12`, `shatter_drop_q12`, `spall_q12` | `MaterialDef` | static-table fields; widening is a patch — but shipping 4 channels and adding 4 later means re-deriving and re-balancing every row |
| `config_schema: SchemaId` + `max_config_bytes` | `FunctionDef` | P9's TLV blob and its anti-grief cap; the envelope already exists (`core/src/tlv.rs`) |
| `gravity: Option<GravityKind>` | `crates/sim/src/capability.rs` | §2.5.3's HR4 split; a validated-lattice field, free today |
| The arm names `BlockEdit` (P6) and `Signal` (P9) | `crates/wire/src/intershard.rs` | already reserved in the closed 27-arm taxonomy; **no new arm from this section** |

**And the detail ladder's own reservations — every one of them permanent data or an API shape:**

Folding it in is free before the hash is pinned. ~~`NO_OVERRIDE = 0xFFFF` in the `BlockTypeId` space~~ is struck with the delta record: an empty coarse cell carries the realm's declared EMPTY substance id, so there is no sentinel to carve out |

A flag bit in an existing `u16` is free; adding the concept after content is authored means re-auditing every block type. The transient state-light lane it gates is §7's, not this section's |

### 2.8 Registry identity, compatibility, and the decode rule

#### 2.8.1 Identity is not compatibility

A whole-table hash in a durable header would make **every content addition a world-wide migration**:
append one material row, and every persisted planet, station and ship refuses to open. That
contradicts the append-only evolution story the tables exist to provide. Identity and compatibility
are separated:

- **`identity_prefix_digest(n)`** = SHA-256 over the **identity-bearing columns only** —
  `BlockTypeDef.{material, shape, function}` for rows `0..n`, plus each referenced `ShapeDef`'s
  geometry-defining fields (`volume_micro_m3`, the three face masks, `collider`, `mirror_shape`) —
  in fixed-width little-endian tag order, the same canonicalisation `tlv.rs` uses. SHA-256 via the
  already-present `sha2` workspace dependency, **not** BLAKE3, which is not a dependency and would be
  a new-library decision for no benefit at 23 KiB.
- Because the numbering is append-only, a prefix digest is **stable under appends**. A store records
  `(registry_len, identity_prefix_digest(registry_len))`. Opening succeeds iff this binary's
  `registry_len ≥` the stored one **and** its own prefix digest at the stored length matches.
- **What passes:** appending rows; retuning any `GameScale` constant; retuning any resistance,
  thermal or PCU column; adding a 9th damage channel. None of those changes what a persisted id *is*,
  and no channel data is ever persisted per block — so §2.3's claim that widening the channel set is
  "never a world migration" is now *true* rather than contradicted.
- **What fails, loudly:** changing an allocated row's triple, renumbering, reusing a retired slot, or
  changing a shape's geometry. Those genuinely reinterpret a player's wall, and the only safe
  response is a refusal plus an explicit, tested remap pass at an epoch bump.
- The `chunk_meta` row carries `registry_len` per chunk so the check is also available per chunk
  during recovery.

#### 2.8.2 Three placements, three fail-safe behaviours

| Site | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Handshake | full-table digest mismatch → **refuse the connection** with a typed error naming both digests and lengths |
| Store header | prefix-digest mismatch → **refuse to open the store**, exactly as an epoch mismatch already does |
| Epoch record | discard/abort per the existing fail-safe rule |

The handshake rule's **cost, and the alternative.** Cost: a content patch that changes the table is a
fleet-wide reconnect, and every client must patch before it can play — which brushes the seamless
law. The alternative is shipping the table at connect time; it loses, because the client also needs
the *meshes and textures* for any new shape, and it must run the byte-identical terrain generator, so
a data-only handshake removes neither the patch dependency nor the divergence risk while adding a
per-connect payload. The mitigation is operational, not architectural: batch content into release
trains, and version the digest so the error message says "client out of date" rather than a hash pair.
A **client with a shorter but prefix-matching registry is still refused**, deliberately: it would mesh
and collide correctly for old ids but could not generate terrain containing new ones.

The client's *render* registry (§5: textures, warp amplitude, anti-tiling) has its **own, separate,
advisory** digest. A render mismatch changes appearance but never authority — collision comes from
the shape table, which the fatal digest covers — so it is logged and surfaced in client diagnostics.

#### 2.8.3 The decode rule

Unknown ids are an error, never a Default. (This is the `CLAUDE.md` persistence convention —
"decode-to-Default is BANNED for Durable kinds" — **not** HR2, which is generic transfer.)

- **Wire.** An unknown `BlockTypeId` in a delta is a protocol violation and tears the connection. The
  digest makes this unreachable in practice; this arm is the belt to its braces.
- **Persistence.** A WAL entry with an unknown `BlockTypeId` makes the store **refuse to open**. It
  does *not* skip the entry: a silently dropped edit is a lost player build, and P6's DoD requires
  edits to survive `kill -9` and a re-shard.
- **Generation.** Structurally impossible — the generator can only emit ids from its own table.
- **Migration.** A retired id keeps its slot with a `replaced_by` pointer; migration is an explicit,
  tested remap pass at an epoch bump.
- **A break is an edit to `BlockTypeId 0` (`Air` × `FullCube`).** Air is a real allocated row. The
  analytic terrain base returns air without storing anything, and a chunk whose palette is `{Air}` is
  a single-value chunk at **zero index bytes** — which is the concrete answer to "air blocks fill the
  planet's sphere of influence": conceptually yes, at no storage cost.

Note the deliberate contrast with `entity_kind.rs`'s `continuity_of`/`durability_of`, which resolve an
unknown tag to a *conservative* default because they run on a possibly-corrupt `EntityId` in a hot
path where a panic would be worse. There is no conservative default for a block type: "some block" is
not a thing that can be meshed, collided or valued.

### 2.9 Hard-rule conformance, fixtures, and gates

**HR1.** No field mechanic crosses a realm boundary; `flood_terminates_at_realm_boundary` is a
harness assertion. Forwarded edits ride the already-reserved `BlockEdit` arm as
`SideEffecting { FencedKey }` / `ProducerLessReliable`; damage and state deltas never cross a shard.
The edit pyramid is derived realm-private state served on the client lane, so it adds no arm either.
**Zero new `InterShardFlow` arms.**

**HR3.** Nothing here matches on a shard kind. Mechanics are gated by `ShardProfile` capability
values — the existing `voxel`, `block_edit`, `functional_blocks`, `surfaces`, `seats`, plus the new
`gravity` — and `satisfies()` stays branchless bitwise. **A tier is likewise a number, not a kind:** the
palette container, the mesher, the material tables and the shape catalogue take the same code path at
every rung. `tier_is_not_a_code_path` asserts it as a self-similarity property — meshing a synthetic
field at tier *L* through the single `mesh_chunk` call site produces the tier-0 result scaled by 2^L —
so a future `match tier` shows up as a failing test rather than as an architecture review.

**HR4.** Two G-IDENTICAL fixtures, enumerated in §2.5.3: the gravity-free subset on Spherical + a
Cartesian ship, and the gravity subset on a Spherical planet + a Cartesian spin station. The
cube-face-seam question belongs to `GridMapping`, which gets exhaustive table-driven tests (12 edge
pairings × 2 directions × 62 positions), not to the block model.

**HR5.** `def()` is the proven generated `match`. `apply_hit` is a fixed-length branchless const loop
in `i64`. The flood kernel is monomorphic. Registry coverage is the `taxonomy.rs` pattern: an
`ALL` loop plus a full `0..=u16` tag sweep per registry. Tests use `assert_eq!`/`expect_err`
equality, never `assert!(matches!(…))`. The `MATERIAL_OVERRIDES` table is non-empty so its branch is
covered (§2.2.1). The ladder's new Tier-A surface is small and all of it is monomorphic: `coarsen`,
`recompute_pyramid` and `representative` take no type parameter; `COARSE_SHAPE` is a dense
`[[u16; 9]; 256]` table swept exhaustively over both indices, and the bucket function is swept over the
whole `fill_256` range; and `ChunkKey::as_tier0()`'s `None` arm is exercised at every tier 1..=31, so
the write invariant costs one covered branch rather than an uncoverable region.

**The three ladder invariants that are assertions, not tests.**

- **`collision_is_tier_zero_only`** — the collider builder's argument type is `Tier0Key`, so handing
  physics a coarse chunk does not compile. The negative case is `ChunkKey::as_tier0()` returning `None`
  for every tier 1..=31 — a real, covered branch under HR5 — plus the rejected example documented in the
  doc comment. It is deliberately **not** a `trybuild` case: `trybuild` is not a workspace dependency,
  adding one to prove a type signature would be a new-library decision that the standing "never adopt a
  library unilaterally" rule reserves to the owner, and a compile-fail fixture is invisible to the
  coverage gate where the `None` arm is not. This ruling stands over §5.10.3's L5 row, which asked for
  the `trybuild` mechanism.
- **`writes_are_tier_zero_only`** — same mechanism, same negative test, on `BlockStore::write`.
- **`a_chunk_is_shaded_by_its_own_tier`** — a chunk's shadow-caster geometry is the same mesh object as
  its visual geometry. This is stated now, before someone optimises the shadow pass by selecting a
  coarser rung for it, which is the classic way a ladder starts casting a shadow that does not match
  the thing casting it.

The drift tripwire, mirroring `taxonomy.rs`'s shape, with six parts:

```rust
#[test]
fn material_registry_cannot_drift() {
    // 1 — a new variant breaks THIS exhaustive match at compile time.
    for m in MaterialId::ALL { match m { MaterialId::Air | MaterialId::PackedSoil | /* … */ => {} } }
    // 2 — dense, index-aligned, table-aligned.
    assert_eq!(MATERIAL_DEFS.len(), MaterialId::ALL.len());
    for (i, m) in MaterialId::ALL.into_iter().enumerate() {
        assert_eq!(m as usize, i);
        assert_eq!(m.def().tag, m as u16);
        assert_eq!(MaterialId::from_tag(m as u16), Ok(m));
    }
    // 3 — sweep the FULL tag space: exactly ALL is accepted, in both directions.
    let mut accepted = 0usize;
    for tag in 0..=u16::MAX { if let Ok(m) = MaterialId::from_tag(tag) { accepted += 1;
        assert_eq!(m as u16, tag); } }
    assert_eq!(accepted, MaterialId::ALL.len());
    assert_eq!(MaterialId::from_tag(60_000).expect_err("unknown").to_string(),
               "unknown block-registry tag material:60000");
    // 4 — every row coherent (density > 0, integrity > 0, scale <= 4096, mirror closure, …).
    let bad: Vec<MaterialId> = MaterialId::ALL.into_iter()
        .filter(|m| !m.def().is_coherent()).collect();
    assert_eq!(bad, Vec::<MaterialId>::new());
    // 5 — THE ONE THAT MAKES "no magic numbers" MECHANICAL: every row round-trips
    //     through the derivation. A HAND-EDITED ROW FAILS THE BUILD.
    for m in MaterialId::ALL {
        assert_eq!(derive_material_row(facts_for(m), &GameScale::CANONICAL), *m.def());
    }
    // 6 — the identity digest is pinned.
    assert_eq!(identity_prefix_digest(BLOCK_TYPE_DEFS.len()), BLOCK_IDENTITY_DIGEST_PIN);
}
```

The same tripwire exists for `ShapeId`, `FunctionId` and `BlockTypeId`, and for
`derive_tool_row`/`derive_shape_row`.

**Load and performance gates — landing with the subsystem, not deferred.** Five benchmarks with
ratcheted floors, plus their load fixtures:

| Artefact | Benchmark | Load fixture |
|---|---|---|
| `apply_hit` / `resolve` | ns per hit; asserts branchlessness via a constant-time spread | 10⁶ hits/s sustained |
| `FloodField` | cells/ms per field row; asserts the r=15/24/32 ball sizes | 64 concurrent floods against `budget_cells_per_tick` |
| Sparse side table | insert/lookup/drain ns; the measured 33.3 %/20.0 % promotion crossover | a chunk driven from 0 → 100 % occupancy |
| Damage replication | msgs/tick and bytes/tick at 128 sessions | the D-9 density fixture with a firefight |
| PCU accumulator | ns per edit; asserts O(1) | 50,000-block ship fully rebuilt |
| **Pyramid walk-up cost** | **≤ 1 entry write and ≤ 1 pyramid storage-block read per rung per touched coarse cell (a rung-*L* parent's eight children always lie in ONE rung-(L−1) storage block because `CHUNK_EDGE` = 62 is even); ZERO reads of `block_wal` and zero reads of any tier-0 delta — a miss resolves through the GENERATOR, not through disk; all writes ride the WAL's own redb write transaction. p99 ≤ `(tier_depth − 1) × 8 × 5 × 12.19 ns` (5.85 µs at `tier_depth` = 13, 9.75 µs at 21) and ≤ 1 % of the click-to-pixels budget; the early-exit depth distribution is reported. Independent of world size, realm size and edit history** | **10⁶ edits streamed into one realm** |
| **Pyramid fidelity** | **`recompute_pyramid` equals the live table for every touched coarse cell, and `vdctl world verify-pyramid` passes after every edit scenario** | **the same 10⁶-edit fixture, plus a dig-and-refill fixture asserting the pruned table is empty** |
| **Coarse generation is cheaper** | **a tier-*L* chunk costs strictly less than a tier-0 chunk, monotone in *L*** | **against the pinned 0.885 ms per 62³ surface chunk (Appendix A) — this is what proves octave-dropping is real rather than decorative** |

**HR6 visual scenarios (paired `vdctl` runs, with readback screenshots and run manifests):**
`crack_stages_advance_and_heal` (a block is damaged through all 8 stages and heals back — extended to
assert that the overlay *leaves* at the tier-0 boundary with no discontinuity),
`decoration_reacts_to_edit` (place a soil block → grass appears; place several → a meadow), and the
ladder's own acceptance run **`edits_survive_the_ladder`**: dig a 500 m tunnel and build a 40 m tower,
fly to 100 km, assert both are present in the readback at **every** tier boundary crossed, fly back, and
assert zero disappearance and zero pop — at walking speed and at flight speed, since a short fade ramp
pops for a walker even when it looks clean from a ship. Each asserts pixel deltas at named tick
boundaries.

### 2.10 Decisions the user must take

> **[USER DECISION 2-A] — coloured block light, single-channel, or none (server side).**
> **Options.** (i) No server light field — "can this plant grow", "is this dark", "does this solar
> panel see the star" have no answer; (ii) **single-channel** u4 light + u4 sky exposure as flood
> rows, server-side only, never shipped; (iii) three independent RGB channels.
> **Cost.** (iii) triples memory and flood cost; at 62³ a nibble plane is 116.4 KiB/chunk, so RGB is
> 349 KiB/chunk of *server* state before anything reaches a wire.
> **Recommendation: (ii).** ~~The binary render rule already caps the meshed volume~~ — the binary
> render rule is retracted (§2.0), and the reasoning must be restated rather than dropped, because the
> recommendation survives on a different footing. **The cap is now the tier-0 radius — 786 m at the
> default two-pixels-per-cell target, ≈ 505 chunk columns — which is where renderer lights are placed
> and where a voxel light grid would have to live.** Beyond it a coarse cell carries its dominant
> material's `emit_level`/`emit_rgb` (§2.5.5), so distant emission is derived from the same table
> rather than from a shipped grid. A handful of real renderer lights still beats a voxel light grid on
> quality *and* cost inside that radius, and the ladder does not enlarge the radius.
> **One-way door: yes for (iii)** — retrofitting coloured light after the mesher and the state table
> are frozen is a rewrite.

> **[USER DECISION 2-B] — is there a per-block temperature field at all?**
> **Options.** (i) Thermal is purely event-driven (fire is probabilistic, needs a synchronised RNG
> stream); (ii) a **sparse active-set** field (`temp_dk: u16` absolute, entries only for blocks off
> ambient, evicted on relaxation) — deterministic fire, no RNG; (iii) a dense field.
> **Cost.** (iii) is O(all blocks) per tick and categorically cannot work at planet scale. (ii) costs
> one sparse table, one flood row, and a persisted field in the reservation list.
> **Recommendation: (ii).** It removes an RNG stream that would otherwise be synchronised across
> shards, and it is what makes the §2.3 Thermal *gate* (a temperature comparison) legible to players.
> **One-way door: yes** — discovering this after fire and melting are built forces a rewrite of both.

> **[USER DECISION 2-C] — how far does chemistry go?**
> **Options.** (i) Oxidation (`oxidises_to` + rate) plus the Corrosive channel — what this section
> specifies; (ii) a full `reacts_with` web (Dwarf Fortress / Oxygen Not Included).
> **Cost.** (ii) multiplies the content-balance and test surface as n² pairings for the least
> mechanical payoff in an MMO.
> **Recommendation: (i). One-way door: no** — `reacts_with` is an additive table.

> **[USER DECISION 2-D] — do fire, growth and flooding continue in a realm with no players?**
> **Options.** (i) mechanics pause when a realm is dormant; (ii) mechanics continue via §2.5.2's
> three catch-up classes.
> **Cost.** (ii) makes catch-up a first-class property of every mechanic from day one, and forces
> `temp_dk`, `fluid`, `last_ticked_universe_tick` and `column_sky` to be **persisted** — all of which
> are in §2.7's reservation list precisely because of this decision.
> **Recommendation: (ii).** The dormant-world pillar strongly implies it and the cost is bounded.
> **One-way door: yes** — a structural requirement on every mechanic, not a toggle.
>
> **Amended by the detail ladder.** The question now has a second half: *does a distant observer change
> the answer?* **No, and it must not** — that is §2.5.5's rule, because a per-observer quantity gating a
> realm-wide computation is how two players end up in different worlds. What the ladder does add to
> option (ii) is one obligation: **the onset of coarse observation triggers a single catch-up-to-now
> pass**, after which the realm returns to dormant if nobody is inside. Without it a player flying
> toward a sleeping realm watches its terrain jump the moment it wakes. **Cost:** one
> `dormant_catchup_sample_budget` pass per observation onset, damped by the demand scheduler's existing
> hysteresis. It does not change the recommendation; it makes it honest under a 100 km view.

> **[USER DECISION 2-E] — does block damage heal?**
> **Options.** (i) nothing heals; (ii) **natural terrain heals on the random tick, constructed
> materials do not** — what this section specifies; (iii) everything heals.
> **Cost.** With (ii) the measured drain is τ_eff = 546 s and the dense-promotion trip point is a
> sustained 146 damaged blocks/s in one chunk (§2.3.8). (i) makes the table monotonic everywhere;
> (iii) makes sieges pointless. Note that under (ii) constructed materials are still monotonic, which
> is why the lossless dense-promotion bound plus a per-realm cap exists regardless.
> **Recommendation: (ii). One-way door: no** — one derived field and a random-tick row.

> **[USER DECISION 2-F] — where does world simulation go in the roadmap?**
> Fire, fluids, growth, weathering, freezing, falling blocks and structural collapse have **no
> committed phase**. `roadmap.json` P7 is "Player checkpoints + full identity/persistence durability
> (MMO-grade)", and dropping a phase of world simulation onto it would put an unbounded new subsystem
> on top of the crash-durability phase.
> **Options.** (i) a new phase **P6b — World simulation** between P6 and P7; (ii) fold it into P11
> (combat + scale-hardening); (iii) split — support/collapse at P6b, the rest at P11.
> **Cost.** (ii) delays the dormant-world pillar and §7's decoration reactivity by five phases, and
> P7 would have to checkpoint per-block state whose shape is not yet decided. (i) inserts a phase
> into a committed roadmap.
> **Recommendation: (i) P6b.** The flood kernel and the random-tick scheduler are prerequisites of
> both the dormant-world pillar and §7, and P7 must know what per-block state exists before it can
> checkpoint it. **One-way door: no**, but the ordering constraint (P6b before P7) is real.

> **[USER DECISION 2-G] — adopt parry's sparse `Voxels` collider?**
> Rapier itself is **already a committed roadmap deliverable** ("P5 — Physics: Rapier3d per shard"),
> so this is not a rapier adoption question. The question is narrower: whether `ShapeDef.collider`
> resolves to parry's `Voxels` shape for the full-cube lane.
> **Options.** (i) project-owned composite colliders only; (ii) parry `Voxels` for full cubes plus a
> project composite for non-cubes.
> **Cost.** (ii) is ~1 byte per voxel with 8³ chunks, a BVH, and structural elimination of ghost
> collisions on voxel edges — against ~120 B per sub-shape for a `Compound`. But `Voxels` entered as
> experimental in 2025 and correctness fixes were still landing through parry 0.28 ("`Voxels::scaled`
> not scaling the internal chunk BVH, causing queries to miss geometry"), and it would sit on the
> physics-authority path where the Category-C rule constrains what may be trusted. There is also an
> unverified interaction: a cube adjacent to a slope is not marked interior by the `Voxels` shape
> unless a phantom voxel is inserted, which then over-collides.
> **Recommendation: (ii), gated on a spike** that reproduces the cube-adjacent-to-slope case and the
> `combine_voxel_states` chunk-seam case against the pinned version. `ColliderShapeId` keeps the
> decision reversible either way — that indirection is the reason it exists.
> **One-way door: no**, because the id is opaque; but the spike must land before P5 freezes the
> collider architecture.

> **~~[USER DECISION 2-H]~~ — what a coarse cell remembers: the edit-pyramid record. COLLAPSED.**
> This question, §3.9.8's 3-J, §4.3.2's 4-E and this section's 2-I were four separate markers on one
> permanent artefact. They are now **register row 37 / [USER DECISION 8-A]** — the edit-pyramid entry,
> with five sub-questions: (a) contents, (b) how the fill is spent on a shape, (c) storage granularity,
> (d) the write invariant, (e) the divergence policy. Take it in the same session as row 2 (the saved
> block record) and row 1 / door 14 (the chunk-key layout), because all three are written into the
> first world that is ever saved. The adjudicated shape this section now carries is in §2.4.3.

> **~~[USER DECISION 2-I]~~ — what happens when derived data disagrees with its source. COLLAPSED**
> into **register row 37 / [USER DECISION 8-A]**, sub-question (e). This section's position is unchanged
> and is stated in §2.4.3: recompute the entry and increment `pyramid_divergence_total`, which the
> harness asserts is zero — a failing build in development and an invisible self-heal in production —
> rather than refusing to open the store, because the identity digest guards data that *reinterprets a
> player's wall* while the pyramid only summarises data the store still holds.

> **[USER DECISION 2-J] — do cosmetic per-block state and player-placed fluid get a coarse rung?**
> Under §2.5.5 and §2.6 they do not: a shovelled path in snow, a cultivated strip of grass and a
> canal a player dug and flooded are invisible beyond tier 0.
> **Options.** (i) **tier-0 only** — zero bytes, what this section specifies; (ii) a fluid rung in the
> pyramid, spending some of the canonical record's **14 reserved bits** so player-made water bodies
> coarsen — costs one entry set per flooded coarse cell, same **8 B** record; (iii) additionally a
> per-coarse-cell state summary (snow/grass) at **+2 B per entry, a 25 % record** — which is a *width*
> change on permanent data, not a use of reserved bits.
> **Cost.** (ii) is bounded by how much water players move, which is small and clustered — the compact
> 0.143 n regime. (iii) is paid on **every** entry, including the vast majority that have no interesting
> surface state, and it reopens the one-way door row 37 closes.
> **Recommendation: (i) now, with (ii) left to the reserved bits and unimplemented.** A flooded valley
> is a real, legible landmark and worth a rung eventually; a 1 m snow track under a 2 m cell is below
> the representation and is correctly filtered, not lost.
> **One-way door: the reserved bits are not, the width is.** ~~The named `lane` field at bits 18..20~~
> is struck with the delta record; the canonical entry instead carries 14 bits that decode **rejects**
> as non-zero, which is what keeps (ii) an epoch-gated addition rather than a migration. Decide (ii) at
> the world-simulation phase.

### 2.11 What this section commits to, in one paragraph

A block is a triple: **substance**, **form**, and optionally **function**. Three small static tables —
64 materials, 64 shapes, later 64 functions, about 13 KiB at P6 and 23 KiB all-in — generate a
`BlockTypeId` that is a u16 index into an explicitly allocated manifest, and every per-block number is
a lookup. Mass, integrity, structural support, harvest tier, the shatter threshold, the whole
eight-channel gate-and-scale matrix and the simulation-cost weight are **derived** at content-build
time from citable physical facts by a tested pure function against fourteen named constants, so a
hand-edited row fails the build and a half-slab automatically has half of everything. Integrity comes
from work of fracture, not strength, because a 1 m block fragments rather than crushes. Damage is one
branchless integer loop in which a per-channel *intensity gate* decides whether a source couples at
all and a per-channel *scale* decides how much of its delivered energy becomes damage — so a rifle
round shatters a window, needs forty hits for a granite block and five thousand for a titanium hull,
and fire never damages stone because 1,100 K is below 1,500 K. Tools are derived the same way from
power, form and head hardness, so the hand ladder is access and durability while the speed ladder is
watts. What changes lives in per-chunk sparse side tables; the block field itself is a per-chunk
palette with a 4-bit floor and a zero-cost single-value fast path, and orientation lives *inside* the
palette entry so it is free on terrain and paid for only on ships. Twelve mechanics fall out of that
data, six sharing one monomorphic flood kernel; four need gravity and therefore get their own
two-profile HR4 fixture rather than a false claim of geometry-independence. The persisted record is
exactly five bytes — 18 bits of local index, 16 of block type, 5 of orientation and 1 marking a block
as generator-authored, the bit that keeps structural support from collapsing every natural cave roof.
And the tables are digested into the handshake and the store header as a *prefix* over
identity-bearing columns only, so appending content and retuning balance are free while
reinterpreting a player's wall is impossible. All of that is **identical at every rung of the detail
ladder** — the ladder costs this section exactly one new persisted structure, the **eight-byte** sparse
edit pyramid, which remembers per coarse cell **which of its eight octants are occupied, how full it is
on average, and which substance dominates it**, is updated by one exact recompute per rung inside the
WAL's own write transaction with an early exit the moment a summary stops changing, is pruned back to
nothing when a player refills what he dug, and is fully recomputable from the seed and the deltas so a
divergence is a failing assertion rather than a tunnel that is the wrong shape from a hilltop. Only
tier 0 is writable and the type system says so; collision, functional behaviour and every gameplay fact stay at tier 0 always; a
coarse tier changes what the owner *publishes* and never what it *computes*; and dormancy stays a
property of the realm while tier stays a property of an observer, so two players at different distances
see different terrain detail and never a different world.

---

### Adjudicated objections

Where the adversary was right, the design above changed. These four are the ones where it was wrong or
only half right, resolved in one line each — plus one where the *project* was wrong and the owner
overruled it.

- **On the "no level-of-detail" rule (Addendum 2): the section was written under a ban the owner has
  retracted, and it survived almost intact** — which is the interesting part. Two statements leaned on
  the ban and are struck with replacements in place: §2.3.8's delivery scope ("the set of chunks the
  subscriber has meshed, which the binary render rule defines") is now the subscriber's **tier-0** set,
  and §2.10's 2-A rationale now rests on the **tier-0 radius** rather than on a global draw cap. Both
  land on the same 786 m / ~505-column figure the old rule produced, so neither number moved. What the
  ladder genuinely adds is §2.4.3's edit pyramid, §2.5.5's per-observer/per-realm split, and **six**
  reservations — and it removes Addendum 1 §C.4's "drawn radius is the binding constraint" finding
  entirely. (The count fell from eight because the cross-section adjudication struck two of them: the
  `NO_OVERRIDE` sentinel, which the absolute record does not need, and the `column_relief` table, whose
  envelope is derived and never persisted and belongs to §3.5.2.)

- **On `def()` as an array index (M3): the adversary is right and the draft was wrong** — HR5's
  branchless rule is about generics, the repo's proven idiom is a `match`, and an index inserts an
  uncoverable panic path; §2.1.2 restores the `match`, generated.
- **On the ordering of resistance and time quantisation (H3): the adversary is right that the rule was
  missing but wrong about which rule** — applying resistance to the per-*tick* vector makes a
  rate-threshold gate tick-rate dependent, so §2.3.2 resists the per-*second* vector and integrates
  the surplus with a remainder accumulator.
- **On parry/rapier adoption (H9): half right** — `collider_id` is indeed made an opaque
  project-owned `ColliderShapeId` and the `Voxels` lane is escalated as **[USER DECISION 2-G]**, but
  rapier is not an unadopted library: `roadmap.json` P5 is "Physics: Rapier3d per shard". The
  `physical_facts.toml` half is right and is fixed by making the facts a checked-in Rust `const`
  array, which removes the parser, the dependency question and a pile of uncoverable Tier-A error
  branches at once.
- **On the "195 vs 196" shatter arithmetic (M1): correct but moot** — the `K_Ic² × SHATTER_SCALE`
  formula it audits is gone, replaced in §2.3.3 by a fraction of integrity under a per-family policy,
  because every first-principles brittleness index puts at least one material class in the wrong
  order.

## 3. The world — grid mapping, seed generation, storage, and the delta

A planet, a ship, a station and a room are the same object: a **realm that owns a voxel grid**. The
only thing that differs between them is a single value — how an integer grid index becomes a position
— and that value is carried by the realm, not by the shard, not by a type parameter, and never by a
`match` on a shard kind. Everything else in the block system (the chunk container, the palette, the
bit packing, the mesher, the edit pipeline, the collider derivation, the block registry, the signal
graph, the persistence layer) is written exactly once and cannot observe which kind of world it is
running on. That is HR4 stated as a data structure rather than as an aspiration, and it is the single
structural decision this section exists to fix.

This section fixes: the addressing scheme and its `u64` packing, **including the detail tier**; the
grid family and the warp, with exact coefficients and a fixed-step inverse; the radius **ladder**; the
generation pipeline, **its detail-tier contract** and its determinism contract; what "air everywhere"
honestly means and where the planet's grid stops; what the client holds **at every rung of the
ladder**; and the durable format, **including the edit pyramid that keeps a player's tunnel visible
from a hilltop**. Section 4 owns the contents of a block; section 5 owns turning a chunk into
triangles; this section owns everything from the seed to the disk.

**Two addenda are folded in and are binding.** *Addendum 1* removed the single global radius: a body's
radius is per-body data on a 39.47 m ladder, its gravity is derived from an authored mass, and a world
is seed **plus configuration** with a curated starter planet. Those read as **settled** below, not as
open questions. *Addendum 2* retracted the no-detail-levels ban: **detail levels everywhere, one rung
per power of two, a tier is a number on a chunk address and never a second code path.** Its
consequences run through every subsection here, and the one it changes most is §3.7 — the draw-radius
wall that both the original section and Addendum 1 §C.4 called the binding constraint is **dissolved**.

### 3.0 Decision index

Nine decisions in this section are the user's, and they are ordered by dependency — each later one
is only meaningful once the earlier ones are taken. Two (3-D, 3-E) are **reduced** by Addendum 1 from
one-way doors on the whole game to per-body range questions; one (3-I) is **created** by the detail
ladder; and one that this section also created — ~~3-J~~, the edit-pyramid record — has been
**collapsed into register row 37 / [USER DECISION 8-A]** together with §2's 2-H and 2-I and §4's 4-E,
because four sections were each independently specifying the same permanent record. The record itself
is settled below (§3.9.8) and the remaining sub-questions are the owner's, in row 37.

**One question this section used to answer on its own authority is now the owner's, in one place.**
The chunk key's tier-field width and the top of the ladder are **register row 1 / one-way door 14**,
taken in the same session as rows 2 and 37 because all three are written into the first world that is
ever saved. §3.3.6 and §3.7.5 below carry the settled layout (**five** tier bits at 60..56) and the
settled ceiling (the **face-covering rung**); row 1 is where the owner signs them.

| id | decision | kind | recommendation | must be taken by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **3-A** | the grid family (cube-sphere vs literal cube vs hex vs octree) | one-way door | cube-sphere | before any P4 code |
| **3-B** | what `G-IDENTICAL` means for geometry code, and who owns a cross-realm block contact | rule amendment | split gate (`G-IDENTICAL` above the seam, `G-MAPPING-EXHAUSTIVE` below); planet owns the contact | with the seam slice |

### 3.1 One container, one address, one place where geometry differs

#### 3.1.1 The shape of the seam

```rust
// crates/core/src/grid/mod.rs — Tier-A, pure, no Bevy, no I/O, no float transcendentals.

pub const CHUNK_EDGE: u32   = 62;          // committed: roadmap.json P4 — at EVERY tier
pub const CHUNK_CELLS: u32  = 238_328;     // 62³ — at EVERY tier

/// The ONE addressing type for every voxel world in the game, at every detail tier.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash)]
pub struct ChunkKey(u64);

/// The detail rung. Tier L means cells are 2^L metres and a chunk spans 62·2^L metres.
/// A tier is a NUMBER ON AN ADDRESS, never a code path (HR3): nothing in the container,
/// the palette, the mesher, the shape catalogue or the material tables branches on it.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash)]
pub struct Tier(u8);       // 0..=31 representable; the legal ceiling is per-body (§3.4)

/// A key PROVEN to be at tier 0. The only thing the store will accept a write on (§3.9.8).
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash)]
pub struct Tier0Key(ChunkKey);   // ctor is the single place that checks `tier() == 0`

/// Cell index inside a chunk: (c*62 + b)*62 + a, `a` fastest. 0..238_328. Tier-independent.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
pub struct CellIndex(u32);

/// A tier-0 block address — TIER-0 BY TYPE, everywhere. This is what makes "only tier 0 is
/// writable" a compile error rather than an API convention.
pub struct BlockAddr  { pub chunk: Tier0Key, pub cell: CellIndex }
/// The ONLY address that admits any tier. Every coarse-rung consumer takes this.
pub struct CoarseAddr { pub chunk: ChunkKey,  pub cell: CellIndex }
impl BlockAddr { pub fn ancestor(self, tier: Tier) -> CoarseAddr; }   // and NO reverse conversion,
                                                                     // not even a fallible one

/// The ONE container. Palette-indirected, bit-packed, identical on every realm kind.
/// `filled` counts cells whose material differs from the realm's declared EMPTY material
/// (air on a planet, vacuum in a hull) — a cached query over the palette, not a privileged
/// material. Nothing in the container knows what "air" is.
pub struct Chunk { palette: Vec<BlockState>, bits: u8, words: Vec<u64>, filled: u32 }

/// The ONLY place spherical and flat may differ. A VALUE on the realm.
pub enum GridMapping {
    Identity(IdentityGrid),          // ships, stations, asteroids, rooms
    CubeSphereShell(ShellGrid),      // planets, moons
}
```

`GridMapping` exposes exactly six total operations, and no consumer above it may see the enum:

| operation | signature | who calls it |
|---|---|---|
| `addr_of` | `(&self, local: LatticePos, tier: Tier) -> Option<CoarseAddr>` | block targeting, residency binning, collider region select |
| `cell_center` | `(&self, CoarseAddr) -> LatticePos` | mesher vertex emit, entity snap |
| `cell_corners` | `(&self, CoarseAddr) -> [LatticePos; 8]` | mesher, collider trimesh |
| `neighbor` | `(&self, CoarseAddr, Dir6) -> Neighbor` | mesher apron, flood fill, signal walk, edit validation |
| `up` | `(&self, CoarseAddr) -> DVec3` | `gravity_dir`, block orientation |
| `domain` | `(&self) -> GridDomain` | edit admission, band tests |

**The six operations take `CoarseAddr` because they are tier-general; `BlockAddr` is the narrower
type the *write* path takes.** A caller holding a `CoarseAddr` narrows it in exactly one place —
`ChunkKey::as_tier0()`, which returns `None` for every tier `1..=31` (§3.3.6) — and that single
narrowing point is what the collider derivation, the store's write path and the client's edit message
all sit behind. ~~The earlier text defined `BlockAddr` as tier-carrying (`chunk: ChunkKey`)~~; that is
**struck**, because a tier-carrying `BlockAddr` makes "only tier 0 is writable" a convention again.

**The ladder adds no operation and no arm.** `addr_of` gains a `tier` argument (you must say which
lattice you are addressing); every other signature is unchanged because the tier already rides inside
the `ChunkKey`. `neighbor` is defined **within one tier** and never crosses rungs — cross-tier
adjacency is a rendering seam (§5, skirts), not an addressing relation, which is what keeps the flood
fill, the signal walk and the edit validator ignorant of the ladder's existence. This is the concrete
form of Addendum 2 §C.1: *a tier is a number carried by a chunk address, not a second code path.*

`Neighbor` is `Same(CoarseAddr) | AcrossSeam { addr: CoarseAddr, axis_remap: AxisRemap } | Outside`.
`addr_of` returns `Option<CoarseAddr>` — `None` means "outside this grid's domain"; `neighbor`
returns the `Outside` arm for the same condition. Two spellings of one fact, one per return type;
they are never used interchangeably in prose. `Identity` never returns `AcrossSeam`;
`CubeSphereShell` returns it only at the 12 cube-face edges.

**One name per concept, fixed here and propagated.** Four sections were spelling the same objects
four ways; this roster is the whole set and every other spelling is **struck**.

| concept | canonical name | struck spellings |
|---|---|---|
| the `u64` chunk address | `ChunkKey` | `ChunkAddress`, `ChunkAddr` |
| the detail rung | `Tier(u8)` | `detail_tier` as a type name |
| the tier-0-proven key | `Tier0Key` | `Tier0Addr` |
| a tier-0 block address | `BlockAddr` (`chunk: Tier0Key`) | the tier-carrying `BlockAddr` above |
| a coarse cell address | `CoarseAddr` | — |
| the pyramid table | `chunk_pyramid` | `block_pyramid`, "beside `block_wal`" |
| the persisted 8-byte word | `PyramidEntry` | — |
| its unpacked payload | `CellSummary` | — |
| the per-`(tier, chunk)` storage block holding a chunk's sparse entry list | `PyramidRecord` | — |
| the substance-table row id | `SubstanceId(u16)` | `MaterialId` wherever it means the block-registry row |

The two arms are the only `match` on geometry in the workspace. Everything above the seam takes a
`&GridMapping` and calls methods; the arm dispatch happens once, inside `core::grid`, in six
two-armed matches whose bodies immediately delegate to a monomorphic `identity::*` or `shell::*`
function. This is the HR5 shape the codebase already uses (`core/src/tlv.rs`): branchless shim on
top, all branching in monomorphic helpers. It is also the HR3 shape: `G-NO-SHARD-FORK` forbids
matching on a *shard kind*; matching on a *geometry value carried by the realm* is the sanctioned
alternative that the lint exists to force you into.

#### 3.1.2 Relation to `ShardProfile::voxel()`, to `FrameSpace`, and to containment

`crates/sim/src/capability.rs` already ships `voxel: Option<VoxelGeometry>` with
`VoxelGeometry::{Spherical, Cartesian}` as private state plus an accessor, and `satisfies()`
(`capability.rs:155`) already does an **exact** geometry equality test so a Cartesian realm can never
re-home onto a Spherical shard. That is the *selector*; `GridMapping` is the *value*. The wiring is:

- **`ShardProfile::voxel()` selects the `FrameSpace` implementation at `register()` time** — one
  branch, in `node::build_app`, exactly as `sealed_shards.md:210` sketches. It says which arm of
  `GridMapping` this shard is permitted to host.
- **The realm's `PlanetParams`/`HullParams` supply the mapping's parameters at realm activation** —
  radius, face resolution, band, origin. These are per-realm and seed-derived, never per-shard.

Consequence worth naming now: because `voxel` is a single value on the profile, **one shard may host
many realms only if they share a geometry.** Under node-per-realm (landed) that is vacuous, and when
it stops being vacuous the existing `satisfies()` equality check fails loudly rather than silently
mixing two grids in one physics world. No new gate is needed.

`FrameSpace` (`sealed_shards.md:219-232`, unbuilt) is the *stateful* half: it owns the
`SurfaceAnchor` lifecycle and `AnchorGen` fencing, which exist because Rapier wants `f32` and a
planet is 161 km across. `GridMapping` is the *stateless* half: integer addressing. They are
different concerns and the published trait conflates them.

> **Amendment to binding design (`sealed_shards.md:219-234`), stated plainly rather than implied.**
> `FrameSpace`'s **method set is kept verbatim** — `anchor_generation`, `chunk_addr`,
> `to_local_flat`, `from_local_flat`, `gravity_dir`, `reanchor`, and the `StaleAnchor` fence
> semantics are unchanged. **One return type changes.** The published `ChunkAddress` is specified as
> "flat `IVec3` chunk + intra-chunk `(u8,u8,u8)` in `[0,61]`" — it has **no face/sector field and
> therefore cannot express a cube-sphere address at all.** It is replaced by
> `CoarseAddr { chunk: ChunkKey, cell: CellIndex }`, which is sector-carrying, tier-carrying and
> radius-independent; `chunk_addr` narrows to `BlockAddr` through `as_tier0()` at its one write site.
> `SphericalSpace { radius, anchor }` holds a `ShellGrid`, `CartesianSpace` holds an `IdentityGrid`,
> and `FrameSpace::chunk_addr` is one line delegating to `addr_of`. All the covered arithmetic then
> lives in Tier-A `vd-core` where the terrain determinism gate can reach it, and `vd-sim` keeps only
> the anchor state machine.

**Containment: blocks never define containment — but the rule is scoped, and the draft scope was
wrong.** D-45 ledger item (i) is written for a voxel-built **ship/station** realm, and applying it to
a planet would be a defect: `core/src/geometry.rs:230` documents `Boundary::Shell { r }` as *"the SOI
/ planet-descent boundary"*. A planet's containment region **is its SOI shell**, sized by `GM`
(§3.4), and it is never recomputed from blocks — recomputing an inscribed boundary on edit commit
would shrink a planet's containment region to its tallest building. The rule therefore reads:

- **Identity/Cartesian realms** (ships, stations, constructions): the `Boundary` is an `Aabb`/`Obb`
  that the blocks *inscribe*, recomputed off-tick on edit commit, debounced.
- **Spherical realms** (planets, moons): the `Boundary` is `Shell { r = r_SOI }`, derived from `GM`
  and the parent's mass, and is **never** a function of the block grid.

Either way `region_signed_distance` stays cheap and the per-tick membership fold never touches a
chunk. The runtime `RealmRegions` mutator that D-45 (ii) owes is a prerequisite for player-built
hulls and for the sky-structure answer in §3.6.

Landing order: **`FrameSpace` + `GridMapping` land as their own slice, before any mesher or generator
code**, with D-41 plant-items (4) and (5) folded in — a `FrameSpace` shape that *admits* more than
one anchor (defaulting to one) and the degenerate `RegionId{WHOLE}` on the directory key. D-41 states
in as many words that hardening single-anchor/single-writer/single-cluster at P4/P5/P6 forecloses
hundreds-in-one-location, and its own tripwires cannot be written until these types exist. The seam
and its tripwire are one slice.

#### 3.1.3 `LatticePos` and the block grid — the exactness that holds and the exactness that does not

`crates/core/src/pose.rs` freezes the coordinate base: `FINE_CELL_EDGE_M = 1/1024`, a power of two
chosen precisely so `normalize` is exactly idempotent. D-41 says every production pose today has
`cell == ZERO` and that this is about to stop being true. A grid API taking a bare `DVec3` therefore
silently assumes the pre-activation form and will need rewriting mid-P5. **`addr_of` takes a
`LatticePos`, not a `DVec3`**, from the first line of code. The reconciliation:

- **Identity grids: exact, at every tier.** A tier-L block is exactly **1024·2^L fine cells** per
  axis. Integer addressing all the way down; the f64 `offset` only ever resolves the sub-block
  residual. A ship's block address is an integer division by `1024 << tier` — a shift — with no
  rounding anywhere. *The ladder is a power of two precisely so this stays a shift.*
- **Shell grids, radial axis: exact, at every tier.** Radial cells are exactly `2^L` metres tall at
  every altitude, so the radial index is an integer subtraction and an integer shift. This is the
  property that makes "which layer am I standing on" stable across the f32/f64 boundary
  `SurfaceAnchor` introduces, and it is the strongest single property of the single-shell choice
  (§3.3.5). It survives the ladder untouched, and it is why a coarse rung can never disagree with a
  fine rung about *which* radial layer a surface sits in — only about how high it is inside one.
- **Shell grids, tangential axes: not exact, and cannot be.** Tangential block width varies from
  0.708 m to 1.005 m per metre of nominal cell (§3.3.2 — the spread is a *ratio*, so it is
  tier-invariant: a tier-5 cell spans 22.7–32.2 m). The tangential index is therefore the only place
  in the grid where a float divide and a `floor` decide an integer, and it is the reason `addr_of`
  needs the fixed-step inverse warp at all. At tier L the same inverse runs and the result is shifted
  right by L — **one inverse, all tiers**, never a per-tier variant.

Two consequences the implementer must not discover later. First, the tangential `floor` is a
**physics→control boundary** in the determinism doctrine's sense, so it is quantised once, in
`shell::addr_of`, and every consumer takes the resulting integer — no consumer re-derives a
tangential index from a float. Second, `addr_of` is emphatically **not** on the containment hot path:
containment uses the analytic `Boundary` shells in `core/src/geometry.rs` and never asks which block
anything is in, so the three Newton steps of the inverse warp never run per-entity per-tick even
after cell activation.

#### 3.1.4 What `G-IDENTICAL` can and cannot mean here

HR4 requires every feature to pass `assert_feature_anywhere` with an identical fixture on ≥2 shard
kinds, and `assert_all_equal_control_plane` compares *results*. Applied naively to grid code this is
incoherent: a cube-face-seam neighbour test has no meaning on an `Identity` mapping, and `reanchor`
is defined to be a no-op on `CartesianSpace`. Forcing equal results would either test nothing or test
the wrong thing. This is an amendment to a user-mandated hard rule, so it is escalated, not ruled.

> **[USER DECISION 3-B] — what `G-IDENTICAL` means for geometry-specific code, and who owns a
> cross-realm block contact.** Not a one-way door in code, but a one-way door in *confidence*: an
> unresolved gate quietly stops being a gate, and this one guards the geometry seam every other
> block feature is written on top of.
>
> - **(A) Split the gate — recommended.** Two gates, written into `PLAN.md` beside the existing HR4
>   paragraph.
>   - **`G-IDENTICAL` binds every feature whose code lives *above* `GridMapping`.** Chunk container,
>     palette, bit packing, greedy meshing, edit pipeline, block registry, collider derivation from
>     quads, signal propagation, persistence, WAL, compaction. One fixture on a Spherical planet
>     profile and a Cartesian ship profile, control-plane results **equal**. This is exactly what
>     P4's DoD already demands ("the chunk math is shard-agnostic — same code path a ship-interior
>     realm will use") and it is satisfiable. The reanchor-forcing variant D-38 owes lands here, on
>     the first block-edit feature, as designed.
>   - **`GridMapping` itself is exempt from result-equality and carries a stronger gate instead:
>     `G-MAPPING-EXHAUSTIVE`.** One parameterised test body, run on both mappings, where the
>     *expected values* are declared by the mapping and the *invariants* are equal:
>     (i) `neighbor` is involutive under direction reversal, for every cell on every seam;
>     (ii) a four-step lateral loop returns to its origin at every vertex **except** the 8
>     cube-corner vertices, where it is asserted to close in three steps;
>     (iii) every cell has exactly four lateral neighbours (the corner defect is a property of the
>     *vertex*, not of the cell — §3.3.4);
>     (iv) `addr_of(cell_center(x)) == x` for every cell, and `addr_of` returns `None` for every
>     point outside `domain()`;
>     (v) the apron gather (§3.3.3) is watertight at all 24 face-boundary strips and all 24
>     corner-diagonal slots;
>     (vi) **every clause above holds identically at every legal tier**, and the seam table itself is
>     **byte-identical across tiers** — which is a theorem, not a hope, once decision 3-I fixes the
>     coarse lattice to tile the face exactly (§3.3.3). That is the single largest reason to take
>     3-I(A): the exhaustive proof at `N = 62` proves the ladder as well as the grid.
>     The `Identity` mapping runs the same body with "no seams, no corners" expectations. Same
>     fixture, mapping-declared expectations — HR4 in form, provable in substance.
> - **(B) Hold HR4 literally.** `GridMapping` gets no gate at all, because no fixture can produce
>   equal results on both arms. The seam every other feature stands on becomes the one piece of the
>   block system with no permanent gate.
>
> **Recommendation: (A).** The seam table is **independent of `N`** (§3.3.3), so exhaustive
> enumeration at `N = 62` — one chunk per face edge: 12 edges × 62 positions × 2 directions = 1,488
> cases, plus 24 corner cells and 24 corner-diagonal apron slots — is a *complete* proof of the
> table. The production-`N` test then only has to prove index scaling, a handful of cases. That keeps
> `G-MAPPING-EXHAUSTIVE` inside a unit-test budget at 100 % branch coverage.
>
> **The second half of the same ruling: who owns the contact when a ship rests on terrain?** A ship
> is a Cartesian realm with a private Rapier world; the planet is a Spherical realm with a different
> private Rapier world; HR1 forbids either from seeing the other's. This is the P5×P8 intersection
> and it is the *other* place the two shard kinds cannot be made symmetric. Options: **(i) the planet
> owns the contact** — the hull enters the planet's world as a ghost collider through the existing
> `InterShardFlow::Ghost` machinery, the planet integrates, and the resulting pose is shipped back as
> the ship realm's authored placement; **(ii) the ship owns it** — terrain enters the ship's world as
> a ghost heightfield patch. **Recommendation: (i)**, because it matches the standing frame-authority
> law (the containing realm's shard is physics authority and authors its children's positions), the
> ghost machinery already exists in the direction it needs, and a hull is bounded while terrain is
> not. This is stated here, and owed as a build item at P8; it is not built by this section.

---

### 3.2 The grid family — the decision every other decision presupposes

Everything below assumes a cube-sphere. That assumption is worth one page, because it is the largest
one-way door in the section and because it collides with a verbatim user requirement.

The user said **"blocks are 1 m and square."** On a cube-sphere that is **unachievable by proof, not
by tuning.** Two independent distortions exist and only one of them responds to the warp:

1. **Edge-length anisotropy** (a block is a rectangle). Sweeping the entire two-parameter odd-quintic
   warp family, the minimum achievable ratio between the largest and smallest tangential cell edge
   anywhere on a face is **1.4110 ≈ √2**. No coefficients beat it. Every warp is a *redistribution*
   of a fixed √2 between "block size varies" and "block shape varies".
2. **Shear** (a block is a rhombus, not a rectangle). The angle between the two grid directions runs
   from exactly **90° at the six face centres to exactly 120° at the eight cube corners**, and this
   is **warp-invariant** — it is the cube net's 90° angle defect (Gauss–Bonnet: 720° total, however
   you distribute it). Measured: the singular-value ratio of the grid Jacobian is **√3 = 1.732** at
   every cube corner for *every* member of the family, including the so-called shape-optimal one.

Neither the draft this section replaces nor the adversarial review stated (2); both reported only the
edge-length measure, which is why "shape-optimal, square everywhere" looked available. It is not.
**No warp makes blocks square everywhere on a sphere.** The warp decision (3-C) is therefore about
the edge-length half only.

> **[USER DECISION 3-A] — the grid family.** The hardest one-way door in the block system: it decides
> the shape of every planet in the galaxy, every block boundary on it, and whether the ship grid and
> the planet grid are the same grid. Nothing in P4 can start before it.
>
> - **(A) Cube-sphere with a warp — recommended.** Six square faces projected onto a sphere. Planets
>   are round from orbit, gravity points at the centre everywhere, blocks are gravity-aligned
>   everywhere, and the addressing is the same integer machinery as a ship grid (which is what makes
>   HR4's one-container property real). **The price, stated exactly:** tangential blocks span
>   0.708–1.005 m; up to 1.40:1 rectangles along 12 great-circle bands; 60°/120° rhombi at the 8
>   corners. The user's "1 m and square" is met at the six face centres and approached almost
>   everywhere else (median edge 0.959 m), but is not universal.
> - **(B) Literal cube planet.** Cheaper on every technical axis: zero distortion, zero shear, one
>   grid literally shared with ships, no shells, no warp, no seam table, no grid defect. Blocks are
>   exactly 1.000 m and exactly square everywhere — the user's requirement met literally. **Two costs
>   decide it:** (i) it looks like a cube from orbit, fighting the seamless-warp-arrival aesthetic (a
>   system that "grows from a dot" growing into a cube); (ii) gravity has no good answer. Point it at
>   the centre and "down" is normal to the ground only at the six face centres — near an edge you walk
>   on ground tilted up to 54.7° while your blocks stay axis-aligned, which is worse than any
>   cube-sphere distortion. Blend it per-face and the 12 edges become 90° discontinuities in "down".
>   There is no third option, and that is why technical cheapness is not the whole story.
> - **(C) Goldberg polyhedron / hex grid.** Near-uniform cells, only 12 pentagon defects. **Loses on
>   HR4:** a hex grid cannot also be the ship grid (ships need a rectilinear lattice for hulls,
>   pistons, rails and rectangular prefabs), so the one-container property dies and the block system
>   forks into two — the exact structural failure the greenfield rebuild exists to avoid.
> - **(D) Cartesian octree / SVO with an analytic planet surface.** One flat grid, no faces, no warp.
>   **Loses because blocks stop being gravity-aligned:** a wall built at latitude 40° is a staircase
>   of cubes rather than a wall, and every structure on a planet is visibly axis-aligned to the star
>   system rather than to the ground. It also gives up the "chunk column" locality that the height
>   band, the residency policy and the storage layout all key off.
>
> **Recommendation: (A) cube-sphere.** It is the only family that simultaneously keeps blocks
> gravity-aligned, keeps planets round, and keeps one grid for planets and ships. The user's own
> reference (the Bowerbyte blocky-planet article) is a cube-sphere, which is evidence but not
> consent — the √2 edge floor and the corner shear are the parts of that choice nobody usually
> states, and he is entitled to see them before signing. **If (B) is chosen instead, §3.3 is deleted
> wholesale, `GridMapping` collapses to one arm, and 3-C evaporates; §3.4 onward survive unchanged.**

---

### 3.3 The cube-sphere, concretely

#### 3.3.1 The warp — verified coefficients, and a correction to the research

A cube-sphere maps grid coordinates `(a, b) ∈ [-1,1]²` on one of six faces to a point on the sphere.
Without a warp (`u = a`), cells near a face corner have **5.17×** the ground area of cells at the
face centre — Bowerbyte's "clearly squeezed into rectangles". Every practical fix is a separable odd
warp `u = W(a)`, `v = W(b)`, applied before normalisation.

The research pool recommended the JCGT 2018 optimal 5th-order polynomial and transcribed it as
`f(a) = 0.1239a + 0.1305a³ + 0.7456a⁵`. **Read literally, that is wrong.** Its slope is 0.124 at the
face centre and 4.243 at the edge — a factor of 34, an order of magnitude outside the whole
tan-warp family, and it is not the inverse of the paper's stated inverse polynomial. The coefficient
order is reversed. The correct assignment, verified numerically to four digits against the paper's
published round-trip error of 0.00109:

```
forward   W(a) = 0.7456·a + 0.1305·a³ + 0.1239·a⁵
inverse⁰  G(u) = 1.3432·u − 0.4865·u³ + 0.1433·u⁵     round-trip max error 1.0814 × 10⁻³
```

Anyone implementing from the research file directly would have shipped a planet whose face centres
were compressed 6× and discovered it visually, late.

#### 3.3.2 Which warp — the measured trade, and where the distortion actually is

The on-sphere cell metric was measured over a 400 × 400 sample of one face for the whole degree-5 odd
family, normalised so the face-centre cell edge is 1.000 m. "Edge" is the tangential cell-edge length;
"shape" is the singular-value ratio of the grid Jacobian, which includes shear; "area" is the true
Jacobian determinant.

| warp | tangential edge (m) | edge spread | area ratio max/min | shape ratio max | % of surface with shape > 1.30 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| identity (no warp) | 0.472 – 1.000 | 2.12 | 5.17 | 1.73 | 30.8 % |
| JCGT area-optimal | 0.709 – 1.178 | 1.66 | **1.28** | 1.73 | 45.0 % |
| **`VD-ASC5` (recommended)** | **0.708 – 1.005** | **1.42** | 1.42 | 1.73 | 31.6 % |
| shape-optimal `k=(0.88, 0.12, 0)` | 0.665 – 1.000 | 1.50 | 2.61 | 1.73 | 16.6 % |

The `√3` shape column is identical in every row because it is topology, not tuning (§3.2), and
`VD-ASC5` sits at the √2 edge-spread floor (1.4167 measured on the discrete grid). The choice is
settled by the one remaining free property: **the angle-proportional constraint is free.** Requiring
`W'(0) = π/4` makes the face-centre cell edge exactly `(π/2)·R/N`, which is precisely the definition
under which the radius family `R = 62·2ᵏ·(2/π)` yields exactly 1.000 m blocks. Fixing `k₁ = π/4` and
sweeping the one remaining free parameter for minimum edge spread lands at `k₂ ≈ 0.15`; the optimum
is flat (1.4169 at 0.16 versus 1.4176 at 0.15), so the value is not load-bearing.

**Recommended warp — `VD-ASC5`:**

```rust
// crates/core/src/grid/warp.rs
pub const W_K1: f64 = 0.785_398_163_397_448_3;   // = π/4, exactly the f64 nearest
pub const W_K2: f64 = 0.15;
pub const W_K3: f64 = 0.064_601_836_602_551_73;  // K1+K2+K3 == 1.0 exactly in f64 ⇒ W(1) == 1.0
const _: () = assert!(W_K1 + W_K2 + W_K3 == 1.0);

#[inline] pub fn warp(a: f64) -> f64  { W_K1*a + W_K2*a*a*a + W_K3*a*a*a*a*a }
#[inline] pub fn dwarp(a: f64) -> f64 { W_K1 + 3.0*W_K2*a*a + 5.0*W_K3*a*a*a*a }

pub const INV_G1: f64 = 1.270_238_82;
pub const INV_G2: f64 = -0.374_192_98;
pub const INV_G3: f64 = 0.103_954_16;            // G1+G2+G3 == 1.0
pub const WARP_INVERSE_STEPS: u32 = 3;
```

Verified in f64: `K1+K2+K3 == 1.0` **exactly**; `W(1) == 1.0` **exactly** under the stated evaluation
order; `G1+G2+G3 == 1.0` exactly; `W'` is bounded below by 0.7854 on `[0,1]` so the Newton denominator
needs **no zero guard and therefore no branch**; the seed polynomial alone gives max error
1.0024 × 10⁻³, and **exactly three** Newton steps give 2.2204 × 10⁻¹⁶ — f64 round-off. The step count
is a `const`, never a tolerance loop, so the inverse is bit-identical by construction. The whole warp
uses only `+ − × ÷` and literal constants: no transcendental, no `libm`, no target divergence.

Cost of the *forward* warp: 5 multiplies, 2 adds. Cost of the inverse: ~40 flops plus 3 divisions.
**Generation and meshing never call the inverse** — both are index-driven (for each cell index,
forward-warp to a direction). The inverse appears only in `addr_of`: block targeting, entity→chunk
binning, collider region selection. All low-frequency, and none of it on the containment path
(§3.1.3).

> **[USER DECISION 3-C] — the warp, i.e. what "blocky" looks like on a sphere.** Conditional on 3-A
> = cube-sphere. A one-way door: it defines every block boundary on every planet forever, and
> changing it after players build invalidates every stored edit.
>
> **Where the distortion actually is** (this is the part that decides the choice, and the part the
> earlier analysis got wrong). Under `VD-ASC5` the worst tangential block, **0.708 m**, sits at the
> **midpoint of each of the 12 cube-face edges**, in the direction *transverse* to that edge — not at
> the cube corners. This is provable rather than sampled: at `(a=1, b=0)` the transverse edge scale
> is `W'(0)·√2/2` for **any** odd warp, so the 0.7071 ratio is warp-independent. At the corners blocks
> are **0.935 m and equal-edged** — better than average in the rectangle sense, and worst in the shear
> sense (120° rhombi). The >1.30 edge-anisotropy region is **12 lens-shaped bands centred on the 12
> cube-edge great-circle arcs**: each arc is `acos(1/3) = 70.53°` = **199 km** long at R = 161,671 m;
> each band is **±15.6 km at the arc midpoint**, narrowing to nothing about 40 % of the way toward
> each corner. Total: **2,388 km of visible cube outline** drawn across the planet, where blocks are
> up to 30 % narrower one way than the other. That is the honest picture; "7 % of the surface"
> understates it by making it sound scattered.
>
> - **(A) `VD-ASC5`, angle-proportional, `k = (π/4, 0.15, 0.0646)` — recommended.** Blocks 1.000 m at
>   the six face centres, 0.708 m at the 12 edge midpoints (transverse), 0.935 m and square-edged at
>   the 8 corners; median 0.959 m, mean 0.933 m; maximum 1.005 m. Sits at the family's minimum edge
>   spread. Makes the radius arithmetic exact. Transcendental-free.
> - **(B) JCGT area-optimal, `k = (0.7456, 0.1305, 0.1239)`.** Every block covers nearly the same
>   ground area (±13 %), so one block mined is one block's worth of material everywhere — which
>   matters to a player-driven economy with physical goods, since (A) and (D) let a player mine
>   1.4×–2.6× more material per block in some places than in others. The cost is a *wider* distortion
>   band — 45 % of the surface above 1.30 shape ratio, and blocks up to 1.178 m — which is the exact
>   complaint the Bowerbyte article exists to fix.
> - **(D) Shape-optimal, `k = (0.88, 0.12, 0)`.** Best rectangle-ness: edges never differ by more than
>   0.7 % *from each other*. But it does **not** make blocks square everywhere — the 120° corner shear
>   is untouched, and 16.6 % of the surface still exceeds a 1.30 shape ratio. The real cost is that
>   block *size* varies by 1.50× across a face and ground area by 2.61×.
>
> **Recommendation: (A).** It is the only option simultaneously at the achievable minimum of size
> spread, near the minimum of shape distortion, and angle-proportional (which is what makes the radius
> exact). (B)'s material-honesty argument evaporates if a mined block yields one unit regardless of
> its physical size — which is what every voxel game does and what section 4 should specify anyway.
> (D)'s 1.5× size drift changes doorway widths, jump distances and build proportions across a planet,
> which is a gameplay inconsistency the player *can* measure, whereas a 1.40:1 block along 12 known
> arcs is one he mostly cannot.

#### 3.3.3 Addressing, faces, the seam table, and the apron

Face indices `0..5` = `+X, −X, +Y, −Y, +Z, −Z`. Each face declares a signed `(right, up)` basis such
that `right × up` is the outward normal. Write `N` for the tier-0 cell count per face edge and
`N_L = N / 2^L` for the tier-L count. Forward addressing, from index to position:

```
a = (2·i + 1)/N_L − 1;   u = warp(a)        // i ∈ [0, N_L)
b = (2·j + 1)/N_L − 1;   v = warp(b)        // j ∈ [0, N_L)
dir = (face_normal + u·right + v·up);  dir /= sqrt(dir·dir)
r   = floor_radius_m + (ir << L) + (1 << (L−1))     // ir ∈ [0, V_L·62), integer metres
pos = dir · r
```

Inverse: `face` = index of the largest `|component|` and its sign (three comparisons, no float
error); `u = p_right/p_axis`, `v = p_up/p_axis`; `a = W⁻¹(u)`, `b = W⁻¹(v)`;
`i = floor((a+1)·N_L/2)`, `j = floor((b+1)·N_L/2)`; `ir = (floor(|p| − floor_radius_m)) >> L`.

**The radial axis is exact integer arithmetic**, as §3.1.3 states, so `ir` is an integer subtraction
and a shift, then `cy = ir / 62`, `iy = ir % 62`. There is no float rounding hazard on the radial
axis at any tier.

**The seam table (12 edges) is data, and it is derivable.** For each face, each of its four boundary
edges maps to `(dst_face: u8, dst_edge: u8, reverse: bool)`. That is 24 directed records = 72 bytes.
The table is *computed once* from the face basis definitions by a small generator function and a test
asserts the computed table equals a committed literal — derive **and** pin, so a basis typo cannot
silently redefine the net. The table depends only on the cube net, **not on `N`, and therefore not on
the tier**, which is what makes exhaustive testing at `N = 62` a complete proof of the whole ladder.

**How the coarse lattice tiles a face — the one new constraint the ladder puts on the radius.** A
tier-L cell is a `2^L × 2^L` block of tier-0 cells, so the tier-L lattice tiles a face exactly only
if `2^L` divides `N`. Addendum 1 fixes `N = 62·m` with `R = 124·m/π` for any integer `m`, and
`62 = 2·31` contributes exactly one factor of two, so the condition is **`2^(L−1) | m`**. For a body
with `T` rungs (tiers `0 … T−1`) that is **`2^(T−2) | m`**. If it does not hold, the outermost row of
coarse cells on each face edge is *partial*, and a partial cell at a face edge is a partial cell in
the one file Addendum 1 §A.3 names as the one that will hurt.

> **[USER DECISION 3-I] — how the coarse lattice tiles a cube face.** A one-way door: it fixes the
> set of legal radii, and a body's radius is persisted data from the moment its first block is saved.
>
> - **(A) Snap the ladder — recommended.** A `T`-rung body's `m` must be a multiple of `2^(T−2)`.
>   The radius ladder's effective step becomes `39.470 × 2^(T−2)` m for that body. Every rung tiles
>   every face exactly, the seam table and the eight corner columns are **byte-identical at every
>   tier**, `addr_of` gains not one branch, and `G-MAPPING-EXHAUSTIVE` clause (vi) is proved by the
>   existing `N = 62` enumeration. The cost is radius quantisation, and it is small:
>
>   | rungs `T` | deepest tier | ladder reach | `m` divisible by | effective step | worst radius error | Earth's error |
>   |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
>   | 1 | 0 | 786 m | 1 | 39.47 m | ±19.7 m | +0.4 m |
>   | 4 | 3 | 6.3 km | 4 | 157.9 m | ±78.9 m | ≤ ±79 m |
>   | 6 | 5 | 25.2 km | 16 | 631.5 m | ±315.8 m | ≤ ±316 m |
>   | 8 | 7 | 100.6 km | 64 | 2,526.1 m | ±1,263 m | **−157.9 m** (0.0025 %) |
>   | 10 | 9 | 402.4 km | 256 | 10,104 m | ±5,052 m | −5,209 m (0.082 %) |
>
>   Worked bodies at `T = 8`: Earth `m = 161,408` → 6,370,843 m (−158 m); Mars `m = 85,888` →
>   3,390,036 m (+36 m); Luna `m = 44,032` → 1,737,962 m (+962 m); Europa `m = 39,552` →
