>   1,561,134 m (+134 m); Ceres `m = 11,968` → 472,462 m (−538 m); a 200 km moon `m = 5,056` →
>   199,562 m (−434 m, 0.22 % — the worst in the set). **The starter world survives unchanged:**
>   `m = 4,096` is `2^12`, divisible by anything the ladder can ask for, so R = 161,671 m stays
>   exactly legal. A body that wants the full 39.47 m ladder declares fewer rungs, which is the
>   honest trade written as data.
> - **(B) A ragged mid-face row.** Keep the 39.47 m ladder at every depth; place the leftover
>   `N mod 2^L` cells as one narrow row and one narrow column **through the face centre**, so both
>   face borders still end on full coarse-cell boundaries and every seam stays exact. Cost: one
>   comparison per axis inside `addr_of` and `cell_center` — the innermost, hottest, most-covered
>   arithmetic in the section — plus a new `G-MAPPING-EXHAUSTIVE` clause, plus one cell-wide width
>   anomaly per face per tier at the six face centres, which is where players spawn. It buys back at
>   most 5 km of radius on an Earth-sized body that nobody can measure in play.
> - **(C) Ragged at the face borders.** Rejected outright: the raggedness would land exactly on the
>   12 seams and the 8 corners, and each face would have to agree with its neighbour about a partial
>   cell's width. That is a new class of seam bug in the file that already caused the reference
>   implementation's author to say "I think I still missed an edge case" after a month.
>
> **Recommendation: (A).** The error is aesthetic and unmeasurable in play (0.0025 % on Earth,
> 0.22 % on the worst body in the table); (B)'s cost is a permanent conditional in the innermost
> addressing function and a permanent anomaly at the six most-visited places on every planet.
>
> **RIDER, and the owner must see it before signing.** §3.7.5's ceiling is now the **face-covering
> rung** and `tier_depth` is **derived** (`tier_depth = ceil(log2 m) + 1`) rather than authored. Fed
> back into this rule, `2^(T−2) | m` with `T = ceil(log2 m) + 1` tightens to **"`m` is a power of
> two"** for any body running a full-depth ladder. The recommended starter world satisfies it
> (`m = 4,096 = 2^12`). Option (A)'s table above and its worked bodies were computed at a *shallower*
> declared ladder (`T = 8`, `m` a multiple of 64) and are kept because they show the shape of the
> quantisation cost; under the derived full-depth ceiling the legal set for a full-depth body is the
> powers of two, and that is the constraint this decision must record rather than have discovered
> when the second body is authored.

**The apron, and a correction to the "why 62" argument.** `62 = 64 − 2`: a 62-voxel column plus a
one-voxel apron at each end is *exactly* one `u64`, so binary greedy meshing's face-cull step
`col & !(col << 1)` runs on a full machine word with the apron included. That is almost certainly why
62³ is committed and it is worth writing down so nobody "simplifies" it to 64. But the branchless
property belongs to the **meshing pass over an already-gathered apron**, not to the gather itself,
and the draft this section replaces claimed too much. The gather rule, stated:

- **Interior chunks** (per face, at tier L, the perimeter is `4·m/2^L − 4` chunks out of `(m/2^L)²`
  — at the starter world's `m = 4,096` that is 16,380 of 16.78 M at tier 0, and 508 of 16,384 at
  tier 3): apron cells are the neighbouring chunk's boundary plane, a straight copy.
- **Face-boundary chunks**: each apron cell is resolved through `neighbor(...)`, which returns
  `AcrossSeam { addr, axis_remap }`; the copy is a strided/reversed gather under `axis_remap`.
- **The 24 corner-diagonal slots** (three faces meet at a cube corner, not four, so one diagonal
  apron neighbour *does not exist*): the fill is **the nearest in-face cell, duplicated**. This is the
  watertight choice — it guarantees the mesher never emits a face into a hole and never emits a
  spurious face across one. It is exactly the class of bug the reference implementation shipped
  ("mesh discontinuities at specific chunk borders"), and it is covered by `G-MAPPING-EXHAUSTIVE`
  clause (v).

The apron rule is **tier-agnostic by construction** under 3-I(A): the same 24 records, the same 24
corner slots, the same `axis_remap`, with only `m/2^L` changing. The proportion of boundary chunks
rises with the tier (0.098 % at tier 0, 3.1 % at tier 3, 25 % at tier 7 on the starter world),
which is worth knowing because the seam path stops being a rare branch at coarse tiers and must be
as well covered as the interior one — but it is the *same* path, so this is a test-weighting note,
not a design change.

#### 3.3.4 The eight corners, and why there are no poles

A cube-sphere has no polar singularity. Put the planet's spin axis through two opposite face centres
(`±Y`) and the rotational poles land at the *most regular* part of the grid — the exact opposite of a
lat/long grid. The unavoidable defect is concentrated into the **8 cube corners, 90° each**, sitting
at latitude **±35.264°** (`asin(1/√3)`), four per hemisphere at 90° of longitude apart.

State the defect precisely. **Every cell has exactly four lateral neighbours, including at a corner.**
What breaks is the *vertex*: three cells meet at a cube corner instead of four, so circulating around
that vertex closes in three steps, the cells there are 120° rhombi (§3.2), and lateral moves stop
commuting near it — "east then north" and "north then east" land on different cells. Consequences:

- Any operation that assumes a rectangular region — prefab paste, explosion volume, area-of-effect
  signal, world-edit box, physics broadphase cell — must be expressed as a **direction walk** from an
  origin cell, and the walk API must return a typed `CornerDefect` when it revisits a cell. Never a
  silent overwrite (that is the "house wraps in on itself" bug in the reference implementation).
- The generator may place a distinctive landform at the eight corner columns so the anomaly is
  diegetic rather than a bug report. This is free: they are eight known addresses in a table.

**The terrain itself has no seam at all**, because the height field is a function of the 3-D unit
direction, not of face coordinates (§3.5). The grid has defects; the world does not.

**The eight defects do not multiply with the ladder.** They are geometric — properties of the cube
net, not of the cell size — so at tier L they sit at the same eight directions, occupied by rhombic
cells of side `2^L` m with the same 120° interior angle. The `CornerDefect` return from the walk API
is tier-agnostic and the eight corner addresses are one table indexed by tier, computed by the same
generator function that emits the seam table.

#### 3.3.5 One radial shell, not Blocky Planet's doubling shells

Reject the doubling-shell scheme outright. Its costs are documented by its own author: one block
gains four up-neighbours (breaking the one-neighbour-per-direction invariant every mesher, flood fill
and signal walk depends on), box-shaped structure placement becomes impossible, the shell-index
lookup becomes a loop, and the shipped build lists "rendering gaps between vertical shells" and "mesh
discontinuities" as known issues. Its only benefit is constant block width from surface to core, which
matters only on sub-kilometre planets. At the committed radius it buys nothing.

A single shell with a fixed radial band. The band is **asymmetric about the datum** and the two ends
are derived independently — the earlier symmetric presentation only worked because the worked example
happened to use a crust depth equal to the scale height:

```
floor_radius_m = R − D_crust                       (integer metres)
ceiling_m      = R + H_scale                       (integer metres)
V              = ceil((D_crust + H_scale) / 62)    tier-0 chunks   (hard cap V ≤ 1024)
V_L            = ceil(V / 2^L)                     tier-L chunks
```

`D_crust` is the geological crust depth and `H_scale` the atmospheric scale height; both are derived
from the body's authored mass through `BodyPhysical` (§3.4), not authored separately. For an
Earth-like atmosphere at 9.81 m/s², `H_scale = 8,410 m`; with an 8.4 km crust, `V = 272`, a 16,864 m
band. This makes the build ceiling mean something physical — *you can build up to where the air runs
out* — and satisfies the no-magic-numbers rule.

**The band coarsens with the ladder like everything else.** A tier-L cell is `2^L` m *radially* as
well as tangentially, so the radial chunk count falls as `V/2^L`: the `V = 272` band is 5 chunks deep
at tier 6 and 3 at tier 7. The floor and ceiling are the same two radii at every rung — the domain
does not change, only its resolution — so `domain()` needs no tier argument and an edit's
`OutsideDomain` answer is tier-independent.

| band `V` | thickness | tangential width at floor (D_crust = ½ band) | at ceiling | radial chunks at tier 0 / 3 / 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 128 | 7,936 m | 0.9755 | 1.0245 | 128 / 16 / 1 |
| **272** | **16,864 m** | **0.9479** | **1.0521** | **272 / 34 / 3** |
| 512 | 31,744 m | 0.9018 | 1.0982 | 512 / 64 / 4 |
| 1024 | 63,488 m | 0.8037 | 1.1963 | 1024 / 128 / 8 |

(The width columns are *multiples of the nominal cell*, so they are tier-invariant; they scale with
`r/R`, and for an asymmetric band you read the floor column at `(R − D_crust)/R` and the ceiling at
`(R + H_scale)/R`. They are quoted here at the starter world's `R = 161,671 m`; on an Earth-sized
body the same 16.9 km band spans only 0.26 % of the radius, so the spread collapses to
0.9987–1.0013.) Radial block height is exactly `2^L` metres at every altitude; only tangential width
scales. A chunk is therefore a frustum, not a box: at tier L its outer face is `(r + 62·2^L)/r` times
its inner face — 0.04 % at tier 0 on the starter world, 4.9 % at tier 7, and both are index-space
facts the mesher never sees.

#### 3.3.6 The `u64` chunk key — widened for variable radius, and the tier is now spent

The earlier layout is **struck**. It gave the tangential axes 14 bits each and reserved three bits
for a `detail_tier` that was "always 0 at P4". Two things killed it: Addendum 1 made the radius
per-body data, so 14 bits (`m ≤ 16,383`, `R ≤ 647 km`) cannot address a real planet — Earth needs
`m = 161,408`, which is 18 bits; and Addendum 2 made the tier real, so the reserved field must carry
a value and must be wide enough for **every addressable body's face-covering rung**. The replacement:

```rust
// crates/core/src/grid/key.rs — the ONE addressing word. PERSISTED.
// ONE-WAY DOOR (register row 1 / door 14).

pub struct ChunkKey(u64);
  bits 63..61  sector    (3)   cube face 0..=5 for a shell; 0 for an identity grid
  bits 60..56  tier      (5)   0..=31 representable; the legal ceiling is the body's `tier_depth`
  bits 55..36  a        (20)   first tangential chunk index AT THIS TIER   (m ≤ 1_048_575)
  bits 35..16  b        (20)   second tangential chunk index AT THIS TIER
  bits 15.. 6  c        (10)   radial / third chunk index AT THIS TIER     (V ≤ 1_024)
  bits  5.. 0  reserved  (6)   MUST be zero; decode REJECTS non-zero
  // 58 bits used, 6 spare. Ordering is sector → tier → a → b → c.

pub struct Tier(u8);                 // 0..=31 representable
impl ChunkKey {
    pub fn tier(self) -> Tier;
    pub fn as_tier0(self) -> Option<Tier0Key>;   // None for EVERY tier 1..=31 — the ONE narrowing point
}
```

**Why 20 bits per tangential axis.** `m ≤ 1,048,575` ⇒ `R ≤ 41,390 km`, which covers every solid
body and the notional surface of an ice giant. Eighteen bits (`R ≤ 10,347 km`) covers Earth and
stops just short of Uranus and Neptune; two extra bits cost nothing here and foreclose nothing later.
At tier L the index range shrinks to `m/2^L`, so the field is widest at tier 0 and the coarse rungs
run in the low bits of it.

**Why 5 tier bits, and not the 3 that were reserved or the 4 an earlier pass proposed.** ~~"Four
bits, 0–15, because an Earth-sized planet viewed from 10 km of altitude wants ten rungs."~~ **Struck.**
That argument sized the field against a *residency* question — how many rungs a client inside the
atmosphere holds — and the field is a *key*, so it must be sized against the body's own ceiling. The
ceiling is the **face-covering rung**: the rung at which one chunk covers a whole cube face, which is
`log2 m`. That is rung **12** for the 162 km starter body, **18** for an Earth-sized one, and **20**
for the largest addressable body (`m = 1,048,575`). Three bits stop at 7 and reinstate a visible wall
at 100 km; four stop at 15 and cannot express an Earth-sized body's ladder at all. **Five bits give
0..=31 with eleven values to spare**, the key closes at **58 of 64 bits with six spare**, and the bits
are free today because they are already asserted zero on decode — where widening after the first world
is saved is a key-format migration over every persisted chunk record and every edit-pyramid entry.

Both of the numbers this replaces are right about different observers, and neither is discarded: the
atmospheric derivation of §3.7.5 is correct for an observer **inside** the air and survives as a
**residency** bound (`tier_view_max`); the face-covering rung is correct for an observer **outside**
it and is the key's ceiling (`tier_depth`).

**Where the realm discriminator went — Addendum 1's §2.7.1 correction, discharged.** Addendum 1
observed that Earth scale needs about 57 bits for face plus three indices and concluded that "the
realm discriminator §2.7.1 packed alongside it must move out". It is out, and it was never in *this*
section: a `ChunkKey` is **realm-relative and carries no realm identity at all**. The realm is
supplied by the container that holds the key — one redb file per `RealmUid` on disk (§3.9.1), an
explicit `realm: RealmId` field on every wire message that carries a chunk (§3.10), and the owning
realm's `GridMapping` in memory. §2.7.1's assumption that a realm id shares the `u64` is therefore
**struck**, not accommodated; the layout above spends 58 bits on geometry and 6 on future geometry.
(Three different spare-bit counts were circulating — 3, 7 and 16. The arithmetic is
`3 + 5 + 20 + 20 + 10 = 58`, so it is **six**, and every other count is struck.)

**Ordering is sector → tier → `a` → `b` → `c`.** Two properties follow and both are load-bearing.
Within one face and one tier a **chunk column is contiguous in key space**, so a
`BTreeMap<ChunkKey, _>` range-scans a column with one query and iterates deterministically — which
the codebase's ban on default-hasher `HashMap` in sim/node code makes mandatory anyway. And **one
whole rung is one contiguous range**, which is what lets the store fetch "every edit-pyramid record
at tier 3 on face 2" as a single scan (§3.9.8) and lets the client's coarse-first loader (§3.7) ask
for the rungs it wants in the order it wants them.

**A correction that must be carried into the doc comments.** The tier on this key is the
**chunk-local content ladder** — how coarse this chunk's *voxels* are. It is a different surface
from `InterShardFlow::OccupantInterest::coarsen_level` (`intershard.rs:659`), which is documented in
the crate as *"hops from the observer's home realm … the deepest ancestors get the full pose; far
ancestors need only the lineage"* — a **pose-precision hop counter on the up-flow**, not a terrain
tier. Addendum 2 §A described the wire as already carrying "a `coarsen_level: u8` precision ladder"
for this purpose; that is too generous and is corrected here. What `intershard.rs:303` genuinely
reserves is the *concept* — "the WHAT lane (terrain/constructions at the LOD the observed realm
controls) is a future ADDITIVE payload on this SAME routing" — a reserved **lane**, not a reserved
field. The two ladders are never converted into one another and neither is derived from the other.

**There are three ladders, not two, and the doc comment is part of the design rather than a nicety.**
The conflation has already happened once in this document (Addendum 2 §A read a pose hop counter as a
terrain ladder), which is why the following text is **required** on `ChunkKey::tier`, on `tier_floor`
(§3.10) and on `OccupantInterest::coarsen_level`:

> **THREE ladders exist and none is derived from, or converted into, another.**
> (1) `ChunkKey.tier` — the CHUNK-LOCAL CONTENT ladder: how coarse this chunk's voxels are.
> (2) `tier_floor` — the OBSERVER'S DECLARED FLOOR: a non-authoritative client memory hint, clamped
>     by the server, used for egress selection only.
> (3) `OccupantInterest::coarsen_level` — a POSE-PRECISION HOP COUNTER on the up-flow ("hops from
>     the observer's home realm"), not a terrain tier. Addendum 2 §A's reading of it as a terrain
>     ladder is corrected in §3.3.6 and §3.10.

**Merged-quad sagitta stops being a non-issue at coarse tiers, and the merge cap comes back — as a
formula, not a literal.** At tier 0 on the starter world a full 62-block merge deviates from the
sphere by **2.97 mm** and the cap is vacuous, exactly as stated before. At tier L a 62-cell merge
spans `62·2^L` metres and the sagitta grows as the square of that: on the starter world a tier-7 run
sags **48.7 m**. It is viewed from at least `786·2^(L−1)` m, so the honest budget is angular:

```
merge_run_max(L)  = sqrt(8 · R · sagitta_budget(L)) / 2^L      cells
sagitta_budget(L) = px_sag_budget · theta_px · 786 · 2^(L−1)   metres
```

with `px_sag_budget` a field of the render tuning struct and `theta_px = fov_h_rad / render_width_px`
**read from that same struct, never re-derived** — it is the one per-pixel angle in the document
(§3.7.1). At half a pixel on the reference screen the budget is `0.25 · 2^(L−1)` m, and the cap
**bites only on small bodies at
deep tiers**: on the starter world it is 50 cells at tier 6 and 35 at tier 7 and vacuous below; on
Earth it is 223 cells at tier 7 and never bites at all. That asymmetry is worth naming — a coarse
rung is a *flatter* approximation of a *smaller* planet, and the small planet is the one that shows
it.

---

### 3.4 The radius ladder, the tier depth, and the gravity

**This subsection is rewritten. Its former premise is struck.** It used to argue that four
constraints — 1 m blocks, 62³ chunks, the roadmap's 100k–200k block radius band, and shift-based
addressing — intersect only on the family `N = 62·2ᵏ`, `R = N·(2/π)`, and it recommended `k = 12` as
"the unique value". Addendum 1 showed the uniqueness was an artefact of a constraint nothing needed:
**the chunks-per-face count never had to be a power of two**, because the chunk index requires a
division by 62 regardless and 62 is not a power of two. Dropping it gives

> **`R = 124·m/π` metres for any integer `m` — a ladder with a 39.470 m step, with `m` chunks per
> face edge and exactly 1.000 m tier-0 cells at the face centres on every rung of it.**

So the radius is **per-body data, not a global decision**, and any real body can be given its true
radius to within twenty metres on one code path — which is what HR3 requires anyway (a body type is
a configuration, never a code path). The detail ladder adds exactly one constraint on top, and it is
decision 3-I: a body with `T` rungs needs `2^(T−2) | m`.

The former `k`-family table survives as **one row of a bigger one** — `m = 4,096` is still legal, is
divisible by every power of two the ladder can demand, and is still the recommended starter world.
What replaces the table is the per-body view, with the detail ladder's own columns in it. `T` is the
rung count a body needs (§3.7), `Σcols` the resident chunk columns at eye height with the ladder,
and the last column is what the same view cost before the ladder existed.

| body | true R | `m` (mult. of 64) | ladder R | error | horizon at eye height | rungs on the ground | Σcols | Σcols without tiers |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **starter world** | — | **4,096** | **161,671 m** | — (exact) | **741 m** | **1** | **505** | 449 |
| 200 km moon | 200 km | 5,056 | 199,562 m | −434 m | 824 m | 2 | 884 | 555 |
| Ceres | 473 km | 11,968 | 472,462 m | −538 m | 1,267 m | 2 | 884 | 1,314 |
| Europa | 1,561 km | 39,552 | 1,561,134 m | +134 m | 2,304 m | 3 | 1,263 | 4,338 |
| Luna | 1,737 km | 44,032 | 1,737,962 m | +962 m | 2,431 m | 3 | 1,263 | 4,830 |
| Mars | 3,390 km | 85,888 | 3,390,036 m | +36 m | 3,395 m | 4 | 1,642 | 9,420 |
| **Earth** | **6,371 km** | **161,408** | **6,370,843 m** | **−158 m** | **4,654 m** | **4** | **1,642** | **17,703** |

The shape of the last two columns is the whole story of this rewrite: **without the ladder the cost
of standing on a planet grows linearly with its radius; with the ladder it grows with the logarithm
of its radius.** The untiered column is exactly proportional — Earth is 39.4× the starter world's
radius and 39.4× its cost — while the tiered column goes from 505 to 1,642, a factor of 3.25 for that
same factor of 39. The growth from here to a Jupiter-sized body is two more rungs.

The rest of the old table's gameplay arithmetic is unchanged and still worth having for the starter
world specifically: a 1,016 km circumference; 56.4 h to walk right around at 5 m/s and 56 min to fly
it at 300 m/s; a 13.4 min low orbit, 1,259 m/s orbital and 1,781 m/s escape velocity **at 1 g** — and
those last three now read off the body's authored mass rather than a global gravity choice (below).

**The anchor constraint is the one the earlier analysis omitted, and variable radius makes it
worse, not better.** `sealed_shards.md:236` states a **binding single-cluster constraint**: *"ONE
planet shard = ONE player cluster = ONE anchor. A second cluster on one planet realm is a HARD ERROR,
not silent f32 corruption."* A conservative f32 tangent-plane budget for stable Rapier contacts is a
~10 km anchor radius (f32 spacing is 0.6 mm at 10 km, 6 mm at 100 km — already at the edge of contact
stability). The number of *distinct* 10 km patches needed to tile a body is **1,045 on the starter
world, 459,800 on Mars and 1.62 million on Earth** — an upper bound on how many anchors a body could
ever require, **not a partition that must exist**. Anchors are per player-cluster, so a body with one
settlement needs one. But the number says how far the single-anchor constraint is from being safe by
construction: two groups of players 100 km apart on the same planet is an ordinary Tuesday, and it is
a hard error today. **The partition rule** is the same per-cell spatial index that D-9/D-39.5 and
D-41 already need: anchors are allocated per occupied cell-cluster, one Rapier world per anchor, and
cross-anchor contacts are the same ghost-collider problem as 3-B(i). Reserving the multi-anchor
*shape* now (D-41 plant item 4) is free; retrofitting it after P5 hardens on one anchor is the
rewrite D-41 warns about. **The detail ladder does not help here** — collision is tier-0 only
(Addendum 2 §C.7) and coarse rungs never enter a physics world, so the anchor problem is untouched
by anything in this amendment and must be solved on its own terms.

**Gravity is derived from an authored mass, and the "fabricate or be honest" question is settled.**
For a body of uniform density `g = (4/3)·π·G·ρ·R`: at fixed density, surface gravity is directly
proportional to radius. A rock body (ρ = 3,000 kg/m³) at the starter radius pulls at **0.1356 m/s²**
— 1/72 g — and 9.81 m/s² at that radius would need a mean density of 217,043 kg/m³, ten times
osmium. That arithmetic has not changed; what changed is that it is no longer a global decision.
Addendum 1's model, adopted here verbatim:

```rust
// crates/core/src/body.rs
/// Per-body physical definition. Seed-derived by default; every field overridable.
pub struct BodyPhysical {
    pub radius_step: u32,    // `m` on the 124/π ladder — the radius IS this integer (3-I constrains it)
    pub mass_kg: f64,        // AUTHORED, or density × volume. The single source of GM.

    /// Number of rungs this body's ladder has. Rungs are 0 ..= tier_depth-1. DERIVED, not authored:
    /// tier_depth = ceil(log2(m)) + 1 — the rung at which one chunk covers a whole cube face, plus
    /// one. 3-I's divisibility is checked in the constructor.
    pub tier_depth: u8,
    /// The COARSEST rung a client INSIDE this body's atmosphere ever requests. A RESIDENCY bound,
    /// never a key bound: ceil(log2(V_atm / R_0)) + 1, clamped to [1, tier_depth].
    pub tier_view_max: u8,
    /// The FINEST rung this body will serve to ANY client — the lower bound of the server's clamp on
    /// a client-declared `tier_floor` (§3.10). Distinct from `tier_view_max`, which bounds the other
    /// end of the same ladder: `tier_view_max` is the coarsest rung a client asks FOR, `tier_floor_min`
    /// is the finest rung the server is willing to GIVE. Normally 0 (full detail is servable); a body
    /// raises it only as an admission-control policy, so a client cannot demand rung 0 residency over
    /// a whole planet. NEVER authoritative: it selects which already-authoritative rung is sent, and
    /// nothing derived from it may reach a fence, a saga, or a persisted value.
    pub tier_floor_min: u8,

    // derived, never authored: surface_gravity, escape_velocity, soi_radius, orbital_period,
    // rotation_period, atmosphere_scale_height, crust_depth, band V
}
```

~~`tier_depth` is "the rung count `T`, whose default §3.7 derives from the atmosphere".~~ **Struck.**
`tier_depth` is derived from the body's *size*, because it bounds a persisted key; the atmospheric
derivation is a different quantity about a different observer and it survives as `tier_view_max`
(§3.7.5). Worked: the starter body `m = 4,096` → face-covering rung 12, `tier_depth` 13; Earth
`m = 161,408` → rung 18, `tier_depth` 19; the largest addressable body `m = 1,048,575` → rung 20,
`tier_depth` 21. **The rider this puts on 3-I** — that a full-depth body's `m` must be a power of two
— is stated in the decision box in §3.3.3 rather than left to be found.

Both former options are now available **per body**: a small world written as unusually dense pulls at
1 g, an honest rock pulls at 0.14 g, and the difference between two bodies is real and consistent
because everything downstream reads the one `mass_kg`. **The SOI consequence survives and must still
be applied consistently:** SOI scales as `(m/M)^0.4`, so a 72× mass inflation to reach 1 g on a small
world inflates that body's sphere of influence by `72^0.4 = 5.5×` — from roughly 55 R to roughly
302 R (≈ 48,900 km at 1 AU from a solar-mass star). Every system-layout distance, every demand-loop
threshold and every warp approach distance is laid out against *this* `GM`, and `GM` is derived once
from `mass_kg` and never re-derived from a density anywhere else. That is a Category-A determinism
requirement as much as a physics one, and the per-body model satisfies it by construction.

> **[USER DECISION 3-E] — the range of surface gravity the generator may draw.** Reduced by
> Addendum 1 from a one-way door on the whole game to a **feel** question, because both behaviours
> are now per-body data. What remains: what band may a procedurally generated body land in?
>
> - **(A) 0.15 g – 1.3 g, recommended.** Wide enough that bodies feel materially different (a 0.2 g
>   moon is a genuinely different place to build on), narrow enough that a player's movement
>   intuition, jump arcs and ship thrust curves stay usable everywhere without per-body retraining.
>   Implemented as a density multiplier band on the seed-derived mass, so nothing is authored twice.
> - **(B) Physical only** — density in the real 1,500–8,000 kg/m³ range, so a 200 km moon pulls at
>   0.14 g and only genuinely large bodies feel Earth-like. Coherent and unusual; it makes every
>   small body a low-gravity environment and effectively deletes ground combat and aerodynamics there.
> - **(C) Unbounded** — whatever the seed produces. Rejected: it produces bodies you cannot jump on
>   and bodies you cannot leave, and the failure is only discovered by a player.
>
> **Recommendation: (A).** The band is two fields (`g_min`, `g_max`) in the generator's parameter
> table, not literals, and the curated starter world sits inside it by construction.

> **[USER DECISION 3-D] — the starter world's radius, and the generator's radius range.** Reduced by
> Addendum 1 from "pick the one radius the game has forever" to a taste question, because radius is
> per-body data. It is **still a one-way door for the starter world specifically** — that world's
> `m` is written into its saved state the moment the spaceport is stamped, and Space Engineers had
> to ship a *sequel* to change theirs.
>
> - **(A) Starter `m = 4,096` (R = 161,671 m) — recommended, and unchanged from the old ruling.**
>   It survives 3-I(A) trivially (`4,096 = 2^12` is divisible by every power of two the ladder can
>   ask for), it is inside the roadmap's stated 100k–200k block band, and its gameplay numbers are
>   the good ones: 505 chunk columns at walking eye height on a **single rung**, a 13.4 min low orbit,
>   1,781 m/s escape velocity, 56 min to fly right around at 300 m/s. A first planet that a player
>   can circumnavigate in an hour is a place; an Earth-sized one is a job.
> - **(B) Starter `m = 161,408` (Earth-sized).** Now *possible* — that is the whole point of
>   Addendum 1 — and it costs 1,642 columns on the ground instead of 505, which is affordable. It is
>   rejected as the *starter* on gameplay grounds only: 40,000 km of circumference means players
>   never meet, and the economy's transport-cost signal degenerates.
> - **(C) Generator range.** Recommended `13 ≤ m ≤ 1,048,575` — from a 513 m asteroid to a
>   41,390 km body — with `tier_depth` derived per body (§3.7) and 3-I(A)'s divisibility applied at
>   construction. The lower end keeps `T = 1` and therefore the full 39.47 m radius ladder, which is
>   what makes small asteroids land on their exact intended size.
> - **Sub-option: what "1 m" is measured at.** Unchanged. 1.000 m is the tier-0 cell width at the six
>   face centres and the median is 0.959 m. Multiplying `R` by 1.071 makes the *median* cell 1.000 m
>   instead of the largest. The face-centre normalisation is recommended because it keeps tangential
>   width never greater than radial height (which is always exactly `2^L` metres) and because it is
>   the definition under which `R = 124·m/π` is exact.

---

### 3.5 Generation from the seed

#### 3.5.1 The pipeline

Height-first, restricted-3D. The order is not a preference; it is the difference between a playable
demo and an unplayable one (§3.5.3).

1. **`BodyDefinition::resolve(seed, overrides)`** — `radius_step m`, `mass_kg`, `tier_depth T`, datum
   radius, `floor_radius_m`, `ceiling_m`, `V`, `GM`, surface gravity, rotation period (roadmap's
   `t_freefall = √(R³/GM) × calibrated multiplier`), axial tilt, sea level, scale height, crust depth,
   geology octave table, strata table, carver params, public-ore table. All via the landed
   `SplitMix64` `child_seed`/`realm_stream` in **`crates/core/src/rng.rs`** (integer-only,
   bit-identical by construction). Closed-form inverse-CDF samplers with **zero rejection loops**,
   following the `taxonomy.rs` idiom already in the repo.
   **This is `PlanetParams::from_seed` widened by Addendum 1, and the widening is settled, not
   optional.** A world is **seed plus configuration**: every field has a seed-derived value and an
   optional authored override, consulted before generation and keyed by the body's position in the
   realm tree. Procedural bodies carry no overrides and cost nothing; a curated world carries a
   handful. The determinism gate survives because **the override table is part of the body's
   *definition*, not its terrain** — definitions already stream to the client as part of the realm
   description. The table is content-hashed, the hash joins the protocol handshake exactly as the
   block registry's does, and a client whose table disagrees is **refused at connect with a named
   error**. The failure is loud at the door instead of silent in the terrain, which is the whole
   reason to hash it rather than trust it (§3.10).
2. **Height field `h(dir, L)`**, sampled as 3-D noise on the **unit sphere** — never a 2-D face map.
   Because `dir` is a 3-D unit vector, the field is automatically continuous across all 12 edges and
   all 8 corners. One field serves every planet in the galaxy.
   `h = R + sea_offset + A_c·fbm_c(dir·f_c) + A_m·ridged(dir_warped·f_m)·mask + A_d·fbm_d(dir·f_d)`,
   with `dir_warped = dir + A_w·fbm_w(dir·f_w)` and `|A_w|` bounded. Budget ~8 octave evaluations per
   column at tier 0.
   **The second argument is not a hint and not an optimisation — it is part of the contract:
   `h(dir, L)` evaluates the stack with its `L` highest-frequency octaves omitted** (§3.5.6). Every
   consumer that asks for a coarse surface — the mesher, the band, the min/max pyramid, the client's
   long-range shadow horizon in §5 — calls the same function with a tier and gets the *correct*
   coarse answer rather than a filtered fine one.
   **Invariant: `max_relief ≤ H_scale/2`** (see §3.6) so the ceiling clamp is an assertion that never
   fires, not a shaping operation that produces flat mesa tops.
3. **Strata** — a per-biome table mapping integer depth below `h` to a material. Integer lookup, no
   noise. **Required property: the table saturates at a bounded depth `D_sat`** (below `D_sat` the
   material is biome-independent bedrock/mantle rock). Without `D_sat` the deep fast path of §3.5.2
   is unsound, because "depth below `h`" needs `h`, which needs the noise.
4. **Biomes** — a low-frequency `(temperature, humidity)` field over `dir` plus the elevation class,
   through a closed-form classifier.
5. **Water** — this is a generation stage, not an afterthought, and the earlier draft omitted it
   entirely. **Water is an ordinary `BlockState` in the grid**, not an analytic field, because the
   player digs channels and floods them. The generator fills every cell with `h(dir) < r <
   sea_level_r` with water. The consequences are all good: an ocean chunk is **Absent** in the store
   (pure generator output, zero bytes); the height band gets an exact third arm (§3.5.2); and a
   flooded excavation is just a large edit count, which the record format of §3.9.3 already handles.
   Water *flow* is not a P4 feature: at P4 water is static. The seam planted for flow is that water
   is an ordinary material, so a future flow system is a rate-capped batch of ordinary edits through
   the ordinary edit pipeline — never a special container and never a second grid.
6. **Carvers (caves)** — **not** per-voxel 3-D density. Per carver region (a coarse cell of the
   direction sphere × depth), `SplitMix64(seed, region)` seeds a small set of parametric tubes: a
   polyline of control points plus a radius. Carving is a distance test against a handful of
   segments — O(few) per chunk, essentially free, and it produces better-looking caves than
   thresholded noise. Large caverns, if wanted, use a 3-D density field evaluated on a **coarse
   lattice** (every 4th cell) and trilinearly interpolated: 1/64 the samples, exact-deterministic
   (only `+ − ×`), and the interpolation error is invisible because the threshold is applied per
   voxel.
   **The tier rule for the cave field is an integer comparison and it is part of the contract:** a
   carver contributes at tier L **iff its radius `ρ ≥ 2^L` metres** (`ρ` is stored in integer metres,
   so this is an integer test with no float and no rounding), and the cavern lattice's step scales
   with the tier — every 4th *cell*, i.e. `4·2^L` m — with the field's own top `L` octaves dropped.
   A three-metre tube is gone at tier 2 and that is correct, not lossy: you cannot see a three-metre
   cave from ten kilometres, and materialising it would be the aliasing §3.5.6 exists to prevent.
7. **Ores** — a **sparse overlay applied after** everything above, never a stage the fast paths can
   skip. Per chunk, `SplitMix64(seed, chunk_key)` → 0..n deposits, each a centre, radius and material
   from the biome/depth-appropriate table. §3.8 splits this into a public and a concealed half.

#### 3.5.2 The generator band — the thing that makes it cheap, and the invariant that makes it safe

A chunk that has never been resident may still be solid rock. "Absent ⇒ air" is the classic hole bug.
The band answers *without* materialising anything:

```rust
/// Conservative min/max terrain radius over one 62×62 chunk-column footprint AT ONE TIER.
/// NAMED for what it bounds: GENERATOR output only. It says nothing about player edits.
pub struct GeneratorBand { pub min_r: i64, pub max_r: i64 }   // integer metres
```

**The band is per (tier, footprint), and the coarse band must be conservative with respect to the
fine one.** A tier-L band computed from the octave-dropped stack would be *narrower* than the tier-0
band over the same ground — the dropped octaves are exactly the ones that make the terrain rough —
and a narrower band used as a pre-rejection walks a player through a ridge. The rule:

> `band_L(footprint) = coarse_min/max over the surviving octaves, widened by the dropped-octave tail
> bound of §3.5.6.` Then `band_L ⊇ band_0` for every footprint, at every tier, by construction —
> and that containment is a property test in `vd-core`, not a comment.

- Chunk entirely **above** `max(max_r, sea_level_r)` and untouched by any carver's upward extent
  ⇒ **all air**, zero noise evaluations.
- Chunk entirely between `max_r` and `sea_level_r` (only where `max_r < sea_level_r`) ⇒ **all water**,
  zero noise evaluations. Sea level is a constant, so this arm is exact.
- Chunk entirely **below** `min_r − D_sat`, whose AABB misses every carver in the region ⇒ **all deep
  stratum**, zero noise evaluations, *plus* the ore overlay. This arm requires `D_sat` from §3.5.1
  step 3; it is unsound without it, and it is also unsound if the deep table is biome-dependent,
  because a 62 m footprint can straddle a biome boundary. Both are stated as required properties of
  the strata table rather than assumed.
- Otherwise ⇒ run the generator.

For an Earth-like relief profile, a `V = 272` column has 1–3 straddling chunks out of 272 — a
**~100× reduction in chunks needing any generation at all**, on top of height-first's saving.

> **The band invariant, which is the failure mode the earlier draft left open.** `GeneratorBand`
> bounds the **generator only**. A player tower 400 m above the terrain sits in chunks the band
> classifies as all-air. The read path (§3.6) is correct because it unions generator output with the
> delta — but **the band is sold as a pre-rejection, and any consumer that uses it *instead of* the
> read path as an emptiness answer walks a player through a tower.** Therefore: *every band query
> that will be used as an emptiness answer must be unioned with the column's delta-presence bitmap*,
> and the bitmap lives in the **same cache entry** as the band so the two cannot be fetched
> separately. This binds the collider broadphase, the residency scheduler and the mesher-skip path.

The band must be *cheap* and *conservative*, which imposes a real constraint on the noise stack:
**every octave declares an amplitude and a Lipschitz bound**, and `band(footprint)` is computed from
a coarse evaluation of the low octaves (an 8×8 lattice over the footprint) plus the analytic tail
bound `Σ|A_i| + L·Δ` for the octaves not evaluated — ~64 evaluations instead of 3,844. It forbids
unbounded domain warps, which is a rule to write into the noise stack now rather than discover later.
Bands are cached in a bounded LRU keyed on `(tier, column footprint)`; they are never persisted,
because they are pure functions of the seed. **The declared per-octave amplitude the band already
requires is the same declaration §3.5.6's error bound reads** — one table, two consumers, no second
description of the noise stack.

**The min/max height pyramid — one small derived structure, four jobs.** Alongside the band, cache a
per-`(tier, chunk column)` pair of solid-radius extremes, stored as two `u16` at the coarse levels and,
at the finest level, as the child extremes normalised into the parent's range as two `u8` (the CDLOD
encoding, measured at roughly 45× smaller than a naive node struct and ~3.5 MiB for a 32K × 32K
field). It does four things at once and none of them needs a second structure:

1. **Tier selection traversal** — the screen-space test of §3.7 needs the column's vertical extent,
   not just its footprint.
2. **Vertical chunk culling** — it is what turns "about three vertical chunks per column at tier 0"
   from an assumption into a measured number, per column, per tier.
3. **The skirt height** (§5's seam mechanism). §5 owns the formula and it is the one that accounts
   for the rim-warp displacement, so it is quoted rather than restated:

   ```
   skirt_drop_m(chunk at tier L) =
         ( relief_max(chunk.column_footprint, L + 1)   // max − min solid height over ONE cell of the
                                                       // NEXT COARSER rung, from THIS structure
         + A_max )                                     // registry MAXIMUM rim-warp amplitude, metres
         * skirt_safety                                // render-tuning field, default 1.25
   ```

   The first term is what this pyramid supplies; `A_max` and `skirt_safety` are §4's and §5's.
4. **The conservative-envelope property test** — `band_L ⊇ band_0` above is checked against it, and
   so is the **envelope property** `min_fine ≤ h_coarse ≤ max_fine` over a coarse cell (§5.9.4).

It is **derived and never persisted**: a pure function of the seed and the edit pyramid (§3.9.8),
recomputable at any time, and therefore outside the format-freeze problem entirely.

**This structure is the relief envelope's ONE home, and that is now a ruling rather than a
preference.** Two alternatives were live and both are **struck**: §2.7.1's persisted `column_relief`
redb table and record, and the proposal to carry a min/max solid-height pair inside the edit-pyramid
entry. The second loses on structure rather than cost — min/max solid height is a per-**column**
quantity and a pyramid entry is a per-**cell** record, so persisting it there replicates it up to 62×
per column — and both lose on the one-way-door argument, because freezing a third permanent format to
cache a computation that is exactly reconstructible from the generator (closed form for the unedited
part) unioned with the pyramid entries (an entry with `occ_mask != 0` bounds the edited part to within
one coarse cell) is the opposite of conservative. Striking `column_relief` also restores §2's headline
claim that the ladder costs it *exactly one* new persisted structure.

**Two proof obligations ride with the skirt and they are not duplicates.** `terrain_tier_agreement`
(§3.5.4 rule 10 / §3.5.6) bounds the **magnitude** of the coarse-vs-fine disagreement; the envelope
property test fixes its **sign** — it proves the crack can only open *downward*, which is what a
downward apron closes. The second is empirically true for zero-mean fBm and is **not a theorem**,
which is exactly why it is a test. A skirt needs both; either alone leaves a hole in the argument.

#### 3.5.3 The measured constant, and the benchmark that must run first

**This subsection's premise is discharged.** It was written when noise evaluation cost was the only
unmeasured number in the design that could invalidate P4's demo. It has since been measured and
pinned (Appendix A, Apple M4 Pro, one core): **one noise evaluation is 12.19 ns, and one complete
62³ surface chunk is 0.885 ms** using a height field plus a coarse-lattice 3-D cave field sampled
every 4th cell and interpolated. The sensitivity table below is kept because it shows how little the
answer depended on the constant, with the measured column marked.

| ns/eval | per 62×62 column-stack (8 evals/col) | 505-column tier-0 disc, single core | *per-voxel 3-D for comparison* |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 0.15 ms | 0.08 s | 4 s |
| 10 | 0.31 ms | 0.16 s | 9 s |
| **12.19 (measured)** | **0.375 ms height + 0.51 ms caves = 0.885 ms** | **0.45 s** | 11 s |
| 20 | 0.62 ms | 0.31 s | 17 s |
| 50 | 1.54 ms | 0.78 s | 43 s |

The height-first decision is worth **62×**, and it converts snowflow's alarming 24-second horizon
into a **sub-second** one. *Height-first is not an optimisation; it is what makes P4 shippable.*
Generation risk is now closed; the mesher is the flight-speed gate.

**The ladder is a second, independent saving on the same path.** A tier-L chunk drops `L` octaves
from the height stack and every carver thinner than `2^L` metres from the cave stack, so it costs
strictly less than a tier-0 chunk while covering `8^L` times the volume. With the measured 8-octave
stack the predicted per-chunk cost runs 1.00 / 0.90 / 0.79 / 0.68 / 0.57 / 0.47 / 0.40 / 0.36 of the
tier-0 figure for tiers 0…7 (the floor is the three lowest octaves, which never drop). Addendum 2
§D.3 makes "a tier-L chunk costs strictly less than a tier-(L−1) chunk" a **gate**, not an
expectation — it is the proof that octave-dropping is real rather than decorative, and it is one
extra row per tier in `just bench-noise`.

**The benchmark, to run before any mesher or generator code lands.** A plain timing binary — no new
dependency, no criterion — under `crates/core/benches/`, driven by `just bench-noise`, using
`std::time::Instant` over a fixed 10 M-sample loop with `black_box`, reporting ns/eval on the dev
machine and one Linux runner. Five measurements: (1) one 3-D simplex octave in f64; (2) a 6-octave
fBm; (3) the full candidate stack per sample; (4) one complete 62×62 column-stack; (5) one complete
straddling 62³ chunk. Publish the numbers as pinned figures in `docs/design/`.

The decisions it feeds: whether large caverns get a coarse-lattice 3-D field at all or carvers only;
whether the client can generate ahead of the camera, which sets the **maximum flight speed** — a
gameplay one-way door, since ship performance gets tuned around it; whether `rayon` becomes a
dependency (a user decision, and one that interacts with determinism: chunk-parallel generation is
order-independent and safe, a parallel *reduction* is not); and whether the band pre-rejection is an
optimisation or a prerequisite.

**The ladder softens the flight-speed door substantially and it is worth saying how.** Without tiers,
flying faster means generating a linearly larger disc ahead of the camera, so speed traded directly
against generation throughput. With tiers, moving forward invalidates a **constant** number of
columns per rung — about 379 per tier, and the coarse rungs both cover the most ground and cost the
least to produce. Flight speed now trades against *tier-0 residency* near the vehicle, which is a
small fixed disc, rather than against the whole view. The gate that remains is the mesher, not the
generator.

#### 3.5.4 Determinism — the exact rules

P4's DoD is byte-identical terrain on server, client, and two target-cpu builds. The rules are
narrower than the research proposed:

1. **Primitive f64 arithmetic is already safe.** `+ − × ÷ sqrt`, casts, `floor/ceil/trunc/round/
   round_ties_even` and `mul_add` are bit-exact IEEE-754-2008 on every conforming target, and Rust
   deliberately never contracts `a*b + c` into an FMA. Optimisation level cannot change a result.
   **The FMA half of SPIKE-6a can be struck**; the spike's real content is libm and glam.
2. **The killer is the transcendental library.** `std` documents `sin/cos/tan/asin/acos/atan/atan2/
   powf/powi/exp/ln/log*/cbrt/hypot/to_radians/to_degrees` as having precision that "varies by
   platform, Rust version, and can even differ within the same execution". LLVM may additionally
   const-fold them using the *build host's* libm.
3. **Do not ban them globally.** `celestial.rs` legitimately uses them and has a documented
   Tier-1/Tier-2 story plus an authority-independence argument. A blanket clippy ban breaks shipped
   code.
4. **Instead, make them unreachable on the generation path by construction.** Wrap the generator's
   float in a newtype:

   ```rust
   // crates/core/src/grid/gf.rs
   #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, PartialOrd)]
   pub struct Gf(f64);      // Add/Sub/Mul/Div/Neg + sqrt/floor/abs/min/max/from_i64/to_f64 ONLY.
   ```

   No `sin`, no `powf`, no way to reach one. This is the same enforcement idiom the codebase already
   uses for `EffectFree` in `sim/src/coupling.rs`: a type-level guard rather than a grep or a lint.
   Every op is a `#[inline]` one-liner, so it is zero-cost and trivially 100 % region+branch covered.
   The whole warp, the whole height field, the whole strata lookup and the whole carver distance test
   are expressible in `Gf`.
5. **No `glam::Vec3A` and no `Vec3::normalize` on this path** — glam guarantees SIMD/scalar parity
   only for serde and Debug output, not for `dot`/`length`/`normalize`. Write `v / v.dot(v).sqrt()`
   explicitly in `Gf`.
6. **No runtime-SIMD noise.** `simdnoise` dispatches between SSE2/SSE4.1/AVX2 at runtime on the same
   binary — two players on different CPUs would get different planets, invisibly, from one build.
7. **Fixed iteration counts everywhere.** `WARP_INVERSE_STEPS = 3`, exactly as `KEPLER_FIXED_ITERS`
   is already a constant in `celestial.rs`.
8. **Integer hashing only.** Reuse the landed `SplitMix64`; introduce no second hash.
9. **Per-planet variation comes from the gradient hash, NOT from a coordinate translation** — the
   research's "the seed is a translation in noise space" is numerically unsound at `u64` magnitudes.
   Adjacent blocks are `(π/2)/N = 6.185 × 10⁻⁶` radians apart, i.e. `6.185e-6·S` in noise space at
   feature scale `S`. f64 spacing near an offset `|T|` is `2.22e-16·|T|`, so keeping 1,000
   distinguishable levels between adjacent blocks requires `|T| < S · 2.79 × 10⁷` — at `S = 1,000`,
   `|T| < 2.8 × 10¹⁰`. A raw `u64` is `1.8 × 10¹⁹`: **nine orders of magnitude too large**, with an
   f64 spacing (≈ 2,200 noise units) five orders *above* the entire inter-block step. The failure is
   silent — terrain quantises into stair-stepped plateaus, the byte-identical gate still passes (the
   same wrong answer everywhere), and it gets diagnosed as "the noise stack is bad". **Rule: the
   planet's identity enters through `child_seed`-derived gradient selection inside the noise
   function; any coordinate offset used at all is bounded to a documented cube
   (`T ∈ [0, 2²⁴)³`, decorrelated by `child_seed`), and the bound is published with the pinned
   figures.** Two tests: seeds differing only in high bits must produce different terrain; adjacent
   cells' sample coordinates must differ by at least 2²⁰ f64 ULPs.

10. **Every tier is its own byte-identity fixture.** `h(dir, L)` for each `L` is a *different
    function* — a different subset of octaves summed in a different-length loop — so a tier that
    passes the pin proves nothing about its neighbours. Two players standing at different distances
    from the same hill are evaluating two different tiers of it, and if those two disagree beyond the
    §3.5.6 bound the ladder visibly breathes. The rule: **the digest set is indexed by
    `(seed, chunk key, tier)`, and the cross-build diff covers every legal tier.**

**The gate.** `crates/core/tests/terrain_pin.rs` — deliberately an *integration* test, following the
`celestial_ephemeris_pin.rs` precedent, because the justfile coverage recipes exclude `/tests/` via
`--ignore-filename-regex '(/bin/|/tests/)'` and an exactness assertion must not be able to turn the
HR5 gate red. For one fixed seed and ~64 chunk keys spanning all 6 faces, all 12 edges, all 8 corners,
the band floor and ceiling, a water column, and both hemispheres — **each generated at every legal
tier, so the fixture is ~64 × `T` digests, 512 at an eight-rung body** — assert a 128-bit digest
equals a committed literal. The digest is a 30-line integer-only mixer in `core` (no new dependency,
fully coverable). `just terrain-crossbuild` then builds and runs that test on
`x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, `aarch64-apple-darwin`, `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` at opt-level 0 and 3 and
diffs the digests. With `Gf` in place this gate should pass *by construction* — which is the point of
the newtype and the reason it is worth the ceremony.

A **third** gate joins it, and it is the one the ladder specifically needs:
`terrain_tier_agreement` asserts `|h(dir, L) − h(dir, 0)| ≤ 4·k_rough·2^L` over a large deterministic
sample of directions at every tier (§3.5.6). It is a property test, it lives in `vd-core` at Tier-A,
and it is what makes the skirt height in §5 a derived constant rather than a tuned one.

A second gate, `client_server_terrain_parity`, has the client crate and the sim crate each generate
the same chunk list and assert equal digests. It is trivially true today and it exists to fail the
day someone forks the generator — which is precisely what the ore decision in §3.8 makes possible.

#### 3.5.5 The noise implementation

`noise = "=0.9.0"` is declared at `Cargo.toml:73` and unused; nothing else is in `Cargo.lock`. Its
arithmetic is deterministic f64, but `PermutationTable::new(seed)` seeds a `XorShiftRng` and calls
`rand`'s `SliceRandom::shuffle` under caret-ranged `rand = "0.9"` / `rand_xorshift = "0.4"`. A patch
bump inside 0.9.x that changes the shuffle's RNG-consumption pattern regenerates **every planet in
the game**, with no compile error and no test failure — and every already-stored player edit becomes
misaligned with the terrain beneath it.

> **[USER DECISION 3-F] — where the noise comes from.** A new-dependency question, so it is yours by
> the standing rule. One-way-door-adjacent: changing the noise implementation after players build
> requires a full world regeneration under their existing edits.
>
> - **(A) Vendor ~400 lines of OpenSimplex2 into `crates/core/src/grid/noise.rs`, written in `Gf`,
>   with `SplitMix64` gradient selection — recommended.** The entire generation path then sits inside
>   the newtype, the determinism gate passes by construction, there is no version-drift class at all,
>   and no new dependency. It is also the only option that implements rule 9 of §3.5.4 natively: the
>   planet's identity enters through seeded gradient selection, so no coordinate translation is
>   needed at all. The repo already prefers owning its math (it declares `brahe` and deliberately
>   hand-rolls Category-A celestial code). **Honest cost:** ~400 lines with roughly 10–20
>   data-dependent branches — lattice-cell selection, a per-candidate-corner falloff rejection
>   (`if a > 0` for each of 4–8 corners) and gradient-index selection. Under HR5's
>   per-monomorphisation region+branch rule each of those needs a directed test; the falloff
>   rejections are the awkward ones. It is *not* branchless, and the earlier claim that it was
>   understated the cost.
> - **(B) `noise = "=0.9.0"` with our own `NoiseHasher` supplying a `const [u8; 256]` table.** Uses
>   the already-declared pin, sidesteps the `rand` hazard entirely, but the crate's float surface sits
>   outside `Gf` and is trusted by review rather than by the type system.
> - **(C) `fastnoise-lite` with the `f64` feature.** The best determinism profile of the surveyed
>   crates — static `const` gradient tables, float surface of only `sqrt`/`trunc`/`abs` — but it is a
>   new dependency, it defaults to f32 (which cannot address distinct 1 m voxels above ~100 km
>   radius), and it too sits outside `Gf`.
>
> **Recommendation: (A).** If (B) or (C) is preferred, the golden-hash gate of §3.5.4 becomes
> mandatory rather than confirmatory, because it is then the *only* thing standing between a
> `cargo update` and a regenerated galaxy.

#### 3.5.6 The tier contract — octave dropping belongs to the generator, not the renderer

This subsection is new and it is the most important thing the detail ladder adds to §3.5. It states a
rule, its determinism consequence, and its error bound, and it explains why coarsening this world is
a *saving* rather than a cost — which is the fact the whole of Addendum 2 is built on.

**The rule.**

> **Tier L evaluates the height stack and the cave stack with their `L` highest-frequency octaves
> omitted.** Not filtered afterwards, not downsampled from tier 0, not averaged — **not summed in
> the first place**.

A cell of size `s` cannot represent detail finer than about `2s`; sampling it anyway produces
aliasing, which is the shimmer everyone associates with distant terrain. The octaves finer than `2s`
are exactly the ones a tier-L cell cannot carry. So dropping them is *simultaneously* the correct
anti-aliasing filter, the correct level of detail, and a reduction in work. **This is not an
approximation of the fine answer; for a fractal field it is the exact answer at that resolution.**

**Why it is a saving and not a cost.** Every other approach to voxel detail levels pays twice — once
to build a pyramid and once to store or ship it. Here the coarse rung is *cheaper to produce than the
fine one it replaces*, by exactly the octaves it does not evaluate (§3.5.3's 1.00 → 0.36 ladder), and
it occupies **zero bytes on disk and zero bytes on the wire**, because it is a pure function of the
seed like everything else in §3.5. The stored pyramid this design does need (§3.9.8) exists only for
the half of the world the generator does not author — the player's edits.

**The error bound, exactly.** For a stack of `n` octaves with lacunarity 2 and persistence `p`,
dropping the top `L` changes the height by at most

```
|h(dir,L) − h(dir,0)|  ≤  Σ_{i=n−L}^{n−1} A_i  =  A_{n−L}·(1 − p^L)/(1 − p)  <  A_{n−L}/(1 − p)
```

`A_{n−L}` is the amplitude of the **finest surviving** octave, whose wavelength is `2·s_L` where
`s_L = 2^L` metres is the cell size. For a self-similar stack (amplitude proportional to wavelength
with declared roughness `k_rough`) that is `A_{n−L} = 2·k_rough·s_L`, and with `p = ½`:

> **`|h(dir,L) − h(dir,0)| < 4·k_rough·s_L` — the error is a fixed multiple of the cell size at every
> rung, forever.** At a characteristic 30° slope (`k_rough = 0.5`) that is **two cells**, whether the
> cells are 1 m or 128 m.

That is precisely the property a detail ladder is supposed to have and rarely gets: the error never
exceeds what the representation can express, so it is invisible by construction rather than by
tuning. Two consequences are consumed elsewhere and both are *derived*, not chosen: §3.5.2's coarse
band widens by this tail and is therefore conservative; and the bound above is the **closed-form
conservative fallback** for §5's skirt depth whenever the relief pyramid is not resident.

~~"§5's skirt depth is `(relief across one coarse cell) + 4·k_rough·s_L ≈ 3 cells` at every tier."~~
**Struck**, and replaced by §5.9.4's formula (quoted in §3.5.2), which this section does not own. Two
things were wrong with the sentence rather than one. It omitted the **rim-warp displacement** entirely
— up to `A_max` metres of it, which is a real vertical offset a skirt must cover — and the "≈ 3 cells"
was this error bound evaluated at `k_rough = 0.5` and then quoted as a constant, so it fails for any
rougher noise stack. What survives, and is genuinely useful, is the bound *as a bound*:

```
relief_max(_, L+1)  ≤  4 · k_rough · 2^(L+1)
  ⇒ skirt_drop_m  ≤  (4 · k_rough · 2^(L+1) + A_max) · skirt_safety
  ⇒ at k_rough = 0.5 and A_max = 0.20 m that is ~5 cells at every rung.
```

So skirts still need no case analysis and no knowledge of the neighbour's tier — the depth is still a
constant number of cells at every rung — but the constant is derived from `A_max` and `skirt_safety`
as well as from `k_rough`, and the fallback figure is five cells rather than three.

`k_rough` is a **declared field of the noise stack**, alongside the per-octave amplitude and Lipschitz
bound §3.5.2 already requires. It is not a literal and it is not a shader constant; it is the same
table read by the band, the bound and the property test.

**The determinism consequence, stated so nobody discovers it in a bug report.** `h(dir, L)` is a
different function for each `L`. The Category-A rules of §3.5.4 apply to *all* of them: the whole
ladder lives inside `Gf`, uses fixed iteration counts, and is pinned per tier (§3.5.4 rule 10). Three
specific traps:

1. **Never derive a coarse chunk by downsampling a fine one.** It would be slower, it would require
   the fine chunk to be resident (defeating the entire memory argument), and it would produce a
   *different* answer from `h(dir, L)` — so two clients at the same distance could disagree depending
   on what happened to be in their caches. The generator's answer is the only answer.
2. **The octave count must come from the tier, never from a distance.** A float distance compared
   against a threshold is a float decision on the generation path; `L` is an integer on the chunk key.
3. **The dropped set is a prefix from the top, never a filtered subset.** `L` octaves, always the
   highest `L`, always in the same summation order as tier 0's first `n−L` terms — so the surviving
   partial sum is bit-identical to the corresponding prefix of the fine sum. That is what makes rule
   10's per-tier pins cheap to reason about and what makes the bound above tight rather than
   heuristic.

**What this does not cover.** The generated half of the world coarsens for free; **player edits do
not**, and if that is ignored a dug tunnel vanishes at 200 m and reappears at 100 m. That is the one
genuinely hard piece of work in the ladder and it is §3.9.8.

---

### 3.6 Air, the build band, the sphere of influence, and floating structures

The user asked for air blocks filling the planet's sphere of influence. The honest engineering answer
has four parts, and the last one gives him what he actually wants.

**What "air is addressable everywhere" must mean.** Air is a first-class material with a `BlockState`
and real properties (breathability, pressure, flammability propagation) — never a special case in the
container. Inside the grid band, every cell has a defined state and air is one of them; it costs zero
storage wherever it is the generator's answer, because only *changes* are persisted. (The `Chunk`'s
`filled` counter counts cells differing from the realm's **declared empty material** — air on a
planet, vacuum in a hull — so the skip-empty optimisation exists without privileging any material in
the type.) Outside the band there are no cells, but the *medium* is still defined, as an analytic
field `atmosphere(seed, r)` returning pressure, density and composition. So "air exists everywhere in
the SOI" is true as a **field** and addressable as a **block** only inside the band. Every consumer
that needs to know whether you can breathe, whether a fire spreads, or how much drag a ship feels
queries the field; only the block system queries the grid.

**Why materialising the grid to the SOI is quantitatively wrong, and why the detail ladder does not
rescue it.** At the starter world's radius:

| grid extends to | volume | 1 m cells | bits of address | at 1 bit/cell |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 R | 1.77 × 10¹⁹ m³ | 1.77 × 10¹⁹ | 64 | 2.2 × 10¹⁸ B |
| 50 R | 2.21 × 10²¹ m³ | 2.21 × 10²¹ | 71 | 2.8 × 10²⁰ B |
| 100 R | 1.77 × 10²² m³ | 1.77 × 10²² | 74 | 2.2 × 10²¹ B |

The address space alone breaks at 10 R — 64 bits with zero left for a face, a tier or a reserved
field. At a typical SOI the answer is 2.2 zettabytes of *nothing*, and a body written dense enough to
pull at 1 g inflates its SOI by a further 5.5× (§3.4). **The obvious objection now that the ladder
exists — "address the sky at tier 7 and it is 128× cheaper per axis" — does not survive arithmetic:**
eight rungs buy `2^21 ≈ 2.1 × 10⁶` in volume against a gap of `10¹⁹`, thirteen orders of magnitude
short, and the coarse cells would still all be air. The other alternative within the grid — freezing
the *angular* resolution so blocks grow with altitude — is a different thing from the ladder and is
still rejected: it makes a 1 m surface block a 100 m block at 100 R **on the same rung**, which
contradicts "blocks are 1 m and square" and destroys the single-container property HR4 rests on. The
ladder is a resolution choice *per chunk*, not a coordinate warp; it never changes what a tier-L cell
means from one place to another.

**Where the planet's grid stops, exactly.** The domain is the closed radial band
`[floor_radius_m, ceiling_m)` over all six faces (§3.3.5). Below the floor: the core, not addressable,
presented as the indestructible bottom face of the lowest chunk layer and justified diegetically as
the mantle. Above the ceiling: not part of the planet's grid. `addr_of` returns `None` and `neighbor`
returns `Outside` for both, so the boundary is a total typed answer, not a clamp. An edit above the
ceiling is rejected with a typed `OutsideDomain` error, never silently dropped. And the generator
carries the invariant `max_relief ≤ H_scale/2` from §3.5.1: the ceiling clamp is an assertion that
*never fires*, rather than a shaping operation. (The earlier draft let the generator clamp against the
ceiling, which both produces flat mesa tops wherever it bites and leaves a player standing on an 8 km
peak with only `margin` metres of build height. With the invariant, the worst case is a mountain at
half the scale height and a guaranteed ≥ `H_scale/2` of build room above every peak.)

**The three-state chunk model, so a restart never produces holes — restated per tier.**

The three states survive the ladder unchanged; what changes is that "the delta" means two different
records depending on the rung, and the *store* answer at a coarse rung is the edit pyramid rather
than the edit list.

| state | store record | tier 0 | tier L > 0 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Absent** | none | no player has ever edited this chunk | no edited fine cell lies anywhere beneath this chunk |
| **Derived** | none | materialised in memory; pure generator output | materialised in memory; pure **octave-dropped** generator output (§3.5.6) |
| **Delta'd** | present | generator output **+ the edit list** (§3.9.3) | octave-dropped generator output **+ the edit pyramid** (§3.9.8) |

Absence in the *store* means "no delta", which is a total and meaningful answer at every rung.
Absence in the *residency map* means "cache miss", which is not an answer at all. The
missing-terrain-after-restart bug is prevented structurally: there is exactly one read path,

```rust
fn chunk_at(&mut self, key: ChunkKey) -> &Chunk    // never Option; `key` carries the tier
```

backed by a `ChunkSource` that generates on miss. It takes `&mut self` — a `&self` method that
generates on miss would need interior mutability over the residency map, in sim code that bans
default-hasher `HashMap` and must stay deterministic; the guarantee is the return type, not the
receiver. No API anywhere returns `Option<Chunk>` to gameplay. The only `Option` in the system is the
store lookup, and its `None` arm is a delta answer.

**The read path at a coarse rung is two steps and the order is fixed:** generate the tier-L field by
dropping octaves, then **overwrite only where the pyramid has an entry**. Never the reverse, and
never a merge that averages the two — the pyramid entry is the authored truth for its coarse cell and
the generator is the baseline everywhere else. That ordering is what makes a dug tunnel a partially
hollowed coarse cell instead of a disappearance, and a built tower a solid coarse cell of the right
material. It is **one function**, and the mesher, the coarse ground tint and the pyramid walk-up all
call it, so the three cannot disagree:

```rust
fn coarse_summary(a: CoarseAddr) -> CellSummary {
    chunk_pyramid.get(a).map(PyramidEntry::summary)
                        .unwrap_or_else(|| generate_summary(a))
}
// then: representative(coarse_summary(a), &ADMITS) -> (BlockTypeId, Orient)
```

**One law governs the whole ladder and it belongs here rather than in the renderer:**

> **Two players at different distances legitimately see different terrain *detail*. They must never
> see different terrain *facts*.**

The edit pyramid is the mechanism that makes the second half true — an edit is visible at *every*
rung — and the exclusion list of Addendum 2 §C.7 is the mechanism that keeps it true for everything
that is not terrain. Two of that list's items are enforced in this section rather than asserted:
**collision is tier-0 only**, which is a type, not a convention (`Tier0Key` is the only thing the
collider derivation and the store's write path accept, §3.9.8); and **the writable grid is tier 0**,
for the same reason. A coarse chunk can be handed to a mesher and to nothing else.

**How a player builds a floating structure in the sky.** He does, and it is better than sky voxels.
Placing a block on a **construction anchor** — a real, craftable, quota'd item — mints a new realm: a
construction realm with `VoxelGeometry::Cartesian`, `GridMapping::Identity`, parented to the planet,
with an analytic bounding `Boundary` (Obb) that the blocks inscribe (D-45 (i), scoped per §3.1.2). It
gets its own redb store, its own demand-driven spin-up through the landed RLM machinery, its own
physics authority, and its own place in the containment tree. It is *literally the same object as a
ship without engines* — HR2's position anyway — so a floating base can later grow thrusters and fly
away with no new machinery.

The earlier draft made this an *implicit* consequence of placing an untethered block, which is an
unbounded resource-exhaustion vector and leaves four questions unanswered. All four are answered here:

| question | rule |
|---|---|
| **Admission** | Minting requires placing a `ConstructionAnchor` item, which must be crafted from materials. Per-account concurrent anchors are capped by `max_anchors_per_account` in `BlockStoreTuning`; the mint is refused (typed error, surfaced as UI text) past the cap. One click never mints a realm; one crafted item does. |
| **Adjacency** | A block placed against an existing construction realm's inscribed boundary **joins that realm** through the ordinary cross-realm forward path (§3.9.7) — it never mints a third. Only an anchor mints. |
| **Merge** | Two construction realms whose boundaries come to intersect do **not** auto-merge. A deliberate *weld* action performs a one-time durable transfer of the smaller realm's whole chunk-delta set into the larger through the existing transfer FSM, as a new `TransferableKind::VoxelVolume`, followed by retirement of the emptied realm. Reserving the kind tag now is free; this is a P8 build item, ledgered, not built at P4. |
| **Abandonment / GC** | A construction realm with no anchor owner, no player-authored blocks beyond the anchor, and no demand for `reap_after` (in `BlockStoreTuning`) is reaped: its store is archived to a single compressed record and its directory entry retired. Reaping runs as an ordinary owner-authority operation at spin-up, never as a background writer. |
| **Detachment** | Removing the block that connects a ground structure to terrain does **not** spontaneously mint a realm. That would be a re-home of a voxel volume across a grid-mapping boundary (Spherical → Identity), which `satisfies()`'s exact geometry equality forbids by construction. Ground-built structures are part of the planet grid, permanently, and float when unsupported. Structural detachment is a P8 mechanic requiring an anchor and a deliberate action. |

The awkward remaining case — a tower built from the ground *through* the ceiling — is engineered away:
the ceiling sits at `R + H_scale` (~8.4 km above the datum) and, with the `max_relief ≤ H_scale/2`
invariant, at least 4.2 km above every generated peak. The client surfaces the refusal as "you have
reached the top of the atmosphere; place a construction anchor to start a floating structure", which
turns a limit into the mechanic that already exists.

Air *simulation* (sealed volumes, pressure, flow) is section 4/6 territory. The seam this section
plants: a sealed volume is discovered by a flood fill over the chunk container using
`GridMapping::neighbor`, so it works unchanged on a planet and inside a ship, and the per-cell air
state is a derived overlay, never a stored one.

---

### 3.7 What the client holds — the draw-radius wall, and why it is gone

**This subsection is rewritten, and the thing it is rewriting is a wall.** The former text concluded
that the visible chunk count grows with the square of the draw radius, that no atmospheric derivation
produces an affordable number, and that the gap between an affordable 449 columns and 1.28 million at
5 km of altitude *was the open no-LOD ruling and could not be closed here*. Addendum 1 §C.4 then
sharpened the same finding into its central claim: **"the binding constraint is the drawn radius, not
the planet radius — roughly 700 m to 1 km of fully meshed terrain is what one-metre blocks with no
detail tiers can afford, on any planet."**

> **That finding is dissolved.** The ruling came back as *detail levels everywhere*, and with one rung
> per power of two the visible chunk count grows with the **logarithm** of view distance instead of
> its square. There is no draw-radius wall, at any planet size, at any altitude. Both constraints that
> the section and the addendum called binding are gone at once, and what replaces them is a
> residency *budget* — a number you spend, not a distance you cannot cross.

Everything below replaces the old policy. The parts that survive unchanged are named as such.

#### 3.7.1 Choosing the rung — the existing rule, one level down

The locked area-of-interest model is *"angular size above a threshold, one generic rule for every
realm kind, never branching on type."* Tier selection is the same rule applied to chunks:

> **Pick the coarsest tier whose cells still subtend at least the target number of screen pixels.**

That is screen-space error, the standard correct metric, and — this is the point — it composes with
the existing demand loop instead of introducing a second scheduler. **One per-pixel angle, one range
formula, one reference screen, all of them fields of the render tuning struct and never literals:**

```
render_width_px    = 1920            // the ONE reference screen
render_height_px   = 1080
fov_h_rad          = 1.2217          // 70 degrees HORIZONTAL
px_per_cell_target = 2.0

theta_px = fov_h_rad / render_width_px              // ON AXIS. 6.363e-4 rad at the reference screen.
R_L      = 2^L / (px_per_cell_target · theta_px)    // 785.8 m · 2^L  ⇒  786 m at rung 0.
```

So **tier L is used out to `785.7 × 2^L` metres**: 786 m, 1.6 km, 3.1 km, 6.3 km, 12.6 km, 25.2 km,
50.3 km, 100.6 km, 201 km, 402 km. Every figure in this section, and §5's, §6's and §8's, is built on
that on-axis value.

**One calibration note, stated once and used in no arithmetic:** the screen-edge worst case is
`2·tan(fov_h_rad/2) / render_width_px = 7.294e-4` rad, 14.6 % tighter than the on-axis value. That is
*why* `px_per_cell_target` defaults to 2.0 rather than 1.75. It is not a second formula and the
`685 · 2^L` range it would imply appears nowhere.

`px_per_cell_target` is the one knob that trades sharpness against everything else, and it must be
runtime-tunable for the tuning overlay. Its shipped value and the governor above it are register
row 38 / **[USER DECISION 8-B]**.

This ladder has a published name and a published parameter set: it is **CDLOD** (Strugar, JGT 2010),
whose quadtree uses exactly this relation — *"each successive LOD level is used to render four times
as many triangles"* with *"the range of each level being two times larger than that of the previous
one"*. Two things transfer as citations rather than guesses: the crossfade band should cover **the
last 15–30 % of each rung's range** (§3.7.4 takes 15–20 %), and the grid resolution is explicitly a
runtime knob usable to draw cheaper versions for reflections and low-quality shadow passes.

#### 3.7.2 What it costs, in numbers

Each rung occupies an annulus between its own range and the previous rung's. The arithmetic falls out
**constant**: the annulus area grows by four and the chunk footprint grows by four, so

> **every rung above the first holds about 379 chunk columns, regardless of which rung it is.**
> Tier 0 is a disc and holds about 505. Both figures are **independent of the planet's radius.**

`columns(T rungs) = 505 + 379·(T − 1)`. Taking three vertical chunks at tier 0 and two above (the
min/max pyramid of §3.5.2 measures the real number per column; these are the conservative defaults):

| view distance | rungs | chunk columns | chunks | mesh @ 17.6 KB (V2 packed, **measured**) | mesh @ 40 KB (V2 packed, **conservative**) | mesh @ 480 KB today | gen, 1 core | gen, 8 cores | columns **without** the ladder |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 786 m | 1 | 505 | 1,515 | 27 MB | 61 MB | 727 MB | 1.34 s | 0.17 s | 505 |
| 1.6 km | 2 | 884 | 2,273 | 40 MB | 91 MB | 1.09 GB | 1.9 s | 0.24 s | 2,019 |
| 6.3 km | 4 | 1,642 | 3,789 | 67 MB | 152 MB | 1.82 GB | 2.9 s | 0.37 s | 32,300 |
| 25 km | 6 | 2,400 | 5,305 | 93 MB | 212 MB | 2.55 GB | 3.7 s | 0.46 s | 517,000 |
| 100 km | 8 | 3,158 | 6,821 | 120 MB | 273 MB | 3.27 GB | 4.3 s | 0.53 s | 8,170,000 |
| 402 km | 10 | 3,916 | 8,337 | 147 MB | 333 MB | 4.00 GB | 5.1 s | 0.63 s | 132,000,000 |

**Both mesh figures are quoted, always, and both are labelled.** 2,200 quads/chunk is the **measured**
figure for natural terrain (0fps's 1.3× merge ratio against the culled count); 5,000 quads/chunk is a
**conservative allowance** for high-relief or heavily-built chunks. At the V2 8-byte-per-quad format
that is 17.6 KB and 40.0 KB per chunk. The earlier table quoted only the conservative column and did
not say so, which reads as a measurement and inflates every downstream storage line by 2.3×.

Generation uses the measured 0.885 ms per tier-0 chunk and ~0.55 ms averaged over the coarse rungs
(§3.5.3). Meshing at binary greedy meshing's ~65 µs per 62³ chunk is 0.44 s for the whole 100 km set
on one core and is not the constraint.

**The mesh column is where the honesty has to be, and Addendum 2 understated it.** Addendum 2 §C.3
quoted a 100 km view as "about 270 MB of mesh at the packed vertex format". That is the **V2
conservative** number and it is correct as such — the measured-terrain figure for the same view is
120 MB — and it is **the packed format doing the work**: at the 24-byte `MeshPrim` vertex the client
ships today, the identical view is **3.27 GB**. So the correct statement about decision row 21 is
narrower than Addendum 2's:

> Row 21, the vertex format, **no longer decides whether a planet can exist** — on foot, at any planet
> size, on today's format, the ladder needs 727 MB and that fits. It **still decides whether flight at
> altitude fits a VRAM budget**: 3.27 GB at 100 km on today's format against 273 MB packed
> (conservative) / 120 MB packed (measured). It
> de-escalates out of the "blocks all terrain" set and into "blocks the flight gate", which is a real
> de-escalation and not a dismissal.

#### 3.7.3 The residency policy

Only the seed and deltas cross the wire, so residency is a purely local decision and the client can
be aggressive. Four of the six rules below are the old ones, unchanged.

1. **Meshes are resident for the whole tiered render set** — now ~6,800 chunks at a 100 km view
   instead of 24.5 million. *(Unchanged in kind; the set is what changed.)*
2. **Voxels are resident only for tier-0 chunks within the edit/collider radius, and for any chunk
   carrying a delta.** Everything else is dropped after meshing and regenerated on demand — legal
   only because generation is Category-A, deterministic and sub-millisecond per column. Determinism
