   here is not only a correctness property; it is a memory optimisation, and the ladder makes it a
   larger one because coarse rungs are cheaper to regenerate than the fine rung they replace.
   *(Unchanged, and strengthened.)*
3. **Tier 0 is always resident wherever a player is** — which is exactly the region physics runs in,
   and is how Addendum 2 §C.7's "collision is always tier 0" is satisfied without a special case.
4. **Coarse-first, refine-later, as an ordering constraint on the demand queue.** Never request a fine
   rung for a column that has no coarse rung resident. This is the operational content of the one
   scheduling idea worth taking from Pearl Abyss's *hierarchical proxy loading* — it is what makes a
   world look *loaded* during traversal instead of showing holes — and it composes directly with the
   existing demand loop, which already spins realms up ahead of reach. It also makes Addendum 2's
   *"the realm proxy is the coarsest rung"* operationally true rather than merely conceptual: the
   proxy is the always-resident fallback that guarantees there is never a hole. Cost: an ordering rule
   plus a resident-rung bitmask per chunk column in the request queue. Near zero.
5. **Scheduling is the same AoI predicate as the realm demand loop, with the same hysteresis. No
   second scheduler.** Chunk generation, meshing, pipeline warm-up and GPU residency are declared
   phases of the existing demand loop, and the per-cell spatial index D-9/D-39.5 need for entity AoI
   is the same index chunk residency keys off. *(Unchanged, and now doing more work.)*
6. **A residency budget governor sits above the pixel target.** The pixels-per-cell figure is the
   *target*; when resident bytes exceed `resident_chunk_byte_cap` the governor raises it globally
   toward `px_per_cell_ceiling`, with hysteresis, until they fit. This exists because of a specific
   cautionary case: Crimson Desert's most-criticised flaw traces to a fixed ~8 GB texture-memory
   target enforced by uniformly aggressive detail reduction rather than by adaptive shedding, so
   dense scenes read as cut everywhere instead of cut where it is cheapest. Its fields and defaults
   (`px_per_cell_target` 2.0, `px_per_cell_ceiling` 4.0, `resident_chunk_byte_cap`,
   `governor_hysteresis` 0.15, `crossfade_band_fraction` 0.15) are register row 38 /
   **[USER DECISION 8-B]**; tens of lines, purely client-local cosmetic policy: no server state, no
   determinism exposure, no fence — **and its output reaches the server only as the clamped,
   non-authoritative `tier_floor` hint of §3.10, from which no server-authoritative quantity may be
   derived.** It must be smoothed or it becomes a pop source, which §3.7.4's crossfade already
   handles. Two constraints ride with it and neither is optional: it may never shrink tier 0 below
   `max_tool_reach + one chunk edge`, or building stops working at range; and it may never change
   collision, physics or any gameplay-visible fact.

#### 3.7.4 Crossfade residency, and the fade-direction rule that costs 4×

Addendum 2 §C.6 requires a distance-banded dither crossfade between two rungs of the same terrain, so
both rungs are resident and drawn for the width of the band. It did not state the price, and the price
depends on a choice nobody would otherwise notice:

> **The coarse rung fades in over the fine rung's outer band; the fine rung dies at its own range.
> Never the reverse.**

With a band covering the last fraction `f` of a rung's range, the doubly-resident area is
`R²(1 − (1−f)²)` against an annulus of `0.75 R²`. If the *coarse* rung is the one brought in early,
the extra columns are coarse ones with a 4× larger footprint, costing about 45 columns per boundary at
`f = 0.2` — **about +10 %** on the 100 km view's 3,158 columns across all seven boundaries. If the
*fine* rung is instead kept alive into the coarse annulus, the extra columns are fine ones and the
same band costs **about +40 %**. That one-line ordering rule is the difference between the residency
gate — **≤ 7,500 resident chunks including crossfade residency, measured while moving** — passing and
failing at the exact moment the player is moving.

Cross-checked against CDLOD's published 15–30 % morph band: `f = 0.15` costs about +8 % and `f = 0.3`
about +14 %. **The tuning field is `RenderTuning::crossfade_band_fraction`** — one field, shared with
§4's AO ramp, §6's prop impostor band and §5's shadow-distance derivation, never a second copy — **and
its shipped value is bounded by the residency gate rather than chosen freely**: `f = 0.15` passes at
7,353 chunks and `f = 0.20` fails at 7,510, which is why the shipped default is 0.15.

#### 3.7.5 The draw radius, and a derivation that now works

The old ruling stands where it still applies and is **struck where it does not**. It said `D` is a
budget-derived operational parameter because the atmospheric derivation produced numbers three orders
of magnitude beyond every budget. Re-run it against the ladder. Koschmieder gives visual range
`V = 3.912/β_ext` at a 2 % contrast threshold: a hazy but normal day is 20–30 km, aerosol-loaded "very
clear" air about 50 km, clean Rayleigh air at sea level 200–330 km.

| derived visual range | old cost (single rung) | rungs **resident** (`tier_view_max`) | columns | chunks | mesh @ 40 KB (conservative) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 741 m | 449 columns — the only affordable point | 1 | 505 | 1,515 | 61 MB |
| 30 km (hazy day) | 735,500 columns, **706 GB** | 7 | 2,779 | 6,063 | 243 MB |
| 50 km ("very clear") | 2.04 M columns, **1.96 TB** | 7 | 2,779 | 6,063 | 243 MB |
| 200 km (clean Rayleigh) | not computable | 9 | 3,537 | 7,579 | 303 MB |
| 330 km | not computable | 10 | 3,916 | 8,337 | 333 MB |

> **So the derivation that failed now succeeds, and the design is better for it — but it derives a
> RESIDENCY bound, not the key's ceiling.** ~~"The top of a body's ladder is `tier_depth =
> ceil(log2(V_atm / d₀)) + 1`, clamped to `[1, 10]`."~~ **Struck**, and split in two, because the
> earlier text used one number for two different observers.
>
> - **`tier_view_max = ceil(log2(V_atm / R_0)) + 1`, clamped to `[1, tier_depth]`** — the coarsest
>   rung a client **inside** this body's atmosphere ever requests, where `V_atm` comes from the
>   seed-derived scale height and optical depth and `R_0` is tier 0's reach from the pixel target
>   (§3.7.1). A vacuum body clamps at its ceiling; a fog-bound one needs three rungs. This is the
>   derivation the table above computes, it is correct, and it is a **residency** bound: it says which
>   rungs get *asked for*, never which rungs are *addressable*.
> - **`tier_depth = ceil(log2 m) + 1`** — the face-covering rung plus one, derived from the body's
>   size rather than its air, because it bounds a **persisted key** and an observer outside the
>   atmosphere sees the whole body. This is the ceiling the five tier bits of §3.3.6 are sized
>   against, it is what decision 3-I's divisibility rule is applied to, and its rider (a full-depth
>   body's `m` is a power of two) is in §3.3.3.
>
> Both are fields of `BodyPhysical` (§3.4) and they are the only new per-body numbers the ladder
> introduces. The `[1, 10]` clamp is gone: it was a cap on the wrong quantity, and it would have made
> §5's recommended "blocks all the way to the face-covering rung" unbuildable on an Earth-sized body.
> Where the ladder *stops* — blocks to the face-covering rung versus an earlier hand-off to a proxy —
> is register row 1 / **one-way door 14**, taken with the key layout because the two are the same
> decision seen from two ends.

#### 3.7.6 Spin-up, and what a player actually waits for

Arrival at a body is now a **coarse-to-fine fill, not a radius sweep**, and the arithmetic is
comfortable everywhere:

| moment | what must be resident | one core | eight cores |
|---|---|---|---|
| first frame at 100 km (all rungs, coarse-first) | 6,821 chunks | 4.3 s | 0.53 s |
| …of which the coarse rungs alone, drawn first | 5,306 chunks | 2.9 s | 0.36 s |
| descending to the ground | +1,515 tier-0 chunks | 1.34 s | 0.17 s |
| walking one chunk forward | ~7 columns per rung | ~5 ms | — |
| after an edit | one tier-0 column-stack + ≤ `tier_depth − 1` pyramid entries (12 at the starter world's `tier_depth = 13`), walk-up ≤ 5.85 µs | ~0.9 ms | — |

The demand loop already spins a realm up *before* the player reaches it; the ladder adds the same
hysteresis one level down, and because the coarse rungs both cover the most ground and cost the least
to produce, **the thing that arrives first is a complete world rather than a nearby fragment of one.**
That is what makes warp arrival seamless rather than merely fast, and it is the same property the
seamless law demands of every other transition in the game.

**Everything the old text listed as "not foreclosing the ruling" is now spent rather than reserved.**
The three key bits became **five** and carry a value (§3.3.6); the height-first generator's ability to
produce a tier-L chunk *directly and exactly* became the generator contract (§3.5.6); and the
genuinely hard part — folding a player's dug tunnel into a coarse rung so it does not vanish at 200 m
and reappear at 100 m — is built rather than gestured at (§3.9.8).

---

### 3.8 Ore foreknowledge

P4's DoD guarantees, by construction, that every player can compute the location of every deposit on
every planet in the galaxy before anyone mines. This is structurally worse than the Minecraft X-ray
problem — X-ray needs the chunk to be loaded and sent; here an offline tool enumerates the galaxy from
the seed the moment the client binary is extracted. It collides directly with the already-decided
player-driven economy, whose price signal depends on scarcity producing information.

The structural requirement, whichever way this goes, must be planted at P4: **the generator is split
into a public half and a concealed half.**

```rust
pub fn gen_public   (params: &PlanetParams, key: ChunkKey) -> Chunk;        // compiled into the client
pub fn gen_concealed(secret: &ServerSecret, key: ChunkKey) -> SparseDelta;  // server-only crate
```

The client links only the first; `client_server_terrain_parity` (§3.5.4) is the gate that fails the
day someone links the second into the client. Splitting it at P4 is free. Splitting it after P6
persists deltas is a schema migration plus a regeneration of every planet's resources under players'
existing builds.

> **[USER DECISION 3-G] — ore placement and what discovery is worth.** A genuine one-way door: it is
> irreversible the moment the client ships.
>
> - **(A) Accept it. All deposits are public and computable.** Scarcity becomes about access,
>   transport cost and territorial control rather than prospecting. Coherent, with precedent (EVE's
>   static belts). Costs nothing. Prospecting gameplay has no value; first-mover advantage is decided
>   by travel time, which is decided by ship technology, which is player-driven.
> - **(B) All ore is a server-only overlay.** Deposits are generated from a `ServerSecret` that never
>   ships and delivered as deltas on the P6 path. Bandwidth is proportional to *digging*, not to
>   terrain: a chunk's ore delta ships only when the chunk enters the player's small collider/edit
>   radius, so foreknowledge is bounded at tens of metres and ore genuinely reveals itself as you
>   mine. Storage cost is zero (the overlay is regenerable from the secret). Cost: the "only the seed
>   crosses the wire" rule acquires a documented exception for one material class.
> - **(C) Hybrid — recommended.** Common ores (iron, copper, coal) are seed-derived and public; rare
>   and strategic deposits are concealed and revealed by exposure or by a survey action the server
>   validates. The bulk of terrain keeps the byte-identical gate meaningful and the early game needs
>   no network at all, while the high-value tier — the part the economy's price signal actually
>   depends on — keeps real scarcity and real discovery value.
>
> **Recommendation: (C).** It costs one `MaterialClass::{Public, Concealed}` field in the block
> registry and the generator split above, both of which are free at P4.

---

### 3.9 Persistence

#### 3.9.1 One writer, and a key that cannot move

The store is per realm and single-writer. Two different keys are involved and conflating them is the
defect the earlier draft shipped.

- **The directory key is the `RealmPath`, never a bare `RealmId`.** `realm_coord.rs:49-52` documents
  in the type itself that `lowered()` is lossy — Universe→System(0), Galaxy→System(1), and every
  System seed collapses across galaxies — and says *"NEVER use as a directory/saga/dedup key at
  multi-galaxy scale"*. D-RLM-10 is already an open finding for exactly this mistake made once. Block
  edits are the longest-lived durable state in the game, so a key collision there silently merges two
  planets' builds and is unrecoverable. **This amends roadmap P6's committed "DBs keyed by RealmId
  (not shard_id)"**; the amendment is named rather than inferred, and its reason is the documented
  lossiness plus the open finding.
- **The *file name* is an immutable `RealmUid`, never the `RealmPath`.** `RealmPath` is by definition
  *"a realm's ordered lineage from the Universe root"*, and the project's own travel model is
  lineage-changing: fly out of System A's SOI and the deepest container becomes the Galaxy, so the
  path shortens; approach System B and it lengthens again. P8 makes a ship its own persisted voxel
  realm, and §3.6 lets a construction realm grow thrusters and fly away. **Naming the database file
  after the path means every interstellar trip renames a ship's block store**, and a crash between
  the rename and the directory CAS loses the interior — the `last_owner_fence` protection does not
  help, because the file the new owner opens is a *different file*.

```rust
/// Immutable for the realm's entire life. Never derived from the current lineage.
pub struct RealmUid(u128);
```

- For **seed-derived realms** (planets, moons, systems) the uid is a deterministic `SplitMix64` fold
  over the realm's **birth** lineage — reproducible from the seed alone, with no directory round-trip,
  and stable because a planet's birth lineage never changes.
- For **minted realms** (ships, constructions) the uid is directory-minted at birth in the same
  `(mint_shard, seq, rand)` shape `EntityId` already uses, and recorded in the parent's manifest.

The file is `realm-<uid:032x>.redb`. A `RealmDescriptor` record inside it repeats the uid, the
*current* path, `universe_epoch_id`, `epoch_schema_version`, `gen_schema_version`, the `PlanetParams`
digest, and `last_owner_fence`. The path inside the file is advisory metadata that gets rewritten on
re-home; nothing is ever renamed.

This still couples the block store to the one genuinely load-bearing owed P4 piece: `path_for_realm`
at real scale is backed by a fixed 7-realm roster today, and `universe_generator.md` names the general
inversion as *"the load-bearing owed piece"* at P4. **The inversion lands with the storage layer, not
after it.**

Two reservations follow and both are free today. `RealmKindTag` has exactly six arms — `Universe,
Galaxy, System, Planet, Station, Area` — and it is a **frozen append-only postcard discriminant
surface** by its own doc comment. It has no `Ship` and no `Construction`. §3.6 mints construction
realms and P8 mints ships. **Append both arms now**; appending after ships persist is a wire-version
event. Likewise reserve `TransferableKind::VoxelVolume` for the weld path (§3.6).

#### 3.9.2 The record

roadmap.json P6 specifies "5-byte dedup-to-final edits". Five bytes is 40 bits. A 62³ chunk needs
**18 bits** of local index (238,328 < 2¹⁸), leaving 22. Material plus shape plus orientation alone is
25 bits at any sane width. The 5-byte figure predates the non-cube-shape discussion and cannot carry
the format.

```
WAL edit record — 8 bytes, one u64:
  bits 63..46  cell index   (18)   0..238_327
  bits 45..14  block state  (32)   material | shape | orientation | damage | flags — §4 owns the split
  bits 13..0   reserved     (14)   MUST be zero
```

This section fixes the record's *shape* and the state word's *width* at 32 bits; section 4 fixes the
state word's internal fields. A WAL frame batches records for one `(chunk, tick)`:
`{ chunk: Tier0Key, fence: u64, universe_tick: u64, epoch: EpochTag, count: u32, records: [u64] }`.
"Dedup-to-final" is a `BTreeMap<(Tier0Key, CellIndex), BlockState>` drained in sorted order, so only
the final state per cell per batch is written and the byte output is deterministic — which is what
P6's "deterministic WAL byte output (sorted drain)" scenario asserts.

**The frame's key is a `Tier0Key`, not a `ChunkKey`, and that is the ladder's single most important
storage invariant** (§3.9.8): only tier 0 is writable, every coarser rung is derived. A WAL frame
addressed at a coarse tier is not a rejected input, it is an **unrepresentable** one.

> **[USER DECISION 3-H] — the durable edit record width.** roadmap.json commits 5 bytes; the
> arithmetic says it cannot work. One-way door: P6's DoD requires edits to survive `kill -9` and a
> re-shard, so widening after players have built is a migration over every saved world.
>
> - **(A) 8 bytes — recommended.** 18-bit index + 32-bit state + 14 reserved. Aligned, one `u64`,
>   generous headroom for shapes, damage, ownership and signal ports.
> - **(B) 6 bytes.** 18-bit index + 24-bit state (10-bit material = 1,024 materials, 7-bit shape,
>   5-bit orientation, 2 flags) + 6 reserved. This does fit, and 1,024 materials is ample. It leaves
>   no room for per-block damage state in the durable word.
> - **(C) Variable-width TLV per record.** `core/src/tlv.rs` already provides the machinery, but it
>   costs the fixed-size property that makes the sorted drain cheap and deterministic.
>
> **Recommendation: (A).** The 3-byte saving of (B) is worth ~300 MB across 100 M edits — noise
> against the cost of a format migration.
>
> **Addendum 1 §B reframed the same question and it is worth carrying here.** Its §2.7 layout closes
> at **five** bytes — 18-bit index, 16-bit combined block type, 5-bit orientation, 1 bit
> generated-or-player-placed — but only because of two upstream verdicts: **mirroring is a separate
> shape rather than a flag**, and **identity is one combined `(substance, form, function)` number
> rather than separate substance and shape fields**. If both verdicts hold, five bytes fits with a
> bit spare and the roadmap's committed figure survives. If either is reversed, five stops fitting
> and the answer is eight. So 3-H is really *"do you accept those two verdicts, or do you want
> fifteen reserved bits"* — and the ~300 MB is the price of the slack either way. What is **not**
> defensible is leaving it open past the point the chunk format freezes.

Every operational number in this subsystem lives in one config struct, **`BlockStoreTuning`**,
alongside `TransferTuning`/`TransportTuning`: the WAL fsync interval (~250 ms), the per-realm delta
budget, `max_anchors_per_account`, `reap_after`, the per-session edit rate cap and `max_reach_m`. No
inline literals.

#### 3.9.3 The chunk record — one delta, two encodings, no terrain

The compactor folds WAL frames into `chunk_delta: ChunkKey → ChunkRecord`. The earlier draft offered
two *semantically different* forms — a sparse delta and a dense chunk "taken verbatim, ignoring the
generator" — and that difference caused two separate defects: a dense record **is terrain** and
shipping it contradicts P4's *"only the seed crosses the wire"* and P6's *"the binding no chunk
streaming rule"*; and a `gen_schema_version` bump on a dense record has only two outcomes, discard
(delete a player's rebuilt chunk) or abort (the planet will not load). Both disappear if the two forms
are **two encodings of the same thing**:

> **A `ChunkRecord` is always, semantically, the set of player-authored cells.** It never embeds
> generator output. Two encodings, and the compactor picks whichever is smaller — computed exactly,
> not against a guessed threshold:
>
> - **Sparse:** the ascending list of `(cell, state)` 8-byte records. `8n` bytes.
> - **Masked-dense:** a 238,328-bit authored-cell bitmask (**29,791 bytes, fixed**) plus the palette
>   plus the bit-packed states of the authored cells only, in ascending index order.
>   `29,791 + palette + n·bits/8` bytes.
>
> Crossover at an 8-bit packed state: `8n ≥ 29,791 + n` ⇒ **n ≥ 4,256 cells (1.8 % of a chunk)**. A dug
> tunnel stays sparse; a heavily rebuilt chunk flips masked-dense at a fifth of the edit count the
> old rule required, and the masked-dense form is strictly smaller than sparse from that point on.

Three properties fall out for free. **(1) The wire never carries terrain**, because there is no
encoding that contains an unedited cell — §3.10's payload is authored cells in either encoding, and
the "no chunk streaming" rule holds literally. **(2) A `gen_schema_version` bump is survivable**: the
unauthored cells are re-derived from the *new* generator and the authored cells are kept verbatim, so
the mismatch path is a re-derive, not a discard-or-abort. A version mismatch is still recorded and
still surfaces a warning (a player's tunnel may now open into different rock), but nothing is lost and
nothing refuses to load. **(3) The delta index the band invariant of §3.5.2 needs is the mask** — the
same bytes, no second structure.

A `ChunkRecord` is **tier-0 only**, by the same invariant as the WAL frame. Its coarse-rung
counterpart is the edit pyramid of §3.9.8, which reuses this subsection's two encodings and its
crossover arithmetic rather than inventing a third form — and which inherits property (2) for the
same reason and by the same construction.

`ChunkRecord` is TLV-framed (`core/src/tlv.rs`) with an `encoding` tag, the payload, `last_lsn`,
`last_fence`, the epoch tag, and a **reserved tag for a future `ClaimId`** (§3.9.7) — giving
skip-unknown evolution, a hard version floor, and canonical ascending-tag bytes that are
content-hash-dedup safe for free.

Compaction uses P6's three-step durable checkpoint verbatim: write snapshots and fsync → record the
durable LSN and fsync → prune WAL entries strictly ≤ LSN. Recovery tolerates an older WAL and is
idempotent last-writer-wins. Write amplification is bounded by an off-tick batched WAL writer.

**Scale check.** Pre-generating the starter world's full band is `6 × 4096² × 272 = 2.74 × 10¹⁰`
chunks = **2.9 PiB** at 4 bits/cell; on an Earth-sized body it is 1,551× that. Ten thousand players
making 100 M edits, clustered at ~500 edits per touched chunk, touch ~200 k chunks: **~800 MB sparse
plus a few hundred MB of chunks that flipped masked-dense — under 1.5 GB per heavily-played planet**,
and **under 1.7 GB once the edit pyramid's ~1.1 entries per edit are added** (§3.9.8). Both figures
are independent of the body's radius, because storage tracks *edits* and not world size — which is
the same reason the ladder makes view cost independent of radius, arriving from the other direction.
Seed-derivability is not an optimisation; it is the only reason a planet is storable at all.

#### 3.9.4 Re-shard, its saga step, and the anti-pattern

P6's DoD includes "a re-sharded planet keeps its edits". The store lives on a persistent volume, named
by the immutable uid, so a new owner opens the same file. The handoff rides the existing transfer FSM
— **with its own step id, not by overloading someone else's.**

`FLUSH_SOURCE_STEP = 7` is documented at `intershard.rs:52` as *"the orchestrator→source **pose-flush**
request AND its source→orch `TransferAck::SourceFlushed` reply"*. It keys `(transfer, step_id)`
idempotency for the entity-state ack family. Overloading it with a block-store flush means a source
that flushed poses but crashed before the block WAL fsync is seen by the orchestrator as having
completed step 7; the `applied_steps` journal then **suppresses the retry** — a lost block WAL flush
with a green saga. That is also a straight violation of the user's standing law ("never hack/repurpose
messages; add proper new types"). Steps 7–18 are allocated, so:

```
pub const BLOCK_STORE_FLUSH_STEP: u32 = 19;   // NEW: drain WAL, fsync, write last_owner_fence, release
pub const BLOCK_EDIT_FORWARD_STEP: u32 = 20;  // NEW: the §3.9.7 forward arm
```

`BLOCK_STORE_FLUSH_STEP` is sequenced **before** the pose flush, with its own ack. **On failure or
timeout the directory CAS must not commit**, the saga takes the ordinary abort path, and the source
retains authority and its store — preserving the established rule that source authority is held until
the destination is Committed.

On open, a shard whose fence is not strictly greater than the stored `last_owner_fence` refuses
loudly. **The fence is the mechanism; a file lock is a courtesy.** The cloud plan puts these stores on
a network-backed persistent volume and advisory locks over network filesystems are not reliable, so
nothing may depend on the lock for correctness. Double-open is detected by the fence, not by the OS.

**The anti-pattern, and how it is made unrepresentable.** D-39.1 names the most likely single defect in
P6: an implementer writes the edit locally on the shard that received the input instead of forwarding
it to the realm owner, breaking single-writer redb safety and HR1 together. Prevent it in the type
system:

- The writable handle is `OwnedBlockStore`, obtained **only** through
  `BlockStore::open_owned(uid, owner_proof)` where `owner_proof` is produced by a directory read that
  returned this shard as the `RealmRef` owner.
- Every mutating method takes `&OwnedBlockStore` **and a `Tier0Key`**. Two orthogonal proofs on the
  same call: *you are the owner* and *this is the writable rung*.
- A non-owner holds a `GhostGrid` — generator output plus received deltas — whose type has **no
  mutating method at all**. There is nothing to call.

#### 3.9.5 How a dormant world advances without a writer

The type-level defence above is correct and must be kept — and, read literally, it makes a **user
pillar impossible**: *99 % of the galaxy is off, yet the world and economy advance believably from NPC
life, materials and constructions.* A dormant realm has no owner and no shard, so nothing can ever
author a block delta on it: an NPC settlement cannot grow, a mine cannot deepen, a half-built
construction cannot finish. The earlier draft never noticed.

The answer is not to grant a background writer. It is to make dormant advance **Category-A**, exactly
like celestial motion:

> **A dormant realm's advance is a closed-form fold `f(realm_seed, tick_span)` evaluated by the owner
> at spin-up, not an accumulation written while it sleeps.** The dormant scheduler is not a shard,
> never opens a block store, and holds no writable handle. What it maintains per realm is a tiny
> `DormantSummary { last_advanced_tick, population, stockpiles, project_states }` — economy-layer
> state on the economy's side of the one-way dependency, never on the realm/physics/lifecycle path.
> On spin-up the owner reads the summary, computes the advance for the elapsed span in one closed-form
> step, and **emits ordinary WAL edits under its own fence**. The advance is therefore idempotent,
> re-shard-safe, crash-safe, and auditable — it is indistinguishable from a player's batch of edits
> once written.

This answers the "what if it never spins up for six months" question directly: nothing accumulates,
nothing is replayed, and the cost of a six-month absence is the same O(1) evaluation as a six-hour
one, because the fold is a function of the span, not a sum over it. It also bounds the result: the
fold is clamped by a `max_advance_span` in `BlockStoreTuning`, so a realm dormant for a year does not
materialise a city.

The alternative — a short-lease "dormant writer" role granted by the directory — is rejected: it
introduces a second writer class into the one place the design has a type-level single-writer proof,
it needs its own fence/lease/renewal machinery, and it makes the dormant tier a scaling cost
proportional to the *dormant* galaxy rather than the played one.

#### 3.9.6 Delta lifecycle: budget, revert, reap

The store must not grow monotonically forever, and griefing must be recoverable.

- **Budget.** A per-realm delta byte budget in `BlockStoreTuning`, **counting the edit pyramid as well
  as the delta** — the pyramid is derived but it is persisted, it grows at ~1.1 entries per edit on the
  mixed-edit planning figure (the shape-dependent range is §3.9.8's four-row table, which spans a
  factor of fifty), and a budget that ignored it would be wrong by 14 % at exactly the moment it
  matters. Exceeding it does not
  silently drop edits; it refuses new edits with a typed error and raises an operational alarm.
  Shedding must be loud, per the transport doctrine already adopted. **The failure mode being avoided
  is documented and shipped elsewhere:** No Man's Sky keeps terrain edits in a fixed set of 255 buffers
  per save, evicts edits outside base bounds when the budget overruns, and visiting a heavily-edited
  base can wipe a player's own edits. That is what an unbudgeted pyramid retrofitted onto a fixed cap
  looks like from the player's side, and it is why the budget must be pyramid-aware from the first
  line rather than after the delta format freezes.
- **Revert.** An admin `RevertRegion { realm, chunk_range }` operation writes **reverting edits through
  the ordinary WAL** — it never deletes records behind the log. Revert is therefore auditable,
  fence-ordered, re-shard-safe, and fans out to clients through the same delta path as any other edit.
  A raw record delete would be none of those things, and — because the pyramid is maintained by the
  ordinary edit path — a revert repairs the coarse rungs for free rather than needing its own pass.
- **Reap.** Abandoned construction realms are reaped per §3.6. Planet realms are never reaped.

#### 3.9.7 The cross-shard forward path, and edit admission

Two `InterShardFlow` arms are needed and both must respect the four structural gates.

`InterShardFlow::BlockEdit(BlockEditForward)` — appended at the **end** of the enum (postcard is
positional and non-self-describing); classified `SideEffecting { IdempotencyKey::TransferStep }` with
`BLOCK_EDIT_FORWARD_STEP = 20`; classified `ProducerLessReliable` in `durability_class`, because no
saga re-drives a block edit — which means **its `push_flow` site must carry `Durability::Retained`**
so the durable outbox mirrors and replays it; and represented in `intershard_closed.rs`'s
`arm_tripwire` and `every_arm()` in the same commit or it does not compile. Payload as already fixed
by `sealed_shards.md`:
`{ realm, fence, edits: Vec<BlockEdit>, origin: EditSource, corr: (TransferId, StepId) }`.

The client→shard leg is the reliable discrete-action carrier D-39.1 says does not exist. roadmap P6
already sanctions the shape: *"RELIABLE discrete actions (BULK[sub] C→G action frames **or CONTROL
with their own seq+ack**)"*. Take the CONTROL variant — `ClientControlMsg` already exists and is
already reliable+ordered — and **build it once, with both consumers named in the code**, because P11's
fire trigger needs the identical thing and `action_bits` rides the unreliable latest-wins
`InputDatagram` today (with a live tripwire in `stub.rs` that flips red the day the sim reads it).

```rust
ClientControlMsg::WorldAction { seq: u32, action: WorldAction }
enum WorldAction {
    BlockEdit { target: WorldBlockRef, op: EditOp },
    // RESERVED: Fire { .. }  — P11, the second consumer
}
struct WorldBlockRef {
    realm: RealmId, chunk: Tier0Key, cell: CellIndex,
    anchor_gen: AnchorGen,        // stale-anchor rejection, the FrameSpace fence
    expected: BlockState,         // CAS guard
}
```

`chunk` is a `Tier0Key`: a client cannot express an edit at a coarse rung, so the owner never has to
reject one. That is one fewer typed error and one fewer adversarial input, obtained by picking the
narrower type.

`expected` earns its bytes twice: it stops a client whose 100–150 ms interpolation buffer is showing
stale state from clobbering a block someone else already changed, and it makes retries idempotent for
free, since a replayed edit sees its own result and returns success without acting.

**But a CAS is not an authorisation.** As written, `WorldBlockRef` is a grant to any
`(realm, chunk, cell)` in the game, gated only by a comparison against the current state — and the
chunk-key layout is published and radius-independent, so an adversarial client enumerates keys and
deletes another player's base from the other side of the planet at line rate. `domain()` does not
help; it only answers "inside the band". **The admission predicate is part of the carrier, not a
later hardening pass:**

1. **Server-side reach.** The edit target must be within `max_reach_m` of the **server's**
   authoritative pose for that session — never a client-supplied position. This is the only thing that
   makes the CAS meaningful.
2. **Realm membership.** The session's current containment realm must be the target realm, or a realm
   whose ghost/overlap region covers the target — and on the forward path (`BlockEditForward`), the
   origin shard ships the *server's* pose for the originating session so the owner can re-run the
   reach test itself. The owner never trusts the forwarder's admission decision.
3. **Rate.** A per-session edit rate cap in `BlockStoreTuning`, enforced at the owner, shed loudly.
4. **Ownership.** A stated but deferred model: a `ClaimId` TLV tag is reserved on `ChunkRecord` now
   (§3.9.3) so a claim/permission layer can land without a record migration. Until it lands, reach +
   rate + membership are the whole policy, and that is stated rather than implied.

While adding the arms, re-sync the four stale prose arm counts (`intershard.rs` says 16,
`wire/src/lib.rs` says 24, `intershard_closed.rs` says 22, the code has 27). The compile-time gates
hold, but HR1's "one reviewed file" story depends on its prose being trustworthy.

**One thing the forward arm does *not* need: a tier.** `BlockEditForward` carries `Tier0Key`s and
nothing else, because only tier 0 is writable (§3.9.8). Whoever owns the realm maintains every coarse
rung locally from the edits it commits, so no coarse data ever crosses a shard boundary and the arm's
payload is unchanged by the entire detail ladder. That is worth noticing: **the ladder adds zero
inter-shard bytes**, which is the strongest possible form of "it does not weaken HR1".

#### 3.9.8 The edit pyramid — the coarse rungs' delta

This is the one genuinely hard piece of the detail ladder and the only part of it that is real work.
The generated world coarsens itself for free (§3.5.6). **Player edits do not** — and if that is
ignored, a tunnel a player dug vanishes at 200 m and reappears at 100 m, and a base they built pops in
and out as they fly. That artefact is forbidden by the seamless law, so this subsection is load-bearing
rather than supporting.

**The invariant that comes first, because everything else depends on it.**

> **Only tier 0 is writable. Every coarser rung is derived from it.**

This is copied verbatim from shipped practice: Space Engineers' voxel storage documents that *"the
storage system can only write to LOD0, with higher LODs computed based on that level"* — you may read
any level, but if you intend to write you must read LOD0. We take it one step further and make it a
**type-level impossibility rather than an API convention**: the writable methods take a `Tier0Key`
(§3.1.1), so `write(tier != 0)` does not compile. The cost of doing it this way is one newtype and one
constructor; the cost of *not* doing it is a class of bug in which a coarse rung is authored directly,
diverges from the fine data it was supposed to summarise, and the divergence is discovered by a player
noticing their tunnel is the wrong shape from a hilltop.

**The record.** One entry per coarse cell that has at least one edited fine cell beneath it. This is
the version four sections were each specifying differently, and it is now **one** record — settled,
not proposed.

```rust
// crates/core/src/block/pyramid.rs — Tier-A, 100 % region+branch. Pure integer arithmetic.
// PERSISTED, PERMANENT, ONE-WAY DOOR (register row 37 / door 43). No branch on tier.

/// The unpacked payload of one coarse-cell summary. Closed under its own update rule:
/// a parent's summary is a function of its eight children's summaries ALONE.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)]
pub struct CellSummary {
    /// Octant o (canonical order: x fastest, then z, then y) set iff child o is non-empty.
    /// At tier 0 this is the drawn variant's baked `octant_mask` (ShapeDef.octant_mask under Orient).
    pub occ_mask:  u8,
    /// Mean fill fraction of the eight children, 0..=255.
    pub fill_256:  u8,
    /// Dominant substance by SUMMED fill over non-empty children; ties -> lowest SubstanceId.
    /// When `occ_mask == 0` this MUST be the realm's declared EMPTY substance id.
    pub substance: SubstanceId,   // u16, the §2.1 substance-table row id
}

/// The persisted 8-byte word. ONE width at EVERY tier: a tier is a number, not a code path.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct PyramidEntry(u64);

Edit-pyramid entry — 8 bytes, one u64, MSB-first:
  bits 63..46  cell       (18)  CellIndex within the tier-L chunk, 0..=238_327
  bits 45..30  substance  (16)  SubstanceId — dominant by summed fill; ties -> lowest id
  bits 29..22  occ_mask    (8)  octant o set iff child octant o is non-empty
  bits 21..14  fill_256    (8)  mean fill fraction of the eight children, 0..=255
  bits 13.. 0  reserved   (14)  MUST be zero; decode REJECTS non-zero (never decode-to-Default)
```

**Two fields this section previously specified are gone, and a reader who remembers them should learn
why.** ~~`authored` (8 bits, the player-authored fraction)~~ is **dropped**: `occ_mask` needs those
eight bits, and §6.5 — the only named consumer the authored fraction ever had — states that it needs
no new pyramid field. ~~`dominant block type` (16 bits, the combined `(substance, form, function)`
id)~~ is replaced by **`substance`**: a `BlockTypeId` carries a shape and possibly a function, and a
coarse cell's shape must come from the mask and the fill rather than from whichever child happened to
dominate. What is *added* is the **octant mask**, and it is the field that earns the record: an
eight-metre ramp built from eight wedges is a *feature* at rung 3, and a fill count thresholded to a
boolean is exactly the documented "castles read as voxel-based blobs" failure.

`fill_256` is what makes a dug tunnel survive — a coarse cell containing a tunnel is *partially*
hollowed rather than binary-solid. ~~"It is drawn solid iff `fill ≥ solid_threshold`, a render tuning
field, default 128."~~ **Struck, and not relocated: there is no threshold on this path at all.**
`occ_mask == 0` means empty and every other mask selects a shape:

```
bucket = (fill_256 as u16 * 9) >> 8                     // 0..=8, exact
(ShapeId, Orient) = COARSE_SHAPE[occ_mask][bucket]      // [[u16; 9]; 256], 4,608 bytes
BlockTypeId = the row for (substance, ShapeId), else the substance's `Cube` row
```

`COARSE_SHAPE`, the bucket function and `representative()` live in `crates/core/src/block/coarsen.rs`
(Tier-A, 100 %) and are **folded into `BlockRegistryHash`**, so a client/owner mismatch is a refused
connection rather than a silently wrong distant silhouette. A client-tunable threshold on that same
decision was the one place a *detail* knob could have produced a visible *fact* difference between two
clients, which the fact/detail law of §3.6 forbids outright — and under this record it is not needed,
so deleting it is free. The one-step `admits` fallback is total because every substance with any block
type row has a `Cube` row.

> ~~**[USER DECISION 3-J]**~~ — **collapsed into register row 37 / [USER DECISION 8-A]**, together
> with §2's 2-H (what a coarse cell remembers) and 2-I (what happens when derived data disagrees with
> its source) and §4's 4-E (the coarse-cell record). Four sections were each asking the owner about
> the same permanent record. Row 37 asks it once, with five sub-questions — (a) contents, (b) how the
> fill is spent on a shape, (c) storage granularity, (d) the write invariant, (e) the divergence
> policy — and the record above is its recommendation (a) A1 + (b) B1 + (c) C1 + (d) D1 + (e) E1. It
> is a one-way door for the same reason 3-H is: Addendum 2 §D.1 puts the pyramid on the list of
> formats that must be frozen before the first world is written, because it is **permanent delta
> data**. Everything §3 argued for survives in row 37 — the 8-byte one-`u64` width, the reserved-bit
> discipline, the absolute (not delta) semantics, the per-`(tier, chunk)` storage block — so this is a
> collapse of the *question*, not a reversal of the answer.

**Absolute, not relative — and why that is the opposite choice from §3.9.3.** `fill_256` is the
post-edit fill fraction, not a signed delta against the generator. §3.9.3 chose "authored cells only,
never generator output" precisely to survive a `gen_schema_version` bump, so the inconsistency needs a
reason and it has one, and it is the reason this section's semantics won over the competing signed-
delta form: a coarse cell's generator baseline is **binary** (one octave-dropped evaluation says solid
or not), so a signed delta would need the coarse cell's *generated solid count* at read time — `8^L`
tier-0 evaluations, **2,097,152 at rung 7** — which is the same four-orders-of-magnitude cost §4.3.2
prices and rejects, and it contradicts §3.5.6's whole premise that a coarse cell is one evaluation.
Absolute fill is smaller, simpler, and its staleness on a generator bump is repaired by the same
recompute-from-deltas pass that §E of Addendum 2 requires anyway. The pyramid is **derived data that
happens to be cached on disk**; the delta is **authored data that cannot be recomputed**. Different
natures, different rules.

**The update rule.** One rule, and it is byte-identity-gated **per tier**, so it is stated exactly
rather than sketched.

```rust
// crates/core/src/block/coarsen.rs — Tier-A, 100 %, FOLDED INTO BlockRegistryHash.
// Branchless shim over monomorphic helpers (HR5's generic-code discipline).
pub fn coarsen(children: &[CellSummary; 8]) -> CellSummary;

  occ_mask  = Σ_{o=0..7} ((children[o].occ_mask != 0) as u8) << o
  fill_256  = ((Σ_{o=0..7} children[o].fill_256 as u16) + 4) >> 3        // round-half-up, exact
  substance = argmax over distinct s of
                Σ { children[o].fill_256 as u32 : children[o].substance == s
                                               && children[o].occ_mask != 0 }
              ties broken by LOWEST SubstanceId
              if occ_mask == 0 then substance = realm.empty_substance and fill_256 = 0

// THE TIER-0 LEAF — the only place the block field is read:
summary_of_tier0_cell(a: BlockAddr) -> CellSummary {
    occ_mask  = BAKED_VARIANT[variant_index[shape][orient]].octant_mask
    fill_256  = ((volume_units as u64 * 255) + CELL_VOLUME_UNITS/2) / CELL_VOLUME_UNITS
    substance = the cell's SubstanceId
}   // CELL_VOLUME_UNITS = 196_608; full cube -> 255, half slab -> 128
```

On commit of the edits touching tier-0 chunk `C` — once per batch, coarse cells deduped — the owner
walks *up*, **inside the WAL's own redb write transaction**:

```
for each touched tier-0 cell a:
    mark a.ancestor(1) dirty
for L in 1 ..= tier_depth - 1:
    for each dirty CoarseAddr parent at rung L (deduped, ascending key order):
        siblings = [ chunk_pyramid.get(s).map(PyramidEntry::summary)
                     .unwrap_or_else(|| generate_summary(s))   // MISS -> GENERATOR, never Default
                     for s in parent.children() ]              // 8 lookups, ONE storage block
        next   = coarsen(&siblings)
        stored = chunk_pyramid.get(parent).map(PyramidEntry::summary)
        if Some(next) == stored { continue }                   // EXIT ON SUMMARY EQUALITY
        if next == generate_summary(parent) { chunk_pyramid.remove(parent) }   // PRUNE
        else { chunk_pyramid.put(parent, PyramidEntry::new(parent.cell, next)) }
        dirty_coarse_chunk(parent.chunk, L)
        mark parent.ancestor(L+1) dirty
```

Four properties of that loop are load-bearing and none of them is decoration.

- **A miss resolves through the GENERATOR, never through disk and never to `Default`.**
  `generate_summary(a)` is the same call the coarse mesher makes — one evaluation of `h(dir, L)` plus
  one strata lookup, in `core/src/grid/gen/`, Category-A deterministic — so the read path, the mesher
  and the walk-up cannot disagree. Composition at read time is one function:
  `coarse_summary(a) = chunk_pyramid.get(a).map(PyramidEntry::summary).unwrap_or_else(|| generate_summary(a))`,
  then `representative(coarse_summary(a), &ADMITS)`.
- **The early exit is on SUMMARY equality, not on representative equality.** Two different summaries
  can share a drawn representative, so exiting on the representative would leave an ancestor whose
  *stored* summary is stale while the pixel is right — and the recompute-from-deltas audit below then
  fails on visually correct data. An unchanged parent implies unchanged ancestors, so exiting on the
  summary is exact.
- **Pruning is exact.** An entry is deleted iff it equals `generate_summary` of its own address. Dig a
  hole, fill it back in, and nothing is left behind at any rung.
- **Order-independence holds at every rung at every instant.** `coarsen` is a pure function of the
  eight children's *current* summaries with a total tie-break (lowest `SubstanceId`, values distinct),
  so its output depends on the tier-0 state and nothing else. That answers — rather than ignores —
  the objection that a live running majority can never match a replay of a dedup-to-final,
  sorted-on-drain WAL: the objection defeats a *streaming estimator*, and this is an *exact
  recompute*. There is therefore **no dirty-dominant bit and no deferred compaction pass**; the
  competing blind-increment rule (`for tier in 1..=TIER_MAX { e.solid_delta += d }`) is **struck**
  along with it, because it cannot produce this record at all.

**Cost.** `walk_up_budget_ns = (tier_depth − 1) · 8 · 5 · 12.19 ns` with every sibling missing —
**5.85 µs at `tier_depth = 13`, 9.75 µs at 21**, ≤ 1 % of a ~1 ms edit budget. With the early exit the
common single edit inside solid rock terminates at rung 1 or 2 (~0.5 µs). Because `CHUNK_EDGE = 62` is
**even**, a rung-L parent's eight children always lie in ONE rung-(L−1) storage block, so the eight
sibling reads are eight lookups inside one block: **≤ 1 entry write and ≤ 1 pyramid storage-block read
per rung per touched coarse cell, zero reads of `block_wal`, zero reads of any tier-0 delta.**

**Storage, and a figure this section previously overstated as a rule.** ~~"The pyramid costs roughly
one seventh of the edits it summarises, in writes and in time."~~ **Struck as a general claim.** One
seventh is `Σ 8^-L`, the compact-3-D case only, and the tunnel example in this very subsection is the
1-D case at ~1×, which is why the two contradicted each other. The cost depends on the **shape** of
the edit set and the four cases span a factor of fifty:

| edit shape | entries per edit | bytes per edit |
|---|---|---|
| compact 3-D cluster | `Σ 8^-L` = 0.143 n | 1.14 B |
| surface / wall (2-D) | `Σ 4^-L` = 0.333 n | 2.67 B |
| line / pipe (1-D) | `Σ 2^-L` ≈ 1.000 n | 8.00 B |
| isolated (hard bound) | `tier_depth − 1` per edit | `8·(tier_depth − 1)` B |

Worked at `tier_depth = 13` (the starter world, `m = 4,096`): a 1,000-edit one-wide tunnel is
`250+125+63+32+16+8+4+2+1+1+1+1 = 504` entries = 4,032 B ≈ **3.9 KiB**; an 8,000-edit 20×20×20 tower
is `1,000+125+27+8+1·8 = 1,168` entries = 9,344 B ≈ **9.1 KiB**; 100 M mixed edits at the ~1.1
entries/edit planning figure is **~880 MB of pyramid**. Deeper ladders do not move the clustered rows
— the series converge — and only the adversarial isolated row grows, bounded by `tier_depth − 1` by
construction. §3.9.3's scale check uses the ~1.1 mixed-edit figure and absorbs it.

**Encoding and keying.** Entries are grouped **per `(tier, chunk)`, not per entry** — one persisted
record holding that chunk's sparse entry list, in the same two encodings as §3.9.3 (sparse `8n`, or
masked-dense `29,791 + palette + n·bits/8`, compactor picks the smaller, same 4,256-cell crossover).
Keying the *storage block* coarser than the *addressing node* is CDLOD's own separation and it is what
keeps redb key counts sane on a heavily built planet: the thousand-block tunnel above becomes ~40
records rather than ~500 keys. The table is **`chunk_pyramid: ChunkKey → PyramidRecord`** — that name
and no other; `block_pyramid` and "beside `block_wal`" are struck — in the **same redb file** as the
delta, so it moves with the realm on a re-shard, flushes under the same `BLOCK_STORE_FLUSH_STEP`
fence, and cannot be separated from the deltas it was derived from. Because §3.3.6 orders keys
`sector → tier → a → b → c`, "every tier-3 pyramid record on face 2" is one range scan.

**Player-built realms are simpler, not harder.** A ship, a station or a floating base has no generated
baseline at all, so its coarse rungs are **pure pyramid**: `generate_summary` returns an empty summary
(`occ_mask == 0`) everywhere and the recursion bottoms out on the hull's own cells. A ship's distant
representation is therefore a downsampled occupancy-and-substance grid maintained on edit, which
degrades continuously into the realm proxy — Addendum 2's *"the proxy is the coarsest rung"* holding
literally for constructions.

**Why the octant mask is the field that earns its bytes.** The most-reported visual failure of a
merged region proxy is that it keeps mass and loses *form* — players describe Crimson Desert's distant
castles as "voxel-based blobs". That is exactly what the pure-pyramid path produces for player-built
structures if occupancy is thresholded to a boolean, which is why this record spends eight bits on the
mask and none on a threshold. The `(occ_mask, fill bucket) → (ShapeId, Orient)` mapping is the
4,608-byte `COARSE_SHAPE` table stated above; it must be identical on server and client, so it lives
in **`vd-core` (Tier-A, 100 % coverage)** and is folded into `BlockRegistryHash`, not left in the
renderer. It adds no representation and no second catalogue, so it is not an HR3 fork.

**The audit, which Addendum 2 §E asks for and which is cheap only if it is built in.** The pyramid is
*derived* data, so it can silently disagree with the truth it came from. Two mitigations, both from
the first line:

- `vdctl world verify-pyramid <realm>` rebuilds every entry from `generator ∪ deltas` and asserts
  **byte-equality** against what is stored.
- The test suite runs that command after **every** edit scenario, so a divergence is a failing
  assertion in CI rather than a player noticing a hilltop. This is the audit that the summary-equality
  early exit above exists to keep passing: an exit on the drawn representative would leave stale
  ancestors that look right and fail here.

**The gate** is Addendum 2 §D.3's, and it writes itself: dig a tunnel and build a tower, fly away,
confirm both are visible at *every* rung boundary, fly back, confirm nothing popped. It is an HR6
`vdctl` scenario on machinery that already exists, and it must run at walking speed as well as at
flight speed — the walk is the case that catches a short crossfade band, and the walk is the case
Crimson Desert visibly failed.

---

### 3.10 The wire

**Terrain never crosses the wire, and §3.9.3 makes that literally true rather than approximately
true** — no `ChunkRecord` encoding contains an unedited cell, so there is nothing to ship but authored
cells. P4's "only the seed crosses the wire" and P6's "the binding no chunk streaming rule" both hold
without exception.

**Server → client.** `crates/wire/src/channels.rs` already ships the message family: `BulkMsg` is a
closed enum on the "uni per sub G→C, reliable, **paced**" carrier, documented as *"chunk payloads land
at P4/P6"* and *"concrete chunk schemas arrive with terrain (P4) as additive variants"*, and
`BulkKind` already reserves `ChunkSnapshot`, `ChunkDelta` and `Catalog`. So the *wire family* is
committed; what is missing is the `MsgClass` **routing arm** in `sim/src/io/mod.rs`, which is what
DEFERRED D-4 owes.

D-4 says *"TWO independent consumers need this ONE arm (build it once; it is shared infra, never
per-feature — HR3/DRY)"*, and its two named consumers are both `EventMsg` consumers (AoI eviction,
cross-shard signals). Chunk deltas are a `BulkMsg` consumer. The question is therefore whether
`MsgClass` gains one arm or two:

- **One arm plus a priority/rate field on the send — rejected.** `MsgClass` is the *routing
  discriminator*: postcard is non-self-describing, so the carrier class is what tells the receiver
  which enum to decode into (this is stated verbatim in the `RealmSnapshot` doc comment, which exists
  as a separate class for exactly that reason). One arm carrying two different payload enums cannot be
  decoded. Worse, `class_to_byte` in io-prod's outbox is a golden-pinned per-class mapping and
  `Reliability` is a per-class function, so a pacing property carried on the *send* would not survive
  a durable-outbox replay.
- **Two arms, `Event` and `Bulk`, appended in ONE slice — adopted.** This satisfies D-4's actual
  requirement (build the shared infra once, not per feature) while respecting the committed channel
  table's distinction between reliable and reliable-paced. The slice lands both arms, their
  `Reliability` and `class_to_byte` entries, and the append-only discriminant pin, with all three
  consumers named in the doc comments.

```rust
BulkMsg::ChunkDelta {            // an additive variant, as the existing doc comment anticipates
    realm: RealmId,
    chunk: ChunkKey,             // CARRIES THE TIER — tier 0 = an edit list, tier L = a pyramid record
    epoch: EpochTag,             // universe_epoch_id + epoch_schema_version + gen_schema_version
    encoding: DeltaEncoding,     // Sparse | MaskedDense
    payload: TlvBytes,           // {1: sparse records, 2: mask+packed, 3: concealed reveals,
                                 //  4: pyramid entries}
}
```

**The detail ladder adds no field to this message.** The tier rides inside `ChunkKey` (§3.3.6), and
the pyramid's payload is a new TLV tag on an envelope that was built to take one — which is exactly
the skip-unknown evolution property `tlv.rs` exists for. A per-session Bulk rate cap lives in
`TransportTuning` — the one config struct — never as an inline literal. A client at an older protocol
minor skips tags it does not know (3, concealed-material reveals, §3.8; 4, pyramid entries) and still
renders correctly at the rungs it understands.

**A client that already has the generator only ever receives deltas, at any rung.** For most chunks
that means *nothing at all*: the overwhelmingly common state is Absent, at every tier, and a coarse
rung of an unedited region costs zero bytes exactly as a fine one does. To know which chunks it should
be waiting for, the client receives one compact manifest per AoI cell:

```rust
BulkMsg::DeltaManifest { realm: RealmId, cell: CellId, keys: Vec<ChunkKey>, digest: u64 }
```

Eight bytes per key — tier-tagged, because the key carries it — so one manifest covers every rung of
a cell and the client's coarse-first loader (§3.7.3) picks the order. A heavily built cell with 1,000
edited chunks is 8 KB. The digest lets a reconnecting client skip a manifest it already holds.
Manifests and deltas are demand-driven by the same AoI predicate and the same hysteresis as chunk
residency and realm spin-up — no second scheduler.

**One byte to reserve now, and a claim to correct.** Addendum 2 §A said the wire "already carries a
`coarsen_level: u8` precision ladder, always 0 today". That is too generous and it should not be
cited as a reservation: `coarsen_level` at `intershard.rs:659` is a field on `OccupantInterest`
documented as *"hops from the observer's home realm"* — a **pose**-precision hop counter on the
up-flow, not a terrain tier, and it is on an inter-shard arm rather than a client lane. What
`intershard.rs:303` genuinely reserves is the **lane** — *"the WHAT lane (terrain/constructions at the
LOD the observed realm controls) is a future ADDITIVE payload on this SAME routing"* — which is a
reserved concept, not a reserved field. There is no terrain-tier field anywhere yet and, in
particular, **no way for a client to say which rungs it wants**. So:

> Reserve **`tier_floor: u8`** on the client's AoI interest report — the message that already drives
> realm demand — always 0 today. It is the *finest* rung the client will accept, raised by its own
> residency governor (§3.7.3 rule 6) when it is short of memory. It is a hint about local memory, in
> the same category as the AoI radius the client already declares. One byte in a message that exists
> is free today; adding it later is a `PROTO_MINOR` bump plus a client-compatibility window during
> which the server must guess.

**THE TIER-HINT RULE, which is now a ruling across four sections and not just this one's framing.**
Two sections asserted flatly that *"the server never learns what tier anything is being drawn at"*.
That sentence is **struck** and replaced, because it is wrong on the merits and was contradicted in
the same sections by the largest bandwidth saving the ladder has. Routing a delta to the rung an
observer is resident at selects **what to send**, exactly like routing by AoI membership, and never
selects what is true. The replacement:

> A client may declare `tier_floor`. The server **CLAMPS** it to `[body.tier_floor_min,
> body.tier_depth − 1]` and uses the clamped value for **EGRESS SELECTION ONLY** — which rung of a
> chunk delta to send, and at what rate a `Telemetry` channel is refreshed. **NO fence, NO arbitration
> outcome, NO admission decision, NO scheduling deadline, NO persisted value and NO simulation state**
> may read it, directly or transitively. A shard's trajectory must be **byte-identical for every value
> of every observer's `tier_floor`.**

That invariant is **asserted, not merely written down**: the `tier_invariance` fixture runs the
identical scenario with every observer's clamped `tier_floor` forced to 0 and to `tier_depth − 1` and
requires byte-identical shard state, an identical beacon blink count, an identical spin-up order and
identical fence/arbitration/grant outcomes.

**Which tier fields exist, exhaustively, so a fourth is not invented.** The three-ladder doc comment
of §3.3.6 is required on the first and third of these:

- **KEEP `tier_floor: u8`** on the client AoI interest report (`crates/wire/src/channels.rs`) — the
  ONE observer-side tier field. Client-declared, server-clamped, non-authoritative.
- **KEEP `tier: u8`** on the chunk / block-edit **request** shape and on the delta **payload**
  (`crates/wire/src/intershard.rs`, the reserved `BlockEdit` arm; one-way door 45,
  **[USER DECISION 4-F]**) — a **payload descriptor** naming which rung the entries are at, not an
  observer property. The two are different kinds of thing and must never be merged into one field to
  save a byte. Door 45 is restated as *"the requested-tier byte on the chunk / block-edit request lane
  AND the tier descriptor on its delta payload — one arm, both fields, landed together, because
  postcard is positional (D-39.6)"*.
- **STRUCK: `OccupantInterest::observer_tier: u8`, `LedgerCell::min_demanded_tier`,** and the
  `PROTO_MINOR` 7 → 8 bump that was raised for them. `observer_tier` was to be *"computed server-side
  from the render tuning's pixels-per-cell target"* and folded into a spin-up **lead time** — a
  server-authoritative scheduling input derived from a client-local, governor-modified number the
  server cannot have. The insight (derive the lead, do not tune it) is kept and only the source is
  replaced: `lead_time_s = d_demand(r) / max(v_closing(o, r), v_closing_floor)` with
  `d_demand(r) = r.bounding_radius_m / tan(aoi_theta_min_rad / 2)`, both server-known since the A5
  flip. The resulting lead is strictly better than the tier form because it is continuous rather than
  quantised into rungs.

**And one hash to add, from Addendum 1.** A world is seed **plus configuration** (§3.5.1), so the
per-body override table is part of a body's *definition*. Its content hash **joins the protocol
handshake exactly as the block registry's does**, and a client whose table disagrees is refused at
connect with a named error. The failure is loud at the door instead of silent in the terrain. This
costs one more hash in an existing handshake and is the only wire consequence of making worlds
configurable.

**Client → server** is the `WorldAction` carrier of §3.9.7: reliable, sequenced, acked, CAS-guarded,
reach-checked, rate-capped, retried on loss. Movement stays on latest-wins datagrams. A block edit can
never ride a coupling or a datagram, and this is enforced rather than documented: `sim/src/coupling.rs`'s
sealed `EffectFree` marker cannot be implemented for a discrete authority event, so a `BlockEdit` is
structurally incapable of being smuggled onto a latest-wins lane.

**Live-edit fan-out**, once the edit is committed on the owner: the same `BulkMsg::ChunkDelta` goes to
every session whose AoI includes that chunk. This inherits D-9's unresolved fan-out shape — emit is
whole-realm broadcast with no within-realm AoI, measured at 357,248 gateway messages for 128 sessions
in one realm — so **the D-9/D-39.5 per-cell reshape is a precondition of block edits, not a
follow-on.** The per-cell index it introduces is the same index chunk residency, delta manifests, edit
fan-out and (per §3.4) anchor partitioning all key off, which is the argument for doing it once,
first, with one consumer instead of five.

**The ladder makes fan-out *cheaper*, not dearer, and this is the one place that is worth spelling
out.** A naive reading says an edit must now be broadcast at every rung — eight messages instead of
one. The opposite is true, for two reasons. First, a session receives the rung it is *resident at*,
and each session is resident at exactly one rung for a given chunk column, so an edit still produces
one message per interested session. Second, and more importantly, **the pyramid attenuates**: 500
edits inside one chunk collapse to ~63 tier-1 entries, ~8 at tier 2 and one above, so a distant
observer receives roughly `n/8^L` bytes for an edit burst that a nearby observer receives in full.
Mining out a whole chunk is a torrent up close and a single coarse cell changing colour from 50 km.
That is the correct shape for a fan-out budget and it falls out of the pyramid rather than needing a
throttle.

---

### 3.11 What this section reserves now, and the landing order

Two rows are **spent rather than reserved** now that the detail ladder is a ruling: the tier field
carries a value, and the pyramid record joins the list of formats that must be frozen before the
first world is written.

| reserve | where | why now |
|---|---|---|
| ~~`detail_tier: u8` in bits 18..16, always 0~~ → ~~4 bits at 60..57~~ → **`tier: u8` in bits 60..56 (5 bits), carrying a real value** | `core/src/grid/key.rs` | **spent.** The ruling arrived; **five** bits because the ceiling is the face-covering rung — 12 for the starter body, 18 for Earth, 20 for the largest addressable body — which four bits cannot express and three would reinstate a wall at 100 km. Register row 1 / one-way door 14 |
| 20-bit tangential axes and a 10-bit radial axis in `ChunkKey` | same | Addendum 1 made radius per-body data; 14 bits addressed 647 km and Earth needs 18. Twenty covers 41,390 km and costs nothing |
| ~~7~~ **6** zero-checked reserved bits in `ChunkKey` | same | region ids, multi-anchor, whatever D-41 resolves into. `3 + 5 + 20 + 20 + 10 = 58` of 64, so **six**; the tier field took the seventh, and it was the reserved field's intended consumer |
| `Tier0Key` as a distinct type, with `ChunkKey::as_tier0() -> Option<Tier0Key>` as the ONE narrowing point | `core/src/grid/key.rs` | the write path, the collider derivation and the client's edit message all take it; it is what makes "only tier 0 is writable" a compile error rather than a convention, and `as_tier0()` returning `None` for every tier `1..=31` is the covered negative branch that proves it under HR5 |
| **`BlockAddr { chunk: Tier0Key, … }` and `CoarseAddr { chunk: ChunkKey, … }` as two distinct types** | same | **new.** One address is tier-0-by-type and one admits any tier; there is no reverse conversion, not even a fallible one |
| `tier_depth: u8` **and `tier_view_max: u8`** on `BodyPhysical`, with 3-I's divisibility checked in the constructor | `core/src/body.rs` | `tier_depth` is derived from the body's size and bounds a persisted key; `tier_view_max` is derived from its atmosphere and bounds only residency. Enforcing the divisibility at construction is free, discovering it after a world is saved is not |
| 14 reserved bits in the 8-byte WAL record | `io-prod` block store | section 4's state word will grow (damage, ownership, signal ports) |
| **14 reserved bits in the 8-byte edit-pyramid record** (`cell 18 \| substance 16 \| occ_mask 8 \| fill_256 8 \| reserved 14`) | same | **new.** Permanent derived-but-persisted data (Addendum 2 §D.1); a coarse damage/power/claim summary is the obvious future consumer. Register row 37 / one-way door 43 |
| the table name **`chunk_pyramid`** and the type names `PyramidEntry` / `CellSummary` | same | **new.** Three spellings were circulating for one table; fixing the name is what stops a second one being invented |
| a `ClaimId` TLV tag on `ChunkRecord` | same | the deferred ownership/permission model lands without a record migration |
| **TLV tag 4 (`pyramid entries`) on `BulkMsg::ChunkDelta`** | `wire/src/channels.rs` | **new**, and free — the envelope was built for exactly this; a client at an older minor skips it and renders the rungs it knows |
| **`tier_floor: u8` on the client AoI interest report, always 0 — client-declared, server-CLAMPED, egress-selection only** | `wire/src/channels.rs` | **new.** There is no way for a client to say which rungs it wants today, and `coarsen_level` is a pose hop counter, not a terrain tier (§3.10). One byte now versus a `PROTO_MINOR` bump plus a guessing server later. It carries the three-ladder doc comment, and `observer_tier` / `min_demanded_tier` are struck rather than reserved |
| **the body-override table's content hash in the handshake** | protocol handshake | **new**, from Addendum 1: a world is seed *plus* configuration, so a disagreeing client must be refused at the door rather than desynced in the terrain |
| `RealmKindTag::Ship` and `::Construction` | `core/src/realm_path.rs` | a frozen append-only postcard discriminant surface; appending after ships persist is a wire-version event |
| `TransferableKind::VoxelVolume` | `core/src/entity_kind.rs` | the P8 weld/merge path for construction realms |
| `MaterialClass::{Public, Concealed}` + the `gen_public`/`gen_concealed` split | `core/src/grid/gen/` | free at P4; a schema migration plus a galaxy-wide regeneration after P6 |
| `BLOCK_STORE_FLUSH_STEP = 19`, `BLOCK_EDIT_FORWARD_STEP = 20` | `wire/src/intershard.rs` | new steps, never a repurposed one; 7–18 are allocated |
| `Warp` as an enum with one variant | `core/src/grid/warp.rs` | keeps the wire encoding closed if a second geometry family is ever wanted |
| a `FrameSpace` shape admitting >1 anchor (default 1) and `RegionId{WHOLE}` on the directory key | `sim/src/feature/voxel/`, directory | D-41 states plainly that hardening single-anchor/single-writer/single-cluster at P4–P6 forecloses hundreds-in-one-location, and its tripwires cannot be written until these types exist; §3.4 says how far that is from safe — and note the ladder does **not** help, because collision is tier-0 only |
| `WorldAction::Fire` named as a reserved arm | `wire/src/channels.rs` | forces P11's carrier to be the same one, which is the whole point of building it once |

And the ordering, which is the section's single most consequential recommendation: **`GridMapping` +
`FrameSpace` + the `Gf` determinism newtype land as one slice, before the mesher, before the
generator, before any chunk code.** Everything in P4 is defined to live above that seam; every line
written before it exists is written against an unknown interface, and the retrofit is a rewrite of
every producer plus its 100 %-coverage tests.

**Where the ladder lands, per Addendum 2 §D.2 — two pieces of it are not optional extras.**

| slice | what lands | why it cannot wait |
|---|---|---|
| **the seam slice** | `Tier`, `Tier0Key`, the widened `ChunkKey`, 3-I's divisibility check | the key is persisted; every other item here is addressed by it |
| **P4, the terrain slice** | octave dropping in the generator (§3.5.6); tier selection from screen-space error (§3.7.1); the per-tier band and min/max pyramid (§3.5.2); skirts | the generator change is *removing* work and tier selection reuses the existing angular-size machinery — both are small, and both are rewrites if they arrive after the mesher |
| **P6, the edit slice** | the edit pyramid (§3.9.8), maintained on every edit and persisted beside the delta, with `verify-pyramid` and the fly-away/fly-back gate | it is permanent delta data; the format must be right before the first world is saved |
| **later, with their own subsystems** | shadow cascades, mipmaps, decoration density falloff, the dither crossfade | ordinary rendering work; none of it is addressed by anything in this section |

### Adjudicated objections

Four review findings were checked and are wrong, or right for the wrong reason; they are recorded here
so they are not re-raised. Five statements this section itself made and has now retracted are recorded
below them, so a reader who remembers the old rule learns that it changed rather than quietly reading
past it.

- **"A second reliable client class where D-4 says build exactly one"** — half wrong. `BulkMsg` and
  `BulkKind::ChunkDelta` are already **committed, closed types in `channels.rs`** with "chunk payloads
  land at P4/P6" in their own doc comment, and the channel table already distinguishes Bulk (reliable,
  *paced*) from Event (reliable). Proposing a Bulk lane is not inventing a per-feature carrier. The
  finding was right that the alternative was never stated and the structural difference never argued;
  both are now in §3.10, and the conclusion is two `MsgClass` arms landing in one slice, not one arm.
- **"The >1.30 aspect band is ~10.9 km wide"** — right location, wrong shape. 10.9 km is an
  area-average over the full 199 km arc; the band is lens-shaped, **±15.6 km at the arc midpoint**,
  narrowing to zero about 40 % of the way to each corner. §3.3.2 states the profile rather than the
  average. (The "7.9 % of surface" figure is also unweighted; solid-angle weighted it is 7.1 %.)
- **"The radius implies a ~1,000-way cluster partition of a subsystem whose design says more than one
  is a hard error"** — right that the row was missing, wrong that the number is a required partition.
  1,045 is the count of distinct 10 km patches needed to *tile* the planet, i.e. an upper bound on how
  many anchors a planet could ever need. Anchors are per player-cluster; a planet with one settlement
  needs one. The row is in §3.4 framed that way.
- **Both the original draft and the review reported "shape distortion" as the edge-length ratio
  only**, which is why "shape-optimal: every block square to within 0.7 %" looked available. Measuring
  the grid Jacobian's singular values shows a **warp-invariant √3 = 1.732 shear at all eight cube
  corners** (the grid directions meet at 120° there, for every warp). No warp makes blocks square
  everywhere on a sphere; the warp decision is about the edge-length half only, and option (D) of 3-C
  buys 31.6 % → 16.6 % of the surface above a 1.30 shape ratio, not 0 %.

### Retractions

- **"There is one radius, `k = 12`, and it is the unique value."** Retracted by Addendum 1 §C. The
  uniqueness came from requiring chunks-per-face to be a power of two, which nothing needed. Radius is
  per-body data on `R = 124·m/π`; `m = 4,096` survives as the recommended *starter* world and nothing
  more. §3.4.
- **"Gravity must be fabricated or honest, once, for the whole game."** Retracted by Addendum 1 §D.
  Mass is an authored per-body field and gravity, escape velocity, SOI, orbital period and scale
  height are all derived from it, so both behaviours are available per body. What survives is the
  SOI-inflation consequence, which must still be applied from the one mass field. §3.4.
- **"`D` is a budget-derived operational parameter, not a physically derived one, because the
  atmospheric derivation produces numbers three orders of magnitude beyond every budget."** Retracted
  by the ladder. The derivation now produces 243–333 MB for visual ranges of 30–330 km, so it is worth
  running — but what it derives is `tier_view_max`, a **residency** bound for an observer inside the
  air, not the ladder's ceiling. §3.7.5.
- **"The gap between `D` and the horizon is exactly the open no-LOD ruling; this section does not
  pretend it is closed."** The ruling arrived and the gap is closed. Visible chunk count grows with
  the logarithm of view distance, so **Addendum 1 §C.4's "the binding constraint is the drawn radius,
  not the planet radius" is dissolved along with it** — there is no wall at any planet size or any
  altitude, only a residency budget. §3.7.
- **"Merged-quad sagitta is a non-issue and the merge-width cap can be dropped."** Retracted for
  coarse rungs on small bodies: a tier-7 run on the starter world sags 48.7 m. The cap returns as an
  angular formula (§3.3.6) that is vacuous below tier 6 and never binds on an Earth-sized body.

Six more, all from the cross-section reconciliation of the detail-ladder sweep. Each is a statement
**this section made** and no longer makes, recorded so a reader who remembers it learns that it
changed rather than reading past it.

- **"The tier field is four bits at 60..57, because a ten-rung ladder is what an Earth-sized body
  needs at altitude; the key spends 57 bits on geometry and 7 on future geometry."** Retracted. It
  sized a *key* against a *residency* question. The field is **five bits at 60..56**, the ceiling is
  the face-covering rung (12 / 18 / 20 for the starter body / Earth / the largest addressable body),
  and the key closes at **58 of 64 with six spare**. §3.3.6, and register row 1 / one-way door 14.
- **"`tier_depth = ceil(log2(V_atm / d₀)) + 1`, clamped to `[1, 10]`."** Retracted and split.
  `tier_depth = ceil(log2 m) + 1` bounds the persisted key; the atmospheric derivation survives
  unchanged as `tier_view_max`, a residency bound. The `[1, 10]` clamp is gone — it capped the wrong
  quantity, and it would have made "blocks all the way to the face-covering rung" unbuildable on an
  Earth-sized body. §3.7.5. **It carries a rider onto 3-I**: a full-depth body's `m` is a power of two.
- **"The edit-pyramid entry is `cell 18 | dominant block type 16 | fill 8 | authored 8 | reserved 14`,
  and it is drawn solid iff `fill ≥ solid_threshold` (a render tuning field, default 128)."**
  Retracted on three counts. `authored` is **dropped** (its only named consumer needs no pyramid
  field, and `occ_mask` needs the bits); `dominant block type` becomes **`substance`** (a
  `BlockTypeId` carries a shape and possibly a function, and a coarse cell's shape must come from the
  mask and the fill); and `solid_threshold` is **deleted outright, not relocated** — a client-tunable
  knob on a decision that `BlockRegistryHash` exists to keep byte-identical is the one place a
  *detail* setting could produce a visible *fact* difference between two clients. §3.9.8, register
  row 37.
- **"The pyramid update rule is `fill_L = mean over 8 children`, `dominant_L = argmax over children
  types`, `authored_L = mean over 8 children`."** Retracted and made exact, because the walk-up is now
  byte-identity-gated per tier: `coarsen(children: &[CellSummary; 8]) -> CellSummary`, with a
  round-half-up mean, dominance by **summed fill** over non-empty children, a total tie-break, a
  generator fallback on a miss, an early exit on **summary** equality, pruning against
  `generate_summary`, and every write inside the WAL's own redb write transaction. §3.9.8.
- **"The pyramid costs roughly one seventh of the edits it summarises, in writes and in time."**
  Retracted as a general claim — it is the compact-3-D case only, and the tunnel example in the same
  subsection was the 1-D case at ~1×. The four shape-dependent rows span a factor of fifty and are now
  quoted as a table. §3.9.8.
- **"§5's skirt depth is `(relief across one coarse cell) + 4·k_rough·s_L ≈ 3 cells` at every tier."**
  Retracted: it omitted the rim-warp displacement entirely and quoted one substitution of `k_rough` as
  a universal constant. §5.9.4 owns the formula; this section owns the relief envelope it reads
  (§3.5.2, derived and never persisted) and the closed-form fallback bound (~5 cells). §3.5.6.

One near-retraction from outside the section, recorded because it would otherwise be cited as fact:
**Addendum 2 §A's claim that the wire "already carries a `coarsen_level: u8` precision ladder"** for
terrain detail is too generous. `coarsen_level` is a pose-precision hop counter on `OccupantInterest`;
what is genuinely reserved at `intershard.rs:303` is the WHAT *lane*, not a field. §3.10 plants the
field that is actually missing.
