## 4. Shapes — half blocks, slopes, corners: encoding, meshing lanes, collision, and building

The user's ask is one sentence: *"Blocks are 1 m and square. Also half-blocks, slopes etc. so buildings
and ships can be more beautiful."* That sentence costs more than any other in the block system, because
a non-cube block touches seven subsystems — the persisted record, the wire, the mesher, the collider,
the character controller, the build UI and the mass model — and five of those are places where a wrong
choice becomes a migration over saved worlds rather than a refactor.

This section fixes: the encoding (which turns out to need **no new persisted field at all**), the map
from a baked template onto a *warped* cube-sphere cell, the catalogue and its exact-integer volume and
slope lattice, the one `ShapeDef` row, the two meshing lanes and their culling contract, the four
collision lanes, the derived character-controller parameters, the build loop, the placement-latency
and validation protocol, and — as of Addendum 2 — **what a shape becomes when its cell is eight metres
wide**.

Three facts from outside this section govern everything below. **(1)** §2 defines a block as a
`BlockTypeId(u16)` triple index over (substance, form, function), so "shape" is already inside the
persisted identity. **(2)** §3 commits to the `VD-ASC5` cube-sphere: tangential cell width runs from
**0.672 m to 1.052 m** across a planet and the lattice is sheared by up to **30°** near the eight cube
corners, while radial cell height is exactly **1.000 m everywhere**. A design written in an axis-aligned
unit cube is not a design for this planet. **(3) — new, and it re-opens four of this section's
subsections —** `block_system_design_addendum_2.md` retracts the no-detail-levels ban and installs a
**one-rung-per-power-of-two ladder**: at tier *L* a cell is 2^L m, a chunk is still 62³ cells, and the
tier is *a number on a chunk address, never a second code path* (HR3). Tier 0 is used out to 786 m and
tier 7 to 100 km.

> **Amendment [C3] — the ladder's ceiling is data, not the number seven.** ~~Above tier 7 sits the realm
> proxy as the coarsest rung.~~ **Replaced by:** the top rung is the body's derived
> `tier_depth = ceil(log2 m) + 1` — the rung at which one chunk covers a whole cube face, plus one —
> which is **13** for the 4,096-chunk-per-face-edge starter body, **19** for an Earth-sized one and
> **21** for the largest addressable body. The persisted tier field is therefore **FIVE bits at
> `ChunkKey` 60..56** (§3.3.6), not three, and where the realm proxy takes over is register row 1 /
> one-way door 14. Every "rung 7" figure that survives below is an *evaluation at a rung*, not a
> ceiling.

**The one-sentence summary of what the ladder does to §4, so the rest can be read against it:** every
type, table, mask, rasterisation and assertion in this section is authored in **index space** and is
therefore **tier-invariant** — a 32×32 coverage pattern of the unit cell means the same thing whether
the cell is one metre or 128 — while every *semantic* reading of them (mounting, sealing, structural
support, mass, collision, targeting, editing) is **tier-0-only** and is confined there by the type
system rather than by discipline. §4 gains one new pure function (`coarsen`), one new baked table
(4.5 KiB), one newtype (`Tier0Key`), one wire field (`tier: u8`) and **one user decision of its own —
[USER DECISION 4-F] — plus its half of register row 37**, the collapsed decision that now owns the
edit-pyramid record. It loses nothing.

---

### 4.1 The encoding: one identity, one orientation, no new field

**Verdict: shape is `ShapeDef` inside §2's `BlockTypeId` triple, plus §2's 6-bit `orient`. §4 adds no
persisted field, no wire field, and no new bit. Neighbour-derived sub-shapes are a *refinement layer*
computed at mesh/collide time and never persisted. Pinned (player-forced) connection state lives in
§2's existing sparse `block_state` side table, never in `orient`.**

**The ladder does not change this and consumes zero additional rows.** A coarse cell is expressed with
the *same* `(BlockTypeId, orient)` pair drawn from the *same* authored rows — §4.3.2's coarsener is
constrained to shapes the substance already admits — so the combination cap below is untouched by the
existence of a ladder, at any depth. Coarse chunks are **derived, never persisted, never on the wire as
placements**; only the sparse edit pyramid (§4.9.5) is durable, and it carries an **8-byte geometric
summary — C1's `PyramidEntry`, one `u64`** — rather than a block record.

#### 4.1.1 Reconciliation with §2 and §3 — and the decision that actually exists

§2.7.1 fixes the durable record at `local_index 18 | block_type 16 | orient 6` = 40 bits = the five
bytes `roadmap.json` P6 already commits to. On the reasoning that "material plus shape plus orientation
alone is 25 bits at any sane width" — which is true only for *independent* fields — the record has been
proposed at eight bytes. With a triple index it is 16 + 6 = 22 bits and the committed five bytes fit
exactly.

> **Correction [M4] — §4 cited the wrong decision, and must not close this one.** ~~§3.8.2 independently
> proposed widening to eight bytes and raised **[USER DECISION 3-E]** … §4's ruling: the five-byte record
> stands; §3's [USER DECISION 3-E] is answered "keep 5 bytes" and should be struck.~~ **Replaced by:**
> §3.9.2 independently proposes eight bytes and raises **[USER DECISION 3-H]** (3-E in the final §3 is
> the surface-gravity range, a different question — as written, §4 struck the wrong decision). §4's
> position is that the triple index makes five bytes sufficient; §8.6 item 1's counter-argument is that
> five bytes cannot carry BOTH the placed marker and the mirror flag and both are load-bearing. **This is
> register row 2 and it is the OWNER'S; §4 states its argument and does not strike 3-H.**

A `GeometryId` field pairing a 16-bit material with a 16-bit geometry is 32 bits and
is the wrong model anyway — it re-authors per (material × shape) exactly the drift surface §2.1.1 exists
to remove. **That half — the identity model, one combined `BlockTypeId` rather than independent material
and geometry fields — is settled and is all any other section depends on** (§5.10.2 cites it).

There is a **second** one-way door underneath, beside the record width that register row 2 owns, and §4
does own this one: the **combination cap**.

| Growth point | Rows consumed | % of the 65,536 `BlockTypeId` space |
|---|---|---|
| v1: 40 build materials × 23 shapes + 24 terrain-only materials × `Cube` | 944 | 1.4 % |
| 64 materials × 23 shapes + 64 functions × ~4 shapes | 1,728 | 2.6 % |
| 256 materials × 64 shapes | 16,384 | 25 % |
| 512 materials × 64 shapes | 32,768 | 50 % |
| 1,024 materials × 64 shapes | 65,536 | **100 % — the wall** |

Adding one shape costs one row *per material that admits it*. That is the mechanism by which the
per-material admits-mask of §4.2 is implemented: a `(material, shape)` pair is admitted **iff a
`BlockTypeDef` row exists for it**, so admission needs no separate bitmask and no separate validation
path. It is also why the cap must be watched.

**One new bake assertion the ladder requires, and it is one line: every substance that has any
`BlockTypeDef` row has a `Cube` row.** That is what makes §4.3.2's one-step admits fallback *total* —
a coarse cell whose best-matching shape is not admitted by its dominant substance falls back to `Cube`,
and `Cube` is guaranteed to exist. Without the assertion the fallback has an undefined case, which is
the shape of bug that only appears on the first world containing an exotic material.

> **[USER DECISION 4-A] — does the persisted identity stay a triple index?**
> This replaces the first draft's spurious "widen the WAL record" question, which §2 had already solved.
> **[M4] The record WIDTH half of this question is register row 2 and is not §4's to close** — §4 states
> the argument below and leaves 3-H standing. What follows is §4's position on the identity MODEL.
>
> - **A1. Keep §2's `BlockTypeId(u16)` triple index and the 5-byte record** *(recommended)*. Every
>   `(material, shape, function)` combination that a designer authorises costs one row; unauthorised
>   combinations cost nothing and are unrepresentable, which is a validation property, not just a saving.
>   The cap binds at 1,024 materials × 64 shapes.
> - **A2. Split the record into independent material and shape fields.** Needs `18 + 16 + 10 + 6 = 50`
>   bits, i.e. §3's 8-byte record, and contradicts the `roadmap.json` deliverable. Buys an unrestricted
>   cross product nobody has asked for and loses the "the row IS the permission" property.
>
> **This is a ONE-WAY DOOR.** Both the record width and the identity model bind every persisted planet,
> ship, station and blueprint. **Mechanical guards for A1:** the content build FAILS at
> `BLOCK_TYPE_ROWS > 65_536` and WARNS at 49,152 (75 %); the manifest is append-only and the build fails
> if an existing row's triple changes.

#### 4.1.2 The runtime handle, and the frozen orientation code

```rust
// crates/core/src/block/shape.rs — Tier-A, frozen, covered by BlockRegistryHash.

pub struct ShapeId(u16);   // dense, append-only, cap 1_024 (§2)

/// 6 bits: bits 0..4 = one of 24 proper rotations, bit 5 = mirror. The rotation
/// NUMBERING is part of the frozen contract — a renumber silently reinterprets every
/// persisted build. Pinned by a golden table test.
pub struct Orient(u8);

/// RUNTIME ONLY — the index into the baked variant table. NEVER persisted, NEVER on
/// the wire, never in a hash. Derived as variant_index[shape][orient].
pub struct VariantId(u16);
```

Rotations are **integer matrices**, a `const [[[i8;3];3]; 24]` table of 216 bytes, exact under
composition. Rotating a template vertex, a coverage bitmask or a collider hull is integer arithmetic
with no rounding — which matters because the rotated coverage bitmask feeds the culling matrix, and a
one-texel rasterisation difference between two builds is a visible hole.

**The mirror bit is reserved from the first commit** even though every shape in the starting catalogue
is achiral. One bit today, versus later auditing every shape for a mirror twin, adding a winding-order
flip to the bake, and mirroring every collider hull — after players have built.

#### 4.1.3 Why the two alternatives lose, briefly

**Micro-voxel sub-grids.** Dense sub-voxels at 1 byte each per 62³ chunk, against the palette-packed
baseline of 232.7 KiB at 8 bits/block: 2³ = 1.82 MiB (8×), 4³ = 14.55 MiB (64×, SE2's resolution),
8³ = 116.4 MiB (512×), 16³ = 931 MiB (4,096×, Vintage Story's chisel). RAM is not the decisive argument;
the wire is. P6 networks edits as deltas, and a 25 cm chisel stroke is up to 64 sub-cell edits inside one
1 m cell, which the five-byte record cannot express at all. Rendering is worse again: a 45° slope at 8
sub-voxels per metre becomes 8 stair steps per metre per axis. Teardown is the honest end state — 10 cm
voxels and a GPU raymarcher instead of a mesher, a different renderer from the Bevy PBR pipeline this
project has already built against. Vintage Story's version is *additive on top of* the explicit id
(merged cuboids at one `u32` each, gated behind a world setting) and remains available at P6+.

**One new argument against sub-grids, supplied by the ladder.** A sub-grid extends the world *downward*
in scale by a fixed factor and pays for it in bytes at every cell. The ladder extends the world *upward*
in scale by an unbounded factor and is paid for by *removing* octaves. The two are not symmetric: going
finer is always storage, going coarser is always a saving. A project that wants both should build the
free direction first and measure whether the paid one is still wanted.

**SDF / dual contouring.** Memory is not the argument either (a 63³ i8 corner lattice is ~245 KiB, 1–4×
the palette). Three other things kill it. **Block identity dissolves** — a functional block needs an id,
an owner, a damage state, mount points and, from P9, a signal address and ports, and a density field has
nowhere to put any of them; every one of the user's functional-block asks presumes "this block, here, is
a thing". **Player-built geometry melts** — §5.6.5 rejects iso-surface extraction on the same ground, and
the user asked for *"real life, but voxely"*, which is a rim wobble on natural edges (§5.6), not a melted
hull. **It contradicts a committed deliverable** — P4 commits to "the binary-greedy-meshing adapter on
62³ chunks". The determinism objection is narrower than the research pool stated: primitive float ops
including `sqrt` are bit-exact and Rust never contracts into an FMA, so a QEF solve in `+ − × ÷ sqrt`
would reproduce; the real hazard is that practical solvers reach for `atan2`/`hypot` in Givens rotations,
which `std` documents as platform-varying.

#### 4.1.4 Where neighbour-derived sub-shapes ARE right — and the pin, done correctly

Minecraft never stores a shape id, and the numbers are the most important ergonomics datum in the
survey: **walls have 324 block states and a player chooses zero of them.** Stairs have 80 and a player
chooses two (facing from look direction, half from where in the face the ray hit); the inner/outer corner
is a pure function of the two neighbouring stair blocks. Fences are 32 states, all derived.

> Derive a sub-shape when **(1)** the number of visually-required states is large, **(2)** none of them
> is a choice a player would deliberately make, and **(3)** getting it wrong reads as a *missing
> connection* rather than a *wrong build*. Use an explicit id whenever a player would ever want the
> "wrong" one.

Minecraft satisfies (1)–(3) for walls and gets no complaints; it fails the escape hatch and players
resent being unable to build a deliberately disconnected stub. **Every derived family therefore ships
with a pinned twin — and the pin does NOT live in `orient`.** Packing four connection bits plus an up bit
into the six orientation bits (the first draft's proposal) breaks three things at once: it makes the
encoding non-uniform so every decoder must branch on the shape family before reading orientation; it
makes the bake's group-action assertion false, because composing two connection masks is meaningless;
and it leaves no bit to distinguish a *derived* wall from a *pinned wall with zero connections*, which is
precisely the escape hatch being designed.

**The pin lives in §2's `block_state` side table**, which already exists, is already sparse, and already
carries a `state_bits: u16` with a `PERSIST_MASK`:

```
block_state.state_bits:  bit 0 = CONNECT_PIN
                         bits 1..5 = connection mask (−X +X −Z +Z, up)
```

A derived block has **no side-table row at all** (the common case, zero cost). A pinned block has one
8-byte row. `orient` keeps a single uniform meaning for every shape, the group action stays total over
all 48 codes, and the pin flag exists.

Three consequences of the derived layer that are easy to miss:

- **Derived state is never persisted and never on the wire.** The persisted identity is the player's
  intent (type + facing + half). The derived variant is presentation-and-collision, recomputed from the
  same integer table over the same block field.
- **An edit dirties a 3×3×3 neighbourhood** in render *and* collision. The mesher already reads a
  1-voxel apron; the collider builder does not and must gain one.
- **Connective families need a 2-cell read window.** The derived variant of an apron cell depends on
  *its* neighbours, two cells out. Do **not** widen the padded buffer to 66³ — that breaks the 64-bit
  column trick the whole binary mesher rests on. Instead a **resolve pass** reads a 66³ window and writes
  a 64³ *resolved variant* buffer (`u16` per cell, 512 KiB, reused per worker); the bitmask mesher and
  the collider builder both consume the 64³ resolved buffer unchanged.
- **Divergence at the data edge is real and must be ruled on** (the first draft's "there is no divergence
  risk" is false). Three cases: the client holds only the chunks it has generated or received, so a
  connect family at the loaded-region edge resolves against absent neighbours; an in-flight edit delta
  makes the two fields differ for at least one round trip; and P6 forwards ghost-region edits to the
  realm owner, so a neighbouring shard's observer sees them later still. **The rules:** (i) the client
  renders the *disconnected* variant for any cell whose 2-cell window is not fully loaded, and re-meshes
  when the neighbour arrives — a deterministic, benign fallback, never a guess; (ii) the server never
  resolves against an absent neighbour *inside its own realm*, and at the realm boundary
  `GridMapping::neighbor` returns the typed `Outside` arm, which resolves deterministically to "no
  connection"; (iii) **a bake assertion bounds the blast radius**: every connect variant's collider must
  contain the family's declared `core` and be contained in its declared `envelope`, so a mis-derived
  variant can at worst look wrong, never open a hole a player can walk through.
- **A fourth case, added by the ladder: the neighbour is resident at a *different tier*.** The rule is
  the same one, not a new one — `neighbor` returns `Outside`, the connect family resolves to
  "disconnected", and the chunk re-meshes if the same-tier neighbour later arrives. Connect families are
  a **tier-0 vocabulary in practice** (fences, railings and conduits are metre-scale objects that fall
  below one pixel long before tier 2), so this path is exercised only in the single-rung band around a
  seam, and its worst outcome is a visually detached railing at 800 m. §4.5.8 gives the general form of
  this rule and its proof.

#### 4.1.5 One-way doors, stated plainly

| Item | One-way? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 m cell size **at tier 0** | **YES** (already answered) | Keen could not migrate SE's 2.5 m/0.5 m grids to 25 cm — it took a new engine and a sequel. Every saved ship, station and blueprint binds to it. Note the ladder does **not** reopen this: tiers 1–7 are derived views of the same 1 m field, never a second authoring scale |
| §2's 5-byte record and the triple-index identity | **YES** | [USER DECISION 4-A] |
| The 6-bit `orient` field and its rotation **numbering** | **YES** | A renumber silently reinterprets every persisted build |
| The mirror bit | **YES** | Retrofitting means auditing every shape for a twin, winding-flip in the bake, and a mirrored twin per collider hull, after players have built |
| `ShapeId` numbering append-only | **YES** | Same reinterpretation failure |
| Explicit ids rather than an iso-surface representation | **YES in content terms** | Players build against the vocabulary; you cannot take faceted hulls away later |
| One geometry per cell (no sub-grid) | **YES** | A chisel layer must be strictly additive; making the base cell sub-divisible is the SE1→SE2 door |
| Templates authored in **index space** (§4.2) | **YES** | It is what makes the same catalogue legal on a warped shell **and** on a flat grid **and at every rung of the ladder** — one authoring space, three independent payoffs |
| **The edit-pyramid entry** — 8 bytes, one `u64`, `cell 18 \| substance 16 \| occ_mask 8 \| fill_256 8 \| reserved 14` (C1) | **YES — new** | It is durable delta data. **Register row 37 / [USER DECISION 8-A]** (one-way door 43), which absorbed §4's own 4-E |
| **A `tier: u8` on the block-edit wire arm** | **YES — new** | postcard is positional; the arm freezes on first ship. [USER DECISION 4-F] |
| The `COARSE_SHAPE` table's *contents* | No | Derived data, recomputable, covered by `BlockRegistryHash`; retuning it re-meshes, it does not migrate |
| Whether the pin lives in `block_state` vs its own table | No | Server-internal, behind the store seam |
| The Lane-B collider representation | No | Server-internal; swap when measured |

---

### 4.2 The index-space contract — how a template meets a warped cell

This is the subsection the first draft did not have, and without it every geometric claim in the section
is false on a planet. Addendum 2 makes it load-bearing a second time: **index space is also what makes
the catalogue tier-free.**

**Ruling: every template is authored in INDEX space — the unit cell in fractional cell coordinates
`p ∈ [0,1]³` — and is mapped to world space by the grid mapping, per vertex, at emit time. There is no
world-space template and no "per-cell integer translation".**

The map is the fractional generalisation of §3's existing `cell_corners`, and it must be added to the
`GridMapping` seam as a seventh total operation:

```rust
/// The fractional-coordinate generalisation of `cell_corners`. p ∈ [0,1]³.
/// cell_corners(addr) == the 8 evaluations at the corners of the unit cube.
/// `addr.chunk` carries the tier in ChunkKey bits 60..56 (five bits, C3); the map reads it
/// and scales by 2^tier. `CoarseAddr` is the ONLY address type admitting a tier >= 1 (M3);
/// the earlier spelling `ChunkAddrAnyTier` is STRUCK.
fn cell_point(&self, addr: CoarseAddr, p: DVec3) -> DVec3;
```

On `IdentityGrid` it is `origin + p·2^L`. On `ShellGrid` it is exactly §3.3.3's forward addressing
evaluated at fractional indices, with the tier folded into the index step:

```
k = 2^tier                                       // cells per tier-L cell, integer
a = (2·k·(i + p.x))/N − 1;   u = warp(a)         // warp: 5 mul, 2 add — no transcendental
b = (2·k·(j + p.z))/N − 1;   v = warp(b)
dir = normalize(face_normal + u·right + v·up)
r   = floor_radius_m + k·(ir + p.y)              // radial cells are exactly 2^tier m
world = dir · r
```

Four properties follow, and they are the whole justification:

**(a) Cracks are impossible *within a tier*, by construction.** Two cells of the same tier sharing a face
agree on the fractional index coordinate of every point on that face, and `cell_point` is a pure function
of that coordinate. So a template vertex lying on a cell-boundary plane maps to the *identical* world
point from both sides — bit for bit, since it is the same expression on the same inputs. This replaces
the first draft's arithmetic crack budget with a proof, and it is why the "template geometry lies inside
the closed unit cell" invariant is now load-bearing rather than tidy. **Assert it at bake:** every
template vertex satisfies `0 ≤ p ≤ 1` on the 1/32 lattice.

> **Amendment (Addendum 2).** ~~Cracks are impossible, by construction.~~ **Replaced by: cracks are
> impossible *within a tier*.** Across a tier boundary the two sides evaluate `cell_point` at different
> values of `k`, so the shared-input argument does not apply and the surfaces genuinely disagree. That
> disagreement is bounded (§4.5.8) and closed by a skirt, and it is the *only* place in this section
> where geometry is concealed rather than proved. It is worth being explicit that the proof narrowed,
> because "cracks are impossible" was previously an unqualified claim in this document.

**(b) Shear and taper are in the map, so the catalogue does not have to know about them.** At a cube
corner the lattice is 30°-sheared; a template placed in index space is sheared with it automatically. No
`Isometry` and no per-axis `voxel_size` is asked to express shear, because nothing does — the map does.
**The same sentence now covers scale:** a template placed in index space is *scaled* with the tier
automatically, so no shape, no coverage pattern, no collider template and no assertion in this section
carries a metre anywhere. That is why the ladder costs §4 one function and not a second catalogue.

**(c) Faces become bilinear patches, and the non-planarity is negligible at 1 m — but it grows with the
tier, and here is the bound.** A planar quad in index space maps to a bilinear patch. The four side faces
of a cell are *exactly* planar (each contains two radial rays through the planet centre). Only the two
constant-radius faces bow, by the chord sagitta `s²/(8R)`. At tier 0 on the 161,671 m reference planet
that is `1²/(8 × 161,671) = 0.77 µm`. At tier *L* it is `4^L` times larger:

| Tier | Cell edge | Sagitta on a 162 km planet | Sagitta on an Earth-sized planet | Screen size at that tier's range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 m | 0.77 µm | 0.020 µm | — |
| 3 | 8 m | 49 µm | 1.3 µm | 0.016 px |
| 5 | 32 m | 0.79 mm | 0.020 mm | 0.063 px |
| 7 | 128 m | 12.7 mm | 0.32 mm | 0.25 px |

The last column is the one that matters: the sagitta is measured *at the distance its tier is used at*
(786·2^L m), and it grows as `4^L / 2^L = 2^L` in screen terms while the pixel budget is constant — so a
tier-7 cell's bow is a quarter of a pixel on the smallest planet in the range and less on every larger
one. **Triangulating a template as if planar remains exact for every practical purpose at every rung**,
and no tessellation, no patch primitive and no re-derivation is needed. Had the number come out above a
pixel the answer would have been to cap the tier, not to add a patch primitive; it does not, so there is
no cap.

**(d) The cost, honestly.** "Never rotate at mesh or collide time" survives — the baked variant table
stays integer, in index space, deduped and shared. What does *not* survive is "instanced at a per-cell
integer translation". Each emitted vertex costs one `cell_point`: ~25 flops (two degree-5 polynomials,
one normalise, one scale) against a bare copy. At 24 vertices per shaped cell that is ~600 flops/cell,
so a 3,000-shaped-cell chunk costs ~1.8 Mflop ≈ 0.6 ms, roughly double the first draft's memcpy estimate
and still an order below the GPU upload. On `IdentityGrid` the map is an add and the cost is zero. **The
tier changes none of this** — `k` is a shift, and coarse chunks carry strictly fewer shaped cells
(§4.5.8), so `cell_point` cost per chunk falls monotonically up the ladder.

**Cross-lane precision.** If Lane B is GPU-instanced (§4.5.4) the map runs in WGSL in f32 chunk-local
coordinates while Lane A's vertices are computed on the CPU in f64 and stored as f32 chunk-local. Worst
disagreement at a shared face is **≤ 0.1 mm** at tier 0 (f32 rounding at a 62 m chunk extent, ~15
accumulated ULP) — about a tenth of a pixel at 1 m viewing distance, three orders below §3's 3.0 mm
merged-quad sagitta threshold. At tier *L* the chunk extent is `62·2^L` m so the f32 error scales with
it: 12.8 mm at tier 7 over a 7.9 km chunk, viewed from 100 km — 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ px. The margin *widens* up
the ladder, because the extent grows by 2^L while the viewing distance grows by the same factor and the
pixel budget is fixed. If it ever proves visible at tier 0 the fallback is contained: emit Lane B
vertices on the CPU for the cells adjacent to Lane A, using the same `border_peel` machinery §5.5.2
already introduces.
---

### 4.3 The catalogue

The catalogue is a set of **geometries**, not blocks. A geometry becomes placeable in a material by the
existence of a `BlockTypeDef` row, so one 23-entry shape table produces the equivalent of Space
Engineers' per-armour-family variant lists for every material at zero marginal content cost. (SE's wiki
lists 46 pages under Light Armour and 46 under Heavy Armour — the same ~23 topologies enumerated twice
across two materials and three sizes.)

**The exact volume lattice.** Volume is an integer number of `1/196,608` of a *cell*, where
`CELL_VOLUME_UNITS = 196_608 = 6 × 32³`. This is the exact volume lattice of any polyhedron whose
vertices lie on the 1/32 cell grid (a lattice tetrahedron has volume `|det| / (6 · 32³)`), so **every
catalogue value and every future authored mesh is exactly representable with no tolerance constant**.
It supersedes both §2's `volume_micro_m3` (which cannot express 1/3, 1/6, 2/3 or 5/6) and the first
draft's `volume_48ths` (which cannot express an arbitrary authored mesh). 1/48 of a cell is exactly
4,096 units, so the catalogue below sits on both.

**The mass and yield ruling** — §3.3.2 explicitly delegated this here, and the first draft specified the
opposite. On the committed grid the *physical* volume of a full cube ranges 0.452 m³ to 1.107 m³, a 2.45×
spread. Therefore:

> **The cell is the unit of matter.** `volume_units` is a **cell fraction**, never a cubic metre. One
> full cube of material X yields exactly one unit of X wherever it is mined; mass is
> `density_kg_m3 × volume_units / CELL_VOLUME_UNITS`, evaluated in µkg integer arithmetic, treating
> every cell as nominally 1 m³. Material cost, thermal capacity, structural load, buoyancy and salvage
> all read the same nominal quantity.
>
> **Addendum 2 rider, and it closes an exploit before it exists: "the cell" here means a TIER-0 cell,
> always.** A coarse cell's `volume_units` is its *representative's*, which is a silhouette summary and
> not a mass. Mass, yield, structural load, thermal capacity and buoyancy are summed over the tier-0
> field and nowhere else. This is not a discipline note — §4.6.3's `Tier0Key` newtype makes every mass
> reader structurally incapable of being handed a coarse chunk. Without it a ship's mass would depend on
> how far away it was being rendered, which is both a physics bug and a duplication exploit.

Consequences, all deliberate: on Cartesian realms this is physically exact; on planets it removes a
2.45× position-dependent mining exploit that would be invisible to the player and durable in a
scarcity-driven economy; a structure's mass does not change with where on the planet it was built; and a
planet's gravitational mass is `PlanetParams`-derived closed-form (Category A), never summed from
blocks — which was already true.

All coordinates are in the unit **index** cell with +Y up (radially outward on a shell). "Full faces" is
the set of cell faces the shape covers completely in the canonical orientation — one mask that doubles
as the greedy-culling fast-reject, the airtightness mask (§2.5's pressurisation) and the mount-point set.
"Slope" is the exact index-space `tan²` of the steepest upward-facing facet, stored as a rational; the
degree column is the datum-face-centre reading and is derived, not authored. "Orients" is the deduped
orbit size under the 48 transforms. **"Octant mask" is new** and is derived at bake: the 8-bit set of
half-cell octants the shape's solid region touches at all. It is what §4.3.2 coarsens by, and its
presence in this table costs one derived column.

| Id | Name | Family | Volume (/196,608) | = | Slope tan² | ≈ index ° | Full faces | Orients | Octant-mask class |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `Cube` | Full | 196,608 | 1 | 0/1 | 0 | all 6 | 1 | full (1) |
| 1 | `Slab` | Plate | 98,304 | 1/2 | 0/1 | 0 | −Y | 6 | face-half (6) |
| 2 | `Plate` | Plate | 49,152 | 1/4 | 0/1 | 0 | −Y | 6 | face-half (6) |
| 3 | `Panel` | Plate | 24,576 | 1/8 | 0/1 | 0 | −Y | 6 | face-half (6) |
| 4 | `Wedge` | Ramp | 98,304 | 1/2 | 1/1 | 45.000 | −Y, −X | 12 | six-octant (12) |
| 5 | `RampLow` | Ramp | 49,152 | 1/4 | 1/4 | 26.565 | −Y | 24 | six-octant (12) |
| 6 | `RampHigh` | Ramp | 147,456 | 3/4 | 1/4 | 26.565 | −Y, −X | 24 | six-octant (12) |
| 7 | `CornerOut` | Corner | 65,536 | 1/3 | 1/1 | 45.000 | −Y | 24 | five-octant L (24) |
| 8 | `CornerIn` | Corner | 131,072 | 2/3 | 1/1 | 45.000 | −Y, −X, −Z | 24 | seven-octant (8) |

| 10 | `RampLowIn` | Corner | 65,536 | 1/3 | 1/4 | 26.565 | −Y | 24 | six-octant (12) |

| 14 | `TetraIn` | Facet | 163,840 | 5/6 | 2/1 | 54.736 | +X, +Y, +Z | 8 | full (1) |
| 15 | `Quarter` | Post | 49,152 | 1/4 | 0/1 | 0 | none | 12 | edge-pair (12) |
| 16 | `Post` | Post | 49,152 | 1/4 | 0/1 | 0 | none | 3 | edge-pair (12) |

| 18 | `Stairs` | Step | 147,456 | 3/4 | step 512 FINE | — | −Y, −X | 24 (8 legal) | six-octant (12) |

| 22 | `Conduit` | Connect | per variant | — | — | — | none | 12 | per variant |

**23 topologies. Baked geometries: 286 (ids 0–18) + 4 × 12 (connect) = 334. Distinct rendered placements:
286 + 4 × 32 = 414**, because each connect family's 32 connection masks resolve to one of 12 baked
geometries under one of four lateral rotations. Both numbers matter and the first draft's "≈382" was
neither. At ~976 B of template plus collider per baked geometry the table is **0.33 MB** — which is why
baking every rotation at load is not a trade.

Reading the table:

- **The ramp arithmetic works out.** `RampLow` + `RampHigh` side by side is a continuous 1:2 ramp — cell
  one carries the 0 → 0.5 rise, cell two the 0.5 → 1.0. Rotating either 90° about its extrusion axis
  swaps its legs and yields the steep 2:1 roof piece for free: **same `ShapeId`, different `orient`, zero
  catalogue cost.** That is why there is no separate steep-wedge entry.
- **The corner quartet is not optional.** Ship `RampLow`/`RampHigh` without ids 9–12 and a player cannot
  turn a shallow roof. That is precisely the SE2 alpha complaint ("12–16 classic shapes unreproducible").
  The corner variants are clipped unions of the family's own planes, so they add no *new* slope — which
  is what keeps the walkability analysis in §4.7 to two distinct angles.
- **Curves are excluded by construction, deliberately.** SE's `RoundSlope`/`RoundCorner` have no exact
  volume, no exact coverage rasterisation and no clean convex collider.
- **The last column is the finding that made §4.3.2 cheap, and it is not a coincidence.** The octant-mask
  classes and the shape orbits are orbits of *the same* octahedral group acting on *the same* cube, so
  they line up exactly: 8 single-octant masks ↔ `Nub`'s 8 orients; 12 adjacent-octant-pair masks ↔
  `Quarter`'s 12; 6 face-half masks ↔ `Slab`'s 6; 12 six-octant masks ↔ `Wedge`'s 12; 24 five-octant
  L masks ↔ `CornerOut`'s 24. **The catalogue was already a basis for coarsening; nobody designed it to
  be.** That is the whole reason a coarse cell can be an ordinary catalogue block rather than a second
  representation.

#### 4.3.1 Closure under the 48 transforms

```
for each ShapeDef s:
    orbit = { T · s.template : T ∈ OCTAHEDRAL_48 }      // 24 proper + 24 improper
    dedupe by EXACT integer vertex equality             // 1/32 units — no epsilon
    for improper T: reverse triangle winding            // else front faces point inward
    variant_index[s][o] = the deduped slot for orient code o   // all 48 codes resolve

ASSERT total mirror closure:  ∀ baked v, ∀ axis a:  mirror_a(v) ∈ variants[*]
ASSERT group action:          ∀ (o1,o2):  variant_index[s][compose(o1,o2)] is defined
ASSERT exact volume:          true_volume(v) == v.volume_units          // EQUALITY, no tolerance
ASSERT cell containment:      every template vertex p satisfies 0 ≤ p ≤ 1 on the 1/32 lattice
ASSERT connect envelope:      ∀ connect variant: core ⊆ collider(v) ⊆ envelope
ASSERT cube row exists:       ∀ substance with any BlockTypeDef row: (substance, Cube) has a row
ASSERT octant coverage:       the 40 silhouette-critical masks each have an EXACT variant match
```

The group-action and mirror-closure assertions are **total** — including the connect families, which is
only possible because their connection state was kept out of `orient` (§4.1.4). The last two assertions
are new and are what make §4.3.2 total; both are one line each and both fail loudly at content-build
time rather than at render time on a world nobody has generated yet.

Mirroring is the trap. Space Engineers needed *two* fields — a `Mirrored: bool` and a `MirroringBlock`
naming a **different block** to substitute on the mirrored side, because a left-hand slope's mirror is a
right-hand slope — plus a 26-value `MySymmetryAxisEnum`, because a mirror plane can sit on a cell
boundary *or* through a cell centre. Every shape in the starting catalogue is achiral, so closure is
automatic today — which is exactly why the assertion must exist now, to catch the first chiral shape
someone adds. The 26-value enum has a cleaner generalisation: `MirrorPlane { axis: Axis,
position_half_cells: i64 }` — half-cell units make a boundary plane even and a centre plane odd, so **one
integer replaces a 26-value enum** and there is no case to forget.

**Never rotate at mesh or collide time.** godot_voxel's documentation is blunt ("rotating or flipping
voxels automatically is not supported, so you have to create each rotated version") and the reasons are
concrete: a transform per vertex per remesh, re-rasterisation of a 1,024-bit coverage mask per side per
cell, and the loss of `SharedShape` `Arc` dedup for colliders. Baking costs 0.33 MB and makes the hot
path an array index. (Note the distinction from §4.2: *rotation* is baked; the *index→world map* is
per-vertex and unavoidable on a shell. And note that neither is a tier concern — the baked table is
shared verbatim by **every** rung, whatever the body's `tier_depth`.)

#### 4.3.2 The coarse cell — what a shape becomes at eight metres, and the rule that decides

This subsection answers the ladder's first question, and it starts by rejecting the premise it is usually
posed with.

> **"At 8 m cells a slope is just a cube."** That is true of *one* slope and false of a *ramp*. A single
> `Wedge` at tier 3 is one part in 512 of the coarse cell that contains it — it should vanish, and any
> scheme that preserves it is preserving noise. But an eight-metre ramp built of eight `Wedge`s fills a
> tier-3 cell with a diagonal half, and **that** must still read as a ramp, because it is a metre-scale
> feature only at tier 0 and an eight-metre feature at tier 3. The distinction is not "does the shape
> survive" but "does the *feature* survive at the scale where it is a feature", and that is exactly what
> an octant mask measures and a solid count does not.

**Ruling: coarsening is octant-mask-preserving, recursive one rung at a time, and constrained to shapes
the dominant substance already admits.**

**The record is register row 37's, and it is not §4's alone.** §4's four-byte
`CellSummary { occ_mask, fill_256, substance }` and §3's eight-byte absolute `u64` and §2's ten-byte
signed delta have been adjudicated into **one** record (C1): §4 wins the octant mask and
substance-not-`BlockTypeId` on the arguments below, §3 wins the width, the absolute semantics and the
reserved-bit discipline, `authored` and `solid_delta` are both dropped. §3 owns its persistence; §4 owns
the payload's shape semantics and the pure kernel over it.

```rust
// crates/core/src/block/pyramid.rs — Tier-A, 100 % region+branch. Pure integer arithmetic.
// PERSISTED, PERMANENT, ONE-WAY DOOR (register row 37 / door 43). No branch on tier.

/// The unpacked payload of one coarse-cell summary. Closed under its own update rule:
/// a parent's summary is a function of its eight children's summaries ALONE.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)]
pub struct CellSummary {
    /// Octant o (canonical order: x fastest, then z, then y) set iff child o is non-empty.
    /// At tier 0 this is the drawn variant's baked `octant_mask` (ShapeDef.octant_mask under Orient).
    pub occ_mask:  u8,
    /// Mean fill fraction of the eight children, 0..=255.
    pub fill_256:  u8,
    /// Dominant substance by SUMMED fill over non-empty children; ties -> lowest SubstanceId.
    /// When `occ_mask == 0` this MUST be the realm's declared EMPTY substance id.
    pub substance: SubstanceId,   // u16, the §2.1 substance-table row id
}

/// The persisted 8-byte word. ONE width at EVERY tier: a tier is a number, not a code path.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct PyramidEntry(u64);
```

```
Edit-pyramid entry — 8 bytes, one u64, MSB-first:
  bits 63..46  cell       (18)  CellIndex within the tier-L chunk, 0..=238_327
  bits 45..30  substance  (16)  SubstanceId — dominant by summed fill; ties -> lowest id
  bits 29..22  occ_mask    (8)  octant o set iff child octant o is non-empty
  bits 21..14  fill_256    (8)  mean fill fraction of the eight children, 0..=255
  bits 13.. 0  reserved   (14)  MUST be zero; decode REJECTS non-zero (never decode-to-Default)
```

**Keying and storage (§3's, restated once so §4's readers can follow the walk-up).** Table
`chunk_pyramid: ChunkKey -> PyramidRecord`, in the **same redb file as the block deltas** (it moves with
the realm on a re-shard and flushes under the same `BLOCK_STORE_FLUSH_STEP` fence). The *storage block*
is one `(tier, chunk)` pair holding that chunk's sparse entry list, in §3.9.3's two encodings — sparse
`8n`, or masked-dense `29,791 + palette + n·bits/8`, the compactor picking the smaller at the same
4,256-cell crossover. `ChunkKey` orders sector → tier → a → b → c, so one whole rung is one contiguous
range scan. **The names `block_pyramid` and "beside `block_wal`" are STRUCK** (M3), including where §4.9.5
and §4.10 used the latter.

**Composition at read time** (Addendum 2 §C.4, made exact):

```
fn coarse_summary(a: CoarseAddr) -> CellSummary {
    chunk_pyramid.get(a).map(PyramidEntry::summary)
                        .unwrap_or_else(|| generate_summary(a))
}
// then: representative(coarse_summary(a), &ADMITS) -> (BlockTypeId, Orient)
```

`generate_summary(a)` is THE SAME generator call the coarse mesher makes — one evaluation of `h(dir, L)`
plus one strata lookup — in `core/src/grid/gen/`, Category-A deterministic. It is also the call §6.2 and
§6.5's coarse ground tint make (M8), so the mesher, the tint and the walk-up cannot disagree.

**The pure kernel over that payload, which is §4's:**

```rust
// crates/core/src/block/coarsen.rs — Tier-A, 100 %, FOLDED INTO BlockRegistryHash.
// Branchless shim over monomorphic helpers (HR5's generic-code discipline).
// Pure integer arithmetic. No float, no transcendental, no allocation, no branch on tier.

/// One rung. Children are in canonical octant order (x fastest, then z, then y).
pub fn coarsen(children: &[CellSummary; 8]) -> CellSummary;

/// The summary -> drawable block. `admits` is the BlockTypeDef row test of §4.1.1.
pub fn representative(s: CellSummary, admits: &AdmitsTable) -> (BlockTypeId, Orient);
```

**`coarsen` is stated exactly, because byte-identity is now gated PER TIER** (C2):

```
occ_mask  = Sum_{o=0..7} ((children[o].occ_mask != 0) as u8) << o
fill_256  = ((Sum_{o=0..7} children[o].fill_256 as u16) + 4) >> 3        // round-half-up, exact
substance = argmax over distinct s of
              Sum { children[o].fill_256 as u32 : children[o].substance == s
                                               && children[o].occ_mask != 0 }
            ties broken by LOWEST SubstanceId
            if occ_mask == 0 then substance = realm.empty_substance and fill_256 = 0
```

**The tier-0 leaf — the only place the block field is read at all:**

```
summary_of_tier0_cell(a: BlockAddr) -> CellSummary {
    occ_mask  = BAKED_VARIANT[variant_index[shape][orient]].octant_mask
    fill_256  = ((volume_units as u64 * 255) + CELL_VOLUME_UNITS/2) / CELL_VOLUME_UNITS
    substance = the cell's SubstanceId
}   // CELL_VOLUME_UNITS = 196_608; full cube -> 255, half slab -> 128
```

The tie-break is **total** (distinct `SubstanceId`s, lowest wins) and the sum is over the children's
*current* summaries, so `coarsen`'s output depends on the tier-0 state and on nothing else — no
insertion order, no arrival order, no compaction pass. That answers §2.4.3's order-independence
objection rather than ignoring it: §2 was right that a *streaming majority estimator* can never match a
replay of a dedup-to-final, sorted-on-drain WAL, but this is an exact recompute, not an estimator, so
order-independence holds at every rung at every instant — more strongly than §2's deferral achieved.
**STRUCK with it:** §2.4.3's `DOMINANT_DIRTY` bit, its deferred compaction argmax over a transient
histogram, and its `dominant_recompute_batch` field.

**The three rules, each with its reason:**

1. **Occupancy is `non-empty`, not `half-full`.** Octant *o* is set iff child *o* has any solid at all.
   The alternative — a volume threshold — makes a wall of `Panel`s (1/8 fill) vanish at tier 1 and a
   distant hull disappear, which is precisely the artefact Addendum 2 §C.4 exists to prevent. Rounding
   *toward solid* is the safe direction here because the failure mode of over-solid is "the wall looks a
   metre thicker than it is at 800 m" (a 1.3 px error) and the failure mode of under-solid is "the wall
   is not there". Note this is a **different** threshold from §4.5.5's `occ_ao`, which uses `≥ half`, and
   deliberately so: `occ_ao` is a shading term where over-occlusion is the visible error, and coarsening
   is a silhouette term where under-occupancy is. Two questions, two answers, both stated with their
   reason rather than one constant reused because it was to hand.
2. **The shape is chosen by the mask; the fill only breaks ties.** `COARSE_SHAPE[mask][bucket]` is a
   baked `[[u16; 9]; 256]` table — `(ShapeId 10 | Orient 6)` packed into one `u16`, **4,608 bytes** —
   where `bucket = (fill_256 as u16 * 9) >> 8 ∈ 0..=8`. The entry is the baked variant whose own octant
   mask equals `mask`, tie-broken by minimum `|variant.volume_units/CELL_VOLUME_UNITS − fill|`, then by
   lowest `(ShapeId, Orient)`. Where no variant has that exact mask (184 of the 256 masks; §4.3's orbit
   correspondence covers at least 72 exactly, and the bake reports the precise figure), the entry is the
   variant minimising Hamming distance to `mask` first and volume error second. The whole table is
   computed at bake by 256 × 9 × 334 = 769,536 integer comparisons — microseconds, once.
   **[M1] There is NO fill threshold and NO solid-or-empty decision anywhere on this path.** `occ_mask ==
   0` means empty and every other mask selects a shape through the hashed table; §3.9.8's *"drawn solid
   iff `fill >= solid_threshold` (a render tuning field, default 128)"* and the `solid_threshold` field
   itself are **STRUCK**, not relocated. A client-tunable knob on this decision is the one place a DETAIL
   setting could produce a visible FACT difference between two clients, which is exactly what folding
   `COARSE_SHAPE` into `BlockRegistryHash` (§4.4.1) exists to prevent. C1's record makes the knob
   unnecessary, so deleting it is free.
3. **The admits fallback is one step, and it is total.** `representative` returns
   `(substance, COARSE_SHAPE[..])` if that row exists, else `(substance, Cube)`. It is exactly one step
   rather than a declared fallback chain because the only substances that restrict their shape set are
   terrain-only substances, whose set is `{Cube}` — so the one step is exact for every case that exists.
   §4.3.1's new `cube row exists` assertion is what makes it total.

**Recursive, not direct-from-fine, and the reason is four orders of magnitude.** Tier *L*'s summary is
computed from tier *L−1*'s summaries, never from the tier-0 field. Direct-from-fine would read 8^L cells
per coarse cell — **2,097,152 at rung 7** — against 8. An edit therefore costs **8 summary reads per
rung**, `8 × (tier_depth − 1)` in the worst case (96 on the starter body's 13-rung ladder), against a
direct-from-fine sum that is already 19,173,960 by rung 7 and grows by a factor of eight per rung after
it. **This is also why §2.4.3's signed `solid_delta` against the generated baseline loses:** turning a
delta back into a fill fraction needs the coarse cell's *generated solid count*, which is 8^L tier-0
evaluations — the exact cost this paragraph prices and rejects — whereas an absolute summary needs one
octave-dropped evaluation. The cost of recursion is that information loss compounds; it is bounded by one
bucket per rung and it is measured, not assumed (§4.10's property test drives random fields through both
paths and reports the worst-case silhouette divergence).

**Two properties that fall out, and one that does not:**

- **It terminates early — on SUMMARY equality, not on representative equality.**

  > **Correction [C2].** ~~The walk up stops at the first rung whose `representative` output is
  > unchanged.~~ **Replaced by: the walk up stops at the first rung whose stored `CellSummary` equals
  > the recomputed one.** Two different summaries can share a representative, so exiting on
  > representative equality leaves an ancestor whose *stored* summary is stale while the drawn pixel is
  > right — and §4.9.5's recompute-from-deltas audit then fails on visually correct data. Exiting on
  > summary equality is exact, because an unchanged parent implies unchanged ancestors.

  The bound is unchanged and the worked example still holds: breaking one block inside solid rock changes
  rung 1 (`Cube` → a seven-octant `CornerIn`) and then rung 2's fill goes from 8/8 to (7 + 2/3)/8 = 0.958,
  which differs from the stored 1.000 only in `fill_256` and settles by rung 2 or 3, so **the common
  single edit dirties one or two coarse chunks**. The worst case (removing the last solid child of a
  chain of representatives, e.g. the final block of an isolated pillar) is `tier_depth − 1` rungs.
- **The generated half never uses it.** Terrain's coarse tiers come from the octave-dropped generator
  directly (Addendum 2 §B), which emits `Cube`-or-empty; the coarsener runs only over the *edit* pyramid.
  So a dug tunnel at tier 2 appears as missing `Cube`s rather than as invented wedges, which is the
  correct reading of Addendum 2 §C.7's derived-from-versus-substituted-for test: **coarsening never
  invents a shape that was not there, it only preserves one that was.**
- **It is not volumetrically conservative, and it does not need to be.** A six-octant mask coarsens to a
  `Wedge`, which does not fill all six of its octants; strict containment therefore fails. The property
  the design actually needs is weaker and is trivially true: both the coarse solid and the union of its
  children lie inside the same coarse cell, so their Hausdorff separation is at most one coarse cell
  edge. That single sentence is what makes §4.5.8's skirt provably sufficient with no case analysis, and
  it is why the design does not need — and should not pay for — a containment guarantee.

**What this costs at the wide end.** Player builds coarsen shape-preservingly and their cell count falls
8× per rung, and a structure is drawn at exactly one tier at a time, so a 10,000-block ship is 10,000
Lane-B instances at tier 0, **1,250 at tier 1, 156 at tier 2, 20 at tier 3, 2 at tier 4** — 80 KB, 10 KB,
1.2 KB, 160 B, 16 B of instance data. **Lane B is self-bounding under the ladder**, and §4.5.4's 1.91 MB
per-chunk ceiling is revealed as a tier-0 ceiling that no coarse rung can approach.

> **~~[USER DECISION 4-E]~~ → REGISTER ROW 37 / [USER DECISION 8-A] — the edit-pyramid entry.**
> §4 raised this as its own; §2.10 raised it as 2-H and 2-I and §3.9.8 as 3-J. All four are **collapsed
> into register row 37**, which asks one question with five sub-parts: (a) contents, (b) how the fill is
> spent on a shape, (c) storage granularity, (d) the write invariant, (e) the divergence policy.
>
> **§4's argument, which the row carries and which is why the recommended option is A1:** the octant mask
> is what keeps an eight-metre ramp reading as a ramp and a wall of thin panels from vanishing. The
> alternative — a solid count thresholded to a boolean — is the documented "distant castles read as
> voxel-based blobs" failure, and the mask costs one byte per entry on a record the shape bake already
> computes for the catalogue. §4 also argues **substance, not `BlockTypeId`**: a `BlockTypeId` carries a
> shape and possibly a function, and a coarse cell's shape must come from the mask and the fill rather
> than from whichever child happened to dominate. The remaining judgement is **taste**, and it is stated
> in the row: A1 means a distant player build reads as *faceted* (its slopes and corners survive) and A2
> means it reads as *blocky*. §4 does not prefer A2, because it contradicts what the player built, but it
> is a real position on a world whose art direction is deliberately blocky.
---

### 4.4 The one `ShapeDef` row, and where it lives

**One row, one crate, one unit per field.** `ShapeDef` lives where §2 puts it —
`crates/core/src/block/shape.rs`, Tier-A, covered by `BlockRegistryHash`. **No new `vd-voxel` crate**:
introducing one would be a change to CLAUDE.md's dependency rule that this section has no need to make.
The baked variant table, the coverage patterns, the occlusion matrix and (new) the `COARSE_SHAPE` table
are pure integer data and live beside it in `crates/core/src/block/bake.rs`; only the construction of
parry `SharedShape`s from `collider_id` happens in `vd-sim`, which is exactly what §2's
`collider_id: u16` indirection was for.

```rust
pub struct ShapeDef {
    pub tag: u16,
    pub name: &'static str,               // debug only; EXCLUDED from the registry hash
    pub family: ShapeFamily,
    pub template: &'static [TemplateTri], // canonical orientation, 1/32-cell INTEGER coords
    pub volume_units: u32,                // EXACT, /196_608 of a CELL (never m³)
    pub face_full_mask: u8,               // DERIVED: sides whose conservative cover is FULL.
                                          //   == solid == airtight == greedy-cullable. One field,
                                          //   replacing §2's three authored masks.
    pub mount_face_mask: u8,              // DERIVED: sides whose conservative cover is non-empty
    pub octant_mask: u8,                  // DERIVED (new): octants the solid region touches at all.
                                          //   The coarsening key of §4.3.2. Costs one byte per row.
    pub cover_cons: [u8; 6],              // interned conservative 32×32 pattern id per side
    pub cover_lib:  [u8; 6],              // interned liberal 32×32 pattern id per side
    pub collider_id: u16,                 // → ColliderTemplate: Cuboid | Convex | Parts(&[..])
    pub mirror_shape: [u16; 3],           // TOTAL: this shape mirrored in x / y / z
    pub slope_tan2_num: u32,              // EXACT index-space tan² of the steepest upward facet
    pub slope_tan2_den: u32,
    pub step_rise_fine: u16,              // Step shapes: 512 FINE = 0.500 m exactly
    pub orientation_group: u8,            // deduped orbit size under the 48 transforms
    pub legal_rotation_mask: u8,          // §2's MyBlockRotation policy (2 bits); the 48-bit legal
                                          //   set is DERIVED at bake from policy × symmetry
    pub connect: u8,                      // ConnectRule id, or NO_CONNECT
    pub autorotate: u8,                   // Free | MountToSurface | Upright | Fixed
    pub flags: u8,                        // IS_FULL_CUBE | PLACEABLE | RETIRED | AO_OCCLUDES
}
```

64 bytes per row (`octant_mask` lands in existing padding; the row width does not change); 32 rows is
2 KiB (§2's byte budget line moves from 0.9 KiB to 2 KiB — noise).

Notes on the fields that are not self-evident:

- **Two coverage rasterisations, not one.** The occluder side is rasterised *conservatively* (a texel is
  set only if fully covered) and the occludee side *liberally* (set if covered at all). The justification
  is a containment property, not a bug attribution: `conservative ⊆ true ⊆ liberal`, so the only possible
  error is **under**-culling. **Under-coverage produces overdraw, never a hole** — that is the safety
  property the whole two-lane design rests on, and §4.5.8 shows it is also the safety property the whole
  *tier* design rests on. Cost: 2 × 128 B per interned pattern, ~40 KB total.
- **The authored source is a mesh; the row is derived.** §2's pipeline authors `shape_meshes/*.obj`; the
  content build snaps vertices to the 1/32 lattice (**failing** if a vertex is off-lattice) and derives
  `volume_units`, both cover arrays, all three masks and `slope_tan2` from the snapped template by a
  tested pure function. §2's tripwire 5 — "the derivation is the only author; a hand-edited row fails the
  build" — applies unchanged, and now covers `octant_mask` too: a hand-written octant mask is exactly the
  way a coarse tier would silently stop matching the shape it summarises.
- **`slope_tan2` is exact and index-space.** Every upward-facing facet's normal is an integer vector, so
  `tan²θ = (nx² + nz²) / ny²` is an exact rational. §4.7 converts to physical with one division. There
  is no millidegree field and no rounding-direction question.

#### 4.4.1 `ShapeId` numbering, and version skew

**Append-only. Never renumbered. Never reused. A retired shape keeps its id, loses `PLACEABLE`, and must
still bake, collide and render, because a persisted world contains it.**

Skew is handled by §2's mechanism, not a duplicate one: `BlockRegistryHash([u8;32])` sits in the
connection handshake, the `chunk_snapshot` header and the epoch record, and a mismatch **refuses the
connection / refuses to open the store**. An unknown `BlockTypeId` or `ShapeId` on the wire is a protocol
violation that tears the connection — it is **never** rendered as `Cube`, because a client rendering a
slope where the server collides a corner is the failure this exists to prevent. §4 adds only a **golden
roster pin** (`(id, name, volume_units, octant_mask, family)`, one literal line per shape) as a *review*
tripwire so that appending appends a line and changing one is a visible diff; it lives in `tests/`,
following the `celestial_ephemeris_pin.rs` precedent, where the justfile's
`--ignore-filename-regex '(/bin/|/tests/)'` keeps it out of the HR5 gate.

**`COARSE_SHAPE` joins the registry hash, and that is not optional.** The client and the realm owner both
compute coarse cells — the client to render them, the owner to maintain the pyramid — so a table
mismatch means two machines disagree about what a distant tower looks like. Folding it into
`BlockRegistryHash` makes that a refused connection instead of a silent divergence, at the cost of one
more input to a hash that is already computed.

And the HR3/HR5 corollary: **there is no `match` on `ShapeId` anywhere in feature code, and there is no
`match` on a tier anywhere at all.** Everything is an array index into the baked table (§2.1.2's
dense-tag idiom); the tier is an integer that scales an index and selects a table row, never a branch.
A 23-arm match inside a generic mesher function is precisely the per-monomorphisation coverage trap
CLAUDE.md documents; all branching lives in one monomorphic `resolve_variant` helper, and `coarsen`
is written to the same shape (a branchless shim over monomorphic helpers) for the same reason.

#### 4.4.2 Which of these fields are tier-invariant, and which are tier-0 semantics

This is the ladder's third question — *"the per-face coverage bitmasks and mount points are tier-0
concepts; say what the coarse tier uses instead"* — and the answer has two halves, one of which corrects
the premise.

**Half one: none of the geometry is a tier-0 concept, because all of it is index-space.** A 32×32
rasterisation of the unit cell says "this fraction of this face is covered"; that statement is scale-free
and means exactly the same thing whether the cell is one metre or 128. `cover_cons`, `cover_lib`,
`face_full_mask`, `octant_mask`, `volume_units`, `slope_tan2`, the collider templates and the 48-element
rotation orbit are therefore **tier-invariant and shared verbatim by every rung of every body's
ladder**, whatever its `tier_depth`. There is no
coarse coverage table, no coarse occlusion matrix and no coarse catalogue. That is the direct payoff of
§4.2's index-space ruling, taken for a completely different reason two months earlier.

The containment property survives with one clarification worth stating precisely: `conservative ⊆ true ⊆
liberal` is a statement about **the variant that is drawn**, and at a coarse tier the variant that is
drawn *is* the coarse representative. So the property holds against what is on screen. It says nothing
about the fine field the representative summarises, and it was never asked to.

**Half two: every *semantic* reading of those fields is tier-0-only, and the list is exactly four.**

| Reader | What it reads | Valid at tier ≥ 1? | Why not, and what the coarse tier uses instead |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Culling** (`occludes`, `face_full`, `face_partial`) | `cover_cons`/`cover_lib` | **YES** | It is a statement about two adjacent representatives at the same tier. Unchanged code, unchanged matrix, unchanged safety property |
| **Airtightness / pressurisation** (§2.5) | `face_full_mask` | **NO** | Pressurisation is gameplay state. A coarse cell over-reports solidity by construction (§4.3.2 rule 1), so a coarse-sealed room would be a room the player cannot actually breathe in. Coarse tiers use **nothing** — they are never sealed, because nothing at 8 m is a room |
| **Mount points** (`mount_face_mask`) | `mount_face_mask` | **NO** | Mounting is a placement operation and placement is tier-0 by §4.6.3's typing. Coarse tiers use **nothing** — a coarse cell is never a mount target, because it is never placed on |
| **Structural support** (§2.2.4) | `face_full_mask` + the generated/placed bit | **NO** | Same over-reporting problem, with a worse failure: a coarse cell would report support that the fine field does not provide, and a build would stand at distance and collapse on approach. Coarse tiers use **nothing** |
| **Mass / yield / thermal / buoyancy** | `volume_units` | **NO** | §4.3's rider. A representative's volume is a silhouette summary, not a mass |
| **Collision** | `collider_id` | **NO** | §4.6.3, and it is an assertion rather than a rule |
| **Ambient occlusion** | `occ_ao` | **at tier 1 only** | ~~§4.5.5 already confines AO to a 16 m sphere, which is inside tier 0 by 49×. Coarse tiers use nothing and need nothing.~~ **Replaced by [H3]:** the slab exists iff `2^L <= ao_max_cell_size_m` (default 2.0 m ⇒ tiers 0 **and 1**). Tiers ≥ 2 use **nothing** and need nothing, because §5.9.6(d)'s analytic coarse-height horizon term captures the occlusion that is real at that scale, and the two hand over inside the tier-1/tier-2 crossfade band |
| **Walkability** (§4.7) | `slope_tan2` | **NO** | It feeds the character controller, which sits on the collider |

**So the honest answer to "what does the coarse tier use instead of mount points and airtightness" is:
nothing, and it needs nothing.** The four semantics all exist to answer questions about a place a player
is standing in, holding a block, breathing, or being held up by — and a player is always inside tier 0.
This is not an accident of the numbers; it is the same fact stated twice. Tier 0 runs to 786 m
(Addendum 2 §C.2) and every one of those semantics has a physical reach measured in metres.

The mechanism that enforces it is §4.6.3's newtype, and it is worth saying why a type is the right answer
rather than a runtime check: all eight readers above are *correct today* and would remain correct for
years, because nothing hands them a coarse chunk. The failure arrives the first time someone optimises a
distant-structure query by reading the coarse field, and it arrives as a physics bug on a shipped world.
A type turns that from a future incident into a compile error today, for one newtype and roughly a dozen
signature characters.
---

### 4.5 The two meshing lanes and the culling matrix

§5 fixes the mesher's architecture, tiering and worker model. This subsection fixes the **contract
between the lanes** — the part that decides whether a cube next to a slope leaves a hole — and, as of
§4.5.8, the part that decides whether a fine chunk next to a coarse one leaves a hole.

#### 4.5.1 Lane assignment is computed, not declared

```
is_cube(v) = (∀ s: v.cover_cons[s] == FULL) ∧ (v.volume_units == CELL_VOLUME_UNITS)
```

Computed at bake from the geometry, so no shape can lie about it; the volume clause excludes a
pathological hollow shell with six full sides.

- **Lane A (cube lane)** — every `is_cube` variant. Binary greedy meshing, ~65 µs per 62³ chunk.
- **Lane B (shaped lane)** — everything else. Instanced from the baked template through `cell_point`,
  never merged, appended to the same chunk mesh.

**Lane assignment is tier-blind and that is the point.** A coarse cell whose representative is `Cube`
goes to Lane A; one whose representative is a `Wedge` goes to Lane B. Because generated terrain is
`Cube`-only at every rung (§4.9.4) and player builds shrink 8× per rung (§4.3.2), **coarse chunks are
overwhelmingly Lane A** — which is the arithmetic reason the ladder does not multiply the shaped lane's
cost by eight.

#### 4.5.2 Six face masks, not one occupancy mask

The first draft said Lane B cells contribute 0 to the occupancy bitmask "so a neighbouring cube's face is
still considered". That is wrong for three catalogue entries — `CornerIn` (−Y, −X, −Z), `TetraIn`
(+X, +Y, +Z) and `RampHighIn` (−Y, +X, +Z) all have FULL faces, and a cube facing one of them *should*
be culled. Left as drafted, every cube/`…In` interface emits a hidden face.

The fix stays bitwise rather than adding a scalar pass. The mesher's step-1 integer pass produces:

| Mask | Bits/chunk | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `face_full[6]` | 6 × 29.8 KiB | side *s* of this cell is fully covered — culls the facing neighbour's quad |
| `face_partial[6]` | 6 × 29.8 KiB | side *s* is non-empty but not full — a **greedy merge barrier** |
| `occ_ao` | 29.8 KiB | AO occupancy (§4.5.5) — chunks where `2^L <= ao_max_cell_size_m` (**tiers 0–1** at the default); coarser chunks emit none. ~~tier-0 chunks only~~ corrected by [H3] |

Building them costs one `memcpy` of `face_full` from the cube occupancy (6 × 29.8 KiB ≈ 15 µs), one
`memset` of `face_partial` (≈ 15 µs), then a scatter over Lane B cells only. **Lane A rises from ~65 µs
to ~95 µs plus ~6 bit-ops per shaped cell.** Scratch per meshing worker: 358 KiB of masks + the 512 KiB
resolved-variant buffer ≈ **870 KiB**; at eight workers, 7 MB. The resolved buffer is cleared through a
dirty list, not a full memset, so a sparse chunk does not pay for the whole 512 KiB. **All of this is
per-chunk and therefore tier-invariant** — a tier-7 chunk has the same 62³ cells and the same scratch as
a tier-0 one, which is why the worker pool needs no tier awareness and no second budget.

#### 4.5.3 The occlusion matrix

```
BAKE
  for each baked variant v, each side s ∈ 0..6:
      v.pat_cons[s] = intern( rasterize_conservative(v.template ∩ plane(s), 32×32) )
      v.pat_lib[s]  = intern( rasterize_liberal    (v.template ∩ plane(s), 32×32) )
  occludes[a][b] = (pattern[a] & pattern[b]) == pattern[b]        // P × P bits

MESH (Lane B and the cube/shaped interface)
  emit face (cell c, side s)  iff
      ! occludes[ variant(neighbour(c,s)).pat_cons[opposite(s)] ][ variant(c).pat_lib[s] ]
```

334 baked geometries × 6 sides = 2,004 rasterisations before dedup, collapsing to an expected 60–150
distinct patterns (most sides are FULL, EMPTY, half, triangle or quarter). At 150 the matrix is 150² bits
= 2.8 KB and the pattern store is 150 × 128 B × 2 = 38 KB. godot_voxel's shipped bound is 65,536 models;
we are at 334.

Degenerate cases fall out correctly: `occludes[FULL][x]` is true for every `x`, so a full face culls
everything (which is why the bitwise `face_full` shortcut in §4.5.2 is exactly equivalent and cheaper);
`occludes[EMPTY][x]` is true only for `x == EMPTY`. **That second identity is what §4.5.8's tier-seam
proof turns on** — an absent or different-tier neighbour is `EMPTY`, and `EMPTY` occludes nothing.

**Z-fighting cannot arise given one invariant:** any face lying exactly on a cell-boundary plane must be
registered in that side's coverage pattern. Registered faces participate in culling; unregistered
coplanar geometry would be drawn twice. Assert at bake, alongside the containment assertion of §4.2.

#### 4.5.4 Lane B must be instanced, and that is what bounds it

Lane B "never merged" plus real emitted vertices is unbounded and the first draft's 3,000-cell figure was
asserted, not derived. At 24 vertices × 20 B = 480 B per shaped cell:

| Shaped-cell density in one 62³ chunk | Cells | Vertices emitted | Instanced at 8 B/cell |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.26 % | 3,000 | 1.44 MB | 24 KB |
| 10 % (a facade built of `Slab`s and `Panel`s — an ordinary build) | 23,833 | **11.4 MB** | 191 KB |
| 100 % | 238,328 | **114 MB** | **1.91 MB — the hard ceiling** |

§5's budget is "edit echo → pixels ≤ 33 ms" against ~480 KB/chunk of Lane A upload. The 10 % row blows it
by 24×. **Therefore instancing is not an optimisation; it is the mechanism that makes Lane B bounded, and
it must land in the same slice as Lane B.** The instance record is `(cell_index 18 | block_type 16 |
resolved_orient 6)` = 40 bits padded to 8 B — deliberately the same shape as the WAL record — and the
vertex shader applies `cell_point` per vertex (§4.2(d)), reading the cell scale `2^L` from
`ChunkHeader.detail_tier`, which §5.2.2 already reserves. Draws are grouped by baked variant **across all
resident chunks and across all tiers** — the baked table is shared, so a `Wedge` at tier 0 and a `Wedge`
at tier 4 are the same instanced draw with different per-instance headers — so the draw count is bounded
by the number of distinct variants in view (≤ 334), not by the chunk count and not by the rung count.

**This table is now explicitly a tier-0 table.** Every figure in it is a worst case over a 62 m chunk of
one-metre cells; a coarse chunk covering the same *world volume* holds 8^L times fewer shaped cells and a
coarse chunk covering the same *cell count* is drawn only from a range 2^L times further away. The
ceiling is unreachable above tier 0 and the ladder therefore only ever relaxes this budget.

**Sparse constructs.** A 10k-block player ship fits inside a single 62³ chunk, so a naive implementation
re-runs the whole-chunk resolve, remesh and collider rebuild on every edit: O(238,328) work for O(1)
change, a 24× waste, on P8's normal case. Two requirements:

1. **Sparse iteration.** §3's `Chunk` already tracks `non_air: u32`. When `non_air ≤ 29,791` (12.5 % of
   the chunk — the crossover where per-cell neighbour gather at ~8 ops/cell equals the dense sweep), the
   resolve and mesh passes iterate the occupied-cell list, not the volume. **Coarse chunks are sparse by
   construction** (a tier-3 chunk of a 10k-block ship holds 20 occupied cells), so they take this path
   always and a coarse remesh is microseconds, not the ~1 ms a dense tier-0 remesh costs.
2. **Sub-chunk mesh sections.** Lane B (and Lane A) must be re-meshable at sub-chunk granularity;
   **31³ cells, 8 sections per chunk** is the natural split (62 = 2 × 31), so a single edit re-meshes 1/8
   of a chunk. The merge barrier this introduces every 31 cells costs a 62×62 wall four quads instead of
   one. §5 owns the partition; this section owns the requirement and the number.

#### 4.5.5 Ambient occlusion across the lane boundary

godot_voxel's shipped compromise is to set `contributes_to_ao = false` for any model whose side pattern
is not full, so non-cube blocks neither cast nor meaningfully receive baked vertex AO. That is the right
fallback and the wrong target. §5.7's fragment-shader AO from the per-chunk occupancy bitmask is
**lane-agnostic by construction** — the shader samples an occupancy field and does not care whether a
texel's geometry came from a merged quad or a slope template. The one addition:

> **A second occupancy bitmask, `occ_ao`** — a shaped cell sets it when `volume_units ≥
> CELL_VOLUME_UNITS / 2` (**98,304 of 196,608**; half-solid or more occludes). The threshold is a stated
> rule, not a tuned constant, and its one tunable lives in §5's render config struct, not inline. Known artefact: a
> vertical `Slab` reads as occluding from all six directions; directional AO occupancy would cost six
> masks and is not worth it.

Without it a slope reads as a hole in the AO field and every wedge gets a bright halo.

**Residency.**

> **Correction [H3 / M5].** ~~At §5.8's 449 ground-level surface chunk-columns and ~4 resident chunks per
> column, keeping `occ_full` + `occ_ao` GPU-resident for every rendered chunk is ~1,800 × 59.6 KiB =
> **107 MB**, and at 1 km altitude it is impossible. AO is a contact-shading term with a visual reach of a
> few metres, so: **the occupancy slab is GPU-resident only for chunks intersecting a 16 m sphere around
> the camera — at most 27 chunks, 1.6 MB.** Beyond it AO is simply absent.~~
>
> **Replaced by the DERIVED residency rule.** The slab is built, uploaded and sampled for a chunk iff
>
> ```
> 2^L <= ao_max_cell_size_m        // RenderTuning::ao_max_cell_size_m : f32, default 2.0 m
>                                  // => tiers 0 and 1
> ```
>
> and `ChunkHeader.ao_slot` carries the **absent sentinel** for every chunk that fails the test. That is
> **2,273 chunks, ≤ 71 MiB dense and ~45 MiB sparse** (§5.3.6's VRAM table row already books it).
> The 449-column, 107 MB and 16 m-sphere figures were all sized against the retracted single-tier horizon
> and are struck with it. The rule is an authored size in **metres**, not a tier list, so it obeys §5's
> generic sub-cell law rather than being grandfathered past it.

> **Amendment (Addendum 2, as corrected).** ~~This does brush the open "what counts as LOD" question
> (`snowflow_technique_analysis.md` §5.4/§7); it is flagged here and deferred to that existing decision,
> not re-opened.~~ **Replaced by: register row 7 is ANSWERED and CLOSED, so nothing is deferred and
> nothing needs flagging.** Distance-driven AO falloff is now an explicitly permitted *parameter falloff*
> under Addendum 2 §C.8 — the same mesh, the same material identity, one term ramping to zero. Three
> consequences, two of which are themselves corrected above:
>
> 1. ~~**AO is a tier-0-only term.** The 16 m sphere sits inside tier 0's 786 m by a factor of 49, so
>    `occ_ao` is never computed for, uploaded for, or read from a coarse chunk. `ChunkHeader.ao_slot`
>    carries the absent sentinel at every tier ≥ 1.~~ **STRUCK by [H3]: AO covers tiers 0–1.** At tier 2 a
>    "block" is 4 m, so darkening the corner where two 4 m cells meet is a four-metre dark band painted on

>    AO covers tiers 0–1, the horizon term covers tiers ≥ 2, and they meet inside the tier-1/tier-2 band.

>    has its own `warp_frac_on` (0.15) / `warp_frac_off` (0.05) pair applied to `A_max / 2^L` (§5.6.7).
