>    ~6,800 chunks, which at 59.6 KiB is **406 MB** …~~ **STRUCK.** The question is not full-view
>    residency; it is the tiers-0-and-1 set, which is 2,273 chunks at ≤ 71 MiB dense and ~45 MiB sparse,
>    and which §5.3.6 books. The cost objection that motivated the 16 m sphere is answered.

#### 4.5.6 Merge barriers, and the cost argument corrected

A merged N×M greedy quad has only four corner vertices; if the adjacent geometry subdivides that edge, a
benign sub-pixel T-junction becomes a visible crack. **Rule: any cube face whose in-plane neighbour has
`face_partial` set is a barrier in the greedy sweep.** Implement it as the *same* `border_peel(quad,
predicate) -> (core, ring)` operation §5.5.2 introduces for material seams and §5.6.2 for warped corners.
**Three consumers, one operation, one set of tests** — the most reusable piece of machinery in the mesher,
and it should be written once, first.

The first draft's cost argument was backwards. It claimed the peel "removes merging exactly on the
surfaces where merging was already earning 1.3×", citing 0fps's 31–64× win on flat-regular geometry
versus 1.3× on noisy terrain — but the peel fires where *shaped* cells are, i.e. on player-built hulls,
which are the flat-regular 31–64× case. The peel removes merging exactly where merging earns the most.

The correct bound is **perimeter, not area**: a barrier splits a sweep along the boundary of a shaped
region. A 62×62 wall with a slope trim on one edge costs one 1×62 ring — negligible. The worst case is
adversarial and must be stated: a **checkerboard** of `Slab` and `Cube` collapses merging on that plane
entirely, 3,844 quads per 62² plane ≈ 369 KB of vertices, ~22 MB if repeated on all 62 planes. That is a
griefing vector, and it is caught by the same per-chunk upload budget that bounds Lane B (§4.5.4) — a
chunk over budget degrades to per-cell quads, which is already what it is, and the pathological build
becomes a performance cost to its own builder rather than to the server. **The ladder shortens its reach
rather than lengthening it:** at tier 1 the checkerboard's alternating cells coarsen to a single
representative apiece, so the pathology exists only inside tier 0's 786 m and cannot be used to attack a
distant observer's frame time.

**No barrier is needed at a tier seam.** The greedy sweep is per chunk and terminates at the chunk edge
regardless, so a differing neighbour tier changes nothing about merging. It changes what happens to the
boundary *faces*, which is §4.5.8.

#### 4.5.7 Material blending, and the vertex ABI Lane B needs

§5.5's blend width is bounded by the emitting primitive's extent, which is why merged quads need a
seam-strip peel. **Lane B primitives never exceed one cell, so Lane B is blend-correct for free** — a
shaped face abutting a different material carries the two-material path over its whole face. At tier *L*
"one cell" is 2^L m, so the blend width scales with the tier automatically and is always the same
fraction of the screen; there is no second blend-width constant and no tier term in §5.5.

One requirement flows back to §5. §5's packed `u32` derives the tangent from the face axis plus a
handedness bit, which is exact for axis-aligned faces and meaningless for a diagonal. Lane B therefore
needs a fourth arm on §5's proposed `VertexStream`:

```rust
VertexStream::Shaped { verts: Vec<ShapedVertex> }   // { pos: [f32;3], packed: u32,
                                                    //   normal_oct: u16, tangent_oct: u16 }  20 B
```

The correct argument for adding it now is **not** that the enum already exists — it does not; §5 is
proposing it, and today `crates/client/src/realm_scene.rs:540` defines only `MeshPrim`. The argument is
that §5 is landing the enum in one slice, and a fourth arm added in that slice is free, whereas a fourth
arm added after three producers exist re-specialises every pipeline and re-covers every producer test.
**The ladder adds a second free rider to that same slice:** §4.5.8's skirt quads need one spare bit in
the packed `u32` (§5.2.2 reserves bits 28–31) so the fragment shader can suppress AO and decoration on
them. One bit in the landing slice; a vertex-ABI revision afterwards.

#### 4.5.8 The tier seam — why culling cannot leave a hole, and what the skirt is actually for

This subsection discharges the ladder's second obligation: *the two-lane culling matrix must still work
when one side is coarse.* The proof is four steps and the first one does most of the work.

**Step 1 — a tier boundary is always a chunk boundary, so the culling matrix never sees one.**

> **Correction [C3].** ~~The tier lives in `ChunkKey` bits 18..16 (§3.10 already reserves them; three bits
> hold rungs 0–7 exactly, and tier 7's 7.9 km chunk is the last rung before the realm proxy, so the field
> is right-sized rather than merely sufficient).~~ **Replaced by §3.3.6's published layout: the tier lives
> in `ChunkKey` bits 60..56 — FIVE bits, 0..=31 representable — and the legal ceiling is the body's
> `tier_depth`, which is 13 for the starter body, 19 for an Earth-sized one and 21 for the largest
> addressable one.** Three bits could not express any of those; the layout §4 was citing had already been
> struck by §3.3.6. The key is `sector 3 | tier 5 | a 20 | b 20 | c 10` = **58 of 64 bits used, six
> reserved and asserted zero on decode.**

**There is no per-cell tier.** Every cell inside a chunk therefore has the same cell
size as every other, and §4.5.3's `emit face iff !occludes[...]` compares two variants at one scale, as
it always did. The matrix is not extended, not parameterised and not re-derived. This is the whole reason
the answer is short.

**Step 2 — across a chunk face whose neighbour is at a different tier, `neighbor` returns `Outside`.**
Not a new arm: §3's `Neighbor` enum already has `Same | AcrossSeam | Outside`, and `Outside` already
means "there is no addressable neighbour here". A neighbour at a different cell size is not addressable
in this chunk's index space, so it is the same fact. Nothing in `GridMapping` changes; the residency
manager simply does not supply an apron for that face.

**Step 3 — `Outside` resolves to `EMPTY`, and `occludes[EMPTY][x]` is true only for `x == EMPTY`.** So
every boundary face on both sides of a tier seam is **emitted**. That is under-culling, and §4.4 already
established the direction of that error: **under-coverage produces overdraw, never a hole.** The tier
axis inherits the safety property of the shape axis for free, because it inherits the same mechanism.
The cost is bounded and small: of the ~379 chunk columns in each tier's annulus, the seam ring is
`2π · 786 / 62 = 79.7` columns — **21 %, and tier-invariant**, falling straight out of Addendum 2's
constant-379 arithmetic. Those columns emit their outward boundary faces uncalled; the rest do not.

**Step 4 — the residual disagreement is geometric, is bounded by one coarse cell, and a skirt of that
depth closes it with no case analysis.** §4.3.2 established the bound and it is deliberately weak:
the coarse solid and the union of its children both lie inside the same coarse cell, so they cannot
differ by more than one coarse cell edge. Therefore:

> **Skirt rule.** Every chunk emits a downward apron around its four lateral borders. It is emitted
> unconditionally, so it does not depend on which neighbour is at which tier, which is the property that
> matters because that neighbour's tier changes as the camera moves.
>
> **The DEPTH is §5.9.4's, not §4's** — §4's `2^(L+1)` metres is **STRUCK** [H2]. It was §3.5.6's error
> bound evaluated at `k_rough = 0.5`, presented as a universal bound, and it omitted the rim-warp
> displacement entirely (up to `A_max = 0.20 m`):
>
> ```
> skirt_drop_m(chunk at tier L) =
>       ( relief_max(chunk.column_footprint, L + 1)   // max - min solid height over ONE cell of the
>                                                     // NEXT COARSER rung, from the DERIVED min/max
>                                                     // relief pyramid (§3.5.2)
>       + A_max )                                     // registry MAXIMUM rim-warp amplitude, metres
>       * skirt_safety                                // render-tuning field, default 1.25
>
> // Closed-form conservative fallback when the relief pyramid is not resident (§3.5.6's bound):
> relief_max(_, L+1)  <=  4 * k_rough * 2^(L+1)
>   => skirt_drop_m  <=  (4 * k_rough * 2^(L+1) + A_max) * skirt_safety
>   => at k_rough = 0.5 and A_max = 0.20 m that is ~5 cells at every rung.
>
> // What ChunkHeader.skirt_drop carries, in the chunk's OWN cell units, 8.8 fixed point:
> skirt_drop_cells = ceil(skirt_drop_m / 2^L)
> ```
>
> The relief envelope has **one home and it is not §4's**: §3.5.2's per-`(tier, chunk column)` min/max
> structure, **derived and never persisted**. §2.7.1's `column_relief` table is struck with it.

Three supporting rulings, each needed for the skirt to be sufficient rather than merely usual:

- **Adjacent chunks differ by at most one rung.** Tier selection is `floor(log2(distance / base))`, which
  is monotone in distance and 1-Lipschitz over chunk adjacency for every chunk beyond one chunk-width of
  the camera; inside that radius everything is tier 0. That is what makes "one cell of the *next coarser*
  rung" the right footprint for `relief_max` above, rather than an assumption about which neighbour turns
  up. It is cheap to assert in the residency manager (a debug assertion over resident
  neighbours), and it should be, because a residency-budget governor that raised the pixel target
  non-uniformly could break it silently.
- **Tier is assigned per chunk COLUMN, not per chunk.** Vertical neighbours are therefore always at the
  same tier, so only the four lateral faces need skirts and the top and bottom faces keep exact
  crack-freeness by §4.2(a). This is a free 33 % saving on the skirt and it also removes an entire class
  of seam (a horizontal tier boundary, which a downward skirt could not have closed anyway).
- **Skirts are single-sided, outward-facing, and flagged.** They carry the boundary cell's material and
  the `SKIRT` bit of §4.5.7, so decoration and AO skip them. Viewed from below they are backface-culled;
  the only viewpoint that would reveal a crack from underneath is one already inside solid rock. The one
  honest exception is flying beneath a coastal overhang at a seam, where a sliver of sky could show
  through — that is the case Addendum 2 §C.5 holds vertex snapping in reserve for, and it should be
  measured by the pop gate before any code is written for it.

**The cost, in bytes — quoted in both regimes, per L3's rule that a quad figure without its label is
meaningless.** *Unmerged worst case:* 4 lateral faces × 62 cells = 248 skirt quads per chunk, at 8 B/quad
packed = **1,984 B ≈ 2 KB per chunk**; over Addendum 2's 6,800-chunk 100 km view that is **13.6 MB on
270 MB — plus 5.0 %**, and this is the number to budget against. *Greedy-merged measured case
(§5.9.4):* a skirt run merges along its border like any other quad, giving **typically under 20 quads,
248 only on a fully broken border — under 1 % against the measured 2,200 quads/chunk.** The 5× spread is
the merged-versus-unmerged gap, not a disagreement; budget the 5 %, expect the 1 %. Against the alternative (transvoxel-class transition cells: a second 512-case
lookup table, a second vertex representation and a per-boundary mesh with its own lifetime and dirty
rules, built for smooth iso-surfaces that we do not have) the skirt is the correct trade by a wide
margin, and it is one this section can take without a user decision because it is server-internal
geometry that can be swapped behind the mesher.

**One caveat on Addendum 2's headline memory figure, because §4.5.4 quotes it.** The 270 MB is stated at
the **V2 packed vertex format** (8 B/quad). At V1 (4 vertices × 16 B + 6 indices × 4 B = 88 B/quad) the
same view is 1.3–3.0 GB depending on whether one takes §5.2.1's measured 2,200 quads/chunk or the ~5,000
implied by the 270 MB figure — either of which consumes or exceeds §5.3.6's 3.0 GiB client VRAM cap. So
the precise statement is: **the ladder dissolves the planet-size constraint completely at any vertex
format (on foot, any radius, ~4,000 chunks) and dissolves the flight constraint only at V2.** Register
row 21 de-escalates out of the blocking set for *rendering a planet at all*, which is what Addendum 2
claims, and remains the gate on a 25–100 km flight view. Lane B is unaffected either way, because its
8 B/cell instance record is already V2-shaped.

**And the corresponding caveat on cost.** Per-chunk mesh cost is close to tier-invariant: a chunk's top
surface is 62² = 3,844 cells at every rung, and dropping the top *L* octaves of an fBm field reduces
slope roughly linearly in *L* (each octave contributes equal slope), so going from 8 octaves to 5 removes
about 37 % of the side-face quads rather than dividing the count by four. **The ladder does not make a
chunk cheaper to mesh; it makes far fewer chunks necessary.** The generation half *is* cheaper — that is
Addendum 2 §D.3's "coarse generation is cheaper" gate and it is real — but the mesh half is not, and any
budget written on the assumption that it is will be wrong by 4× per rung.
---

### 4.6 Collision

#### 4.6.1 Four lanes, not two

Shape lane (cube / shaped) crosses realm geometry (Cartesian / Spherical). The dispatch is on the
`GridMapping` **value** carried by the realm, which §3.1.1 establishes as the HR3-sanctioned alternative
to a shard-kind match — never on a shard kind. **It is four lanes and not eight: there is no tier axis
here, by §4.6.3.**

| | **Cartesian realm** (ships, stations, interiors) — exact 1 m axis-aligned cells | **Spherical realm** (planets) — warped, sheared, tapering cells |
|---|---|---|
| **Cube cells** | parry `Voxels`: ~1 B/voxel, 8³ sub-chunks of 512 B, only non-empty allocated, BVH over sub-chunks, per-voxel Empty/Vertex/Edge/Face/Interior classification so a character never snags on inter-voxel seams. A 10k-block hull ≈ 150 KB. `ColliderBuilder::voxels(voxel_size, &coords)` is the whole API | **`Voxels` is structurally impossible** — it is a uniform axis-aligned lattice positioned by an `Isometry`, and no parry API expresses shear. Instead: greedy-box decomposition in **index space**, boxes capped at 8 cells per axis, each emitted as a `ConvexPolyhedron` over its 8 `cell_point` corners. ~500 B/box; a surface chunk is 200–2,000 boxes = 100 KB–1 MB |
| **Shaped cells** | `ColliderTemplate` from the baked table, `SharedShape` `Arc`-deduped across every cell with the same variant. ~116 B per sub-shape × ~1.6 parts avg ≈ 186 B/cell as a `Compound`; ~8 B/cell + BVH as a hand-rolled `TypedCompositeShape` after measurement | Per-cell warped convex parts through `cell_point`; **`Arc` dedup is lost** because every cell's geometry differs. ~500 B × ~1.6 parts = 800 B/cell |

**Why the 8-cell box cap.** The convex hull of a merged box's 8 warped corners under-approximates its
bowed constant-radius faces by the chord sagitta. At 8 cells (8.42 m) that is `8.42²/(8 × 161,671)` =
**55 µm**; at 62 cells it would be 3.0 mm, exactly §3's stated merged-quad threshold. 55 µm is 50× below
it and the box count rises only ~8×; that is the trade, and it is why the cap is 8 and not 62. (This is a
tier-0 number and stays one — §4.6.3. Had colliders been allowed a coarse tier, the same sagitta at tier
3's 8 m cells would be 3.5 mm, i.e. straight through the threshold, which is an independent second reason
the tier-0 rule is right rather than merely convenient.)

**Nine of 23 shapes are non-convex** — `CornerIn`, `RampLowIn`, `RampHighIn`, `TetraIn`, `Stairs` and the
four connect families are unions of half-spaces or stacked boxes. `ColliderTemplate::Parts` exists for
them; the ~1.6 parts average above is what makes the per-cell figures honest (the first draft's
one-sub-shape-per-block assumption understated Lane B collision by ~60 %).

**Collider residency is not render residency.** Colliders exist only within a `physics_radius` of a
dynamic body — 64 m, one chunk edge, derived as "greater than any body's per-tick swept motion at 20 Hz
plus the character's reach". That is at most 3³ = 27 chunks per dynamic-body cluster, and at the ≤ 1 MB
per-chunk worst case, **≤ 27 MB of collider per cluster** — including the D-9 density case of 128
co-located sessions, whose radii overlap into one cluster. **This sentence is now doing double duty and
is the load-bearing argument of §4.6.3:** 64 m of collider inside 786 m of tier 0 is a **12.3× margin**,
so "collision is always tier 0" is not a constraint the renderer has to respect — it is a fact the
geometry hands us, and the type system merely records it.

**Per-chunk `TriMesh` is rejected** for dynamic bodies: ~860 KB per chunk, `FIX_INTERNAL_EDGES` mitigates
but does not remove internal-edge snagging, full rebuild per edit, and Rapier's own documentation warns
that objects get trapped. Ships **are** dynamic bodies. (§3.1.1's parenthetical "collider trimesh" beside
`cell_corners` is a loose label for "any collider construction", not a commitment to parry's `TriMesh`;
`cell_corners` is exactly what feeds the convex-hexahedron path above.)

#### 4.6.2 The named pitfalls

- **`Voxels::combine_voxel_states(&mut other, origin_shift)` across every Cartesian chunk-collider seam,
  or ghost collisions come straight back at chunk boundaries** — the hardest kind to reproduce, because
  it depends on where a chunk happens to be cut. Make it a harness assertion (walk a character across a
  chunk boundary at 20 sampled offsets; assert no vertical velocity impulse), not a review item.
- **Never call `Voxels::scaled`.** Set `voxel_size`. The scaled-BVH bug — queries silently missing
  geometry — was only fixed in parry 0.28. **Note the ladder's temptation here and refuse it explicitly:**
  a coarse collider would be spelled `Voxels::scaled` or a scaled `voxel_size`, and it is exactly the
  API this bullet already bans. There is no cheap coarse-collider shortcut lying around; the tier-0 rule
  costs nothing it was not already costing.
- **The unvalidated cross-lane seam (Cartesian only).** The `Voxels` shape and the shaped-cell shapes are
  separate colliders and do not share neighbourhood classification, so a cube adjacent to a slope will not
  have its shared face marked interior and a character sliding along the boundary can catch on it. There
  is no "filled for classification, empty for geometry" API. **No shipped implementation validates this;
  it must be a spike, run before P5 commits.** The greedy-box fallback does not have the problem, because
  one composite has one uniform contact story — which is also the reason the spherical lane is immune.
- **Rigid-body mass properties are computed from the block field, never from the collider.** The
  colliders are geometric and (on a shell) physically smaller or larger than a nominal cell, while §4.3's
  ruling makes block mass cell-nominal. A ship whose thrusters are balanced against a geometric mass
  centre and whose fuel cost is computed from a nominal one will mis-behave. **Rule:** colliders are built
  with zero density and `RigidBodyBuilder::additional_mass_properties` receives the sum over the block
  field of `density × volume_units / CELL_VOLUME_UNITS` at each cell's centre. `MassProperties::from_voxels`
  is not used. **And the sum is over the tier-0 field, structurally** (§4.3's rider, §4.6.3's typing).

**Determinism.** CLAUDE.md classifies rapier state as Category C — checkpoint-carried, never re-simulated
cross-host — so the *solver* need not be bit-identical across binaries. What must be deterministic is
**collider construction from the block field**, because it feeds checkpoints; both the greedy-box
decomposition and the `Voxels` construction are pure integer operations over the resolved buffer, and
`cell_point` uses only `+ − × ÷ sqrt` with no transcendental. **The tier ladder does not enter this
argument at all, which is the point of §4.6.3** — the coarsening function is a client-and-owner
*rendering and summary* path, and no coarse value ever reaches a checkpoint.

> **[USER DECISION 4-B] — adopting `rapier3d` / `parry3d`, and the Cartesian cube lane.** Neither crate
> is in `Cargo.lock` today and both sit on the physics-authority path, so this falls under the standing
> "never adopt a new library unilaterally" rule. **The ladder does not change this decision and, if
> anything, simplifies it: neither option ever has to represent a coarse cell.**
>
> | Option | Commits to | Maturity risk | Cost if wrong |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **B1. rapier3d + parry `Voxels` on the Cartesian cube lane; convex-hexahedron composites everywhere else** *(recommended)* | rapier3d 0.34 / parry3d 0.30 (Aug 2026) | `Voxels` entered experimental in 2025; fixes were still landing through parry 0.28 (`scaled` BVH), 0.25 (sparse rewrite), 0.25.3 (`combine_voxel_states`). The cross-lane classification seam is unvalidated anywhere | Fall back to B2 — a contained, server-internal swap behind the collider seam |
> | **B2. rapier3d + our own greedy-box composite on ALL four lanes** | rapier's `Compound`/`TypedCompositeShape` only | Low; `Compound` is a decade old | Slower per-edit rebuilds (full sub-chunk re-decompose vs `set_voxel`) |
> | B3. `avian3d` instead of rapier | Bevy-native ECS integration; **still parry underneath** | Parry adoption is implied either way; avian is younger than rapier | Same as B1/B2 |
> | B4. Hand-roll collision | Nothing | — | Unshippable for an MMO with Newtonian physics and colliding players |
>
> **Recommendation: B1**, with B2 pre-designed as the fallback and the cross-lane seam spike run before
> P5 commits. Note that `Voxels` buys us the *Cartesian* lane only — a genuine planet/ship divergence in
> the collider layer, which is legitimate because it sits below the `GridMapping` seam, but which must not
> be described as an HR4 win. What *is* an HR4 win is that all four lanes read the **same `ShapeDef`
> table**, which is why it must be one table in one crate.
>
> Sequencing: SPIKE-6a / DEFERRED D-19 (rapier snapshot/restore + cross-binary determinism) already gates
> P5 and rapier is not yet a dependency, so this decision is on the critical path regardless.

#### 4.6.3 Collision is tier 0, always — and the type system is what says so

Addendum 2 §C.7 lists this first: *"Collision. Always tier 0, no exceptions. Physics never sees a coarse
tier."* §D.3 sharpens it further: *"an assertion, not a test."* This subsection makes it exactly that.

**The assertion, stated once:**

> **A collider, a mass property, a raycast target, a structural-support query, a pressurisation query, a
> mount test, a block edit and a WAL record are all defined over tier-0 cells and over nothing else. No
> code path exists by which any of them can be handed a chunk at tier ≥ 1.**

**The mechanism is one newtype and roughly a dozen characters of signature change.** Not a runtime check,
not a `debug_assert`, not a code-review convention:

```rust
// crates/core/src/grid/key.rs — the ONE addressing word. §3.1.1 fixes the name roster (M3);
// §4 owns exactly one entry in it, BlockAddr, and owns it because that is what makes the
// write invariant a compile error rather than an API convention.

pub struct ChunkKey(u64);   // sector 3 | tier 5 (bits 60..56) | a 20 | b 20 | c 10 | reserved 6
                            // 58 of 64 used. The earlier "bits 18..16, three bits" is STRUCK (C3).
pub struct Tier(u8);        // 0..=31 representable; the legal ceiling is the body's tier_depth

/// A ChunkKey PROVEN to be at tier 0. The only constructors are the two below,
/// so a value of this type cannot exist for a coarse chunk.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash)]
pub struct Tier0Key(ChunkKey);

impl ChunkKey {
    pub fn tier(self) -> Tier;                        // 0..=31, NOT 0..=7
    pub fn as_tier0(self) -> Option<Tier0Key>;        // the ONE narrowing point;
                                                      // None for EVERY tier 1..=31
}
impl Tier0Key {
    pub fn new(face: Face, i: i32, j: i32, k: i32) -> Self;   // builds at tier 0 by construction
}

/// The authoritative address. Tier-0 by TYPE, everywhere in the workspace.
/// This DIFFERS from §3.1.1's draft, which made BlockAddr tier-carrying; §4's definition wins
/// on the merits because every section agrees the write invariant must be a compile error,
/// and only this shape delivers it. One narrowing call at one boundary is the whole cost.
pub struct BlockAddr  { pub chunk: Tier0Key, pub cell: CellIndex }

/// The mesher's read address, and the ONLY type that admits any tier.
pub struct CoarseAddr { pub chunk: ChunkKey,  pub cell: CellIndex }

impl BlockAddr { pub fn ancestor(self, tier: Tier) -> CoarseAddr; }   // and NO reverse conversion,
                                                                     // not even a fallible one
```

**Names, once, so nothing drifts again (M3).** `ChunkKey` (never `ChunkAddress`/`ChunkAddr`/
`ChunkAddrAnyTier`), `Tier0Key` (never `Tier0Addr`), `CellIndex`, `BlockAddr`, `CoarseAddr`,
`chunk_pyramid` (never `block_pyramid`, never "beside `block_wal`"), `PyramidEntry`, `CellSummary`, and
`SubstanceId(u16)` for the substance-table row — `MaterialId` survives only in §5's *renderable* sense
(texture-array addressing) and must never name a registry row.

**Why this is the right shape, and what it costs.** Every consumer named in the assertion already takes
`BlockAddr`; changing `BlockAddr::chunk` from `ChunkKey` to `Tier0Key` propagates the guarantee to all of
them with **no change at any call site that was already correct**. The only code that must say anything
new is the residency manager and the mesher, which are the only two places a coarse chunk is legitimately
produced or consumed, and they say it once: `key.as_tier0()`. Handing a coarse chunk to the collider
becomes a compile error with a type name that explains itself.

The cost is **zero at runtime** (a newtype is a `u64`) and **one narrowing call at one boundary** at
authoring time. The cost of *not* doing it is that all eight readers in §4.4.2's table are correct today
and stay correct until someone optimises a distant-structure query, at which point the failure is a
physics bug on a shipped world with saved builds in it.

This is the read-side twin of Space Engineers' shipped storage invariant — their `MyOctreeStorage`
documents that "the storage system can only write to LOD0, with higher LODs computed based on that
level", so a caller intending to write must read LOD0. That is the correct rule, and they enforce it in
prose. **We can enforce it in the signature, so we should**, and the write side follows for free from the
same type: `block_wal`, the edit command, the undo table and the pyramid's *source* all key on
`BlockAddr`, so `write(tier != 0)` is unrepresentable rather than merely forbidden.

**Three consequences worth writing down:**

- **`CoarseAddr` is not a lesser `BlockAddr`; it is a different thing and should not be convertible into
  one.** There is deliberately no `CoarseAddr -> BlockAddr` at all, not even a fallible one, because
  every legitimate use is the other direction (a tier-0 address has a unique ancestor at each rung, given
  by shifting the indices). Provide `BlockAddr::ancestor(tier) -> CoarseAddr` and nothing else.
- **The pyramid writer takes `BlockAddr` and returns `CoarseAddr`s.** §4.9.5's walk-up is the one place
  the two meet, it is a dozen lines long, and it lives in `vd-core` under HR5's 100 % gate.
- **It does not need a `ShardProfile` capability, a config flag or a runtime mode.** Nothing branches on
  a tier; a `Tier0Key` is either constructible or it is not. HR3 is satisfied in the strongest available
  form — not "we do not branch on the tier" but "there is no value here to branch on".

**Is it a one-way door?** No. It is server-internal typing behind the store and collider seams and can be
widened later if some future subsystem genuinely wants a coarse collider (nothing in this design does).
It gets more expensive every week, though, in exactly the way §4.10's ship order describes: the newtype
costs one line today and a mechanical edit across ~40 call sites once P5's physics and P6's edit pipeline
are written against `ChunkKey`.

---

### 4.7 The character controller, derived from the catalogue and the warp

Rapier's `KinematicCharacterController` defaults are actively hostile to a 1 m grid:
`max_slope_climb_angle` and `min_slope_slide_angle` both default to exactly 45.000°, which is exactly a
`Wedge` on a flat grid — sitting on the float boundary produces intermittent, un-reproducible "sometimes
I can't walk up this ramp"; `autostep` defaults to `None`, so nobody can step onto a `Slab` at all; and
`CharacterAutostep::default().max_height` is `Relative(0.25)` = 0.45 m on a 1.8 m character, just short of
clearing a 0.5 m `Slab`.

**Everything in this subsection is a tier-0 quantity and is unaffected by the ladder**, because the
controller sits on the collider and the collider is tier-0 by §4.6.3. Two sentences are worth having
anyway, because the alternative reading is tempting and wrong. First, `w` — the tangential-to-radial
cell-width ratio — is **tier-invariant**: at tier *L* the tangential width is `w·2^L` m and the radial
height is `2^L` m, so the ratio, and therefore the physical-slope law below, is identical at every rung.
Had a coarse tier ever reached the controller, the constants would still have been right. Second, that is
belt and braces and not a licence: the reason no coarse tier reaches the controller is the type, not the
arithmetic.

**The physical-angle law.** Radial cells are exactly 1.000 m and tangential cells are scaled by `w`, so
an index-space facet's physical slope is

```
tan θ_physical  =  tan θ_index / w
```

with `w ∈ [w_min, w_max]` supplied by an eighth `GridMapping` operation, `cell_width_bounds() ->
(f64, f64)`: `(1.0, 1.0)` for `IdentityGrid`, and for a `ShellGrid` the product of the warp's corner/centre
range and the band's floor/ceiling scale — **(0.6721, 1.0521)** at §3's recommended `V = 272`.

The consequence the first draft missed entirely:

| Placement | `w` | `Wedge` (tan 1) | `RampLow` (tan ½) | `Tetra` (tan √2) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| face centre, band ceiling | 1.0521 | **43.55°** | 25.42° | 53.35° |
| datum, face centre | 1.0000 | 45.00° | 26.57° | 54.74° |
| cube corner, band floor | 0.6721 | **56.10°** | 36.65° | 64.58° |

A single `Wedge` spans 12.55° across one planet, and the **ordering inverts**: a `Wedge` at a cube corner
(56.10°) is steeper than a `Tetra` at a face centre (53.35°). Any threshold placed between two
catalogue-declared classes using datum angles is a tripwire wired to nothing.

**The derivation, restated on the physical bounds:**

```
walkable_max_tan   = max over PLACEABLE walkable shapes of  sqrt(slope_tan2) / w_min
nonwalk_min_tan    = min over PLACEABLE non-walkable shapes of sqrt(slope_tan2) / w_max
                     (or tan 90° = ∞, i.e. vertical, if that set is empty)

BAKE ASSERTION: angle(nonwalk_min_tan) − angle(walkable_max_tan) ≥ MIN_SLOPE_SEPARATION

climb = walkable_max + (gap)/3        slide = walkable_max + 2·(gap)/3
```

Placing the two thresholds at the thirds is not arbitrary: they must be distinct (equal thresholds make a
surface both unclimbable and non-sliding, the "sticky then slippery" flip-flop), and equidistant thirds
is the unique placement maximising the minimum distance among the four values.

`MIN_SLOPE_SEPARATION` is derived, not chosen. The dominant error on the contact normal is f32
quantisation of collider vertices in the `SurfaceAnchor` frame: at a 4,096 m anchor radius,
`2 × 4096 × 2⁻²³` = 0.98 mm over the narrowest 0.672 m facet gives `ε = 0.084°`. Requiring each of the
three sub-intervals to exceed 10 ε gives `MIN_SLOPE_SEPARATION = ceil(30 ε) = **3.000°**` — and note the
coupling this creates: **shrinking the anchor radius buys slope separation**, which is a real constraint
on `FrameSpace` and should be recorded there.

> **[USER DECISION 4-C] — which catalogue shapes are walkable?** The geometry, not taste, has removed one
> option: **"`Wedge` walkable AND `Tetra` non-walkable" is not expressible**, because `Wedge` reaches
> 56.10° somewhere and `Tetra` drops to 53.35° elsewhere on the same planet (gap = −2.75°). The real
> choice is between two consistent worlds. **The ladder does not touch this decision.**
>
> - **C1. Everything in the catalogue is walkable; only vertical is not** *(recommended)*.
>   `walkable_max = 56.10°`, `nonwalk_min = 90°`, gap **33.90°**, `climb = 67.40°`, `slide = 78.40°`.
>   Costs nothing on terrain, because §4.9.4's ruling makes generated terrain `Cube`-only at every tier —
>   natural terrain has 0° and 90° surfaces and nothing between, so cliffs remain cliffs (a 1 m step
>   exceeds autostep) and the thresholds only ever judge *player-built* ramps. A 45° hull ramp is walkable
>   everywhere, which is what a builder expects. The `WalkClass::NonWalkable` arm stays in the type for
>   future shapes and for material-driven slipperiness, but is empty in v1.
> - **C2. `Wedge` and `Tetra` are hull-only; the 1:2 pair is the steepest walkable.** `walkable_max =
>   36.65°`, `nonwalk_min = 43.55°`, gap **6.90°**, `climb = 38.95°`, `slide = 41.25°`. Makes ramp choice a
>   real decision (the way Avorion makes edge blocks half-cost/half-function), but every interior corridor
>   needs two cells per metre of rise, and players *will* try to walk on wedges and be confused.
> - C3. Per-realm thresholds (walkable on ships, not on planets). **Rejected:** the same block behaves
>   differently in two places, and it breaks G-IDENTICAL result-equality for a feature that lives *above*
>   the `GridMapping` seam.
>
> **This is close to a one-way door in content terms** — players build stairs and ramps around whatever
> ships, and reversing it either breaks existing builds (C1→C2) or trivialises them (C2→C1).

**Every remaining length is an exact integer number of FINE lattice cells** (2⁻¹⁰ m = 0.9765625 mm, from
`crates/core/src/pose.rs:163`), and every constant below is derived:

| Parameter | Value | Derivation |
|---|---|---|
| `offset` (skin) | 16 FINE = **1/64 m** | the smallest power-of-two cell fraction exceeding 10× the f32 position quantisation at the anchor radius |
| `autostep.max_height` | 512 + 16 + 16 = 544 FINE = **0.53125 m** | max catalogue `step_rise_fine` (0.5 m, **radial and therefore warp-independent on both geometries**) + `offset` + one `offset` of collider registration margin |
| `autostep.min_width` | **256 FINE = 0.25 m** | narrowest physical tread `512 × w_min` = 344 FINE, minus `offset`, minus margin = 312 FINE; rounded **down** to the next power of two so a later warp-bound refinement cannot invalidate it |
| `snap_to_ground` | `ceil_fine(max_walk_speed × tick_dt × walkable_max_tan) + offset` | at the 6 m/s reference walk speed, 20 Hz, C1: 458 + 16 = **474 FINE = 0.46289 m**. `walkable_max_tan` is `sqrt(rational)` — bit-exact, **no `tan()` call** |
| `jump_clear` | 1024 + 16 + 16 = 1056 FINE = **1.03125 m** | one cell (the dominant terrain feature, and exactly 1.000 m radially on both geometries) + `offset` + margin. **Assert `jump_clear < 1536 FINE`**, or a `Slab` on a `Cube` becomes climbable and walls stop working |
| jump impulse | `v₀ = sqrt(2 · g · jump_clear)` | `g` from `PlanetParams`; `sqrt` is bit-exact |
| `up` | `FrameSpace::gravity_dir(pos)` | |

Note that "one cell" in `jump_clear` means one *tier-0* cell, as every other length in this table does.
That is not a caveat; it is the same assertion as §4.6.3 read from the other end.

**The one transcendental, and why it is legal.** Converting `walkable_max_tan` into the *angle* rapier's
KCC wants needs `atan`. It is evaluated **once per realm at activation**, quantised to millidegrees, and
**carried in the realm checkpoint** rather than recomputed — so a re-home to another host cannot change a
player's climb behaviour by a millidegree. This is the correct reading of CLAUDE.md's Category C: what
must be bit-identical is collider construction (integers plus `+ − × ÷ sqrt`), not the solver
configuration.

**Phase anchors.** The catalogue table is **declared in full at P4** even though `PLACEABLE` is false for
everything but `Cube` until P6, so the derivation is well-defined from the first commit and L4's
empty-set bootstrap never arises: the KCC lands at P5 reading the same derived constants it will read at
P6. The bake assertion is `if the non-walkable set is non-empty then gap ≥ MIN_SLOPE_SEPARATION`; under
C1 that set is empty and `nonwalk_min` is vertical, which is well-defined.

**The G-IDENTICAL discharge, stated accurately.** The first draft claimed `up` is the only value that
differs between a planet and a ship; that is false — `w_min`/`w_max` differ, and every threshold derived
from them differs unless C1/C2 is chosen (both of which use planet-worst-case bounds *globally*, which is
what restores equality). PLAN.md:42 lists `gravity_dir` among the things **above** the seam, shared
write-once; the seam is `FrameSpace` itself. And DEFERRED.md:294 records **D-38 as 🟩** with only the
`reanchor()`-forcing variant re-owed at P5, whose content both DEFERRED.md and roadmap P6 name as
"**block edits on planet AND ship**". So the fixture this section owes is not "walk up a wedge" — it is:

> **place a `Wedge`, break it, and re-place it as a `RampLow`, then walk the resulting surface**, run on a
> Spherical planet profile and a Cartesian ship profile from one fixture, with the Spherical run roaming
> far enough to force a `reanchor()` mid-sequence, asserting identical control-plane results (final cell,
> climb outcome, resulting block field).
>
> **The ladder adds one assertion to the same fixture, and it belongs there rather than in a new one:**
> after the edits, assert the **coarse field** produced by §4.3.2's `coarsen` is byte-identical on both
> profiles. Coarsening is pure index-space integer work and therefore lives *above* the `GridMapping`
> seam, so G-IDENTICAL binds it in the strong form (result equality, not merely both-run-clean). This is
> the cheapest possible discharge — one extra assertion on a fixture that already places, breaks and
> re-places on two profiles — and it is exactly the kind of coverage that would otherwise be discovered
> missing at P6 when a ship's distant silhouette differs from a planet build's.
---

### 4.8 Build ergonomics: at most ONE explicit decision per placement

The target, restated as an engineering budget: **walls have 324 states and a player chooses zero; stairs
have 80 and a player chooses two, both by pointing.** SE2 shipped linear variant cycling in its alpha and
immediately drew two support tickets ("new block variant and size cycling feels tedious", "Selection wheel
for block sizes/variants"); Empyrion's shape window drew a community mod to fix it. Cycling works to about
six variants and collapses beyond that.

**Build ergonomics are unaffected by the ladder, and that is a ruling rather than an omission.** Every one
of the five inference layers below reads the tier-0 block field through a `BlockAddr`, so none of them can
observe a tier at all. The single place the ladder touches building is the *residency floor* stated after
the table, and it exists to keep that true.

The five inference layers, in the order they fire on a single click:

1. **Face + hit octant → variant.** The raycast returns a target cell, a face, and a hit point
   `(u,v) ∈ [0,1]²` on that face. The face gives the placement axis; `v < 0.5` selects the bottom
   `Slab`/`Stairs` half; the `(u,v)` quadrant selects which corner piece. Eight octants and three
   face-halves, free. **Zero UI.**
2. **Look direction + `autorotate` → orientation.** `MountToSurface` (SE's `MyAutorotateMode::OneDirection`)
   plus the derived legal-orient set collapses 24–48 rotations to the 1–4 that make sense: `Stairs`
   exposes 8 of 24, `Slab` 6, `Cube` 1.
3. **Neighbours → connective sub-shape.** `Wall`, `Fence`, `Railing`, `Conduit` and the `Stairs`
   inner/outer corner are computed, never chosen. Escape hatch: the pin (§4.1.4).
4. **Symmetry/mirror mode → the mirrored twin**, via the total `mirror_shape` map and
   `MirrorPlane { axis, position_half_cells }`.
5. **Explicit UI, for the shape *family* only.** A hold-to-open radial picker plus a most-recently-used
   shortlist; the scroll wheel cycles *within* the family last picked (≤ 6 entries, where cycling still
   works). A full grid palette is the long-tail escape hatch — opened twice an hour, not twice a minute.

| Feature | First release (P6) | Why it cannot wait |
|---|---|---|
| Hit-octant variant inference | **Yes** | Free, and the UI is designed around whether it exists |
| `autorotate` + derived legal orients | **Yes** | Without it every placement is a rotation puzzle |
| Radial picker + MRU | **Yes** | 23 families is already past the ≤ 6 cycling limit |
| Neighbour-derived `Stairs` corners | **Yes** | The resolve pass and the 2-cell window shape the mesher's buffer layout; retrofitting means re-laying it |
| Symmetry / mirror mode | **Yes** | It is the only thing that *exercises* mirror closure; ship it later and the assertion rots untested until a player finds the hole |
| Batched line/plane placement | **Yes** | It is the latency mitigation (§4.9) and the remesh amortiser: 4,096 edits, one remesh, **one pyramid walk-up per touched coarse cell rather than per edit** |
| Server-side undo | **Yes** | See §4.9.3 — the inverse must be journalled at commit or nothing placed before the retrofit is undoable |
| Blueprint copy-paste | Polish | A pure addition on top of the batch command |
| `Wall`/`Fence`/`Railing`/`Conduit` | Polish (`Conduit` waits for P9 anyway) | `Stairs` proves the machinery; the rest are data |
| Shape "paint" tool (change shape, keep material) | Polish | One more command arm |

**The tier-0 residency floor, and why building needs one.** Placement targets a cell through a client-side
raycast against the client's own block field (§4.9.2), and §4.6.3 makes that field tier-0-only. So a
player can only build where the client holds tier 0. That is trivially satisfied today — build reach is
about 5 m against tier 0's 786 m — but the constraint must be *written down*, because the first feature
that would break it is one somebody will want: a ship-mounted mining beam, a terraforming tool, a
long-range welder.

> **Rule: the client's tier-0 residency radius has a floor, `tier0_min_radius = max_tool_reach +
> CHUNK_EDGE`, and the render-side residency budget governor may never shrink tier 0 below it.** The floor
> is a field in the render tuning struct derived from the longest reach in the tool catalogue, never a
> literal.
>
> **Correction [H1] — the absolute version of this rule was wrong, and §4 contradicted it two subsections
> later.** ~~The server is not involved and must not be: it holds tier 0 and the pyramid and validates in
> tier-0 terms only, so *the server never learns what tier anything is being drawn at.* Tier is a purely
> client-side residency concept, and keeping it that way is what stops the ladder from leaking into
> authority.~~ **Replaced by THE TIER-HINT RULE:**
>
> > A client may declare `tier_floor`. The server **CLAMPS** it to `[body.tier_floor_min,
> > body.tier_depth - 1]` and uses the clamped value for **EGRESS SELECTION ONLY** — which rung of a chunk
> > delta to send, and at what rate a `Telemetry` channel is refreshed. **NO** fence, **NO** arbitration
> > outcome, **NO** admission decision, **NO** scheduling deadline, **NO** persisted value and **NO**
> > simulation state may read it, directly or transitively. **A shard's trajectory must be byte-identical
> > for every value of every observer's `tier_floor`.**
>
> That is the line, and it is a stronger statement than "the server never learns the tier", because it is
> one the design can actually keep: §4.9.2 rule (iii) routes a delta to the rung an observer is resident
> at, exactly as it routes by AoI membership, and selecting **what to send** is not selecting **what is
> true**. The build-side conclusion is unchanged — the server holds tier 0 and the pyramid and validates
> in tier-0 terms only — and it is enforced by §4.6.3's types rather than by a sentence.
>
> **Asserted, not merely written down:** `tier_invariance` runs the identical fixture with every
> observer's clamped `tier_floor` forced to 0 and to `tier_depth - 1` and requires **byte-identical**
> shard state, an identical beacon blink count, an identical spin-up order and identical
> fence/arbitration/grant outcomes.

This matters more than it looks because the AAA reference case fails exactly here: Crimson Desert's
observed behaviour is a fixed ~8 GB memory target enforced by uniformly aggressive detail reduction, and
its most-reported complaint is near-field clutter cut too hard. A budget governor that trades pixels per
cell against resident bytes is the right answer to that (it belongs in §5's tuning struct, with
hysteresis, and it is cosmetic and client-local: no server state, no determinism exposure, no fence — its
output reaches the server only as the clamped, non-authoritative `tier_floor` hint above)
— but an ungoverned governor would eventually decide that the cheapest thing to drop is the tier-0
disc around the player, which is the one thing that must never go. The floor is two fields and one
comparison, and it is the difference between a governor and a bug.

---

### 4.9 Placement: latency, validation, undo, and what terrain may emit

#### 4.9.1 Latency

Every builder in the survey commits the block locally the instant you click, because none of them is a
server-authoritative MMO. Here the click becomes a command to the realm shard.

The often-quoted ~215 ms includes the full 100–150 ms *pose* interpolation buffer. That buffer exists for
interpolated poses on the unreliable datagram lane; a block edit is a reliable discrete action on a
different lane (P6: "RELIABLE discrete actions … with their own seq+ack — a lost block-edit is retried;
movement stays latest-wins datagrams"), and nothing requires a reliable, non-interpolated, absolute event
to be buffered.

| Stage | Naïve | Corrected | Under the ladder |
|---|---|---|---|
| Client → shard | ~20 ms | ~20 ms | ~20 ms |
| Wait for the applying tick | up to 50 ms at 20 Hz | **up to 50 ms — this row cannot be zeroed** | unchanged |
| Shard → client | ~20 ms | ~20 ms | unchanged |
| Pose interpolation buffer | 125 ms | **0 — the edit is not an interpolated quantity** | unchanged |
| Resolve + mesh + upload (§5.1.2) | ~33 ms | ~33 ms | unchanged — **the edited chunk is always tier 0 for the editing player** |
| Pyramid walk-up (§4.9.5) | — | — | **≤ 5.85 µs at `tier_depth` = 13 (9.75 µs at 21), inside the tick, off the critical path** |
| **Total** | **~248 ms** | **73–123 ms, mean ~98 ms** | **73–123 ms, unchanged** |

**The ladder's ruling on the editing player's budget is therefore "no change", and it is a proof rather
than a hope.** The player is standing within reach of the edit; reach is metres; tier 0 runs to 786 m; a
world location is drawn at exactly one tier at a time. So the chunk the player just edited is resident at
tier 0, is the chunk that gets remeshed, and is the chunk whose pixels the 33 ms row is measuring. No
coarse rung is on the path between a click and the pixel that answers it.

The first draft zeroed the tick wait by "acking on the tick it arrives". That is not free: a block edit
mutates authoritative state that must be ordered against the tick for the fixed `step_tick` model, for
P6's sorted-on-drain deterministic WAL bytes, and for P6's "edits land exactly once on the realm owner
during a transfer" gate. **The protocol is two-stage:** an off-tick, `EffectFree` **validation receipt**
(`{ nonce, accepted_for_tick }`, no world mutation) plus the **authoritative echo** at tick N. The client
renders the block against the echo only; the receipt exists to dismiss the placement preview and to
surface a rejection early. Restoring the tick wait moves the range only from 73–120 to 73–123 ms, because
the draft's upper bound already carried it implicitly.

**The second budget, which the ladder creates and which is a different class entirely.** A *distant*
observer with that location resident at tier *L* must eventually see the edit too, and their path is:
pyramid walk-up (owner, ≤ 5.85 µs at `tier_depth` = 13) → tier-*L* delta on the wire (§4.9.2) → coarse
chunk remesh. Two facts
make this a **background-class** job under §5.1.3's two-latency-class model rather than an interactive
one, and both are numbers rather than judgements: the walk-up terminates after 1–2 rungs for a single
edit (§4.3.2), so most edits produce *no* coarse work at all; and a coarse chunk is sparse by
construction, so its remesh takes microseconds against a dense tier-0 chunk's ~1 ms. The stated budget is
**one tick (50 ms) to enqueue and best-effort thereafter**, because nobody is watching a four-metre cell
at three kilometres with millisecond expectations, and pretending otherwise would put a low-value job on
the same queue as the one that answers a click.

Dependencies on the critical path: DEFERRED **D-4** (🟥) owes a reliable client-facing event class —
`MsgClass` today has nine append-only wire-frozen arms (`Control, Saga, Snapshot, Input, Membership,
GhostReliable, GhostDelta, RealmSnapshot, SignalDelta`) and no `Event`/`Bulk` arm — and
`InterShardFlow::BlockEdit` is a reserved *name*, not yet a variant.

#### 4.9.2 What the client ships, everything the server must check, and the tier-tagged delta lane

With a pose buffer the player *aimed* using a view 125 ms old, so a server that re-derives the raycast
from server-now can target a different cell than the player saw. The fix removes the class: **the client
ships the resolved target — cell, face, hit octant, intended `BlockTypeId` + `orient`, and a nonce — and
the server VALIDATES.** Validation is cheap integer work against the same block field both sides hold, the
command is self-describing and idempotent under retry, and rejections become genuinely rare (concurrent
edits, permissions, resources) rather than routine aim drift.

The full validation list, all of them cheap and all of them exploitable if omitted:

reach · line of sight · target cell occupancy · build permission for the realm/region ·
**the `BlockTypeId` row exists** (which *is* the per-material admits check) ·
**`orient` is in the shape's derived legal set** · **the shape is `PLACEABLE`, not `RETIRED`** ·
**pin permission** for a connect family · structural support (§2.2.4) · inventory contents ·
**batch cap** · **rate limit** · **nonce dedup**.

There is deliberately **no "is the target at tier 0" check in that list**, because the target address is a
`BlockAddr` and §4.6.3 makes it unrepresentable at any other tier. A validation check that can never fail
is a check nobody maintains; a type that cannot be constructed is one the compiler maintains.

- **Batch cap = 4,096 edits per command**, derived as one chunk face (62² = 3,844) rounded up to a power
  of two. Cost: 20.5 KB of WAL and **exactly one chunk remesh**, which is why batching is cheaper per edit
  than singles. Under the ladder it is cheaper still: a 4,096-cell plane touches at most 512 tier-1
  cells, 64 tier-2 cells and so on, so **one batch produces about 585 pyramid entries rather than 4,096
  walk-ups** — the coarse cost of a batch is sub-linear in the batch size, which is the same reason
  batching is the right latency mitigation.
- **Rate limit**: a per-player token bucket, both parameters per-entity fields, never inline literals —
  reference values 4,096 cells capacity refilling at 512 cells/s.
- **Fan-out, and this is where the ladder pays for itself on the wire.** With D-9 (whole-realm broadcast,
  no within-realm AoI; 128 sessions measured at 357,248 gateway messages peaking 1,920/tick), an edit
  storm on the *reliable* lane is the dangerous case. Three rules make it bounded:
  **(i)** all edits committed in tick N for chunk C are emitted as ONE delta per observer per chunk
  **per tier** per tick; **(ii)** block deltas are addressed by chunk residency, which the client already
  declares — so fan-out is `observers-with-that-chunk-resident × dirty-chunks`, not `observers × edits`;
  **(iii) the delta is tier-tagged, and an observer resident at tier L receives pyramid entries at
  tier L rather than fine placement records.** Rule (iii) is new and it is the largest single saving in
  the section: a 1,000-block tunnel is 5,000 B of tier-0 records, **128 B at tier 2 (39×) and 16 B at
  tier 3 (312×)**. Without it every distant observer pays full fine-delta bandwidth for edits they are
  rendering at four-metre resolution. Together these partially discharge D-9 for the block lane.
  **[H1] This is EGRESS SELECTION and is legitimate for exactly that reason:** the rung is taken from the
  observer's *clamped* `tier_floor` hint (§4.8), it selects **what to send** the way AoI membership
  already does, and no fence, arbitration outcome, admission decision, scheduling deadline, persisted
  value or simulation state may read it. `OccupantInterest::observer_tier` — a server-side tier derived
  from the client's render tuning — is **STRUCK** and was never §4's; so is
  `LedgerCell::min_demanded_tier` and the `PROTO_MINOR` 7 → 8 bump raised for them.
- **Nonce durability.** The nonce is `(session_id, client_seq)`, written into the dedup set in the **same
  redb write transaction** as the WAL append, so it survives `kill -9` between append and ack. It crosses
  with the realm at handoff (drained in `FLUSH_SOURCE`, step id 7). Separately, HR1 requires the
  side-effecting `InterShardFlow::BlockEdit` arm to carry `(TransferId, step_id)` idempotency — the client
  nonce does not substitute for it; both exist, at different layers. **The pyramid rows written by the
  walk-up join that same transaction**, which is what makes the pyramid crash-consistent with the WAL for
  free rather than needing its own recovery path.

> **[USER DECISION 4-F] — does the block-edit lane carry a tier from its first commit?**
> This exists because HR1's `InterShardFlow` arms and the client-facing delta are **postcard-positional**:
> DEFERRED D-39.6 records that appending a field to a shipped struct is *not* safe. An arm freezes when it
> ships. Note also that the field Addendum 2 §A cites as already present is not this one — the
> `coarsen_level: u8` at `crates/wire/src/intershard.rs:659` is a **pose-precision hop counter on
> `OccupantInterest`**, documented as "hops from the observer's home realm". What line 303 genuinely
> reserves is the *concept* ("the WHAT lane … at the LOD the observed realm controls") — a reserved lane,
> not a reserved field. **There is no terrain-tier field anywhere in the wire today, and in particular no
> way for a client to request one.** That request side is the thing to plant.
>
> | Option | What lands now | Cost now | Cost later |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **F1. Land `BlockEdit` with `tier: u8` and both payload shapes** *(recommended)* | one `u8` plus a two-arm payload (fine records / pyramid entries) on an arm that does not exist yet | **One byte and four structural conformance tests that already gate every arm.** Free today | — |
> | F2. Tier-0 only now; add the tier when coarse rendering lands | nothing | zero | a `PROTO_MINOR` bump, a re-serialisation of every persisted pyramid, and — until it lands — every distant observer receiving full fine deltas at **39–312× the necessary bandwidth** |
>
> **Recommendation: F1.** This is the clearest reserve-now-retrofit-never case in the section: the arm is
> unwritten, the byte is free, and the alternative is a protocol migration on a lane that carries durable
> edit data. **It is a ONE-WAY DOOR in the sense that matters** — once shipped the arm's field order is
> frozen — which is exactly why it should be shipped with the field rather than without it. One-way
> **door 45**, restated per [L5] to name both halves: *"the requested-tier byte on the chunk /
> block-edit request lane AND the tier descriptor on its delta payload — one arm, both fields, landed
> together, because postcard is positional (D-39.6)."*
>
> **[L5] The `tier: u8` here is a PAYLOAD DESCRIPTOR, not an observer property, and the field carries this
> doc comment so the three ladders are never conflated again** — the conflation has already happened once
> in this design, which is why the comment is part of the reservation rather than a nicety:
>
> ```

> /// (1) `ChunkKey.tier` — the CHUNK-LOCAL CONTENT ladder: how coarse this chunk's voxels are.
> /// (2) `tier_floor` — the OBSERVER'S DECLARED FLOOR: a non-authoritative client memory hint,
> ///     clamped by the server, used for egress selection only.
> /// (3) `OccupantInterest::coarsen_level` — a POSE-PRECISION HOP COUNTER on the up-flow ("hops from
> ///     the observer's home realm"), not a terrain tier. Addendum 2 §A's reading of it as a terrain
> ///     ladder is corrected in §3.3.6 and §3.10.
> ```

> **[USER DECISION 4-D] — the placement ghost.** **The ladder changes nothing here, and the reason is
> §4.9.1's proof: the edited chunk is always resident at tier 0 for the player doing the editing**, so
> there is no case where an echo arrives and the coarse representative happens not to change, and
> therefore no new "the ghost never pops" failure mode. The three options stand exactly as written.
>
> | Option | What it is | Standing law touched | Verdict |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **D1. The two-stage protocol only** — reliable lane, off-tick receipt, batching, client-resolved target | ~73–123 ms; no new client state | **None** | **Do this regardless** |
> | **D2. D1 + a translucent, unlit, non-colliding client ghost**, popped on the receipt or the echo | The placement *preview*, which must exist anyway, simply persists past the click | Arguably none: no simulation state, no collider, no rollback, and it cannot desync because it is discarded on the next authoritative message. But it *looks* like prediction, so it needs a ruling rather than an implementation | **Recommended if D1 alone still feels soft** |
> | D3. A narrow prediction exemption — apply the edit to the client's local block field and remesh | Directly contradicts **"NO client-side prediction"** and **"server does ALL math"**. The client block field *is* simulation state: it feeds the mesher and the collider-free render, and a reject forces a visible remesh | **Reject** |
>

> material difference: D2's failure mode is a translucent box vanishing; D3's is the world visibly
> rewriting itself. **One rider if D2 is taken:** the ghost is drawn in the tier-0 pass only and is never
> composited against a coarse chunk. That is automatic rather than enforced — §4.8's residency floor makes
> the whole reach volume tier-0 — but it should be written down, because a future long-range build tool
> that ignored the floor would produce a ghost hovering in front of coarse geometry, which is the one way
> this decision could be reopened by accident.

#### 4.9.3 Undo — the mechanism, corrected

The first draft said the inverse is recorded "in the WAL write". It cannot be: the WAL is dedup-to-final
by definition, so the prior state of an overwritten cell is exactly what it discards, and neither the
5-byte record nor any spare bits can carry a second block state.

**Undo is a separate redb table, written in the same transaction as the WAL append:**

```
block_undo:  key (realm, player, group_seq, item_seq)
             val { chunk: u64, cell: u32, prev_block_type: u16,
                   prev_orient: u8, prev_state_bits: u16, tick: u64 }   = 25 B
```

- **Atomic with the edit**, so it survives `kill -9`; it is a *different table with a different key order*
  and therefore does not touch the WAL's sorted-on-drain byte determinism.
- **A batch is one group**, so undoing a 4,096-cell line is one action.
- **Depth bound**: a per-player ring of 256 groups. 1,000 players × 256 × 25 B ≈ 6.4 MB.
- **Retention**: survives relog; pruned at the realm's next compaction checkpoint or after 24 h.
- **Undo is a new forward edit**, not a WAL rewind — it re-enters the ordinary command pipeline, carries
  its own fence, respects permissions, and is therefore re-shard-safe by construction. **This is also what
  makes undo pyramid-safe for free:** because an undo is a forward edit, it runs the same walk-up as any
  other edit, so the pyramid needs no inverse operation, no journal of its own and no rollback path. Had
  undo been a WAL rewind, the pyramid would have needed all three.
- **Concurrency rule**: an undo whose cell no longer matches `prev_*` is refused and its entry dropped, so
  undo can never silently overwrite another player's later build.
- **`chunk: u64` is a `Tier0Key`** by §4.6.3, so an undo record cannot name a coarse cell. The column
  width does not change; the type does.

#### 4.9.4 May the terrain generator emit non-cube geometry — at any tier?

**Ruling: no. Generated terrain is `Cube`-only at P4 and P6, and — new — at every rung of the ladder.**
Non-cube generated geometry is a later, explicitly-gated feature and is not foreclosed by anything here.

Four reasons, each load-bearing and each unchanged by the ladder: it bounds Lane B on planets to *player
builds*, which are small and near players, which is what makes the spherical per-cell collider budget of
§4.6.1 hold; it keeps the P4 DoD ("same seed ⇒ byte-identical terrain") to a pure
`(seed, address) → BlockTypeId` function with no shape resolution in it; generated shapes are not edits
and must never appear in `block_wal`, which stays true trivially if none exist; and the user's actual
ask — *"dirt should not have perfectly lined edges if it is the last block"* — is answered by §5.6's
**render-side** rim warp, not by geometry.

**A fifth reason, and it is the one that settles the tier question.** The tempting move is to let a coarse
tier use ramps to smooth a distant mountain, since a tier-5 mountain built of 32 m cubes sounds
unacceptably blocky. It is not, and the arithmetic says why: tier selection targets a **constant cell size
in pixels** (Addendum 2 §C.2, two pixels per cell), so a 32 m step at tier 5's range of 25 km subtends
exactly the same two pixels that a 1 m step subtends at tier 0's range. **Blockiness is scale-invariant in
screen space at every rung.** Using ramps at coarse tiers would make distant terrain *smoother* than near
terrain — the world would become less blocky as you flew away and re-blockify as you approached, which is
precisely the discontinuity the crossfade exists to eliminate, applied to the art direction instead of to
the geometry. Cube-only at every tier is not a simplification; it is the only choice that keeps the world
looking like itself.

The asymmetry with player builds (which *do* coarsen shape-preservingly, §4.3.2) is principled rather than
arbitrary, and it is Addendum 2 §C.7's own test: **coarsening never invents a shape that was not there; it
only preserves one that was.** A player's 45° roof was a 45° roof at tier 0, so keeping it at tier 3 is a
coarser rung of the real thing. A generated hillside was never made of wedges, so giving it wedges at
tier 3 would be substituting for rather than deriving from.

That hands §4 the render/collide divergence budget the two sections were each assuming the other owned:

> **The collider is the unwarped tier-0 cell. §5.6's rim warp is render-only, inward-biased, and bounded
> at `|d|∞ ≤ 0.20 m`, so the visual hull is a strict subset of the collision hull.** The failure direction
> is therefore always "a chipped-looking edge that still holds you up", never "you fall through what looks
> solid". §5.6 already proves the inward-bias property exhaustively over all 256 corner-occupancy
> configurations; §4 adds the collider-side half of the contract and the assertion
> `render_hull ⊆ collider_hull` to the same test.
>
> **The rim warp is a tier-0-only effect**, on its own reasoning: it is a sub-metre silhouette
> perturbation and at tier 1 its 0.20 m bound is a tenth of a cell and a fifth of a pixel. **[M6] It does
> NOT fade on `crossfade_band_fraction`** — ~~it fades out with the same crossfade-band tuning field~~ is
> struck, along with §4.5.5's three-way sharing claim. The rim-warp fade is a different mechanism with its
> own two fields, `warp_frac_on` (0.15) and `warp_frac_off` (0.05), applied to `A_max / 2^L` (§5.6.7);
> numerically similar, causally unrelated. Above tier 0 the warp is simply not evaluated — a
> saving in the shader, not a loss on the screen. It therefore never interacts with the
> `render_hull ⊆ collider_hull` assertion, which is stated over tier-0 geometry and has no coarse
> counterpart to be stated over.

**Economy seam (one sentence, because the yield ruling touches it).** Placement validation reads the
player's **inventory**, which is game state; it never reads a price, a market or a currency, which is the
economy overlay. Yield is a game quantity (one tier-0 cell → one unit, §4.3); value is an economy
quantity. The one-way dependency holds and the economy-absent CI gate covers block placement and mining
unchanged.
#### 4.9.5 The edit pyramid's geometric half, and the walk-up

Addendum 2 §C.4 makes the sparse edit pyramid the whole of the real work and §E names it the one thing to
watch: it is **permanent data**, so its format must be right before the first world is saved, and it is
**derived data**, so it can silently disagree with what it was derived from. §3 owns its persistence. §4
owns what it must *carry*, because that is a shape question, and the answer is §4.3.2's `CellSummary`,
persisted as C1's **8-byte `PyramidEntry`** in the **`chunk_pyramid`** table, keyed per `(tier, chunk)`
in the **same redb file as the block deltas**. ~~four bytes, beside `block_wal`~~ — both spellings are
struck (C1, M3).

**The walk-up, in full, because every line is load-bearing.** This is C2's rule, and it replaces both
§2.4.3's blind-increment form and §4's own earlier eight-line sketch, whose `if before == after { break }`
on **representatives** is struck:

```
// Once per COMMITTED BATCH, coarse cells deduped, inside the WAL's own redb write transaction.

on commit of the edits touching tier-0 chunk C:
  for each touched tier-0 cell a:
      mark a.ancestor(1) dirty
  for L in 1 ..= tier_depth - 1:
      for each dirty CoarseAddr parent at rung L (deduped, ascending key order):
          siblings = [ chunk_pyramid.get(s).map(PyramidEntry::summary)
                       .unwrap_or_else(|| generate_summary(s))   // MISS -> GENERATOR, never Default
                       for s in parent.children() ]              // 8 lookups, ONE storage block
          next   = coarsen(&siblings)
          stored = chunk_pyramid.get(parent).map(PyramidEntry::summary)
          if Some(next) == stored { continue }                   // EXIT ON SUMMARY EQUALITY
          if next == generate_summary(parent) { chunk_pyramid.remove(parent) }   // PRUNE
          else { chunk_pyramid.put(parent, PyramidEntry::new(parent.cell, next)) }
          dirty_coarse_chunk(parent.chunk, L)
          mark parent.ancestor(L+1) dirty
```

**Pruning is new and it is what keeps the pyramid honest:** an entry is deleted iff it equals
`generate_summary` of its own address, so digging a hole and filling it back in leaves nothing behind at
any rung.

Five properties, each with the number that makes it true:

- **It is closed under itself.** A parent's summary is a function of its eight children's *summaries*,
  never of the tier-0 field, which is what makes eight bytes enough and what makes the walk 8 reads per
  rung instead of 8^L. §4.3.2 priced the alternative at rung 7 alone: 8 reads against 2,097,152.
  **And the eight sibling reads are eight lookups inside ONE storage block**, because `CHUNK_EDGE = 62`
  is even, so a rung-L parent's eight children always lie in one rung-(L−1) chunk. That is what makes the
  §8.4 gate *"≤ 1 entry write and ≤ 1 pyramid storage-block read per rung per touched coarse cell, zero
  reads of `block_wal`, zero reads of any tier-0 delta"* passable — tighter than any of the three
  competing update rules claimed.
- **A missing entry is generated, not defaulted.** The sparse pyramid has no row for unedited regions, and
  the owner holds the generator, so a miss is one octave-dropped evaluation at that child's tier — not a
  zero, not a `Default`, which for durable data is banned outright by CLAUDE.md. At the measured
  12.19 ns per noise evaluation and roughly five evaluations per cell, the worst-case walk with **every**
  sibling missing is `(tier_depth − 1) × 8 × 5 × 12.19 ns` = **5.85 µs at `tier_depth` = 13** and
  **9.75 µs at 21**. That is the whole cost of maintaining the ladder per edit, against a ~1 ms edit
  budget: **≤ 1 %.**
- **It terminates early, and usually at rung 1 or 2.** §4.3.2 walked the arithmetic; with the early exit
  the common single edit inside solid rock terminates at rung 1 or 2 (~0.5 µs). The
  worst case is `tier_depth − 1` rungs and it requires removing the last solid child of a chain — the
  final block of an isolated pillar.
- **It is crash-consistent for free.** The rows ride the transaction the WAL append already opens
  (§4.9.2), so `kill -9` between the two is impossible. The pyramid needs no recovery path of its own,
  which is the second reason to write it at commit time rather than in a background job.
- **It is re-derivable, and that must be a command and a test rather than a hope.** Addendum 2 §E asks for
  exactly this: **`vdctl world verify-pyramid <realm>`** (~~`recompute-pyramid`~~) rebuilds every entry
  from the generator plus the deltas and asserts byte-equality against what is stored, and **the test
  suite runs it after EVERY edit scenario**. A divergence becomes a failing assertion instead of a player
  noticing their tunnel is the wrong shape from a hilltop. It is cheap because the walk-up is pure and
  deterministic; it is *necessary* because derived durable data with no auditor is how silent corruption
  ships — and it is the audit that the struck exit-on-representative-equality would have failed on
  visually correct data.

**Storage, honestly — and the cost per edit depends on the SHAPE of the edit set, not on one ratio.**
Entries are 8 B, stored as sorted runs keyed per `(tier, chunk)` rather than per cell, which is CDLOD's
separation of storage-block granularity from node granularity and is what keeps redb key counts sane on a
heavily-built planet. §4's earlier three-row table is superseded by C1's four-case series, which spans a
factor of fifty and is the one form that will not mislead a capacity plan (§3.9.8's "roughly one seventh"
is the compact-3-D row only, and is struck as a general claim):

| Shape of the edit set | Entries per edit | Bytes per edit |
|---|---|---|
| compact 3-D cluster | `Σ 8^-L` = 0.143 n | 1.14 B |
| surface / wall (2-D) | `Σ 4^-L` = 0.333 n | 2.67 B |
| line / pipe (1-D) | `Σ 2^-L` ≈ 1.000 n | 8.00 B |
| isolated (hard bound: nothing shares a coarse cell) | `tier_depth − 1` | `8·(tier_depth − 1)` B |

Worked at `tier_depth = 13` (the starter world, m = 4,096):

| Case | Entries | Bytes |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000-edit 1-wide tunnel | 250+125+63+32+16+8+4+2+1+1+1+1 = **504** | 4,032 B ≈ **3.9 KiB** |
| 8,000-edit 20×20×20 tower | 1,000+125+27+8+1×8 = **1,168** | 9,344 B ≈ **9.1 KiB** |
| 100 M mixed edits at the ~1.1 entries/edit planning figure | ~110 M | **~880 MB** |

Deeper ladders do not move the clustered rows — the series converge — and only the adversarial isolated
row grows, bounded by `tier_depth − 1` by construction. That is the price of a tunnel still being there
at three kilometres, and it is the right
price. **The one thing to watch is not the size but the shape:** §3.9.6's delta budget, revert and reap
must be made **pyramid-aware from the start**, because the failure mode of not doing so is documented and
severe — No Man's Sky caps terrain edits at 255 fixed buffers per save, evicts edits outside base bounds
when the budget overruns, and players report visiting heavily-edited bases wiping their own edits. That
is what a pyramid designed for a bounded delta set does when the delta set is unbounded.

**Load fixtures, landing with the slices that bear them** (the standing law is that they do not defer):
(i) a 10k-block construct, full remesh + collider rebuild, p99 budget, sparse path verified;
(ii) a 50 %-shaped 62³ chunk against the 1.91 MB Lane-B tier-0 ceiling;
(iii) an N-player edit storm measuring `observers × dirty-chunks × tiers` fan-out against the D-9 baseline,
**with and without the tier-tagged delta** so the 39–312× saving is measured rather than assumed;
(iv) a checkerboard-`Slab` wall against the §4.5.6 merge-barrier worst case;
(v) **a sustained-edit run measuring the pyramid walk-up against its `(tier_depth − 1) × 8 × 5 × 12.19 ns`
budget — 5.85 µs at `tier_depth` = 13, 9.75 µs at 21 — and its early-exit depth distribution**, which is
the number that decides whether the coarse remesh queue can ever back up.

**Gates the ladder adds, all of them §4's half of an Addendum 2 §D.3 row:**

| Gate | What §4 must hold |
|---|---|
| **Collision is tier-0 only** | An *assertion*, not a test: `Tier0Key` has no coarse constructor, so `collider_from(coarse_chunk)` does not compile. The negative test is `ChunkKey::as_tier0()` returning `None` for **every tier 1..=31** (~~1–7~~, C3) — a real, covered branch under HR5, plus the rejected example in the doc comment. **No new workspace dependency**, which is also why §5.10.3's `trybuild` mechanism is replaced by this one [H6] |
| **Edit survival across tiers** | Break a `Wedge` at 10 m, fly to 3 km crossing every tier boundary, assert the notch is present in the drawn geometry at each rung, fly back, assert nothing popped |
| **Coarsening is exact and agrees with itself** | **`verify-pyramid`** byte-equality over a fixture world, run **after every edit scenario**; and a property test driving random fields through recursive vs. direct-from-fine coarsening, reporting worst-case silhouette divergence rather than asserting they are equal (they are not, and the bound is the deliverable) |
| **Pyramid walk-up cost** (§8.4's row, §4's half) | **≤ 1 entry write and ≤ 1 pyramid storage-block read per rung per touched coarse cell** — the eight siblings lie in ONE storage block because `CHUNK_EDGE = 62` is even. **Zero reads of `block_wal`, zero reads of any tier-0 delta**; a miss resolves through the GENERATOR. All writes ride the WAL's own redb write transaction |
| **Tier invariance of authority** [H1] | The identical fixture with every observer's clamped `tier_floor` forced to 0 and to `tier_depth − 1` produces **byte-identical** shard state and identical fence/arbitration/grant outcomes |
| **The skirt closes every crack** | A property test over all 256 masks × 9 buckets asserting the coarse solid and its children's union lie within one coarse cell, plus a rendered seam sweep with the camera at the annulus boundary |
| **No pop** | The pop detector sees no discontinuity at any tier crossing — **at flight speed and at a forward walk at eye height.** The walking traverse is not redundant: it is the case the AAA reference visibly failed (near-field clutter and grass appearing metres ahead), and a fade ramp tuned only on a flyover will pass a flyover and fail a walk |

**The HR6 artefact** is a single cheap and unusually high-value one: a **shape sheet** — one `vdctl`
scenario placing every distinct rendered placement in a labelled grid and taking one screenshot. 414
placements at 1 m spacing is a **21 × 20 m plate**. A broken template, a reversed winding, a wrong mirror
twin, a missing coverage pattern or an off-lattice vertex becomes a pixel diff rather than a bug report.
Run it on both a Spherical and a Cartesian profile and the warp contract of §4.2 is visually verified in
the same artefact.

**The ladder adds a second sheet, and it is the same idea applied one level up: a coarsening sheet.** For
each of the 40 silhouette-critical octant masks, place the 2×2×2 fine group and its coarse representative
side by side and take one screenshot — an 80-cell plate, one scenario, one diff. A wrong `COARSE_SHAPE`
row, a mis-derived `octant_mask`, a broken tie-break or an admits-fallback that fires when it should not
becomes a pixel diff instead of a report from a player who noticed their tower looked wrong from a hill.
Both sheets are the same machinery and should be written as one scenario with two fixtures.

### Adjudicated objections

The adversarial critique raised 27 findings. Twenty-three were correct and are fixed above — the
index-space contract (§4.2) and the warped-slope derivation (§4.7) are new subsections; the encoding now
adopts §2's triple index; `ShapeDef` is one row in one crate on one unit per field; the pin moved out of
`orient`; volume, mass and yield are cell-nominal on an exact 196,608 lattice; Lane B is instanced and
bounded; undo has a real table; the terrain-geometry, occ_ao-residency, jump, phase-anchor and
economy-seam rulings are stated. Four are wrong or overstated:

- **C3 (the record) is right in substance but wrong to call [USER DECISION 4-A] spurious.** §3.9.2
  independently raises the same width question as **[USER DECISION 3-H]** (~~3-E~~ — a citation fault
  corrected under [M4]; 3-E is the surface-gravity range) and explicitly delegates the state
  word's split to §4, so a document-level decision does exist — what was wrong was §4 raising it as its
  own and recommending 8 bytes. **The width itself is register row 2 and §4 does not close it**; §4
  states its argument for five and leaves 3-H standing. C3's related claim that the triple index "caps
  material × shape × function at 65,536" is
  imprecise: the cap is on *authored* rows, which is 944 at v1 and 25 % of the space at 256 materials × 64
  shapes.
- **H2's citation of §3's `cell_corners` "for mesher, collider trimesh" as a contradiction is a misread.**
  That parenthetical is a loose label for collider construction generally; `cell_corners` is precisely
  what feeds the convex-hexahedron composite recommended in §4.6.1. §4's rejection of parry `TriMesh` for
  dynamic bodies stands unchanged. The rest of H2 — that `Voxels` cannot represent a sheared shell and
  that [USER DECISION 4-B] hid a planet/ship divergence — is correct and is fixed.
- **M3 is right that the tick wait cannot be zeroed, but its proposed restatement (~125–170 ms) is
  wrong.** The corrected range is 73–123 ms, because the draft's own 120 ms upper bound already carried
  the tick wait implicitly; only the lower bound's justification changes.
- **L1's arithmetic is right (54,735, and the rounding direction was inverted) but the finding is moot**:
  the millidegree field no longer exists — slopes are exact rationals (§4.4) and the one `atan` is

**Addendum 2 pass (2026-08-03).** The detail-level ladder amends this section in eight places and
contradicts it in one. Amended: §4.2's crack proof is narrowed to *within a tier* and gains the tier-scaled

Three of Addendum 2's own statements are corrected here rather than repeated. Its §A claim that the wire
