## 5. Rendering the surface — mesher, materials, big textures, blending, and the un-square edge

This section owns the path from an authoritative block field to lit pixels. Three of the user's
explicit asks live here and nowhere else: **big textures spanning many blocks**, **materials that
blend into each other**, and **edges that are not perfectly square**. All three are solvable, none
is free, and two of them force decisions that cannot be cheaply reversed.

**Addendum 2 changed this section more than any other, and it is worth being exact about how.** The
"no level-of-detail" preference is retracted by owner ruling; detail levels are mandatory everywhere,
on one generic ladder, and **a tier is a number on a chunk address, never a second code path**. Four
consequences, each of which the rest of the section is written against:

1. **The mesher, the material, the peel, the blend and the warp are structurally unchanged.** A tier
   changes the metre size of a cell and nothing else. Everything above the geometry seam already works
   in *cell index space*, so it is tier-agnostic by construction (§5.1.4). HR3 is satisfied the same
   way it is for shard kinds: nothing here branches on a tier, and the two places that look like they
   do are one generic rule reading a tier-derived parameter (§5.5.4's and §5.6.7's **sub-cell rule**).
2. **Mipmapping stops being an open question and becomes mandatory** — and with it arrives a
   correctness bug this design never named: the roughness mip chain must carry the normal map's lost
   variance, or every distant surface sparkles under a moving sun (§5.3.7). That is a **bake-spec**
   change, so it shares the one-way door with USER DECISION 5-C.
3. **§5.9 is now a different subsection.** It used to be "the no-LOD collision, and the orbital view" —
   a subsection about a wall. It is the detail ladder itself, and USER DECISIONS 5-F and 5-G are both
   discharged inside it.
4. **The vertex format stops being a feasibility question and becomes a bandwidth question** (§5.2).
   That is a de-escalation, not a reprieve: the ladder makes *residency* logarithmic in view distance
   while leaving *ingest* proportional to speed, so **the upload budget is now the tightest number in
   the section** and V2 acquires a dated trigger it did not have before.

~~Addendum 1 §C.4: "the binding constraint is the drawn radius, not the planet radius — roughly 700 m
to 1 km of fully meshed terrain is what one-metre blocks with no detail tiers can afford".~~
**Dissolved.** That finding was true only of a single-tier renderer, and the clause that made it true
is the clause the ruling deleted. With the ladder a 100 km view costs about 6,800 chunks and a 786 m
view about 1,500, so the drawn radius stops being a budget at all; what replaces it is a **rung
count**, which grows with the logarithm of view distance. Say this where Addendum 1's finding is
cited, because it was the headline of that document and readers will remember it.

The whole path, stated once, with the tier in it:

```
chunk address (sector, a, b, c, detail_tier = L)      ← L is DATA, not a code path
  │
  ├─ [Tier-A, vd-voxel-gen]  height + cave fields evaluated on the tier-L lattice with the
  │                          top L octaves DROPPED (§3.5; cheaper AND correctly pre-filtered)
  │                          ⊕ edit-pyramid overwrite wherever an entry exists (§3.9)
  │                          → block field at tier L + a 1-CELL apron of full block records
  │                            read at the SAME tier
  │
  ├─ [Tier-A, vd-voxel]  occupancy masks → face-mask cull → greedy runs → border peel
  │                       → rim warp (baked, integer, amplitude scaled by the sub-cell rule)
  │                       → skirt apron → ChunkGeometry (pure integer + fixed point)
  │
  ├─ [Tier-A, vd-client] ChunkGeometry → MeshPrim { stream, indices,
  │                                                 transform.scale = 2^L,
  │                                                 chunk header carrying L }
  │
  └─ [Tier-B, vd-client-render]  MeshPrim → GPU buffers, ExtendedMaterial, WGSL:
                                  world-UV, anti-tiling, seam blend, AO, emission,
                                  the material feature ladder keyed on L,
                                  and one dither crossfade between adjacent rungs
```

**The tier line is the load-bearing structural decision of this section.** Everything above it is
integer and fixed-point manipulation with no floats-with-transcendentals and no Bevy types, which is
simultaneously the shape that reaches 100 % region+branch coverage easily (HR5) and the shape that is
byte-identical on server and client by construction. Everything below it touches wgpu or WGSL, which
has no coverage instrumentation at all.

Two corrections to the naive reading of that line, both of which the first draft got wrong:

1. **`vd-voxel` is Tier-A only if it is *added to the justfile's `tier_a` list*.** That list is
   `-p vd-core -p vd-devproto -p vd-wire -p vd-sim -p vd-node -p vd-connection-plane -p vd-harness
   -p vd-client -p vd-client-harness` (justfile:12). A new crate is Tier-B by omission. Adding
   `-p vd-voxel` is part of the slice that creates the crate, not a follow-up.
2. **`vd-client-render` is not a leaf that "nothing depends on".** `crates/bins/Cargo.toml:66` has
   `render = ["dep:vd-client-render", …]`. Its Tier-B status is a justfile fact, not a dependency
   fact, and no design argument may lean on an isolation it does not have.

**The frame budget every number below is measured against**, stated once because the research pool
computed triangle, quad and tap counts against no denominator: **1920×1080 at 60 Hz (16.67 ms) on an
8 GB discrete desktop GPU of the RTX 4060 / RX 7600 class, with a mandatory depth prepass.** Derived
sub-budgets, ~~terrain vertex+index residency ≤ 256 MiB~~ **restated for the ladder**: resident chunk
count ≤ 7,500 across every rung **including crossfade residency, measured while moving** (§5.9.5's
restatement of Addendum 2 §D.3's gate); terrain vertex+index residency ≤ 1.60 GiB at V1 and ≤ 160 MiB
at V2 (§5.3.6 — the 256 MiB figure was a 741 m single-tier horizon and no longer describes anything);
**terrain mesh UPLOAD ≤ 8 MiB/frame = 480 MB/s, which the ladder makes the
binding number** (§5.2.3); total client VRAM ≤ 3.0 GiB; per-pixel texture taps 24 soft / 32 hard, now
reached only in the tier-0 near field (§5.4); main-pass triangles ≤ 6 M. The macOS development machine is explicitly *not*
the sizing target — Bevy's `AUTO` bindless slab limit is 64 there versus 2048 elsewhere, a 32× gap —
and that divergence is a listed risk, not a design input.

Two hard rules bind the section and are satisfied structurally. **HR3:** nothing here matches on a
shard kind. The mesher's inputs are a padded block-record buffer, a material table and a
`GridMapping`; the cube-sphere lives inside `GridMapping` (§3.1) and the mesher never learns the word
"planet". **HR4:** §3.1.4 already issues the binding ruling — G-IDENTICAL binds everything *above*
`GridMapping` and is satisfiable there; `GridMapping` itself carries `G-MAPPING-EXHAUSTIVE` instead.
The mesher, the peel, the seam pass and the warp all sit above the seam, so they take G-IDENTICAL:
**one fixture, meshing a chunk containing a material seam, a shaped block and a warped rim, run on a
Spherical planet profile and a Cartesian ship profile, with equal control-plane results.** The one
piece that is chart-dependent — corner identity across a cube-face seam — is pushed *into*
`GridMapping` as a seventh operation (§5.6.1) precisely so it lands under the other gate. Nothing in
this section re-opens or quietly widens either ruling.

**HR3 and the tier, ruled once so it is not re-argued per subsection.** A tier is a `u8` on the chunk
address. The mesher, the peel, the coverage matrix, the merge predicate, the AO masks, the
transparency dual-mask, the shape catalogue and the material table are byte-identical code at every
rung. Where a *feature* must weaken with tier — the seam blend (§5.5.4), the rim warp (§5.6.7), POM,
hex-tiling, the normal map (§5.4) — it does so through **one generic law**, stated once here and
referenced everywhere else:

> **The sub-cell rule.** Every geometric or shading feature carries an authored size in **metres**. A
> tier expresses that feature with weight `w = clamp(size_m / (cell_size_m · min_cell_fraction), 0, 1)`
> and no branch. A feature smaller than one cell of the current tier is not represented at that tier;
> it is folded into the shading instead. `cell_size_m = 2^L`; `min_cell_fraction` is a render-tuning
> field.

That is a data-driven continuous weight, not a `match L`, and it generalises for free: a material
authored with a 20 m blend width still blends at tier 4. The G-IDENTICAL fixture of §5.1 gains one
clause — **the same fixture is meshed at tier 0 and at tier 3 on both profiles, and the tier-3 result
is a pure function of the tier-3 field** — which is the cheapest possible proof that no tier fork
exists.

### 5.1 The mesher

#### 5.1.1 Verdict on the named candidates

| Option | Maintained | Throughput / 62³ chunk | Non-cube shapes | Transparency | Per-face materials | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `block-mesh` 0.2.0 | **No.** Last release 2022-04-17. A negative-stride integer-overflow fix and `merge_value_facing_neighbour` are stranded unreleased on git main. "Road to 1.0" open since 2024-03-02, no maintainer reply. | ~3 ms (`greedy_quads`) | No (issue #33) | `VoxelVisibility::Translucent` exists | No (one `merge_value`) | **Reject** |
| `bevy_voxel_world` 0.15.0 | Yes, but main has moved to Bevy 0.19 and it depends on `block-mesh` 0.2.0. | n/a — uses the **non-merging** `visible_block_faces` | No | — | Via a `[u32;3]` callback | **Reject as a dependency; read three mechanisms** |
| `binary-greedy-meshing` 0.5.2 | Yes — 2026-01-07, MIT, engine-independent, extracted from a shipped Bevy game | **65 µs** (`fast_mesh`), **90 µs** with transparency | No | Yes, dual-mask | No | **Closest usable, but forked on day one** |
| Ours, from the published bit expressions | — | 65 / 90 µs class | Yes (two-lane) | Yes | Yes | **Recommend** |

Maintenance disqualifies `block-mesh` on its own; the decisive fact is the **non-cube gap**. §4 commits
the palette to half-blocks, slopes and corners. No bitmask algorithm emits a diagonal — greedy merging
expands axis-aligned rectangles inside a plane and a hypotenuse has no rectangle decomposition. Every
off-the-shelf Rust option assumes full cubes. The mesher is therefore **two-lane** regardless of
starting point, and §4.5.1 already fixes the lane predicate (`is_cube` computed at bake from coverage
and volume, so no shape can lie about it).

`binary-greedy-meshing`'s hard lock to 62³ happens to match the committed chunk size, so that
limitation does not bite. What bites is that Lane B, the per-side coverage matrix (§4.5.3), the
seam-quad pass (§5.5), the rim border-peel (§5.6) and the dual transparency masks (§5.7) all require
editing the merge predicate and the quad emitter — a fork before the first planet renders. Owning
~300–800 lines of branchless integer code we can cover to 100 % is cheaper than owning a fork of a
crate whose generic monomorphisation is the exact coverage foot-gun `CLAUDE.md` documents.

**Three mechanisms to read out of `bevy_voxel_world` and reimplement, not depend on:**
(1) `prepare_voxel_texture` — the Bevy recipe for reinterpreting a vertically-stacked PNG as a
`D2Array` view with all address modes `Repeat`; (2) the `AsyncComputeTaskPool` throttle
(`remaining_threads = max_threads.saturating_sub(in_flight)`, `max_spawn_per_frame`, non-blocking
harvest via `poll_once`); (3) the `MaterialExtension` binding-100+ pattern. Its mesh cache is
**deliberately not on that list** (§5.1.3), and its world model — camera-ray chunk spawning, a
per-chunk LOD system, a flat grid with no parent frame — is structurally incompatible with a realm tree
whose chunk residency is decided by realm membership and the demand loop.

> **[USER DECISION 5-A] — dependency adoption for the mesher.** None of these crates is in
> `Cargo.lock`; adopting any is a user decision under the standing rule.
>
> | Choice | Cost now | Cost later | Risk |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **A1. Write our own from the published bit expressions** *(recommended)* | ~300–800 lines + a coverage suite + a determinism fixture | Zero version drift; two-lane, peel and dual-mask are natural | We own every bug |
> | A2. Depend on `binary-greedy-meshing` 0.5.2 | ~0 | Fork required at the first slope, the first seam strip, the first rim peel | One maintainer; a fork with no upstream is A1 with worse ergonomics |
> | A3. Vendor it (copy, MIT, attribute) | ~0 | Same as A1 from slice two onward | Loses upstream fixes silently |
> | A4. Depend on `block-mesh` | ~0 | Cannot express slopes, AO or per-face materials | Unmaintained since 2022; a released correctness bug |
> | A5. Depend on `bevy_voxel_world` | ~0 | Its world model must be fought; drags in `block-mesh` | Pulls Bevy into whatever crate meshes |
>
> **Recommendation: A1**, with A3 acceptable if the first slice must move faster. **Not a one-way
> door**: `ChunkGeometry` is the seam and swapping the producer behind it is contained.

#### 5.1.2 The two lanes, and the one operation all three cut rules share

Lane assignment, the coverage matrix, the shaped-vertex ABI and the AO mask pair are fixed by §4.5 and
are adopted here verbatim. What §5 owns is the **cut rule**, and there are three of them:

| Predicate | Fires when | Ring granularity needed |
|---|---|---|
| **Material seam** (§5.5) | an in-plane neighbour across this edge has a different render material | 1-block **strip** |
| **Shaped neighbour** (§4.5.2) | the in-plane neighbour's coverage pattern is not FULL | 1-block **strip** |
| **Warped corner** (§5.6) | a lattice corner on this edge has non-zero warp amplitude | **unit** (1×1) quads |

All three are the same operation, and it is the single most reusable piece of machinery in the mesher.
Specified completely, because the first draft's "shrink Q inward by 1 block" is undefined for small
quads and non-deterministic at corners:

```rust
/// Total, order-independent, and exact for every rectangle down to 1×1.
/// `fire[k]` is the peel predicate for edge k in the fixed order [-u, +u, -v, +v].
pub fn border_peel(q: Rect, fire: [bool; 4]) -> (Option<Rect>, ArrayVec<Rect, 4>) {
    let u0 = q.u0 + fire[0] as u32;  let u1 = q.u1 - fire[1] as u32;
    let v0 = q.v0 + fire[2] as u32;  let v1 = q.v1 - fire[3] as u32;
    if u0 >= u1 || v0 >= v1 {                      // nothing left to keep
        return (None, once(q).collect());          // the whole quad IS the ring
    }
    let core = Rect { u0, u1, v0, v1 };
    let mut ring = ArrayVec::new();                // fixed emission order: -v, +v, -u, +u
    if fire[2] { ring.push(Rect { u0: q.u0, u1: q.u1, v0: q.v0, v1: v0 }); }
    if fire[3] { ring.push(Rect { u0: q.u0, u1: q.u1, v0: v1,   v1: q.v1 }); }
    if fire[0] { ring.push(Rect { u0: q.u0, u1: u0,   v0,        v1 }); }
    if fire[1] { ring.push(Rect { u0: u1,   u1: q.u1, v0,        v1 }); }
    (Some(core), ring)
}
```

If the **warped-corner** predicate fires anywhere on the quad's boundary, each ring rectangle is then
passed through `split_unit` and emitted as 1×1 quads; otherwise the ring stays as strips. One
operation, three consumers, one set of tests, one cost. Write it first.

**The two-material reduction is a total order, not a "dominant" heuristic.** A ring quad carries its
core's material `m` plus a second material chosen as the **lowest `MaterialId` among the differing
in-plane neighbours across its firing edges**. `MaterialId` is a `u16` with distinct values, so this is
total, tie-free, order-independent and chunk-independent — the two chunks that share a boundary corner
reach the same answer from their own aprons, which is the same property `min` buys for the warp
amplitude.

#### 5.1.3 The worker architecture, two job classes, and two latency budgets

The mesher is never called on the main thread.

1. **Dirty flags.** An edit marks its chunk dirty. Meshing needs a 1-block apron of *full block
   records*, so an edit at a chunk corner dirties up to 2³ = **8** chunks. Dirty is a set, not a
   queue — repeated edits coalesce.
2. **Scheduling is the demand loop, not a second scheduler.** §3.7 already rules that chunk
   generation, meshing, pipeline warm-up and GPU residency are declared *phases of the existing AoI
   demand loop with the same hysteresis*. Frustum membership, camera distance and dirty-flag age are a
   **tiebreak inside the AoI set**, never an alternative residency policy. This is why
   `bevy_voxel_world`'s camera-ray spawning is rejected as a *world model* while its throttle is
   adopted as a *mechanism*. **The ladder adds a dimension to this queue, not a second scheduler**
   (§5.9.2): a request is `(chunk address, tier)`, and tier selection is the existing angular-size
   rule applied one level down.
3. **Coarse-first ordering, and it is a rule rather than a heuristic.** *Never issue a fine-tier
   request for a region that has no coarser rung resident.* This is the operational content of the
   only part of Pearl Abyss's "hierarchical proxy loading" that survives transfer to a player-editable
   world (the offline HLOD bake does not — §5.9.7), and it is what makes Addendum 2's "the realm proxy
   is the coarsest rung" operationally true instead of merely conceptual: there is always a resident
   rung covering every direction, so a missing chunk is a *blurrier* chunk, never a hole. Cost: an
   ordering constraint plus one resident-tier bitmask per chunk column in the request queue —
   near-zero CPU. Its real cost is a wire consequence, discharged in §5.10.1: the coarse edit-pyramid
   record for a region must be fetchable *before* the fine deltas under it, which means the P6 block
   lane needs a `tier: u8` on its request shape. One byte in an arm that does not exist yet is free;
   after the arm ships it is a `PROTO_MINOR` bump plus a pyramid re-serialisation.
4. **Two job classes with separate in-flight caps.** Generation and meshing have different cost
   distributions and must not share a queue. With §3.5's height-first generator a column-stack is
   **0.15–1.5 ms** and a chunk mesh is **65–90 µs**; both caps are fields on one render-tuning config
   struct, never inline literals.
5. **A cost estimator, because worst-case chunk content is 566× the average and a player can build
   it.** The same source that publishes 65 µs publishes the range: **0.174 ms (empty) to 36.8 ms (3-D
   checkerboard)** — an afternoon's work for a creative player and a deliberate act for a griefer. The
   policy: the estimator is the previous mesh's quad count (a free integer); chunks above a threshold go
   to an **expensive queue** with at most one job in flight per worker, so a 36.8 ms job cannot
   monopolise the pool; **there is no quad cap and no visual degradation** — dropping quads makes holes
   and material-blind merging makes lies, both worse than a slow remesh, so the bound is on the
   *scheduler*, not the *output*; and a **degenerate-content short-circuit** skips the peel passes
   entirely when the merged quad count exceeds 60 % of the culled count (merging bought nothing, every
   quad is already 1×1, so the peels are no-ops). That last rule is exact, free, and collapses the
   pathological case's triple multiplier to a single one.
6. **The mesh swap, designed rather than asserted.** Bevy has **no partial mesh upload** — any `Mesh`
   mutation raises `AssetEvent::Modified` and re-extracts the whole mesh — and `RenderAssetBytesPerFrame`
   defers *whole assets* by an unbounded number of frames, so the main world cannot observe upload
   completion and "upload before dropping the old handle" is not directly expressible. The implementable
   form: hold both handles alive; a render-world system watches `RenderAssets<RenderMesh>` for the new id
   and sends `MeshReady(AssetId)` back over a channel; the main world swaps `Mesh3d` on receipt. ~50
   lines. The named fallback, if that proves fragile across a Bevy release, is a single-frame gap on
   remesh only (≤ 16.7 ms) — visible, and ledgered rather than silently accepted.
7. **`RenderAssetBytesPerFrame` is set to 8 MiB/frame** (480 MiB/s at 60 Hz). It defaults to *unlimited*,
   which is what the client runs today; its guarantee is at least one asset of forward progress per
   frame, so a large budget cannot deadlock but an unbounded one can spike a frame.

**Budget 1 — edit echo to pixels.** Mesher CPU for one block at a chunk corner is 8 × 65 µs = 520 µs
of worker time, ~150 µs wall on a 4-thread pool. Upload dominates.

| Stage | Budget | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Authoritative echo → dirty flag | 0 | Same frame the reply lands |
| Dirty → worker start | ≤ 1 frame | Bounded pool may defer |
| Meshing | ≤ 1 ms wall (typical), ≤ 60 ms (pathological chunk) | Expensive queue keeps it off the critical path |
| Upload | ≤ 1 frame at 8 MiB/frame | 3.52 MB worst click |
| **Edit echo → pixels** | **≤ 33 ms (2 frames)** | Main thread stalls **0 µs** |

**The ladder does not touch this budget, and the reason is worth stating because it is not obvious.**
An edit also writes the sparse edit pyramid — at most one small write per rung, and the walk-up exits
as soon as a rung's summary is unchanged (§3.9) — but it triggers **zero coarse remeshes on the editing
client**. Rung `L` is only resident *beyond* `786·2^(L−1)`
metres, and a player editing a block is at zero distance from it, so the region under his hands exists
at tier 0 and nowhere else. A distant observer does see one coarse chunk re-mesh, on his own client,
bounded by the same queue. So the interactive loop the player feels is unchanged: **8 fine chunks,
3.52 MB at V1, two frames.**

That sits on top of the latency the no-prediction rule already costs — the 100–150 ms interpolation
buffer plus one server tick plus RTT, of order 200 ms, whose exact value follows from the transport
tuning and not from this section. Which is why *jitter* matters more than the mean: a multi-megabyte
upload spike that drops a frame is far more noticeable than 33 ms of extra latency.

**Budget 2 — first appearance, which the draft omitted and which is the one the P4 demo is judged on.**
~~Under the binary render rule a chunk entering the draw radius must be generated, meshed and uploaded
before it is visible, or the seamless law is broken by a hard pop-in edge with no LOD to hide it.~~
The binary render rule is retracted, so the *failure mode* changes: a chunk that arrives late is now
covered by its own coarser rung, which is already resident by the coarse-first rule above. There is no
edge and no hole — only a region that is briefly blurrier than it should be, and the dither crossfade
of §5.9.5 means even that arrives without a step. **The warm ring survives, with a smaller job:** it
exists to keep the *finest* rung ahead of the camera, and its failure is soft rather than structural.

The rule: **maintain a generated-and-meshed warm ring of width `v · t_warm` beyond each rung's own
range, with `t_warm = 2.0 s`, and evaluate each chunk's tier at the PREDICTED camera position
`p + v·t_warm` rather than the current one.** The prediction is not a new mechanism — it is the
velocity lead already in the locked AoI model. It matters because above `R_0 / t_warm = 393 m/s` the
tier-0 warm ring is *wider than tier 0's entire range*, so warming "tier 0 ahead of you" without the
lead generates fine chunks that will be drawn at tier 1 by the time you reach them: pure waste, and it
is the exact speed band a ship operates in.

**The structural result, and it is the reason the ladder is affordable at all.** New columns per second
entering rung `L` is `ρ_L = 2π·R_L·v / (62·2^L)²`, and with `R_L = 786·2^L` the `2^L` cancels twice
over: `ρ_L = 1.284·v·2^(−L)` columns/s. Summing the rungs is a geometric series, so

> **the entire ladder costs at most twice its innermost rung, no matter how many rungs it has.**

(The convention is §5.1.3's conservative one — the full leading circumference sweeping at `v`, which
over-counts by about π because columns also leave behind you. It is kept for continuity with the
number it replaces.) Weighting each rung by its octave discount `(8−L)/8` gives **2.25·v tier-0
equivalent columns per second** for generation and **6.40·v chunks per second** for meshing.

| | Single tier (786 m view) | Full 8-rung ladder (100 km view) |
|---|---|---|
| Column ingest | 1.28·v /s | 2.56·v /s |
| Generation, octave-discounted | 1.28·v tier-0 equivalents | **2.25·v** tier-0 equivalents |
| Chunks meshed | 3.85·v /s | 6.40·v /s |
| `v_max` at `W = 2` cores, pessimistic `c_gen = 1.5 ms/col` | 919 m/s | **528 m/s** |
| `v_max` at `W = 2` cores, typical `c_gen = 0.15 ms/col` | 4,600 m/s | 2,653 m/s |
| View distance bought | 786 m | **100,608 m** |

**Maximum sustainable flight speed is a derived quantity, not a tuning constant:**
`v_max = W / (2.25·c_gen + 6.40·c_mesh)`. ~~The draft's `v_max = (W · 62 m) / c_col ≈ 760 m/s`~~ is
**withdrawn** — that formula does not reproduce its own table (it evaluates to 76,073 m/s at the stated
inputs) and it predates the ladder. The corrected pessimistic figure is **528 m/s for a 100 km view**,
against 919 m/s for a 786 m view: the ladder costs **1.74×** and buys **135×** the view distance. It
remains a gameplay one-way door — ship performance gets tuned around it — and it remains the second
reason §3.5.3's noise benchmark must run before any mesher code lands.

**And the case everyone expects to be expensive is the cheap one.** At altitude `h` the finest resident
rung is `L_min = ⌈log₂(h / 786)⌉`, because everything finer is sub-2-pixel and simply not requested. At
10 km altitude `L_min = 4` and the ingest collapses to `Σ_{L≥4} 1.284·v·2^(−L) = 0.16·v` columns/s —
**16× cheaper than the same speed at eye height.** The old §5.9 table read altitude as a 2,854×
multiplier; under the ladder altitude is a *discount*, and the genuinely expensive case is fast flight
at eye height, which is a hovering gunship, not a spacecraft.

**On the mesh cache: it is deleted from the design.** A content-keyed `Handle<Mesh>` cache (the
`bevy_voxel_world` pattern) does not work here. The emitted mesh depends on the 1-block apron — face
culling, the seam predicate, the warp's `min` combiner — so a rock chunk buried in rock and one with air
above hash identically under "the chunk's voxel array" and mesh completely differently. Once the key
includes the apron, the only byte-identical chunks are fully interior ones, which emit **zero quads**
and are therefore never worth meshing at any tier. (The draft justified that last clause with the
binary render rule; the rule is retracted but the clause survives on its own arithmetic — an
all-solid chunk emits nothing because every face is culled, not because a policy said so.) The cache
saves nothing, `mesh_key` is absent from the widened ABI, and no other decision in this section may
lean on it.

#### 5.1.4 The tier is a parameter of the same mesher — what changes, and what provably does not

This is the subsection Addendum 2 makes necessary, and its content is mostly a list of things that do
not change.

**Provably unchanged, because the mesher works in cell index space and never in metres:**

| | Why it is tier-invariant |
|---|---|
| The greedy sweep, the face-mask cull, the merge predicate | Operate on `u64` bit columns over a 62-cell axis. `62 + 2 = 64` holds at every rung (§3.3.6) |
| `border_peel`, `split_unit`, the ring emission order | Pure rectangle arithmetic on cell indices |
| The per-side coverage matrix, Lane A/Lane B assignment, `is_cube` | Properties of a shape, not of a scale |
| The three occupancy masks (`occ_ne`, `occ_solid`, `occ_ao`) and the face-emission table | Bit operations on the same 62³ lattice |
| The two-material reduction (`min` over `MaterialId`) | Total order on a `u16`; scale-free |
| The durable block record (its width is register row 2, not §5's), the chunk palette, `ChunkGeometry` | Cell indices, 18 bits, at every rung |
| **The chunk container is 62³ cells at every rung** | A per-tier chunk size would be exactly the HR3 fork §5.8 already refuses for shard kinds |
| The per-chunk mesher COST — 65 µs typical, 36.8 ms pathological | See below; this is the one people assume falls with tier and it does not |
| The exactness of the integer-modulo UV (§5.3.1) | A tier-`L` cell's tier-0 index is `index · 2^L`, an exact integer, so every modulo stays exact |
| The edit-echo budget (Budget 1) | An edit only ever re-meshes tier 0 on the editing client |

**What actually changes, and it is a short list:**

1. **The field the mesher is handed.** Tier `L`'s block field is the generator with its top `L` octaves
   dropped, overwritten wherever the edit pyramid has an entry. That is §3's work, not §5's; §5's
   requirement on it is one sentence, and it is load-bearing: **the apron must be read at the same tier
   as the chunk.** A tier-3 chunk aproned with tier-0 records would compute different face culls on its
   two sides of a chunk boundary and crack.
2. **`PrimTransform.scale = 2^L`.** The emitted positions stay in cell units; the metre size of a cell
   lives in the transform. This is why the vertex ABI needs no tier field beyond the `ChunkHeader` one
   it already reserves, and why the same encoder serves every rung.
3. **The sub-cell rule is evaluated**, weakening the seam blend (§5.5.4), the rim warp (§5.6.7) and the
   shader feature ladder (§5.4). All three are continuous weights from a tier-derived parameter.
4. **A skirt apron is emitted** (§5.9.4). About twenty lines, one loop over the chunk border, no case
   analysis, and — decisively — **no dependence on the neighbour's tier.**
5. **`detail_tier` in `ChunkHeader` stops being always-zero.** It becomes the per-draw uniform that
   drives the material feature ladder, which is the single highest-leverage consequence of the ruling
   for the shader (§5.4).

**The number that surprises people: per-chunk mesher cost is very nearly tier-invariant.** A chunk's
top surface is 62² = 3,844 cells at *every* rung, so a coarse chunk is not a cheaper chunk. Octave
dropping reduces slope roughly linearly in `L` (each fBm octave contributes an equal share of slope,
because amplitude and wavelength halve together), which trims side-face quads and improves greedy
merging — going from 8 octaves to 5 removes about 37 % of the slope — but it does not divide the quad
count by four. Two effects push the other way and are real: at tiers ≥ 1 the material-seam predicate
stops firing (§5.5.4) and at tiers ≥ 2 the warp predicate stops firing (§5.6.7), so **coarse chunks
peel less and merge better.** The honest summary is that a coarse chunk costs somewhat less than a
fine one and never four times less; **the ladder's saving is in chunk COUNT, not in per-chunk cost**,
and any budget that assumes otherwise is wrong. The cost estimator, the expensive queue and the
degenerate-content short-circuit of §5.1.3 are unchanged and still needed — a player can build a
3-D checkerboard at any tier's scale.

---

### 5.2 The vertex format and the `MeshPrim` widening

> **Register row 21 is DE-ESCALATED out of the blocking set (Addendum 2 §D.1), and the argument for it
> is rewritten rather than weakened.** ~~Addendum 1 §C.3: "the vertex format gates how big a planet can
> be — 2.1 GB packed versus 25.5 GB today for an Earth-sized surface".~~ That was arithmetic over a
> single-tier horizon that grew linearly with planet radius. Under the ladder the resident chunk count
> is a function of the *rung count*, not of the radius, so **no vertex format decides whether a planet
> exists.** What the format now decides is **upload bandwidth under motion**, which the ladder makes
> the tightest budget in the section (§5.2.3). The recommendation is unchanged; its justification, its
> trigger and its deadline are not.

`scripts/snowflow_technique_analysis.md` §3.3 flags this as due before the P4 mesher and is right that
P4 is the deadline. The crate comment on `MeshPrim` promises terrain will emit greedy quads "through
this SAME type with zero renderer change"; that promise is false as written. `MeshPrim` is
`{ vertices: Vec<Vertex{pos,normal}>, color_rgba, transform }` with no indices, no UVs, no material id,
and `PrimTransform { translation, scale }` has **no rotation** — so a rotating planet or a banking ship
cannot be drawn correctly *today*, independent of voxels.

#### 5.2.1 The three formats, with corrected arithmetic

Horizon arithmetic is §3.7's, and this section stops recomputing it: at R = 161,671 m the eye-height
horizon is **741 m**, **449** surface chunk-columns, **~900** surface chunks. The horizon disc is
1.73 M one-metre top faces; side faces from relief bring the culled count to ~2.6 M; greedy merging on
noisy terrain is measured at only 1.3× (0fps: 2,198 → 1,670), so the resident working set is
**~2.0 M quads, ~2,200 per chunk**.

| | V0 — today | V1 — position + packed u32 | V2 — vertex pulling |
|---|---|---|---|
| Layout | `pos: Float32x3`, `normal: Float32x3`, **non-indexed** (`mesh_from_prim` builds a `TriangleList`, `client-render/src/lib.rs:795`) | `pos: Float32x3` + one `Uint32`, indexed | 8 B per **quad** in a storage buffer, no vertex buffer |
| Bytes/quad | 6 × 24 = **144 B** | 4 × 16 + 6 × 4 = **88 B** | **8 B** |
| Ground horizon, 2.0 M quads | **288 MB** | **176 MB** | **16 MB** |
| Re-mesh, one high-relief chunk (~5,000 quads) | 720 KB | 440 KB | 40 KB |
| **One click at a chunk corner (8 chunks)** | **5.76 MB** | **3.52 MB** | **0.32 MB** |
| Bevy 0.18 reality | Works today | Works: `MeshVertexAttribute::new("Voxel", <large u64>, VertexFormat::Uint32)` + `Material::specialize` setting `descriptor.vertex.buffers` | Custom `SpecializedMeshPipeline` + `RenderCommand` tuple, hand-written prepass/shadow/deferred shaders, manual `Aabb` |
| GPU-driven path (bindless, MDI, two-phase occlusion culling — free since Bevy 0.16) | Free | **Free** | Lost; must be rebuilt |
| Shadows / prepass / TAA motion vectors | Free | Free | Hand-written |

(snowflow's committed 3.8 MB for the same click assumed 480 KB/chunk at 20k indexed 24-byte vertices;
the V1 figure of 3.52 MB is the same computation at 16 B/vertex with a measured quad count. They
agree.)

The decisive numbers are the *upload* rows, not the VRAM rows — and under the ladder that statement
gets stronger, not weaker. 288 MB versus 176 MB is not a real difference on an 8 GB card;
**5.76 MB versus 0.32 MB per click** is an 18× swing on the interactive loop the player feels, and it
becomes a per-frame swing the moment a mining beam or an explosion dirties chunks continuously — or,
now, the moment the player *moves* (§5.2.3). Against that, V2 costs the entire Bevy 0.16+ GPU-driven path — bindless,
multi-draw indirect, two-phase occlusion culling, prepass, shadow and motion vectors all consume
`Mesh::ATTRIBUTE_POSITION` — a permanent maintenance surface on a renderer that migrates every ~4
months (0.17 → 0.18 alone moved types into `bevy_material`, replaced `MaterialPlugin`'s
`prepass_enabled`/`shadows_enabled` with `Material` methods, split `MaterialDrawFunction` into per-phase
labels, required `label()` on hand-written `AsBindGroup` impls, and changed the meshlet asset format).

> **[USER DECISION 5-B] — the vertex format.** Reversible in principle, but only while
> `realm_scene.rs` is the sole producer.
>
> - **B1. V1 now, V2 declared as the endgame** *(recommended)*. 16 B/vertex with a real `POSITION`,
>   the whole Bevy pipeline free, and the `ChunkGeometry → GPU bytes` encoder as a single Tier-B
>   function so a later switch changes the encoder and the shaders — not the mesher, not `MeshPrim`'s
>   producers.
> - **B2. V2 immediately.** Best numbers, 18× better click upload, but it front-loads a custom render
>   pipeline before there is a planet to look at and it must be re-derived every Bevy release.
> - **B3. Stay on V0.** No work now; guarantees a second migration of every producer later.
>
> **Recommendation: B1, with a dated trigger the ladder supplies.** 3.52 MB worst-case click is
> acceptable at 8 MiB/frame with dirty-chunk coalescing, and P4 does not need V2. ~~"V2 becomes a
> measured decision once mining and combat exist"~~ is too vague now that the ingest arithmetic exists:
>
> **V2 must land before sustained flight over a long view ships — that is P8 (ships) at the latest, not
> P11.** The trigger is a measured one and it is §5.2.3's table: at V1, 528 m/s of low flight consumes
> **63 % of the entire 480 MB/s upload budget on terrain streaming alone**, leaving nothing for edits,
> decoration, entity meshes or a second player; at V2 the same flight is **5.7 %**. That is the number
> that decides it, and it is not a taste call — it is a budget breach with a date. **Still not a
> one-way door**: `ChunkGeometry → GPU bytes` stays a single Tier-B function, so the switch changes the
> encoder and the shaders, not the mesher and not `MeshPrim`'s producers.

#### 5.2.2 What the `MeshPrim` seam must widen to

`MeshPrim` and `Vertex` live in `crates/client/src/realm_scene.rs`, Tier-A at 100 % region+branch.
Today there is exactly **one** producer (`to_render_prims`, two shapes). After P4 terrain, P6 edits,
§4's shaped lane and P8 hulls there will be four or more plus their golden fixtures. Widening then is a
simultaneous migration of all of them — which is why this is **one atomic slice, now**.

```rust
/// Four build-time-bounded vertex ABIs. NOT a content kind — the renderer picks a pipeline from a
/// set of size 4 fixed at BUILD time (snowflow §3.5: the pipeline set is a function of the build,
/// never of the world).
pub enum VertexStream {
    /// The existing VU proxy path — arbitrary normals (UV spheres). Unchanged, byte-identical.
    Proxy  { verts: Vec<ProxyVertex> },   // { pos:[f32;3], normal:[f32;3] }             24 B
    /// Interior greedy quads: one material, unwarped, axis-aligned.
    Voxel  { verts: Vec<VoxelVertex> },   // { pos:[f32;3], packed:u32 }                 16 B
    /// Every peeled RING quad: material seams AND warped rim quads. 1×1 or 1×N.
    Detail { verts: Vec<DetailVertex> },  // { pos:[f32;3], packed:u32, aux:u32 }        20 B
    /// Lane B shaped templates — a real basis is required (§4.5.7).
    Shaped { verts: Vec<ShapedVertex> },  // { pos, packed:u32, normal_oct:u16, tan_oct:u16 } 20 B
}

pub struct MeshPrim {
    pub stream:     VertexStream,
    pub indices:    Vec<u32>,            // NEW — greedy quads are indexed: 4 verts, not 6
    pub transform:  PrimTransform,       // NEW field: rotation
    pub pass:       PassClass,           // NEW — Opaque | Cutout | Translucent (§5.7)
    pub chunk:      Option<ChunkHeader>, // NEW — per-draw voxel data
    pub color_rgba: [f32; 4],            // RETAINED, and MEANINGFUL ONLY on `Proxy`
}

pub struct PrimTransform {
    pub translation: [f32; 3],
    pub rotation:    [f32; 4],           // NEW — quaternion; owed regardless of voxels
    pub scale:       [f32; 3],
}

/// One row per resident chunk in a storage buffer. The draw reaches its row through
/// Bevy 0.18's `MeshTag(u32)` — the app-controlled per-instance u32 (§5.8).
pub struct ChunkHeader {
    pub origin_local: [i32; 3],  // chunk origin in REALM-LOCAL block coords — the UV phase key
    pub realm_salt:   u32,       // seed-derived; keeps the warp constant out of the source
    pub ao_slot:      u32,       // offset into the sparse occupancy slab (§5.8)
    pub biome:        u16,       // macro-variation layer index (§5.4)
    pub detail_tier:  u8,        // ~~RESERVED, always 0~~ → LIVE (Addendum 2). Cell size is 2^tier m;
                                 // this is THE per-draw uniform driving the material feature
                                 // ladder (§5.4) and the sub-cell rule. Never branched on.
    pub skirt_drop:   u16,       // NEW — border-skirt depth in the chunk's OWN cell units, 8.8
                                 // fixed point (max 255.996 cells, i.e. 255·2^tier m). Tier-relative
                                 // by construction, so it needs no rescaling. Value:
                                 // skirt_drop_cells = ceil(skirt_drop_m / 2^L), where
                                 // skirt_drop_m = (relief_max(column footprint, L+1) + A_max)
                                 //                · skirt_safety   (§5.9.4)
}
```

The 32-bit `packed` field:

| Bits | Field | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 0–2 | face axis (6 values) | Replaces `normal`; also selects the UV plane |
| 3–5 | tangent handedness + in-plane rotation | A full `[f32;4]` tangent is **not stored** — on an axis-aligned face it is derivable from the face axis plus a handedness bit at zero cost. Only `Shaped` needs a real basis and carries baked oct-encoded vectors |
| 6–17 | render material id (12 bits = 4,096) | Indexes both the texture-array layer and the material-parameter storage row |
| 18–20 | AO corner index | Used only by the merge-key AO fallback (§5.8) |
| 21–23 | cosmetic variant tag (8) | Hash-selected model/texture variant of a **cube** (§5.6.4). NOT `GeometryId` — that lives in the chunk palette (§4.1.1) and drives Lane B |
| 24–27 | reserved: material-id widening | Earmarked so the render id can grow to 16 bits and match §4's persisted `MaterialId` |
| 28–31 | reserved | `detail_tier` promotion, rim flag, spare |

The 32-bit `aux` field, present only on `Detail` vertices:

| Bits | Field | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 0–11 | second material id | The other side of the seam blend (§5.5) |
| 12–29 | unwarped cell index (18 bits, 238,328 < 2¹⁸) | Makes the AO lookup exact where the geometry moved (§5.8) — closes the one artefact a baked warp would otherwise introduce |
| 30–31 | reserved | |

**Note what is deliberately absent: UV.** §5.3 derives it in the vertex shader from
`chunk.origin_local + chunk-local position` at zero vertex bytes and full integer exactness. A
`Float32x2` UV would push V1 from 16 B to 24 B for nothing.

**Note what was removed from the draft.** `mesh_key: u64` (the cache saves nothing — §5.1.3) and
`uv_base: [u8;3]` (redundant with `origin_local`, and its LCM-16 form would have hard-coded a 16-cell
tile ceiling into the per-draw ABI — §5.3.1).

**On the HR5 cost of slice one.** Landing four arms with one real producer means the `Voxel`, `Detail`
and `Shaped` arms must be constructed and exercised by synthetic tests *on that slice*; the coverage
cost is paid immediately, not deferred. The mitigation that turns a cost into an asset: those synthetic
constructions **are** the golden fixtures the Tier-A mesher will later be asserted against, so they are
written once and used twice.

#### 5.2.3 The ingest budget — the number the ladder actually makes tight

Residency is now logarithmic in view distance. **Ingest is not.** It is proportional to speed, because
the ladder's column intake is `2.56·v` columns per second (§5.1.3) regardless of how far you can see.
That inverts which budget matters: the ladder made the VRAM question easy and the upload question hard.

Chunks per second uploaded at speed `v`: 3 vertical chunks per tier-0 column and 2 above, giving
`1.284·v × 3 + 1.276·v × 2 = 6.40·v` chunks/s. At the measured **2,200 quads per chunk** that is
193.6 KB/chunk at V1 (88 B/quad) and 17.6 KB/chunk at V2 (8 B/quad).

| Speed | Chunks/s | V1 upload | % of 480 MB/s | V2 upload | % of 480 MB/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Walking, 5 m/s | 32 | 6.2 MB/s | 1.3 % | 0.56 MB/s | 0.12 % |
| Ground vehicle, 30 m/s | 192 | 37 MB/s | 7.7 % | 3.4 MB/s | 0.70 % |
| Low flight, 100 m/s | 640 | 124 MB/s | **26 %** | 11 MB/s | 2.3 % |
| `v_max`, 528 m/s | 3,379 | **654 MB/s** | **136 % — breach** | 59 MB/s | 12 % |
| Sustainable ceiling at V1 (the budget's own answer) | 1,550 | 300 MB/s | 63 % | — | — |

Read the last two rows together: **at V1 the upload budget, not the CPU, becomes the flight-speed
limit somewhere around 240 m/s**, well below the 528 m/s the generator can sustain, and pushing to
528 m/s over-commits the whole 480 MB/s to terrain. At V2 the same flight is 12 %. That is the entire
case for V2, it is measurable before it hurts, and §5.10.3's `bench-upload` gate is where it gets
caught: **assert sustained terrain upload ≤ 50 % of `RenderAssetBytesPerFrame` at the declared
`v_max`.**

Two mitigations belong here rather than in the format choice, because they apply at either format:

1. **Coarse rungs upload once and are never re-uploaded.** A chunk crossing a tier boundary is a
   *different* chunk (different address), so there is no re-upload of the same data — the crossfade
   holds both resident, then drops one. Peak residency during a crossing is priced in §5.9.5.
2. **The 3-frame remesh floor of §5.10.5 generalises to a per-tier upload quota, and the priority runs
   coarse-first.** A coarse rung is the fallback that guarantees no hole, so it is never deferred; a
   *fine* rung may arrive a few frames late, because the coarser rung covering that direction is
   already resident and the crossfade band absorbs the difference. Deferring the fine rung degrades to
   "briefly blurrier"; deferring the coarse rung degrades to "briefly missing". This is the
   coarse-first rule (§5.1.3) paying for itself a second time.

---

### 5.3 Big textures across many blocks

The user's ask: *"apply BIGGER textures to BIGGER surfaces combined from multiple blocks."* Greedy
meshing hands it over almost free, because the merge predicate is face-equality — **a greedy quad
always carries exactly one material**, so it needs no per-quad 0..1 UV. Set the UV to the two in-plane
grid coordinates divided by the tile period and a 40-cell quad gets 10 tiles of a 4-cell texture,
continuously, with no seam anywhere inside it.

#### 5.3.1 World-space UV by exact integer modulo — and why floats disintegrate

`uv = worldpos / P` in the fragment shader is the obvious implementation and it is **wrong at this
planet's scale, at the planet's own surface**. f32 has a 24-bit mantissa, so
ULP(uv) = 2^(⌊log₂ uv⌋ − 23). With P = 4 cells and a 1024² texture (256 texels/cell):

| Distance from UV origin | ULP in texels |
|---|---|
| 1 km | 0.016 — fine |
| 10 km | 0.25 — marginal |
| **161.7 km (our own surface, realm-local)** | **≈ 4 texels — visibly swimming** |
| 1,000 km | 16 texels |
| 10,000 km | 256 texels — the texture is destroyed |

This is the *default* at the planet's own radius using the smallest possible coordinate. It is exactly
why Mikkelsen ships a separate `hextiling_rws.h` variant "to maintain fractional precision as we move
far away from the center of absolute world space".

**The fix costs nothing**, because 1-cell blocks plus a power-of-two tile period make the reduction
exact integer arithmetic:

- Lock the tile period `P` to a **power of two in cells** — `tile_period_cells: u8`, a per-material
  data field, never a constant even while every material shares a value.
- The vertex shader computes, per in-plane axis:
  `uv_axis = f32((chunk.origin_local[axis] & (P − 1)) + pos_local[axis]) * (1.0 / P)`.
- `x & (P − 1)` on a two's-complement `i32` **is** the Euclidean remainder for a power-of-two `P`
  (`(−9) & 7 = 7`), which is the behaviour we need — `%` would give `−1` and mirror the texture on
  negative coordinates. Exactness needs no separate `rem_euclid` call in the shader.
- The magnitude bound is `uv ≤ 1 + 62/P` — at most 16.5 for P = 4, and it **shrinks** as P grows, so
  there is no ceiling on `P` at all. ULP at 16.5 is 2⁻¹⁹ = 1.9 × 10⁻⁶ tiles = **0.002 texels**.
  Bit-exact for every purpose, at every altitude, for every tier.

This is a real CI gate, in the spirit of the seed-determinism gate: assert bit-identical UVs for the
same block at the realm origin and at 10⁹ m. **Extend it by one row for the ladder:** the same physical
point sampled at tier 0 and at tier 5 must produce bit-identical *macro* UVs (see below), because a
tier-`L` cell's tier-0 index is exactly `index · 2^L` and the shift is exact in `i32`.

**Two UV frames, and the ladder needs both — this is the one genuinely new rule in §5.3.**

| | Period measured in | World-space period at tier `L` | Screen-space period | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Detail tile** (albedo/normal/ORMH) | **cells of the chunk's own tier** | `P · 2^L` metres | **constant, ~2·P pixels** | The tile must stretch with the cell or it turns into its own average at every rung ≥ 1. Keeping it cell-relative keeps texel density per screen pixel constant across the whole ladder |
| **Macro variation** (§5.4) | **metres, world-locked, power of two** | fixed | grows with `L` | It must not slide when a chunk changes rung, or a whole hillside would appear to shift colour at a tier boundary. Instead it is an *octave stack*: at tier `L` the shader samples the two octaves whose metre periods are `64·2^L` and `1024·2^L` |

Both are exact integer reductions. The detail tile uses the chunk's own cell index; the macro layer
uses `index · 2^L`, the tier-0 index, which is a left shift and therefore exact. Neither ever calls
`fract()` (§5.3.2), and neither has a ceiling on `P`.

**The residual difference between two rungs is the crossfade's job, and there is exactly one
crossfade.** At a tier boundary the two rungs disagree about the terrain height (dropped octaves),
about the detail tile's world period (2×), about which macro octaves are sampled, about the seam blend
(§5.5.4) and about the warp (§5.6.7). All five differences are hidden by the *same* dither band of
§5.9.5. Stating that once is what stops five separate anti-pop mechanisms from being invented, each
with its own tuning field and its own failure mode.

**Two unit corrections the draft got wrong.** (i) The period is in **cells**, not metres: on a
cube-sphere a cell is 1.000 m only at the six face centres and 0.709 m at the eight cube corners
(§3.3.2), so "256 texels/m" is a nominal density that ranges 256–361 texels/m across a face. The field
name must say `cells` because the material registry is what the art pipeline reads. (ii) The in-plane
axes are the cube face's integer (u, v) grid axes, so the tile follows the block grid and distorts
exactly as the blocks do — which is what you want.

**Tile phase is continuous across a cube-face seam** because N = 62 · 2¹² = 253,952 = 2¹³ · 31 is
divisible by every power of two up to 8192, so `N mod P == 0` for every plausible `P`. Tile
**orientation** is not: crossing a cube edge swaps and may flip the axis pair, so the tile rotates 90°
along the 12 cube-edge lines. For stochastic natural materials that is invisible, and it lands where
cube-sphere distortion is already maximal. It **is** visible on structured materials — one more reason
structured materials belong on constructions, not on natural terrain (§5.4).

#### 5.3.2 The no-`fract()` rule

**Never call `fract()` on a UV in the fragment shader.** It makes `ddx`/`ddy` discontinuous across the
wrap line, the GPU picks the coarsest mip, and you get grey bands between every tile. That is the
canonical reason texture *atlases* fail for tiled multi-block textures: the atlas workaround is a
4-tap 2×2 pattern plus per-tile periodic mipmap generation, costing 4× the taps and up to 2× the
memory — and 4× would stack on top of every other multiplier in §5.4. With integer-reduced UVs and
array storage there is nothing to wrap manually; `AddressMode::Repeat` does it in hardware, correctly,
with correct mips.

**And mips are now mandatory rather than contested.** ~~"A literal Option-A reading of the no-LOD rule
bans mipmapping, which would make the entire §5.3 design unshippable" (old §5.9).~~ Addendum 2 §C.8
settles it: mipmaps are explicitly permitted and explicitly required. The full statement, so nothing is
left implicit: **every layer of every array ships with a complete mip chain, generated offline into
KTX2, trilinear-filtered, with 16× anisotropy.** Runtime mip generation is banned — it is a
render-target pass per layer at load, which is the spin-up stutter the seamless law forbids, and it
would produce a *different* chain from the bake tool's, which §5.3.7 shows is not merely a quality
question but a correctness one.

#### 5.3.3 Storage: one `texture_2d_array`, the 256-layer myth, and the refusal rule

`max_texture_array_layers = 256` is wgpu's **guaranteed minimum in the default limit set, not a device
cap** — "Limits 'better' than the default must be supported by the adapter and requested when
requesting a device." The Vulkan hardware database (Windows) reports `maxImageArrayLayers`:
**2048 on 19,179 devices, 8192 on 1,201, 4096 on 4, 1024 on 1, and 256 on zero.**

**Rule:** request 1,024 layers at device creation. If the adapter cannot supply them, the client
**refuses to start with a named error**. There is no LRU layer-residency fallback: it is a
texture-streaming subsystem with its own hitching, built for a device class that does not exist on the
target platforms (WebGL2's 256 is not a target; Metal reports 2048). Deleting that fallback is a
strict simplification of the draft.

Do **not** go bindless. Bevy's `AUTO` bindless slab limit is **64 on macOS/iOS versus 2048 elsewhere**
— a 32× gap that would make the development machine exercise a materially different code path from the
shipping target — and `PARTIALLY_BOUND_BINDING_ARRAY` is Vulkan/DX12 only.

**The palette numbers, stated once so they stop diverging:** 65,536 representable (§4's persisted
`u16 MaterialId`) → 4,096 addressable in the vertex ABI (12 bits, +4 reserved) → **1,024 renderable
layers** (the universal hardware floor, and the bake-time assertion `renderable_material_count ≤ 1024`)
→ **128 shipped at launch** (§5.3.6's VRAM cap).

**The resident texture set is tier-invariant, and that fact does most of the work in §5.3.8.** The
array holds every material the game ships, always, whether the player is looking at a 786 m disc or a
100 km panorama. The ladder adds **zero bytes** to it — a coarse chunk indexes the same layers as a
fine one. So the one property a virtual-texturing system exists to buy, namely resident texture memory
that does not grow with what you can see, this design already has for free, because its materials tile.

#### 5.3.4 The one material — three arrays, and where height and emission live

`StandardMaterial` has **no `Texture2dArray` support** — Bevy issue #20134, open since 2025-07-14,
`S-Needs-Design`, no assignee, filed for exactly this voxel use case. A custom material is mandatory,
and "custom" means **extension, not replacement**:

```rust
#[derive(Asset, TypePath, AsBindGroup, Clone)]
pub struct VoxelSurface {
    // layer index = render material id.  ALL THREE ARRAYS SHARE ONE LAYER INDEX.
    #[texture(100, dimension = "2d_array")] #[sampler(101)] albedo_e: Handle<Image>, // BC7 RGB=albedo, A=emissive mask
    #[texture(102, dimension = "2d_array")] #[sampler(103)] normal:   Handle<Image>, // BC5 RG
    #[texture(104, dimension = "2d_array")] #[sampler(105)] ormh:     Handle<Image>, // BC7 R=AO G=rough B=metal A=height
    #[texture(106, dimension = "2d_array")] #[sampler(107)] macro_v:  Handle<Image>, // BC1, one layer per biome (§5.4)
    #[storage(108, read_only)] materials: Handle<ShaderStorageBuffer>, // per-material rows
    #[storage(109, read_only)] chunks:    Handle<ShaderStorageBuffer>, // ChunkHeader rows
    #[storage(110, read_only)] occupancy: Handle<ShaderStorageBuffer>, // sparse AO slab (§5.8)
}
// type TerrainMaterial = ExtendedMaterial<StandardMaterial, VoxelSurface>;
```

**Three PBR arrays, not four.** The first draft declared a separate `height` array and then omitted it
from the VRAM table — a 17 % error in the one table the user is told is a re-do rather than a refactor.
The fix is a design change, not an arithmetic one: **height goes in the ORM array's alpha channel.** BC7
encodes alpha with separate endpoints from RGB, so a packed ORMH block does not suffer the
cross-channel correlation artefacts that packing four correlated channels into RGB would. This keeps
the per-material cost at exactly **4.00 MiB at 1024²** and keeps 3 taps per material. *Contingency, to
be settled by a bake-time PSNR check on the shipped set:* if BC7 alpha proves inadequate for parallax
heights, a separate BC4 height array costs +0.667 MiB/material (4.667 MiB, 583 MiB at 128 materials).

**Emission has a home and costs nothing.** The albedo array's alpha is an emissive **mask**; the
material row carries `emissive_rgb: [f16;3]` and `emissive_nits: f16`. A glowing block, a thruster
plume face and a lit sign are all one material row, zero extra taps, zero extra arrays. For blocks that
must *illuminate* rather than merely glow, the client spawns a real clustered point light per
light-emitting block, budgeted at **≤ 128 within the draw radius**, chosen by distance — Bevy 0.18's
clustered forward handles this without a second material path.

`ExtendedMaterial<StandardMaterial, E>` with `#import bevy_pbr::pbr_fragment` in the fragment override
inherits shadows, clustered lights, fog and atmosphere free; extension bindings live at 100+
(`StandardMaterial` occupies 0..30). This is **exactly one material type for every voxel surface in the
game** — planet crust, ship hull, station deck. A per-content material type is a kind-branch in the
renderer, which the agnostic-client law forbids, and every extra `MaterialPlugin` is a distinct
pipeline family and warm-up set. All variation is data fetched by index.

> **Named risk, and the one prototype that must run before the vertex ABI is frozen.**
> `StandardMaterial` is declared `#[bindless(index_table(range(0..31)))]`. Whether extending a bindless
> base forces, disables or breaks bindless for the extension — and whether extension **storage buffers**
> survive it (there is a known Bevy issue class here, bevyengine/bevy#18853) — decides whether the
> block above is implementable as written. **The spike:** one `ExtendedMaterial` with one storage
> buffer and one `MeshTag`, drawing two chunks with different `ao_slot`s, on Vulkan and Metal.
> **The named fallback if it fails:** a standalone `Material` that `#import`s `bevy_pbr::pbr_functions`
> and reimplements the fragment, at the cost of a re-merge every Bevy release. Ledger it (§5.10).

#### 5.3.5 Triplanar: where it is genuinely needed (almost nowhere)

Triplanar is three fetches per map blended by `pow(abs(n), k)`. It exists because smooth voxel surfaces
have arbitrary normals and no UVs. **A 1-cell blocky world's faces are axis-aligned by construction** —
the normal is one of six values, *known at mesh time* — so a single planar projection is exact, with
zero blending and zero per-pixel branching. Skipping triplanar is a flat **3× saving on every texture
tap in the frame** and it is the single largest performance decision in this section.

For Lane B shaped blocks the normals are not axis-aligned — but the shape palette is **finite and known**,
so the projection axis and its blend weights are baked into `ShapeDef.render` at authoring time and ride
the quad in the `Shaped` stream's oct-encoded normal and tangent (§4.5.7). That gives biplanar's quality
at zero ALU, with implicit derivatives, and without `textureGrad` (which biplanar requires because its
axis selection is discontinuous, and which disables the hardware's cheap derivative path).

**Rule, written into the material contract: the fragment shader never selects a projection axis.** The
cost of the exception is 4 B/vertex on the `Shaped` stream, which is under 5 % of vertices on terrain
and bounded by shape density on hulls.

#### 5.3.6 Tile period, authored resolution, and the total VRAM budget

> **[USER DECISION 5-C] — tile period and authored resolution, as a locked pair.** Fixed **before any
> material is authored**. This is the highest-cost reversal in the section: re-authoring hundreds of
> materials at a different period is not a refactor, it is a re-do. **ONE-WAY DOOR.**
>
> | Pair | Texel density | Per material (BC7 albedo+E, BC5 normal, BC7 ORMH, with mips) | 128 materials | 256 materials |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | 4 cells @ 512² | 128 texels/cell | 1.00 MiB | 128 MiB | 256 MiB |
> | **4 cells @ 1024²** | **256 texels/cell** | **4.00 MiB** | **512 MiB** | 1,024 MiB |
> | 8 cells @ 2048² | 256 texels/cell | 16.00 MiB | 2,048 MiB | 4,096 MiB |
> | 4 cells @ 2048² | 512 texels/cell (hero) | 16.00 MiB | 2,048 MiB | 4,096 MiB — not shippable |
>
> **Recommendation: 4 cells @ 1024², with a hard cap of 128 materials (512 MiB) in the shipping set.**
> 256 texels/cell is normal AAA environment density. 2-cell tiles read as almost-per-block and lose the
> multi-block effect that motivates the exercise; 16-cell @ 1024² drops to 64 texels/cell, visibly soft
> at walking distance.
>
> The per-material `tile_period_cells` field then makes 8 or 16 cells a **free** per-material choice
> *within the same array* — the same 1024² layer over 8 cells is 128 texels/cell, which large rock faces
> carry fine. **A `texture_2d_array` requires uniform layer dimensions**, so a 2048² hero pair is not a
> per-material field — it is a *second array trio* and a second set of sampler bindings. If hero
> materials are wanted, budget ≤ 16 (256 MiB) and decide the two-array addressing now, because layer
> addressing propagates into the packed vertex, the material registry and every shader.
>
> **Why 4 cells is enough for the "bigger textures on bigger surfaces" ask:** a 4-cell tile already spans
> 16 block faces on a flat top surface, and the *perceived* period is set by the macro-variation layer
> at 64 and 1,024 cells (§5.4), not by the detail tile. Enlarging the detail tile instead trades texel
> density for the effect and reads soft at walking distance.
>
> **The paired question, already open as snowflow §7.8:** are we willing to **ship authored texture
> data** (CC0 PBR scans, BC-compressed, vendored with licences, through the KTX2/zstd path Bevy's
> default features already include), or must every texel be synthesised from seed on the client? Fully
> procedural is stronger for thousands of planets but moves real GPU cost to realm spin-up — exactly
> where the seamless law says we must not stutter. **Recommendation: ship authored data**; variety comes
> from the seed-selected macro layer and per-block hash variation, not from synthesising the detail tile.

**Total client VRAM, re-summed for the ladder.** The draft's single column assumed one rung and a
741 m horizon; that column is kept as the "on foot" case and two more are added. Chunk counts are
Addendum 2 §C.3's: tier 0 holds 505 columns × 3 vertical chunks = 1,515; each rung above holds
379 × 2 = 758; eight rungs total **6,821 chunks**. Quads per chunk is this section's measured 2,200,
not Addendum 2's implied ~5,000 (see §5.9.4 for the reconciliation).

| Item | On foot, tier 0 only (786 m) | Full 8-rung ladder (100 km), **V1** | Full ladder, **V2** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Terrain vertices + indices (×1.5 headroom at tier 0, ×1.2 above — coarse rungs have less relief) | 420 MiB | **1,595 MiB** | 147 MiB |
| Material arrays, 128 × 4.00 MiB — **tier-invariant** | 512 | 512 | 512 |
| Macro-variation layers, 32 biomes × 256² BC1 + mips (one layer, many periods — the octave stack costs nothing extra) | 1.4 | 1.4 | 1.4 |
| Occupancy slabs (AO), **tiers 0–1 only** (§5.8), 2,273 chunks, sparse | ≤ 71 | ≤ 71 | ≤ 71 |
| Decoration (§6's measured total) | 39 | 39 | 39 |
| Render targets at 1080p (HDR, depth, prepass normal+motion, 4-cascade shadow atlas) | ~200 | ~200 | ~200 |
| Bevy residency, entity meshes, MSDF atlas, misc | ~200 | ~200 | ~200 |
| **Total** | **≈ 1,443 MiB (1.41 GiB)** | **≈ 2,618 MiB (2.56 GiB)** | **≈ 1,170 MiB (1.14 GiB)** |

Three readings, all of them load-bearing:

1. **The material budget did not move.** 512 MiB covers a 786 m view and a 100 km view identically.
   That is the argument of §5.3.8 in one row.
2. **V1 fits the 3.0 GiB cap at a 100 km view with about 0.44 GiB to spare — at 1080p.** It does not
   fit at 4K (render targets roughly quadruple, +600 MiB), and it does not fit alongside a 2048² hero
   array (+256 MiB). So V1 is not merely a bandwidth compromise; it is also what makes 4K a *format*
   decision. V2 leaves 1.86 GiB spare and both fit.
3. **The AO line moved from ≤ 29 to ≤ 71 MiB**, and only because §5.8 rules the occupancy slab a
   tiers-0-and-1 resource. Uploading it for all eight rungs would be 6,821 × 32 KiB = 213 MiB for
   contact shading on 128-metre cells, which is not a thing worth shading.

Against a 3.0 GiB self-imposed cap on an 8 GB card. **The VRAM budget is now genuinely tight at V1 and
comfortable at V2; the upload budget (§5.2.3) is tight at V1 and comfortable at V2.** Both point the
same way, which is why §5-B's trigger is dated rather than open.

#### 5.3.7 Texture level of detail — and the correctness bug this design never named

Mipmaps are mandatory (§5.3.2). What nobody wrote down is that **shipping a mip chain is not the same
as shipping a correct one**, and the incorrect version has a visible, specific failure: distant terrain
sparkles under a moving sun.

**The mechanism.** Mipmapping a normal map preserves the *mean* normal and destroys its *variance*. A
mip-4 texel holds the average of 256 normals that pointed in 256 directions; the surface it describes
is rough, but the fetched normal describes a surface that is flat. The lost variance has to reappear
somewhere, and the only place it can go is roughness. If it does not, the specular lobe at that mip
stays too tight, and every sub-texel bump that used to average into a broad highlight becomes a
one-pixel firefly that flickers as the sun, the camera or the ship moves. This is not a subtle
quality issue at our scale: at tier 5 a 4-cell detail tile spans about 8 screen pixels, so the GPU
selects mip 6–7 of a 1024² map — an 8×8-to-16×16 average — and **the entire normal detail of a 128 m
chunk lives inside one pixel.**

**Why the usual fix is impossible here, which is the part that makes this a design decision rather
than a shader task.** The classical correction is the Toksvig factor, computed from the *length* of
the averaged normal — and that is exactly what §5.3.4's locked **BC5 two-channel normal format cannot
supply.** We store RG and reconstruct `z = sqrt(1 − x² − y²)`, so every fetched normal is unit length
by construction and `|avg(n)|` is unrecoverable at runtime. The incompatibility is documented, not
inferred. Reverting to three-channel normals to enable the runtime version would cost +0.667 MiB per
material (+85 MiB at 128) and buy nothing the bake does not.

**The ruling: variance goes into the roughness mip chain at BAKE time.** Written as a spec because it
changes the asset pipeline, not the renderer:

```
for each material, for each mip level m > 0:
    r_m(x) = | mean of the UN-normalised three-channel source normals in x's footprint |   # pre-BC5
    s      = 2/α² − 2                       # Blinn power from the authored GGX roughness α
    s'_m   = r_m · s / (r_m + s·(1 − r_m))  # Toksvig
    α'_m   = sqrt(2 / (s'_m + 2))           # back to GGX roughness, monotonically ≥ α
    ORMH.g at mip m := α'_m                 # THEN BC7-compress the ORMH chain
```

- **Box-filtering the roughness map — the default in every texture tool — is a defect**, not a
  simplification. The bake tool must be incapable of emitting a roughness chain that was not produced
  this way: a flag in the KTX2 key/value metadata, checked at load, refusing the material by name.
- **Cost: zero runtime, zero memory, one bake-tool step.** The Order: 1886 shipped exactly this
  (baked Toksvig into roughness, plus temporal AA).
- **ONE-WAY DOOR, and it is the same door as USER DECISION 5-C.** Materials baked without it must be
  re-baked; if the shipped set has been authored by then, that is a re-do rather than a refactor. This
  must be fixed **before the first material is authored**, which is why it appears here as a locked
  rule and not as a decision — there is no defensible alternative to pick between.

**The runtime half, which is separate and also mandatory: geometric specular anti-aliasing.** The bake
handles sub-*texel* normal detail. It does nothing for sub-*pixel* **geometric** detail, and §5.6
deliberately manufactures an entire planet's worth of that: the rim warp puts a high-frequency
displaced normal on every exposed block edge in the world, and the ladder means those edges are viewed
at every scale from 1 m to 100 km. The answer is Tokuyoshi & Kaplanyan 2019 (the projected
half-vector formulation), which filters the microfacet distribution using screen-space derivatives of
the half vector. **~10 ALU and two derivative pairs per pixel, no memory, no bake, no asset change.**
Take the 2019 variant rather than the 2016 original specifically because it removes the large errors
the original produced at grazing angles and near edges — and on a sphere, every horizon pixel is a
grazing-angle pixel, permanently.

**The gate (§5.10.3, slice 3).** A `vdctl` scenario that parks the camera on a distant slope, sweeps
the sun through 90°, and asserts the frame-to-frame luminance variance in a fixed screen region stays
under a threshold. It fails loudly with box-filtered roughness and passes with the bake above, which
is what makes it worth writing.

#### 5.3.8 Virtual texturing versus a cached material bake — the ruling, with the arithmetic

Three distinct things get called "virtual texturing". Each gets its own verdict.

**(a) Hardware sparse / partially-resident textures — UNAVAILABLE, and this is not a cost question.**
`wgpu` 27.0.1 exposes no sparse, tiled or partially-resident texture feature of any kind: a grep of the
vendored `wgpu-types-27.0.1/src/features.rs` for `sparse|partially_resident|tiled_resources` returns
zero hits, and no such flag appears in the published `Features` list. WebGPU's own investigation
(gpuweb#455) is parked at "Milestone 4+" with no assignee, because WebGPU lacks the heap abstraction
two of the three backends need, Vulkan exposes nine separate sparse-residency capability flags, and
Metal forbids tile sharing across resources. The consequence closes a whole family: PLAYERUNKNOWN
Productions' Melba engine gets its 70–80 % texture-memory reduction from DX12 *reserved resources*
plus *sampler feedback* in `MIN_MIP` mode with 64 KiB tiles, and **neither primitive exists on our
stack.**

**(b) Software / megatexture virtual texturing — REJECTED, because we have no unique texels.** The
sizing first, so the rejection is not hand-waved: at 1920×1080 = 2.07 Mpx, with 4× slack for mip
transitions, overdraw and anisotropy, the working set is ~8.3 M texels ≈ a 2,896² atlas, so a 4096²
BC7 physical cache is 16 MiB per map and **48 MiB for the albedo/normal/ORMH trio** — against 512 MiB,
an apparent 10.7× win. It is not the same product. VT's headline property is resident memory that is
`O(screen pixels)` instead of `O(unique world texels)`, and **our unique-world-texel count is zero**:
§5.3.1 derives UV by exact integer modulo of a 4-cell period, and all variation comes from the macro
octaves and the per-block hash, not from authored uniqueness. Our 512 MiB array is *already* the
complete resident set for an Earth-sized planet at any view distance, and the ladder adds nothing to
it (§5.3.3). So VT would spend a subsystem to replace a constant with a smaller constant, and the
subsystem is not small: an indirection texture, a physical page atlas, a reduced-resolution feedback
render target, a GPU→CPU readback loop with 2–3 frames of latency, hand-rolled mip selection from
screen-space derivatives, ≥ 4-texel page borders for BC block alignment (more for anisotropy) and a
custom eviction policy — several thousand lines of Tier-B code on a renderer that migrates every ~4
months. It also **deletes hardware `AddressMode::Repeat`** (page borders break wrapping — the exact
atlas failure §5.3.2 already rejected on its own merits) and degrades anisotropic filtering across
page seams. **Not a one-way door in either direction**; if we ever ship genuinely unique per-planet
texels the premise changes and the question reopens.

**(c) An RVT-style cached material bake per terrain tile — TAKE LATER, with a measured trigger.** This
is the cheaper 80 % idea and it deserves an honest number rather than a dismissal. Unreal's Runtime
Virtual Texture caches *shading results* over large areas into an LRU page pool (tiles up to 1,024
texels; YCoCg encoding costs +25 % memory), and it pays there because a Landscape material stack with
decals and splines is expensive to composite and is re-read across many frames. Ours is cheap: 3 taps
per material (albedo+E, normal, ORMH), 6 at a seam where §5.5 blends two, plus 2 macro taps — **about
8 taps on the worst ordinary terrain pixel.** An RVT bake collapses steady state to 3 taps + 1
indirection = 4. Saving ~4 taps over the ~1.45 M terrain pixels of a 1080p frame is 5.8 M fetches per
frame, i.e. roughly **0.03–0.06 ms** on a 100–200 Gtexel/s GPU. Below noise.

Two further arguments against building it now, both specific to us:

- **A cache pays only when re-reads greatly exceed re-bakes**, and every block edit invalidates the
  tiles it touches. §5.10.5's sustained-edit regime — a mining beam, an explosion — is precisely where
  such a cache thrashes. Our edit rate is what makes an RVT cache pay *less* here than it does for
  Unreal, which is the opposite of the usual intuition.
- **The ladder reduces the case for it further.** §5.4's feature ladder already drops the composite to
  ~2 taps at tiers ≥ 5, and in a long view most pixels are at coarse tiers. RVT would be caching the
  cheap pixels.

> **Trigger to revisit, stated so it can be checked rather than argued:** terrain fragment tap count
> sustained above ~16, or a GPU profile showing the terrain composite above ~1 ms. The things that
> would push it there are known — edit stains, wetness and thermal overlays, block-cover projections
> (§6.7) and dense decals. Reserve cost today: **nothing.** Ledgered as **D-R9**.

#### 5.3.9 What Crimson Desert's "texture mapping" actually is — and what of it survives here

The owner singled this out, so it is worth separating what Pearl Abyss has *said* from what has been
*measured* from what has been *invented about them*, because the last category is large.

**What is traceable to Pearl Abyss staff is three phrases and no numbers**, all from a closed-door
GDC 2025 session: *"we use something called proxy LODs to optimize distance rendering"*, *"the seamless
rendering uses hierarchical level subdivision for distance rendering"*, and — separately — *"by
incorporating the shape variation feature … it is possible to place trees of various shapes with simple
manipulation"*. Their own press release and their "Dev Archives: BlackSpace Engine" notice contain
**zero** statements about LOD, impostors, proxies, streaming, terrain or textures; there is no GDC
Vault talk, no SIGGRAPH/NDC paper and no engineering blog. **Treat the lineage as undocumented at the
technical level, and discard any article that describes their terrain algorithm — it is fabricating.**
In particular, nothing external validates or contradicts §5.9.4's skirts choice or §5.9.5's dither
crossfade; both stand on their own reasoning.

**On textures specifically, there is no evidence of virtual texturing, sparse residency or a
megatexture — and two things that ARE primary.** Patch 1.03.00 added a user-facing *"Displacement
Scale"* option and a *"Detail Decorative Mesh"* option. Community reverse-engineering identifies the
first as **screen-space displacement mapping**, and it was split into its own toggle because it made
the image *"really blurry when using DLSS, especially on balanced or performance"* — the documented
failure mode of a screen-space post-process at reduced internal resolution. The second adds *"moss,
short grass, and small pebbles to terrain, walls and objects"*, which is derived decoration (§6), not
texturing.

So **the "amazingly detailed texture mapping" is high texel density plus parallax relief, not a
residency system.** That validates two choices already made here — §5.3.6's 256 texels/cell and §5.4's
per-material fragment-shader POM on the ORMH height — and supplies two concrete additions:

1. **POM with silhouette refinement is what sells it**: clip where the displacement overshoots the mesh
   boundary, and march a second short ray along the light direction for self-shadowing. In a 1 m blocky
   world the silhouette case *is* the block edge, so this is worth evaluating as a **per-pixel
   complement** to §5.6's geometric edge rather than a competitor to it. It does not and cannot replace
   the warp — POM leaves the rasterised triangle's edge against the sky unchanged (§5.6.5) — but it
   sharpens the edge against the surface *behind* it. Cost: one `discard` plus roughly double the march
   for edge pixels, tier-0 only since POM is already dropped at 20 m.
2. **Ship the displacement scale as a user-facing slider from day one**, as a field in the render
   tuning struct with a settings entry — never a shader constant. They had to retrofit exactly that in
   a patch.

**The cautionary number, and it is the most useful thing in the whole study.** Their texture budget is
player-measured at ~7.7–8 GB and it is the direct cause of their most-criticised flaw: players
attribute *"very aggressive LODs for environmental details"* to an 8 GB target, raising Model Quality
to Cinematic paradoxically *worsens* pop-in for some, DSOGaming reports *"severe pop-in problems"*
including shadows and lights appearing abruptly, and distant castles are described as *"voxel-based
blobs"*. The GDC narrative ("I could not tell the difference") does not survive the retail build: the
far field is genuinely excellent, the near-field clutter and the mid-distance *structure* proxies are
visibly cut. Two lessons land directly:

- **Enforce a memory cap by adapting the target with hysteresis, not by picking a uniformly aggressive
  fixed ladder.** That is §5.9.6's residency governor and it exists because of this evidence.
- **"Distant structures read as blobs" is the exact failure mode our pure-pyramid path for
  player-built geometry will hit by default**, because a coarse cell rendered as solid-or-empty keeps
  mass and loses form. The fix is §3/§4's to make and §5 only consumes it, and it is now ruled
  (register row 37): the pyramid entry carries an **octant mask and a mean fill** — ~~"a solid *count*"
  is struck, because a count thresholded to a boolean is precisely what produces the documented blobs~~
  — and the drawn geometry is `COARSE_SHAPE[occ_mask][bucket]` over §4's existing catalogue, where
  `bucket = (fill_256 · 9) >> 8`. Zero extra stored bytes, one small deterministic table, **no fill
  threshold anywhere on this path**, and it must live in Tier-A and be folded into `BlockRegistryHash`
  because server and client must agree byte-for-byte — a mismatch is a refused connection, not a
  silently wrong distant silhouette.

**One calibration that reorders our own risk register.** Digital Foundry confirms per-pixel ray-traced
diffuse global illumination across a ~200 km² open world on base PS5, and DSOGaming measures the PC RT
cost at 3–4 fps with a barely-stressed 7950X3D. Their frame goes to crowds, battles and
**streaming-heavy transitions** — not to lighting. So §5's lighting ambitions are not what will sink
the frame; **residency and upload under motion are**, which is exactly where §5.2.3 and §5.9 spend the
