engineering, and it argues for spending the next benchmark slot on chunk upload under motion rather
than on shading.

**Explicitly not taken from them**, each for a structural reason rather than a taste one: baked HLOD
merged region proxies (their world is authored and static; one player edit invalidates a merge —
§5.9.7); baked impostor atlases for terrain, structures or ships (you cannot bake an atlas of a base
the player finished thirty seconds ago, and doing it at runtime is a render-to-texture stall in the
exact moment the seamless law forbids one); authored occluder/visibility volumes (a player can dig
through the ridge that was the occluder); and SpeedTree-style hand-authored vegetation (§6 derives
vegetation from the block field by rule). The one cheap idea that *does* transfer — **shape variation**,
one authored prop procedurally varied per instance — belongs to §6, and our version must be
hash-derived rather than "real time random" so it is identical on every client, which costs nothing
because the instance already carries a cell-derived seed.

---

### 5.4 Anti-repetition on huge surfaces

A 4-cell tile across a 741 m horizon repeats ~185 times in each direction. In strict cost order:

**Layer 1 — macro variation (2 taps, cache-resident).** Decided, because the draft left it as
"per-planet or per-biome … produced how, never stated", and both loose readings break a rule (a unique
per-planet map is 94.5 Mtexels and must be generated at spin-up — the stutter the seamless law forbids;
an in-shader float-noise map reintroduces the transcendental determinism hazard §3.5.4 exists to
remove). **The decision: the macro layer is a shipped, authored `texture_2d_array` of ≤ 32 biome
archetype layers at 256² BC1 (1.4 MiB total), indexed by `ChunkHeader.biome`, sampled at TWO periods
from the same layer and multiplied over the *blended* albedo.**

~~The two periods are 64 cells and 1,024 cells.~~ **Amended for the ladder (§5.3.1): the periods are
world-locked and expressed in METRES on a power-of-two octave stack, and the tier selects which two
octaves are sampled — `64·2^L` m and `1024·2^L` m at tier `L`.** Cell-relative periods would slide
whenever a chunk changed rung, so a whole hillside would appear to shift colour at a tier boundary;
metre-locked octaves keep the *function* identical at every rung and let the crossfade absorb the
octave change like every other rung-to-rung difference. At tier 0 the behaviour is exactly as before —
64 m and 1,024 m — so nothing about the P4 look changes; at tier 5 the same two taps supply 2 km and
32 km variation, which is the scale that reads at 25 km. **Still two taps per pixel at every rung**,
regardless of how many materials are blended, because it is applied *after* the blend, and still
1.4 MiB total because an octave stack is a sampling rule, not a second asset. Frostbite shipped the
same idea (a unique low-res colour map plus 3–6 tiled detail maps plus a macro detail map); Space
Engineers 2 ships three texture sets per voxel material transitioning by distance.

**Layer 2 — per-block hash variation (0 taps).** Perturb albedo tint, roughness and a wear scalar by
`SplitMix64` of the **realm-local integer block coordinate** — the same key as the warp (§5.6) and the
same key snowflow §4.2 identified for the glint hash. Exactly-integer, bit-stable across frames and
re-homes, identical on every client. The 1-cell grid is a natural variation unit and the coordinate is
already in the shader.

**Layer 3 — hex-tiling, per-material opt-in (3× per map).** Mikkelsen's *Practical Real-Time
Hex-Tiling* (JCGT 11(2), 2022): 3 `SampleGrad` per map on the original texture, no precomputation, no
transform textures, per-tile random rotation. Weights are barycentric ω on a simplex lattice,
exponentiated ω^γ (γ = 7), modulated by a significance metric (β = 0.6) and renormalised; a Perlin
S-curve restores contrast for colour with r ∈ [0.65, 0.75], and r = 0.5 (ramp off) for normal maps.
**Normal maps must be blended as partial derivatives, not as normals.** `SampleGrad` is mandatory
because of the per-tile random offset.

**Tap budget — corrected, complete, and internally consistent** (3 maps per material, axis-aligned
projection ×1 per §5.3.5, macro counted once per pixel):

| Configuration | Detail | Macro | POM | **Total** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 material, plain | 3 | 2 | — | **5** |
| 2 materials on a ring quad, height-blended | 6 | 2 | — | **8** |
| 1 material + hex-tiling | 9 | 2 | — | **11** |
| 2 materials + hex-tiling | 18 | 2 | — | **20** |
| 1 material + POM (8 fixed steps) | 3 | 2 | 8 | **13** |
| 2 materials + POM on the dominant material | 6 | 2 | 8 | **16** |
| 2 materials + Laplacian, 3 levels (4 samples × 3 maps × 2) | 24 | 2 | — | **26** |
| *(if we had used triplanar: multiply the detail column by 3)* | | | | |

**Three combinations are forbidden by a bake-time assertion over material pairs**, which is what keeps
the worst case inside the budget: hex-tiling + POM on the same material; hex-tiling + Laplacian on the
same pair; Laplacian + POM. The worst shippable configuration is therefore **26 taps**, above the 24
soft budget and inside the 32 hard one, and it occurs only on Laplacian-blended ring quads, which are a
small fraction of pixels.

**What the tap budget actually constrains, stated honestly.** At 1920×1080/60 the pixel rate is
124.4 Mpx/s, so 26 taps is 3.2 Gtap/s against an RTX 4060-class fill rate of order 240 Gtexel/s — about
1.3 % of peak. **The budget is not fill-rate-bound; it is a cache-locality and overdraw budget.** A
26-tap pixel touches up to 18 independent array layers, which thrashes L1 and defeats the texture
cache's spatial locality, and a 1-cell voxel world has heavy overdraw. That is why the **depth prepass
is mandatory** and why the budget is stated at all. Geometry is comfortable at the same target:
2.0 M quads = 4.0 M triangles in the main pass, ~4.0 M in the prepass and ~6.4 M across shadow cascades
(a ×1.6 cascade multiplier) = 14.4 M/frame = 864 Mtri/s against ~7.5 Gtri/s of setup throughput.

**The honest warning.** Every stochastic anti-tiling method in the literature works on *stochastic,
non-periodic* inputs: moss, granite, sand, bark, dirt, rock. Hull plating, deck grating, planks, bricks
and panel lines are **periodic by design**, and hex-tiling shears and rotates them into mush —
Mikkelsen's own paper shows the repeated pebble as the motivation for random rotation, which is
precisely the transformation that destroys oriented features. "Star Citizen meets Minecraft" means the
game is *full* of constructed periodic surfaces. Therefore, as a locked engineering rule rather than a
decision: **`anti_tiling: AntiTilingMode` is a per-material data field from day one**
(`None | HexTile { r, gamma, beta }`), defaulting to `None`. Constructed materials get repetition
control from Layers 1 and 2 plus wear decals and panel-line variation. There is no global stochastic
path to build and later throw away.

**Anisotropic filtering** is specified, because it dominates quality at grazing angles on a ground plane
and the draft omitted it: **16× on all three PBR samplers**, and it composes with hex-tiling's
`SampleGrad` (the gradients are supplied explicitly, so aniso applies normally).

#### 5.4.1 The distance ladder — granted, and mandatory rather than merely permitted

~~"The natural saving is to drop expensive layers with distance — POM beyond ~20 m, hex-tiling beyond
~60 m, the second seam material beyond ~100 m. **This section does not grant itself that carve-out.**
It is Option-B-shaped under the unresolved no-LOD ruling and is routed to §5.9."~~ **Granted by
Addendum 2 §C.8**, which names "distance-blended detail-normal scales" and "parameter falloff" as
dissolved questions. §5.4's budget is no longer the shipped budget with no distance relief.

It is also stronger than "permitted", and this is the sentence Addendum 2's list is missing: **without
a feature ladder a coarse rung looks *worse* than no rung at all.** At tier `L` the detail tile's world
period is `P·2^L` metres while its screen footprint stays ~2·P pixels (§5.3.1), so hardware mip
selection returns mip 6–7 of a 1024² map — the tile's own average colour. Draw a 128 m cell with a
tile that has averaged to a flat swatch and the far field reads as coloured paper. The tile must hand
over to something whose features are still resolvable, which is the macro octave stack.

**Key the ladder on `ChunkHeader.detail_tier`, a per-draw uniform, for everything above tier 0; key it
on per-pixel distance only *inside* tier 0.** Four reasons, and the fourth is the one that matters:

1. A per-draw uniform makes each fade a branchless `mix()` with a uniform weight — no per-pixel
   distance maths, no divergence, and it is the field §5.2.2 already reserved.
2. It is identical for every pixel of a chunk, so it is deterministic and cannot shimmer along an
   arbitrary iso-distance line crossing a surface.
3. It composes with the crossfade band instead of fighting it. A per-pixel distance fade and a
   per-entity dither band **disagree inside the band** — the two rungs would be shading themselves
   with different feature weights while being blended together, which is a seam the crossfade cannot
   hide because the crossfade is what created it.
4. Tier 0 is the exception because tier 0 is a *disc*, not an annulus: it spans 0 m to 786 m, three
   decades of screen-space cell size. Every rung above it spans exactly one octave (2–4 px per cell),
   which is why a single per-draw weight is enough there and only there.

| Feature | Weight from | Full | Zero | Why the cut is honest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| POM, 8 fixed steps | per-pixel distance, **tier 0 only** | ≤ 15 m | 20 m | Relief that is under one texel of parallax offset costs 8 taps to produce nothing |
| Hex-tiling, 3× per map | per-pixel distance, **tier 0 only** | ≤ 45 m | 60 m | Its entire purpose is defeating a repetition the eye can still resolve |
| Second seam material (2× detail taps) | sub-cell rule on the authored blend width | tier 0 | tier ≥ 1 | At tier ≥ 1 the ring strip is not emitted at all (§5.5.4), so the shader path is never reached — the saving is in the mesher, not the shader |
| Detail tile (albedo + normal + ORMH) | **per-draw tier**, weight `w_tile` from the material's authored `tile_max_tier` (default 3) | `L ≤ tile_max_tier` | one-rung fade, zero at `L > tile_max_tier + 1` | Below its own mip-6 average; the macro octaves carry the colour |
| Detail **normal** map | **per-draw tier**, weight `w_normal` from the material's authored `normal_max_tier` (default 4) | `L ≤ normal_max_tier` | one-rung fade above it | A normal map whose features are sub-pixel is a sparkle source (§5.3.7), not detail |
| Macro octave pair | always | every rung | — | 2 taps; this is what makes a coarse rung look like terrain |
| Per-block hash variation | always | every rung | — | 0 taps |
| 16× anisotropy | always | every rung | — | Dominates quality at grazing angles, and every horizon pixel is grazing |
| GSAA (§5.3.7) | always | every rung | — | ~10 ALU |

```rust
// material registry — per material, authored, never a literal, never a `match L`.
pub tile_max_tier:   u8,   // default 3 — the coarsest rung whose cell size this tile's CONTENT
                           //             remains plausible at
pub normal_max_tier: u8,   // default 4

w_tile   = clamp((tile_max_tier   as i32 + 1 - L as i32) as f32, 0.0, 1.0)   // one-rung fade at the top
w_normal = clamp((normal_max_tier as i32 + 1 - L as i32) as f32, 0.0, 1.0)

// RenderTuning, making §5.8's row obey the generic law:
pub ao_max_cell_size_m: f32,   // default 2.0 m => tiers 0-1; occ_ao exists iff 2^L <= this
```

These two rows are **tier-indexed data and not derivations, and that is deliberate.** The generic
sub-cell law converts an authored size in **metres** into a weight; the detail tile is authored in
**cells** (`tile_period_cells`), so its screen footprint is `tile_period_cells · px_per_cell_target`
pixels at *every* rung and no metres-denominated criterion can ever fire for it. What degrades at a
coarse rung is the plausibility of the tile's *content*, not its resolution — a four-cell gravel tile
is gravel at 1 m cells and a 512 m gravel pattern at tier 5 — and the compliant expression of an art
judgement is a per-material authored field, not an inline literal. Everything else in this table —
POM, hex-tiling, the seam blend, the rim warp, the AO slab — **is** derived from an authored size in
metres and stays that way. (~~"tiers 0–3 full, fades across tier 4, off at tier ≥ 5" and "tiers 0–4,
off at tier ≥ 5"~~ were literal rung numbers and are struck; the numbers above are the same defaults
expressed as data.)

**Tap count by rung** — the same worst case, now confined to a shrinking part of the frame:

| Where | Detail | Macro | POM | **Total** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tier 0, ≤ 20 m, 2-material ring + POM | 6 | 2 | 8 | **16** |
| Tier 0, ≤ 20 m, Laplacian ring, 3 levels (the worst shippable configuration, unchanged) | 24 | 2 | — | **26** |
| Tier 0, 20–60 m, hex-tiled, 1 material | 9 | 2 | — | **11** |
| Tier 0, > 100 m | 3 | 2 | — | **5** |
| Tiers 1–4 | 3 | 2 | — | **5** |
| Tier ≥ 5 | 0 | 2 | — | **2** |

Two consequences worth naming. First, **the 26-tap worst case is unchanged and the forbidden-combination
bake assertion stays load-bearing** — the ladder relieves distance, not the near field, and the near
field is where the assertion binds. Second, **the payoff mirrors the generator's exactly**: coarse rungs
get cheaper per *pixel* as well as per triangle, so the far field of a 100 km view is the cheapest part
of the frame, and Addendum 2's "coarsening is a saving" argument extends from the octave sum all the
way into the fragment shader. A companion bake assertion makes that structural rather than accidental:
**tap count must be monotonically non-increasing in tier.**

---

### 5.5 Blending between block types

The user's ask: *"ideally different block types BLEND into each other, like real life."*

#### 5.5.1 Why per-vertex material weights are structurally broken here

Every established per-vertex blend scheme comes from **smooth** voxel meshers where vertices are ~1
voxel apart: Godot Voxel Tools' `Mixel4` (4 indices + 4 weights at 4 bits, packed into two 16-bit
channels, 8 B/vertex, max 4 blended textures) and bonsairobo's `[f32;4]` weights (16 B/vertex,
L1-normalised in the vertex shader).

Neither survives greedy merging. A greedy quad has **exactly four corner vertices** no matter how large
it is, and the binary mesher's 6-bit position field permits quads up to 62 cells across. Bilinear
interpolation between four corners 62 m apart produces a **62 m gradient**. The blend width equals the
quad size. That is a topology problem, not a tuning problem.

#### 5.5.2 The fix: the seam predicate on the shared border-peel

Fire the peel of §5.1.2 on the material predicate:

```
For each greedy quad Q with material m, for each of Q's four edges E:
    fire[E] = ∃ block adjacent across E (in-plane, same face) with render material ≠ m
(core, ring) = border_peel(Q, fire)
core  → VertexStream::Voxel   (single material, 3+2 taps)
ring  → VertexStream::Detail  (two materials via `aux`, 6+2 taps; blend width exactly 1 cell)
```

Interior quads stay single-material. Only ring strips run the two-material path, and the two-material
choice is the lowest-`MaterialId` rule of §5.1.2 — deterministic and chunk-independent.

**The area cost is O(perimeter), not O(area)** — the fact that reconciles this with greedy meshing and
that the draft never stated:

| Greedy quad | Culled quads | Merged | Peeled (**strip** ring: material/shape predicate) | Border fraction of area |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 × 4 | 16 | 1 | 5 | 75 % |
| 8 × 8 | 64 | 1 | 5 | 44 % |
| 16 × 16 | 256 | 1 | 5 | 23 % |
| 62 × 62 | 3,844 | 1 | 5 | 6.3 % |
| *A grass field or a hull plate (no abutment)* | — | 1 | **1** | **0 %** |

The extra mesher pass is a linear scan of each quad's border — +10–15 % on the 65 µs baseline, inside
the §5.1.3 budget — and it is short-circuited entirely on degenerate chunks (§5.1.3 item 5).

#### 5.5.3 The blend operator

**Start with height blending — free.** Each material carries a height channel (ORMH alpha, needed for
parallax anyway). Instead of `lerp(a, b, w)`, select by comparing `height_a + w` against
`height_b + (1 − w)`, which makes gravel poke through dirt along real gravel edges rather than
producing a soft airbrushed ramp. **0 extra taps** — it reweights samples already taken. Jason Booth
(MicroSplat) reports it averages ~1.5 samples instead of a hard 3 because the selection lets samples be
branched away, and argues it beats the variance-preserving operator because the latter "washes out the
detail".

**Upgrade to Laplacian blending only if height blending is not good enough.** Wronski's *GPU-Friendly
Laplacian Texture Blending* (JCGT 14(1), 2025): sample each texture and the mask at LOD 0..n via
`textureSampleLevel`, form Laplacians in place as `level[i] − level[i+1]` from the existing mip chain,
blend each band with a *different* mask sharpness proportional to feature size, then add the coarsest
Gaussian. Low frequencies blend wide (no seam), high frequencies blend narrow (no ghosting, no contrast
loss). n+1 taps for n levels, **all extra taps from lower mips** that stay in L1/L2 — max bandwidth
133 % of the base mip chain — zero precomputation, zero extra memory. Measured at 3840×2160 on an RTX
4090: 4 levels = **0.087 ms**, 5 = 0.113, 6 = 0.125, 7 = 0.134. It is the only operator in the survey
that provably preserves normal-map detail across a blend (linear narrow = visible seam; linear wide =
normals flattened toward +Z). **Capped at 3 levels** by the §5.4 assertion, giving the 26-tap worst
case.

> **[USER DECISION 5-D] — the art direction for material transitions.** These are genuinely
> different-looking games and the technical stacks diverge immediately.
>
> - **D1. Soft blending** *(recommended if the target is "believable real-life ground")*. Needs the
>   seam predicate, the two-material shader path and 8 taps in transition regions (26 with Laplacian).
>   Blend width exactly 1 cell.
> - **D2. Hard 1-cell edges decorated with overlay geometry** — the Minecraft/Vintage Story
>   grass-overhang look. The mesher emits an extra alpha-tested quad carrying the neighbour material
>   with a noise-edged mask. **No shader blending at all**; cost is geometry and overdraw rather than
>   taps, and it preserves the blocky honesty of a 1 m voxel world. A smooth blend on a surface that
>   visibly steps in 1 m cubes can read as *inconsistent* rather than higher quality.
> - **D3. Hybrid** — D1 for natural terrain pairs (dirt/grass/sand/stone), D2 for gameplay-legible
>   boundaries (ore, farmland, hull). Technically fine; means building and maintaining both paths and
>   defining a per-material-pair policy.
>
> **Recommendation: D1**, because the user's words are "blend into each other, like real life", and
> because the border-peel is needed for the rim warp and the shaped lane anyway, so the marginal cost is
> the shader path only. A taste call that gates roughly a month of shader work in one direction or the
> other. **Not a one-way door** — the peel machinery is shared, so switching later replaces the ring
> quad's shader, not the mesher.

#### 5.5.4 Blending across the ladder — the seam strip at coarse rungs

At tier `L` a coarse cell's material is the **dominant** material of the `2^(3L)` fine cells beneath
it, taken from the edit pyramid where an entry exists and from the coarse generator's own strata
evaluation everywhere else. That is one call — `coarse_summary(addr)` (register row 37) — and it is
the same call the pyramid walk-up and §6's coarse ground tint make, so the three cannot disagree.
Material seams therefore exist at every rung; nothing about coarsening removes them.

**Two facts that need no re-derivation.** First, §5.5.2's cost table is expressed in *cells*, so it
holds verbatim at every rung — a 16×16 coarse quad still peels to 5 rectangles with a 23 % border
fraction. Second, the blend width is one cell, and one cell is 2–4 screen pixels at every rung by
construction, so **a 1-cell blend is tier-invariant in screen space.** Taken alone that argues for
blending at every rung.

**The sub-cell rule overrules it, and the arithmetic is why.** The blend width is a per-material
authored quantity in **metres** (`blend_width_m`, default 1.0), and the mesher computes
`blend_cells = floor(blend_width_m / 2^L)`. The material-seam predicate fires iff `blend_cells ≥ 1`.
For a 1.0 m authored width that is **tier 0 only**; for a hypothetical material authored at 20 m it
would blend up to tier 4. **There is no branch on the tier anywhere** — one data field, one division,
one comparison, and the generic law of the section header does the rest.

Three consequences, and the second is the one people miss:

1. **At tiers ≥ 1 the ring is not emitted for material reasons at all.** The quad stays merged, the
   `Detail` stream is not produced, and the two-material shader path is never reached. The saving is in
   the *mesher* first and the shader second, which is the right order — it is also part of why coarse
   chunks peel less (§5.1.4).
2. **The peel is still exercised at every rung, by a different predicate.** The shaped-neighbour
   predicate (§4.5.2) fires wherever a coarse cell's dominant *shape* is not a full cube — which is
   common, because a partially-filled coarse cell should be a slope or a half rather than
   solid-or-empty (§5.3.9's count-to-shape rule; it is what stops a distant tower reading as a blob).
   So `border_peel` is not dead code above tier 0: **one machine, three predicates, each gated by its
   own sub-cell weight.**
3. **The visible loss is sub-pixel, provably.** The finest rung that ever draws unblended material
   boundaries is tier 1, whose innermost radius is 786 m; a 2 m hard edge at 786 m subtends 2.5 px, and
   inside the crossfade band a blended tier-0 strip is dithered against an unblended tier-1 strip whose
   disagreement is confined to that same ≤ 2.5 px. ∎

**One discipline this inherits and must not lose: "dominant" has to be a total order.** ~~Highest
solid count wins; ties break to the lowest `MaterialId`.~~ **Struck, and replaced by the one canonical
rule (register row 37).** Dominance is §4's `coarsen()` kernel: the dominant substance is the argmax
over distinct substances of the summed `fill_256` of the **non-empty** children, and **ties break to
the lowest `SubstanceId`**. `SubstanceId` is a `u16` with distinct values, so the rule is total,
tie-free, order-independent and chunk-independent — which is what lets the realm owner's pyramid entry
and a client's local recompute agree bit for bit. The *shape* of the rule is §5.1.2's two-material
reduction, but the id space is not: §5.1.2 reduces over the **render** `MaterialId`, which is §5's only
legitimate use of that name (the texture-array addressing of §5.10.2) and is never the block-registry
row. Addendum 2 §E's recompute-from-deltas assertion is the test that keeps them honest.

---

### 5.6 The un-square edge

The user's words: *"edge blocks must NOT be perfectly squared like Minecraft. Dirt should not have
perfectly lined edges if it is the last block — should feel like real life, but voxely."* Note
precisely what it says: **edges**, not surfaces. That is a rim requirement, and the whole design turns
on it.

#### 5.6.1 The rim-only deterministic lattice warp — baked, in the Tier-A mesher

**The single largest correction to the first draft: the warp is computed on the CPU, in the Tier-A
mesher, and baked into the emitted vertex position. It does not run in the vertex shader.**

A vertex-shader warp is **not implementable as specified**, and that is the reason, not a preference.
The amplitude `A(p) = min over the SOLID blocks touching p of A_mat(block)` is a reduction over the
**materials** of the eight blocks around a lattice corner. The only per-chunk GPU resource in the design
is a 1-bit occupancy slab; a 1-bit mask supplies the outward direction but not eight neighbours'
material amplitudes. The escapes both lose: a per-chunk material volume costs 256 KiB/chunk —
**1,706 MiB across the ladder's 6,821 resident chunks**, which strengthens rather than weakens the
rejection (~~"112 MiB at 900 resident chunks"~~ was the superseded single-tier horizon) — and a single
global amplitude constant violates no-magic-numbers and voids the per-material design. The three usual arguments for a shader warp also fail here: a content-keyed mesh
cache saves nothing (§5.1.3); untunable amplitude is a development-iteration cost covered by a dev
`remesh-all`; and positions are f32 in V1 regardless.

Baking additionally **removes four failure modes for free**: the prepass/shadow shader-duplication trap
(a displaced `vertex_shader()` without a byte-identical `prepass_vertex_shader()` makes shadows and TAA
motion vectors disagree with visible geometry, *silently*); the frustum-culling trap (culling uses the
undisplaced `Aabb`, which would need manual inflation); the WGSL reassociation-and-fusion question (WGSL
§15.7.5 explicitly permits fusing a multiply-add and reassociating, so a Rust↔WGSL bit-equality gate
would be either flaky across vendors or vacuous); and the AO-sampling discontinuity at rims. And it puts
the warp inside the crate that *already needs it*: §5.6.3's peel rule makes `A(p)` an input to the
**merge predicate**, so the amplitude table has to be Tier-A regardless.

**The hash is `SplitMix64`, not a new mixer.** §3.5.4 rule 8 is explicit: "Integer hashing only. Reuse
the landed `SplitMix64`; introduce no second hash." Three 10-bit fields of the 64-bit result give 1,024
distinct offsets per axis (Minecraft ships 16), and the conversion to a signed unit value uses **only
powers of two**, so every intermediate is exactly representable:
`((bits as f64) + 0.5) * (1.0 / 1024.0) * 2.0 − 1.0`. No float noise function — no Perlin, no simplex,
no `sin` — because two machines must agree and noise implementations differ in evaluation order.

**The key is a chart-independent canonical corner identity, and it lives in `GridMapping`.** A
cube-sphere block address is `(face, u, v, h)`, and the same *physical* corner on a cube edge has **two
different `(u, v)` values**, one per adjoining chart. Hashing the raw triple gives different
displacements on the two sides — up to `2 × 0.20 × √3 ≈ 0.69 m` of disagreement along **12 seams each
N = 253,952 corners long**, i.e. 3.05 million lattice corners of guaranteed cracking. (The texture
analogue of this is benign — "the tile rotates 90° along the 12 cube-edge lines" — which is exactly why
it is easy to notice for textures and miss for geometry.) The raw key would also reproduce an identical
pattern on all six faces, making every planet's rubble 6-fold symmetric.

The fix is a **seventh `GridMapping` operation**, alongside the six of §3.1.1:

```rust
/// Chart-independent identity of a lattice CORNER. Identity grids return the raw triple;
/// CubeSphereShell canonicalises boundary corners to the representative on the LOWEST
/// adjoining face index, using the same 24-record seam table §3.3.3 derives and pins.
/// The 8 cube-corner vertices (three faces meet) take the lowest of the three.
fn corner_key(&self, corner: LatticeCorner) -> CornerKey;   // packed u64
```

This places the only chart-dependent line of the warp *below* the geometry seam, where §3.1.4's
`G-MAPPING-EXHAUSTIVE` gate applies rather than result-equality — and it adds one clause to that gate:
**(v) `corner_key` agrees for both charts at every one of the 12 × N boundary corners and at all 8 cube
corners.** The mesher above the seam never learns the word "face". Including the canonical face index in
the hash also removes the 6-fold symmetry.

**The amplitude field is binary.** `A_mat` is a per-material field in metres, and the registry asserts
at bake that **every value is either exactly 0.00 or at least 0.08** — because a non-zero amplitude
triggers the peel identically at 0.02 m as at 0.20 m, and a 2 cm wobble is below one texel at
256 texels/cell while costing the full merge reduction. (The draft recommended 0.02 m for hand-laid
stone; that recommendation is **withdrawn**.) Starting table: dirt 0.20, sand 0.18, gravel 0.16, snow
0.14, loose stone 0.10, bedrock and ore 0.08; every constructed material — metal, glass, planks, brick,
concrete — exactly 0.00.

At a corner `p` with 2×2×2 block occupancy `o`:

```
A(p) = 0                                                if o is all solid or all air
A(p) = 0                                                if p is not on an exposed CONVEX silhouette corner
A(p) = min over the SOLID blocks touching p of A_mat     otherwise
```

`min` is load-bearing: it is commutative and order-independent, so both chunks sharing `p` compute the
same value from their own 1-block apron; and a single hard material adjacent to a corner **pins it to
zero**, so a steel beam set into dirt stays razor-sharp with no branching and no shard-kind test.

**A requirement this places on the chunk buffer:** the `min` combiner reads the *material* of each of the
eight neighbours, so **the 1-block apron must carry full block records, not a 1-bit occupancy mask**.
This is already how §3's `Chunk` container works; state it in the chunk-store contract so nobody
optimises the apron down to a bitmask.

**There is deliberately no "1-wide air gap" clause.** Such a clause is not expressible in a 2×2×2
neighbourhood — solid–air–solid is a property of cells at distance 2, needing a 4×4×4 window and
therefore a **2-block apron**, which would break the 256-entry table, the continuity proof, *and* the
`62 + 2 = one u64 column` property that is why 62³ was chosen (§3.3.6). It also addresses the
wrong-signed problem. Under inward-only bias a 1 m air **gap** gets visually *wider* (both walls recede:
1.4 m visual, 1.0 m physical), which is benign; a 1 m **solid** feature gets visually *thinner* (0.6 m
visual, 1.0 m physical), which is a phantom hit — consistent with everything else, and on natural
material it reads as a rammed-earth berm, which is the intended look. On structural material
`A_mat = 0.00` and the case does not arise.

#### 5.6.2 The rim predicate and the containment proof

Let `o` be the 8-bit occupancy of the 2×2×2 block neighbourhood at corner `p`:

```rust
/// A coplanar 4-slab is EXACTLY one of the six half-space masks of the 2×2×2 cube.
/// Those are the corners in the MIDDLE of a flat face — the ones that must not move,
/// because they are what lets a plain merge into a handful of quads.
const fn is_rim(o: u8) -> bool {
    let s = o.count_ones();
    s >= 1 && s <= 4
        && !matches!(o, 0x0F | 0xF0 | 0x33 | 0xCC | 0x55 | 0xAA)
}
// Materialised as a const [bool; 256]; one unit test walks all 256 entries.
```

`s ≥ 5` (a concave inside corner) is deliberately excluded: that is where a floor meets a wall, where a
displaced vertex opens a crack toward the interior, and where nothing about the silhouette improves.

**Inward bias.** Derive an integer outward direction `o⃗ ∈ {−1,0,+1}³` at `p` from the 2×2×2 occupancy
octants, then take `d = −o⃗ ⊙ |raw| · A(p)` componentwise, **quantised to 2⁻¹⁰ m** — the project's
existing FINE lattice unit (`LatticePos`, §D-41), so the offset is an exact integer quantity with an
exact f32 image, and the "every physics→control boundary quantised to an integer grid" law is honoured
rather than approximated.

**The containment guarantee, stated so that it is actually provable.** "The visual hull is a subset of
the collision hull, proved by enumerating 256 corner configurations" is *not* a valid claim: a corner
enumeration says nothing about triangle interiors, and the union of blocks touching a rim is generally
non-convex (an L-shaped step is the ordinary case on terrain), so a straight edge between two contained
points can leave the set. The true statement is stronger where it matters and weaker where it must be:

> **Per-face outward containment.** For every emitted face `f` and every vertex `v` of `f`,
> `d(v) · n_f ≤ 0`, where `n_f` is `f`'s outward normal — because `d = −o⃗ ⊙ |raw| · A` and `o⃗`'s
> component along `n_f` is `+1` for any face incident to that corner. A plane through three points each
> at-or-below a reference plane lies entirely at-or-below it. **Therefore no point of any emitted
> triangle protrudes outward through its own unwarped face plane.** ∎
>
> **Bounded divergence.** `|d|∞ ≤ A_max` at every vertex, so the Hausdorff distance between the warped
> and unwarped surfaces is ≤ `A_max` everywhere.

What is *not* claimed: a rim triangle may slide **laterally** past its block's edge into the adjoining
empty cell by up to `A_max`, producing at most a 0.20 m visual overhang above a solid block at a convex
step. That is the chamfer, it is the intended look, and it is stated rather than proved away.

The exhaustive test enumerates all 2⁸ corner configurations and asserts (i) `d · n_f ≤ 0` for every
incident face and (ii) `|d|∞ ≤ A_max`; the per-triangle result follows from the two-line planarity
argument above rather than from enumeration. Cheap, complete, and in the Tier-A crate that owns the
predicate — which is `vd-voxel`, once it is on the justfile list.

**Bounding.** `|d|∞ ≤ 0.20 m` keeps the minimum lattice edge at 1 − 2(0.20) = 0.60 m, guaranteeing no
cell inversion, no fold-over and no self-intersection.

**Chunk-seam continuity, proved rather than asserted.** `d` is a pure function of
`(realm_salt, corner_key(p), occupancy(p), A_mat table)`. Both chunks sharing `p` read the same 2×2×2
from their own 1-block apron; `min` is order-independent; `corner_key` is chart-independent and a pure
function of the corner. Therefore both compute bit-identical `d`. No cross-chunk communication, no seam
machinery, no ordering constraint. ∎

#### 5.6.3 The greedy-run cut rule, T-junctions, and the true price

A merged N×M quad has only four corner vertices — the interior lattice points along its shared edge are
gone. If a neighbouring 1×1 quad's corner moves 0.20 m, the merged quad's straight edge no longer meets
it and a benign 1-pixel T-junction becomes a **0.20 m hole**. That is the most alarming possible visual
failure.

**Rule: any lattice point with `A(p) ≠ 0` is a barrier in the greedy sweep** — the third peel predicate
of §5.1.2, with `split_unit` applied to the ring. No merge boundary ever crosses a warped point, so the
warp creates zero cracks. Residual T-junctions from ordinary greedy size mismatch remain; those *are*
sub-pixel and the standard mitigation (render quads ~1 px larger, compute positions in eye space) is
calibrated for exactly that.

**The price, with the arithmetic the draft owed and the adversary overstated.** The peel replaces one
N×M quad with `1 + (2N + 2M − 4)` unit quads, versus `N × M` un-merged:

| Quad | Culled | Merged | Warp-peeled (unit ring) | Merge win retained | Effective merge ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 × 4 | 16 | 1 | 13 | 20 % | 1.2× |
| 8 × 8 | 64 | 1 | 29 | 56 % | **2.2×** |
| 16 × 16 | 256 | 1 | 61 | 76 % | 4.2× |
| 32 × 32 | 1,024 | 1 | 125 | 88 % | 8.2× |
| 62 × 62 | 3,844 | 1 | 245 | 94 % | **15.7×** |

The cost is **O(perimeter)**, so it is asymptotically free on large surfaces. A player-laid 8×8×8 dirt
cube goes from 6 quads to 174 against 384 culled — a 2.2× win retained, and 174 quads is nothing in
absolute terms. A 100 × 100 dirt platform goes from 1 quad to 397 against 10,000 culled. The warp does
not *delete* the merge win on player construction; it reduces it to between 1.2× and 15.7× depending on
quad size, and it survives comfortably where surfaces are large.

0fps's own measurements complete the picture:

| Geometry | Culled | Greedy | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8³ solid cube | 384 | 6 | 64× |
| Authored structure | 690 | 22 | 31× |
| Sphere | 4,770 | 2,100 | 2.3× |
| **Noisy terrain** | 2,198 | 1,670 | **1.3×** |

Greedy merging buys almost nothing on noisy natural terrain — which is precisely where the warping
materials live — and buys 31–64× on flat regular geometry, which is precisely where `A_mat = 0.00`. **One
binary data field per material decides both whether a block wobbles and whether it merges freely, and
the two decisions want the same answer** — with the honest caveat that a *player-built structure out of
natural material* is the case where they conflict, and the table above prices it at 2.2× rather than
64×.

#### 5.6.4 Two cheap layers on top

**Hash-selected model variants + rotation** for exposed natural blocks. Vintage Story ships
`randomDrawOffset` ("randomly offseted by 1/3 of a block") and `randomizeRotations` as per-blocktype
JSON data; Hytale gets natural variation from weighted texture-variant arrays plus custom-geometry model
blocks built from cubes and quads only. Both are pure functions of position, both are invisible to the
server, both survive greedy meshing because variants replace individual cells. A hand-authored "slumped
dirt edge" reads better than any hash, and combining a small variant library with the continuous warp
defeats the repetition a variant library alone produces. This rides the 3-bit cosmetic variant tag in
the packed vertex (§5.2.2).

**A per-edge chamfer catalogue is the available upgrade, and it is cheaper than it sounds.** An edge is
convex-exposed iff both faces meeting at it are air; a corner is exposed iff its three faces and three
edges are air — **20 O(1) boolean tests per block, not a 256-case marching table**. A fully chamfered
cube is 44 triangles versus 12 (3.7× worst case, ~1.5–2× on real terrain), the bevel width is a
per-material field (steel 0 mm, dirt 120 mm), and it composes with the same border-peel: merge the flat
interior, emit the bevel frame only around the exposed boundary. Combined with the warp this reads as
"chipped and slumped" rather than merely "eroded". It is the reserved second half of USER DECISION 5-E.

**Instanced rim decoration** — pebbles, grass fringe, chipped-corner shells — is **§6's territory, not
this section's.** §6.1–6.5 own the two-tier scatter design, its GPU compute cull/compact path, its four
phase registrations and its measured VRAM and millisecond envelope. §5's only obligation is to hand §6
the **exposed-rim classification the mesher already computes**, as a per-cell bit alongside the
occupancy masks.

#### 5.6.5 Explicitly ruled out

**Iso-surface extraction (marching cubes / surface nets / dual contouring / Transvoxel) — rejected, and
it is a ONE-WAY DOOR.** It breaks player-built geometry: naive surface nets rounds every corner, so a
1-block wall becomes a slab with a soft edge; only dual contouring with Hermite/QEF data preserves sharp
features, and that needs gradient data a binary block field does not have plus inter-cell dependency.
Godot Voxel Tools' documented way to "get blocky output back" is to saturate SDF values to ±1 — an
admission the two representations do not coexist. Critically, an iso-surface makes the visual surface
diverge from the 1 m collision cells by **up to 0.5 m everywhere**, the maximum-hazard configuration for
§5.6.6. The shipped warning is 7 Days to Die: smoothed terrain voxels meeting cube building blocks "do
not blend perfectly", and its POI editor exposes a manual density adjustment so builders can hand-fix
the gaps — disqualifying for a game whose premise is player-built ships sitting on planets.

~~"Transvoxel additionally exists only to stitch LOD seams and is void under a no-LOD rule."~~ **That
reason is retracted and replaced by a better one**, because the ladder makes tier seams a real problem
this design now has to solve. Transvoxel (Lengyel 2009) adds a second lookup table over transition
cells — 13 sample points instead of 8, 512 cases — and `godot_voxel` implements it by carrying a
secondary vertex position per vertex and morphing between the two in the vertex shader. It exists
because two *smooth iso-surfaces* at different resolutions genuinely disagree along a curve. **Our
surfaces are axis-aligned quads at every rung**; a tier only changes the cell size, so a fine chunk and
a coarse chunk meet in a vertical *step*, not an interpolated curve. Adopting transvoxel would mean a
second mesher and a second shape catalogue — an HR3 violation, and precisely the "the block system
forks in two" failure Addendum 1 §A.2 rejected hex grids to avoid. §5.9.4's skirts close the same crack
in about twenty lines with no case table and, decisively, with no dependence on the neighbour's tier.
Dual-contouring seam octrees (Gildea-style) are rejected as the same class for the same reason: they
build a third mesh kind, with its own lifetime, its own dirty rules and its own coverage cost, to
reconcile a disagreement our representation does not have.

**Tessellation / geometry shaders — unavailable.** wgpu's `Features` list contains **zero**
tessellation and **zero** geometry-shader entries; mesh shaders exist only as
`EXPERIMENTAL_MESH_SHADER`, native-only, Naga-supported on Vulkan only. Amplifying a greedy quad back
into a per-cell lattice on the GPU would need a compute pass writing an indirect-drawn buffer — a far
larger commitment than the mesher-side peel.

**Parallax occlusion mapping as a silhouette technique — impossible by construction.** POM displaces
the sampled texel along the view ray *inside* the surface; the rasterised triangle's edge is unchanged,
so against the sky the block edge is still a straight line, and depth-correct inward carving requires
`frag_depth`, which disables early-Z on the largest material in the game. POM stays for surface richness
— it is unusually cheap on voxel faces because the tangent frame is constant per quad, and Space
Engineers 2's VRAGE3 ships exactly this for "subtle rounded bevels on armor edges" — under three
constraints now in the material contract: **per-material opt-in, default off; a fixed 8 ray-march steps
with no grazing-angle escalation; on a non-hex-tiled height channel, dominant material only.** With those
it costs 8 taps and fits (§5.4).

#### 5.6.6 Confronting the standing law head-on

The warp is client-side geometry math. The standing law says **"server does ALL math; client renders"**,
it is worded emphatically, and a previous slice was already reworked for drifting into client-compose.
This must be ruled on, not inferred.

1. **The client already turns a block field into triangles, by design.** P4's deliverable is explicit —
   "no chunk streaming, no networked terrain; only the seed crosses the wire", and "the client-side
   mesher mirrors the server's chunk math". Meshing *is* client-side math, mandated by the roadmap;
   shipping server-computed vertices for a 741 m horizon is hundreds of megabytes per player per remesh.
2. **The warp is a pure function of authoritative data with no feedback path.** Inputs: the block field,
   the material amplitude table (registry data) and the seed-derived realm salt. Its output is consumed
   by the rasteriser and by nothing else.
3. **It is the *same code* the server would run.** Baked in the Tier-A `vd-voxel` mesher rather than in a
   shader, it is not a client-only reimplementation of anything — it is one function in one crate that
   both sides link, exactly like the generator. This is a stronger position than "it lives in a crate the
   sim cannot reach", which would also have been factually wrong (`vd-client-render` is a dependency of
   `bins`).
4. **There is no server artefact to diverge from.** Collision is exact 1 m cells. If parry's `Voxels`
   collider is adopted (§4.6), the server never builds a triangle mesh at all.

**The failure modes, and what inward-only bias actually does to them.** Visual-vs-collision divergence
has eight distinct gameplay failures: (1) a visual ledge that is not standable; (2) *phantom miss* — a
shot visually intersecting geometry that passes through; (3) *phantom hit* — a shot visually through a
notch that connects; (4) camera near-plane clipping; (5) placement-preview mismatch; (6) the selection
outline not hugging the mesh; (7) a 1 m solid feature reading 0.6 m; (8) unfairness if decoration were
per-client random.

Per-face outward containment (§5.6.2) eliminates (2) and (4) outright and converts them into (3), which
players tolerate far better because the world reads as *solid*. It **bounds but does not eliminate** (1):
a lateral chamfer overhang of ≤ 0.20 m above a solid block can be mistaken for standable — a 0.20 m
error, not the 0.5 m one an iso-surface would give. (5) and (6) are closed by warping the placement
preview and the selection outline with the same baked function (eight corners, trivial). (7) is the
thin-solid case: a phantom hit, the intended erosion look on natural material, impossible on structural
material. (8) is closed by determinism. Minecraft's precedent is instructive: its Y offset is always ≤ 0
(a block may sink, never rise), and for two of its three offset types Mojang moved the *interaction box*
along with the visual rather than let them diverge.

**The determinism gate is one artefact, not two.** P4's DoD is a property of the **block field**; the
warp is strictly downstream of it. But it needs its own gate for *fairness* as much as for looks — if
two players saw different rubble, one would have cover the other does not. Because the warp is baked in
Tier-A integer code, that gate is a single **golden-vector table**: 10,000 corner configurations,
including a mandatory cube-face-seam continuity block and all 8 cube corners, with the expected
quantised `d` checked in. It lives in `crates/voxel/tests/` following the `celestial_ephemeris_pin.rs`
precedent, so the justfile's `--ignore-filename-regex '(/bin/|/tests/)'` keeps an exactness assertion out
of the HR5 gate. A GPU-readback WGSL↔Rust equality test is **not** needed, because there is no WGSL
implementation to disagree — a direct saving from the bake decision.

> **[USER DECISION 5-E] — the un-square edge: amplitude, direction, and who wobbles.** Close to a
> **ONE-WAY DOOR**: art is authored against whatever amplitude is chosen.
>
> **Sub-decision 1 — the divergence budget, in metres, and whether outward is allowed.**
>
> | Option | Max visual↔collision divergence | Look | Failure profile |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | E1. No warp (pure cubes) | 0.00 m | Minecraft | None |
> | E2. 0.10 m, inward-only | 0.10 m, never outward through a face plane | Subtly eroded | Phantom hit; ≤0.10 m chamfer overhang |
> | **E3. 0.20 m, inward-only** *(recommended)* | 0.20 m | Crumbling, eroded edges; min lattice edge 0.60 m | Phantom hit; ≤0.20 m chamfer overhang |
> | E4. 0.25 m, outward permitted (Minecraft XZ parity) | 0.25 m both directions | Genuinely chipped, protruding — reads best | Adds real visual ledges and phantom **misses** |
> | E5. 0.33 m (Vintage Story parity) | 0.33 m | Strongly organic | As E4, larger |
>
> **Recommendation: E3.** Inward-only is the difference between "the world is solid and I sometimes hit
> slightly more than I see" and "the world lies to me"; players complain about the second. Note
> Minecraft's own Y offset is inward-only for the same reason.
>
> **Sub-decision 2 — do player-built blocks wobble, or only natural terrain?** Boundless's developer
> framed this publicly as "Lego versus modelling clay" and chose deformation for a natural feel. The
> opposite case is strong here: natural material wobbles, structural material is machined-sharp, and the
> *contrast* is the art direction. Mechanically it is one binary field per material — but it also decides
> how much greedy merging survives, priced in §5.6.3 at 2.2× retained on an 8³ player-built box.
> **Recommendation: natural wobbles (0.08–0.20 m), every constructed material exactly 0.00.** The
> middle position the draft offered (hand-laid stone at 0.02 m) is **withdrawn**: it is below one texel
> at 256 texels/cell and costs the whole merge win, and the registry now asserts `A_mat ∈ {0} ∪ [0.08, ∞)`.
>
> **Sub-decision 3 — is a per-edge chamfer catalogue wanted on top of the warp?** +1.5–2× triangles on
> exposed rims, 20 boolean tests per block, per-material bevel width, shares the border-peel. It is what
> takes the look from "eroded" to "chipped and slumped". **Recommendation: reserve the `bevel_mm: u8`
> field in the material registry now (free) and land the catalogue after the warp ships and is judged on
> screen.**
>
> **Sub-decision 4 — confirm that a deterministic, baked geometry warp is compatible with "server does
> ALL math; client renders".** The argument is above; the bake decision makes it a shared Tier-A function
> rather than a client-only shader. The alternative reading requires the server to ship warped vertex
> positions, which contradicts P4's "only the seed crosses the wire". **Recommendation: rule it
> compatible and write the general amendment down once** — *"authoritative pose composition is the
> server's; deterministic derivation of geometry from already-authoritative field data is shared code,
> run wherever it is needed"* — so this class of question is settled permanently rather than re-litigated
> per feature.

#### 5.6.7 The warp across the ladder — the fade rule, and the proof it stays seamless

A 0.20 m displacement on a 1 m cell is the art direction. On an 8 m cell it is 2.5 % of a cell and
0.05 screen pixels: invisible, and it costs the entire greedy merge win to produce (§5.6.3). **The warp
must fade out with tier**, and the rule is the section's generic sub-cell law with one deliberate
choice about its input.

> **The rule.** `A_eff(p, L) = A(p) · w(L)`, where
> `w(L) = smoothstep(warp_frac_off, warp_frac_on, A_max / 2^L)`,
> `A_max` is the **registry maximum** over all materials (not the per-material `A_mat`),
> `warp_frac_on = 0.15` and `warp_frac_off = 0.05` are render-tuning fields.

At the recommended `A_max = 0.20 m` that gives **tier 0 → 1.00, tier 1 → 0.50, tier ≥ 2 → 0.00.**

**Why `A_max` and not `A_mat`, which is the one place this deviates from the generic form.** If each
material faded on its own schedule, `A(p) = min over the solid blocks touching p` would be non-zero at
a scattering of corners and zero at their neighbours on the same rung — so the warp peel predicate
would fire at isolated corners, unit-splitting a handful of rectangles in an otherwise mergeable quad.
That is the worst of both: no visible wobble and no merge win. Feeding the registry maximum makes all
materials fade together, so `w(L) = 0` means `A_eff ≡ 0` **everywhere** at tier ≥ 2 and the predicate
is uniformly off. One value, read from the registry at bake, no magic number.

**The thresholds are derived, not chosen.** `A_max / 2^L` is the displacement as a fraction of a cell,
and a cell subtends 2 px at its own rung's outer range. So `0.15` is "0.3 px at the rung's far edge"
and `0.05` is "0.1 px" — the same screen-space criterion the entire ladder is built on, applied to a
displacement instead of to a cell.

**What it buys, in the numbers §5.6.3 already computed.** A 62×62 greedy quad with a warped rim is 245
unit quads at tier 0. At tier ≥ 2 it is **1**. Since tiers 2–7 hold 6 of the ladder's 8 rungs and
5,306 of its 6,821 chunks, the warp's `O(perimeter)` cost is paid only where the player can see it,
and the coarse two-thirds of the resident set merges at full efficiency.

**One requirement on the mesher's warp input, and it is what makes the next proof work.**
`corner_key` must always be evaluated at the **tier-0 corner identity**, `coarse_index · 2^L` — an
exact integer shift. Every coarse lattice corner *is* a fine lattice corner, so the coarse rung warps a
**subset of the same corners with the same raw hash**, merely scaled by `w(L)`. The fade is therefore
an amplitude scaling of one displacement field, not a switch between two different ones.

**The seamlessness proof across a tier boundary**, in four parts, because this is the one place the
ladder could plausibly have broken the warp:

1. **Two rungs never share a lattice edge.** They overlap for the width of the crossfade band and are
   stitched by skirts (§5.9.4); they are never welded, so there is no vertex to disagree about.
2. **The skirt bound already covers the warp.** §5.9.4 sets
   `skirt_drop_m = (relief_max(column footprint, L+1) + A_max) · skirt_safety`. Per-face outward containment (§5.6.2) proves `d · n_f ≤ 0` — the warp
   moves a surface **inward only**, never outward through its own face plane — so a warped fine surface
   can only ever sit at or below its unwarped coarse counterpart at the border. **The crack can only
   open downward, and downward is the direction a skirt closes.** ∎
3. **The residual visual difference inside a band is bounded and sub-pixel.** Because the two rungs
   displace the same corners with the same hash, their disagreement is
   `A(p) · (w(L) − w(L+1)) ≤ A_max`. At the tier-0/tier-1 band (630–786 m at the default pixel target)
   that is at most 0.20 m at 630 m = **0.40 px**. At the tier-1/tier-2 band (1.26–1.57 km) it is at
   most 0.10 m = **0.10 px**. Every band above is exactly 0, because `w = 0` on both sides. **The
   largest geometric disagreement the fade can produce anywhere in the world is four tenths of a
   pixel**, and it is dithered by §5.9.5 on top of that. ∎
4. **Chunk-seam continuity within a rung is unchanged.** `d` remains a pure function of
   `(realm_salt, corner_key(p), occupancy(p), A_mat table, w(L))`, and the two chunks sharing a corner
   are always at the same rung — they are the same rung. §5.6.2's proof holds verbatim with `w(L)`
   appended to the tuple. ∎

**The determinism gate gains one axis.** §5.6.6's golden-vector table (10,000 corner configurations)
is checked in at tier 0, tier 1 and tier 2, with the tier-2 block asserting `d == 0` for every
configuration. That is 3× the rows and 0× the new machinery.

**Decoration follows the same law and it is §6's to write**: instance density is a continuous function
of the same weight, reaching zero rather than switching off, with a ramp wide enough that a walking
player never sees clutter appear — which is the single most-reported complaint about the game the
owner cited (§5.3.9).

### 5.7 Transparency, cutout, and what `color_rgba` becomes

Transparency is a whole rendering class and it is load-bearing here: the user's own block-cover ask is
literally *"a **transparent** block-cover"*, `realm_scene.rs:8` documents `MeshPrim` as carrying "a
**translucent** color", and §6's grass is alpha-tested geometry.

**The mesher: two occupancy masks for culling, a third for AO.** Following engineersbox's dual-mask
extension of binary greedy meshing — `occ_ne` (non-empty: opaque ∪ cutout ∪ translucent cubes) and
`occ_solid` (opaque cubes only) — with `col & !(col << 1)` applied to each and OR-ed. §4.5.5's `occ_ao`
(anything with `volume_units ≥ CELL_VOLUME_UNITS / 2`, i.e. 98,304 of 196,608 — §4's exact cell-fraction
lattice; ~~`volume_48ths ≥ 24`~~ names a unit §4 deleted) is the third. Measured cost of the transparent path in the reference
implementation: **90 µs versus 65 µs**, a +38 % mesher cost that only chunks containing transparent
blocks pay. **Only `occ_ao` is uploaded to the GPU**; the other two are CPU-side mesher intermediates, so
the VRAM figure in §5.3.6 is unaffected.

**Face emission rules, stated exactly:**

| This face's class | Neighbour | Emitted? |
|---|---|---|
| Opaque | opaque, full coverage | No |
| Opaque | cutout, translucent, air, or partial coverage | Yes |
| Cutout | anything | Yes (cutout never occludes) |
| Translucent | **same render material**, full coverage | No — a body of water has no internal faces |
| Translucent | different material (incl. other translucent), air | Yes — glass against water shows both |

**Three passes, chosen by a `PassClass` on `MeshPrim` (not a content branch — one material, three
pipeline specialisations):**

| Class | Bevy phase | Prepass | Shadow | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Opaque` | `Opaque3d` | yes | yes | The overwhelming majority |
| `Cutout` | `AlphaMask3d` | yes | yes | Leaves, grates, fringe; alpha-test threshold is a material-row field |
| `Translucent` | `Transparent3d` | no | **no** (a shadow-casting pane of glass is wrong) | Depth-write off; back faces then front faces as two draws per chunk |

**No order-independent transparency.** Bevy ships none, weighted-blended OIT desaturates, and the
per-chunk two-draw back-then-front ordering plus Bevy's per-entity distance sort is correct for the
overwhelmingly common cases (a window, a pool surface, a canopy). The known limitation, stated rather
than hidden: two translucent surfaces of *different* materials inside one chunk at overlapping depths
may sort wrongly. That is a P8 ship-interior concern (a glass cockpit inside a glass dome) and the
reversal cost is contained — OIT is a pass change, not an ABI change. Ledger it.

**Water is a block.** A translucent material with an animated scroll offset and a depth-based absorption
term, both material-row parameters. A flat sea surface is exactly the geometry greedy merging is best at
(the 64× column of §5.6.3), so an ocean costs almost nothing in quads. Underwater tinting is a
camera-side full-screen effect, not geometry. Fluid *flow* simulation is out of §5's scope entirely.

**Across the ladder, transparency is the cheapest thing on it, and it needs no new machinery.** A
coarse cell's pass class follows from its dominant material (§5.5.4), so an ocean at tier 5 is a
128 m-cell flat sheet — exactly the geometry greedy merging is best at, the 64× column of §5.6.3 — and
a 100 km sea view costs a handful of quads. Cutout behaves correctly by disappearing: a 1 m grate hole
loses the dominant-material vote to the hull around it at tier ≥ 1, which is right, because a 2 m hole
at 786 m is under three pixels. And because **`PassClass` is already a per-`MeshPrim` split rather than
a per-chunk property**, a chunk that has a translucent prim at one rung and none at the next is not a
special case: that prim's dither ramp simply has no partner and fades against the background, which is
what a dither ramp does. The one known limitation is unchanged and does not worsen — two translucent
surfaces of different materials at overlapping depths inside one chunk may sort wrongly — and it gets
*rarer* with tier, because coarse translucent surfaces are large, few and far apart.

**`color_rgba` is retained on `MeshPrim` and is meaningful only on the `Proxy` arm.** The VU realm-proxy
path (translucent boundary boxes and shells) is the type's original consumer and keeps working
byte-identically. On `Voxel`, `Detail` and `Shaped` streams the field is ignored: per-material colour
lives in the material storage row, where it is data addressed by index rather than a per-prim constant.
A debug assertion in the Tier-A producer tests fixes it to a sentinel on voxel streams so nobody starts
using it.

### 5.8 Ambient occlusion

AO is what makes a blocky world read as lit rather than flat-shaded, and it is in direct tension with
everything §5.6 paid to preserve.

**Why baking it into greedy vertices breaks merging.** The 0fps rule is that you may only merge facets
whose four vertex AO values are identical. Vertex AO is
`if side1 && side2 { 0 } else { 3 − (side1 + side2 + corner) }`, plus a quad flip when
`a00 + a11 > a01 + a10` to avoid interpolation anisotropy. On any non-flat surface the AO pattern changes
cell to cell, so the merge predicate fragments quads back toward the culled count. The ecosystem's three
answers are all bad trades: cgerikj's binary-greedy-meshing v2 **deleted AO entirely** to keep merging;
`bevy_voxel_world` **abandoned merging entirely** to keep AO; TanTan keeps both by putting a 9-bit 3×3
neighbourhood pattern into the merge key (`ao_index | (block_type << 9)`), which is correct and
branch-free but fragments quads on any non-flat surface.

| Option | Merge cost | Extra GPU resources | Look | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Merge-key AO (TanTan) | Severe on terrain | None | Correct blocky corner shading, per-vertex bilinear | **Fallback only** |
| Per-texel AO baked into a per-chunk atlas (Veloren-style) | None | A texture allocation + upload **per chunk, on every edit** | Best static quality | **Reject** — the per-edit cost is worse than what it replaces and it collides with §5.1.3's upload budget |
| **Fragment-shader AO from the occupancy bitmask** | **None** | The sparse `occ_ao` slab, already built in the mesher | Smoother than per-vertex bilinear; no quad-flip hack; **lane-agnostic** (§4.5.5) | **Recommend as the target** |
| Screen-space GTAO / Bevy `ScreenSpaceAmbientOcclusion` | None | A full-screen pass | Different, non-blocky look; misses contact darkening at grazing angles | **Recommend as the P4 stopgap** |

**Why the bitmask option wins.** `occ_ao` is built anyway in the mesher and is pure integer data;
evaluating the 0fps rule per-fragment decouples AO from merging completely, restores full merge
efficiency, sidesteps the quad-flip anisotropy hack, and — per §4.5.5 — is the only option correct across
the cube/shaped lane boundary without giving up (godot_voxel's shipped compromise marks non-cube models
AO-inert, which halos every wedge). The same mask feeds a DDA raycast that skips 64 empty cells per test.

**The slab is sparse, and that is what makes ships affordable.** A dense 64³ 1-bit mask is exactly
32 KiB. Store it as parry's `Voxels` does — 8³ sub-blocks of 512 B, allocating only non-empty ones.
The resident set is the tiers-0-and-1 set below: **2,273 chunks, ≤ 71 MiB dense and ~45 MiB sparse**
(§5.3.6) — ~~"a 900-chunk terrain horizon is ≤ 29 MiB"~~ was the superseded single-tier figure. A
10,000-block ship interior occupies ~20 sub-blocks = **10 KiB**,
which is the answer to "62³ chunks are wasteful for small ships". **Chunk size stays 62³ everywhere** — a
per-shard-kind chunk size would be an HR3 violation (G-NO-SHARD-FORK), and the const generic §5.9
reserves is for a *detail tier*, a different input to the same code on the same shard, not a fork.

**The per-draw route.** The mesh *instance index* cannot be used: it is assigned by Bevy's batching and
binning in the render world, and the application neither controls nor observes its ordering, so an
app-side buffer cannot be built to match it. The correct mechanism is **`MeshTag(u32)`**, Bevy 0.18's
app-controlled per-instance `u32` readable in the shader without leaving the standard path (§6.5
independently inventories it). `MeshTag` = the chunk's row index; the row carries `ao_slot`,
`origin_local`, `realm_salt` and `biome`. No bindless, no per-chunk bind group, no
`PARTIALLY_BOUND_BINDING_ARRAY`. Bundled into the same pre-freeze spike as §5.3.4's bindless question.

**Sampling at rims, which is where the geometry moved.** A baked warp displaces the interpolated
position by up to 0.20 m, so a naive `floor(world_pos)` AO lookup can index a neighbouring cell and
produce a hard discontinuity precisely along the silhouette the warp exists to soften. Closed exactly:
warped quads are always 1×1 `Detail` quads (§5.6.3), and the `Detail` stream's `aux` field carries the
**unwarped 18-bit cell index** (§5.2.2), so the AO sample cell is a constant per rim quad rather than a
function of the displaced position. Interior `Voxel` quads are never warped, so their interpolated
position is exact and needs nothing.

**AO across the ladder — a hand-off, not a cut.** The slab's size is tier-invariant (62³ bits per
chunk), so uploading it at every rung costs 6,821 × 32 KiB = **213 MiB** to draw contact shading on
128-metre cells. **Ruling — and it is expressed as a derived rule rather than as a literal tier list,
so that §5's own generic law reaches it too:**

```
the occupancy slab is built, uploaded and sampled for a chunk iff  2^L ≤ ao_max_cell_size_m
RenderTuning::ao_max_cell_size_m : f32, default 2.0 m   ⇒  tiers 0 and 1
ChunkHeader.ao_slot carries the ABSENT SENTINEL for every chunk that fails the test
```

That is **2,273 chunks, ≤ 71 MiB dense and ~45 MiB sparse** (§5.3.6's table) at the default. The
justification is not the budget. AO is contact darkening at *block* scale; at tier 2 a "block" is 4 m,
and darkening the corner where two 4 m cells meet is not ambient occlusion of anything real, it is a
four-metre dark band painted on a hillside. The occlusion that *is* real at that scale — a valley in
the shadow of a ridge — is captured exactly by the analytic coarse-height horizon term of §5.9.6, which
is a different and strictly better mechanism. **AO strength ramps linearly to zero across the
tier-1/tier-2 crossfade band, using `RenderTuning::crossfade_band_fraction` — the one shared field
(§5.9.5), never a second one.** So per-cell AO covers tiers 0–1, the horizon term covers tiers ≥ 2, and
they meet inside the band where the same dither ramps one into the other.

**Note that `occ_ao`'s threshold is deliberately a *different* threshold from §4.3.2's coarsening
rule 1.** A shaped cell sets `occ_ao` when `volume_units ≥ CELL_VOLUME_UNITS / 2` (98,304 of 196,608);
coarsening's rule is *non-empty*, not half-full. `occ_ao` is a shading term where over-occlusion is the
visible error; coarsening is a silhouette term where under-occupancy is. Two thresholds, two failure
modes, and neither may be "unified" into the other.

Two happy alignments fall out for free: the `aux` unwarped-cell-index trick is needed only where the
warp is expressed, which is the same tiers 0–1 (§5.6.7), so no rung ever has AO without the cell index
it needs; and Bevy's SSAO is screen-space, so the P4 stopgap covers every rung at no extra cost.

That also sharpens the case against the merge-key fallback. If merge-key AO were ever taken, the AO
pattern would enter the merge key at **every** rung, fragmenting coarse quads exactly where the ladder's
whole saving lives. The bitmask path was already recommended; the ladder makes the fallback worse.

**Ship order.** P4 lands with Bevy's SSAO (one line) so the first planet does not look flat; the bitmask
path lands at P6 alongside the block-edit loop that needs the mask uploaded anyway. Merge-key AO stays
documented as the fallback if the storage-buffer binding proves intractable under a future Bevy release.
