### 5.9 The detail ladder

This subsection used to be called *"the no-LOD collision, and the orbital view"* and its job was to
describe a wall honestly and route the question elsewhere. Addendum 2 removed the wall. Its job now is
to specify the ladder, price it, prove its seams, and discharge the two user decisions it was holding.

#### 5.9.1 The table that used to justify the wall, now read in the other direction

The old arithmetic was correct and is kept, relabelled as **the cost of *not* having a ladder**:

| Eye altitude | Horizon | Surface chunk columns, single tier | Step vs. ground |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.7 m | 741 m | **449** | 1× |
| 10 m | 1,798 m | 2,642 | 5.9× |
| 100 m | 5,687 m | 26,409 | 59× |
| 1,000 m | 18,009 m | 262,634 | **585×** |
| 5,000 m | 40,518 m | 1,281,653 | **2,854×** |

~~"Vertex bytes at ground level are 288 MB (V0), 176 MB (V1), 16 MB (V2). All three are affordable.
Multiply any of them by 585 and none is. That is the honest finding, and it reframes §5.2: the vertex
format does not solve the altitude problem — no vertex format does. Altitude is structurally impossible
at every format."~~ **Retracted.** The clause doing the work was "single tier". With the ladder, the
finest resident rung at altitude `h` is `L_min = ⌈log₂(h / 786)⌉` — everything finer is under two
pixels per cell and is simply never requested — so **altitude is a discount, not a multiplier**:

| Eye altitude | Finest resident rung | Rungs carried to 100 km | Resident columns | Single-tier equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.7 m | 0 | 8 | **3,158** | 449 (for 1/135 of the view) |
| 100 m | 0 | 8 | 3,158 | 26,409 |
| 1 km | 1 | 7 | 2,779 | 262,634 |
| 5 km | 3 | 5 | 2,021 | 1,281,653 |
| 10 km | 4 | 4 | 1,642 | 7,927,749 |

The expensive case is not altitude. It is **fast flight at eye height**, where every rung is resident
at once and the ingest rate (§5.1.3) is at its maximum — a hovering gunship, not a spacecraft.

#### 5.9.2 The ladder, and how a rung is chosen

One rung is one power of two. At tier `L` a cell is `2^L` metres and a chunk is still **62³ cells**, so
it covers `62·2^L` metres. The chunk container, the palette, the mesher, the material tables and the
shape catalogue are identical at every rung (§5.1.4).

**Rung selection is the existing angular-size AoI rule applied one level down**, not a second
scheduler: *pick the rung whose cells subtend a fixed number of pixels on screen.* With a target of `k`
pixels per cell and a per-pixel angle `θ_px`, rung `L` is used out to

```
R_L = 2^L / (k · θ_px)
```

**There is ONE per-pixel angle, ONE range formula and ONE reference screen in this document, and they
live here.** Every field is on the render tuning struct — runtime-adjustable for the tuning overlay,
never a literal — and §6 and §7 *read* them rather than defining their own:

```rust
render_width_px:      u32,    // reference screen: 1920
render_height_px:     u32,    // reference screen: 1080
fov_h_rad:            f32,    // reference screen: 1.2217 (70 degrees HORIZONTAL)
px_per_cell_target:   f32,    // 2.0
text_cap_px_min:      f32,    // 8.0 — the legibility primitive §6 and §7 both derive from
```

```
θ_px = fov_h_rad / render_width_px            // ON AXIS. 6.363e-4 rad at the reference screen.
R_L  = 2^L / (px_per_cell_target · θ_px)      // 785.8 m · 2^L  ⇒  786 m at rung 0.
θ_text_min = text_cap_px_min · θ_px           // 5.090e-3 rad at the reference screen.
```

**One calibration note, stated once and used in NO arithmetic:** the screen-edge worst case is
`2·tan(fov_h_rad/2) / render_width_px = 7.294 × 10⁻⁴ rad`, 14.6 % tighter than the on-axis value. That
is *why* `px_per_cell_target` defaults to 2.0 rather than 1.75. It is not a second formula, and
~~`685 · 2^L`~~ appears nowhere else in this document. (The draft's "both are kept because they bracket
the truth" is struck: two ranges that no other section's arithmetic uses is how a design ends up with
two ladders.) Every existing figure survives unchanged — `θ_px = 6.363e-4`, `R_0 = 786 m`, 505 tier-0
columns, 379 per rung above, 3,158 columns and 6,821 chunks at 100 km.

| Rung | Cell | Chunk span | Used out to (on axis) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 m | 62 m | 786 m |
| 1 | 2 m | 124 m | 1.57 km |
| 2 | 4 m | 248 m | 3.14 km |
| 3 | 8 m | 496 m | 6.29 km |
| 4 | 16 m | 992 m | 12.6 km |
| 5 | 32 m | 1.98 km | 25.2 km |
| 6 | 64 m | 3.97 km | 50.3 km |
| 7 | 128 m | 7.94 km | **100.6 km** |

#### 5.9.3 What it costs, and the one number Addendum 2 left ambiguous

Each rung occupies an annulus between its own range and the previous rung's, and the arithmetic falls
out constant: the annulus area grows by four and the chunk footprint grows by four, so **every rung
above the first holds about 379 chunk columns whatever rung it is.** Tier 0 is a disc and holds 505.

| View distance | Without tiers (columns) | With tiers | Rungs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 786 m | 505 | 505 | 1 |
| 1.6 km | 2,019 | 884 | 2 |
| 6.3 km | 32,300 | 1,642 | 4 |
| 25 km | 517,000 | 2,400 | 6 |
| 100 km | 8,170,000 | **3,158** | 8 |

At three vertical chunks per column at tier 0 and two above: `505×3 + 7×379×2` = **6,821 chunks** for a
100 km view. **Visible chunk count now grows with the logarithm of view distance instead of its
square.**

**The reconciliation this section owes.** Addendum 2 quotes "about 270 MB of mesh at the packed vertex
format" for 6,800 chunks, which implies ~39.7 KB/chunk ≈ **5,000 quads/chunk** at 8 B/quad. This
section's measured figure is **2,200 quads/chunk** (0fps's 1.3× merge ratio on noisy terrain against
the culled count, §5.2.1). Both are right about different chunks: 2,200 is measured natural terrain,
5,000 is a fair allowance for high-relief or heavily-built ones. Quote both, always:

| 100 km view, 6,821 chunks — **raw, before §5.3.6's relief/excavation headroom** | 2,200 quads/chunk (measured) | 5,000 quads/chunk (conservative) |
|---|---|---|
| **V1**, 88 B/quad | 194 KB/chunk → 1,320 MB | 440 KB/chunk → **2,999 MB** |
| **V2**, 8 B/quad | 17.6 KB/chunk → 120 MB | 40.0 KB/chunk → **273 MB** |

Addendum 2's 270 MB is the **V2 conservative** figure and it is correct. **Both numbers are quoted
everywhere, always, labelled** — 2,200 is *measured* natural terrain (0fps's 1.3× merge ratio against
the culled count), 5,000 is the *conservative* allowance for high-relief or heavily-built chunks — and
§3.7.2's storage table carries both columns for the same reason. The same allowance at V1 is
3.0 GB — the entire VRAM cap. So the precise form of row 21's de-escalation is:

> **The ladder dissolves the planet-size constraint at every vertex format. It dissolves the 100 km
> flight view only at V2.** On foot, at any planet size, V1 is comfortable (§5.3.6's 1.41 GiB).

Stated with the three qualifiers, because "only at V2" is doing real work: at the **measured** 2,200
quads/chunk, V1's 100 km residency fits the VRAM cap at 1080p with 0.44 GiB spare (§5.3.6) — but it
does **not** fit at the conservative allowance, it does **not** fit at 4K, and the **upload** budget
fails at V1 under motion regardless of either (§5.2.3). So the VRAM question is "tight and
resolution-dependent" and the bandwidth question is "breached"; they point the same way and V2 answers
both.

**A width problem raised here and SETTLED elsewhere, because the field is persisted.** The ladder as
specified above is eight rungs. But the ladder's *true* top rung is data-derived, not eight: it is the
rung at which one chunk covers a whole cube face, `2^L ≥ N/62`. For a 162 km body (`N = 253,952`) that
is **L = 12**; for Earth (`N = 10,007,544`) it is **L = 18**; for the largest addressable body it is
**L = 20**. Three bits are exactly enough for a 100 km view and short for a planet seen from space
(§5.9.8).

> **RULED, and §5 records the outcome rather than re-arguing it: the tier field is FIVE bits at
> `ChunkKey` bits 60..56** — `sector 3 | tier 5 | a 20 | b 20 | c 10` = **58 of 64 bits used, SIX
> reserved** (MUST be zero; decode rejects non-zero). Five bits give 0..=31 with eleven values to
> spare; the legal ceiling for any given body is its own `tier_depth`, which §3 derives as
> `ceil(log2 m) + 1` — the face-covering rung, plus one. ~~"widen `detail_tier` to 5 bits, taken from
> `ChunkKey`'s 16 zero-checked reserved bits"~~ is struck in its *provenance*, not its conclusion:
> §3.3.6's layout leaves **seven** reserved bits, not sixteen, and taking one of them leaves six —
> still free, because they are already asserted zero on decode. ~~`ChunkKey` bits 18..16~~ is a layout
> §3.3.6 explicitly struck and §5 no longer cites it.
>
> The decision itself is **register row 1 / one-way door 14** (the chunk address bit layout, taken in
> the same session as rows 2 and 37, because all three are written into the first world that is ever
> saved). §5's contribution to it is the arithmetic above and §5.9.8's recommendation; the choice is
> the owner's. **Effectively a one-way door once P6 persists a pyramid.**

#### 5.9.4 Seams — skirts, and the bound that makes them provable

Where a fine chunk meets a coarse one the surfaces do not exactly agree, so there is a crack. Addendum
2 §C.5 rules for **skirts**: each chunk emits a short downward apron around its border, hiding the
crack behind geometry that is never seen from above.

**The decisive argument is not "about twenty lines".** It is that vertex snapping and transvoxel make
the emitted geometry **a function of the viewer**, and skirts keep it a pure function of
`(chunk address, tier)`. Three things depend on that:

- **Meshing stays a function of the world**, so the same code can run on the server. A viewer-dependent
  mesh cannot.
- **A camera pan cannot trigger a remesh storm.** At the tier-0/tier-1 boundary there are
  `2π·786/62 ≈ 80` columns; a scheme in which a chunk's border geometry depends on its neighbour's rung
  re-meshes those columns' border chunks every time the boundary sweeps them — at 100 m/s that is
  roughly 80 chunk re-meshes per second of pure waste, plus their upload, and it scales with speed
  exactly when the budget is already tightest.
- **The mesh-cache question stays closed** (§5.1.3), because the emitted mesh still depends only on the
  chunk and its apron.

**The skirt's height is a computed bound, not a guess.** This is the one canonical formula — it is the
only one of the three that were in circulation that accounts for `A_max`, and the two that did not
(`2^(L+1)` metres unconditionally, and "≈ 3 cells at every tier") are both §3.5.6's error bound
evaluated at `k_rough = 0.5` with the rim-warp displacement omitted:

```
skirt_drop_m(chunk at tier L) =
      ( relief_max(chunk.column_footprint, L + 1)   // max − min solid height over ONE cell of the
                                                    // NEXT COARSER rung, from the DERIVED min/max
                                                    // relief pyramid (§3.5.2)
      + A_max )                                     // registry MAXIMUM rim-warp amplitude, metres
      × skirt_safety                                // render-tuning field, default 1.25

// Closed-form conservative fallback when the relief pyramid is not resident, from §3.5.6's bound:
relief_max(_, L+1)  ≤  4 · k_rough · 2^(L+1)
  ⇒ skirt_drop_m  ≤  (4 · k_rough · 2^(L+1) + A_max) · skirt_safety
  ⇒ at k_rough = 0.5 and A_max = 0.20 m that is ~5 cells at every rung.

// What ChunkHeader.skirt_drop carries, in the chunk's OWN cell units, 8.8 fixed point:
skirt_drop_cells = ceil(skirt_drop_m / 2^L)
```

**Skirts are emitted UNCONDITIONALLY on the FOUR LATERAL borders only.** §4.5.8's ruling that a tier is
assigned per chunk *column* stands, so vertical neighbours are always at the same rung and the top and
bottom borders need no apron — a free 33 % saving. Skirt quads are single-sided and outward-facing and
carry the **SKIRT bit**, so decoration (§6) and AO skip them.

**Why the bound suffices — Nanite's crack-freeness principle, stripped of Nanite.** Nanite is watertight
under any cut because it locks shared group boundaries and makes error monotonic up the hierarchy. We
need no DAG, only the same *property*: **the coarse surface must be a conservative envelope of the fine
surface it replaces at the boundary.** Octave dropping supplies it — the coarse height is the fine
height's low-pass, so over a coarse cell it lies between the fine height's min and max. Combined with
per-face outward containment (§5.6.2), which proves the warp only ever moves a surface inward, **the
crack can open only downward**, and downward is what a skirt closes. ∎

Two honesty notes on that argument, both of which turn into tests rather than assertions:

1. The envelope property is **empirically true for zero-mean fBm and is not a theorem** — it requires
   the dropped octaves to attain both signs somewhere within the coarse cell, which holds for
   band-limited noise over a region larger than its own wavelength but is not guaranteed pointwise, and
   would need re-checking if a domain warp were ever added. **So it is a property test**: over random
   seeds and random coarse cells, assert `min_fine ≤ h_coarse ≤ max_fine`. It fails before the cracks
   appear, which is the whole point of writing it.
2. `skirt_safety` exists to cover the residual. It is a field, not a fudge, and its value is asserted
   against the property test's measured margin rather than tuned by eye.

**The relief envelope has exactly one home, and it is not this section's and not a persisted one.** It
is §3.5.2's per-(tier, chunk column) min/max structure — two `u16` at the coarse levels and, at the
finest level, the child extremes normalised into the parent's range as two `u8` (CDLOD's encoding,
~45× smaller than a naive node struct, ~3.5 MiB for a 32K×32K field). It is **derived and never
persisted**: a pure function of the seed and the edit pyramid, recomputable at any time, and therefore
outside the format-freeze problem entirely. Two consequences a reader who remembers the alternatives
needs told: the `column_relief` redb table §2.7 reserved is **struck**, and persisting a min/max pair
*inside* the pyramid entry (§8 decision 37(a) option A2) is **rejected** — min/max solid height is a
per-*column* quantity and a pyramid entry is a per-*cell* record, so it would replicate up to 62× per
column, and it is exactly reconstructible from the generator unioned with the pyramid entries anyway.
37(a)'s real point — that the envelope is what makes skirts *provably* sufficient rather than hoped —
survives in full; only its storage home changes.

**And there are TWO proof obligations here, not one, and they are not duplicates:**
`terrain_tier_agreement` (§3.5.4 rule 10 / §3.5.6) asserts `|h(dir,L) − h(dir,0)| < 4·k_rough·2^L`,
which **bounds the magnitude** of the disagreement; the envelope property test above asserts
`min_fine ≤ h_coarse ≤ max_fine`, which **fixes the sign** — it is what proves the crack can only open
*downward*, which is the only direction a downward apron closes. A skirt needs both; either alone
leaves a hole in the argument.

**Cost.** A chunk's border ring is `4 × 62 = 248` cells, greedy-merged along each side into a handful
of runs — typically under 20 quads, at most 248 — against 2,200 quads for the chunk. **Under 1 %**, and
the skirt quads face outward and downward so they are back-face-culled from above and contribute
nothing to overdraw in the common case.

**Held in reserve, and explicitly rejected.** Vertex snapping stays in reserve per Addendum 2 §C.5 if
skirts prove visible from a low grazing angle. **Per-vertex CDLOD morphing is rejected outright for
us**: it works by degenerating vertices to collapse eight grid triangles into two, which destroys both
the blocky silhouette that is the entire art direction and the exact integer world-space UV of §5.3.1
(a morphed position is not on the lattice, so the modulo stops being exact). Skirts plus the dither
crossfade achieve the no-pop requirement **without moving a single vertex off the grid**, which is a
property this design should not trade away for anything.

#### 5.9.5 No pop — the dither crossfade, and the fade-direction rule that is worth 4×

**The mechanism exists by name in the version we vendor**, so Addendum 2's "the mechanism already
exists in the engine" is verified rather than hoped:
`bevy_camera-0.18.1/src/visibility/range.rs` defines
`VisibilityRange { start_margin: Range<f32>, end_margin: Range<f32> }`, documented as *"also known as
hierarchical level of detail or HLOD"* and *"to avoid an artifact known as popping between levels, each
level has a margin, within which the object transitions gradually from invisible to visible using a
dithering effect"*. The docs even state the composition rule we need: *"the `end_margin` of a higher
LOD is always identical to the `start_margin` of the next lower LOD; this is important for the
crossfade."* It is driven per entity by camera distance, gathered into `VisibleEntityRanges` before
`check_visibility`; the shader side is `mesh_functions::get_visibility_range_dither_level`, gated by
the `VISIBILITY_RANGE_DITHER` shader def and the `MeshPipelineKey::VISIBILITY_RANGE_DITHER` bit.

Our chunks are entities and the ladder is a distance ladder, so **two rungs of the same column get
complementary ranges and Bevy crossfades them with no custom code — one pipeline bit.** The dither
wants a temporal resolve to look clean, which our TAA/motion-vector path already provides, and the
prepass sets the same bit (`bevy_pbr-0.18.1/src/prepass/mod.rs:960`) so the fade is consistent between
the depth and colour passes.

**Band width: the last 15–20 % of each rung's range.** That is CDLOD's published figure — *"the morph
area usually covers the last 15 %–30 % of every LOD range"* — and it is the number Addendum 2 left as
"a tuning field". `RenderTuning::crossfade_band_fraction`, default **0.15**, and §5.4.1's whole point
is that both rungs shade themselves with the same per-draw weight inside the band.

**It is ONE field, and here is its exhaustive consumer list**, written down so a second copy is never
declared:

1. the tier dither bands between two rungs of the same column (this subsection);
2. the AO strength ramp across the tier-1/tier-2 boundary (§5.8);
3. the prop P0 → P1 impostor dither band (§6.2);
4. the shadow-distance derivation (§5.9.6b).

**Not a consumer:** the rim-warp fade, which is a different mechanism with its own two fields
`warp_frac_on` (0.15) and `warp_frac_off` (0.05) applied to `A_max / 2^L` (§5.6.7) — numerically
similar, causally unrelated. `DecorTuning::crossfade_band_frac` is **deleted**; §6 reads this field.
(§6's `micro_plateau_frac` and `prop_plateau_frac` are a *different* concept — the plateau before
falloff begins, not a two-rung blend band — and they survive.)

**Its shipped value is not free to choose: it is bounded by the residency gate below.**

**The fade-direction rule, because getting it backwards costs 4×.** With a band covering the last
fraction `f` of a rung's range, the doubly-resident area is `R²(1 − (1−f)²)` against an annulus of
`0.75 R²`. At 379 columns per rung and `f = 0.2`:

| Direction | Extra columns per boundary | Over 7 boundaries | On 3,158 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Coarse rung fades IN over the fine rung's outer band** (extra columns are coarse, 4× footprint) | **45** | 318 | **+10 %** |
| Fine rung kept alive into the coarse annulus (extra columns are fine) | 182 | 1,272 | **+40 %** |

> **The coarse rung fades in early, over the fine rung's outer band. The fine rung dies at its own
> range. Never the reverse.** It is the ordering of two margin ranges and it costs nothing to get right.

That also fixes a gate that would otherwise pass in a screenshot and fail in play. Steady-state
residency is 6,821 chunks; with the crossfade it is 6,821 × 1.078 = **7,353** at `f = 0.15` and 7,510
at `f = 0.2`. Addendum 2 §D.3's gate reads "under ~7,000 resident chunks", which the *steady state*
meets and the *moving* case does not.

> **Restate the gate as: ≤ 7,500 resident chunks including crossfade residency, measured while
> moving.** A residency gate that excludes the transient peak is not a residency gate. **And read the
> direction of that dependency the right way round: this gate is what BOUNDS
> `crossfade_band_fraction`, not the reverse — the shipped default is 0.15 because 0.2 (7,510) does not
> pass.**

#### 5.9.6 Shadows — permitted now, and three genuinely separate problems

**(a) The cascade ceiling is a compile-time constant.** `bevy_pbr-0.18.1/src/render/light.rs:191`
declares `pub const MAX_CASCADES_PER_LIGHT: usize = 4;`, backing a fixed `[GpuDirectionalCascade; 4]`
in the light uniform and the matching `array<DirectionalCascade, 4>` in `mesh_view_types.wgsl`.
Raising it is an engine fork carried across every Bevy release. Defaults from
`bevy_light-0.18.1/src/cascade.rs`: 4 cascades, `minimum_distance` 0.1 m, `maximum_distance` 150 m,
`first_cascade_far_bound` 10 m, `overlap_proportion` 0.2 — an exponential split with base
`(150/10)^(1/3) = 2.466`, giving bounds at 10.0, 24.7, 60.8 and 150.0 m. Against a 100 km view that is
**0.15 % of the distance**, and pushing `maximum_distance` to 1 km with only four cascades makes the
first cascade cover 0.1–5.6 m and quadruples texel footprint everywhere else. Shadow maps cannot
follow the ladder; something else has to cover the rest.

**(b) A verified Bevy defect that would otherwise appear as an unexplained band of acne on the first
flight test.** `VISIBILITY_RANGE_DITHER` is set into the pipeline key in exactly three places —
`material.rs:1098` (main pass), `prepass/mod.rs:960`, `wireframe.rs:812` — and consumed at
`render/mesh.rs:2648` and `prepass/mod.rs:502`. **`render/light.rs`, which queues the `Shadow` phase,
never sets it**; it sets only `DEPTH_PREPASS`, `UNCLIPPED_DEPTH_ORTHO`, `LIGHTMAPPED` and
`MAY_DISCARD`. Consequence for our ladder: **during a crossfade both rungs are fully opaque shadow
casters** — two surfaces up to one coarse cell apart — so the shadow map receives the union, producing
double-darkening and self-shadow acne along every tier boundary, permanently, at exactly the distance
the player is flying toward.

> **The fix that costs nothing: keep the shadow horizon inside the first crossfade band.** This is the
> canonical relation, and it is a **derived relation clamped by the governor, never two numbers
> configured side by side**:
>
> ```
> // Asserted at startup AND re-asserted whenever the residency governor changes px_per_cell.
> R_0                 = 1.0 / (px_per_cell · θ_px)      // tier 0's outer range; MOVES WITH THE GOVERNOR
> shadow_max_distance = min(shadow_max_distance_authored,
>                           (1 − crossfade_band_fraction) · R_0)
> ```
>
> At the defaults (`px_per_cell_target = 2.0`, `θ_px = 6.363e-4 rad`, `crossfade_band_fraction = 0.15`):
> `R_0 = 786 m` ⇒ **`shadow_max_distance ≤ 668 m`** — four times Bevy's default and a defensible shadow
> horizon in its own right. No tier crossing is then inside the shadow-casting set, so the missing
> dither cannot bite. ~~"Cast shadows only from tiers 0–2, which the 300–500 m horizon delivers for
> free"~~ is **struck**: tiers 0–2 reach 3.14 km and therefore *contain* the tier-0/1 band (668–786 m)
> and the tier-1/2 band (1.33–1.57 km), so that formulation guarantees the artefact twice rather than
> making it not arise — and "300–500 m" is an authored literal where this is derived. The authored
> value is free to be *lower* than the cap; it may never be higher.

Two named fallbacks if the horizon ever has to exceed that bound: **(i)** put `NotShadowCaster` on the
fading-in rung for the width of the band — trivial, but the shadow itself then pops; **(ii)** carry the
dither into the shadow pipeline key, which is a small upstream patch or a fork. **D-R12 / D-RND-11
records both.**

**(c) The shadow-LOD versus visual-LOD mismatch, stated as an invariant before someone optimises it
into existence.**

> **A chunk's shadow-caster mesh IS its visual mesh — one mesh object, both passes.** Bevy gives us
> this by default; the value is entirely in asserting it, because the "optimisation" of shadowing from
> a coarser rung than the one being drawn is both obvious and wrong: a mountain's shadow stops matching
> the mountain, and the error is largest exactly where the crossfade is already working hardest. **If a
> separate shadow rung is ever introduced, it must be selected by the LIGHT's screen-space error, not
> the camera's**, because a shadow map's texel footprint is a property of the light frustum. CDLOD's
> runtime grid-resolution knob (a coarser grid for reflections and low-quality shadows) is a real
> saving and is worth having later — driven by the light.

**(d) The long-range answer, which is free, deterministic, and unique to a generated world.** Because
tier `L`'s height is *the same closed-form octave sum with the top `L` octaves dropped*, the client can
evaluate the sun-direction horizon angle at any point by marching the coarse height function directly.
No shadow map, no cascade, no memory — and by construction **it cannot disagree with the drawn mesh,
because it is the same function that produced it.** Cost: a fixed number of taps of a cheap coarse
field per pixel (the measured 12.19 ns/eval is a CPU number; a 3–5 octave evaluation on GPU is a few
dozen ALU), amortisable into a per-chunk-column horizon-angle texture updated when the chunk is. It
gives correct mountain-shadow-across-a-valley at 20 km, which no four-cascade system can, and it is the
"the generated world coarsens itself for free" argument applied to lighting. It also supplies §5.8's
coarse-tier occlusion term, so one mechanism answers two subsections.

**What it cannot capture is player-built geometry**, which has no closed form. **Builds cast real
shadows only inside the cascade horizon.** That is what every open-world game already does, and saying
so plainly is honest rather than a hack.

> **~~[USER DECISION 5-I]~~ — COLLAPSED.** The shadow horizon is **register row 41 /
> [USER DECISION 8-E]**, which absorbs this section's I1/I2/I3 options; §5 states the mechanism and the
> derived relation above and does not raise a second marker for the same question. §5's position,
> recorded there: four cascades out to the derived, governor-clamped horizon of §5.9.6(b), plus the
> analytic coarse-height horizon term of §5.9.6(d) for the whole 100 km view. ~~"~500–668 m"~~ is
> struck as a *range*: the cap is derived, and the authored value is free to be lower.

#### 5.9.7 The residency governor, and the list that must never coarsen

**The governor.** Addendum 2 §C.2 specifies a fixed 2 px/cell target. A fixed target undershoots on an
empty plain and blows the budget in a dense, heavily-edited region — and §5.3.9's evidence is that a
fixed memory target enforced by a uniformly aggressive ladder is precisely how a shipped AAA title
earned its worst reviews: dense scenes end up cut *everywhere* instead of cut where it is cheapest.
The compliant fix keeps §C.2's rule as the **target** and adds a governor above it:

```
if resident_chunk_bytes > resident_chunk_byte_cap:   raise px_per_cell toward px_per_cell_ceiling
if resident_chunk_bytes < cap · (1 − governor_hysteresis): lower it toward px_per_cell_target
```

smoothed between frames, with the crossfade of §5.9.5 absorbing the movement so the adjustment is
never itself a pop source. It is **client-local cosmetic policy**: no server state, no determinism
exposure, no fence; ~~no wire~~ — **the governor's output reaches the server only as the clamped,
non-authoritative `tier_floor` hint.** That hint is the ruled seam and its rule is exact: a client
declares `tier_floor`, the server clamps it to `[body.tier_floor_min, body.tier_depth − 1]` and
may use the clamped value for **egress selection only** — which rung of a chunk delta to send, and at
what rate a `Telemetry` channel is refreshed. No fence, no arbitration outcome, no admission decision,
no scheduling deadline, no persisted value and no simulation state may read it, directly or
transitively; a shard's trajectory must be byte-identical for every value of every observer's
`tier_floor`, and that is asserted by a `tier_invariance` fixture, not merely written down. Every
quantity of the governor itself is a field on the render-tuning struct —
`px_per_cell_target`, `px_per_cell_ceiling`, `resident_chunk_byte_cap`, `governor_hysteresis` — and
none is a literal. Tens of lines.

> **~~[USER DECISION 5-H]~~ — COLLAPSED.** "Is sharpness constant, or is memory constant?" is
> **register row 38 / [USER DECISION 8-B]** — the ladder's tuning fields and its residency governor,
> which absorbs this section's H1/H2/H3 options and §1's 1-A. §5 states the mechanism above and does
> not raise a second marker for the same question. §5's position, recorded there: fixed target plus a
> smoothed, hysteretic governor now, a user-facing slider at the first settings pass, with defaults
> `px_per_cell_target` 2.0, `px_per_cell_ceiling` 4.0, `resident_chunk_byte_cap` sized from §5.3.6's
> terrain row, `governor_hysteresis` 0.15, `crossfade_band_fraction` 0.15. Three riders ride with it
> and row 38 carries them: the governor **clamps the shadow distance** (§5.9.6(b), since raising the
> pixel target shrinks `R_0` and would otherwise walk a crossfade band into the shadow-casting set); it
> may never shrink tier 0 below `tier0_min_radius = max_tool_reach + one chunk edge`, or building stops
> working at range; and it may **never** change collision, physics or any gameplay-visible fact (the
> table below) — a cosmetic policy whose scope is asserted, not assumed.

**What must never coarsen** — Addendum 2 §C.7, restated with §5's own consequences so each line is
enforceable rather than aspirational:

| Never coarsened | The §5 consequence |
|---|---|
| **Collision. Always tier 0.** | The collider builder takes a distinct `Tier0Key` type, so `build_collider(tier ≠ 0)` is **not expressible**, not merely forbidden. This is Space Engineers' shipped invariant — *"the storage system can only write to LOD0, with higher LODs computed based on that level"* — applied to the read side as well |
| **Other players, ships, projectiles — anything that can shoot or be shot** | No impostors, no billboards, ever, at any distance. The test is **derived-from versus substituted-for**: a coarser rung of the real thing is derived-from and allowed; a picture standing in for a player is substituted-for and forbidden |
| **Signal-bearing behaviour** | A beacon's housing may coarsen; its blink may not. §7's evaluation never reads a tier |
| **Anything whose appearance carries actionable state** | Coarsen geometry, never state. A docking clamp's light is state |

And the positive form, which is the part that keeps the ladder honest: **two players at different
distances legitimately see different terrain *detail*; they must never see different terrain *facts*.**
The realm proxy is the **coarsest rung**, not an exception to the rule (§5.9.8).

**Coarsening techniques rejected, each on a verified fact rather than a preference:**

| Technique | Why not |
|---|---|
| Bevy 0.18's `meshlet` module, or any hand-rolled Nanite | Four disqualifications quoted from the crate we vendor: *"the conversion step is very slow… not suitable for dynamically generated geometry"*; *"materials have no control over the vertex shader or vertex attributes"* (deletes §5.2.2's packed ABI); *"materials must be opaque… alpha masked not supported"* (deletes §5.7's cutout lane); *"performing manual arithmetic on texture coordinates is forbidden"* (deletes §5.3.1's integer-modulo UV). Structurally, one edit invalidates an `O(log n)` chain of cluster groups, each needing a fresh boundary-locked decimation — seconds against a ~1 ms edit budget. Also MSAA-incompatible, Vulkan/Metal-only, and it forces a global forward-or-deferred choice |
| A hand-rolled cluster-culling pipeline | `wgpu-types-27.0.1/src/features.rs` declares `EXPERIMENTAL_MESH_SHADER` as Vulkan-only and explicitly experimental, and there is **no tessellation stage at all**. The dev machine would exercise a materially different path from the shipping target — the same objection §5.3.3 used against bindless |
| Geometry clipmaps | Level selection is a function of 2D distance *in the clipmap plane*, so — per CDLOD's own paper — when the observer is high above the mesh it selects far more detail than the screen can resolve, giving both complexity blow-up and aliasing. Our binding case is a ship at 100 m to 10 km. It also assumes a single 2D heightfield, which cannot express caves, overhangs, or six cube-sphere charts with a 24-record seam table |
| Baked HLOD / merged region proxies | An offline cook, and a single player edit invalidates the merge. §C.4's sparse edit pyramid is exactly the online, incremental replacement. **Take the loading order from them (§5.1.3's coarse-first rule); do not take the bake** |
| Impostors for terrain, structures or ships | You cannot bake an atlas of a base a player finished thirty seconds ago, and baking at runtime is a render-to-texture stall in the one moment the seamless law forbids one. Impostors survive only over a fixed, shipped prop catalogue, which is §6's territory |
| Authored occluder / visibility volumes | Presume a static occluder set an artist placed and a cook validated. A player can dig through the ridge that was the occluder |
| Per-vertex CDLOD morphing | §5.9.4 |

#### 5.9.8 The far field — USER DECISIONS 5-F and 5-G, discharged

> **[USER DECISION 5-F] — ANSWERED AND CLOSED by Addendum 2 §D.1 (register row 7).** The two narrow
> sub-rulings it was holding for this section are both resolved in our favour: **(i)** mipmapping is
> *mandatory*, not banned (§5.3.2, §5.3.7); **(ii)** a per-pixel shader-cost ladder that changes no
> geometry and no material identity is granted, and §5.4.1 specifies it. DEFERRED entry **D-R2**
> ("`detail_tier` reserved and always 0") flips at P4.

**5-G is mostly dissolved and the residue is smaller and sharper.** The old text said *"the altitude
band from ~2 km to ~50 km is unsolved by any option in this document and is the single largest open
rendering risk in the block system."* That band is **rungs 2 through 6**, it costs 379 columns each,
and §5.9.1 shows altitude is a discount. It is solved. The analytic displaced-sphere shell (old option
G1) is **no longer needed**, which is a strict simplification: G1 would have been a second surface
representation and would have collided with §5.3.4's "exactly one material type for every voxel
surface in the game".

What remains is a real question with a cheap answer, and it belongs to the owner because it decides
what a planet looks like from space:

> **~~[USER DECISION 5-G′, REPLACED]~~ — COLLAPSED.** "How far up the ladder do blocks go before the
> realm proxy takes over" and "how many tier bits does the persisted chunk key carry" are **the same
> decision**, and it is **register row 1 / one-way door 14** — the chunk address bit layout, taken in
> the same session as rows 2 and 37. §5 raises no separate marker; what follows is §5's evidence and
> its recommendation *into* that row.
>
> The ladder's natural top rung is data-derived: the rung at which one chunk covers a whole cube face,
> `2^L ≥ N/62`. A 162 km body reaches it at **L = 12**; Earth at **L = 18**; the largest addressable
> body at **L = 20**. And the cost of running blocks all the way is *lower than standing on the
> ground*, because from a camera at distance `d` the resident rungs run from `L_min = ⌈log₂(d/786)⌉`
> upward: from 400 km above Earth that is rungs 9 through 18, ten rungs ≈ 3,800 columns. **Orbit was
> never the expensive case; single-tier arithmetic just made it look that way.**
>
> | Option | What you see at 2,000 km | Cost | Constraint it adds |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **G1. Blocks all the way to the face-covering rung; the proxy only beyond it** *(§5's recommendation)* | Real terrain, octave-dropped to continental scale, shaded by the macro octaves | ~3,800 columns, cheaper than ground level | Needs a **five-bit** tier field; four bits cannot express an Earth-sized body (§5.9.3) |
> | G2. Cross over to a textured analytic sphere at a fixed angular size | A good sphere, but a *second* surface representation | Small | Re-opens §5.3.4's one-material rule |
> | G3. Cross over to today's flat VU proxy at rung 7 | A grey ball at 200 km — visibly wrong while the body still subtends hundreds of pixels | Zero | None, but it fails the seamless law's "grows from a dot" requirement in the middle |
>
> **§5's recommendation into row 1: G1, with five tier bits at `ChunkKey` 60..56.** It keeps one
> representation from a block in your hand to a planet seen from another star, which is exactly what
> Addendum 2 §C.1 describes, and the macro octave stack (§5.4) is what makes a rung-15 planet read as a
> planet rather than a coloured sphere. **The one-way door inside it is the key width, not the
> rendering.** Two riders the owner must see, both recorded on row 1: the per-body rung ceiling becomes
> the **face-covering rung** (`tier_depth = ceil(log2 m) + 1`), and §3.7.5's atmospheric derivation is
> demoted to a **residency** bound named `tier_view_max` — both are right, about an observer inside and
> outside the air respectively; and this tightens [USER DECISION 3-I]'s divisibility rule to "the
> body's radius step is a power of two" for any body running a full-depth ladder (the recommended
> starter world, m = 4,096, satisfies it).

The draft's sixth insurance item — *"on a 161.7 km planet the atmosphere can plausibly fade the far
field to sky before the single-tier cut"* — was correctly called out as a render-distance cut hidden by
fog. **It is now simply unnecessary**: the far field is drawn, not faded, and atmospheric extinction
goes back to being an atmosphere rather than a budget.

#### 5.9.9 What the ladder requires from §3, stated as consumer requirements

Four things §5 needs and does not own. Each is cheap now and a migration later.

1. **A per-chunk-column min/max solid-height pyramid — derived, and never persisted.** Its one home is
   §3.5.2. CDLOD's encoding: two `u16` per node at the coarse levels and, at the finest level, the
   child min/max normalised into the parent's range as two `u8` — reported at roughly 45× smaller than
   a naive node struct, ~3.5 MiB for a 32K×32K field with 32-cell leaves. It does **three** jobs at
   once: it is the traversal metric for rung selection, it culls vertical chunks (which is what turns
   "three vertical chunks at tier 0" from an assumption into a measured number), and it is the exact
   source of `skirt_drop` (§5.9.4). ~~"It rides the edit pyramid naturally"~~ is **struck as a storage
   claim**: it is a pure *function* of the seed and the edit pyramid, recomputable at any time and
   therefore outside the format-freeze problem entirely — which is exactly what lets a coarse rung know
   a tunnel exists without decompressing anything, and is a strictly better position than reserving a
   third permanent format for it (§5.9.4).
2. **The write invariant, as a type rather than a convention.** Only tier 0 is writable; every coarser
   rung is derived. `write()` takes a `Tier0Key`, so writing to a coarse rung is a compile error, and
   the negative test is `ChunkKey::as_tier0()` returning `None` for every tier 1..=31 — a real, covered
   branch under HR5, not a compile-fail fixture the coverage gate cannot see. Plus Addendum 2 §E's
   recompute-from-deltas debug command and its test-suite assertion, which is what turns "derived data
   can silently disagree with its source" from a risk into a failing test.
3. **Storage-block granularity coarser than addressing-node granularity** (CDLOD's separation). One
   persisted block serves many pyramid nodes. This is what makes §C.4's "≈1.1× the edit count" hold in
   practice and keeps redb key counts sane on a heavily built planet. A layout decision taken once, free
   now, a migration later.
4. **A pyramid-aware delta budget.** The instructive counterexample is No Man's Sky: terrain edits live
   in a fixed set of 255 buffers per save, edits outside base bounds are evicted when the budget
   overruns, and visiting heavily-edited bases can wipe a player's own edits. That is a hard cap chosen
   because the pyramid was not designed for unbounded deltas. §3.9.6's budget/revert/reap must be
   pyramid-aware from the start so we never ship that failure mode.

---

### 5.10 What this section reserves, gates, ledgers, and ships

#### 5.10.1 Reserves — free now, expensive later

| Reserve | Where | Free now / expensive later |

| `rotation: [f32;4]` on `PrimTransform` | `crates/client/src/realm_scene.rs` (Tier-A, 100 %) | A rotating planet or banking ship is **already** undrawable; adding it after four producers exist migrates all of them plus their golden fixtures |
| `indices: Vec<u32>` on `MeshPrim` | same | Without it every greedy quad is 6 vertices instead of 4 — a permanent 1.6× on all terrain |
| `VertexStream` with 4 build-bounded arms | same | Adding a vertex ABI later re-specialises every pipeline and re-covers every producer test |
| `pass: PassClass` on `MeshPrim` | same | Retrofitting three passes after the opaque path ships touches every producer |
| `ChunkHeader { origin_local, realm_salt, ao_slot, biome, detail_tier, skirt_drop }` | same | `ao_slot` is the per-draw indirection AO needs; ~~`detail_tier` is the LOD insurance~~ **`detail_tier` is now LIVE and is the per-draw uniform driving the whole material feature ladder (§5.4.1)**; `skirt_drop` is new and cannot be recomputed on the GPU; `origin_local` is what makes UVs cost zero vertex bytes |
| 8 reserved bits in the packed `u32` (4 earmarked for a 16-bit material id) | encoder, Tier-B | The material ABI is what every shader and the mesher agree on; changing it touches all three |
| 18-bit unwarped cell + 12-bit second material in `Detail.aux` | same | Both are unrecoverable after the fact from a warped position |
| `corner_key` as a seventh `GridMapping` operation | `core/src/grid/mod.rs` | Without it the warp cracks along 3.05 M cube-edge corners, and the fix is not expressible above the geometry seam |
| `A_mat: f32` (binary: 0 or ≥ 0.08 m) per material | material registry | Makes the warp/merge trade one data field; makes amplitude tunable without a code change |
| `bevel_mm: u8` per material | material registry | The chamfer catalogue upgrade (§5.6.4 / 5-E sub-decision 3) |
| `tile_period_cells: u8` (power of two) per material | material registry | The integer-modulo UV depends on it; no-magic-numbers requires it even while every material shares a value |
| `anti_tiling: AntiTilingMode` per material | material registry | Prevents building a global stochastic path that structured materials would force us to throw away |
| `emissive_rgb`, `emissive_nits`, `pom: Option<Pom8>`, 4 animation `Fx` params in the material row | material registry | Every "dynamic surface" the user might want — scrolling conveyors, damage stages, pulsing lights — becomes a parameter rather than a second material path |
| ~~`SurfaceShell` prim kind~~ | ~~render seam~~ | **WITHDRAWN.** It was insurance for old 5-G's analytic displaced sphere, and the ladder makes that second surface representation unnecessary (§5.9.8). Reserving it now would preserve a seam for something we have decided not to build, and it would sit in tension with §5.3.4's one-material rule. Deleting a reserve is the rare free win |
| `-p vd-voxel` in the justfile `tier_a` list | justfile:12 | A crate omitted from the list is Tier-B by default and its 100 % gate silently never runs |
| **A FIVE-bit `tier` field at `ChunkKey` bits 60..56** (`sector 3 \| tier 5 \| a 20 \| b 20 \| c 10` = 58 of 64 used, **six** reserved) | `core/src/grid/key.rs` (§3.3.6) | Three bits hold exactly 8 rungs and four hold 16; the ladder's true top rung is `2^L ≥ N/62`, which is 12 for a 162 km body, **18 for Earth** and 20 for the largest addressable body. Free today — the reserved bits are already asserted zero on decode (there are **seven**, not the sixteen the draft assumed, and taking one leaves six). After P6 persists a pyramid it is a key-format migration over every saved chunk AND every pyramid entry (§5.9.3, register row 1 / door 14) |
| **`tier: u8` on the P6 block/chunk REQUEST shape AND on its delta PAYLOAD** — one arm, both fields, landed together (one-way door 45, [USER DECISION 4-F]), because postcard is positional | `wire/src/intershard.rs`, the reserved `BlockEdit` arm | Coarse-first loading (§5.1.3) is useless if a client must pull every tier-0 delta under a region to see it at tier 5. It is a **payload descriptor** naming which rung the entries are at — *not* an observer property, which is the distinction that keeps it separate from `tier_floor` (§5.10.2). Today `coarsen_level` at `intershard.rs:659` is a *pose*-precision hop counter on `OccupantInterest`, not a terrain tier, and line 303 reserves a **lane**, not a field — so there is no terrain-tier field anywhere yet and no way to request one. One byte in an arm that does not exist is free; afterwards it is a `PROTO_MINOR` bump plus a pyramid re-serialisation |

The first five are the **one reference screen** every other section's angular arithmetic reads (§5.9.2) — §6 and §7 consume them rather than defining their own; `crossfade_band_fraction` is the **one** crossfade field with an exhaustive consumer list (§5.9.5); `ao_max_cell_size_m` is what makes §5.8's AO cutoff a derivation instead of a literal tier list. Every one of them is the kind of value that gets inlined as a literal in the first prototype and is then impossible to expose to the tuning overlay |

Authored data with a bake assertion (tap count monotonically non-increasing in tier) beats both an inline literal and a fake derivation |
| **`blend_width_m: f32` per material** | material registry | This is what makes §5.5.4's seam rule the *generic* sub-cell law instead of a hard-coded "tier 0 only". Free as a field; a code branch otherwise |
| **The `Tier0Key` newtype on the collider-builder entry point**, with `ChunkKey::as_tier0() -> Option<Tier0Key>` as its one narrowing point | `vd-voxel` public API | Makes "collision is always tier 0" (§5.9.7) a compile error rather than a code-review convention, and gives it a *covered* negative branch under HR5. Retrofitting a type through an API that already has callers is the expensive version |
| **A variance-aware-roughness flag in the KTX2 key/value metadata** | the bake tool + the material loader | §5.3.7. Without it, a material baked with box-filtered roughness is indistinguishable from a correct one at load, and the defect is only visible as sparkle on a moving sun months later |

#### 5.10.2 Cross-section reconciliations, resolved rather than handed off

- **The material palette, one number per role.** 65,536 persisted (`u16 MaterialId`, §4.1.1) / 4,096
  addressable in the vertex ABI / 1,024 renderable array layers (the universal hardware floor) / 128
  shipped at launch. Bake assertions: `renderable_material_count ≤ 1024` and `material_count ≤ 4096`
  until the four reserved vertex bits are spent. The draft's "12-bit geometry id + 12-bit material id
  does not fit in 5 bytes" analysis is **moot for a different reason than the draft gave.** The durable
  record's WIDTH is register row 2 ([USER DECISION 3-H] / [4-A]) and is **not settled**: §4.1.1 rules
  "the five-byte record stands", §3.9.2 recommends eight, and §8.6 item 1 recommends eight on a
  different argument (at five bytes you can have the placed marker or the mirror flag, not both, and
  both are load-bearing). What **is** settled and is all §5 needs: the persisted identity is ONE
  combined `BlockTypeId`, never independent material and geometry fields (§4.1.1), and the RENDER
  material id was never the persisted id. (~~"§3.8.2 and §4.1.2 independently settle the WAL record at
  8 bytes with a 16-bit material and a 16-bit geometry id"~~ is struck: it was wrong about §4 on both
  the width and the identity model, and §5 does not settle another section's record width in a
  reconciliation bullet.)
- **Where the warp lives.** `vd-voxel`, Tier-A, shared by client and server, covered at 100 % with the
  golden-vector table in `crates/voxel/tests/` outside the gate. This supersedes the draft's
  `vd-client-render` placement, which was both incoherent (the peel needs `A(p)` in the Tier-A merge
  predicate) and factually wrong about isolation.
- **Realm origin and salt are immutable.** The warp key and the UV phase are both functions of
  realm-local block coordinates and `realm_salt`. Therefore: **a realm's block-local grid origin and its
  `realm_salt` are immutable for its lifetime, and no rebase of either is permitted.** A rebase by a
  non-multiple of the tile period would shift every texture tile's phase across the whole realm in one
  frame; any rebase at all would re-randomise every warped corner simultaneously — a whole-world geometry
  shimmer. This costs nothing because §3.1.2's `SurfaceAnchor` is already the *float* rendering-origin
  mechanism: it moves the f32 frame, never the integer grid. `realm_salt` derives from the realm's
  `RealmPath` seed, never from a shard identity or an incarnation.
- **Meshing is gated on delta resolution.** Terrain is seed-derived client-side, but P6 edits are a
  delta overlay owned by one shard. **A chunk is meshed only when its delta state is resolved** —
  §3.9's `DeltaManifest` for the AoI cell has arrived and says either "no delta" or "here it is". Under
  the seamless law a chunk appearing *late* beats a chunk appearing *wrong* and then correcting (a
  player's house missing, then popping in). The warm-ahead ring of §5.1.3 resolves chunks well before
  they enter the draw radius; if the owner is unreachable the realm is not spun up and the player cannot
  be there. **The ladder strengthens this rather than complicating it:** because the coarse edit-pyramid
  entry for a region is smaller than the fine deltas under it and is fetched first (§5.1.3's
  coarse-first rule), the degraded state is *"coarse but correct"* rather than *"absent"*. The rule
  becomes **a chunk appearing coarse beats a chunk appearing wrong**, which is a better trade than the
  one the draft could offer.
- **The ladder is a demand-loop dimension, not a second system, and this is where that is enforced.**
  §3.7 already rules chunk generation, meshing, warm-up and residency to be phases of the AoI demand
  loop. A request is `(chunk address, tier)`; tier selection is the angular-size rule one level down
  (§5.9.2); coarse-first is an ordering constraint on the same queue. **If a second scheduler ever
  appears for tiers, that is the defect** — it is how `bevy_voxel_world`'s camera-ray world model would
  re-enter through the back door after §5.1.1 rejected it through the front.
- **THREE ladders exist and none is derived from, or converted into, another.** (i) `ChunkKey`'s
  `tier` is the *chunk-local content* ladder — how coarse this chunk's voxels are; it is what
  `ChunkHeader.detail_tier` carries to the shader. (ii) `tier_floor` on the client's AoI interest
  report is the *observer's declared floor* — a non-authoritative client memory hint, clamped by the
  server, used for **egress selection only** (§5.9.7), and never an input to any authoritative
  quantity. (iii) `OccupantInterest`'s `coarsen_level` (`intershard.rs:659`) is a *pose-precision hop
  counter* on the up-flow ("hops from the observer's home realm"), **not** a terrain tier — Addendum 2
  §A's reading of it as one is corrected in §3.3.6 and §3.10. §3.3.6 already ruled (i) against (iii);
  the ruling matters more now that (i) is live and (ii) exists, because all three are `u8`, all three
  were "always 0" in the old code, and all three are about distance. The doc comment on each of the
  three names the other two, because this confusion has already happened once in this design.
  Separately: the delta lane's `tier: u8` is a **payload descriptor**, not a fourth ladder — it names
  which rung the entries in *that message* are at.
- **What §5 hands §6 grows by one field.** Alongside the exposed-rim bit, the mesher hands the
  decoration evaluator the chunk's **tier**, which is its natural density cutoff for free (Addendum 2
  §C.8). §6 owns the falloff curve; §5 owns only the fact that the number is already there.
- **Rim classification is handed to §6.** The mesher emits an exposed-rim bit per cell alongside the
  occupancy masks; §6 owns everything instanced on top of it.
- **Dynamic surfaces are not a voxel-material problem.** The user's block-cover is §6.7's face-slot
  attachment drawn by one instanced world-space pass with server-authored draw commands — a different
  *primitive class*, not a content-kind branch in the voxel material. Every other "dynamic" case
  (conveyor scroll, damage stage, pulsing emission) is a material-row parameter. There is deliberately
  **no** per-block render-target path: Space Engineers ships one and its documented failure is panels
  literally displaying "OFFLINE" when `m_currentFreeResources` runs out.

The negative test is `ChunkKey::as_tier0()` returning `None` for every tier 1..=31 — a real, covered branch under HR5 — plus the rejected example documented in the doc comment. ~~checked by a `trybuild` case~~ is struck: **no new workspace dependency**, because adopting one to prove a type signature is a library decision reserved to the owner |

#### 5.10.5 The sustained-edit budget (P11's case, priced)

| Event | Chunks dirtied | Bytes at V1 | Frames at 8 MiB/frame |
|---|---|---|---|
| One block at a chunk corner | 8 | 3.52 MB | 1 |
| A 10 m-radius explosion | 27 | 11.9 MB | 2 |
| A mining beam, 4 blocks/s in one chunk, coalesced per frame | 1/frame | 26.4 MB/s | continuous, 5.5 % of the budget |
| A mining beam with a 3-frame remesh floor (the shipped policy) | 1/3 frames | 8.8 MB/s | 1.8 % |

The 3-frame remesh floor for a continuously-edited chunk is the policy that keeps a backlog from
converting into visibly stale geometry. It is a field on the render-tuning config struct.

**Edits and motion share one budget, and motion is now the larger claimant.** Every figure above is a
*tier-0* cost and none of it changes under the ladder (§5.1.3's Budget 1). What changes is what it
shares the 480 MB/s with: §5.2.3's ingest is 124 MB/s at 100 m/s and 654 MB/s at `v_max`, both at V1.
So the honest composite statement is that **a mining beam is 5.5 % of the budget standing still and
unaffordable while flying at V1** — which is the same conclusion as §5-B's trigger, reached from the
other end, and the reason the per-tier upload quota of §5.2.3 exists rather than a single global one.

#### 5.10.6 Ship order

**Slice 1** is the `MeshPrim` widening and it lands **alone**, while `realm_scene.rs` is still the only
producer — the only item here that gets dramatically more expensive with every week of delay, and the
one whose synthetic-arm tests double as the mesher's future acceptance fixtures. **Slice 2** is
`vd-voxel` (added to the justfile `tier_a` list in the same commit): the integer mesher, Lane A only,
cube blocks, no warp, with its determinism fixture and its `bench-mesh` gate. **Slice 3** is the Tier-B
encoder, the `ExtendedMaterial`, the integer-modulo UVs and the texture array — the first thing that
looks like a planet — preceded by the §5.3.4 bindless/`MeshTag` spike. **Slice 4** is `border_peel` and,
on top of it, the seam strips. **Slice 5** is the rim warp, which reuses the peel unchanged. **Slice 6**
is the transparency pass split. **Slice 7** is bitmask AO, alongside P6's edit loop. **Slice 8** is Lane
B, following §4's shape encoding and reusing everything above it.

**Where the ladder lands, and it is deliberately not a slice 9.** Addendum 2 §D.2 rules that two pieces
of it must land *inside* the terrain slice or they become retrofits, and §5 agrees for its own reasons:

- **Inside slice 2** (the Tier-A mesher): the tier as a parameter, the tier-`L` apron contract, the
  `2^L` transform scale, the skirt apron, and the sub-cell rule with `w = 1` everywhere at first. This
  is *smaller* than not doing it — the generator change is removing work, and the mesher change is
  three lines and a field. Doing it later means re-covering the mesher to 100 % a second time.
- **Inside slice 3** (the Tier-B encoder and material): the feature ladder keyed on
  `ChunkHeader.detail_tier`, the world-locked macro octave stack, the variance-aware roughness bake,
  GSAA, and mip/aniso sampler state. Gate L1 rides here.
- **Inside slice 4** (the peel): §5.5.4's `blend_width_m` gating, which is what keeps the seam rule
  generic instead of hard-coded to tier 0.
- **Inside slice 5** (the warp): §5.6.7's fade and the tier-0/1/2 golden-vector rows.
- **A new slice 3b, small and standalone**: rung selection from screen-space error, the demand-loop
  tier dimension, `VisibilityRange` crossfade wiring, the fade-direction rule, the residency governor
  and the shadow-distance clamp. It is one file plus a pipeline bit, and it is what makes the ladder
  *visible* rather than merely *representable* — so it must not be deferred behind slices 4–8.
- **With P6**: the edit pyramid and gate L5. This is the only genuinely hard part (Addendum 2 §C.4/§E)
  and it is the one whose format is permanent.

**The three user asks, answered in one line each.** *Big textures across many blocks* — greedy quads are
single-material by construction, so world-space UVs reduced by exact power-of-two integer masking give a
continuous 4-cell tile across a 62-cell quad with no seam and no float precision loss anywhere on a
161.7 km planet, at zero vertex bytes. *Materials blending into each other* — one shared border-peel
shrinks greedy quads by one cell wherever they abut a different material and emits a two-material ring,
so the blend width is 1 m instead of the quad size, with a free height blend and a measured 0.087 ms
Laplacian upgrade in reserve. *Edges that are not perfectly square* — a rim-only, inward-only,
integer-hashed lattice warp baked in the Tier-A mesher, keyed on a chart-independent canonical corner so
it does not crack along the twelve cube-face seams, seamless across chunk boundaries by proof rather
than machinery, provably never protruding through its own face plane, and paid for at O(perimeter) so it
retains 94 % of the merge win on a full-size quad.

**And the fourth ask, added by the ruling** — *detail levels everywhere, in the smartest way.* One rung
per power of two, selected by the same angular-size rule the realm loop already uses, so there is no
second scheduler; the generated half of the world coarsens itself by dropping octaves, which is
simultaneously the correct anti-aliasing filter and a saving, so the smart part is free; the stored
half survives coarsening through a sparse edit pyramid, which is the only genuinely hard piece and is
gated hard; seams close with skirts, which keeps the mesh a function of the world rather than of the
viewer; rungs cross over with one dither band that hides all five of the differences between them at
once; every shading feature weakens through one generic sub-cell law rather than a `match` on the tier;
and the list of things that never coarsen — collision, players, projectiles, signal behaviour, anything
a player could act on — is enforced by types and assertions rather than by discipline. A 100 km view
costs 6,821 chunks against 24.5 million, altitude becomes a discount instead of a multiplier, and the
realm proxy stops being an exception and becomes the top rung of the same ladder.

---

### Adjudicated objections

Where the adversarial review was right, the design above is changed rather than reworded. These are the
findings where it was wrong, or right about a fact but wrong about the consequence.

- **C3 (HR4 declared satisfied over an open ruling).** Not open. §3.1.4 issues the two-gate ruling
  (G-IDENTICAL above `GridMapping`, `G-MAPPING-EXHAUSTIVE` for the mapping itself). This section cites it
  and adds one clause to the second gate; it does not re-escalate a settled question.
- **H2 (worker architecture sized against the wrong dominant cost, "generation is 150–1,500× meshing").**
  The 57 ms/chunk figure comes from the per-voxel 3-D generation pipeline §3.5.1 rejects. With height-first
  generation a column-stack is 0.15–1.5 ms, comparable to a chunk mesh. The *structural* point — two job
  classes and a first-appearance budget — is right and is adopted; the magnitude is not.
- **H7 ("the 31–64× merge win is deleted").** The peel is O(perimeter): an 8×8 quad retains a 2.2× win and
  a 62×62 quad 15.7×. The warning is adopted at the corrected magnitude, and the finding's strongest point
  — that the 0.02 m hand-laid amplitude buys nothing and costs everything — is adopted outright.
- **H1 (the mesh cache is worthless).** Correct, and the cache and `mesh_key` are deleted. Its inference
  that this "weakens the case for shader-side warp to tunability alone" is inverted: removing the cache
  removes the main argument *against* baking, which is why the warp is now baked.
- **M5 (the WAL bit-budget comparison compares the wrong quantities).** Correct, and moot — but for a
  different reason than this bullet originally gave. ~~"§3.8.2 and §4.1.2 both settle the record at 8
  bytes with 16-bit material and geometry ids"~~ is struck: the durable record's width is **register
  row 2 and is not settled** (§4.1.1 rules five bytes, §3.9.2 and §8.6 item 1 recommend eight), and §5
  does not settle another section's record width in passing. What is settled, and is all §5 depends on,
  is that the persisted identity is ONE combined `BlockTypeId` and that the *render* material id was
  never the persisted id (§5.10.2).
- **M11 (horizon arithmetic 5.7 % low).** §3.7 is the authority for horizon and column counts; this
  section adopts its table verbatim and stops recomputing. The cross-reference errors (shapes are §4,
  decoration §6) and the non-indexed V0 arithmetic are corrected.
- **P3 / H10 (the 12-bit static material id forecloses BLOCK-COVER).** BLOCK-COVER is §6.7's per-face
  attachment drawn by a separate instanced world-space pass with server-authored draw commands; it was
  never a voxel-material surface, so the ABI does not foreclose it. The finding is redirected, not
  accepted. The adjacent half — that emission had no home — is accepted and fixed (albedo alpha plus a
  material-row emissive colour).
- **M6 ("`vd-client-render` is not a leaf"; "`vd-voxel` is Tier-B by default").** Both correct, and both
  were load-bearing errors in the draft: the first invalidated an isolation argument, the second would
  have silently switched off the 100 % gate on the largest new Tier-A crate in the project.

## 6. The living surface — decoration, props, and in-world panels

This section designs the layer that sits *on top of* the block field: the grass, moss, pebbles,
bushes, ferns, rocks and leaf clusters that make a 1 m voxel world read as a place rather than a
grid — plus the transparent block-cover HUD that turns any block face into a readout. It answers
"add a soil block, grass appears; add several, you get a meadow; add a wood column and leaf blocks,
you get beautiful 3D leaves".

The design thesis: **decoration is a total, pure, integer function of (authoritative block field,
authoritative growth log, world seed, universe tick), keyed on an anchor-invariant global cell
address, costing zero bytes per instance and zero bytes on the wire** — **and it is presented on a
detail ladder that is the same generic angular-size rule the rest of the project already uses,
applied to each decoration class's own feature size.** Everything below is the machinery that makes
those two sentences true, fast, and provably identical on every machine — and the decisions the owner
must take before any of it is built.

---

### 6.0 What Addendum 2 changes in this section, stated so nothing is silently deleted

Addendum 2 retracts the "no level-of-detail" ban and the "binary render rule". Both were load-bearing
in the original §6, so the affected statements are listed here with their replacements rather than
edited away. Everything not in this table stands unchanged.

| Was, in this section | Now | Why the ladder forces it |
|---|---|---|
| §6.2: "Radius is a knob that is *fully compliant* with the binary render rule: in range gets the proper mesh, out of range gets nothing." | **Struck.** The radius is now the outer end of a continuous density ramp. Nothing switches on or off at a distance, ever. | The ban is retracted, and a hard cut at 40 m is precisely the pop the seamless law forbids. §6.2's new falloff. |
| §6.3, worked example 3(b): "the cube must not be meshed"; `RenderModel::ShellCluster` emits no cube geometry. | **Struck and replaced** by `RenderModel::CubeWithShell`: the leaf cube is *always* meshed, and the cluster cards are a near rung drawn on top of it. | It hands the distant canopy to the terrain ladder for free at every tier, removes the cosmetic→mesher coupling entirely, and costs 300 triangles instead of 150 opaque backing cards. This **closes D-DEC-7**. |
| §6.8: "Synty's LOD chains are wasted under the no-LOD rule, so we import **LOD0 only — the heaviest mesh in each chain**, inverting the usual assumption that Synty assets are cheap." | **Struck.** The shipped chains become an asset: each chain rung maps onto a prop rung. Synty assets return to being cheap. | The ban is retracted. This is the one place the retraction makes the art pipeline strictly easier. |
| §6.9: "Below θ_min the panel simply stops drawing — the binary render rule gives the right answer at the far end without an LOD." | **Struck and replaced.** The panel ladder now has four rungs (C0 live, C1 chrome, C2 reduced, C3 off). The far end is C3, reached by the same angular-size rule. | A panel that is legible-then-gone is a two-rung ladder pretending not to be one; naming the middle rungs is what buys the wire budget back. |
