The second is what keeps the prop `DecoCell` tables affordable once the prop range triples. Both are free today and are a universe-wide re-roll after S1. |
| §6.10's GPU contract, **2.80 ms**. | **1.90 ms**, while the prop range grows 2.2–3.9× and the micro radius holds at 40 m on *every* tier including VD-MIN. | The falloff removes 71.9% of micro instances; impostors replace mesh triangles with a bounded fill budget. 0.90 ms returns to the frame table. |
| §6.11 **D-DEC-7** — "distant tree canopies beyond the prop radius, before the first planet flyover". | **Resolved by design**, closing at S4. | `CubeWithShell` plus the terrain tier ladder. |

Two things Addendum 2 does *not* change, and this section does not weaken to make room for the
ladder: **[USER DECISION 6-1]**'s authority model (§6.1), and §6.6's promotion boundary. The second
turns out to be exactly the line the impostor question needed (§6.2).

---

### 6.1 The decision everything else is downstream of

> **[USER DECISION 6-1] — who evaluates decoration.**
>
> Decoration's inputs are all server-authored. The question is whether the *output* is derived
> independently on each client under a byte-identity gate, or shipped by the server.
>
> - **A. Client-derived under a CI byte-identity gate (recommended).** Zero wire bytes; the server
>   can sample the same function at O(1) per query whenever it wants to. Costs: a WGSL↔Rust parity
>   gate that must never be allowed to go red, and a modified client can choose not to render grass.
> - **B. Server-authored scatter on the snapshot lane.** Correct-by-construction under the most
>   literal reading of the standing law. Costs: a minimal 12-byte per-instance record at 100/m² over
>   a 40 m radius is 502,655 instances × 12 B = **6.0 MB per player per region entry**, ~150× the
>   whole snapshot budget, and it pushes cosmetic bytes across sealed-shard boundaries (HR1) for zero
>   gameplay benefit. This option is not foreclosed by choosing A — it is simply never affordable.
> - **C. Derived, plus a mandatory server-side sampler for any value the simulation ever reads.**
>   A, with the `vd-sim → vd-decor` dependency edge and its query API present from the first slice
>   so that concealment, foliage-density sensors or fire spread can be added without a graph change.
>
> **Recommendation: C.** It is A's cost with B's escape hatch. The three properties that distinguish
> this from the floating-origin S2/S3 client-compose failure are precise and must be held: (1) the
> inputs are already replicated and the client adds no information; (2) the function is *total,
> stateless and recomputed from scratch*, so there is no accumulation order to get wrong — S2/S3 was
> an accumulating composition; (3) nothing in the simulation reads the output by default.
>
> **Why this is a decision and not an engineering call:** the standing "server does ALL math; client
> only renders" law is recorded emphatically and has already forced one rework. The section tags a
> €46 asset pack as a user decision; it would be dishonest to take this one silently. It is a
> **one-way door in code shape** (not in bandwidth): the crate graph, the gate, and the Tier-A
> placement of the evaluator are cheap now and are a whole-subsystem rework later.

The rest of §6 assumes **C**. Under A or B the rule table, the key, the growth model and the panel
half are unchanged; only §6.6's render path and §6.10's gate list move.

**Does the detail ladder reopen this?** No, and the reason must be stated rather than assumed,
because this is exactly where a standing law gets eroded by accident. The falloff of §6.2 is a
*camera-dependent subset selection with a soft edge*. The client already performs camera-dependent
subset selection — frustum culling, and the radius cut this design has always had. A ramp instead of
a step is the same operation with a continuous boundary; it introduces no new information, no new
arithmetic over authoritative values, and no accumulation. **Culling is not composition.** The three
properties above survive verbatim: the derived instance set is still camera-free (§6.2 proves it),
the falloff is a monotone selector over that set, and the simulation still reads nothing by default.
Impostors (§6.2) are the same argument one step further: they change *how* an instance is drawn,
never which instances exist or where they are.

---

### 6.2 Two tiers, three rungs each, and the arithmetic that forces them

No single system serves both "50–200 blades per square metre" and "one believable bush every few
metres". Take the worst case the storage model must survive — VD-HIGH at a 64 m micro radius, a disc
of π·64² = 12,868 m², 100 tufts/m², **1,286,796 resident tufts** at uniform density — and cost it
three ways.

| Storage model | Bytes/instance | 1.29 M tufts | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bevy entity | ~600 B (96 B `MeshInputUniform` + 176 B `MeshUniform` + 32 B `MeshCullingData` + ~110 B `RenderMeshInstanceGpu` + ~200 B main world) | **774 MB** | Dead on memory alone. Bevy 0.18's `many_cubes` implies ≈30.9 ns of *whole-frame* cost per static entity (49.47 ms ÷ 1.6 M, on a **laptop mobile RTX 4090** — not a CPU submit cost and not VD-REF hardware); 1.29 M of them is 39.9 ms of frame. |
| Packed per-instance record | 16 B | **20.6 MB**, plus 3.2 MB/s of buffer writes while walking at 5 m/s and 64 MB/s in a ship at 100 m/s | Affordable and pointless — the data is derivable. |
| Derived from an integer hash | **0 B** | **0 MB** | The design. |

The prop tier inverts it: at 0.05–0.5 props/m² the same disc holds 643–6,434 props, which a
per-instance record serves comfortably. **Two tiers, one renderer, one instance format.**

- **MICRO** — grass, moss fringes, pebbles, sand ripples, small flowers. 50–200/m² at full density.
  Geometry: a **crossed quad, 2 planes, 4 triangles, pipeline `cull: None`**, with
  Ghost-of-Tsushima-style view-space thickening so edge-on blades do not vanish. Zero per-instance
  storage.
- **PROP** — bushes, ferns, rocks, logs, leaf clusters, mushrooms. 0.05–0.5/m². Geometry 24–400
  triangles. Also derived; the 16-byte record exists only as the transient compacted GPU format the
  cull pass emits and as the shape of the sparse authoritative override set.

**On the triangle budget for a tuft.** The research pool costed a tuft at 12 triangles. That figure
assumes duplicated double-sided geometry and a three-plane blade. We get two-sidedness from
`cull: None` at *zero* triangle cost (with a two-sided normal flip in the fragment shader) and use
two planes, not three, giving 4. This is a deliberate, load-bearing departure: at 12 triangles the
micro tier is 3× over budget and the whole tier fails. It is therefore enforced, not assumed — a
Tier-A test asserts every micro archetype in the catalogue is ≤ 4 triangles, and art is authored
against that ceiling. **One-way door:** art authored to a 4-triangle blade cannot cheaply become a
12-triangle blade later.

#### The ladder rule — one rule, applied to each class's own feature size

Addendum 2 §C.2 picks a terrain tier by asking *what does a cell subtend on screen*, which is the
locked area-of-interest rule applied one level down. Decoration applies the identical rule one level
down again:

> **A decoration class is drawn at the rung whose representation subtends a fixed number of pixels.
> The class's *feature size* — a blade's height, an archetype's bounding height, a cluster card's
> edge — is authored data on the rule row, not a constant.**

There is no second scheduler, no second distance system and no branch on class. ~~With the screen
parameters as tuning fields (`render_width_px`, `fov_y_rad`), one pixel is
`rad_per_px = fov_y_rad / render_width_px`.~~ **Struck.** That expression divides a *vertical* FOV by
a *horizontal* pixel count and is dimensionally wrong. **§6 defines no per-pixel angle of its own; it
reads the one the render tuning struct owns**, on axis:

```
theta_px = fov_h_rad / render_width_px            // ON AXIS. The ONE per-pixel angle.
R_L      = 2^L / (px_per_cell_target * theta_px)  // the ONE range formula
```

At the **reference screen** (1920 × 1080, 70° **horizontal**) that is `theta_px = 6.363 × 10⁻⁴` rad
and `R_0 = 786 m` — the value §2, §3, §5 and §8's arithmetic is built on. At **VD-REF's resolution**
(2560 px wide, the same 70° horizontal FOV) the identical formula gives `4.772 × 10⁻⁴` rad, which is
the value every worked range in this section was evaluated at. A feature of height *h* subtends *n*
pixels at `h / (n · theta_px)`.

**VD-REF is the HARDWARE tier §6.10's GPU budgets are stated against — it is not a second reference
screen.** The formula is what is normative; the tables below are labelled with the resolution they
were evaluated at; and `assert(prop_range_max_m <= tier0_range_m)` therefore compares two quantities
computed from the same runtime `theta_px`, not two numbers from two screens.

Three consequences fall out and they are the whole of §6's ladder:

1. **The micro tier is a density ramp**, because a blade is never the thing you swap — it is the
   thing you have fewer of.
2. **The prop tier is a representation ladder**, because a prop *is* a thing you can swap for a
   cheaper picture of itself.
3. **Both are bounded by a residency governor, not by the pixel target alone.** The pixel rule gives
   a *ceiling*; the governor gives the shipped value and only ever lowers it. This is taken directly
   from the study's clearest cautionary finding: Crimson Desert's most-criticised flaw traces to a
   fixed memory target enforced by uniformly aggressive detail cuts rather than by adaptive
   shedding, so dense scenes look cut everywhere instead of cut where it is cheapest.

**An invariant that removes an entire subsystem.** At every shipping configuration below, the
outermost decoration rung ends well inside tier 0's range (786 m at 2 px/cell). So
**decoration is a tier-0 phenomenon**: no coarse-tier decoration evaluator exists, no coarse rule
table, no pyramid-keyed scatter. What survives to every tier is a single ground-tint term (below).
The invariant is asserted, not assumed: `assert(prop_range_max_m <= tier0_range_m)`, and if the
terrain governor ever raises pixels-per-cell far enough to shrink tier 0 below the prop range, the
prop range is clamped to it in the same frame. One assertion, one clamp, and a whole class of work
never has to exist.

#### The micro ladder, and the falloff curve

| Rung | Extent at VD-REF | What is drawn | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| **M0** | 0 → 10 m (`micro_plateau_frac` = 0.25 of the radius) | full density, 100/m², the 4-triangle crossed quad, all four phases | plateau |
| **M1** | 10 → 40 m | the same blades, progressively fewer, each retiring one shrinking smoothly to nothing | rank retirement (below) |
| **M2** | beyond 40 m | no instances. The meadow is carried by the terrain's **ground tint** | one rule-table field, zero instances |

The curve is a plateau followed by a squared ramp, in q8 fixed point:

```
x         = sat_q8( (d − r_full) / (r_max − r_full) )        // 0 on the plateau, 1 at the radius
S(d)      = (1 − x)²                                          // q8, monotone non-increasing
r_full    = micro_plateau_frac × r_max                        // DecorTuning, default 0.25
```

**Why squared, and why a plateau.** Under perspective, a ground annulus at distance *d* occupies
screen area falling as 1/d³, so holding *screen* density constant would demand ρ ∝ 1/d⁴ — the
standard result, and far too aggressive to look right in the mid field. A plain 1/d family, at the
other end, saves almost nothing. The squared ramp with a quarter-radius plateau is the point where
the arithmetic is exact and checkable: the retained fraction is

`f² + 2(1−f)[1/3 − (1−f)/4]`, which at f = 0.25 is **exactly 9/32 = 0.28125**.

That is a closed-form constant a test can assert to the last instance, not a measured approximation.
At VD-REF it takes the resident micro count from 502,655 to **141,372**, and the micro GPU line from
1.52 ms to **0.43 ms** — which is the relief the retired **[USER DECISION 6-4]** promised, now
delivered with its curve. The prop tier uses the same family with `prop_plateau_frac = 0.60`,
retaining **54.7%**, because a thinning bush field is far more visible than thinning grass.

**Rank retirement — why this is a ramp and not a re-roll.** The naive way to implement a density
falloff is to scale the density and re-test the presence roll, which re-rolls *which* instances
exist every time the camera moves — flicker, and a different meadow for every observer. Instead,
every slot carries a fixed **rank** drawn once from its own hash, and the falloff is a threshold on
that rank:

```
rank_q8(cell, slot)  = h[2] bits 24..31          // already in the ABI: the "presence roll"
alive_q8(cell,slot,d)= sat_q8( (S(d) − rank_q8) / retire_band_q8 )
final_scale          = base_scale × ease(alive_q8) × grow_in_scale
```

The presence roll was already in the output bit table for sub-1.0 densities; it now does double duty
and **no ABI bit changes for this**. A slot whose rank sits just under the current threshold is drawn
at partial height and shrinks away as the camera recedes; a slot below the threshold by more than the
retire band is not appended at all, so the bandwidth is saved as well as the fill.

Eight bits of rank against K = 128 micro slots means about 32 collision pairs per cell, i.e. roughly
32 of the 128 retirements happen two-at-a-time. Two blades shrinking together over a retire band is
not a pop, so the collision is priced and accepted rather than paid for with more bits.

**Proof that this is still a pure deterministic function.** Write `emit(cell, slot)` for the derived
instance — position, yaw, scale, variant, tint, lean, wind phase, rank — which is the existing pcg3d
evaluation and **never sees the camera**. Then:

1. **Purity.** `S` is a closed-form q8 function of one integer: the camera distance quantised to
   `falloff_quantum = r_max / 256`. `rank` is a hash output. So `alive_q8` is a pure integer function
   of `(cell, slot, quantised distance)` — no float, no state, no iteration order, no accumulation.
   Quantisation is not cosmetic: without it the comparison is a float compare and the golden test
   cannot be exact.
2. **Nesting.** `S` is non-increasing in *d*, so `alive` is non-increasing in *d*, so the drawn set
   at `d₂ > d₁` is a **subset** of the set at `d₁`. **No instance ever appears as you walk away, and
   none disappears as you approach.** That single property kills the entire flicker class.
3. **Identity invariance.** Every attribute except the scale multiplier comes from `emit`, which is
   camera-free. A blade seen at 5 m and at 35 m is the same blade in the same place.
4. **Agreement.** Two clients at the same quantised distance draw the identical set, bit for bit.
   The golden gate (§6.10 test 1) is extended to `(GlobalCell, slot, quantised distance)` triples,
   which is a wider fixture over the same machinery.
5. **Server superset.** `S(0) = 1.0`, so `vd_decor::query` evaluated at the plateau returns the union
   of every client's set. The server is never surprised by an instance a client drew.

Property 5 has one consequence that must be stated before it becomes a bug: if
**[USER DECISION 6-5]** turns concealment into a mechanic, the server must evaluate concealment at
the *observer's* distance-conditioned density, not at the plateau — otherwise a distant sniper is
told a target is concealed by grass the sniper is not being shown. The server authors both positions,
so this is one extra argument to `sample_concealment`, and it is free to reserve now.

**Where the meadow goes at M2.** The terrain material's macro-variation layer already exists (§5.4).
`ScatterRule` gains two bytes — `ground_tint: u8` (index into the same 256-entry palette the instance
tint uses) and `ground_tint_q8: u8` (its weight) — and the terrain fragment shader, on top faces
only, blends the tint of the matching micro rule row. 200 rows × 2 B = **400 bytes**, one extra
storage-buffer read on the ~1.45 M terrain pixels that are top faces, ≈0.01 ms. This is derived from
the same rule table and the same clump field that produced the blades, so it is a rung of the real
thing and not a substitute; and it removes the "bald ring at the grass radius" artefact completely.
At tier ≥ 1 the tint is taken from the coarse cell's **dominant substance** — **from the edit pyramid
where an entry exists, and from the coarse generator's own strata evaluation everywhere else**
(§5.5.4). ~~which the edit pyramid (Addendum 2 §C.4) already stores~~ — **struck, because it was
incomplete rather than wrong**: the pyramid is sparse by construction and holds entries only where a
player edited, so for unedited terrain, i.e. almost the entire surface, the generator is the source
and "the pyramid already stores it" would leave coarse terrain with no tint source at all. It is one
call — `coarse_summary(addr)`, the composition rule of register row 37 (§3) — and it is the *same*
call the coarse mesher and the pyramid walk-up make, so the three cannot disagree. A player-built
stone tower at 400 m therefore reads as stone and grows no green, with no extra data and no extra
code.

#### The prop ladder, and the impostor rung

| Rung | Extent at VD-REF (archetype height *h*) | What is drawn | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| **P0** | 0 → `32.7·h` m (`impostor_px` = 64) | the full mesh — LOD0, or, where a bought chain exists, that chain's own rungs | — |
| **P1** | `32.7·h` → the governed range (≈ e × P0's end) | a **hemi-octahedral impostor**: 2 triangles, three-frame barycentric blend, one parallax offset from the baked depth map | `VisibilityRange` dither band over the last 15–20% of P0 |
| **P2** | across P1 | the same instances, progressively fewer, each retiring one shrinking away | rank retirement, `prop_plateau_frac` = 0.60 |
| **P3** | beyond | nothing emitted; the ground tint carries the colour | — |

Worked ranges at VD-REF (2560 px, 70°), with the governor's output in the last column:

| Archetype class | *h* | Density | P0 ends | P1 ends (governed) | Resident meshes | Resident impostors |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pebble / shard | 0.4 m | 0.05/m² | 13 m | 35 m | 27 | 166 |
| Fern / small plant | 1.0 m | 0.02/m² | 33 m | 89 m | 67 | 430 |
| Bush | 2.0 m | 0.06/m² | 65 m | **178 m** | 808 | 5,163 |
| Boulder | 3.5 m | 0.005/m² | 114 m | **310 m** | 204 | 1,305 |
| Leaf cluster (tree) | 1.8 m card set | 0.01/m² tree | 59 m | **no impostor rung** | 109 trees | — |

**Why 64 pixels and not 128.** A 128²-texel frame can stay convincing to roughly 128 screen pixels,
which is the *ceiling* of what the atlas supports, not the right swap point. Swapping at 128 px leaves
3,234 full-mesh bushes resident (970 k triangles) to save fill that a 4× minified impostor gives for
free; swapping at 32 px leaves the impostor doing 4× the screen area and the fill budget collapses.
64 px balances the two: the mesh rung costs **0.21 ms** across all passes and the impostor rung costs
**0.40 ms** of bounded fill. `impostor_px` is a tuning field, and these are the numbers it was chosen
against.

**The atlas layout, and why it is one array rather than one atlas per archetype.** The reference
implementations bake a 2048² atlas of 16×16 frames per prop type — 18.67 MiB per type with mips, 597
MiB for 32 types, which breaches §5.3.6's 3.0 GiB cap on its own. They also do not support mipmaps,
so the atlas aliases at exactly the distances it is used at. Both problems dissolve with a different
layout:

> **One `texture_2d_array` of 64 layers, one layer per view frame (an 8 × 8 hemi-octahedral lattice).
> Each layer is a 1024 × 512 grid of 32 archetype tiles at 128 × 128. Four maps: BC7 albedo, BC5
> normal, BC7 ORM, BC4 depth. Five mip levels, stopping at 8 × 8 per tile so mips never bleed across
> tile borders.**

- Memory: 64 × (1024 × 512) × 3.5 B/texel × 1.29 (5 mips) = **151.5 MiB** for the entire prop
  catalogue, against 597 MiB for per-type 2048² atlases.
- **64 array layers total**, comfortably under wgpu's *guaranteed* 256-layer minimum — so this works
  on the floor device, not just on the 2048-layer majority.
- Mip-safe by construction, because minification happens within a tile and the chain stops before a
  tile is small enough to bleed.
- **One draw call for every impostor in the world**, because every archetype shares one quad mesh and
  one material. The variant count goes 32 → 33, not 32 → 64, so the indirect-loop fallback goes from
  192 to 198 calls rather than to 384.

The mapping itself — normalise the camera→instance direction, fold it onto the upper hemi-octahedron,
unfold to a [-1,1]² square, take the three lattice points of the containing triangle and blend
barycentrically, then apply one parallax offset from the depth map — uses only `abs`, `add`,
`multiply` and `sign`. **No transcendentals**, so it introduces no cross-platform divergence even
though it is float shader code. Like wind (§6.10), it sits outside the byte-identity gate because it
affects shading only; unlike wind, it must be said explicitly that it affects *no instance
attribute*, only the pixels of an instance the gate already pinned.

**The line between a legitimate coarse rung and a banned placeholder.** Addendum 2 §C.7 gives the
test — derived-from versus substituted-for — and the ban on impostors for entities stands absolutely.
This section sharpens the test into four clauses, each with a CI assertion, so it is not a judgement
call at review time:

1. **Derivation.** The impostor is baked mechanically from the *same mesh asset* the P0 rung draws,
   with the same material and the same shading inputs. Not an artist's approximation, not a
   simplified silhouette. **Assertion:** every impostor tile records the content hash of its source
   mesh; the build fails if a mesh changes and the atlas does not.
2. **Identity.** The impostor rung changes only how an instance is drawn. Position, yaw, scale,
   aspect, variant, tint, lean, wind phase and rank are all emitted by the camera-free `emit`, and
   presence is decided by rank retirement, which is impostor-independent. **Assertion:** the
   `decor_rule_golden` vectors are identical whether the instance is destined for P0 or P1.
3. **Lighting.** The impostor carries normal *and* depth and is lit by the identical GI, shadow and
   tonemap stack as the mesh. This is not decoration on the point — it is the measured difference
   between the best-reviewed part of Crimson Desert's world and a flat billboard: Digital Foundry's
   analysis of the shipped build specifically notes that distant trees are "lit and shadowed
   convincingly" rather than relying on flat impostors. A pre-lit sprite is a substitute; a
   normal-plus-depth impostor sampled by view direction is a compression of the same geometry.
   **Assertion:** a CI check that every decoration material's pipeline key is one of exactly two
   (opaque, alpha-mask) already exists in §6.8 — the impostor material is required to be one of them,
   which structurally forbids an unlit path.
4. **Consequence.** The instance has no gameplay consequence at *any* rung, because §6.6's promotion
   boundary already guarantees it: cosmetic scatter never collides, is never raycast, is never
   persisted, and is never read by the simulation except through a sampler that runs on the derived
   set rather than on drawn geometry.

Clause 4 is the whole answer, and it is worth stating as a rule because it removes every future
argument:

> **Impostors are legal exactly on the cosmetic side of §6.6's promotion boundary, and nowhere else.**

That boundary already partitions the world into "has consequence" and "has none". Anything promoted —
a harvestable `Bush` block, a `PottedFern` a player placed, a functional block, a ship, a player, a
projectile — is on the wrong side and gets the *terrain* ladder (the edit pyramid, which coarsens the
real block field) rather than a picture. Anything cosmetic may have an impostor rung. Zero new
judgement calls, and **[USER DECISION 6-6]** acquires a second consequence: answering "yes, props are
placeable" moves that prop class across the boundary and off the impostor path entirely.

> **[USER DECISION 6-8] — build the impostor rung, and at what size.**
>
> - **A. No impostor rung.** Props end at P0 — roughly 33 m for a bush, 114 m for a boulder — and the
>   mid field is bare ground with a tint. Costs nothing, ships nothing, and is the one option that is
>   visibly worse than what the section had before, because the old 80 m radius was *further* out
>   than P0 alone.
> - **B. One 64-layer array, 1024 × 512 per layer, 32 archetypes at 128² (recommended).** 151.5 MiB
>   of VRAM — 95% of this section's total memory, and **10.5% of §5.3.6's on-foot V1 total of
>   1.41 GiB (1,443 MiB), or 5.8% of the 2.56 GiB full-ladder V1 total**, against a 3.0 GiB cap.
>   (The "12.6% of a 1.20 GiB baseline" figure is struck: §5.3.6's table was re-summed for the
>   ladder.) Buys 2.2–3.9× the prop range for 0.40 ms of bounded fill and one draw call.
> - **C. 2048² per-archetype atlases, 16 × 16 frames.** 597 MiB for 32 types. Sharper at the swap
>   point, breaches the VRAM cap, loses the single-draw-call property, and — in the reference
>   implementations — has no mipmap support, so it aliases where it is used.
> - **D. Cluster impostors for whole distant forests** (one billboard cloud per co-planar leaf group,
>   built by k-means). Strictly better per byte for a forest seen from 2 km, needs an offline
>   clustering pass per archetype, and is a different *granularity* question. Not now; ledgered.
>
> **Recommendation: B.** **One-way door — but in the art convention, not in the data.** The atlas
> itself is rebakeable at any time; what is not, is that every prop archetype must be authored to a
> fixed pivot and bounds convention for the bake to be mechanical. Retrofitting that convention means
> re-authoring the catalogue, so it must be fixed before the first archetype is authored, and it
> interacts with **[USER DECISION 6-2]**.

**Shipping configuration.** All fields of one `DecorTuning` struct; no inline literals anywhere. The
micro radius no longer falls on the weaker tiers, because the falloff pays for it.

| Tier | Micro radius | Micro resident (9/32) | Micro visible (25%) | Prop range, bush class | Impostor coverage cap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| VD-MIN | **40 m** (was 28 m) | 141,372 | 35,343 | 120 m | 0.35 screens |
| **VD-REF** | **40 m** | **141,372** | **35,343** | **178 m** | **0.60 screens** |
| VD-HIGH | 64 m | 361,911 | 90,478 | 260 m | 0.90 screens |

~~Radius is a knob that is *fully compliant* with the binary render rule: in range gets the proper
mesh, out of range gets nothing.~~ **Struck.** Radius is the outer end of a ramp; the governor may
move it every frame within a smoothed hysteresis band, and nothing switches state at a distance.

**The residency governor.** Two fields and one loop, and it must be smoothed or it becomes the very
pop it exists to prevent:

```rust
pub struct DecorGovernor {
    pub micro_instance_budget: u32,        // default 150_000 at VD-REF
    pub impostor_screen_coverage_max: Fx,  // default 0.60 of the framebuffer, q8
    pub adjust_per_second: Fx,             // default 0.08 — a full traverse takes >12 s
    pub hysteresis_band: Fx,               // default 0.10 — enter/leave asymmetry
}
```

The governor reads last frame's compacted instance count and the impostor rasteriser's coverage
counter, and adjusts `micro_radius_m` and the prop range at `adjust_per_second`. It only ever
*lowers* below the pixel rule's ceiling. Because the adjustment is slower than the crossfade band's
own duration, every instance the governor sheds leaves through the retire ramp, never through a cut.
The alternative — a fixed pixels-per-cell target with no governor — is what produced Crimson
Desert's shipped complaint pattern: an 8 GB budget enforced uniformly, so raising Model Quality to
Cinematic paradoxically *worsened* pop-in for some players. Two fields is a cheap way not to ship
that.

#### The hash, and the key it consumes

Every derived attribute comes from **pcg3d** (Jarzynski & Olano, *Hash Functions for GPU Rendering*,
JCGT 9(3) 2020, pp. 20–38). Chosen for one property that outranks quality: it is **pure u32
multiply / add / xor / shift**, so it is bit-identical in WGSL, in Rust on the client and in Rust on
the server. A trig hash (`fract(sin(dot(p,k))*43758.5453)`) cannot make that promise — `sin` is
documented non-deterministic across platform and toolchain — and the paper's Figure 1 shows `lcg`
and `trig` producing visible banding.

The repo already ships a deterministic integer generator, `core::rng::SplitMix64`, documented as
"the deterministic RNG for … seed-derived world decisions … no dependency, no platform variance".
It loses here on shape, not on quality: it is a 1→1 *stream* generator that must be seeded and
stepped, whereas decoration needs a stateless 3→3 *positional* hash evaluated a million times per
frame inside a shader with no state to carry. SplitMix64 remains the harness and seed RNG; the two
coexist without conflict because both are integer-only.

```rust
// vd-decor (Tier-A, pure integer, 100% region+branch, no float anywhere).
// Byte-identical twin in WGSL — pinned by the golden-vector gate in §6.10.
#[inline]
pub const fn pcg3d(mut v: [u32; 3]) -> [u32; 3] {
    v = [
        v[0].wrapping_mul(1664525).wrapping_add(1013904223),
        v[1].wrapping_mul(1664525).wrapping_add(1013904223),
        v[2].wrapping_mul(1664525).wrapping_add(1013904223),
    ];
    v[0] = v[0].wrapping_add(v[1].wrapping_mul(v[2]));
    v[1] = v[1].wrapping_add(v[2].wrapping_mul(v[0]));
    v[2] = v[2].wrapping_add(v[0].wrapping_mul(v[1]));
    v = [v[0] ^ (v[0] >> 16), v[1] ^ (v[1] >> 16), v[2] ^ (v[2] >> 16)];
    v[0] = v[0].wrapping_add(v[1].wrapping_mul(v[2]));
    v[1] = v[1].wrapping_add(v[2].wrapping_mul(v[0]));
    v[2] = v[2].wrapping_add(v[0].wrapping_mul(v[1]));
    v
}
```

**The key must be anchor-invariant, and this is the single most expensive thing to get wrong.**
`sealed_shards.md:236` defines the chunk address as a **flat `IVec3` chunk + intra-chunk `(u8,u8,u8)`
in `[0,61]`** relative to the one mutable `SurfaceAnchor` (that document spells it `ChunkAddress`;
§3.1.1's name roster canonicalises the spelling as **`ChunkKey`**, which is what this section uses
from here on), and `sealed_shards.md:234` says every
block address carries the `AnchorGen` it was computed under, with stale-gen coordinates rejected.
`reanchor()` recentres that flat grid on the cluster centroid, so **every flat cell index changes**.
If the hash consumed the flat key, one reanchor — a routine event on a 161 km planet, and the event
PLAN.md:42 mandates a G-IDENTICAL fixture must force — would simultaneously re-roll every blade,
prop, clump and leaf cluster in the realm in front of the player. The section's headline invariant
("recompute from scratch and everything converges") would be false across an `AnchorGen` bump.

So `FrameSpace` grows one method, and it is the only geometry-touching part of decoration:

```rust
/// The anchor-INVARIANT global cell address. Never derived from a flat ChunkKey alone.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct GlobalCell { pub a: u32, pub b: u32, pub c: u32 }

trait FrameSpace {
    /// SphericalSpace: (a) = face(3) | u(24) ; (b) = v ; (c) = shell index, signed-biased,
    ///   measured in blocks from the planet's nominal surface radius. Independent of SurfaceAnchor.
    /// CartesianSpace: the realm-local integer block coordinate, zig-zag encoded.
    ///   Already anchor-invariant — CartesianSpace::reanchor is a no-op and AnchorGen never advances.
    fn to_global_cell(&self, addr: ChunkKey, gen: AnchorGen) -> Result<GlobalCell, StaleAnchor>;
}
```

The pcg3d input triple is fixed by contract and never varied per rule — **with one amendment the
ladder forces, taken now because it is free now**:

- `v[0]` = `(GlobalCell.a >> row.stride_log2)` ⊕ (realm_salt low 32)
- `v[1]` = `(GlobalCell.b >> row.stride_log2)` ⊕ (world_seed high 32)
- `v[2]` = `(GlobalCell.c >> row.stride_log2)` ⊕ `(slot_index << 8 | rule_salt)` ⊕ (world_seed low 32)

`stride_log2` is a per-row `ScatterRule` field: **0 for micro rows (the 1 m lattice, unchanged), 2
for prop rows (a 4 m lattice)**. The reason is arithmetic, not taste. Props run at 0.05–0.5/m², so a
1 m evaluation lattice is 12–20× oversampled for them, and once the prop range grows from 80 m to 310
m the per-cell `DecoCell` tables that feed the prop tier would grow to 18.4 MB. At stride 4 a chunk
column's prop table is (62/4)² = 240 surface cells instead of 3,844, and the same 310 m range costs
**432 KB**. The slot budget K = 4 on a 4 m cell is a 0.25/m² ceiling, which covers the authored band.
A row wanting sparser, larger objects (a landmark boulder field) sets `stride_log2 = 3`.

This **amends one-way door #3** (the input contract). It is free today and is a universe-wide re-roll
after the S1 golden vectors ship, so it must land in S1 or never.

Output bit assignment — **this is an ABI; changing it re-rolls every meadow in the universe.** One
amendment, also taken now:

| Output bits | Attribute | Range |
|---|---|---|
| `h[0]` 0..11 / 12..23 | in-cell offset U / V | **12-bit** fraction of the cell (was 16-bit; 1/4096 of a cell is 0.24 mm, which is 30× finer than anything visible) |
| **`h[0]` 24..31** | **aspect / bend** | **NEW — u8, signed non-uniform scale on the archetype's minor axis plus a branch-bend phase** |
| `h[1]` 0..15 | yaw | 16-bit turn in the face tangent basis (see below) |
| `h[1]` 16..23 | scale | u8 mapped into the rule row's `[scale_lo, scale_hi]` |
| `h[1]` 24..31 | variant | u8, weighted-selected against the rule row's variant list |
| `h[2]` 0..7 | tint | u8 into the rule row's tint ramp |
| `h[2]` 8..15 | lean | u8, signed lean off the surface normal |
| `h[2]` 16..23 | wind phase | u8 (§6.10) |
| `h[2]` 24..31 | **rank** (was "presence roll") | u8 — the fixed retirement order of §6.2's falloff, and still the sub-1.0 density test |

**The new byte is *shape variation*, and it is the cheapest quality idea in the whole study.** Pearl
Abyss's one dev-attributed technique in this area is placing "trees of various shapes with simple
manipulation" by varying branch and leaf geometry per instance from a single authored model, rather
than shipping N authored variants. Our version is strictly better for free: it is **hash-derived**
rather than "real time", so it is deterministic and identical on every client, and the instance
already carries a cell-derived seed. It costs one byte of hash output (taken from U/V precision
nobody can see), one byte in the packed record's former pad, and a handful of vertex-shader ALU. It
buys visual variety on the axis §5.3.6's budget is tightest on — **no new assets, no new material
slots, no new atlas tiles** — and it compounds with the impostor rung, because variation applied to
the instance transform and a shader parameter means **one impostor array still serves a whole varied
forest**.

**The tangent basis, and what happens at a cube-face seam.** Yaw is measured in the face-local
`(u,v)` basis supplied by `FrameSpace`. On a cube-sphere that basis swaps and flips axes across each
of the 12 face-edge pairings — the exact place the reference blocky-planet implementation is
documented to have broken. Three rules make that harmless: (a) micro yaw is uniformly random, so it
is *statistically* invariant and the seam is invisible; (b) prop rows needing real orientation use
`YawMode::AlignToSlope`, whose alignment vector is the gravity-projected downhill direction — a
geometric vector, continuous across the seam by construction; (c) `YawMode::SnapToFace` is legal
only on realms whose `FrameSpace` is Cartesian and is **rejected by the rule-table validator at load
time** on a Spherical profile. (c) is data validation at config load, not a shard-kind match in
feature code, so it is HR3-clean.

#### The clump field

A meadow that is not a lawn needs a low-frequency density field. It is derived from the
**anchor-invariant surface coordinate**, not from the packed key: right-shifting a packed
`(face, chunk, local)` key groups eight consecutive indices that wrap across rows and layers — a
62-stride is not a power of two — producing stripes and chunk-boundary discontinuities, not a
lattice. The correct form is:

```
clump_uv = (GlobalCell.a_u >> 3, GlobalCell.b >> 3)   // an 8 m lattice in face-local u/v
value    = bilerp_q8( H(c00), H(c10), H(c01), H(c11), frac_u_q8, frac_v_q8 )   // FOUR hashes
```

Four hashes, not one, hoisted to the *cell* level in compute pass A (not per slot), ~80 integer ops
per decorated cell. Interpolation is q8 fixed point — there is no float in the evaluator. The clump
value modulates density ×0.4..×1.6 and biases variant weights. Note that it modulates `S(d)`'s input
density, **not** the rank threshold: clumping changes how many blades a cell wants, retirement
changes how many of them the camera is close enough to be shown, and the two must not be folded
together or a distant tussock and a near scuffed patch become indistinguishable. **Seam behaviour:**
because the `(u,v)` basis changes at the 12 cube-face edges, the clump lattice is discontinuous
there. That is acceptable *only* because clump drives density and variant weighting, both of which
read as natural variation; it must never drive a spatial *pattern* (rows, paths, rings), which would
show a visible seam. Enforced by construction: `ScatterRule` has no pattern-generating field.

#### The packed instance record (transient scratch, and the override representation)

| Field | Bytes | Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| position | 6 | 3 × u16 chunk-local at 1/1024 m (0..64 m — a 62 m chunk plus 2 m for warp and shell-push) |
| yaw | 1 | u8 turn; pitch/roll derive from the surface normal, never stored |
| scale | 1 | u8, log-encoded over 0.5×–2.0× |
| variant | 1 | u8 into the rule row's palette |
| tint | 1 | u8 into a 256-entry palette |
| spawn time | 2 | u16 in **1/16 s units** relative to the chunk decoration epoch |
| flags | 1 | grounded / normal-aligned / stale / override-suppressed / **rung (mesh or impostor)** |
| lean + wind phase | 2 | u8 + u8 |
| ~~pad~~ **aspect / bend** | 1 | **NEW — the shape-variation byte from `h[0]` 24..31** |
| **total** | **16** | unchanged |

The record does not grow: the ladder is paid for out of the pad byte and one flag bit. At VD-REF the
resident compacted set is 35,343 micro + 1,106 prop meshes + 7,064 impostors + ~7,500 cluster cards =
**51,013 × 16 B = 0.82 MB**, double-buffered for async compute = **1.63 MB** — *less* than the 4.06 MB
the section budgeted before the ladder, because the falloff removes more instances than the longer
prop range adds.

---

### 6.3 The rule table: a flat table, not a solver

Placement is a **local transduction** — a cell's decoration depends only on its material, its
block-state bits, its shape class and its immediate neighbourhood — so the answer is a lookup table.

```rust
/// The packed match key. Exactly 32 bits, no spare. Shared byte-for-byte with WGSL.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct RuleKey(u32);
//  bits  0..9   material_id  (1,024 materials — matches the 10-bit block-record field)
//  bits 10..17  state_bits   (the material-interpreted state byte, §6.5)
//  bits 18..23  neigh_mask   (6-face occupancy of the outward neighbour)
//  bits 24..26  up_face      (the face whose outward normal is most anti-parallel to gravity_dir;
//                             7 = NONE, i.e. free-fall/zero-g — see below)
//  bits 27..30  geom_class   (16 shape classes, mapped from the 12-bit GeometryId)
//  bit  31      tier         (0 = micro, 1 = prop)

pub struct ScatterRule {
    pub pattern: RuleKey,
    pub care: RuleKey,               // match is (k & care) == (pattern & care)
    pub density_q8: u16,             // instances per m², 8 fractional bits — no float in the table
    pub slots: u8,                   // K: fixed slot budget (micro 128, prop 4)
    pub stencil: Stencil,            // the declared read neighbourhood (§6.4)
    pub place: PlaceConstraint,
    pub variants: &'static [Variant],
    pub growth: GrowthParams,        // PER-ROW, not global (see below)
    pub needs_sky: bool,             // reject cells with no sky column above

    // --- added by the detail ladder; all per-row, none a literal anywhere else ---
    pub stride_log2: u8,             // 0 for micro (1 m lattice), 2 for prop (4 m lattice)
    pub feature_h_q8: u16,           // the authored feature height that drives the rung rule
    pub plateau_frac_q8: u8,         // 0.25 micro, 0.60 prop — the falloff plateau
    pub impostor: Option<ImpostorId>,// Some => this row has a P1 rung; None => cards/cubes only
    pub ground_tint: u8,             // palette index the terrain shader blends at M2/P3
    pub ground_tint_q8: u8,          // its weight
}

pub struct GrowthParams {            // all DURATIONS in seconds — never ticks
    pub spread_s_q8: u32,            // bare → full for one cell
    pub jitter_s_q8: u32,            // per-cell ragged-front jitter
    pub step_s_q8: u32,              // delay added per taxicab step away from an existing source
    pub grow_in_s_q8: u32,           // the pop-free scale-up on appearance
}

pub enum PlaceConstraint {
    SurfaceCentre,                   // the shape template's surface plane, not the nominal cube face
    Jitter { radius_q8: u16 },
    ShellPush { out_q8: u16 },       // push out along the surface normal — the leaf overhang
    AlignToNormal,
}
```

Four corrections encoded here that the naive version gets wrong:

1. **`up_face`, not the grid face.** "Grass grows where there is air overhead" is a *gravity*
   statement. PLAN.md:42 names `gravity_dir` as the one shared "up" seam above the geometry seam;
   `up_face` is derived from it through `FrameSpace`. On a cube-sphere the answer is the outward
   radial face by construction; on a ship it is whatever the ship's artificial gravity says; in
   vacuum or free fall it is `NONE` and the table's zero-g rows apply (moss on every face, no
   gravity-aligned lean). Without this, the G-IDENTICAL fixture would pass while meaning "+Y" on one
   profile and "up" on the other.
2. **`geom_class`.** The block record carries a 12-bit `GeometryId` (§4). Without a shape class in
   the key, grass placed on a slope's nominal top face floats in mid-air, a half-block's tufts sink
   half a metre, and `ShellPush`'s normal on a corner piece is undefined. `geom_class` is a 16-entry
   projection of `GeometryId`, and `PlaceConstraint::SurfaceCentre` resolves against the shape's
   **surface template** (top-plane offset and normal) from the shape catalogue — the same
   render/collider template split §4 recommends and Minecraft ships.
3. **Per-row growth.** The user's brief is explicit that "each block can have different params".
   Grass, moss, lichen, vines and fungus do not spread at one rate. Moving the four growth constants
   onto the row costs 16 bytes × ~200 rows = 3.2 KB and removes four globals.
4. **`needs_sky`.** An enclosed cave floor with air above matches a naive grass rule and grows grass
   in the dark. `sky_exposed` is a pure function of the chunk's height column, which the mesher
   already computes — **zero stored bits**, computed during the `DecoCell` build.

**The ladder adds nothing to the key.** `RuleKey` is unchanged, and in particular **the rung is not a
key bit**. That is deliberate and it is HR3 by construction: a rung selects how a matched row is
*presented*, never which row matches. If the rung were in the key, a distant cell could match a
different row than a near one, two clients would disagree about *which rule fired*, and the section's
purity proof would collapse. The six new `ScatterRule` fields are presentation parameters read after
the match, and the six of them together add **9 bytes per row** — 200 rows × 57 B = **11.4 KB**, still
L1-resident on the CPU and one small storage buffer on the GPU.

**Everything is fixed point.** No `f32` in the table, no `f32` in the evaluator, no `f32` crossing
between the Rust and WGSL implementations. Exact `assert_eq!` in tests, no uncoverable epsilon
branches, no cross-binary drift.

**Matching** is not a linear scan: rows sort by `(material_id, up_face)`; a fixed 10-iteration binary
search finds the run, then a linear scan over ≤ 8 rows tests `(k & care) == pattern`, most-specific
first, first match wins. Uniform cost, no data-dependent iteration count, identical in WGSL where
the table is a storage buffer. Measured shape: ~60 ns per cell on the CPU.

| Surface | Naive cross-product | With don't-care masks | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Grass on soil | 1,024 × 256 × 64 | **6 rows** | soil→grass; soil at a vertical edge → longer overhanging tufts; soil under water → none; snowy → snow tuft; burnt → ash. Coverage scales K; it is not a key bit. |
| Leaves | 64 masks × 7 distances = 448 | **19 rows** | key on `(up_face, distance_band)` with the mask a don't-care — a leaf emits one cluster per *exposed* face, so the mask is consumed by the per-face iteration. |
| Launch palette | — | **~200 rows** | ~12 natural materials × ~8 + ~24 constructed × ~2 + leaves + special states + a catch-all `geom_class != FullCube ⇒ no decoration` row for slice 1. |

**Why not WFC or Wang tiles.** WFC solves a *global* consistency problem: it assigns over a region
so every adjacency constraint holds. Wrong shape in three independent ways. (1) Not local — a single
edit can force a global re-solve, and §6.4 exists to make an edit touch a bounded declared stencil.
(2) Not a pure function of position — output depends on solve order and the random stream, so
determinism across two binaries means replicating solver state, the exact replication we avoid.
(3) It solves a problem we do not have: "grass on top of soil, not the side of stone" is a predicate
over one cell's local key, not a tiling problem. Wang tiles are local but solve edge-*matching* for a
tile set — a texturing answer. Cellular automata are the right tool for growth *simulation* and the
wrong tool for choosing meshes. The flat table wins on four concrete properties: it is data
(diff-able in review), 100%-branch-coverable as a pure function (HR5), shareable byte-for-byte with
the shader, and cache-resident. It is also what Minecraft ships (`blockstates` JSON: `variants` with
weights, `multipart` with `when`/`apply`) and Vintage Story ships (a `behaviors` array plus variant
groups) — both at planetary scale, for over a decade.

#### Worked example 1 — soil placed → grass

1. The grass rule declares `stencil = {(0,0,0), (0,+1,0)}` (own cell plus the cell "above" along
   `gravity_dir`).
2. The dirty set is the reflected stencil `p ⊖ N = {p, p − up}` — **two cells**, recomputed from
   scratch.
3. `RuleKey(material = soil, up_face, state, neigh_mask, geom_class = FullCube, tier = micro)`
   matches row 1: `density_q8 = 100 << 8`, `slots = 128`, `place = Jitter { radius 0.45 }`,
   variants `[blade_a w=6, blade_b w=3, clover w=1]`, `stride_log2 = 0`, `feature_h = 0.15 m`,
   `plateau_frac = 0.25`, `impostor = None`, `ground_tint = meadow_green @ 0.55`.
4. Instances = `floor(128 × coverage(cell, t) × clump)` from the closed form in §6.4, then rank
   retirement against `S(d)`. At coverage 1.0, clump 1.0 and the plateau that is 128 tufts on 1 m² —
   inside the requested 50–200 band. At 30 m it is roughly 14, each of them a blade that was already
   there at 10 m, at reduced height.
5. The prop row for soil also matches at `density_q8 = 0.08 << 8` with `slots = 4` and
   `stride_log2 = 2`; the rank test passes for roughly 1 four-metre cell in 3, so a clover clump or
   pebble appears sparsely.
6. **Nothing is written to any instance buffer.** The writes are one 8-byte `DecoCell` record and, if
   the cell is not yet mature, one 8-byte growth-log entry.

#### Worked example 2 — several soil blocks → a meadow

There is **no meadow rule**. A 20 × 20 m patch is 400 cells → **51,200 tufts** at the plateau and ~34
props from three mechanisms that already exist: per-cell jitter (every cell hashes differently, so no
two adjacent square metres repeat — this is what separates a meadow from a texture); sub-unit prop
density by rank test (Poisson-ish, not gridded); and the 8 m clump field (thick tussocks and thin
scuffed patches). Storage: **0 bytes of instances**, 400 `DecoCell` records = 3.2 KB, plus 400
growth-log entries = 3.2 KB that expire as the patch matures. Walk 30 m away and the same patch is
~5,700 tufts and the ground beneath them is tinted meadow green; walk back and the identical 51,200
return, because retirement is nested and re-entrant (§6.2, property 2).

#### Worked example 3 — wood column + leaf blocks → clusters that overhang the cube

**(a) The distance field.** Copy Minecraft's shipped state: leaves carry `distance: 1..7` (3 bits)
and `persistent: bool` (1 bit) in the block record. `distance` is the taxicab distance to the nearest
wood block, recomputed by a **bounded BFS capped at 7** (a 15³ = 3,375-cell box worst case, ~200 in a
typical canopy) **on the server at edit time**. It mutates authoritative block state and replicates
on the P6 chunk-delta path — no second lane, no new fence discipline (HR3). Player-placed leaves set
`persistent = true` and never decay; decay is a deterministic consequence of the same bounded pass,
not a stochastic random tick.

**(b) ~~The cube must not be meshed~~ — the cube is ALWAYS meshed, and that is what gives us the
distant canopy for free.**

> **Struck.** The original design declared `RenderModel::ShellCluster`, under which "the mesher emits
> no cube geometry and the decoration layer emits cluster props on the shell", with an opaque backing
> card per cluster so a canopy is never see-through.
>
> **Replacement:** `RenderModel::CubeWithShell`. The mesher **always** emits the leaf cube — with the
> leaf material, the rim warp and the cutout lane, exactly like any other block — and the cluster
> cards are a **near rung drawn on top of it**.

Three reasons this is strictly better, and the third is the one the ladder forces:

1. **Cheaper.** A 5 × 5 × 5 canopy has 98 shell cells and 150 exposed faces. As cubes that is 300
   triangles. The opaque backing cards it replaces were 150 × 2 = 300 triangles *plus* they were
   alpha-mask-pipeline geometry sitting inside the cluster's own overdraw. Net: the same triangle
   count, one fewer pipeline key, and no "is the canopy see-through" question because the interior
   mass is real geometry.
2. **No cosmetic→mesher coupling.** The original had to argue carefully that the flag lives on
   `BlockDef` rather than on the scatter rule, because a render mesh must not be a function of the
   cosmetic table. `CubeWithShell` removes the argument: the mesher does the ordinary thing for a
   block, and decoration is purely additive on top. The chunk mesh stays a pure function of
   `(block field, block-definition table)` with no reference to decoration at all.
3. **★ The distant canopy stops being an open problem.** A leaf block is a block. It therefore rides
   the *terrain* ladder — the tier ladder for the generated part, the edit pyramid for the planted
   part — with no work from this section at all. At 400 m a canopy is coarse blocky green mass, lit
   by the same lighting, correct in silhouette, present in the edit pyramid if a player planted it.
   **That closes D-DEC-7**, which the original section named as "the honest edge of this design" and
   "the most jarring pop available".

**(c) The shell, the push, and the near rung.** A leaf block emits a cluster only on a face whose
outward neighbour is neither leaf nor wood. For a 5 × 5 × 5 canopy: 125 cells, 27 interior (emitting
nothing, costing nothing), 98 shell, 150 exposed faces = 150 clusters.
`place = ShellPush { out_q8 = 0.30 }` puts each cluster centre 0.30 m out along the surface normal
plus hash jitter; the cluster mesh has ≈0.9 m radius, so clusters on adjacent shell faces are 1 m
apart with 1.8 m diameters and overlap by 0.8 m — the overlap is what dissolves the silhouette, and
the leaf cube behind it is now the dark interior mass rather than a card. Distance banding does the
rest: band 1–2 large, dark, dense; band 3–4 medium; band 5–7 small, lighter, higher-jitter, so the
canopy thins toward its edge with no extra rule.

**(d) The cluster's ladder has two rungs and no impostor.** A cluster is *procedurally assembled from
the rule row's parameters* — its shape depends on the neighbour mask and the distance band — so a
baked impostor would need one bake per (variant × mask × band), which is combinatorial and pointless
when a better rung already exists underneath. So `impostor = None` for every leaf row, and:

| Rung | Extent at VD-REF | What is drawn |
|---|---|---|
| **L0** | 0 → 59 m (`cluster_range_m`, ceiling from the rung rule: a 1.8 m card set at 64 px) | cluster cards on the shell, plus the leaf cubes behind them |
| **L1** | beyond 59 m | the leaf cubes alone, at whatever tier the chunk is on |

The crossfade between them is the standard dither band (§6.7) applied to the *cards*; the cubes never
change, so there is nothing to fade against. Both rungs are the same block field, so this is a rung,
not a substitution, and it passes all four clauses of §6.2's impostor test trivially — there is no
impostor.

**Cost.** A cluster is ~11 alpha-masked cards (22 tris) + the leaf cube's share of the shell (2 tris
per exposed face) = **24 triangles** of decoration per cluster, unchanged. A 5³ canopy tree is
150 × 22 = **3,300 triangles of cards** plus **300 triangles of cube**. Inside the 59 m cluster range
a forest at one tree per 100 m² is 109 trees = 360 k triangles of cards resident, ~90 k visible,
~324 k submitted across three passes ≈ **0.24 ms** — down from the original 0.43 ms at 80 m, and the
canopy now continues past 59 m instead of vanishing.

**One cost this hands to §5, honestly.** Leaf cubes are terrain, and terrain at tier 0 runs to 786 m.
A dense forest at one tree per 100 m² over that disc is 19,400 trees × 300 triangles = **5.8 M
triangles of leaf cube inside tier 0** — a 5 m canopy drawn with 1 m cells at 786 m, where it subtends
5 pixels. That is not a decoration problem and this section does not invent a private fix for it. It
is the general "tier 0 is expensive for high-frequency materials" problem, and the rule-shaped answer
is one §5 already has the data for: **per-chunk tier selection should take the chunk's own measured
quad count as a second input to the pixels-per-cell target, so a chunk producing 10× the quads
coarsens one rung earlier.** That is still one rule (screen-space error against a budget), it is
per-chunk data the mesher already produces, and it is the exact form of the residency-governor
argument in §6.2. Registered as **D-DEC-12** and routed to §5's tier selection, not owned here.

Note the consequence for §6.8 that survives: a cluster's *shape* depends on the neighbour mask and
the distance band, so **a bought asset structurally cannot serve this class** — leaf clusters must be
procedurally-assembled card clusters generated from the rule row's parameters.

---

### 6.4 The surface a tuft actually stands on

§5 recommends a **rim-only deterministic lattice warp**, `W(p) = p + d(p)` with `|d|∞ ≤ 0.2 m`
biased inward, applied to mesh vertices at exposed convex edges so block edges are not perfectly
straight. Decoration placed at the *nominal* face plane therefore floats up to 0.2 m above a warped
surface, or sinks into it — visibly, on exactly the rim cells the warp exists to make interesting.
Neither the draft nor the adversary caught this; it is a hard cross-section coupling.

**Rule.** Decoration anchors are placed at `W(surface_point)`, evaluating the *identical* warp
function. This forces two things:

1. **One warp implementation, in one place, callable from three.** `W` lives in a small Tier-A crate
   (`vd-lattice`) depended on by the mesher, by `vd-decor`, and mirrored by one shared WGSL include.
   §5 proposed keeping the warp in the Tier-B render crate; that is no longer viable once decoration
   consumes it under a byte-identity gate.
2. **`W` becomes integer/fixed-point and bit-pinned.** §5 argued the warp is renderer-only and so
   float-tolerant. Once decoration reads it, either `W` joins the gate or decoration's anchor is
   carved out of the gate. Making `W` integer costs a handful of operations per lattice point and
   removes a whole class of ambiguity. **Verdict: integer, in the gate.**

**What the ladder adds: `W` is tier-parameterised, and decoration only ever evaluates it at tier 0.**
The warp displaces a *cell rim*, so at tier L its amplitude scales with the cell — a tier-3 chunk's
rim warp is up to 1.6 m. If decoration ever anchored on a coarse chunk it would have to evaluate `W`
at that chunk's tier or every prop would float by up to 1.6 m. §6.2's invariant makes that impossible
by construction (every decoration rung ends inside tier 0's range), so **`W` is evaluated at tier 0,
always**, and this is stated as an assertion in `vd_decor::emit` rather than left as an accident of
the current tuning values. The ground tint at coarse tiers needs no `W` at all, because it is a colour
on a surface the mesher already warped.

Two corollaries. The mesher's greedy-versus-per-face decision does not affect decoration at all —
decoration keys on the block field, never on emitted quads. And because §5's warp is biased *inward*
(the visual mesh is a subset of the collision volume), a tuft anchored at `W(p)` sits at or below the
collision surface, which is the harmless side of the visual/collision divergence.

---

### 6.5 Edit reactivity with no pop

#### Stencils, the dirty set, and the bulk path

Every rule declares its read neighbourhood as a compile-time `Stencil`. An edit at `p` invalidates
exactly `{ c : p ∈ N(c) } = p ⊖ N`.

| Rule | Stencil | Dirty set |
|---|---|---|
| Grass (needs air above) | `{0, +up}` | 2 |
| Leaf cluster (6 outward neighbours) | `{0} ∪ 6-face` | 7 |
| General 3×3×3 | 27 offsets | 27 |

**The correctness rule: always recompute a dirty cell from scratch from the block field, never mutate
it incrementally.** Recomputation is idempotent and order-independent, so replay, a late-joining
client, a re-sharded realm and the server converge regardless of arrival order. Incremental mutation
makes the result path-dependent, which is how this class of system quietly desynchronises.

**Chunk seams need a one-cell apron**: only evaluate cells whose full stencil is loaded, and
re-evaluate the apron when the neighbour chunk arrives. Same apron the mesher needs; skipping it is
the hardest-to-reproduce bug in this section, because it only manifests at AoI boundaries where
chunk arrival order differs per client.

**Prop rows widen the apron to their stride.** A prop row at `stride_log2 = 2` reads a 4 m cell, so
its dirty set is the *coarse* cell containing the edit plus the coarse cells its stencil reaches — at
most 2 coarse cells for the standard grass-like stencil, and the apron is one coarse cell wide, i.e.
four block cells. This is the one place the stride amendment costs something, and it costs four cells
of apron.

**Bulk edits are a separate path, not a loop.** P5/P6 terrain tools and P11 combat produce single
operations that change thousands of blocks. A 10 m spherical crater is (4/3)π·10³ ≈ 4,189 blocks.
Naively that is 4,189 × 27 = 113,103 dirty-record writes; in truth the dirty sets overlap almost
completely inside a solid volume, so the deduplicated set is the crater's cells plus a one-cell
shell — ≈5,575 cells, of which only the exposed bowl (~630 cells) is decorated. Still 45 KB of
records and far past the per-edit design point, and this subsection's scheduling constraint says the
recompute must land in the same frame as the remesh. So:

```
edits arrive as an EditBatch → union the reflected stencils → dedup by (chunk, cell)
if |dirty in chunk| > DecorTuning::bulk_rebuild_threshold   (default: chunk_decorated_cells / 8)
      → rebuild that chunk's whole DecoCell table on the task pool, one write
else  → span-write the dirty records inline
```

#### The `DecoCell` table, and the honest write shape

Instances are never stored; the thing an edit writes is one fixed-size record per decorated cell,
**dense and sorted by chunk-local index**, with a per-chunk free list of tombstones:

```rust
#[repr(C)]
pub struct DecoCell {            // 8 bytes
    pub packed: u32,             // 0..17 chunk-local cell index, 18..29 rule row (0 = tombstone),
                                 // 30..31 tier + override-present
    pub spawn_rel: u16,          // 1/16 s since the chunk decoration epoch — tick-rate independent
    pub state: u16,              // 8 state bits | geom_class(4) | sky_exposed | growth-present | 2 spare
}
```

- **Micro tables** (`stride_log2 = 0`): per chunk 62² = 3,844 surface cells, up to ~2× with overhangs
  and caves, × **1.25 headroom** = ~9,600 slots × 8 B = **80 KB**. They exist only inside the micro
  radius plus hysteresis — at VD-REF the 40 m disc is π·40²/62² = 1.3 chunk footprints, so ~24 tables
  resident with vertical stacking and margin = **1.92 MB**.
- **Prop tables** (`stride_log2 = 2`): (62/4)² = 240 coarse surface cells, × 2 for overhangs, ×1.25 =
  600 slots × 8 B = **4.8 KB per chunk column** — 16.7× smaller than a micro table, which is exactly
  why the stride amendment exists. They must reach the *outermost* prop rung: 310 m for the boulder
  class is π·310²/62² = 78.5 chunk footprints, so ~90 tables = **432 KB**.
- Total resident `DecoCell` = **2.35 MB**, against 1.92 MB before the ladder — a 0.43 MB increase for
  a 3.9× longer prop range. Without the stride amendment the same range would cost **18.4 MB**.
- **The write is spans, not one contiguous range.** A 3×3×3 dirty set in a 62³ chunk is 9 disjoint
  runs of 3 (row stride 62, layer stride 62²), so the honest statement is **≤ 9 write ranges
  totalling ≤ 216 bytes per edit**. The earlier "one contiguous `write_buffer`" claim is
  incompatible with any allocator and with the addressing itself. A gap-claiming free-list allocator
  is *also* rejected for the same reason — it destroys the sorted order that makes spans coalesce.
  Insert cost is O(log n) into the sorted dense array with a tombstone-reuse fast path; the full
  rebuild happens on the bulk path only.
- For scale: the block edit this accompanies is ~480 KB of chunk remesh upload, up to ~3.8 MB if it
  sits on a chunk corner. Decoration is **0.005%** of the edit's upload cost. It is correctly not the
  thing the player waits for.
- **The recompute must happen in the same frame as the chunk remesh**, or grass hangs in the air for
  a frame where a block was removed. A scheduling constraint, not an optimisation.

#### Grow-in with no pop — and its second job

`spawn_rel` drives a vertex-shader scale animation,
`scale *= ease_out(clamp(elapsed / grow_in_s, 0, 1))`, with `grow_in_s` a **per-rule duration**
(default 0.30 s). On removal the instance shrinks and the slot frees one grow-duration later.

**The ladder reuses this machinery unchanged, and that is the point.** `final_scale =
base_scale × ease(alive_q8) × grow_in_scale` — the retirement ramp and the grow-in ramp are two
multipliers on one animated scale. There is no second fade path, no alpha lane, no extra pipeline
key. A blade that is retiring because you walked away and a blade that is growing because someone
placed soil use the same three lines of vertex shader.

**The clock is the client's interpolated authoritative tick converted to seconds, never wall time.**
The client already runs a 100–150 ms interpolation buffer against a server tick; using that same
delayed tick makes the grow-in land at exactly the tick the server said the block changed,
identically on every client, and it replays exactly under `vdctl`.

**Epoch handling.** `spawn_rel` is u16 in 1/16 s units, covering 68 minutes. When it would exceed
60,000 the CPU rewrites that chunk's table subtracting the offset and saturating at 0 — one 80 KB
background write per chunk per ~62 minutes, on the task pool. This is deliberately not "wrap the u16
and hope", which makes a handful of instances per chunk spuriously re-grow.

**Alternatives rejected:** alpha cross-fade (needs alpha *blending*, which destroys opaque batching
and depth order for 125,000 instances); instant appearance (fine for pebbles, very visible for
grass, and the user asked specifically about growth).

#### Growth over time — and where `placed_tick` actually lives

```
elapsed_s(cell, t)   = (t − placed_tick) / tick_hz × realm_time_multiplier
coverage(cell, t)    = sat( (elapsed_s − step_s·dist_to_source + jitter_s(cell)) / spread_s )
instances(cell)      = floor(K × coverage)            // BEFORE rank retirement, which is separate
jitter_s(cell)       = (pcg3d(global_cell, seed, GROWTH_SALT)[0] % J) − J/2
```

Coverage and retirement compose in one direction only and it matters: **coverage decides how many
slots the cell has grown; retirement decides how many of those the camera is close enough to be
shown.** Implemented as `effective_threshold = S(d) × coverage`, so a half-grown patch seen from 30 m
is thin for two independent reasons and neither is confused with the other. Walking toward a
half-grown patch reveals more blades; waiting reveals more blades; the two are commutative, which is
what makes the visual read correctly.

**Every constant is a duration in seconds in `DecorTuning` / `GrowthParams`, converted to the local
tick base at boot against the live `tick_dt_s`** — the pattern `worldgen::grace_ticks_from_seconds`
already establishes, and which `celestial.rs:264` states as law ("a global `TICKS_PER_SECOND` const
would be a magic number silently splitting a 10 Hz vs 50 Hz shard"). The dev cluster runs 50 Hz, not
20 Hz; tick-denominated constants would silently run 2.5× fast there.

Calibrated against Minecraft's familiar feel (random tick speed 3 ⇒ mean interval 68.27 s, median
47.30 s per block):

| Constant | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `spread_s` | 60 s | one cell, bare → full |
| `jitter_s` (J) | 30 s (±15 s) | the ragged front |
| `step_s` (k) | 12 s per taxicab step | spreading speed away from an existing source |
| `D_GROW_MAX` | 62 (one chunk edge) | the distance cap |

**Calibration rule: `J ≈ 2.5 × step_s`.** With 12 s per step and ±15 s of jitter, the front is ragged
over ~2.5 cells — enough to look organic, not so much that the front scrambles. A 20-block-wide bare
patch (centre distance 10) greens in 60 + 120 = **3 minutes**; a 124-block-wide field (centre
distance 62) takes 60 + 744 = **13.4 minutes**, with a visibly creeping edge throughout. The naive
version capped the distance at 7, which meant *every* cell more than 7 blocks from grass shared one
distance term and the whole interior of any field wider than 14 blocks flipped inside a ±15 s window
— the synchronised flip the closed form exists to avoid.

**Where `placed_tick` and `dist_to_source` live: a small, expiring, authoritative growth log.**

```rust
#[repr(C)]
pub struct GrowthLogEntry {   // 8 bytes, per (chunk, cell)
    pub packed: u64,          // 0..17 chunk-local cell, 18..49 placed_tick (u32),
                              // 50..55 dist_to_source (u6, cap 62), 56..63 rule row
}
type GrowthLog = BTreeMap<CellLocalIndex, GrowthLogEntry>;   // per chunk, normally near-empty
```

The naive design declared this free by recovering the tick from the append-ordered WAL frame and
defaulting to "mature" when absent. That breaks in two ways, both fatal. The tick is recoverable only
while the record is still in the un-compacted WAL; P6 specifies WAL + `chunk_snapshot` compaction,
and a snapshot carries no tick — so **at the instant compaction runs, every in-progress patch jumps
to full coverage in one frame**, on the one feature whose stated purpose is "no pop". And a client
receiving a delta (with a tick) computes different coverage from one receiving a post-compaction
snapshot, which falsifies the design's own late-joiner invariant.

The growth log fixes both and stays cheap because it is **self-expiring**: an entry is deleted, by
both server and client, when `elapsed_s > spread_s + step_s·dist + J/2`. Maximum lifetime is 13.7
minutes. Absent an entry, coverage = 1.0 — now *correct*, because absence means matured, not
unknown. Costs: 8 B/entry; a player building a 20 × 20 m camp writes 3.2 KB that evaporates in three
minutes; a 4,189-block crater's bowl writes ~5 KB. It rides the chunk-load path alongside the block
deltas and is persisted in the per-realm redb store. It is a **new persisted record type** (see
§6.6) and must be declared as such, not smuggled in as "no new machinery".

`dist_to_source` is **snapshotted at edit time, never evaluated live.** Two reasons. Cost: a per-cell
bounded BFS at D=7 visits up to 3,375 cells, and ~8,000 decorated cells per chunk is 27 M visits
≈ 135 ms — 390× the chunk budget; even the correct shared formulation (one multi-source BFS per
chunk) is 5–10 ms if run over the full voxel volume. The affordable form is **one multi-source BFS
over the chunk's ~3,844 *surface* cells, seeded from every existing source cell**: ~31 k visits
≈ 0.16 ms, run once per bulk edit or chunk build. Correctness: evaluating the distance against the
*current* field makes coverage non-monotonic — mining one grass block near a maturing patch adds a
step and subtracts 12 s of progress from every cell behind it, so grass that was 80% grown visibly
drops to 60%. Nobody reports that as a bug; it just looks wrong.

**The realm time multiplier.** `StubConfig::time_multiplier` is a live per-realm knob that dilates
occupant movement (`stub.rs:2280`). The standing user law says it dilates occupant movement only,
never the parent-authored orbit. Growth is neither, and the section owes a verdict: **growth runs on
realm-subjective time**, because a player standing in a ×10 realm experiences ten subjective minutes
per universe minute and grass that took thirty subjective minutes to grow would read as broken. The
closed form multiplies elapsed universe time by the multiplier, which stays exact **only while the
multiplier is constant for the realm's life**. It is a boot-time config today
(`resolve_time_multiplier` reads the environment once). **Invariant: a realm's `time_multiplier`
must not change at runtime**; if it ever must, the growth log has to store subjective elapsed at the
change point (D-DEC-8).

#### The edit pyramid, and the one thing decoration owes it

Addendum 2 §C.4 makes the sparse edit pyramid the load-bearing piece of the whole ladder. **The
record, its keying and its update rule are not §6's to state and are no longer open: they are
register row 37 (the collapsed [USER DECISION 8-A]), owned by §3 for persistence and §4 for shape,
and §6 cites them.** What matters here is only what a consumer needs to know:

- one entry is **8 bytes, one `u64`** — `cell 18 | substance 16 | occ_mask 8 | fill_256 8 |
  reserved 14` — carrying an **absolute** mean fill and an **octant mask**, not a signed delta and
  not a solid count;
- its unpacked payload is a `CellSummary { occ_mask, fill_256, substance }`, where `substance` is a
  `SubstanceId` (the substance-table row), **not** a `BlockTypeId`;
- entries live in the `chunk_pyramid` table, one storage block per (tier, chunk), in the same redb
  file as the block deltas;
- a coarse cell's summary is read as `coarse_summary(addr)`: the pyramid entry if one exists, and
  **the generator's own octave-dropped evaluation if not**.

~~for every coarse cell containing an edited fine cell, the realm owner stores the solid count and
the dominant material, updated on every edit at most eight small writes deep~~ — **struck.** The
solid-count form is superseded (a count thresholded to a boolean is exactly the "blobs" failure §6
complained about below), and the update rule is the recursive walk-up of §3, not a fixed eight
writes. Decoration touches the pyramid in exactly one place and owes it exactly one thing.

**It touches it** only for the ground tint at tier ≥ 1 (§6.2): the tint is the coarse cell's
**dominant substance**, read through `coarse_summary(addr)` — the pyramid where an entry exists, the
coarse generator's own strata evaluation everywhere else (§5.5.4). No new field, no new read path, no
decoration data in the pyramid. **§6 needs no new pyramid field of any kind**, which is on the record
because it is the reason row 37 could spend the `authored` bits on the octant mask instead: §6 is the
`authored` bit's only named consumer, and it does not want it.

**It owed it a shape, not just a mass — and that debt is now paid in the record itself.** The study's
clearest transferable finding here is that Crimson Desert's visible weak point is distant
*structures* — players describe castles at moderate distance as "voxel-based blobs" — which is the
exact failure mode of a merged proxy that keeps mass and loses form. §6 asked for the solid *count*
to be spent on a shape from §4's catalogue rather than thresholded to a boolean. **Row 37 answers it
more strongly than §6 asked:** the entry carries an **octant mask** rather than a count, and the
drawn geometry is `COARSE_SHAPE[occ_mask][bucket]` where `bucket = (fill_256 * 9) >> 8` — so an
eight-metre ramp built of eight Wedges still reads as a ramp, and there is **no fill threshold
anywhere on the path** to be tuned differently by two clients. The table is folded into
`BlockRegistryHash`, so a mismatch is a refused connection rather than a silently wrong distant
silhouette. §6 keeps **D-DEC-13** only as the traceable record of the dependency, now discharged.

**And it must not silently disagree.** Addendum 2 §E names this as the one thing to watch: the
pyramid is derived data that can drift from the deltas it was derived from. The divergence policy is
row 37(e) and is §3's to carry — recompute the entry and increment a divergence counter the harness
asserts is zero, never refuse to open the store — and the audit is `vdctl world verify-pyramid
<realm>`, which rebuilds every entry from generator plus deltas and asserts byte-equality; the test
suite runs it after every edit scenario. Decoration benefits from both directly, because the ground
tint reads the pyramid. Copy the invariant from Space Engineers' shipped voxel storage, which
documents that only the finest level is writable and every coarser level is computed from it, and
make it **a type-level impossibility rather than a convention**: the store's `write` takes a
`Tier0Key`, not a `ChunkKey`, so `write(tier != 0)` does not compile.
