## 7. Signals and functional blocks — one generic bus that scales to a galaxy

This section owns the user's largest ask and his hardest one: *"every functional block becomes an
extremely generic emitter/receiver"*, *"all types of communication — including text/voice/video —
should be signals"*, *"signals that travel far should arrive later"*, and, in the same breath,
*"this is not really scalable; you will need an approach that scales indefinitely to all star
systems and galaxies."*

Those four sentences are in tension. A single uniform reliable bus carrying everything is trivially
generic and provably unscalable. A bus specialised per message type scales and violates HR3. The
resolution taken here, stated once:

> **One channel namespace, one wire arm, one subscription mechanism, one authorisation model, one
> block-behaviour dispatch — and behind them exactly TWO delivery lanes and exactly THREE routing
> planes, each chosen by a declared field on the channel rather than by a branch in feature code.**
> Genericity lives in the namespace and the dispatch. Scale lives in the delivery discipline and in
> the *bounded radius* of every routing plane. Nothing in block code, and nothing in the
> player-facing model, ever asks which lane or which plane it is on.

The section is long because it is the section that has to prove a number rather than assert an
architecture. Where an earlier draft asserted a number that does not survive arithmetic, the number
has been recomputed and the design changed to match; §7.19 lists the corrections that changed a
recommendation rather than a sentence.

*Amended 2026-08-03 by Addendum 2 (detail levels everywhere, on one ladder), and again the same day by
the cross-section adjudication. §7 is the least affected section in the document: the bus has no
camera, no distance and no observer anywhere on its hot path, so there is nothing in it for a tier to
change. What the amendment adds is the invariant that keeps it that way (§7.1.6), the one rung this
section is allowed to have, a demand-scheduler lead time derived from server-known distance and closing
speed (§7.8.1), the panel refresh restated as a rung rather than an exception (§7.9), and the retraction
of the ban §7.15.1 was written to defend.*

*The adjudication struck three things this section had asked for — `OccupantInterest::observer_tier`,
`LedgerCell::min_demanded_tier` and `SignalTuning::telemetry_divisor_for_tier(L)`, together with the
`PROTO_MINOR` 7 → 8 bump raised for them. Each is marked struck where it was stated rather than deleted,
with its replacement named, so a reader who remembers it learns what changed. What survives on the
observer side is ONE non-authoritative, server-clamped `tier_floor` hint (§7.1.6), and the rate that
was going to be a divisor is now §6.9's continuous, server-side `refresh_hz`.*

---

### 7.1 The model — what a Signal is

#### 7.1.1 Definition

A **Signal** is a named value, published by an emitter port into a channel, delivered to whoever
holds live interest in that channel. It is not a message to an address. There is no recipient field
anywhere in the design; the emitter is structurally incapable of naming a destination. This is the
single property that makes the dormant galaxy free: with no interest, an emission is one integer
store and zero bytes.

Four things travel with a value, and nothing else:

| Field | Type | Why it exists |
|---|---|---|
| **channel** | `ChannelId(u32)` in-realm; `ChannelKey(u64)` across realms | Identity. Interned per realm; §7.2 and §7.4. |
| **value** | `SignalValue` — fixed-point only | The payload. §7.1.4. |
| **provenance** | emitting `RealmKey` + emitting realm `Fence` + `GrantId` when the write is grant-authorised | Stale-fence rejection (mid-transfer frames die) and the audit trail for "who drove my ship". |
| **timing** | `source_tick: UniverseTick`, plus `arrival_tick: UniverseTick` on the Event lane | Deterministic ordering and light-lag. Never wall-clock. |

There is no sender **entity** id on either lane. Who wrote a value is an arbitration question
resolved *before* the value lands in the table (§7.12), not a field a receiver inspects. A sender
entity id would inflate a 13-byte item by 16 bytes and would tempt receivers into per-sender
branching — the exact thing that would make autopilots and pilots distinguishable, which §7.12
exists to prevent. The emitting **realm** key is present because the receiver must fence-check the
peer, and it is one field per *bundle*, not per item (§7.1.3).

#### 7.1.2 The two lanes behind ONE wire arm

`InterShardFlow` is at **27 arms** today against an original taxonomy of six, with `BlockEdit`,
`Coupling` and `Signal` still reserved names. `sealed_shards.md` §8 warns that freezing a contract
before its first consumer freezes the wrong shape. The design therefore adds **exactly one arm**,
carrying a versioned envelope with an internal sub-type — not one arm per lane, not one per plane,
not one per media class.

```rust
// crates/wire/src/intershard.rs — APPENDED (preserves every existing postcard discriminant)
Signal(SignalBundle),

pub struct SignalBundle {
    pub from_realm:   RealmCoord,
    pub to_realm:     RealmCoord,
    pub fence:        Fence,          // the EMITTING realm's fence — stale frames rejected
    pub source_tick:  UniverseTick,
    pub arrival_tick: UniverseTick,   // == source_tick when no light-lag applies
    pub body:         BundleBody,
    pub auth:         BundleAuth,     // ONE truncated MAC over the encoded body (§7.5)
}

pub enum BundleBody {
    Interest(InterestSet),         // the realm's exported key set, level-triggered (§7.3)
    State(Vec<StateItem>),         // coalesced latest-wins samples
    Event(EventBatch),             // reliable, per-channel ordered
    Receipt(Vec<DeliveryReceipt>), // acks, refusals, shed diagnostics (§7.8)
}
```

`effect_class()` and `durability_class()` already match *inside* payloads — the verified precedent is
`InterShardFlow::Directory(op) => op.effect_class()` at `intershard.rs:376` — so classifying per
`BundleBody` arm is idiomatic, not a new precedent. Because the arm carries both effect-free and
side-effecting bodies, the arm itself is **not** marked `EffectFree`; the classification is per body,
exactly like `Directory`.

| `BundleBody` | `EffectClass` | `FlowDurabilityClass` | Carrier |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Interest` | `FireAndForget` (absolute set; redelivery idempotent) | `ReDriven` (the periodic reconcile IS the re-driver) | `SignalEvent` |
| `State` | `FireAndForget` | `Unreliable` | `SignalState` |
| `Event` — non-durable (chat, door-opened, contact-gained) | `SideEffecting { ChannelSeq }` | `ProducerLessReliable` (push site MUST carry `Durability::Retained`) | `SignalEvent` |
| `Event` — durable config change (grant minted, block reconfigured) | `SideEffecting { TransferStep { corr, step_id } }`, steps **20–23** | `ReDriven` | `SignalEvent` |
| `Receipt` | `FireAndForget` | `ReDriven` (the emitter's next bundle re-triggers it) | `SignalEvent` |

That table costs **one appended variant on `IdempotencyKey`**. The obvious spelling breaks the enum:
`IdempotencyKey` derives `Copy` (`intershard.rs:324`) and `RealmCoord` does **not**
(`realm_coord.rs:18` — it wraps a `RealmPath(Vec<…>)`), so keying on a `RealmCoord` would de-`Copy`
`IdempotencyKey` and transitively `EffectClass`, whose by-value returns run through the G-SEALED
conformance tests. The correct spelling keeps `Copy`:

```rust
ChannelSeq { emitter: RealmKey, channel: ChannelKey, seq: u64 },   // 24 B, Copy
```

where `RealmKey(u64)` is a content hash of the encoded `RealmCoord`, used **only** as a dedup scope —
never as an address. The receiver's peer table holds the authoritative `RealmCoord` and applies the
same loud collision check as §7.4. The existing three keys genuinely cannot express "the third chat
line from this realm on this channel": a fence cannot dedup two distinct events at the same fence,
and minting a `TransferId` per chat line would put a saga correlation id on a lane that must cost
bytes, not sagas.

The two lanes:

| | **State lane** | **Event lane** |
|---|---|---|
| Semantics | latest-wins, absolute | reliable, ordered per channel |
| Carrier | `MsgClass::SignalState` (unreliable datagram) | `MsgClass::SignalEvent` (reliable stream + ack) |
| Loss policy | dropping is correct | loss is retried |
| Coalescing | one bundle per destination per tick, one item per channel | batched, never collapsed |
| Dedup | none per item; one monotone-max fence per **peer realm** | `(emitter, channel, seq)` + a 64-bit sliding replay bitmap, bounded and evicted (§7.5.4) |
| Durability | never | only when the event changes durable config |
| Change gate | integer epsilon deadband **plus a mandatory heartbeat** (§7.1.5) | none — every event matters |
| Staleness | `deadline_ticks` + declared `fallback`, on **imported** channels only | `LIFESPAN` expiry, no fallback |
| Light-lag | **refused** beyond the budget, never queued | queued at the routing node (§7.6) |
| Value types | `Bool`, `Fx`, `Vec3` only | all six |
| Item size | 6 B (`Bool`) / 13 B (`Fx`) / 29 B (`Vec3`) | 40–60 B + 24 B resident replay state per `(peer, channel)` |
| Example | `flight.thrust.fwd`, `hull.gforce`, `reactor.output_W` | `door.opened`, `chat.local`, `dock.autopilot.offer` |

**Why the split, in numbers.** A state sample needs a channel id and a quantised value and *nothing
else* — no sequence, no ack, no retry timer, no idempotency key, no redb touch. Against the reliable
shape that is a 3–7× byte difference per item plus, for the durable subset, one storage write. In the
other direction the resident cost of the reliable lane is not bytes but *state*: a `ReplayWindow` is
a 64-bit bitmap + `high_seq` + a source-tick bound ≈ 24 bytes **per (peer, channel) pair**,
permanently resident until evicted.

**What breaks if you merge them.** Four failures, one per direction:

1. *Everything reliable.* 20 Hz thrust pays a sequence number, an ack, a retry timer and — for any
   sample touching config — a redb write, on the lane that must be free. Worse, reliability means
   back-pressure, and back-pressure on a per-tick lane is a **sim stall**: the tick cannot advance
   until the ack window opens. The old `signal_pipeline.rs` used fire-and-forget `tokio::spawn`
   inside the tick precisely to dodge this, which `roadmap.json` P9 lists as the phase's headline
   risk.
2. *Everything unreliable.* A chat line is silently lost; a door-opened is silently lost; a grant
   revocation is silently lost, which is a **security** failure, not a cosmetic one.
3. *Reliable chat on the State coalescer.* Coalescing is latest-wins per channel; two chat lines in
   one tick become one. The bug is invisible in testing and permanent in play.
4. *Latest-wins thrust on the Event queue.* A queue delivers a four-minute-old thrust command on
   arrival. This is what DDS's `LIFESPAN` policy exists to prevent, and it is why §7.6 refuses rather
   than queues State.

The lane is a declared field on the channel, so no code branches on it: the publisher writes into a
port, the port's `ChannelDecl` names the lane, and one monomorphic function per lane does the rest.

#### 7.1.3 Bundle framing — one header, many items

A bundle carries the peer identity, fence, ticks and MAC **once**, and up to a datagram's worth of
items. Header cost measured against the frozen budget: `from_realm`/`to_realm` are paths, so a
bundle between two known peers carries `RealmKey` pairs (16 B) with the full coords exchanged once
at link setup; plus `fence` 16 B, two ticks 16 B, MAC 16 B, framing 4 B = **68 B per bundle**. A
State bundle is capped at `CONSERVATIVE_DATAGRAM_BUDGET = 1200` (verified,
`crates/wire/src/channels.rs:304`) minus 68 = 1132 B of items, i.e. **87 `Fx` items or 188 `Bool`
items per destination per tick**. That cap is the reason §7.8.4 exists.

#### 7.1.4 The value type set — fixed point only, floats BANNED on the bus

```rust
/// Fixed point, milli-units. 1 unit = 1/1000 of the channel's declared physical unit.
/// Range ±9,223,372,036,854,775.807 units (i64::MAX milli-units ÷ 1000 ≈ ±9.22e15).
/// Starbase's YOLOL is the shipped precedent — 64-bit fixed point, exactly three
/// decimals, documented range −9223372036854775.808 … 9223372036854775.807.
pub struct Fx(i64);

pub enum SignalValue {
    Bool(bool),
    Fx(Fx),
    Vec3(Fx, Fx, Fx),
    Text(TextInline),        // ≤ 127 bytes UTF-8 — signs, labels, nameplates
    Blob(TlvBlob),           // TLV-framed (core/src/tlv.rs), ≤ MAX_SIGNAL_BLOB_BYTES = 1024
    Handle(StreamHandle),    // media/stream handle — Event lane ONLY (§7.7)
}
```

Six variants, closed, `ALL`-looped, wire-frozen by postcard discriminant. **No `F32`, no `F64`,
ever.**

Headroom against the real range, not a mistyped one: a thruster at 10⁹ N is **6.2 orders of
magnitude** inside; a capital-ship battery at 10¹² J is 3.2 orders inside; a fusion reactor at
10¹⁰ W is 5.2 orders inside. The binding constraint is therefore not the range of one value but the
**`Sum` accumulator** (§7.12), which saturates rather than wraps.

The reasons compound rather than add:

- *Determinism.* Every physics→control boundary in this project is already quantised to integer
  grids. A float on the bus re-imports the problem at the exact place the rule was written for.
- *Cross-shard comparison and dedup.* The epsilon deadband must be an integer comparison or two
  shards will disagree about whether a channel is dirty and therefore about whether a bundle exists.
  A float deadband makes the *presence of a network message* floating-point-dependent.
- *Coverage (HR5).* Integer equality lets tests use `assert_eq!`/`expect_err`; float tests need
  `assert!((a-b).abs() < eps)`, whose false arm is an uncoverable region — the exact HR5 note in
  CLAUDE.md.
- *Precedent.* Starbase shipped YOLOL as 64-bit fixed point specifically so chip execution is
  bit-identical everywhere. Same requirement, arrived at independently.

Floats exist inside the physics kernel (Category C, checkpoint-carried) and are quantised at exactly
one place: the coupling→signal adapter in §7.13 step 7. That adapter is the only float→`Fx`
conversion in the subsystem, and it is a named function with a named rounding mode.

**Value type × lane is a declared validity table, checked at declaration time**, not left to the
first implementer:

| | `Bool` | `Fx` | `Vec3` | `Text` | `Blob` | `Handle` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **State** | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ |
| **Event** | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |

Without this table a player can bind a 1 KB `Blob` to a State channel at `EveryTick`: 20 KB/s on one
channel against a 1132 B item budget, so §7.8.4's shed fires permanently and the channel never
delivers — an invisible dead wire the player cannot debug. Radar's `contacts` output is a `Blob` and
is therefore an **Event** channel published on change, which is also what makes §7.15's ordering
invariant necessary. `MAX_STATE_ITEM_BYTES = 29` is asserted structurally by the table above, not by
a runtime length check.

Chat is a `Blob` with a declared `ChatMessage` TLV schema, not a `Text`. 1024 bytes of UTF-8 is
~340 CJK characters or ~1000 Latin, which is longer than any single chat line, so **no chunking,
continuation or reassembly rule exists or is needed** — one line, one Event. `Text(≤127 B)` remains
the inline case for signs, nameplates and widget labels.

#### 7.1.5 The channel declaration — a channel cannot ship without an answer

```rust
pub struct ChannelDecl {
    pub key:       ChannelKey,     // 64-bit content hash of the name (§7.4)
    pub name:      NameRef,        // interned; config-time and HUD only, NEVER hot path
    pub lane:      Lane,           // State | Event
    pub ty:        ValueType,
    pub plane:     RoutingPlane,   // Local | Neighbourhood { hops: 1..=2 } | Relay { net } (§7.3)
    pub epsilon:   i64,            // integer deadband; 0 = publish on any change
    pub heartbeat: HeartbeatTicks, // State + exported: republish period that BYPASSES epsilon
    pub deadline:  DeadlineTicks,  // State + imported: sample must arrive within N ticks
    pub fallback:  SignalValue,    // State + imported: the value adopted on a deadline miss
    pub lifespan:  LifespanTicks,  // Event: expire rather than deliver stale
    pub access:    AccessPolicy,   // OwnerOnly | AllowList | Public, separately read/write
    pub retention: RetentionClass, // Event: Ephemeral | Reportable | Mailbox (§7.8.4)
    pub grantable: bool,           // may a grant ever authorise a foreign writer? (§7.5)
}
```

**The heartbeat is the fix for the failure that kills the engines at steady state.** Compose an
epsilon deadband with a mandatory deadline naively and you get: pilot holds W, `flight.thrust.fwd`
sits at 100% for 400 ticks, the epsilon gate suppresses every publish after the first, the remote
subscriber's deadline expires and it adopts `fallback` — which for a thruster is 0. Holding W would
cut the engines. DDS avoids this because DEADLINE obliges the *writer* to publish at the deadline
period regardless of change; TIME_BASED_FILTER (decimation) and DEADLINE are separate policies. This
design imports both halves:

> **Invariant SIG-HB (validated in `ChannelDecl::build()`, not a convention).** A State channel that
> is exported across a realm boundary must declare `heartbeat_ticks ≥ 1` and
> `2 × heartbeat_ticks ≤ deadline_ticks`. `epsilon > 0` with no heartbeat is a **typed rejection**,
> not a warning.

Two further clarifications collapse the cost:

- **Deadline and fallback apply to *imported* channels only, heartbeat to *exported* ones.** An
  in-realm reader reads `front[c]` out of the same memory the writer wrote; a missing publish means
  *unchanged*, which is correct, so an in-realm State channel has no deadline and no heartbeat and
  costs nothing. Liveness inside a realm is **edge-triggered**: destroying a block removes its
  contribution from the arbitration accumulator (a `Sum` drops, an `Exclusive` lease ends and the
  channel reverts to `fallback`) on the same tick as the edit. Deadlines exist only because you
  cannot see a block in another shard.
- **Defaults.** `heartbeat = 4 ticks` (5 Hz), `deadline = 10 ticks` (500 ms at 20 Hz), both derived
  from `tick_hz` in the ONE `SignalTuning` struct, never inline. One lost datagram at 20 Hz is a
  50 ms gap; hold-last-value heals it invisibly inside the client's 100–150 ms interpolation buffer.

**The bandwidth consequence, honestly.** The wire cost of an exported State channel is
`max(change_rate, 1/heartbeat)`, not `change_rate`. A realm-to-realm link exporting the full
64-channel cap costs, worst case, 64 × 5 Hz = 320 `Fx` items/s = 4.16 kB/s, plus a 68 B header at
20 Hz = 1.36 kB/s → **≈5.5 kB/s ≈ 44 kbps per realm-to-realm link at full export.** That is the
number the rest of this section budgets against; the pre-heartbeat figure was ~7× lower and wrong.

`grantable: false` is the mechanism that makes `flight.abort` un-hijackable no matter what a player
approves (§7.12).

#### 7.1.6 Detail levels and the bus — behaviour never coarsens

Addendum 2 puts every drawn thing on one ladder: one rung per power of two, the tier a number carried
on a chunk address rather than a second code path, and the realm proxy demoted from an exception to
the coarsest rung. The bus is barely touched by that, but it is the place where the ladder's worst
failure mode would land, so the rule is stated as an invariant rather than left to be inferred:

> **Invariant SIG-NO-COARSEN (asserted in tests, not merely written down here).** A detail tier is a
> property of a *drawing*, never of a *simulation*. No tier — of the observer, of the observed realm,
> or of a block's own housing chunk — may change the value in `front[c]`, the contents of `subs[c]`,
> the one-tick propagation delay, an arbitration outcome, a grant check, a fence check, a heartbeat,
> a deadline, a `Retained` port write, or whether a bundle is produced. **A beacon blinks at the same
> rate when its housing is drawn as a 128-metre cell as when it is drawn as a one-metre one, and it
> blinks whether or not anybody is looking.**

Three reasons, and only the first is aesthetic:

1. Addendum 2 §C.7 already requires it — *"anything a signal or a functional block depends on … its
   housing may coarsen, its behaviour may not"*, and *"two players may see different terrain detail,
   never different terrain facts."*
2. **Coarsening behaviour is a determinism break, not a quality setting.** A tier is a function of
   where a client's camera is, which is not authoritative state. Feed it into the sim and a shard's
   trajectory depends on who is watching; two shards replaying the same tick with different viewers
   diverge, and the replay/byte-identity gate that covers everything else in this project stops
   covering the signal pass. It is precisely the client-compose drift that cost the floating-origin
   work S2/S3, re-imported through a rendering knob.
3. It is §7.7.2's rendering test applied one level down: **a derived quantity is *rendering* if and
   only if no server-authoritative state ever depends on it.** A tier passes that test only for
   things nothing reads back.

The bus needs no new machinery to obey this. Nothing in §7.2's hot path takes a camera, a distance or
an observer as an input, and the anti-vacuity assertion for that is §7.18 item 12.

**What the server may know about a rung, stated once because §7 is a consumer of this rule and not its
owner.** The adjudicated tier-hint rule replaces §4.8's earlier absolute — *"the server never learns
what tier anything is being drawn at"* — which is struck:

> A client may declare `tier_floor`. The server CLAMPS it to `[body.tier_floor_min,
> body.tier_depth - 1]` and uses the clamped value for **egress selection only** — which rung of a
> chunk delta to send, and at what rate a `Telemetry` channel is refreshed. **No fence, no arbitration
> outcome, no admission decision, no scheduling deadline, no persisted value and no simulation state
> may read it, directly or transitively. A shard's trajectory must be byte-identical for every value of
> every observer's `tier_floor`.**

SIG-NO-COARSEN is the §7-side statement of the same line, and the two do not collide: selecting *what
to send to one client* is routing, exactly like routing by AoI membership, and never selects *what is
true*. SIG-NO-COARSEN's "whether a bundle is produced" is about the **authority path** — the
`InterShardFlow::Signal` bundles that cross realm boundaries — and those are never touched by a
`tier_floor`. §7.18 item 12 is where the rule is asserted against `tier_floor` rather than merely
written down.

**What a coarse rung IS allowed to change.** A realm resident with every observer far away is the
*normal* state of a realm on the horizon — the demand loop spins realms up ahead of reach — not an
edge case. Three residency states, and the middle one is new with the ladder:

| Realm state | Authority path — the §7.2 pass, arbitration, grants, fences, heartbeats, `Retained` writes, `InterShardFlow::Signal` bundles | Observation path — panel content (§7.9), telemetry-only egress, decoration density, mesh rungs |
|---|---|---|
| **Dormant** (reaped) | not running; §7.6.3's mail-and-spin-up rules apply unchanged | nothing to compose |
| **Resident, drawn only at coarse rungs by every observer** | **runs in full. Nothing is skipped, ever.** | throttled at the client-facing egress (below) |
| **Resident, an observer drawing it at rung 0** | runs in full | full rate |

So the answer to *"what does a coarse tier entitle the signal system to skip"* is **nothing on the
authority path** — not one delivery, not one heartbeat, not one grant check, not one bundle. What it
entitles the system to *throttle* is the composition of things a human is looking at, and only where
the human demonstrably cannot resolve the result.

**Which channels may be throttled is DERIVED, never authored.** A channel is `Telemetry` if and only
if its compiled subscriber list contains no local subscriber outside the `Surface` kernel and it is
not exported; otherwise it is `Control`. That is one bit computed from `subs[c]` on the same
config-apply that already recompiles the list (O(|subs[c]|), §7.2.1), so it costs nothing, a player
cannot lie about it, and there is no new authored field to get wrong. It also supplies the "declared
class" that §7.8.4's shed ordering has always assumed and never defined — which means congestion can
now never shed a control value ahead of a gauge reading.

~~**Decided: the throttle is one divisor, `SignalTuning::telemetry_divisor_for_tier(L) = min(2^L,
max_telemetry_divisor = 32)`, applied to `Telemetry` channels at the CLIENT-FACING EGRESS only, with
the value HELD between refreshes.**~~ **Struck, with `SignalTuning::telemetry_divisor_for_tier(L)` and
`SignalTuning::max_telemetry_divisor` themselves.** The divisor was a tier-quantised approximation of a
rate §6.9 already computes exactly, continuously and server-side; a second throttle on top of it would
be a duplicate mechanism that reopens the seam — and its argument form required the server to hold an
observer's tier as an authoritative input, which the tier-hint rule above forbids. What §7 keeps is the
seam, not the rate:

> **Decided: §7 states FOUR things about the throttle and no rate at all.**
> - **(a) The `Telemetry`/`Control` bit is DERIVED**, computed from `subs[c]` on the same config-apply
>   that already recompiles the list — a player cannot lie about it, and it is what finally defines
>   §7.8.4's shed ordering, so congestion can never shed a control value ahead of a gauge reading.
> - **(b) Only `Telemetry` channels may be rate-reduced, and only at the CLIENT-FACING EGRESS**, never
>   on realm↔realm export: an exported channel's heartbeat is a liveness contract against the
>   importer's deadline, so reducing one without the other trips SIG-HB, and reducing both would make a
>   remote realm's liveness depend on a third party's camera. Realm↔realm export stays bounded by
>   SIG-HB and the 64-key cap.
> - **(c) The value is HELD between refreshes, never zeroed.** A reduction that let a channel miss its
>   deadline and adopt `fallback` would be SIG-HB's engine-cut failure (§7.1.5) with a rendering
>   trigger — a bug this design has already paid for once.
> - **(d) The reduced rate is floored by `SignalTuning::telemetry_min_refresh_hz`.**
>
> **THE RATE ITSELF IS §6.9's**, not §7's: `refresh_hz = clamp(base_hz × (θ/θ_ref)², 0, max_hz)`,
> already computed server-side from a server-authored subscriber position. §7 cites it and does not
> restate it.
> - *Alternative rejected:* a second, observer-distance scheduler inside the bus. It puts a camera on
>   the hot path (violating SIG-NO-COARSEN) and adds the second scheduler Addendum 2 §C.2 exists to
>   refuse.
> - *Cost.* Zero new state and zero new mechanism; one floor field in `SignalTuning`, and one derived
>   bit that already had to be computed for §7.8.4.
> - **Not a one-way door.** Every part is a config field plus a derived bit; setting `base_hz` to
>   `max_hz` restores un-throttled behaviour byte for byte.

---

### 7.2 The hot path — one realm, one tick

#### 7.2.1 The shape

Everything on the hot path is a `u32` index into a `Vec`. Names appear in exactly three places: the
subscribe handshake, the config blob, and the HUD.

```rust
pub struct SignalGraph {
    decls:      Vec<ChannelDecl>,          // indexed by ChannelId(u32)
    by_name:    BTreeMap<NameRef, ChannelId>, // CONFIG TIME ONLY
    front:      Vec<SignalValue>,          // read buffer  (tick N)
    back:       Vec<SignalValue>,          // write buffer (tick N+1)
    dirty:      Vec<u64>,                  // one bit per channel — plain words, not `bitvec`
    dirty_list: Vec<ChannelId>,            // the changed set, ascending id order
    subs:       Vec<SubList>,              // COMPILED at configuration time
    pending:    Vec<PendingAgg>,           // O(1) inline arbitration accumulator
    imported:   Vec<ImportedChannel>,      // bounded by MAX_IMPORTED_INTEREST — §7.2.4
}
/// Subscribers of one channel, sorted by (chunk index, local block index) so
/// iteration order is byte-stable across hosts and replays.
pub struct SubList { local: Vec<BlockSlot>, remote: Vec<PeerIdx> }
```

`dirty` is `Vec<u64>` plus shifts, not the `bitvec` crate — `bitvec` is absent from `Cargo.lock`
entirely, adopting it would be a new-dependency user decision for ~20 lines of code, and branchless
integer words are the better HR5 shape anyway.

Five mechanisms, each doing one job:

1. **Interning.** `ChannelId(u32)` indexes a `Vec`. Measured: `Vec<u32>` index 0.5 ns vs
   `HashMap<u64,u32>` (SipHash) 5.2 ns — a 10× per-access gap multiplied by every read on every
   block on every tick.
2. **Compiled subscriber lists.** `subs[c]` is built when a player wires a port and mutated only
   when a player rewires one. A publish walks `subs[c]` and touches nothing else. Recompilation on a
   config change is O(ports on the changed block): a sorted insert/remove into the affected lists.
3. **Dirty flags + inline aggregation.** `PendingAgg` accumulates by the port's arbitration mode in
   O(1) per write (a running saturating sum for `Sum`, a running max for `Max`, a
   `(priority, EntityId)` comparison for `LastWins`) instead of collecting a `Vec<SignalValue>` and
   reducing it.
4. **Double buffering.** The pass reads `front` and writes `back`. No block observes a value written
   this tick, therefore evaluation order is irrelevant, therefore the pass is deterministic and
   (later, if a parallelism dependency is ever adopted) parallelisable with no ordering hazard.
5. **Uniform one-tick propagation delay.** Every hop through every block costs exactly one tick.
   This breaks combinational loops without a topological sort — a player-built oscillator becomes a
   well-defined pipelined clock rather than an infinite recursion. Factorio (1 tick per combinator at
   60 UPS) and Scrap Mechanic (1 tick per gate at 40 Hz, *explicitly* "to ensure nothing happens that
   can cause a loop that crashes the game") both shipped this independently.

The counter-example is instructive. Vanilla Minecraft redstone notifies *while* solving, so one wire
can change its power level half a dozen times before settling, emitting 42 block updates and up to 22
shape updates each time — of which 6 go to itself and cause further recalculation, 12 of the
remaining 36 are duplicates, and 16 shape updates go to blocks that structurally cannot matter. The
Alternate Current rewrite solves the network first and notifies once, measuring **up to 20× lower**
MSPT with vanilla-identical behaviour. Solve-then-notify is not an optimisation; it is the difference
between a bounded and an unbounded per-tick cost.

#### 7.2.2 The measured numbers, and the budget they buy

All figures measured on an Apple M4 Pro, release, `opt-level = 3`:

| Shape | Work | Cost/tick | Relative |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Full interest scan, O(blocks × names) | 10,000 blocks × 200 names = 2,000,000 pairs | **1.023 ms** | baseline |
| (b) Naive pull, `HashMap<String, id>` per read | 10,000 blocks × 3 reads = 30,000 lookups | 0.401 ms | 2.6× better |
| (c) Interned pull, every block every tick | same 30,000 reads | 0.009 ms | **44× better than (b)** |
| (d) Dirty push to compiled lists, 100% churn | 30,000 deliveries | 0.014 ms | — |
| (d) same, realistic 10% churn | 3,060 deliveries | 0.001 ms | **≈400× better than (a)** |
| (d) same, 1% churn | 275 deliveries | below timer resolution | — |

The per-delivery constant is **≈0.5 ns**. That is the number the subsystem is budgeted against.

> **`SignalTuning::deliveries_per_tick_budget = 1_000_000`** per shard per tick — ≈0.5 ms, i.e. **1%
> of a 50 ms tick at 20 Hz.** An operational parameter in the ONE `SignalTuning` struct, derived from
> `tick_hz` exactly as `RlmTuning::cloud` derives its windows, and asserted by a load test that ships
> with the subsystem.

What that buys, in the project's actual deployment model. The landed model is **node-per-realm** — a
ship is its own shard with a private physics world at P8 — so the operative question is not "how many
constructs fit on a shard" but "does one construct's signal pass fit inside its own tick budget with
room for everything else". A 10,000-block construct at a realistic 10% channel churn costs 3,060
deliveries ≈ 1.5 µs, i.e. **0.003% of a 50 ms tick**; even at 100% churn it is 0.03%. The naive scan
costs 1.023 ms for the same ship — twice the entire budget — and at 2,000 channel names it becomes
10 ms/tick, 20% of one core for one construct. That 400× is the difference between the signal pass
being invisible and being the dominant per-tick cost of a large ship. The multi-construct case that
does exist (a station or hangar realm holding docked craft, deployables and dropped items) is priced
by the same budget without a separate model.

#### 7.2.3 Proof that emission is O(actual deliveries)

The claim: the per-tick cost of the signal pass is proportional to the number of value deliveries
that actually happen, with no term in the number of channels, blocks, or subscribers who received
nothing.

```
# Pass A — emission. O(deliveries).
for c in dirty_list:                        # changed channels only
    v = resolve(pending[c])                 # O(1), the arbitration accumulator
    if |v - front[c]| < decls[c].epsilon: continue        # epsilon gate, O(1)
    back[c] = v
    for slot in subs[c].local:  mark_input_dirty(slot, c)         # O(1) each
    for peer in subs[c].remote: stage_into_bundle(peer, c, v)     # O(1) each
clear(dirty_list)

# Pass B — export heartbeat + import deadline. O(exported + imported), both CAPPED.
for e in exported:  if now - e.last_publish >= e.heartbeat: stage_into_bundle(...)
for i in imported:  if now - i.last_arrival >  i.deadline:  front[i.ch] = i.fallback
```

Pass A is O(deliveries): every statement is O(1) and executes once per delivery, except the loop
header, which executes once per *changed* channel — and a channel cannot be in `dirty_list` without
having been written, which is a delivery from the writer's side. There is no scan over `decls`, no
scan over blocks, and no scan over `subs` for channels that did not change. Total
`O(|dirty_list| + Σ_{c ∈ dirty} |subs[c]|)`.

Pass B is the honest cost of §7.1.5's liveness rules, and it is stated here rather than hidden. It is
**not** a per-delivery timer and it does not touch the 0.5 ns constant. It is two flat sweeps over
two capped arrays: `MAX_EXPORTED_INTEREST = 64` and `MAX_IMPORTED_INTEREST = 256` per realm, so Pass
B is ≤ 320 integer comparisons per tick ≈ **0.16 µs**, i.e. 0.0003% of a 50 ms tick. Capping the
imports is what makes this a constant rather than a term in the channel count, and the cap is
enforced at subscribe time with a typed refusal.

The mirror-image claim is the **"no listener, no traffic" law**: if `subs[c]` is empty in both halves
and the channel is not exported, the write costs one accumulator merge and one epsilon comparison and
produces zero bundles and zero bytes. This gets an anti-vacuity CI assertion (§7.18 item 12), not a
comment.

#### 7.2.4 Change detection is a WIRE requirement, not an optimisation

The user's thruster example is 20 Hz across thousands of blocks across hundreds of ships. At
20 Hz × 5,000 blocks × 16 bytes that is 1.6 MB/s **per realm before any fan-out**, and the realm
already has a measured scale problem: DEFERRED D-9 (verified 🟥 at `DEFERRED.md:2683`) records 128
sessions in one realm producing 357,248 gateway messages peaking at 1,920 msgs/tick over 7.6 s, with
no within-realm per-entity AoI. Signals landing on an unculled fan-out compound it multiplicatively.

Four enforcement points, all data rather than code:

- `epsilon` on every State channel, integer, mandatory. A write equal to the current value produces
  *no event at all* — not a suppressed send, no event — bounded below by SIG-HB's heartbeat.
- `TickPolicy::OnChange` is the **default** in `FunctionDef`; `EveryTick` is opt-in and reserved for the
  small control-path set (seats, thrusters, gyros, actuators). Factorio's 2.0 change — "up to 25×
  less CPU usage" — was achieved by recalculating only on change, with the honest caveat that a block
  changing every tick (a clock) saves nothing. That caveat is why §7.2.2's budget is asserted against
  a worst case as well as a typical one.
- The emission rate cap `FunctionDef::emit_rate_limit_hz`, refinable downward per port, enforced at the
  port. This is
  the griefing control, and it is a number in a table, not policy code.
- The export cap (64) and import cap (256) bound the cross-boundary surface independently of how much
  a player wires internally.

#### 7.2.5 Determinism and coverage discipline

`ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded` is set deliberately in `build_app` because byte-identical replay
depends on it. The pass is *shaped* for parallelism (double-buffered, no cross-writes, sorted
subscriber lists) but **ships single-threaded**. Factorio's measured 14.9× from multithreading
read-only control behaviours (77,000 combinators / 6,000 networks: 131 s → 8.2 s) is the prize, and
it is available later — but `rayon` is not a workspace dependency and adopting one is a user
decision. When it is taken, the reduction order must be fixed rather than work-stealing order:
Factorio had to strip a global RNG out of its selector combinator to get there.

For HR5 the discipline is: **no generics on the hot path.** `ChannelId` is a concrete `u32`,
`SignalValue` a concrete enum, the delivery functions monomorphic. llvm counts regions per
monomorphisation, and a generic delivery pipeline instantiated over five value types in three test
binaries is a 15× coverage surface for zero benefit. The enum surfaces each get an `ALL`-loop test in
the `taxonomy.rs` idiom. Two cross-products are **real and must be paid for**, because they are
validity tables rather than pipeline branches, and both are resolved once at `ChannelDecl::build()`
rather than per delivery: `ValueType × Lane` (12 cells, §7.1.4) and `ValueType × Arbitration`
(30 cells, §7.12.1). Lane, plane and arbitration are resolved at three separate, independently
coverable points in the pipeline, so the pipeline itself is not cross-producted.
---

### 7.3 Cross-realm routing at galaxy scale

#### 7.3.1 Why "one aggregated set covering the whole subtree" does not survive arithmetic

The academically attractive answer is Rebeca-style **covering**: each realm advertises to its parent
one interest set that is the union of its children's, so routing state at a node is O(children) and
depth adds hops but never state. It is the shape an earlier draft of this section took, and it does
not survive contact with player-authored channel names.

Covering requires the parent's advertised set to *subsume* its children's. With 64-bit content-hashed
names typed by players (§7.4), children's key sets do not overlap, so the union does not compress. A
system realm with 1,000 station children, each exporting the 64-key cap, must advertise
**64,000 keys = 512 KB** in one interest set — 1,000× over the declared cap and 427× over the 1200 B
datagram budget it was supposed to ride. Push it to the root and it is 27,000 realms × 64 keys =
1.73 M keys = **13.8 MB in a single renewal**. Either the cap is enforced and covering silently fails
above the first hop (≈99.9% of cross-realm channels become unroutable while an "empty subscriber
list" anti-vacuity test still passes), or covering is honoured and both the cap and the datagram
budget are violated. Only one of the two invariants can hold, and the "depth adds hops, never state"
claim is false either way.

The resolution is not a bigger cap or a Bloom summary bolted onto covering. It is to notice that
**nothing the user actually asked for needs galaxy-wide content-based routing**, and to bound each
plane's radius explicitly.

#### 7.3.2 Three routing planes, each with a bounded radius

`crates/core/src/realm_path.rs` models a realm as `RealmPath(Vec<RealmLevel>)` with `levels()`,
`parent_realm()` and `lineage_seeds()`; the lowest common ancestor of two realms is the longest
common prefix, an O(depth) computation with **depth ≤ 6** (`RealmKindTag` = Universe, Galaxy, System,
Planet, Station, Area). That machinery is used, but only inside a bounded hop radius.

| Plane | What it reaches | Interest state | Who holds it | Radius |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **`Local`** | the emitting realm only | none — a `Vec` index | the realm | 0 hops |
| **`Neighbourhood { hops: 1..=2 }`** | parent, siblings, and (at `hops = 2`) the grandparent's subtree | the realm's own exported key set, ≤64 keys | the **parent** only; **never re-advertised upward** | ≤ 2 hops up, ≤ 2 down |
| **`Relay { net }`** | anywhere, via the relay plane | `net → { subscriber_shard → lease }` | the relay shard chosen by rendezvous (§7.3.5) | unbounded, metered |

`Neighbourhood` is not a compromise; it is what the gameplay needs. Every cross-realm case the user
named is either proximity-local or explicitly infrastructure-mediated:

- **A station offering autopilot to an approaching ship** is proximity: the station and the ship are
  siblings under the same planet or system realm, one hop up and one down. `ShortRange` filtering
  resolves from the shard-local band/ghost membership the design already maintains for ghosts, never
  from a directory query — `sealed_shards.md` §3's Finding #5 resolution, reused verbatim.
- **A ship talking to its hull host** is parent↔child, zero hops through the tree.
- **A fleet spread across a system** is siblings, one hop up.
- **Interstellar coordination, corp comms, radio nets, text and voice** are `Relay` by construction —
  and in fiction they *should* require infrastructure, be jammable, and cost something.

`hops` is capped at 2 by a validated `ChannelDecl` field, not by convention. Nothing advertises
upward past its parent, so there is no union, no covering, and no unbounded set anywhere.

#### 7.3.3 The interest set, and why it needs no lease of its own

```rust
pub struct InterestSet {
    pub child: RealmKey,
    pub keys:  Vec<ChannelKey>,   // sorted, deduped, ≤ MAX_EXPORTED_INTEREST = 64
    pub epoch: u32,               // monotone; a stale full set is discarded, never merged
    pub universe_tick: UniverseTick,
}
```

Three properties, each load-bearing:

- **Full set, not deltas.** A dropped push costs one reconcile cycle and nothing else; there is no
  diff state that can be lost and no resync protocol to write. This is the same self-healing shape
  `RealmDemand` and `ProxySceneSet` already use, and the reasoning the previous project's
  `ship_frequency_interests.rs` documented for its ~90 s full-set renewal.
- **Liveness comes from the demand ledger, not from a second timer.** This is the correction that
  matters most. `crates/sim/src/rlm.rs:99–121` sizes `RlmTuning::cloud` as `demand_ttl = hz × 4`
  (4 s), `empty_grace = hz/2` (0.5 s), `teardown_drain = hz/2`, `teardown_cooldown = hz` — so a realm
  reporting empty is **reapable in ≈2 s** and, worst case via demand-TTL expiry, ≈5.5 s. Any
  interest lease with an 80 s renewal period therefore *outlives the realm it describes by 75–235
  seconds*, during which a parent keeps compiling a dead child into its inverted index and staging
  bundles into the void — on exactly the lifecycle (spin-up-ahead, teardown-behind) that reaps realms
  continuously behind a moving player. Shortening the lease to ≤ `demand_ttl` would fix the
  correctness bug at 40–160× the renewal traffic. The right fix is to **delete the second timer**:
  an interest set's lifetime is bound to the child's `DemandLedger` entry at the parent, dropped in
  the same transaction as `mark_reaped`. The ledger already knows, already has the hysteresis, and
  was expensive to get right once.
- **Content is edge-triggered on the reliable lane, with a slow reconcile behind it.** A player
  rewiring a port pushes a new full set immediately on `MsgClass::SignalEvent` (reliable, so it
  cannot be lost); `SignalTuning::interest_reconcile_ticks = 20 × RlmTuning::demand_ttl_ticks`
  (≈80 s at any tick rate) is a belt-and-braces re-drive, which is why the body classifies as
  `ReDriven` rather than needing a durable outbox.

#### 7.3.4 The arithmetic at 100,000 players

*Per-endpoint subscription (the shape rejected).* 100,000 players × ~50 named channels = **5M
subscriptions**. At NATS-like ~1 KB of routing state per subscription that is **~5 GB of pure routing
state before a single message moves**, on one logical index, growing linearly. NATS's own guidance
(>1M subscriptions needs >1 GB and grows linearly; JetStream ≲100k consumers, ≲300 disjoint subject
filters per consumer) puts this beyond a single broker and into a sharded-broker problem — a second
distributed system with its own membership sitting next to the directory this project already owns.

*Per-realm exported interest (the shape taken).* Assume 100,000 concurrent players, one construct per
four players ⇒ 25,000 live construct realms plus ~2,000 live celestial realms ⇒ **~27,000 live
realms**. `MAX_EXPORTED_INTEREST = 64` is a hard refusal, not a truncation (§7.8), and it is generous
because a construct's *internal* channels — a ship's own thrust bus, its whole logic graph — are
`Local` and never exported at all.

| Quantity | Per-endpoint | Per-realm exported |
|---|---|---|
| Routing entries | 5,000,000 | 27,000 sets |
| Routing bytes | ~5 GB, centralised | 27,000 × (64 × 8 B + 24 B) = **14,472,000 B ≈ 14.5 MB, distributed** |
| Reconcile traffic | continuous per-subscription churn | 27,000 × 536 B / 80 s = **≈181 KB/s cluster-wide** |
| Discovery messages on join | O(n) per new endpoint against every peer | 1 message to 1 parent |
| Hops per cross-realm emission | broker round trip | ≤ 2 up + ≤ 2 down, or 1 relay hop |

**≈345× less routing state, and none of it in one place.** That headline survives the loss of
covering because it never depended on covering — it depends on aggregating per *realm* rather than
per *block*.

*Per-hop cost, and the honest per-node figure.* A parent must not scan its children per emission. It
keeps an **inverted index** compiled when interest sets are installed: `key → sorted Vec<ChildIdx>`,
the same compiled-list trick as §7.2 one level up. A hop is one binary search plus one write per
matching child, and if nobody is interested the emission terminates at the **first** hop. The cost at
a busy node is real and is stated rather than hidden: a system realm with 1,000 children holds
1,000 × 536 B = 536 KB of raw sets plus an inverted index of up to 64,000 `(key, child)` entries at
12 B = 768 KB, so **≈1.3 MB at a 1,000-child system node.** A galaxy realm holding 1,000 systems
holds the systems' *own* export sets (536 KB) and nothing about their subtrees, because nothing is
re-advertised upward. Depth costs nothing precisely because the plane radius is bounded, not because
of a covering property.

*The reconcile figure in context.* 181 KB/s across an entire 100,000-player galaxy is **six players'
worth of proximity voice** (§7.7: one player at k = 6 × 40 kbps = 30 kB/s). That comparison is stated
identically in both places.

#### 7.3.5 The failure mode this avoids: symmetric discovery collapse

DDS/RTPS discovery traffic scales as **n·(n−1)·(r+w)** — every participant exchanges per-reader and
per-writer detail with every other, so a writer with one reader costs the same discovery as a writer
with a million. Measured ROS 2 degradation on that model: end-to-end latency **5.5 ms at 5 nodes →
1,309 ms at 20 nodes**; at **25 nodes packet loss reaches 94.98%** — the network is functionally dead
— and >100 participants on one host frequently fail to discover each other at all. Multi-process
memory grows O(N²): +2.1 MB for the second process rising to +4.3 MB for the twentieth. Zenoh's
measured counter-example on the same workload: **686 packets / 251,576 bytes → 31 packets / 6,617
bytes (−97.37%)**, and 1 packet / 82 bytes with resource generalisation and a warm start, achieved by
advertising coarse resource interests instead of per-endpoint detail.

The rule this design obeys: **never announce a per-block endpoint across a shard boundary.** A
block's subscription is an entry in a `Vec` inside its own realm. The only thing that crosses is one
coarse set per realm, held one hop up.

#### 7.3.6 The relay plane, and rendezvous that survives churn

`Relay { net }` is different in kind: two ships in different galaxies share only `Universe` as an
ancestor, which is not a locality — routing through it would make one node the galaxy's message bus,
the central bottleneck HR1 exists to prevent.

The relay is a node with the *already existing* `signal_relay` capability
(`ShardProfile::signal_relay()`, granted to `profiles::galaxy()` and `profiles::station()` today). It
holds `net → { subscriber_shard → lease_deadline }` plus a wildcard set, and fans out **only to
leased subscribers** — the shape the previous project's `radio_subscribers.rs` already had.

Which relay holds a net must be **computed**, and the obvious computation is wrong. `relay_index =
key % relay_count` is the textbook counter-example to consistent hashing: moving from 8 relays to 9
remaps **~89% of all nets**. Relays are realms on the same demand-driven lifecycle as everything
else, so membership changes constantly; modulo rendezvous means a galaxy-wide re-subscription storm
on every relay spin-up, and during the fence transition two shards at different relay-set fences
compute different indices and their messages never meet.

> **Decided: highest-random-weight (rendezvous) hashing over the fence-versioned relay set.**
> `relay = argmax_i H(net_key, relay_id_i)` — O(R) per lookup with R in the tens, **O(1/R) of the
> keyspace remapped** when a relay joins or leaves, no ring to build and no virtual nodes to tune,
> and deterministic from data the directory already publishes. Plus a **dual-read window**: for
> `SignalTuning::relay_fence_dual_read_ticks = 4 × demand_ttl_ticks` (≈16 s) after a relay-set fence
> bump, subscribers lease at both the old and the new argmax and emitters publish to both. Cost:
> 2× relay traffic for 16 s per membership change. Not a one-way door — the hash function and the
> window are config — but the *migration protocol* must exist from the first slice, because adding
> one after players have standing radio nets is a visible outage.

Two consequences worth stating plainly:

- The relay is *player-visible infrastructure*, not plumbing. A **Relay/Repeater** block exists in
  the catalogue (§7.11) and rebroadcasts a channel onto a new net. Player-built relay networks are
  content, and they are the in-fiction justification for the relay shard.
- The relay is the natural home for the FTL/light-lag policy split in §7.6: direct antenna traffic
  obeys the speed of light; relay traffic obeys the relay network's own (much shorter,
  infrastructure-dependent, jammable, economically meterable) latency.

#### 7.3.7 The client is not a subscriber

A client never holds a channel lease. It has no channel identity and no interest set. What a client
receives is (a) the draw-command lists the server composed for the panels its player can see (§7.9)
and (b) its own seat's feedback ports — both server-composed, both gated by the *same* per-entity AoI
the D-9/D-39.5 reshape introduces, both on the client protocol's own lanes. This keeps "the server
does all the math" intact, avoids a second interest system with a second set of leases, and means the
numbers on a panel arrive as values rather than being derived client-side — the exact drift that bit
the floating-origin S2/S3 work.

---

### 7.4 Global channel identity — a content hash, not a registry

A global registry of names is the centralised bottleneck and single point of failure the sealed-shard
rule exists to prevent, and it would have to be consulted on a path that must not have a network hop.
So the global identity of a channel is **computed**, never allocated:

> **⚠ AMENDED 2026-08-04 — ruling R19. The bare-name construction below is STRUCK.** Hashing the name
> alone makes every player's `thrust` the *same channel across the galaxy*. On the `Local` plane that is
> harmless (my `thrust` and yours are different array slots and the key is never used — which is exactly
> why a realm-private default makes squatting impossible by construction). On the `Neighbourhood` plane
> it is a live defect: two sibling ships both exporting `thrust` collide in the parent's index, so a
> neighbour's emission routes into my realm and only the ingress permission check stands. The takeover is
> stopped; the forced decode-and-refuse traffic is not. And human-chosen names do not collide at the
> 2.7e-12 below — **everyone names their thrust channel `thrust`, so the real collision rate is close to
> 100%.**
>
> **THE KEY IS SCOPED:**
>
> ```rust
> /// The FIRST 8 BYTES of the workspace hash of (scope_bytes || name_bytes).
> /// Still a u64 on the wire, still a u32 index in-realm, still COMPUTED rather than
> /// allocated — so §7.4's no-global-registry argument survives intact, and the
> /// birthday bound below becomes proven PER SCOPE rather than argued globally.
> pub struct ChannelKey(u64);
>
> pub enum KeyScope {
>     Realm,                  // DEFAULT. Purely internal; the key is never compared outside.
>     Construct(ConstructId), // Neighbourhood exports. My exported name ≠ yours.
>     Net(NetId),             // Two strangers meet iff SAME net AND SAME name — so a public
>                             // distress frequency is DELIBERATE, never accidental.
>     Protocol,               // The game's own names. COMPILED CONSTANTS, MINTABLE BY NOBODY.
> }
> ```
>
> **`Protocol` closes the phishing hole.** `dock.*`, `sys.*`, `hull.*` and `chat.*` are compiled
> constants asserted by an `ALL`-loop, not player-typeable strings. Without it a griefer with a
> short-range antenna publishes a forged autopilot offer with an attractive station identity and every
> ship in the neighbourhood shows the approval dialog.
>
> **This must ship in the FIRST SLICE and is a one-way door.** It changes what `ChannelKey::of()`
> computes, so any player wiring persisted under the bare-name construction re-resolves to *different
> channels* afterwards — the same argument §7.4 already makes for its own loud collision check.

Birthday arithmetic, P(collision) = 1 − exp(−n²/2^(b+1)):

| distinct names | 32-bit | 64-bit | 96-bit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10⁴ | 1.2e-2 | 2.7e-12 | — |
| 10⁶ | — | 2.7e-8 | — |
| 10⁸ | — | 2.7e-4 | 6.3e-14 |
| 10⁹ | — | **2.67e-2** | 6.3e-12 |

32 bits is unusable at any scale. 64 bits is comfortable to ~10⁸ player-authored names and
uncomfortable at 10⁹ — and over the lifetime of an MMO with player-authored names, 10⁹ is not absurd.

**The bound the design holds to is much tighter, because the exposure is not global.** The per-realm
registry holds the *string*, and a collision is detected and **rejected loud** at insert time:

```rust
fn intern(&mut self, name: &str) -> Result<ChannelId, ChannelError> {
    let key = ChannelKey::of(name);
    match self.by_key.get(&key) {
        Some(existing) if self.decls[existing].name != name =>
            Err(ChannelError::KeyCollision { key, existing: ..., attempted: ... }), // LOUD
        ...
    }
}
```

Real exposure is bounded by the number of names **co-resident in one realm** — low thousands, where
the 64-bit collision probability is ~10⁻¹². A collision is a hard, named, player-visible refusal at
configuration time ("this channel name collides with `X`; rename it"), never a silent cross-wire.

**The one place that bound does not hold** is a namespace compared across realms by id alone, and
there is exactly one: `Relay { net }`, where subscribers from unrelated realms meet on a key nobody
holds the string for. The fix costs nothing on the hot path: the relay's subscribe handshake carries
the **full name** alongside the key, the relay stores it, and a subscribe whose key matches a stored
entry with a different name is **refused** with a typed reason. Rendezvous is by hash (cheap, O(1),
no registry); equality is by name (exact). Fan-out to an already-leased subscriber set still touches
only the `u64`.

Verdict: **64-bit content hash, loud collision check at every insert point, name-checked equality at
the relay.** Widening to 128 bits later is a wire change on the subscribe handshake and the bundle
header only, never on the in-realm hot path, which uses `u32` regardless — but it *is* a one-way door
once player channel names are persisted at scale, so the loud check must ship in the first slice.

---

### 7.5 Authentication and authorisation, quantitatively

#### 7.5.1 What the crypto costs

Measured on an Apple M4 Pro with the exact crate versions in this workspace's `Cargo.lock`
(blake3 1.8.5, sha2 0.10.9, hmac 0.12.1, ed25519-dalek 2.2.0):

| Primitive | Cost | Ops/s/core | Per 20 Hz tick, one core |
|---|---|---|---|
| keyed BLAKE3, 16/32/64 B | 51.6 / 50.7 / 51.4 ns | ≈19.5 M | ≈975,000 |
| keyed BLAKE3, 128 B | 102 ns | 9.8 M | ≈490,000 |
| HMAC-SHA256, 64 B, **precomputed key state** | 345 ns | 2.9 M | ≈145,000 |
| HMAC-SHA256, 64 B, fresh key | 570 ns | 1.75 M | ≈87,000 |
| Ed25519 sign, 64 B | 9.00 µs | 111 k | ≈5,550 |
| **Ed25519 verify, 64 B** | **18.86 µs** | **53 k** | **≈2,650** |
| Biscuit token verify (compact) | ≈49 µs | ≈20 k | ≈1,020 |

One Ed25519 verify = **367 keyed-BLAKE3 tags**, or 55 HMAC-SHA256 tags. Batch verification does not
rescue it: curve25519-voi reports 31.7 ms for 1,024 signatures = 31 µs/sig, i.e. batching buys ~2×,
not the ~100× that would be needed.

#### 7.5.2 The three tiers

| Tier | What | When | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1 — link** | Mutual auth once per shard pair; in-realm traffic is implicitly trusted because the realm's shard *is* the authority for everything in it | connection setup | amortised to zero |
| **2 — capability grant** | One grant per `(emitter principal, channel set, epoch)`, verified at **subscribe / grant-mint** time, then cached as a symmetric key | grant issue + subscribe (≲10⁴/s cluster-wide) | 18.86 µs (Ed25519) each — invisible at that rate |
| **3 — hot path** | **ONE truncated MAC over the whole per-destination BUNDLE** | every bundle, every tick | 345 ns per (destination, tick) |

Tier-3 arithmetic with the workspace's existing primitive: a busy shard talking to 200 peer shards
emits 200 bundles per tick; at 345 ns with a cached precomputed HMAC key state that is
**69 µs/tick = 0.14% of a 50 ms tick.** The tag is truncated to 16 bytes, so it costs 16 B per
bundle — 1.4% of a full 1132 B State bundle, and amortised across up to 87 items.

The same work done per *signal* with Ed25519: 5,000 signals/tick × 18.86 µs = **94 ms of verification
for a 50 ms tick** — 1.9 cores, for one shard, doing nothing but checking signatures. Per-signal
HMAC is affordable in CPU but adds 16–32 bytes to a payload whose useful content is 8 bytes, a >2×
byte inflation on precisely the lane that must be cheap. Per-bundle is the only affordable
granularity, and it is sufficient: the bundle proves the *peer shard* sent it, and everything
finer-grained is a grant check against durable rows, not a signature.

> **[USER DECISION 7-D] — the hot-path MAC primitive.** `roadmap.json` P9 already names the
> mechanism: *"remote-access grants in the grants table (HMAC-signed per-channel, base64 key transfer
> for the tablet UI)"*. `hmac 0.12`, `sha2 0.10` and `ed25519-dalek 2` are in
> `[workspace.dependencies]` (`Cargo.toml:77-79`). `blake3` appears in `Cargo.lock` only
> transitively and is **not** a workspace dependency of any crate.
>
> - **Option A (recommended) — HMAC-SHA256, truncated to 16 B, precomputed key state per peer.**
>   Zero new dependencies, matches the written P9 deliverable exactly, 69 µs/tick at 200 bundles =
>   0.14% of a tick.
> - **Option B — keyed BLAKE3.** 20.4 µs/tick at 200 bundles = 0.04% of a tick, i.e. **it buys 0.1%
>   of one tick**, and costs one new direct dependency plus a contradiction with a written
>   deliverable.
>
> **Recommendation: A.** The 367× ratio in §7.5.1 is what kills *per-signal Ed25519*; it is not an
> argument for BLAKE3 over HMAC at *per-bundle* rates, where both are noise. If profiling ever shows
> the MAC on a hot path, B is a one-line swap behind the same `BundleAuth` type — the tag width is
> already 16 B either way, so the wire does not change.

#### 7.5.3 The user's "signed signals" idea, answered directly

The idea as stated — sign signals so only approved receivers act on them — has the right instinct and
the wrong polarity. Making the receiver decide per message puts the cost on **every receiver of every
message**, which is the 94 ms number above. The scalable inversion:

> **No listener, no traffic** (nobody receives what they did not subscribe to) **+ no grant, no
> cross-boundary write** (nobody may write a channel in a realm they do not own without a durable,
> revocable grant held by that realm).

In practice "signed signals" means exactly three things:

1. **Every cross-shard bundle is tagged.** One MAC proves the bundle came from the shard that claims
   to have sent it. Not per signal — per bundle, per destination, per tick. 345 ns.
2. **Every foreign write is grant-bearing.** A signal written into a realm by a principal that does
   not own it carries `SignalAuth::Grant { grant_id }` inside a bundle whose MAC is keyed on the
   grant's own key. The realm checks the grant exists, covers the channel, is unexpired and is not
   revoked; then arbitration decides what the value *does*. The grant is the durable, auditable,
   revocable object; the MAC is the cheap per-frame proof.
3. **A real asymmetric signature is minted where the rate is low and the stakes are high**, and
   nowhere else: at **grant issue** (a station proving it is the station whose autopilot you are
   approving), at **identity assertions across trust domains**, and at **moderation actions** recorded
   against an account. All are tens per second cluster-wide; 18.86 µs is invisible.

> **[USER DECISION 7-F] — the grant token format.**
>
> - **Option A (recommended) — plain per-grant HMAC rows in the per-realm `grants` redb table**, key
>   material transferred base64. This is `roadmap.json` P9's own mechanism, zero new dependencies,
>   and it covers every scenario in this section including the station-autopilot handshake.
> - **Option B — `biscuit-auth`** (Rust, Eclipse project): offline verification with public keys,
>   *attenuation without contacting the issuer*, ≈49 µs to verify a compact token, 340–380 B per
>   delegation block. It buys one thing Option A cannot express: "a station hands an approaching ship
>   a token permitting autopilot-class channels for 300 s, and the ship attenuates it further before
>   handing it to its own docking computer." A new dependency, therefore a user decision.
> - **Not an option — macaroons.** Cheaper (HMAC chains) but they need a shared root secret between
>   issuer and verifier, which contradicts HR1's sealed-shard premise unless made per-shard-pair — at
>   which point it is link-level auth with extra steps.
>
> **Recommendation: A now.** Adopt B only if *delegation* becomes a gameplay requirement (sub-letting
> control of a ship down a chain of principals). The grant row's schema should reserve a
> `token: Option<TlvBlob>` field so B is additive rather than a migration.

#### 7.5.4 Ownership, permission, freshness — who may drive my ship

Three layers, all data:

- **Realm ACL** — an owner, an allowlist and roles, held by the realm, consulted when a player
  attempts to occupy a seat or open a configuration panel. This is where "who is allowed to drive my
  ship" is actually answered, at a **low-frequency** event (sitting down), not per input frame.
- **Channel ACL** — `AccessPolicy ∈ { OwnerOnly, AllowList, Public }` on `ChannelDecl`, separately for
  read and write. A hostile block welded onto your hull cannot write your flight channel, because the
  channel says who may write it and the welded block's owner is not on the list. **Where the decl
  lives is where the policy is enforceable**: in-realm and at the parent, never at a relay (§7.14).
- **Lease + fence** — seat occupancy mints a short-lived, fence-stamped lease id. Every subsequent
  20 Hz intent carries only the lease id and a monotonic sequence number. Cheap, replay-protected,
  and it dies correctly across a shard restart because the fence changes.

Server-side validation must additionally confirm the claimed player is *actually resident in the
realm* and *actually seated* — never trust a client's assertion about its own state. Revocation is a
durable delete of the grant row, fenced, taking effect on the next bundle: the emitter's next bundle
fails the grant check and is dropped with a typed `Receipt::Refusal`.

**Freshness and replay, with the two bounds the design must declare.**

- *State lane, fence.* Provenance carries the emitting realm's `Fence` so mid-transfer frames die.
  Rejecting a stale fence requires remembering the highest fence seen from that emitter — which is
  per-sender resident state, and it must be named rather than waved away. It is held **per peer
  realm, not per (peer, channel)**, in the peer table the receiver already maintains for its imports,
  and the comparison is an explicit **monotone max**: `if incoming.fence < peer.max_fence_seen {
  drop }`, `peer.max_fence_seen = max(...)`. Bounded by `MAX_IMPORTED_INTEREST`-worth of peers, so
  256 peers × 24 B ≈ **6 KB per shard**. Without the monotone-max rule a datagram reordered across a
  re-home is indistinguishable from one after it.
- *Event lane, replay window.* A 64-bit sliding bitmap + `high_seq` + a source-tick bound ≈ 24 B per
  `(peer, channel)` pair. Unbounded, this is a memory attack: emit one Event per second on each of
  10,000 distinct player-authored channel names into a target realm, and §7.8.3's 100/s token bucket
  throttles the *rate* while every accepted message mints a resident entry — ~12 MB/hour per
  attacker, permanently resident on the victim's shard. **Declared bound:
  `SignalTuning::max_replay_entries = 16_384` per shard (≈384 KB), evicted when the channel's
  `LIFESPAN` window closes, LRU within a peer beyond that. A re-delivery arriving past eviction is
  REFUSED with `Receipt::Refusal { ReplayWindowEvicted }`, never accepted** — accepting it would
  reopen the replay hole the window exists to close.
- *Freshness is measured against `source_tick` + declared propagation delay, never wall clock.* The
  previous project's `REPLAY_TIMESTAMP_WINDOW_MS = 5_000` would reject every legitimately
  light-lagged message.

---

### 7.6 Light-lag — far signals arrive later, deterministically

#### 7.6.1 The mechanism, with the two unit traps named

```
delay_ticks  = ceil( d_fine × UNIVERSE_HZ / LIGHT_FINE_CELLS_PER_SECOND )   // i128, exact
arrival_tick = source_tick + delay_ticks
```

Every term is an integer, and two things that look like details are not:

- **`UNIVERSE_HZ` is the universe clock's rate, never a shard's local `tick_hz`.** `arrival_tick` is a
  `UniverseTick` — "the analytic universe clock value … owned by the orchestrator's
  `DurableUniverseClock`" (`crates/core/src/ids.rs:131`), advanced once per orchestrator tick by
  `advance_and_broadcast_clock` and followed by every shard through a monotonic clamp. Shard tick
  rates are explicitly per-deployment ("a 10 Hz cloud shard and a 50 Hz dev shard",
  `crates/node/src/health.rs:55`), so feeding a shard-local rate into a global-clock delta makes two
  shards compute delays differing by 5× for the same distance. There **is** exactly one global rate
  in this system and it is a property of the universe clock, published in the clock sync alongside
  the epoch — that is not a magic number, it is the clock's own definition, and it is the only rate
  the formula may use. (`tick_hz` belongs in the *numerator*, and does: cells × ticks/s ÷ cells/s =
  ticks. The dimensional analysis is fine; the rate's *identity* was the bug.)
- **`d_fine` must be computed in `i128`, and `i64` is not enough.** `FINE_CELL_EDGE_M = 1/1024 m`
  (`core/src/pose.rs`), so `LIGHT_FINE_CELLS_PER_SECOND = 299_792_458 × 1024 = 306_987_476_992`,
  exact because 1024 is a power of two. But one light-year is 9.4607e15 m = **9.688e18 FINE cells**,
  and `i64::MAX` is 9.223e18: **the FINE lattice in `i64` saturates at 0.95 light-years.** Distances
  at interstellar range must be reconstructed from the tiered `(COARSE, FINE)` pair — `LatticePos`
  already carries COARSE at 1 light-year for exactly this reason — and multiplied in `i128`. A
  `d_fine: i64` would silently wrap at the first interstellar signal.
- **Distance comes from the server-authored absolute positions the A5 flip already ships**, never
  from f64 metres: two shards computing the same arrival tick from floats will disagree, and the
  divergence is silent until a replay gate catches it.

**Held at the routing node, in a hierarchical timing wheel.** Varghese & Lauck (SOSP '87) give O(1)
per-tick bookkeeping, O(1) cancel and O(m) start for m wheel levels — the structure Kafka's request
purgatory uses. Three levels of 256 slots at 20 Hz cover 256³ = 16,777,216 ticks ≈ **9.7 days**, well
beyond any sane delivery horizon.

**Which node holds it.** For `Neighbourhood` traffic it is the LCA, which is provably alive: the
demand ledger spins parents up before children and reaps children before parents (verified at
`rlm.rs:492-508` and `reconcile_reaps_child_before_parent`), so the LCA realm outlives both endpoints
of any ≤2-hop path. For `Relay` traffic it is the relay shard. Sender-held loses every in-flight
message when the sender's shard is reaped — routine in this design, not a failure — and
receiver-held is impossible when the destination realm is dormant.

#### 7.6.2 Which lane — and the refusal that makes it honest

Light-lag applies to the **Event lane only.**

State is **not queued and not delayed — it is refused.** A subscribe request for a State channel
whose emitter is beyond the light budget fails at subscribe time with a typed
`SubscribeRefusal::StateChannelBeyondLightBudget { delay_ticks, budget }`. Queueing State delivers a
four-minute-old thrust level (what `LIFESPAN` exists to prevent); silently degrading gives the player
a control that looks connected and is not. Failing loud turns a physics fact into a **legible game
rule**: you cannot fly a ship you are too far from, and the UI can say so.

**With hysteresis, because the project has already paid for this lesson once.** A single threshold on
a continuously varying distance flaps: a ship station-keeping near the boundary would see subscribe
granted / refused / granted at whatever rate its distance oscillates. `RlmTuning` carries
`teardown_cooldown_ticks`, `spinup_cooldown_ticks` and `empty_grace_ticks` sized so "a re-asserted
demand always aborts a drain before a kill fires"; the same discipline applies here:

- **Separate acquire and release radii** from ONE ratio,
  `SignalTuning::light_budget_release_ratio = 1.25` (acquire inside `budget`, release only beyond
  `1.25 × budget`).
- **A minimum hold dwell** of `demand_ttl_ticks` before a refusal can take effect.
- **A subscription refused while held is never yanked mid-manoeuvre.** It runs to its current expiry
  and is simply not renewed, and `sys.signal.link_expiring` fires one dwell before, so a pilot gets a
  visible warning rather than a dead stick.

The structural consequence is intended: **beyond about one light-second, streamed control is
impossible and the design must become "upload a queue."** RemoteTech (KSP) reached exactly this shape
— speed of light as a configurable setting, delay = path length ÷ that value, and each vessel holding
a flight computer with a queue of uploaded commands executed at their scheduled time, automatically
dropping out of time warp a few seconds before a queued command fires. Here the flight computer is
not special-cased: it is the **Nav Computer** block (§7.11, Navigation) whose `waypoints` input is a
`Blob` and whose execution is local. A distant station uploads a *program* (Event lane, reliable,
light-lagged, acknowledged) instead of streaming *inputs* (State lane, refused).

#### 7.6.3 Destination asleep, spun down, moved, or unreachable

| Situation | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Destination realm **dormant** at arrival tick | The pending Event **raises a demand** on the destination through the existing `RealmDemand` machinery — mail spins up the mailbox. Only **grant-bearing** Events may raise a spin-up demand, and doing so is charged and rate-limited (§7.8), or radio becomes a remote realm-spawn attack. |
| Destination **cannot** be spun up (budget, policy, capacity) | The Event expires by `LIFESPAN` and a `Receipt::Undeliverable { reason }` returns to the emitter — itself an Event, itself light-lagged, which is physically honest and gives the player a legible "no reply". |
| Destination realm **reaped mid-flight** | Identical to dormant: the wheel entry survives at the routing node, which outlives both. |
| Destination has **moved** | The delay is **frozen at emit**, computed once by the routing node from both endpoints' absolute positions at the accept tick. Recomputing on arrival is non-deterministic across replays and creates causality inversions (a later message overtaking an earlier one). Photons already in flight arrive even if the target has since moved outside the horizon. |
| **Routing node** reaped | It cannot be while either endpoint lives (parent-before-child ordering); if the whole subtree dies, so do the messages, correctly. |
| **Partition between emitter and its parent** | Named explicitly, because the earlier draft left it silent. After `demand_ttl_ticks` without a parent link, the emitting realm publishes `sys.signal.uplink_lost` on its own diagnostic channel and every antenna block's `link_quality` output goes to 0. The failure is *visible on the player's own HUD* — the same treatment §7.8.4 gives shedding — rather than an antenna that silently does nothing. |
| **Recipient is an offline player** | See `RetentionClass::Mailbox`, §7.8.4. A person gets a mailbox; a machine does not. |

#### 7.6.4 The delivery horizon, and where FTL lives

At 4.2 light-years the delay is 4.2 *years*. Interstellar comms is therefore not "slow", it is
undeliverable, and pretending otherwise fills a timing wheel with messages nobody will read. Two
mechanisms, cleanly separated:

- **Direct antenna traffic obeys physics**, capped by `SignalTuning::light_lag_max_ticks`. Beyond the
  horizon, emission is **refused at the emitter** with a player-visible diagnostic. This is the source
  of the "far signals arrive later" feeling at in-system distances, where it is playable.
- **The relay plane is the in-fiction FTL comms grid**, with its own per-hop latency model (a small
  constant per relay hop, not c). It requires infrastructure, it is jammable (the **EW Jammer**
  block), it is a legitimate economic good, and it is player-extendable via **Relay/Repeater** blocks.
  Interstellar coordination stays possible; it costs something and can be attacked.

> **[USER DECISION 7-A] — the in-system delay policy.** A gameplay one-way door with real content
> cost. It must be settled before the wire shape freezes, because the answer determines whether the
> State lane ever crosses a realm boundary at range.
>
> - **Option A — no light-lag at all.** Simplest; station autopilot and remote control work
>   everywhere; costs the "The Expanse" flavour entirely. Cheapest to build, hardest to add back later
>   (players will have built around zero-delay remote control).
> - **Option B — light-lag everywhere, including in-system.** At 1 AU that is 8.3 minutes. Every
>   cross-system interaction becomes mail; real-time fleet coordination dies; RemoteTech's
>   upload-a-command-queue UI becomes mandatory content, not an option.
> - **Option C (recommended) — a zero-delay bubble plus lag beyond it.** Delay is zero inside
>   `SignalTuning::instant_bubble_fine_cells`, grows with distance beyond it, and refuses beyond
>   `light_lag_max_ticks`.
>   - **Bubble: 2 light-seconds = 599,584,916 m.** Not one — the Earth–Moon distance is 384,400 km
>     = **1.28 light-seconds**, so a one-light-second bubble would put the canonical "a planet and its
>     moons" case *outside* it. Two covers a planet, its moons, a station cluster and any realistic
>     dogfight, with margin.
>   - **Horizon: one light-hour ≈ 72,000 ticks at 20 Hz**, which covers an inner star system.
>   - Relay traffic is exempt and carries its own latency.
>
> **Recommendation: C.** It preserves the station-autopilot feature exactly where the user described
> it (an approaching ship, i.e. metres to thousands of kilometres), it makes distance *felt* on the
> interplanetary scale, and it keeps interstellar play alive through infrastructure rather than
> physics. Both thresholds are config fields, so the *shape* is not a one-way door even though the
> *feature* is; what must be decided now is only whether the State lane may ever be light-lagged.
> Under C the answer is a clean no, which is what lets §7.6.2's refusal be a hard rule.
