### 7.7 Voice, video and text as signals

#### 7.7.1 The architecturally honest shape

The user's model — "all types of communication should be signals" — is correct as a *player-facing*
model and dangerous as an implementation. Three independent facts make media unable to ride the tick
bus:

1. **Granularity.** The sim tick is 20 Hz = 50 ms. Opus real-time frames are 20 ms and conversational
   voice needs <60 ms one-way. The tick is wrong by 2.5× before any queueing.
2. **Volume.** Opus at 16/24/32 kbps with 20 ms frames = 40/60/80 B payloads at 50 packets/s,
   becoming 32/40/48 kbps on the wire with 40 B IP/UDP/RTP headers, or 28/36/44 kbps over QUIC
   datagrams (~30 B overhead).
3. **Determinism.** Media is non-deterministic input. Anything entering the deterministic tick enters
   the replay and byte-identity gates.

So: **a signal carries the handle and the negotiation; media rides a separate real-time path.**

```rust
pub struct StreamHandle {
    pub stream_id: u64,
    pub kind:      MediaKind,     // Voice | Video | Telemetry
    pub codec:     CodecParams,   // fixed-point / integer fields only
    pub endpoint:  RelayEndpoint, // SFU address
    pub grant:     GrantId,       // §7.5 — the authorisation to consume
    pub expiry:    UniverseTick,
}
```

`SignalValue::Handle` is Event-lane only. The **Radio Transceiver** block's `voice` input port takes
a `Handle` and its `rx_voice` output emits one — so at the block layer, and to the player, voice
really *is* a signal. Only the bytes travel elsewhere. Text is a signal with no asterisk: a
`ChatMessage` `Blob` on the Event lane, reliable, ordered, retention-classified (§7.1.4).

RTP-over-QUIC (draft-ietf-avtcore-rtp-over-quic) maps one RTP packet to one RFC 9221 DATAGRAM frame
with no extra framing; datagrams are congestion-controlled and ack-eliciting but never retransmitted
and not flow-controlled — exactly the semantics wanted. **Caveat from this project's own history:**
the BULK-paced-from-RTT work exists because bulk traffic already starved datagrams once. Voice needs
its own pacing budget or its own connection; it must not share an unpaced lane with chunk uploads.

#### 7.7.2 The bandwidth arithmetic — media is 25–40× the entire signal bus

A realm-to-realm link at the full 64-channel export cap costs ≈5.5 kB/s ≈ 44 kbps (§7.1.5). A client
receiving panel content for a busy cockpit costs ≈6.7 kB/s (§7.9). Per-player media, k = 6 audible
speakers at 40 kbps forwarded: **240 kbps = 30 kB/s**, i.e. **≈4.5× a whole realm-to-realm link and
≈4.5× a full cockpit's panel feed.** A single video stream is worse by another order of magnitude.
The whole 100k-player galaxy's *interest reconcile* traffic (§7.3.4) is 181 KB/s — **six players'
worth of voice.**

Unbounded proximity voice, with an SFU forwarding n(n−1) streams for a fully-talking group:

| group size | down per listener | server egress for that one group |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 360 kbps | 3.6 Mbps |
| 20 | 760 kbps | 15.2 Mbps |
| 50 | 1.96 Mbps (above many consumer links) | **98 Mbps** |

The **audible-set cap is therefore not a tuning knob, it is load-bearing**: hard-cap the audible set
at `k = 4..8` loudest-by-distance speakers, **server-side**, and per-listener cost becomes a
constant. Server-side is also required because the cap is simultaneously an anti-griefing control.

**Client-side spatialisation is free here in a way it is not for most games**, because the server
already authors and ships ready-to-draw absolute positions every tick — the panning and falloff data
is already on the wire. This is a deliberate application of the standing "server does all math"
law, not an exception to it, and the test that makes it legitimate is stated once here and reused
in §7.9: **a derived quantity is *rendering* if and only if no server-authoritative state ever
depends on it.** Audio panning passes that test — nothing downstream reads it, no authority derives
from it, two clients disagreeing about a pan angle changes nothing about the world. Floating-origin
position composition failed exactly that test, which is why S2/S3 had to be reworked server-side.
The SFU stays a pure forwarder; server-side mixing (an MCU) would save client bandwidth, cost an
order of magnitude more CPU, and destroy spatialisation.

**SFU capacity.** mediasoup documents ~500 consumers per Worker with one Worker = one core; LiveKit's
16-core benchmark reaches 150 publishers / 150 subscribers at 720p at 85% CPU, and capacity scales
with subscribed *tracks*, not rooms or users. At 100k concurrent players with k = 6: worst case 600k
consumer tracks ≈ **1,200 forwarding cores**; at a realistic 10% simultaneously in a talking group,
≈**120 cores**. That is a real, recurring, per-core operating cost and the largest single
infrastructure line item in the product.

> **[USER DECISION 7-B] — the media transport.** A vendor/licence and recurring-cost decision, not a
> technical one, and it should be taken before the `StreamHandle` fields freeze.
>
> - **Option A — self-hosted SFU (mediasoup or LiveKit) behind our own control plane.** Full control
>   of the audible-set policy and of retention; ~120–1,200 cores at 100k players, billed per
>   core-minute; we own the ops burden and the abuse tooling.
> - **Option B — managed vendor (Vivox-class), billed per monthly active user.** Cheapest to start,
>   asymptotically more expensive, ships moderation tooling, and hands proximity-cap enforcement to a
>   third party that does not know our realm geometry (we would push audible sets to it every tick).
> - **Option C — no voice at launch; text-only, with `MediaKind::Voice` reserved on the wire.** Zero
>   cost, zero moderation surface, and the handle field costs nothing to reserve now.
>
> **Recommendation: C now, A later, never B.** Reserving `StreamHandle` and `MediaKind` costs a few
> bytes in an enum today; building an SFU control plane before there are players to talk to is a
> phase's work spent on the wrong phase. When voice ships, self-hosting is the option that keeps the
> proximity cap and the moderation policy inside a system that knows where the players are.
>
> **Rider (needs an explicit answer whichever option is taken): does voice get a rolling recording
> buffer for report-after-the-fact?** A privacy and jurisdiction question with a legal answer, not an
> engineering one, and genuinely one-way — adding recording after launch is a consent re-collection
> exercise across the whole player base.

---

### 7.8 Anti-abuse, admission, moderation and retention

Four defensive layers, in the order they act. Only the first *prevents* the bomb; the rest contain
it. Moderation and retention are folded in here because they are enforcement on the same egress
points, not a separate subsystem.

#### 7.8.1 Build time — a declared cost, checked when a blueprint or config is applied

Every `FunctionDef` carries a declared simulation cost — `pcu`, the single budget currency §2 already
persists per realm as `realm_pcu`, plus the one column §7 asks for, `probe_cost` (§7.10.2). `pcu` is — Space Engineers' Performance Cost Unit, the proven
mechanism: armour = 1, mechanical blocks/cockpits/connectors = 100–200, weapons = 225–825, default
world budget 100,000 PCU calibrated to ≈100% CPU on minimum-spec hardware, with admins sorting
entities by PCU to find offenders.

The check runs **when a blueprint is pasted or a block configuration is applied**, and the change is
**REFUSED** — not truncated, not queued, not degraded — if the construct's total exceeds
`SignalTuning::realm_signal_budget`. SE's model is the only one of the three shipped precedents that
prevents the bomb rather than surviving it: Second Life's 64-entry event queue silently discards
overflow (a famous source of "my script randomly stopped"), and Roblox's ~500 requests/second/client
platform ceiling still leaves servers crashable and still requires every developer to implement
server-side limiting anyway.

The realm's total is also a first-class input to the demand-driven scheduler's spin-up decision — a
realm costing 10× the median is scheduled accordingly rather than discovered at runtime — and it is
computable from the persisted block deltas without loading the world, as an incremental accumulator
updated at edit time.

**With the ladder, the scheduler gains a second input — and it sizes the *when*, never the *how
much*.** ~~A realm is now demanded *at a tier*: the observer that raised the demand sees it at tier
`L`, so it entered visibility at roughly `786 × 2^L` metres (Addendum 2 §C.2).~~ **Struck: the second
input is not a tier.** The insight that the lead should be *derived* rather than tuned is right and is
kept; only its source was wrong, because a rung is a client-local, runtime-adjustable, governor-modified
quantity the server may not derive an authoritative schedule from (§7.1.6's tier-hint rule). The server
already authors every pose after the A5 flip, so the two quantities the lead actually needs — distance
and closing speed — are server-known, and the derived lead is strictly better than the tier form
because it is continuous rather than quantised into rungs and cannot drift when render tuning changes.
Three consequences, in the order the scheduler applies them:

- **Admission is tier-INVARIANT.** `realm_pcu` is the whole cost, and SIG-NO-COARSEN (§7.1.6) forbids
  discounting it because the realm is far away: a realm you can only see as a dot still runs its full
  signal pass, its full arbitration and its full grant checks. A scheduler that admitted distant
  realms at a discount would be under-provisioning by exactly the amount its beacons still cost, and
  would discover the shortfall as a tick overrun at the moment a player closed — the worst possible
  moment. **Refusing to spin a realm up because the budget is full is legal; spinning up a cheap half
  realm is not.**
- **Lead time is DERIVED from server-known distance and closing speed, and this is the win.**
  ~~`786 × 2^L ÷ v_closing` seconds, with the spin-up queue key `(min demanded tier, then
  realm_pcu)`.~~ **Struck and replaced:**

  ```
  d_demand(r)       = r.bounding_radius_m / tan(aoi_theta_min_rad / 2)   // the LOCKED AoI rule, server-side
  v_closing(o, r)   = max(0, -d/dt |p_o - p_r|)                          // from server-authored poses
  lead_time_s       = d_demand(r) / max(v_closing(o, r), v_closing_floor)
  spin-up queue key = (ascending lead_time_s, then ascending realm_pcu)  // near-and-soon first
  ```

  `aoi_theta_min_rad` and `v_closing_floor` are fields on the existing AoI/demand tuning struct, never
  inline literals. This is computed, not tuned; it is correct at every speed and every scale; and it
  uses only quantities the demand loop already holds, so it asks the lifecycle machinery for **no new
  wire field at all**.
- **Teardown reads the release side only.** A realm receding to coarser rungs sheds observation work
  (§7.1.6's client-facing `Telemetry` throttle, the finer pyramid rungs) and must never trigger a
  reap; a reap still requires the existing `Empty` / `demand_ttl` hysteresis, unchanged. Coupling
  teardown to a rung would let one player's camera reap another player's ship.

> ~~**§7 therefore asks for one number the lifecycle machinery does not carry: the observer's detail
> tier, computed server-side at the observer's home shard and SHIPPED — `OccupantInterest::observer_tier: u8`
> on the existing up-flow, folded at each ancestor into `LedgerCell::min_demanded_tier`.**~~
>
> **STRUCK, with `LedgerCell::min_demanded_tier` and the `PROTO_MINOR` 7 → 8 bump raised for them.**
> The request was a violation of exactly the seam §7.1.6 exists to hold: it derived a
> server-authoritative scheduling input — the spin-up lead time and the queue key — from a client-local,
> runtime-adjustable, governor-modified pixel target the server cannot have. The lead-time bullet above
> keeps the insight and replaces the source, and the replacement asks for **nothing new on the wire**:
> `d_demand` comes from the realm's own bounding radius and the locked AoI rule, and `v_closing` comes
> from the poses the server already authors. §7.18 item 17 is struck accordingly.
>
> The observer-side field that DOES survive belongs to §3.10 and not to §7: `tier_floor` on the
> client's AoI interest report — client-declared, server-clamped, non-authoritative, legal for egress
> selection only. §7 reads it in exactly one place (§7.1.6's client-facing `Telemetry` egress) and
> derives nothing from it.

#### 7.8.2 The pricing rule — charge DELIVERIES, not publishes

```
cost(tick) = Σ_{c ∈ dirty} ( |subs[c].local| + |subs[c].remote_expanded| )
```

Exact and free to compute, because the compiled subscriber list makes `subs[c].len()` O(1). It prices
the actual harm:

- A 10,000-block construct publishing furiously **to nobody** costs ~0 and is **allowed**. Big quiet
  ships should be legal.
- A single publish to 10,000 subscribers is the attack, and it is priced at 10,000.

Charging per publish gets both cases exactly backwards.

#### 7.8.3 Run time — token buckets, bounded queues, and ONE back-pressure rule

Per-session token buckets (never per-IP — NAT makes per-IP both unfair and evadable), calibrated from
the previous project's shipped values: **signal publish 200 burst / 100 per second; remote publish
100 / 50; grant operations 50 / 10.** Plus `FunctionDef::emit_rate_limit_hz`, refinable downward per
port — data, not policy code.

**The back-pressure rule, stated once so it cannot be contradicted twice.** Three outcomes are
possible for an over-budget item and only one is legal:

| Outcome | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Stall the tick until the window opens | **Forbidden.** This is the sim stall §7.1.2 split the lanes to avoid. |
| Queue without a bound | **Forbidden.** Unbounded growth is §7.5.4's memory attack by another route, and it is the Second Life failure §7.8.1 rightly mocks. |
| **Bound the queue and refuse loudly** | **The rule.** |

Concretely: a per-destination Event queue of `SignalTuning::event_queue_depth = 256` items
(≈16 KB at 60 B/item). On overflow the *newest* item is refused — not the oldest dropped, because
Event ordering is a guarantee — with `Receipt::Refusal { QueueFull }` to the emitter, **and the
emitting port latches into a visible `refused` state** that a Display Cover can render and a player
can debug. State items are never queued at all; they are coalesced and, if a bundle still overflows,
shed per §7.8.4.

#### 7.8.4 Bundles are bounded, shedding is LOUD, and retention is declared

A per-destination bundle has a hard byte cap sized against `CONSERVATIVE_DATAGRAM_BUDGET = 1200`
minus the 68 B header, exactly as `partition_entities` already does. On overflow:

1. State items are dropped **lowest-priority-first** (priority = the channel's declared class, then
   staleness), which is correct because State is latest-wins and the next tick heals it.
2. Event items are **never dropped in the bundle** — they remain queued under §7.8.3's bounded queue
   and are refused at its head, not silently discarded at the wire.
3. A `Receipt::Shed { channel, dropped, reason }` goes back to the emitting realm **and** is published
   on a reserved diagnostic channel (`sys.signal.shed`) inside the owning realm.

Point 3 is what matters for the player: a Display Cover bound to `sys.signal.shed` turns an invisible
failure into a **gameplay signal on the owner's own HUD** — "your ship is shedding signals; you have
wired too much". Silent shedding is how Second Life produced a decade of "my script randomly
stopped".

**Retention is a declared field on every Event channel, not an afterthought.**

```rust
pub enum RetentionClass { Ephemeral, Reportable, Mailbox }
```

- **`Ephemeral`** — never stored anywhere. Machine-to-machine traffic; the default for
  `Neighbourhood` channels.
- **`Reportable`** (the default for player-to-player text) — written to an append-only moderation log
  in the **account-tier store**, keyed by `(channel_key, emitter_account, seq)` with a configured
  retention window. Never into a realm's block store, which is world state and is re-shardable.
- **`Mailbox`** — the answer to "a player cannot message a friend who is offline", which is a product
  hole rather than a physics nicety, and which the light-lag feature makes worse precisely where it is
  most interesting (an interstellar message is by definition sent to someone who will not be online
  when it lands). A `Mailbox` Event whose destination **principal is an account** and that account is
  offline is written to the account-tier store and delivered on next login. Bounded:
  `SignalTuning::max_mailbox_items = 256` per account, oldest evicted with a visible notice.
  **A ship is not an account**: a fleet order sent to a machine whose realm is dormant follows §7.6.3
  — it spins the realm up if grant-bearing, otherwise it expires with a `Receipt::Undeliverable`. That
  asymmetry is deliberate and should be surfaced in fiction ("people have inboxes; ships do not").

**Moderation filters DELIVERY TO A HUMAN. It never filters SIMULATION.** This sentence is the whole
architecture. A blocked player's ship still thrusts, their doors still open, their blocks still emit —
because if a personal block list could change what a shard simulates, two shards would disagree about
physics and determinism would depend on social state. Moderation sits strictly on the *egress* side,
at **three** chokepoints:

1. **The client Event/State egress** (the gateway composing a player's bundle) consults a
   `SocialPolicy { blocked: Set<AccountId>, muted: Set<AccountId>, muted_channels: Set<ChannelKey> }`
   held in the **account-tier store** — it must survive the player moving between realms, it must
   never be readable by another realm's shard (HR1), and it is per-account, not per-realm.
2. **The SFU's per-listener consumer set** applies the same policy when composing the audible set,
   which is also where the k-cap is applied, so it is one filter pass, not two.
3. **The panel and sign draw-command composer** (§7.9). This is the chokepoint an earlier draft
   missed: a blocked player's abusive **Sign/Nameplate** text or **Display Cover** content reaches
   the victim through server-composed world state, which is neither of the first two. Text authored
   by a blocked account renders as a **redacted placeholder** — never as removed geometry, because
   removing geometry would be a simulation divergence, while replacing glyphs is presentation and
   passes §7.7.2's rendering test.

A **report** action snapshots the reporter's last K received messages on that channel plus metadata
(tick, realm path, emitter account, grant id if the write was grant-authorised — which is how "a
station's autopilot said something abusive" is attributable to the station's *owner*).

The block-level surface: **mute is a signal.** A player's mute of a channel is an unsubscribe, which
the bus already supports; a player's mute of a *person* is a `SocialPolicy` edit. Both are Event-lane
actions with durable effect, both carry `(correlation_id, step_id)`, both are revocable — moderation
reuses the grant machinery rather than inventing a parallel one.

#### 7.8.5 Walking the 10,000-block bomb

A griefer builds a 10,000-block construct where every block publishes a distinct channel every tick
and subscribes to every other block's channel — the O(n²) shape, 10⁸ deliveries per tick.

| Layer | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Build time** | 10,000 functional blocks × `pcu` exceeds the realm's PCU budget long before the wiring is attempted. **The blueprint is refused**, with a named diagnostic and a number. |
| If the budget were somehow met | Wiring block *k* to 9,999 subscribers is a **config apply**, which recomputes `Σ|subs[c]|` and refuses at the first port pushing the projected delivery count over `deliveries_per_tick_budget = 1,000,000`. |
| Run time | The publish token bucket (200 burst / 100 per second per session) caps the *rate* of new writes regardless. |
| Delivery | Even if all the above were bypassed, the pass is O(deliveries) with a hard per-tick budget; exceeding it sheds State loudly and charges the emitter. |
| Cross-shard | The construct's channels are `Local` unless explicitly exported, export is capped at 64 keys, and `hops ≤ 2`. **The bomb cannot leave the neighbourhood.** |
| Memory | Even a distributed variant (10,000 distinct channel names emitted *into* a victim realm) is bounded by `max_replay_entries = 16_384` with eviction-and-refuse (§7.5.4), not by the attacker's patience. |

The bomb is stopped five times, and the first stop is the only one that costs the victim nothing.

---

### 7.9 The block-cover — the signal seam behind it

The user's requirement is specific: *"the ability to put HUD interfaces on ANY block. A transparent
block-cover where you choose a widget + the signals to show; it renders numbers/graphs on any block,
e.g. the shield-window of a ship."* **§6.7 owns the block-cover**: the `WidgetDef` command set, the
0..4096 fixed-point panel space, the four compositing layers, the static `max_commands`/`max_glyphs`
refusal, the instanced world-space MSDF pass, and the finding that a draw list is a *level* and
therefore rides the existing unreliable latest-wins snapshot lane rather than needing DEFERRED D-4.
None of that is restated here. What §7 owns is the four-line seam between a signal and a pixel, and
its cost — because "the server composes the panels its player can see" is this section's most-cited
client-facing claim and it must not be left unpriced.

**The seam.** A Display Cover is a `Surface`-kernel block occupying a *face overlay*, not a cell: it
changes no occupancy, mass or collision. Its `BlockConfig` binds **input ports to widget slots**, and
the widget's leaves reference those slots — never a channel name, never a raw port. Three rules
follow, and they are all §7's:

1. **The server evaluates; the client draws.** Number formatting, gauge normalisation against
   `lo`/`hi`, and graph windowing all happen server-side, so what crosses is a value already in the
   widget's declared scale. The client never reads a channel, never evaluates a `TransferFn`, and
   never formats. This is §7.3.7's rule applied to the one place it is most tempting to break.
2. **Refresh is ONE RUNG OF THE LADDER, not an exception to a ban.** ~~Below θ_min the binary render
   rule means the panel draws nothing rather than degrading.~~ That framing is retracted with the ban
   itself (Addendum 2 §D.1 row 7): panel refresh was never a carve-out, it was the first rung of the
   ladder the project had not yet admitted to having.

   ~~Restated, the panel content ladder is the ONE locked angular-size rule with three rungs and a
   floor: a full draw list on entry; changed bindings only in steady state; changed bindings **divided
   by `telemetry_divisor_for_tier(L)`** as the housing's tier rises (§7.1.6); and no content at all
   below θ_min.~~ **Struck: §6.9 owns the panel content ladder and it has FOUR rungs, not three.** They
   are `C0 live` (θ above the legibility threshold AND inside the client's byte budget), `C1 chrome`
   (θ above threshold, outside the byte budget), `C2 reduced` (θ between θ_reduced and the legibility
   threshold) and `C3 off` (θ below θ_reduced), filled in **descending angular size** until
   `DecorTuning::panel_bytes_per_client_max` is exhausted. §6 also owns the
   `state_commands`/`detail_commands` split, `WidgetDef::compose(sources, band)`, and the rule that a
   reduced list may drop RESOLUTION but never drop or alter STATE. §7 cites those rungs by name and
   states only the seam: **(a)** the derived `Telemetry`/`Control` bit; **(b)** only `Telemetry` may be
   rate-reduced, and only at the client-facing egress, never on realm↔realm export; **(c)** the value
   is held between refreshes, never zeroed; **(d)** the reduced rate is floored by
   `SignalTuning::telemetry_min_refresh_hz` — and the rate itself is §6.9's server-side
   `refresh_hz = clamp(base_hz × (θ/θ_ref)², 0, max_hz)` (§7.1.6).

   The source ports are `OnChange` by default, so a panel showing a constant value costs **zero bytes
   and zero client work at every rung**; `Divided(n)` on a `Sampler` feeding a panel is a separate,
   block-authored gate that is not part of the ladder at all.

   **The floor is a legibility fact, not a fidelity cut**, which is what keeps it inside Addendum 2
   §C.7's "coarsen the geometry, never the state" rule. Compositing glyphs no eye can resolve is not
   information, and nothing downstream reads the composed list (§7.7.2's rendering test), so removing
   it changes no fact and no authority. Note that the floor is a *distance*, derived per panel from
   its own cap height, not a tier: a big sign stays legible for kilometres and keeps composing.

   **The exception inside the exception, which §C.7 names explicitly: a status light is not a glyph
   run.** A docking-clamp indicator or a hull-breach lamp carries actionable state at an angular size
   two orders of magnitude below readable text, and it must not ride the panel ladder at all.
   **Decided: any `WidgetClass` whose entire output is one colour — `Indicator`, and the lit/unlit
   state of `Button` and `Toggle` — is carried on a separate transient per-realm state-light lane
   composed by the realm owner and shipped at the observer's clamped rung, so it survives to every rung
   including the realm proxy. It is NOT carried in the edit pyramid, which is permanent derived terrain
   data with a different key, a different lifetime and a different write rate. Only the glyph-bearing
   classes (`Display`, `Text`, sign faces, `Holo`) ride §6.9's C0..C3 ladder and have a θ_min floor.**

   ~~"a per-block runtime material state carried on the housing chunk's own draw data, so it rides the
   terrain/construction rung"~~ was the earlier wording and it is struck as written, because §2.6's ban
   on per-block state entering the edit pyramid stands unamended and is right: the pyramid changes at
   EDIT rate and a lamp's colour changes at TICK rate. The mechanism survives in full; only its
   carrier is named properly.

   ```rust
   // crates/sim — TRANSIENT, NEVER PERSISTED, NEVER IN THE PYRAMID.
   /// One entry per coarse cell containing at least one STATE_VISIBLE block whose state is not its
   /// declared default. Composed by the realm owner per (tier, chunk), shipped on the SAME client lane
   /// and at the SAME clamped rung as the chunk delta (§7.1.6's egress-selection rule).
   pub struct StateLightEntry {
       pub cell:  CellIndex,   // within the tier-L chunk
       pub rgb:   [u8; 3],     // the composed colour
       pub flags: u8,          // bit 0 = blinking; bits 1..8 reserved, MUST decode as zero
   }
   // Coalescing when several STATE_VISIBLE blocks share one coarse cell: highest `state_priority`
   // wins; ties → lowest CellIndex. Total, deterministic, order-free.
   ```

   **`STATE_VISIBLE` is ONE reservation, not three.** `BlockTypeDef.flags & STATE_VISIBLE` (§2's
   registry row, with a content-build coherence assertion that every row carrying it has a
   `FunctionRef` with an emitting port, and a `state_priority: u8` for the coalescing key above) **is**
   §2.5.5's `STATE_VISIBLE`, **is** this rule's status-light exemption, and **is** §6.9's status-light
   exemption. Cost: one flag bit, one transient lane, one coalescing rule, and one fewer draw list. The
   alternative — one θ_min for every widget class — either makes text absurdly expensive to keep
   composing or makes a hull-breach lamp invisible at 40 m, and the second is a gameplay defect, not a
   rendering trade. Not a one-way door: both thresholds are tuning fields.
3. **Moderation applies here.** The panel and sign composer is the third `SocialPolicy` chokepoint
   (§7.8.4): glyph runs authored by a blocked account render redacted. Geometry is never removed,
   because that would be simulation divergence; replacing glyphs is presentation.

**The cost, using §6.7's measured widget sizes.** A typical widget (a numeric, a gauge, a label) is
12–30 commands ≈ **150–360 B**, worst case 3 KB. Steady state ships only the changed bound values:
`(panel_id u32, slot u8, value Fx)` = **13 B per changed binding**.

| Case | Panels | Steady-state bytes/s to one client |
|---|---|---|
| Naive "500 visible panels", 4 bindings each, 10% churn at 20 Hz | 500 | 500 × 4 × 0.1 × 20 × 13 B = **52 kB/s** |
| After the θ_min floor — a busy cockpit plus a hangar | 64 | 64 × 4 × 0.1 × 20 × 13 B = **6.7 kB/s** |
| Entering a hangar: full draw lists for newly visible panels | 64 new | 64 × 250 B ≈ **16 kB one-off** |

The floor is what makes the number small, and it is worth stating why the 500-panel row is not the
operative one. ~~At 1080p with a 60° horizontal FOV one pixel subtends 0.000545 rad, so the ~8 px cap
height below which text is unreadable is 0.00436 rad — ≈34 m for a 0.15 m cap height, ≈1.15 km at 5 m,
≈11.5 km at 50 m.~~ **Struck: that was a third reference screen.** There is ONE, and §7 reads it from
the render tuning struct rather than declaring its own — 1920 × 1080 at a 70° **horizontal** FOV, so
`θ_px = fov_h_rad / render_width_px = 6.363e-4 rad` on axis and
`θ_text_min = text_cap_px_min × θ_px = 5.090e-3 rad` at the shared `text_cap_px_min = 8.0`, which is
the one legibility primitive §6.9 and §7.9 both derive from. At the reference screen a display whose
text cap height is 0.15 m is unreadable beyond **≈29.5 m** and stops composing there; 5 m of cap height
reaches **≈982 m**; 50 m reaches **≈9.82 km**.

> **[USER DECISION 7-H] — how far can a stranger read your status lights?** *This row now covers
> mechanism AND range together; §2.5.5's row ("appearance that carries actionable state") and §6.9's
> status-light exemption both cite it rather than restating it, and all three refer to ONE reservation:
> the `STATE_VISIBLE` flag on the block-type row.*
>
> A docking-clamp light, a hull-breach lamp, a running light: how far away can a stranger read it? The
> standing rule is "coarsen the geometry, never the state" — but at three kilometres a ship's housing is
> drawn as a handful of coarse cells, so the state has to be carried by something other than the
> geometry, and whatever carries it is also a passive, unjammable, line-of-sight sensor at whatever
> range it reaches — which competes with the Sensors catalogue (§7.11) and with the EW Jammer, whose
> whole point is denying exactly that kind of knowledge.
>
> - **Option A (recommended) — lights are visible at every rung, out to whatever the ladder draws.**
>   Mechanically it is a small transient per-realm lane of (coarse cell, colour) composed by the realm
>   owner and shipped at the observer's rung — never in the edit pyramid, which is permanent terrain
>   data with a different lifetime and write rate. Consistent with "never coarsen the state" by
>   construction, and it makes lighting a real build decision: a running-dark warship is a stealth
>   choice a player *made*. It is weaker intel than it looks — a stranger sees that a lamp is red, not
>   what channel drove it — but it does compete with the Sensors catalogue and the jammer, and a lamp
>   cannot be seen coming the way a radar can. Cost: one flag bit, one transient lane, one coalescing
>   rule.
> - **Option B — lights fall to the text legibility floor**, so only crew (whose HUD reads the channel
>   directly) see them past about 30 m. Preserves the sensor blocks' value and costs nothing to build —
>   but it puts *state* behind a distance gate, which is the thing the standing rule forbids, and it
>   makes a hull-breach lamp useless at the range you would most want it.
> - **Option C — A, plus physical brightness:** a lamp's visible range falls out of its emissive
>   intensity against the sky's exposure, so a running light dies at 2 km and a landing beacon carries
>   50. Most physical, most work, and it belongs to the lighting subsystem rather than to the signal
>   bus.
>
> **Recommendation: A now, C as a later rendering refinement; never B.** Note that the mechanism
> question is already ruled and is **not** part of this decision: the state rides a separate transient
> lane on the housing's own draw data, NOT the edit pyramid and NOT the signal bus — the signal bus
> cannot deliver it, because clients are not subscribers (§7.3.7) and there is no path by which a
> non-subscribing stranger learns a lamp's colour. Reserving the flag bit and the lane shape costs
> nothing today even if the answer is B, and adding the concept after content is authored means
> re-auditing every block type. Mechanically this is not a one-way door (both are thresholds), but *in
> play* it is: builders who used unlit hulls as stealth will have built around whichever answer ships.

**`SignalTuning::panel_updates_per_tick_budget = 256`** per client per tick caps the worst case at
256 × 13 B × 20 Hz = 66.6 kB/s. Over-budget panels refresh round-robin in `panel_id` order
(deterministic) and the affected panel publishes `sys.panel.throttled` — which, like shedding, is
itself a signal the owner can display.

All of this sits on top of DEFERRED D-9 (whole-realm broadcast with no within-realm per-entity AoI;
measured 357,248 messages and a 1,920 msgs/tick peak at 128 sessions) and does not work without the
D-9/D-39.5 per-entity AoI reshape. That dependency is named in §7.18 item 6, not assumed.

---

### 7.10 Functional blocks — the kernel decomposition and the declarative shape

#### 7.10.1 Six kernels, and the honest dispatch count

Sorting the whole catalogue by *what the tick actually does* yields six behaviours:

| Kernel | Does | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Pure** | read declared inputs, compute, write declared outputs. No world access. | combinators, PID, latch, timer, counter, LUT, event controller, script chip |
| **Actuator** | read a command port, drive a constrained degree of freedom on a sub-assembly, emit measured state | piston, rotor, hinge, rail, clamp, wheel, turret mount, door |
| **Sampler** | probe the world through a declared query, emit the result | every sensor, radar, camera, ore scanner, strain gauge, gravimeter |
| **Converter** | consume resources at a declared rate, produce other resources, gated by an input port | reactor, solar panel, refinery, assembler, scrubber, electrolyser, battery, radiator |
| **Emitter** | inject something outside the block's own cell: force, matter, radiation, or a routed signal | thruster, gyro, gun, shield emitter, antenna, grow lamp, speaker, ejector |
| **Surface** | the player-interaction seam — input (seat, button, keypad) or output (display cover, indicator, sign) | seat, button, lever, display cover, holo-projector |

**The dispatch count, stated honestly rather than as a slogan.** "Six kernels, zero per-block
behaviour functions" is true of the *block* axis and false as a total. Every kernel is parameterised
by a closed sub-enum, and those sub-enums are where behaviour lives:

| Sub-enum | Arms | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `PureOp` | 12 | Const, Arith, Compare, Select, Latch, Timer, Counter, Pid, Curve, EventCtl, BusHub, Expr |
| `DofSpec` | 3 | Prismatic, Revolute, RailPath |
| `DriveSpec` | 3 | Position, Velocity, Force |
| `ProbeSpec` | 5 | Ray, Sphere, Volume, Field, Celestial |
| `MediumSpec` | 5 | Force, Torque, Matter, Radiation, SignalRoute |
| `WidgetClass` | 9 | Seat, Button, Toggle, Slider, Keypad, Display, Indicator, Text, Holo |
| `RecipeRef` | **0** | a recipe is a table row consumed by ONE closed-form integrator (§7.11.3) |

**Total runtime match arity: 6 + 37 = 43 arms**, not 6 and not 143. That is still a 3.3× reduction
against per-block dispatch, and — the property that actually matters — it is *bounded*: adding a
block adds **zero** arms; adding a new kernel *parameter class* adds one arm and is a reviewed event.
Bedrock Minecraft reached the same place (≈38 reusable components composing thousands of blocks) and
so did Factorio (a fixed set of prototype base-types, arbitrarily many data-defined prototypes).

**The rule that makes it hold: no per-block behaviour code, ever.** Adding a block is one enum
row in §2's generated `block_types.manifest` plus zero behaviour code, verified by an `ALL`-loop test
over the static table. The moment someone writes `match ty { PISTON => ... }` in a system, the
decomposition is defeated and the coverage cost explodes.

#### 7.10.2 The declarative shape, and who owns which field

**There is no `BlockDef` in this design, and inventing one would be the defect.** §2 already splits a
block into three authored rows — `MaterialDef` (substance: mass, integrity, the damage-channel
resistance matrix, flammability, thermal, airtightness — the user's "each block has LIFE and different
tools decrease it faster"), `ShapeDef` (form), and **`FunctionDef` (function)** — composed by a
generated `BlockTypeDef { material, shape, function, flags }` indexed by `BlockTypeId(u16)`. §2 owns
`FunctionDef`'s *shape as a table row*, because the row is what the identity digest covers; **§7 owns
its semantics.** The division is exact:

```rust
// §2 owns this row's LAYOUT (21 B → 24 padded). §7 owns what every field MEANS.
pub struct FunctionDef {
    pub tag: u16,
    pub kernel: Kernel,                 // §7.10.1 — the ONLY runtime dispatch point
    pub authority: AuthorityClass,
    pub tick: TickPolicy,               // §7.2.4 — OnChange is the default
    pub ports_off: u16, pub ports_len: u8,        // (offset, len) into a flat static PortDef array
    pub port_growth: PortGrowth,        // Fixed | PlayerNamed { max_in, max_out }
    pub res_off: u16, pub res_len: u8,
    pub config_schema: SchemaId, pub max_config_bytes: u16,
    pub emit_rate_limit_hz: u16,        // §7.8.3 — the block-level publish cap
    pub pcu: u16,                       // §7.8.1 — THE single budget currency
}
```

Three notes where §7 asks something of that row rather than assuming it:

- **`pcu` is the only static cost column, deliberately.** An earlier draft added a separate
  `signal_cost`; it is unnecessary, because delivery cost is priced *dynamically* and exactly by
  `Σ_c |subs[c]|` at config-apply time (§7.8.2), which is strictly better than a static weight. §2
  already persists `realm_pcu` in the realm metadata row for the demand scheduler, so there is one
  currency and one persisted sum.
- **§7 does request ONE new column: `probe_cost: u16`** (row 24 → 28 padded, ≈256 B across a
  64-row table). A world probe costs 1–10 µs against a delivery's 0.5 ns — 2,000–20,000× — and
  folding two quantities that far apart into one currency makes both meaningless. §7.15 spends it.
- **`PortDef` is a §7 type** living in §2's flat static array. Its fields are `name`, `dir`, `ty`,
  `default`, `arbitration` (§7.12), `retention` (§7.10.4), `grantable` (§7.5), and an optional
  per-port `publish_hz` that refines `FunctionDef::emit_rate_limit_hz` downward, never upward.

Instance-level, player-authored, a **TLV blob** using `core/src/tlv.rs` (already built, proptested,
with `schema_id` / `writer_max_tag` / `required_max_tag` / `field_count` and skip-unknown semantics):

```rust
pub struct BlockConfig {                   // ≤ FunctionDef::max_config_bytes
    pub bindings: Vec<PortBinding>,
    pub params:   Vec<(ParamId, Fx)>,
    pub transfer: TransferFn,
    pub widget:   Option<WidgetConfig>,    // §6.7 owns the widget; §7.9 owns the port→slot binding
}

pub struct PortBinding {
    pub port:    PortRef,
    pub channel: NameRef,        // the player's chosen NAME — interned to ChannelId at load
    pub source:  InputSource,    // §7.10.3 — the literal "keyboard press W" requirement
    pub curve:   Option<LutId>,
}

pub enum TransferFn {
    Identity, Const(Fx), Affine { a: Fx, b: Fx }, Deadband { lo: Fx, hi: Fx },
    Curve(LutId), Expr(ExprBytecode), Chip(ChipId),
}
```

TLV framing makes config-blob evolution free and — critically — a destination shard that cannot
represent a newer config **refuses the transfer** rather than decoding to `Default`. The
decode-to-Default ban is already binding for Durable kinds; a ship whose piston config silently
zeroed on a realm crossing would be a catastrophic, unattributable bug.

**The player's channel name lives in the binding, not in the block kind.** This is what makes the
user's model literal: a functional block's configuration panel opens an empty list of signals, the
player adds one by typing a name and choosing a value type, and the block emits or receives it. The
kind contributes only which ports exist and what they mean.

#### 7.10.3 "Config keyboard press W emits thrusters-forward value 100" — where that lives

The user's literal requirement needs a field, and the field must be on the **server** side or a
modified client holds authoritative configuration:

```rust
pub enum InputSource {
    None,
    Slot(InputSlot),                        // a logical slot, 0..32
    SlotPair { neg: InputSlot, pos: InputSlot }, // an axis from two slots (W/S)
    Pulse(InputSlot),                       // edge-triggered, discrete
}
```

Two levels, and the split is what makes it both server-authoritative and personally configurable:

- **The seat's TLV config binds a *logical slot* to a port and a channel**, server-side, durable, ACL-
  gated. This is the "config keyboard press W emits `thrusters-forward` value 100" the user described:
  slot 3 → port `forward` → channel `flight.thrust.fwd`, through a curve LUT, value scaled to 100%.
- **The client maps physical keys to logical slots locally.** That map is pure UI preference with no
  authority — a player who prefers ESDF rebinds nothing on the server, and a modified client can only
  send slot indices it could already send.

The wire consequence is stated so nobody has to guess: analogue slots ride the existing unreliable
latest-wins `InputDatagram` (State semantics — a lost axis frame heals next tick); `Pulse` slots ride
the **reliable client→shard discrete-action carrier** that DEFERRED D-39.1 already owes. The intent
message names a `(seat_entity, slot, value, client_seq)`; it never names a port, a channel or a block.

#### 7.10.4 Retained port state — what survives a spin-down

An empty realm is reapable in ≈2 s (§7.3.3). The catalogue is full of blocks whose entire meaning is
retained state — Latch, Counter, PID integrator, Battery `stored_J`, Gas Tank `pressure`, Timer — so
"the config persists and the values do not" would mean that on respawn every latch resets, every door
unlocks, every counter zeroes and every PID integrator dumps. That is a correctness bug at the
intersection of two user pillars (dynamic realm lifecycle; dormant-world simulation), not an edge
case, and it must be decided now because §7.18 item 4's "the block record needs no new bits"
conclusion depends on it.

> **Decided: `PortDef::retention ∈ { Volatile, Retained }`, declared per port in the static table.**
> Retained port values are written to a per-realm **`port_state`** redb table — a sibling of
> `config_state`, keyed by the same `(chunk, local_index)` plus a port slot — on realm drain, and
> reloaded on spin-up. Retaining the whole `front` table would be the wrong answer: it is 8–24 B ×
> channel count with no eviction and no meaning for a channel whose writer is a live sensor.
>
> - **Cost.** 10 B per retained port (2 B slot + 8 B `Fx`).
>   `SignalTuning::max_retained_ports_per_realm = 4096` ⇒ **40 KB per realm**, refused loudly beyond.
> - **Re-home vs reap-and-respawn are identical by construction.** A re-home moves the realm's own
>   store (the realm keeps its redb; the per-realm store handoff is the existing machinery); a reap
>   drains to the same table and a respawn reads it back. Both paths read the same rows, so there is
>   no second code path and no divergence to test for.
> - **Only outputs whose value is *state* are `Retained`** — a Latch's `q`, a Counter's `count`, a
>   Timer's `elapsed`, a Battery's `stored_J`. A sensor's reading is `Volatile` by definition; on
>   spin-up it is recomputed on the first tick.

### 7.11 The catalogue, and the six subsystems it implies

#### 7.11.1 What this catalogue is, and what P9 actually ships

`roadmap.json` P9's definition of done is *"a switch toggling a lamp"* on a planet and in a ship.
This catalogue is **a long-horizon vocabulary, not a phase's scope**, and the difference must be
stated rather than discovered:

| Tier | Blocks | What it needs beyond §7.1–§7.12 | Phase |
|---|---|---|---|
| **T0 — ships with the bus** | **27**: all 12 Logic/compute, 8 Interface/IO (Seat, Button, Toggle, Lever, Keypad, Display Cover, Indicator, Sign), 4 Communications (Short-Range Antenna, Relay/Repeater, Beacon, Data Recorder), 3 Doors (Door Controller, Lock/Bolt, Access Reader) | nothing — pure logic, pure surfaces, pure routing | **P9** |
| **T1 — needs kinematic articulation** | 12 Mechanical + Turret Mount | §7.16, which is designed here and costs no new simulation subsystem | **P8** |
| **T2 — needs a physics query budget** | 13 Sensors + Hover Pad + Collision Avoidance | §7.15's probe budget, on top of P5 physics | **P5/P8** |
| **T3 — needs a NEW named simulation subsystem** | the remaining ~90 | six subsystems, none of which exists or is scheduled — §7.11.2 | **[USER DECISION 7-E]** |

The 27-block T0 set is a superset of "a switch toggling a lamp" by a wide margin and is genuinely
buildable against machinery this section defines. Every claim in §7.1–§7.12 is proven by T0 alone.

#### 7.11.2 The six subsystems the catalogue presupposes

Naming them is the point; an earlier draft listed 143 blocks and left these implicit, which is a
phase's worth of unowned work hidden inside a table.

| Implied subsystem | Blocks that need it | Shape, if built | Leaned on elsewhere in §7? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Power grid / circuit topology** | 10 Power blocks and every `resources: Power` row | a per-realm connected-components pass over conduits + a per-circuit supply/demand solve, O(circuits) | Yes — every `Converter` gate and the thruster example's `power` port |
| **Fluid + gas + pressure network** | 10 Life-support blocks, hull sealing | a **room graph** (flood-fill over sealed volumes) with O(rooms) pressure, not a cell model — and the same graph gives portal-based audio occlusion, fire oxygen starvation and interior AI regions for free | No |
| **Thermal** | reactor, radiator, laser, thermostat, gas tank | a **sparse active set** of blocks whose temperature differs from ambient, evicted on relaxation. A dense per-block temperature field is the one design that provably cannot work at planet scale | Yes — §7.16 invariant 5's stall/detach thresholds |
| **Item logistics / inventory** | 10 Fabrication blocks, cargo mass → inertia tensor | per-container manifests + conveyor throughput; the mass coupling into the inertia tensor is the only part that touches physics | No |
| **Crafting recipe graph** | refinery, assembler, printer | data, plus the closed-form integrator constraint in §7.11.3 | No |
| **Structural stress** | Starbase-style bolt/frame model | a connected-components + load pass over the block graph — cheap, and the block plan already schedules the BFS/union-find | Yes — §7.16 cites it approvingly and invariant 5 detaches on it |

Three of the six are already load-bearing inside §7's own arguments (power, thermal, structural),
which is precisely why they cannot stay unnamed.

> **[USER DECISION 7-E] — which of the six subsystems are in scope, and in what order.**
> Each is comparable in size to the signal bus itself. None is in `roadmap.json`.
>
> - **Option A (recommended) — two now, two with ships, two behind the economy.**
>   **Structural stress** and the **power grid** first: both are O(components) passes over a graph the
>   block plan already builds, both are already assumed by §7.16 and by every `Converter`, and both
>   deliver disproportionate "physical ship" feeling (Starbase gets most of its physicality from an
>   *analytical* stress model with no joints at all). **Thermal (sparse active set)** and
>   **fluid/pressure (room graph)** land with P8 ship interiors, where they are the point rather than
>   a garnish. **Item logistics** and the **recipe graph** wait behind the economy overlay, because
>   they are the two whose value is almost entirely economic.
> - **Option B — all six before functional blocks ship.** Coherent and enormous; it front-loads the
>   entire simulation surface before a single lamp toggles.
> - **Option C — T0 + T1 only, permanently.** A logic-and-machinery game with no resource simulation.
>   Cheapest by far and a real design (Scrap Mechanic is close to it), but it forecloses most of the
>   catalogue and most of the economy.
>
> **Recommendation: A.** The ordering is chosen so that no subsystem is built before something in the
> shipped game depends on it, and so that the two §7 already leans on stop being assumptions.

#### 7.11.3 The one constraint the catalogue imposes on a subsystem that does not exist yet

A realm reaped after ≈2 s of emptiness and respawned three days later must resolve what its
Converters did in between. There are three possibilities and only one is affordable: (a) a closed-form
`f(elapsed_ticks)` catch-up per recipe; (b) re-simulate 5.2 million ticks on spin-up; (c) do not
advance at all. Whether unobserved realms advance is the dormant-world pillar's decision and belongs
to that section — but **§7 must impose the constraint that keeps (a) reachable, and it must impose it
now**:

> **Binding: `RecipeRef` is closed-form integrable by construction.** A recipe is
> `{ inputs: [(ResourceId, rate_per_tick: Fx)], outputs: [...], gate: PortRef }` where every rate is
> constant per tick given a constant gate value. Advance on spin-up is
> `min(elapsed_ticks, ticks_until_input_exhausted) × rate` — one multiply per resource. A recipe whose
> rate depends on its own accumulated state is **refused at definition time**, asserted by an
> `ALL`-loop test over the static table. This costs nothing today and is impossible to retrofit onto a
> recipe language that already permits state-dependent rates, which is why it is in §7.18's plant-now
> table.

Every row is `FunctionDef` + `MaterialDef` + `ShapeDef` table data; none is code. `f` is the transfer function. Ports are `in → out`.
**T0** rows ship at P9; everything else is gated by §7.11.1's tiering.

#### 7.11.5 Overlay blocks carry no overlay semantics

Four rows touch decoupled overlays: Trade Terminal (economy), Survey Marker (territory/economy),
Respawn Bay and Cryo Pod (identity/persistence). "Removable without breaking anything" is not
achievable by intent, because §2's block-type manifest is **append-only** and covered by the
`identity_prefix_digest` in the wire handshake and the store header, **in `vd-core`** — the bottom of
the dependency arrow. Retiring a row is a `RETIRED` flag, never a deletion, and keeping an
economy-named row means the standing economy-absent CI build compiles a core table naming an economy
concept.

> **Decided: overlay blocks are ordinary `Surface`-kernel blocks with `PlayerNamed` ports and no
> overlay semantics in core at all.** A Trade Terminal declares `listings` in and `sales`/`balance`
> out as *player-named ports* and knows nothing about money; the economy overlay subscribes to those
> channels from outside. A Survey Marker emits a `claim_request` and holds no claim. A Respawn Bay
> emits a `bind_request` and holds no identity state. `vd-core` then knows about a terminal exactly
> the way it knows about a lever, and the economy-absent build simply has nobody listening — which is
> what the one-way economy→game dependency actually requires.

### 7.12 Arbitration — the seat and multiple drivers

#### 7.12.1 Arbitration is a field, not a code path

```rust
pub enum Arbitration {
    Exclusive { lease: bool, priority: u8 },  // strength-ranked single writer — see below
    Sum,                                      // writers add (RCS trim: pilot + stabiliser genuinely add)
    LastWins,                                 // deterministic tiebreak on (priority, emitter EntityId)
    Max,                                      // safety interlocks: any PERMITTED emitter may assert
    Min,                                      // conservative limits: the tightest constraint wins
}
```

`Exclusive` carries a **priority**, because the section's headline scenario depends on one: an
earlier draft's `Exclusive { lease: bool }` could not express "the station's grant outranks the
seat", which §7.12.2 step 5 requires. The semantics are DDS's `OWNERSHIP = EXCLUSIVE` +
`OWNERSHIP_STRENGTH` + `DEADLINE`, adopted verbatim because they are shipped and they answer the
follow-up question correctly:

> **The current owner of an `Exclusive` port is the highest-priority writer that is *alive and
> meeting its deadline*.** A higher-priority writer **outranks** the lease holder; it does **not
> revoke** it. The seat's lease stays valid and fence-stamped throughout, so the instant the
> higher-priority writer stops publishing (grant revoked, link lost, deadline missed) the seat is the
> highest-priority live writer again and control returns on the next tick, with no re-lease
> handshake and no gap. Revocation and outranking are different operations with different fence
> semantics, and conflating them is how a pilot loses their ship to a dropped packet.

Every multi-driver question resolves through the field with **no special cases anywhere**:

| Situation | Resolution |
|---|---|
| Two players in two seats bound to the same flight channel | `Exclusive` lease conflict at equal priority, resolved by the existing Fence discipline. The second seat's `denied` output goes true; the HUD shows "controls held by X". |
| Pilot + flight computer both writing RCS trim | `Sum`. They genuinely add; no arbitration decision is needed because the physics is additive. |
| Pilot vs station autopilot | `Exclusive`, grant priority > seat priority. Preemption is a `(priority, alive, deadline)` ordering, not a branch. |
| A pilot and three turret gunners | Four channels, four leases. Coexist trivially. |
| Emergency stop | `Max` on `flight.abort`, `access: AllowList` = the realm's crew list, `grantable: false`. |
| An NPC ship | A ship whose seat is a **Nav Computer**. Zero NPC-specific control code exists. |

The `flight.abort` rule is stated once because two loose descriptions of it are two different games:
**any *crew member* may assert abort; a stranger who welds a block to your hull cannot**, because the
channel's read/write ACL is an allowlist and `grantable: false` means no grant can ever add to it.
"Any emitter may assert" would hand a boarder your engines.

**Arbitration × ValueType is a real cross-product and is checked, not assumed.** `Sum` of two `Text`
values and `Max` of two `Handle`s are meaningless, and leaving them to the accumulator is undefined
behaviour reachable from player wiring:

| | `Bool` | `Fx` | `Vec3` | `Text` | `Blob` | `Handle` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Exclusive` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `LastWins` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `Sum` | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ |
| `Max` | ✓ (OR) | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ |
| `Min` | ✓ (AND) | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ |

30 cells, resolved once in `ChannelDecl::build()` with a typed rejection enum, never on the hot path.
`Vec3` under `Max`/`Min` is rejected deliberately: a componentwise max of two vectors is a value no
physical quantity has.

**`Sum` overflow is saturating, declared, and surfaced.** Wrapping would make two shards agree on a
nonsense value; a panic in the accumulator would be a shard crash reachable from player-authored
wiring. Saturation clamps at `Fx(i64::MAX)`/`Fx(i64::MIN)` and publishes `sys.signal.saturated` with
the channel key, so the player sees the cause rather than a mysterious ceiling.

The deterministic tiebreak is not optional: `LastWins` without a total order lets two shards disagree
about the winner, and the divergence is silent.

Because arbitration is per-*port* data, **no code anywhere asks "is this a pilot?"** A thruster
consuming `flight.thrust.fwd` cannot tell a human from an autopilot and must not be able to. That is
the property that makes HR3 and HR4 hold at the block layer, and it is the property Space Engineers
reached the hard way (its AI Flight/Basic/Recorder/Defensive/Offensive blocks feed the same interfaces
a cockpit does).

#### 7.12.2 The station-autopilot flow, with the approval handshake

1. **Offer.** The station's Nav Computer emits an **Event** on `dock.autopilot.offer`
   (`plane = Neighbourhood{hops:1}`), carrying `{ offer_id, channels: [flight.*], duration_ticks,
   station_identity, station_pubkey }`. It routes one hop up to the shared parent and back down into
   the ship's realm **only because** the ship realm's exported interest set contains that key — its
   docking computer subscribes. A ship with no docking computer receives nothing and costs nothing.
2. **Verify, THEN resolve, THEN display.** *(AMENDED 2026-08-04 — ruling R19. The original step 2 went
   straight to rendering and verified the station's signature at step 4, i.e. **after** the pilot had
   already clicked approve.)* Three things happen before the pilot is shown anything:
   - **(a) Verify identity first.** The station's Ed25519 signature over its identity assertion is
     checked **before display**, not before mint. One verify, 18.86 µs, once per docking — the same
     cost either way, so the only thing the old ordering bought was a window in which a forged offer
     could be displayed as though it were real.
   - **(b) Resolve the offer into EFFECTS.** A channel name is not a capability a human can evaluate:
     what `flight.thrust.fwd` *does* is whatever **your** ship's subscriber list currently contains —
     your configuration, not the station's. So the ship walks its own compiled subscriber list for each
     requested key (O(1) per subscriber, once per docking) and renders the resolved actuator set.
   - **(c) The dialog is composed by YOUR realm**, never from the station's offer text — the same
     server-composes rule §7.9 already imposes on every in-world panel.

   The pilot therefore sees **"STATION KEPLER-3 REQUESTS CONTROL OF: MAIN ENGINES · RCS · DOCKING
   CLAMPS"**, not a channel name. ~~"STATION KEPLER-3 REQUESTS AUTOPILOT CONTROL — APPROVE / DENY"~~ is
   **struck**: it asks a player to approve a *word* and grants an actuator set they never saw.
3. **Approval.** The pilot's approval is a **reliable client→shard discrete action** (D-39.1's
   carrier, the same one block edits and fire triggers use). It is authenticated as the seated
   occupant with the seat's lease and checked against the **realm ACL** — a passenger cannot approve.
   **RE-RESOLVE AT MINT AND REFUSE IF THE SET CHANGED.** The compiled subscriber list can change
   between display and approval — a crew member with build rights re-points a requested channel at the
   reactor scram while the dialog sits open — so the effect set shown in 2(b) is recomputed at mint and
   the grant is refused, loudly, if it no longer matches what the pilot was shown.
4. **Grant mint.** The ship realm writes a durable row into its per-realm `grants` table:
   `{ grant_id, grantee = station identity + pubkey, channels, priority, expiry_tick, revoked: false }`,
   fenced, with `(correlation_id, step_id)` idempotency on the durable Event lane (steps 20–23). The
   response Event carries the grant id and its HMAC key material, encrypted to the station's public
   key from step 1. **[R19] The Ed25519 verify has MOVED to step 2(a)** — before the dialog is shown,
   not after the pilot approves. Same single verify, same cost, once per docking; the old ordering
   bought nothing but a window in which a forged offer displayed as though it were real. The station's
   identity assertion in step 1 remains where a **real Ed25519 signature**
   is warranted (§7.5.3) — one verify, 18.86 µs, once per docking.
5. **Control.** The station writes `flight.thrust.fwd`, `flight.pitch`, etc. The ship realm verifies
   the **bundle** MAC at ingress (345 ns), checks the grant covers the channel and is unexpired, then
   arbitration runs: `Exclusive`, grant priority > seat priority, **so the seat is outranked**. The
   seat's `denied` port goes true; the HUD shows "AUTOPILOT HAS CONTROL". The thrusters cannot tell
   the difference and never look.
6. **Revocation.** The pilot writes `false` to the seat's `autopilot_enable` port → the realm deletes
   the grant row (durable, fenced) → the station's next bundle fails the grant check and is dropped
   with `Receipt::Refusal { GrantRevoked }`. The seat's lease was never surrendered, so it is the
   highest live writer on the very next tick.
7. **Abort.** `flight.abort` is `Max`, crew-allowlisted, `grantable: false`. No approval, no grant,
   and no bug can ever hand it to a foreign principal.

Light-lag interacts exactly as §7.6 predicts: under **[USER DECISION 7-A] Option C** an approaching
ship is inside the 2-light-second bubble, so step 5 streams. A station a light-minute away cannot
stream — its subscribe request for a State channel is refused — and it must upload a docking *program*
to the ship's Nav Computer on the Event lane instead. That is a coherent, legible game rule rather
than a degradation.

### 7.13 The thruster example, end to end

The user's own worked example, traced through the real architecture, with the plane boundary marked
at every step.

| # | Step | Plane |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Player presses **W**. The client resolves W to logical `InputSlot(3)` from its local preference map and sends an **intent** at the input-resource seam — the same seam `vdctl` injects at, so every acceptance test drives the production path. Analogue slots ride the unreliable latest-wins `InputDatagram` (State semantics: a lost axis frame heals next tick); `Pulse` slots (landing gear, autopilot approve) ride the **reliable client→shard discrete-action carrier** D-39.1 already owes. | client protocol |
| 2 | The realm's shard maps `(seat_entity, slot 3)` → the seat's **binding table** (player TLV config): port `forward` bound to channel `flight.thrust.fwd`, through a curve LUT, arbitration `Exclusive` at the seat's priority with the lease the seat holds. Writes `Fx` into `back[c]`, sets `dirty[c]`. **The client computed nothing and named no channel.** | Signal |
| 3 | One-tick uniform propagation delay. Next tick the pass pushes channel `c` down its compiled subscriber list: 12 thruster blocks, 2 Display Covers, 1 flight recorder. Cost: 15 deliveries ≈ 7.5 ns. | Signal |
| 4 | Each **thruster** (`Emitter{ medium: Force }`) reads three input ports: `throttle` (from `flight.thrust.fwd`), `fuel` (from the tank's channel), `power` (from the reactor bus). Its transfer function is `if fuel == 0 or power == 0 { 0 } else { throttle · rated }` — **exactly the user's specification**, expressed as data. It writes `thrust_N` and `fuel_rate`. | Signal |
| 5 | The realm **aggregates**: sum every thruster's thrust vector and torque about the ship's centre of mass into ONE `ShipOutputs { thrust, torque, mass, com, inertia }`. This aggregation is what keeps the hull host's cost O(ships), not O(blocks). | boundary |
| 6 | `ShipOutputs` leaves the realm as `InterShardFlow::Coupling(ShipThrustPort)` — an **`EffectFree`**, latest-wins sample to the hull-host shard. Per the standing law, **the containing realm's shard is the physics authority**: it integrates the hull rigid body and authors the ship realm's pose in its own frame. The ship shard never integrates its own hull. | **Coupling** |
| 7 | The hull host ships the authored realm placement down the lane the client already receives (`RealmSnapshotDatagram`, absolute positions since the A5 flip). It also returns `HullFeedback { accel, g_load, ambient_density }` on the **same** `CouplingPort`. Inside the ship realm exactly one adapter quantises those floats to `Fx` and injects them on reserved channels (`hull.accel`, `hull.gforce`, `hull.density`). **This is the only float→`Fx` conversion in the subsystem.** | Coupling → Signal |
| 8 | An **IMU** (`Sampler`) reads `hull.accel`; a **PID** (`Pure`) closes an attitude loop against it; a **Display Cover** (`Surface`) binds `thrust_N`, `fuel_remaining` and `hull.gforce`. The server composes the panel's value delta and ships it; the client renders it verbatim and derives nothing. | Signal → client |

#### Why the two planes must not be merged

**The boundary rule, stated once:** *anything the physics solver integrates is a Coupling; anything a
player configured is a Signal.* The thruster's decision to burn is a Signal. The newtons it produces
are a Coupling.

Merging in either direction breaks something specific:

- **Thrust on the Signal bus.** Thrust would inherit grants, ACLs, rate limits, arbitration,
  subscriptions and light-lag. A player could rate-limit your engine. A shard restart would require
  re-establishing a subscription before a 3 g burn resumed — and PLAN.md's declared degraded mode is
  *"normal hull-host transfer ⇒ hold-last-thrust via `last_ship_outputs` carried in the saga handoff
  state — no thrust dropout at 3 g across an SOI"*, which is a **coupling** guarantee carried by the
  **transfer saga**, not something a pub/sub subscription can promise.
- **Signals on the Coupling plane.** `EffectFree` is a *sealed* marker trait; the whole point is that
  a discrete authority-gating payload **cannot implement it** and therefore cannot ride a coupling. A
  grant mint, a door lock and a config change are all authority-gating. Admitting them would delete
  the compile-time guarantee HR1's conformance test exists to enforce, and re-open the old
  dock-clamp-on-a-lossy-datagram bug class by construction.
- **Numerically.** The coupling carries one aggregated ~64 B sample per ship per tick. The signal bus
  carries 12 thruster channels × their subscriber lists, entirely inside the ship realm. Merging would
  push per-block traffic across a shard boundary at 20 Hz — §7.2.4's 1.6 MB/s-per-realm number, on
  the wire instead of in a `Vec`.

### 7.14 Radio confidentiality — decided, and why the relay cannot enforce a read ACL

`ChannelKey` is a content hash of the name, computable offline by anyone — that is the point of §7.4.
The relay holds `net → { subscriber_shard → lease }` and fans out to leased subscribers, and it does
**not** hold the emitting realm's `ChannelDecl`. Therefore `AccessPolicy`, which lives on the decl,
is structurally unenforceable at the relay: any player who guesses or dictionary-attacks a name
(`fleet.alpha.orders`, `corp.<name>.comms`) can lease it and receive everything. This is a real
property and it must be *stated* rather than contradicted by §7.5.4's promise of a read ACL.

> **[USER DECISION 7-G] — is radio interceptable?**
>
> - **Option A (recommended) — radio is OPEN by design.** Any station can tune any net. `AccessPolicy`
>   read enforcement is documented as applying **only where the decl lives** (in-realm and at the
>   parent, i.e. `Local` and `Neighbourhood`), never on the `Relay` plane. Confidentiality becomes a
>   *player-built mechanic*: a **Cipher/Codec** block pair applies a keyed transform to a `Blob`
>   payload before emission and after reception, and the relay forwards ciphertext it cannot read.
>   Signals intelligence, direction-finding, jamming and code-breaking become content; the EW Jammer
>   already exists for the other half.
> - **Option B — the relay enforces read ACLs.** The relay must then hold, per net, the owning realm's
>   allowlist — a second authorisation store outside the owning realm, replicated, fenced and
>   revocable across the galaxy. That is a distributed ACL system, and it puts identity state on a
>   node that HR1 wants to be a dumb forwarder.
>
> **Recommendation: A.** It is cheaper, it is better fiction, and it is honest — B's guarantee would
> be only as strong as the weakest relay. Note the asymmetry: making an open channel private later is
> a straightforward addition, while making a private channel public later breaks every player who
> built around secrecy. The Cipher block's guarantee must be described to players as *game*
> confidentiality, not secrecy against the operator.

### 7.15 Sampler blocks — the probe budget and the ordering invariant

`Sampler` is the only kernel that reads the world, and it is the only kernel whose cost is not priced
by the 0.5 ns delivery constant. A 50 km sphere query against the realm's physics broad-phase costs
**1–10 µs**, i.e. **2,000–20,000× a delivery**. Two things follow, and neither is optional.

**A declared probe budget.** `SignalTuning::probes_per_tick_budget = 64` per realm — 64 × 10 µs =
0.64 ms worst case, 1.3% of a 50 ms tick, on top of the signal pass's 1%. Each `ProbeSpec` carries a
`probe_cost` folded into the block's `pcu` so a radar farm is refused at build time (§7.8.1), and
`TickPolicy::Divided(20)` on a radar means one probe per second per radar, so 64 probes/tick supports
**4,000 radars per realm** before the budget binds — comfortably above anything the PCU cap allows.
Over-budget probes are **deferred to the next tick in round-robin `EntityId` order** (deterministic,
never dropped) and the block's `stale` output goes true so a player can see why their radar is slow.

**A declared sort key.** A broad-phase query returns results in BVH/insertion order, which is a
property of a physics data structure, not of the world. This section sorts subscriber lists precisely
so iteration order is byte-stable across hosts and replays; emitting a `contacts` `Blob` whose
ordering comes from Rapier's BVH would undo that in one field. **Probe results are sorted by
`EntityId` ascending before they become a signal value, asserted by a named invariant test.** Radar
`contacts` is a `Blob` and therefore an Event-lane channel (§7.1.4), which also means the ordering is
observable and diffable in the replay log rather than hidden inside a coalesced sample.

#### 7.15.1 The rate-and-membership ledger, restated against the ladder

~~The standing rules are "no LOD systems for now" and the binary render rule: in range → proper mesh,
out of range → nothing.~~ **Retracted.** Addendum 2 closes decision register row 7 by owner ruling:
detail levels everywhere, on one generic ladder, with §C.7's exclusion list. The three private
carve-outs the source pool had invented for the old rule are no longer carve-outs.

The ledger survives the retraction, because its purpose was never to defend the ban — it was to force
every rate-or-membership decision in this section to be *counted and named* rather than accumulated
quietly. That purpose is stronger now, not weaker: with the ban gone, the only thing standing between
"detail levels everywhere" and "the beacon stopped blinking" is SIG-NO-COARSEN (§7.1.6) and this
table. **Five** decisions, each classified against the ladder:

| Decision | Where | Classification |
|---|---|---|
| State shed lowest-priority-first on bundle overflow | §7.8.4 | **Not a rung.** A congestion response on a latest-wins lane; the next tick replaces the dropped sample. Priority is now the derived `Telemetry`/`Control` bit (§7.1.6), so congestion can never shed a control value ahead of a gauge reading. |
| Audible set capped at k loudest speakers | §7.7.2 | **Not a rung.** Set membership, not fidelity, and an anti-griefing control first. |
| `TickPolicy::Divided(n)` and the probe round-robin | §7.10.2, §7.15 | **Not a rung.** A block-authored sampling rate on a simulation *input*. A 1 Hz radar is a 1 Hz radar at every distance and for every observer, which is exactly what SIG-NO-COARSEN demands. |
| Panel content refresh scaled by angular size, no content below θ_min — §6.9's `C0 live` / `C1 chrome` / `C2 reduced` / `C3 off` | §7.9 | **A rung — and now an ordinary one.** Uses the ONE locked AoI rule, never branches on type, and the floor is a legibility fact rather than a fidelity cut. §6.9 owns the rungs; §7 owns the seam. Derived-`Telemetry` channels only, at the client-facing egress only, value held, floored by `telemetry_min_refresh_hz`, never on realm↔realm export. |

None of the five touches `front[c]`, `subs[c]`, arbitration, a grant, a fence, a heartbeat or a
`Retained` write — which is SIG-NO-COARSEN restated as a checklist, and is how it is tested. All five
are visible in `SignalTuning`, except the one rate §6.9 owns and §7 reads, and they are asserted by
§7.18 items 12 and 13.

Two bans survive Addendum 2 §C.8 intact and this section reinforces them, because they are the part
of the original preference that was always right: **no substitute geometry for anything that can shoot
or be shot**, and **no impostor of anything a player interacts with**. A Display Cover, a Button, a
Seat and a Docking Port are interaction surfaces; none may ever be replaced by a picture of itself.
They coarsen with their housing — a real, coarser rung of the real thing — or they cull.
