### 7.16 Mechanical blocks — kinematic by default

#### 7.16.1 The decision

**Articulation is kinematic. The server computes each actuator's scalar state from its transfer
function, derives the child sub-assembly's pose as an exact analytic rigid offset of the parent, and
moves the sub-assembly's colliders as kinematic-position bodies.** Reaction on the parent is applied
analytically (commanded acceleration × sub-assembly mass, at the anchor). Physics joints are reserved
for a small, explicitly flagged class (loose cranes, rover suspension) and are **multibody trees
only** — never long impulse-joint chains.

This is O(1) per actuator, bit-deterministic, and the only option consistent with *"the server does
all the math and ships ready-to-draw positions."*

#### 7.16.2 The evidence

**Space Engineers' "clang" has one dominant root cause**, and the wiki is explicit: *"Clanging is
caused by the collision boxes of a subgrid intersecting the collision boxes of another grid"* — and
because subgrid damage is off by default the overlapping grids cannot resolve by breaking, so *"it
starts shaking to avoid taking up the same space."* Keen's own fix path was **to remove physics from
the articulation, not to tune the solver**: the 1.185 overhaul dropped welding (performance problems,
simulation flaws, rigid-body warping) and **replaced the piston's prismatic constraint with a
keyframed piston with limited impulse** that stops advancing when the impulse exceeds a player-set
threshold. They also shipped "Share Inertia Tensor", explicitly trading realism for usability.
Remaining known-bad patterns after all that: double-piston connections (redundant constraints →
phantom forces), very high piston force values, and square arrays of connectors.

**Starbase proves the point from the other side.** One rigid body per ship, no joints at all, with a
separate *analytical structural-stress model* over bolts: each part has a Part Strength Factor, the
lowest determines ship strength, and thrusters *"apply a torque around the centre of mass, and stress
to the frame from where the hardpoint is bolted"* — so an unbalanced ship literally snaps in half.
That delivers most of the "physical ship" feeling people wrongly try to get from joint simulation, at
the cost of a cheap connected-components pass the block plan already schedules. It is also the
strongest argument for putting structural stress first in **[USER DECISION 7-E]**.

**Rapier's defaults confirm the arithmetic.** rapier3d 0.34: `num_solver_iterations = 4`,
`num_internal_pgs_iterations = 1`, `min_island_size = 128`. Joints couple bodies into one solver
island, so a 500-actuator machine is *one* island that `min_island_size` cannot split and the parallel
solver cannot distribute. With a projected-Gauss-Seidel inner solve, constraint error propagates
roughly one link per iteration, so a 500-link chain is off by orders of magnitude — the far end
visibly sags, stretches and oscillates no matter how the motors are tuned. Raising iterations is
O(iterations × constraints) and does not converge. Multibody joints cannot be violated (reduced
coordinates) but are tree-only, and Rapier documents them as **slow to add and remove** — fatal when a
player places and grinds blocks every few seconds. (Note that rapier3d and parry3d are **not** in
`Cargo.lock` today; adopting them is a user decision owned by the physics section, and this design
states only what it needs from whichever solver is adopted.)

#### 7.16.3 The invariants (not tuning knobs)

1. **Default: no physics joint.** Kinematic pose derivation from a quantised scalar.
2. **Lock ⇒ merge.** When an actuator is at a limit or explicitly locked, merge the child colliders
   into the parent rigid body. Rapier states plainly that many colliders on one body is *"much more
   efficient"* than connecting separate bodies with fixed joints.
3. **`contacts_enabled = false`** between a parent and its own articulated child; instead **reject the
   commanded motion with a discrete shape-cast before applying it.** This converts the #1 clang cause
   from a physics fight into a control-limit refusal — testable, deterministic, and reportable to the
   player as `stalled`.
4. **Quantise actuator state** to an integer grid (already a project rule), which kills chatter around
   a setpoint.
5. **Declare `max_force_N` per actuator** as a `FunctionDef` param. Exceeding it stalls; a second, higher
   threshold structurally detaches into `EntityKind::Debris` (already registered,
   `BallisticReadvance` continuity). The higher threshold is where the structural-stress subsystem
   plugs in when it exists; until then it is a constant per actuator.
6. **Detect articulation cycles at build time** with union-find and refuse the closing link or convert
   it to a rigid weld. SE's "double piston = phantom forces" becomes one rule.
7. **Budget actuator count** — see §7.16.4, which lowers the cap from the arithmetic below.
8. **Cap physically-simulated joints at ~32 per assembly**, `MotorModel::AccelerationBased` (the
   documented default and recommendation, because spring constants auto-scale by mass), per-DoF
   armature, and joint limits. Treat >32 as unsupported and structure the game so nobody needs them.

#### 7.16.4 The transfer decision that must be taken BEFORE the block system lands

> **An articulated ship is ONE transferable entity. Its actuator states are quantised scalars in its
> state blob. Sub-assemblies are NEVER independently transferable.**

`entity_kind.rs` explicitly warns that a kind needing a new `(DurabilityClass, ContinuityModel,
GhostPolicy)` triple is *"first-class engineering and a crash-matrix multiplication — deliberately
scheduled, never casual"*. Independently transferable sub-assemblies would mean **a transfer saga per
joint** and partially transferred machines: a ship whose turret arrived and whose piston boom did not.

Kinematic articulation makes the correct answer cheap, but the blob arithmetic must be done honestly
rather than asserted:

| Term | Bytes |
|---|---|
| `SHIP_DEF.max_state_bytes` (verified, `crates/core/src/entity_kind.rs:213`) | 8192 |
| TLV envelope header | −16 |
| Ship pose, velocity, ownership, inventory manifest, damage state (allowance) | −512 |
| Available for the actuator array | **7664** |
| Per actuator: 8 B quantised state + 2 B stable slot id, in ONE packed TLV field (not one TLV field per actuator) | 10 |
| **Actuators that fit** | **766** |

766 is **below** invariant 7's SE-derived "500–1,000 actuators at 100k PCU", so the naive claim of
comfortable headroom was false in the direction that matters. Two resolutions exist and the cheap one
is taken:

> **Decided: cap an assembly at 512 actuators** (a `pcu`-checked build-time cap like every
> other cap), leaving ~2.5 KB of blob headroom for growth. Raising `SHIP_DEF.max_state_bytes` is
> available and is a **scheduled `KindDef` change**, not a casual one, and should be spent on
> something better than actuators.

One clarification the arithmetic depends on: **retained port state does not live in the entity blob.**
Once a ship is its own realm (P8) its actuator and port state live in its own redb `port_state` table
(§7.10.4) and move with the realm's store on a re-home. The 8192-byte blob binds only for the
occupant-ship case — a small craft crossing a boundary as an entity rather than as a realm — which is
exactly the case the 512-actuator cap keeps inside budget.

The `rebind_refs` half of the deferred `TransferableKind` trait (DEFERRED D-31) is where an
articulated ship's internal references get remapped, and D-31 already names P6/P8 as when the first
compound kind arrives. **This decision must be recorded before the block system lands**, because a
block system built on independently simulated sub-bodies cannot be retrofitted onto a single-entity
transfer saga without redoing both.

### 7.17 Scripting — staged, with gate conditions

**Stage 1 (ships with the block system, T0/P9).** Combinator / `Pure`-kernel blocks only: Constant,
Arithmetic, Decider, Selector, Latch, Timer, Counter, PID, Curve LUT, Event Controller, Bus Hub. Zero
sandbox surface, deterministic, evaluated in the same double-buffered pass, trivially 100%-coverable.
This alone matches Factorio, Scrap Mechanic and console Space Engineers. **Gate to stage 2:** stage 1
shipped and measured player demand for something it cannot express.

**Stage 2 (P6.5).** A bounded **expression bytecode**: total, loop-free, allocation-free, fixed-point,
with a hard op budget (~256 ops), evaluated inside the same pure pass — no scheduler, no VM, no yield.
It is a `TransferFn::Expr` variant in the config blob, **not a new kernel**, so it costs almost
nothing architecturally. This buys ~90% of what players want from Lua at ~0% of the risk. **Gate to
stage 3:** stage 2 demonstrably runs out — measured, with examples of what players tried to build and
could not.

**Stage 3 (P9+, only if gated).** A Script Chip block. If it ships: **Luau via mlua, never LuaJIT.**
`mlua`'s `sandbox(true)` (safeenv, read-only globals, local write environment) and `set_interrupt()`
are **Luau-only**; on LuaJIT you get `set_hook(every_nth_instruction)`, which the docs themselves call
*"a limited form of execution limits"*, plus JIT-varying float behaviour. Requirements, all mandatory:
`set_memory_limit(~256 KB)` per chip; a per-tick step budget via `set_interrupt`; a CFS-style
scheduler across chips on a bounded worker pool; a **fixed-point-only** exposed API; access restricted
to the chip's own declared ports (no world queries, no spawning, no cross-realm reach except by
writing a port); execution in a separate control phase, **never inside the physics tick**; on budget
overrun the chip is suspended with its last outputs **held**, which the uniform one-tick delay makes
visually invisible; and a high `pcu` so scripting is a deliberate build choice. `mlua` is not a
workspace dependency today, so stage 3 is itself a library adoption decision.

**The cautionary evidence, three games, three ways the same feature kills you:**

- **ComputerCraft/LuaJ** backed each Lua coroutine with a Java thread; the SwitchCraft server was
  repeatedly killed by **250,000 threads accumulating at 50/s**. CC:Tweaked's fix (exception-based
  yielding) dropped a 250-computer server from ~2,000 threads to 50; a further executor redesign cut
  threading overhead ~50%; and it still needs a 7-second soft limit, an 8.5-second hard limit, and a
  Linux-CFS-style fair scheduler. Every one of those is machinery you would have to build.
- **Space Engineers** caps at 50,000 "code junctions" per run on the **main thread** inside a
  16.667 ms frame budget, and the wiki is blunt that the limit *"has no relevance to performance"* —
  it exists only to stop infinite loops. Servers commonly disable scripts outright.
- **Dual Universe** ran player Lua on the **client** and shipped only outputs to the server. Server
  CPU stays flat; every control loop runs on untrusted hardware. That is **directly incompatible**
  with this project's standing law that the server does all simulation math.

> **[USER DECISION 7-C] — the scripting end-state.** A genuine one-way door: once players have written
> chips, removing or throttling the VM is a community incident, not a patch.
>
> - **Option A — stages 1+2 only, permanently.** Combinators plus a bounded expression bytecode. Zero
>   sandbox, zero scheduler, zero determinism risk, and Factorio proves it is enough for enormous
>   creativity. Forecloses the deepest player creations.
> - **Option B (recommended) — stages 1+2 now, stage 3 gated on measured demand.** Ship nothing until
>   it is asked for; the gate conditions above are the contract. Costs a Luau scheduler + sandbox +
>   budget subsystem *if* the gate opens.
> - **Option C — commit to a scripting VM now** as a headline feature (what Starbase and Dual Universe
>   did). Front-loads the scheduler, sandbox, memory-budget and determinism work **before the block
>   system exists**, and is very hard to take back.
>
> **Recommendation: B.** Stages 1 and 2 are cheap and are needed regardless. Stage 3 must not begin
> until stages 1 and 2 have shipped and the demand has been *measured* rather than assumed. Note the
> asymmetry: A→B is free at any time; B→A is not.

(3) `OccupantInterest::coarsen_level` — a POSE-precision HOP COUNTER on the up-flow, not a terrain tier."* Note also that `tier_floor` and the payload `tier` are different KINDS of thing — an observer property versus a payload descriptor naming which rung the entries are at — and must never be merged into one field to save a byte. |

Built four times, it is four forks. |

Two items are explicitly **not** planted now and should not be: the timing wheel (§7.6) and the SFU
control plane (§7.7). Both are self-contained subsystems with no seam in the base they can foreclose —
the wheel lives entirely inside a routing node's own state, and the media path shares nothing with the
tick bus but a handle in an enum that item 16 already reserves.

### 7.19 Adjudicated objections

Five points from the adversarial review are wrong, partly wrong, or superseded by the redesign above.
Each is answered in one line so the record is complete.

- **"`tick_hz` is in the numerator, not the divisor — the formula is unit-inconsistent."** The
  *dimensions* were always right (cells × ticks/s ÷ cells/s = ticks); only the prose said "divisor".
  The real defect was the rate's *identity*, not its position, and §7.6.1 fixes that: the only legal
  rate is the universe clock's own, published in the clock sync.
- **"Honest routing state at the draft's scale is ≈69 MB, not 14.5 MB."** That recomputation still
  assumes upward re-advertisement (depth × 64 keys per realm). §7.3.2 removes covering entirely, so
  nothing is re-advertised and the correct figure is 14.5 MB of leaf export sets plus an O(children)
  inverted index at each parent (≈1.3 MB at a 1,000-child node) — both now stated.
- **"`interest_lease_ticks` must be ≤ `demand_ttl_ticks`, i.e. a 40–160× increase in renewal
  traffic."** The defect is real and verified; the prescription is not taken. §7.3.3 binds interest
  lifetime to the child's `DemandLedger` entry instead of shortening a second timer, which is
  strictly more correct (reaping is edge-triggered, not TTL-approximated) and costs nothing, so the
  181 KB/s reconcile figure survives.
- **"The deadline mechanism is either an O(channels) sweep or a second timing wheel that multiplies
  the 0.5 ns per-delivery constant by 2–10×."** Neither. §7.1.5 confines deadlines to *imported*
  channels and heartbeats to *exported* ones, both hard-capped (256 and 64), so Pass B in §7.2.3 is a
  flat ≤320-comparison sweep costing ≈0.16 µs and touching no per-delivery path.
- **"8192 bytes holds perhaps 400–550 actuators."** That estimate assumes TLV framing per actuator.
  §7.16.4 packs the actuator array into one TLV field at 10 B/actuator, giving 766 — but the
  adversary's *conclusion* stands: 766 is below invariant 7's own 500–1,000 cap, so the cap is
  lowered to 512 rather than the margin being called comfortable.

## 8. Delivery — slices, gates, and the decision register

Sections 2–7 each ended with its own ship order. This section is the single merged plan: one decision
register, one list of doors that must be shut before they cost a world migration, one ordered slice
plan across P4–P9, one list of the numbers this design owes and when each is first measured, the new
`DEFERRED.md` rows it creates, and an honest report of the places two sections still contradict
each other.

**The standing rule that frames everything below** (`CLAUDE.md`, `PLAN.md`): every phase re-runs the
*entire accumulated* transfer / crash / chaos suite, not just its own tests. A slice that lands a new
persisted table, a new wire arm or a new realm kind has not shipped until the P2/P3 matrix, the RLM
demand-loop end-to-end runs and the visual-universe scenarios are green on top of it. This is stated
once and not repeated per slice.

---

### 8.0 Revision note — what the two addenda changed in this section

This section has been amended twice since it was first written. Nothing below is a from-scratch
rewrite; every unchanged decision, table and number stands. What moved:

**Addendum 1** (the radius ladder) turned planet radius into per-body data on a 39.47 m ladder, turned
gravity into a value derived from an authored per-body mass, and introduced worlds that are seed *plus*
configuration. It dissolved register rows 4 and 5 into cheap residual questions and promoted rows 7 and
21.

**Addendum 2** (detail levels) is the larger change, because the owner **retracted the no-detail-levels
ban outright** — *"we will need LODs everywhere, but in the smartest way"*. Six consequences land here:

1. **Register row 7 is ANSWERED and CLOSED.** It was the top of the register after Addendum 1; it is
   now settled, and the three private carve-outs three separate sections had invented for it collapse
   into one ladder.
2. **Row 21 (the vertex format) de-escalates out of the blocking set** — with one honest caveat stated
   in its entry: it no longer decides whether a planet is renderable *on foot*, but it still decides
   whether a 25–100 km *flight* view fits in the video-memory budget.
3. **Row 23 (how a planet is drawn from altitude and orbit) is largely answered**, because the ladder
   builds precisely the thing that row's option G3 was rejected for lacking.
4. **Five new decisions appear** — the edit-pyramid record format, the tier-selection tuning fields, the
   shadow horizon, vegetation impostors, and the virtual-texturing question — numbered 37 to 41 and
   marked `**[USER DECISION 8-A]**` through `**[USER DECISION 8-E]**`. *(Rows 37, 38 and 41 have since
   absorbed the sibling decisions other sections raised for the same three artefacts, and row 1 has
   absorbed a fourth — see the merge note in §8.1.)*
5. **The register is re-sorted.** Three of the old top seven moved: rows 4 and 5 dropped to residuals,
   row 7 closed. The ranking below is therefore materially different from the one first published.
6. **Addendum 1 §C.4's central finding is dissolved.** That addendum concluded *"the binding constraint
   is the drawn radius, not the planet radius — roughly 700 m to 1 km of fully meshed terrain is what
   one-metre blocks with no detail tiers can afford."* **That is now wrong, and the phrase "with no
   detail tiers" is why.** With the ladder, resident chunk *count* grows with the logarithm of view
   distance rather than its square, so there is no drawn-radius cap at all. Everywhere this document
   said "the draw radius is capped near a kilometre" — §3.7, §5.9, Addendum 1 §C.4 — read instead:
   **the resident chunk budget is capped; the drawn radius is not.**

One correction to Addendum 2 itself, because it will otherwise be cited as a reservation that exists:
Addendum 2 §A says the wire *"already carries a `coarsen_level: u8` precision ladder"* for terrain
detail. It does not. `crates/wire/src/intershard.rs:659` carries `coarsen_level` on `OccupantInterest`,
and its own doc comment says it counts *hops from the observer's home realm* — it is a **pose**-precision
counter on the up-flow, not a terrain tier. What line 303 genuinely reserves is the *concept* — "the WHAT
lane (terrain/constructions at the LOD the observed realm controls) is a future ADDITIVE payload on this
SAME routing" — which is a reserved **lane**, not a reserved field. **There is no terrain-tier field
anywhere in the wire today, and in particular no way for a client to request a specific tier.** Planting
that request-side byte is now an item in slice S0.4, where it is free; after the arm exists it is a
protocol migration.

**Forty-one decisions.** Thirty-six were deduplicated from the forty raised across §2–§7 by three merges

- **The table's ORDER is the ranking — by cost of lateness, worst first — and it HAS changed.** Three of

The full entries, in **number** order (the ranking is the table above).

**1. What shape is a planet's grid — and how far up the detail ladder do blocks go?** *(§3, decision 3-A,
plus §5's 5-G′ absorbed 2026-08-03. The largest one-way door in the document.)*
The owner said blocks are one metre and square. On a sphere that is unachievable by proof, not by
tuning: somewhere on every planet blocks are 41 % off square, and at eight points they are rhombic
whatever curve is used.
*Options.* (A) A cube wrapped onto a sphere. (B) A literal cube planet — blocks exactly one metre and
exactly square everywhere. (C) A hexagonal grid. (D) A flat octree with an analytic surface.
*Recommendation.* **(A).** It is the only family that keeps blocks aligned with gravity, keeps planets
round, and keeps one grid for planets and ships. (C) cannot also be the ship grid, so the block system
forks. (D) makes a wall at latitude forty a staircase. (B) is technically cheapest and has no good
answer for which way is down — near an edge you walk on ground tilted up to fifty-five degrees while
your blocks stay axis-aligned. Addendum 1 §A gives the full four-way comparison the owner asked for.

*Second half, absorbed 2026-08-03 from §5's [USER DECISION 5-G′], which is deleted there and points here.
It rides this row because it is the same word: the chunk address. One-way door 14.*
**How far up the detail ladder do blocks go before the realm proxy takes over — and therefore how many
tier bits does the persisted chunk key carry?** The rendering half is reversible; **the key width is
not.** Once a world is saved, changing it is a key-format migration over every persisted chunk record and
every edit-pyramid entry.
*Options.* **(G1) blocks all the way to the face-covering rung** (the rung at which one chunk covers a
whole cube face); the proxy only beyond it. **Needs FIVE tier bits.** You see real terrain from orbit,
octave-dropped to continental scale and shaded by the macro octaves. It is *cheaper* than standing on the
ground — from 400 km above an Earth-sized body the resident rungs are 9 through 18, about 3,800 columns —
because altitude is a discount, not a multiplier. Ceiling: rung 12 for the 162 km starter body, 18 for
Earth-sized, 20 for the largest addressable body; five bits give 0–31 with eleven values spare, and the
key ends at **58 of 64 bits with six spare**. **(G2)** cross over to a textured analytic sphere at a fixed
angular size; **four** bits suffice. A good sphere, small cost, but it is a *second* surface
representation and it re-opens the "exactly one material type for every voxel surface in the game" rule.
**(G3)** cross over to today's flat proxy at rung 7; **three** bits suffice. Zero cost, and a grey ball at
200 km while the body still subtends hundreds of pixels — which fails the seamless law's "grows from a
dot" requirement in the middle of the approach. *Cost of taking fewer bits than G1 needs:* four bits cap
the ladder at rung 15, which cannot express G1 for an Earth-sized body; three cap it at rung 7 and
reinstate a visible wall at 100 km.
*Recommendation.* **G1, with five tier bits at chunk-key bits 60..56.** It keeps one representation from a
block in your hand to a planet seen from another star, which is what the ladder is for, and the bits are
free today (they are already asserted zero on decode) and a migration over every saved world tomorrow.
**Two riders you should see before taking it.** *First:* the per-body rung ceiling becomes the
face-covering rung (`tier_depth = ceil(log₂ m) + 1`), and the atmospheric derivation that currently sets
it is demoted to a **residency** bound — which rungs a client inside the atmosphere requests — rather than
a key bound. Both are right, about an observer inside and outside the air respectively. *Second:* this
tightens **[USER DECISION 3-I]**'s divisibility rule to "the body's radius step is a power of two" for any
body running a full-depth ladder. The recommended starter world satisfies it; the constraint should be
recorded in 3-I rather than discovered when the second body is authored.
*Blocks.* Everything. Decisions 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 12 and 37 all presuppose it, and the tier width is a
persisted field of the same word door 14 freezes.
*Cost of deferring.* Nothing in P4 can start, and a month of cube-sphere work is at risk if the
aesthetic question was never actually settled.

**2. How wide is one saved block change, and what is inside it?** *(Merged: §3's 3-H, §4's 4-A, §6's
6-7. THREE SECTIONS CURRENTLY DISAGREE — see §8.6 item 1.)* The roadmap commits five bytes. Five bytes
is forty bits, and the cell index alone needs eighteen.
*Options.* (A) **Eight bytes** — cell index, the block's identity as one number naming an approved
substance-shape-function combination, an orientation field including a mirror flag, a bit marking a
block as generated rather than placed, a material-interpreted state byte, and fifteen bits reserved
with a decoder that rejects them if non-zero. (B) **Six bytes** — the same minus the state byte, seven
bits spare. (C) **Five bytes as committed** — which forces a choice between the mirror flag and the
generated-versus-placed bit; you cannot have both.
*Recommendation.* **(A) eight bytes.** It is the only width that satisfies every section's stated
requirement at once. The mirror flag is what stops symmetry building punching holes in mirrored
structures; the generated-versus-placed bit is what stops the structural system collapsing every
natural cave roof the first time it runs; five bits of orientation are what a piston with no
configuration still needs. The counter-argument is real and is answered rather than dismissed: one
section argues that "no spare bits" is itself the discipline that keeps state out of the record, and
the mechanical guard is that reserved bits are rejected on decode and spending one is a reviewed
change. The three saved bytes over six-byte records amount to about 300 MB across a hundred million
edits — noise against a format migration. **Also settled by this row:** the identity stays a single
combined number, not independent substance and shape fields, and decoration's state bits are read from
the existing sparse side table rather than requiring the record to grow further. Addendum 1 §B.4
sharpens the question: five bytes *closes* if you accept the two upstream verdicts (mirroring is a
shape, identity is one combined number); the real question is whether you accept them or would rather
have fifteen bits of slack.
*Amended by Addendum 2 — and the amendment is a refusal to widen.* The detail-level ladder does **not**
reopen this row and must not be allowed to. A coarse tier's summary is *derived* data with a different
lifetime, a different key and a different write rate; it belongs in the separate pyramid table of
decision 37, never in more bits on the permanent placement log. Putting it here would break exactly the
discipline §2 defends.
*Blocks.* The chunk format, the save file, the cross-world edit message, undo, and every later phase.
*Cost of deferring.* Deciding after the first world is written is a migration over every saved planet,
ship, station and blueprint — not a refactor.

**3. Which curve wraps the cube onto the sphere?** *(§3, decision 3-C. Conditional on row 1 = A.)*
The honest picture, corrected from the earlier analysis: the worst blocks — about seventy-one
centimetres across one way — sit at the midpoints of the twelve cube-edge arcs, not at the corners; at
the corners blocks are ninety-three centimetres and equal-edged. The distorted region is twelve
lens-shaped bands about thirty-one kilometres wide at their widest along arcs two hundred kilometres
long — roughly two and a half thousand kilometres of faint cube outline drawn across the planet.
*Options.* (A) The angle-proportional curve, at the family's minimum size spread. (B) The area-optimal
curve. (D) The edge-length-optimal curve.
*Recommendation.* **(A).** It is simultaneously at the achievable minimum of size spread, near the
minimum of shape distortion, and angle-proportional — which is the property that makes the radius
arithmetic exact. (B)'s "one block mined equals one block of material everywhere" argument evaporates
once a mined block yields one unit regardless of physical size, which this document rules it does.
(D) does not deliver what it appears to — the corner rhombi are untouched — and it makes block size
drift by half across a face, which changes doorway widths and jump distances measurably.
*Blocks.* Generation, meshing, collision, every stored edit — **and now every tier of the ladder**, since
a tier-L cell is 2^L of these cells and inherits their distortion exactly.
*Cost of deferring.* It defines every block boundary on every planet forever; changing it after players
build invalidates every stored edit.

**4. What radius does the starter world get, and what range may the generator draw from?** *(§3,
decision 3-D. **Settled by Addendum 1 §C.2 — this entry is the residual.**)*
*Struck.* The original entry asked "How big is a planet?" and offered one global radius: **(A) about
162 km, (B) about 81 km, (C) about 323 km**, recommending (A) as "the unique value" giving exactly
one-metre blocks with a whole number of chunks per face. **That uniqueness was an artefact of an
unnecessary power-of-two constraint on the chunks-per-face count, and the recommendation is
withdrawn.**
*Replacement.* Radius is **per-body data on the ladder R = 124·m/π metres for any integer m** — a
39.47 m step, on which every real body lands within twenty metres and Earth within 0.4 m. Gravity comes
from decision 5's authored mass. The residual question is only: what radius does the curated starter
world get, and what range may the procedural generator draw from?
*Doubly settled by Addendum 2.* The original entry carried a rider — *"take (B) instead if row 7 comes
back as 'hold the rule literally', because it halves the flying-altitude costs"*. **That rider is void.**
Row 7 came back the other way, and with the ladder the resident chunk count no longer scales with planet
size in any binding way: an Earth-sized body on foot is about 4,000 resident chunks, the same order as
the 162 km body's 1,348, where before the ladder it was 53,110.
*Blocks.* The starter world only.
*Cost of deferring.* Low, and no longer blocking P4.

**5. What range of surface gravity may the generator produce?** *(§3, decision 3-E. **Settled by
Addendum 1 §D — this entry is the residual.**)*
*Struck.* The original entry asked "does a planet pull like Earth or like a real rock that size?" and
recommended **(A) fabricate Earth-like gravity** globally, accepting a sphere of influence inflated 5.5×.
**That framing is withdrawn: it was a global choice, and it should never have been one.**
*Replacement.* **Mass is an authored per-body field; surface gravity, escape velocity, sphere of
influence, orbital period and atmosphere scale height are all derived from it and never authored.** Both
behaviours are then available *per planet*: a curated 200 km starter world can be written as unusually
dense and pull like Earth, while a procedural asteroid pulls like an asteroid. The honest cost is
unchanged and is now local rather than global — a body written at 72× its natural mass has a
gravitational neighbourhood 5.5× larger than its size suggests, applied consistently from the one field.
*Residual.* What band of surface gravity the generator may produce, which is a feel decision.
*Blocks.* Star-system layout numbers, not architecture.
*Cost of deferring.* Low.

**6. How big is one texture tile, at what resolution, and do we ship authored textures?** *(§5,
decision 5-C. Named the highest-cost reversal in that section.)*
*Options.* Four cells per tile at 512 square (128 texels per cell, 128 MiB for 128 materials); four
cells at 1024 square (256 texels per cell, 512 MiB); eight cells at 2048 square (256 texels per cell,
2 GiB); four cells at 2048 square (512 texels per cell, not shippable at scale). Separately: ship
authored scan-based material data, or synthesise every texel on the client from the seed.
*Recommendation.* **Four cells at 1024 square, a hard cap of 128 materials in the shipping set, and
ship authored data.** 256 texels per cell is normal environment density; two-cell tiles read as almost
per-block and lose the multi-block effect entirely; a coarser tile trades texel density for it and
reads soft at walking distance. Variety comes from a seed-selected macro layer and per-block variation,
not from synthesising the detail tile — synthesising moves real graphics-card cost to the moment a
world spins up, which is exactly where the seamless rule forbids a stutter.
*Amended by Addendum 2 — one clause added to the bake specification, and it is not optional.*
**The roughness mip chain must be generated variance-aware, from the pre-compression three-channel
normal map, not box-filtered from the roughness map.** Mipmapping a normal map preserves the mean
normal and destroys its variance; the lost variance has to reappear as increased roughness at that mip
or the specular lobe stays too tight and the surface scintillates under a moving sun. The classical
runtime fix (a Toksvig factor from the length of the averaged normal) is **mathematically impossible for
us**: §5.3.4 locks two-channel BC5 normals, so the third component is reconstructed and every fetched
normal is unit length by construction — the averaged length the technique needs is unrecoverable at
runtime. So it must be baked: compute the averaged-normal length per mip on the uncompressed map,
convert it to an effective roughness, write it into the ORMH green channel's mip chain, then compress.
*Reason it lands here rather than in the shader:* it is an asset-pipeline change with zero runtime cost
and zero memory cost, and it is a **one-way door on the same schedule as the tile period** — every
material authored before the rule exists has to be re-baked. *Alternative:* three-channel normals to
enable the runtime version, at +0.667 MiB per material (+85 MiB across the shipping set) and it buys
nothing the bake does not. *Why the ladder forces the issue:* before, distant terrain barely existed;
now tier 5 draws a 4 m tile repeating 496 times across one chunk, and every one of those surfaces is
sampled near the top of its mip chain.
*Blocks.* All material authoring; the second-array question if a higher-resolution hero set is ever
wanted (texture arrays require uniform layer sizes, so that is a second array and a second addressing
scheme, not a per-material field).
*Cost of deferring.* Re-authoring hundreds of materials at a different period is not a refactor, it is
a re-do. The same is now true of the mip chain.

**7. What exactly does "no detail levels" ban? — ANSWERED AND CLOSED.** *(Owner ruling, 2026-08-03:
"from where do you get no LOD? Please remove it, we will need LODs everywhere, but in the smartest way."
Merged §5's 5-F and §6's 6-4. Full design: Addendum 2.)*
*Struck.* The original entry recorded that three separate researchers had each invented a different
private carve-out — the signature of a rule about to be broken by accumulation rather than by decision —
declined to grant itself a fourth, and recommended *"take the reserved insurance now, hold the rule
literally through P4, revisit when a ship first makes altitude routine."* Addendum 1 then promoted it to
the top of the register as the single constraint deciding whether flight above ~100 m exists.
**All of that is superseded. The ban is retracted; the answer is not "hold it", it is "everywhere".**
*The ruling, in the form the rest of this section depends on.*
- **One ladder, one rung per power of two.** At tier L a cell is 2^L metres and a chunk is still 62³
  cells. The container, palette, mesher, material tables and shape catalogue are **identical at every
  tier**. A tier is a number on a chunk address, never a second code path — so HR3 (one tooling) is
  satisfied by construction and nothing anywhere branches on tier.
- **For fractal terrain the correct detail level is exact and cheaper.** Tier L drops the L
  highest-frequency octaves. That is simultaneously the right anti-aliasing filter, the right level of
  detail, and a *saving* — the height error is bounded by the sum of the dropped amplitudes, which is
  proportional to cell size, which is exactly the property a ladder is supposed to have. **The generated
  world therefore coarsens itself for free: no stored pyramid, no precomputation, no aliasing.** The same
  argument covers the three-dimensional cave field — a three-metre cave is invisible from ten kilometres
  and correctly disappears.
- **The real work is the sparse edit pyramid** (decision 37), because player edits do *not* coarsen for
  free.
- **Tier selection reuses the existing angular-size rule, one level down**: pick the tier whose cells
  subtend a fixed number of pixels. At two pixels per cell, 70° field of view, 1920 pixels across, tier L
  is used out to 786·2^L metres — tier 0 to 786 m, tier 3 to 6.3 km, tier 7 to 100 km. No second
  scheduler.
- **The numbers.** About 379 chunk columns per tier above the first regardless of which tier, about 505
  in tier 0; a 100 km view is about 3,158 columns ≈ 6,800 chunks ≈ 270 MB packed, against 8.17 million
  columns without tiers. **Resident chunk count is now logarithmic in view distance instead of
  quadratic.**
- **Seams are closed by skirts** (v1): a short downward apron per chunk, about twenty lines, no case
  table, no dependency on which tier the neighbour happens to be at — which matters, because that changes
  as the camera moves. Vertex snapping and transvoxel are held in reserve and rejected for now in §8.6.
- **No pop, ever**: a distance-banded dither crossfade between two rungs of the *same* terrain — a
  crossfade, never an impostor.
- **The realm proxy stops being an exception and becomes the coarsest rung**, so the ladder runs
  continuously from a block in your hand to a planet seen as a dot from another star.
- **What must never get a detail level** (Addendum 2 §C.7, binding): collision — always tier 0, no
  exceptions; other players, ships and projectiles — anything that can shoot or be shot; anything a
  signal or functional block depends on; and anything whose appearance carries gameplay information a
  player could act on. **Two players at different distances may see different terrain *detail*; they must
  never see different terrain *facts*.** Substituted geometry stays banned — a sphere standing in for an
  unbuilt mesh is still forbidden; what is now required instead is *a coarser rung of the real thing*.
  The test is **derived-from versus substituted-for**. *One mechanism note, settled 2026-08-03 because
  two sections had answered it incompatibly:* where a block's **appearance is the state** — a
  docking-clamp light, a hull-breach lamp, a running light — that colour rides a **separate transient
  per-realm state-light lane**, composed by the realm owner and shipped at the observer's clamped rung
  (§7.9), so it survives to every rung including the realm proxy. It is **not** carried in the edit
  pyramid, which is permanent derived terrain data with a different key, a different lifetime and a
  different write rate, and it is not delivered by the signal bus, because a client is not a subscriber.
  How far such a light can be read is **[USER DECISION 7-H]**, which now covers the range only; the
  mechanism is ruled.
- **The four things the old rule left ambiguous now dissolve**: texture mipmaps are mandatory, shadow
  cascades are permitted, distance-blended detail-normal scales are permitted, and parameter falloff
  (grass count reaching zero on the same mesh) is permitted. The two decoration knobs that were blocked
  inside this row are released with them: the grass mat may thin with distance (from 100 per square metre
  near the camera to about 12 at the edge — 503,000 resident instances down to 144,000, 1.52 ms down to
  0.44 ms, and the minimum-spec machine keeps the full forty-metre radius instead of dropping to
  twenty-eight), and grass is dropped from the far shadow cascades (0.54 ms for four, 0.27 ms for the
  near two; a blade forty metres away casts a sub-pixel shadow anyway).
*Blocks.* Nothing any more. It **unblocks** material authoring, the grass radius, the shadow budget and
most of row 23.
*What it costs.* Five new decisions (37–41), two amendments to existing rows (6 and 21), three slice
additions, and five new gates.

**8. Where does the terrain noise come from?** *(§3, decision 3-F. A new-dependency question, therefore
the owner's by standing rule.)* The library already named in the manifest seeds its permutation table
through a loosely-pinned random-number crate, so a patch bump could regenerate every planet in the game
with no compile error and no test failure.
*Options.* (A) Vendor roughly four hundred lines of a known noise algorithm into the core crate, written
inside the determinism guard. (B) Use the already-declared pinned library with our own table supplied.
(C) Adopt a different library with a better determinism profile.
*Recommendation.* **(A) vendor it.** The whole generation path then sits inside the type-level guard,
the determinism gate passes by construction, there is no version-drift class at all, and it is the only
option that natively implements the per-planet-variation rule the design derives. Honest cost, corrected
from the earlier claim: about four hundred lines with ten to twenty data-dependent branches, each needing
a directed test under the coverage rule. It is not branchless.
*Amended by Addendum 2 — one requirement added.* The vendored sampler must expose **an explicit octave
count as a parameter**, so tier L is literally "the same call with L fewer octaves". That is the whole
generator-side implementation of the ladder, it is a *removal* of work, and it must be in the sampler's
signature from the first commit rather than bolted on — a fixed-octave-count sampler makes the ladder a
second code path, which HR3 forbids.
*Blocks.* The generator.
*Cost of deferring.* Changing the noise after players build requires regenerating every world underneath
their existing edits.

**9. Can players compute where every mineral deposit is?** *(§3, decision 3-G.)* Because terrain is
computed from a seed that ships inside the client, an offline tool enumerates the whole galaxy the
moment the binary is extracted. This is worse than the classic see-through-walls problem and it collides
with the already-decided player-driven economy, whose prices depend on scarcity producing information.
*Options.* (A) Accept it — all deposits public. (B) All ore is a server-only overlay delivered as you
dig. (C) Hybrid — common ores public, rare and strategic ones concealed.
*Recommendation.* **(C).** The bulk of terrain keeps the byte-identical determinism gate meaningful and
the early game needs no network at all, while the high-value tier the price signal actually depends on
keeps real scarcity and real discovery value. It costs one field in the block registry and a split of the
generator into a public half and a server-only half — both free now.
*Note added by Addendum 2.* The concealed half is generated server-side and therefore does **not** get
the free ladder — but it also never needs one: a concealed ore body is only ever revealed at tier 0, at
digging range. The public half carries the ladder; the concealed half carries nothing above tier 0. State
that as an invariant in the generator split, or someone will later try to coarsen the concealed field and
leak its distribution through the coarse tier.
*Blocks.* The generator's crate layout and the client-server parity gate.
*Cost of deferring.* Irreversible the moment the client ships; a schema migration plus a galaxy-wide
regeneration afterwards.

**10. Who works out the grass — each client, or the server?** *(§6, decision 6-1.)*
*Options.* (A) Each client works it out under a strict continuous-integration equality test — zero
network cost, but a modified client can decline to draw grass. (B) The server works it out and ships it
— correct under the most literal reading of the standing law, and about six megabytes per player every
time they enter a region, roughly 150× the entire snapshot budget, pushing cosmetic bytes across sealed
boundaries. (C) Client-derived, but with the server-side sampling path and its dependency edge declared
from the very first slice, so anything the simulation ever needs to read is one call away.
*Recommendation.* **(C).** It has (A)'s cost with (B)'s escape hatch. Three properties keep it distinct
from the floating-origin rework that had to be undone: the inputs are already replicated and the client
adds no information; the function is stateless and recomputed from scratch so there is no accumulation
order to get wrong; and nothing in the simulation reads the result by default.
*Note added by Addendum 2.* This row absorbs the grass-radius sub-question that used to be trapped
inside row 7. Decoration now follows the ladder **by density, not by substitution**: instance count per
cell scales smoothly to zero with distance, props stop being emitted past their own range, and the tier
a chunk was meshed at hands the evaluator its cutoff for free. Because decoration is derived rather than
stored that is a parameter change, not a second asset set — so it costs this row nothing and changes no
authority argument.
*Blocks.* The crate layout, the equality gate, and where the evaluator lives.
*Cost of deferring.* Free to set up now, a whole-subsystem rework later.

**11. How far do exposed edges crumble, and which materials do it?** *(§5, decision 5-E.)*
*Options.* Amplitude: none / 10 cm inward-only / **20 cm inward-only** / 25 cm with outward permitted /
33 cm. Who wobbles: everything, or natural material only with every constructed material perfectly
sharp. Plus: reserve a bevel-width field now and build the chamfer catalogue later, or never. Plus: rule
that a pre-computed geometry nudge is compatible with "the server does all the maths".
*Recommendation.* **20 cm inward-only; natural material wobbles between 8 and 20 cm and every constructed
material is exactly zero; reserve the bevel field; rule the pre-computed nudge compatible and write the
general amendment down once so this class of question is settled permanently.** Inward-only is the
difference between "the world is solid and I sometimes hit slightly more than I see" and "the world lies
to me". The registry asserts a material's amplitude is either exactly zero or at least 8 cm, because any
non-zero value costs the same merging penalty and 2 cm is below one texel.
*Note added by Addendum 2 — the amplitude is in cells, and that is a decision.* At tier L a 20 cm
inward wobble on a 2^L-metre cell is 20·2^L cm of displacement, which at tier 4 is 3.2 m of visible
wobble on a mountainside. **Rule: the crumble amplitude is expressed in metres and is not scaled by
tier; it is applied at tier 0 and 1 and is exactly zero at tier ≥ 2.** Reason: the effect exists to
un-square a block you are standing next to, and a 20 cm feature is sub-pixel past about 300 m anyway, so
dropping it costs nothing visible and removes the merge barrier from every coarse chunk — which is where
merging matters most. This is a per-draw uniform decision keyed on the chunk's tier, so it is branchless
and identical for every pixel of a chunk.
*Blocks.* All terrain art authoring; how much face merging survives on player-built structures (measured:
2.2× retained on a small hand-built box, 15.7× on a full-size surface).
*Cost of deferring.* Close to a one-way door — art is authored against whatever amplitude is chosen.

**12. What does the run-anywhere gate mean for geometry code, and who owns a ship-on-ground contact?**
*(§3, decision 3-B.)* A cube-face-seam test has no meaning on a ship grid, so demanding equal results on
both would either test nothing or test the wrong thing.
*Options.* (A) Split the gate — bind the equal-results rule to everything above the geometry seam and
give the seam itself a stronger exhaustive-enumeration gate. (B) Hold the rule literally and accept that
the seam is untested by it. Second half: when a ship rests on terrain, does the planet own the contact or
does the ship?
*Recommendation.* **(A), with the planet owning the contact.** The seam table does not depend on the
planet's size, so exhaustive enumeration at the smallest configuration is a complete proof and fits in a
unit-test budget. Planet-owns-contact matches the standing law that the containing realm authors its
children's positions, and the machinery it needs already exists in the direction it needs.
*Note added by Addendum 2.* The gate now has a second exhaustive obligation, and it is cheap: **the
geometry mapping's nine operations take the tier as a parameter and must be exhaustively enumerated at
more than one tier.** A mapping that is correct at tier 0 and wrong at tier 3 is a class of bug the
existing gate would not see, and the enumeration is over the same smallest configuration, so the cost is
a loop.
*Blocks.* The gate every other block feature is built on top of.
*Cost of deferring.* An unresolved gate quietly stops being a gate.

**13. Where does world simulation live in the roadmap?** *(§2, decision 2-F.)* Fire, fluids, growth,
weathering, freezing, falling blocks and structural collapse currently have no committed phase, and the
phase they were informally assigned to is actually the player-checkpoint and crash-durability phase.
*Options.* (A) Insert a new phase between block edits and checkpoints. (B) Fold all of it into the final
combat and scale-hardening phase. (C) Split — support and collapse early, the rest late.
*Recommendation.* **(A) a new phase between block edits and checkpoints.** The slow-tick scheduler and
the shared propagation engine are prerequisites of both the dormant-world pillar and the auto-decoration
layer, and the checkpoint phase cannot save per-block state whose shape has not been decided yet. The
slice plan below assumes this and labels it accordingly; if (B) or (C) is chosen, those slices move and
nothing else changes.
*Blocks.* Fire, fluids, growth, collapse; and what the checkpoint phase is able to save.
*Cost of deferring.* Not a one-way door, but the ordering is real: putting world simulation after the
durability phase means that phase either saves nothing useful or is reopened later.

**14. Is there a temperature per block at all?** *(§2, decision 2-B.)*
*Options.* (i) Heat is purely event-driven and fire is a dice roll, which needs a random-number stream
synchronised across machines. (ii) A sparse active set of only those blocks currently hotter or colder
than their surroundings, evicted when they settle. (iii) A temperature value for every block.
*Recommendation.* **(ii).** It removes a random-number stream that would otherwise have to stay in step
across machines, and it is what makes the damage model's heat threshold legible — a wood fire at 1,100
degrees simply cannot melt granite that needs 1,500, with no rule anywhere saying so. (iii) is the one
design that provably cannot work at planet scale.
*Blocks.* Fire, melting, freezing; and which per-block values must be written to disk.
*Cost of deferring.* One-way door. Discovering this after fire and melting are built forces a rewrite of
both.

**15. Does the world keep evolving where nobody is watching?** *(§2, decision 2-D.)*
*Options.* (i) Everything pauses while a region is asleep. (ii) Everything continues, caught up when the
region wakes, by three named methods with their costs.
*Recommendation.* **(ii).** The dormant-world pillar requires it. Note the shape it takes: a sleeping
world is not granted a background writer; it advances by evaluating a closed-form step once when it
wakes, so six months asleep costs the same as six hours.
*Blocks.* Every mechanic; and which per-block values are persisted.
*Cost of deferring.* One-way door in a structural sense — catch-up is a requirement on every single
mechanic, not a switch.

**16. Do we adopt the physics and collision libraries, and use the voxel collision shape?** *(Merged:
§2's 2-G and §4's 4-B. §8.6 item 2 resolves who owns the question.)* Neither library is a dependency
today, although the roadmap names one of them as a phase deliverable.
*Options.* (B1) Adopt both, and use the library's purpose-built voxel collision shape on flat realms
only — ships and stations — with hand-built convex composites everywhere else. (B2) Adopt both, use our
own composite everywhere, one uniform lane. (B3) The engine-native alternative, which sits on the same
collision library underneath. (B4) Hand-roll collision.
*Recommendation.* **(B1), with (B2) pre-designed as the fallback and a spike run before the physics
phase commits.** Roughly one byte per block with built-in removal of the snagging problem where a
character catches on the seam between two blocks, against roughly 120 bytes per block hand-rolled. An
important correction: the voxel shape is *structurally incapable* of representing a planet, because a
planet's cells are sheared and tapering and the shape assumes a uniform square lattice — so this is a
genuine planet-versus-ship divergence in the collision layer and must not be sold as a run-anywhere win.
One case is unverified by any shipped implementation anywhere: a cube next to a slope is not recognised
as an internal face unless a phantom block is inserted, which then collides where nothing is.
*Note added by Addendum 2.* Nothing in the ladder reaches this row, and that is the point: **collision
is tier 0 always, and that is an assertion in the code rather than a policy in a document.** Tier 0 is
resident wherever a player is, which is exactly the region physics runs in, so the constraint costs
nothing. The gate is in §8.4.
*Blocks.* The whole collision layer, and the physics-phase architecture.
*Cost of deferring.* Not a one-way door — every shape is routed through an opaque project-owned
identifier — but the spike must land before the physics phase freezes the collider architecture.

**17. Which shapes can a player walk on?** *(§4, decision 4-C.)* The geometry has already removed one
option: because a planet's blocks are between two-thirds and one and a twentieth of a metre wide
depending on where you stand, the same forty-five-degree wedge presents anything from 43.5 to 56.1
degrees, while the steeper corner-cut facet drops as low as 53.4 degrees somewhere else on the same
planet. Those ranges overlap, so "wedge walkable, facet not" cannot be expressed by any single threshold.
*Options.* (C1) Everything in the catalogue is walkable and only vertical is not. (C2) The wedge and the
facet are decorative hull pieces; the shallow one-in-two ramp is the steepest walkable thing. (C3)
Different answers on planets and ships.
*Recommendation.* **(C1).** It costs nothing on natural terrain, because generated terrain is ruled
cube-only, so terrain has only flat and vertical surfaces and cliffs stay cliffs. (C3) is rejected
outright: the same block behaving differently in two places breaks the run-anywhere gate.
*Blocks.* The catalogue; every interior corridor's proportions.
*Cost of deferring.* Close to a one-way door in content terms — players build ramps and stairs around
whatever ships, and reversing it either breaks their builds or trivialises them.

**18. Does distance ever delay a signal, and may a live control stream be delayed?** *(§7, decision
7-A.)*
*Options.* (A) No delay anywhere — remote control works at any range and the sense of distance is lost.
(B) Delay everywhere by the speed of light — at one astronomical unit that is eight minutes, so every
cross-system interaction becomes mail and real-time fleet play dies. (C) A zero-delay bubble, growing
delay beyond it, and outright refusal past one light-hour, with the relay network exempt and carrying its
own much shorter latency.
*Recommendation.* **(C), with the bubble at two light-seconds rather than one** — one light-second does
not even reach a planet's own moon, so the canonical example the feature exists for would fall outside
it. Under (C) a continuous control stream is never delayed, only refused, which is what lets the refusal
be a hard rule and a legible game rule rather than a silent degradation.
*Blocks.* The signal message envelope; whether the station-autopilot feature streams or uploads.
*Cost of deferring.* Players build around whichever answer ships: removing zero-delay remote control
afterwards is a community incident, and adding delay later invalidates every station and fleet design.

**19. How far does player programmability go?** *(§7, decision 7-C.)*
*Options.* (A) Logic blocks plus a bounded arithmetic expression, permanently — no sandbox, no scheduler,
no determinism risk. (B) The same two stages now, with a real scripting language gated behind measured
demand and written gate conditions. (C) Commit to a scripting language now as a headline feature.
*Recommendation.* **(B).** The first two stages are cheap and are needed regardless. The third must not
start until the first two have shipped and demand has been measured with concrete examples of what
players tried to build and could not. Three shipped games each failed differently here: one was killed by
a quarter of a million accumulated threads, one runs scripts on the main frame budget and is commonly
disabled by server operators, and one moved scripting to the player's own machine, which this project's
authority law forbids.
*Blocks.* Whether a scheduler, sandbox, memory-budget and determinism subsystem exists at all.
*Cost of deferring.* A genuine one-way door in one direction: moving from (A) to (B) is free at any time;
once players have written scripts, throttling or removing the runtime is a community incident.

**20. Which of six unscheduled simulation subsystems are in scope, in what order?** *(§7, decision
7-E.)* The block catalogue quietly requires a power grid, a fluid and pressure network, a thermal model,
item logistics, a crafting recipe graph and a structural stress model. None is in the roadmap. Three of
them are already load-bearing inside this document's own arguments.
*Options.* (A) Two now, two with ship interiors, two behind the economy: structural stress and the power
grid first, then thermal and fluids, then logistics and recipes. (B) All six before functional blocks
ship. (C) Only logic, interface and machinery, permanently — a game with no resource simulation.
*Recommendation.* **(A).** Structural stress and the power grid are both cheap passes over a graph the
block plan already builds, and structural stress in particular delivers most of the physical-ship feeling
that people wrongly try to get from joint simulation.
*Blocks.* Most of the block catalogue, and the honest scope of the functional-block phase.
*Cost of deferring.* Each is comparable in size to the signal bus itself. Left unnamed, they get
discovered one at a time during implementation of a phase whose stated goal is a switch toggling a lamp.

**21. What does one mesh vertex look like?** *(§5, decision 5-B. **De-escalated by Addendum 2, with one
caveat that is not a formality.**)*
*Options.* (B1) Sixteen bytes per vertex through the standard engine pipeline now, with a hand-written
eight-bytes-per-quad path declared the endgame. (B2) The hand-written path immediately. (B3) Stay on
today's twenty-four-byte format.
*Recommendation.* **(B1)**, unchanged. The decisive number is upload per player click, not resident
memory: 5.76 MB today, 3.52 MB at B1, 0.32 MB at B2. B2's eighteen-fold win costs the entire
engine-provided graphics-card-driven path — bindless resources, multi-draw, two-phase occlusion culling,
the depth prepass, shadows and motion vectors — all of which must be re-derived on a renderer that
migrates roughly every four months.
*Status, corrected twice.* Addendum 1 **promoted this row to blocking**, because an Earth-sized planet on
foot needed 53,110 chunks — 2.1 GB packed against 25.5 GB at today's format — so the vertex format
decided whether a big planet was renderable at all. Addendum 2 **de-escalates it**, because the ladder
takes that same Earth-sized ground view down to about 4,000 chunks and roughly 160 MB. **It no longer
decides whether a planet can exist.**
*The caveat, stated because de-escalation is not dissolution.* Per-chunk mesh cost is close to
**tier-invariant**: a chunk's top-surface footprint is 62² = 3,844 cells at every tier, and because each
fBm octave contributes an equal share of slope, dropping three octaves removes roughly 37 % of the slope
and therefore only trims side faces — it does not divide the quad count by four. So resident mesh bytes
are (chunk count) × (per-chunk bytes), and Addendum 2's "100 km view ≈ 6,800 chunks ≈ 270 MB" is stated
**at B2's eight-bytes-per-quad format** (it implies ~39.7 KB and ~5,000 quads per chunk — the
**conservative** allowance for high-relief or heavily built chunks, not the measured figure). At B1 the
same view is 6,800 × 5,000 × 88 B ≈ **3.0 GB**, or about **1.3 GB** using §5.2.1's **measured** 2,200
quads per chunk — against §5.3.6's summed **1.41 GiB (1,443 MiB) on-foot V1 total, 2.56 GiB for the full
V1 ladder** *(corrected: the 1.20 GiB figure this row used to quote predates §5.3.6's re-sum for the
ladder)*, and its 3.0 GiB asserted cap. **So the honest
statement is: the ladder dissolves the planet-size constraint completely and dissolves the flight
constraint only at B2.** The consequence is not to re-promote this row — B1 still ships first — but to
put the resident-byte governor of decision 38 in the render tuning struct from the start, because on a
B1 build the 100 km view has to be bought down by raising the pixels-per-cell target, not by hoping.
*Blocks.* Every producer of render geometry; and the maximum affordable flight view distance.
*Cost of deferring.* Reversible only while one producer exists. After terrain, edits, shaped blocks and
hulls there are four or more plus their golden fixtures, and the change becomes a simultaneous migration
of all of them.

**22. Do materials blend softly, or meet at hard decorated edges?** *(§5, decision 5-D.)*
*Options.* (D1) Soft blending across a one-metre strip, using the height information already in every
material so gravel pokes through dirt along real gravel edges. (D2) Hard one-metre edges decorated with
an overlay quad carrying the neighbour material — the classic grass-overhang look, no shader blending at
all. (D3) Hybrid, soft for natural pairs and hard for gameplay-legible boundaries.
*Recommendation.* **(D1)**, because the owner's words are "blend into each other, like real life", and
the border-trimming machinery is needed for the crumbling edge and the shaped-block lane anyway, so the
marginal cost is the shader path only. The genuine counter-argument is stated: a smooth blend on a
surface that visibly steps in one-metre cubes can read as inconsistent rather than higher quality.
*Note added by Addendum 2.* The seam blend is one of the taps the **material feature ladder** drops at
coarse tiers (see decision 38 and §8.6 item 9): a two-material blend across a strip one *cell* wide is
meaningless when the cell is 32 m. Dropping it at tier ≥ 2 is what takes the worst-case tap count from
about 8 at tier 0 to about 2 at tier ≥ 4, so coarse tiers get cheaper per pixel as well as per triangle.
*Blocks.* Roughly a month of shader work in one direction or the other.
*Cost of deferring.* Not a one-way door — the trimming machinery is shared, so switching later replaces
one shader rather than the mesher.

**23. How is a planet drawn from altitude and from orbit?** *(§5, decision 5-G. **Largely answered by
Addendum 2; this entry is the residual.**)*
*Struck.* The original entry offered three options and stated, in bold, that *"the altitude band from
roughly two kilometres to fifty kilometres is unsolved by any option in this document, and it is the
largest open rendering risk in the block system."* It recommended **(G1) an analytic displaced-sphere
shell**, and it **rejected (G3) a genuine chunk detail tier all the way to orbit** on two specific
grounds: "folding player edits into coarsened tiers" and "a two-tier seam algorithm that does not exist
for blocky geometry".
**Addendum 2 supplies both.** Edits fold in through the sparse edit pyramid (decision 37); the seam is
closed by skirts, which work precisely *because* the geometry is blocky — two rungs of axis-aligned
quads meet in a vertical step rather than along an interpolated curve, so a downward apron closes the
crack exactly, with no case table. *(The apron's depth is §5.9.4's derived `skirt_drop`: the relief across
one cell of the **next coarser** rung, plus the registry's **maximum rim-warp amplitude**, times
`skirt_safety`. §5 owns the formula; §3.5.2 owns the relief envelope it reads, which is derived and never
persisted.)* **The rejection no longer holds, and
G3 is now the design.** The unsolved 2–50 km band is solved: it is tiers 2 through 6.
*Residual question, and it is genuinely open.* **Does the analytic shell (G1) survive as an optional rung
above the top tier, or does the realm proxy take over directly from the coarsest chunk tier?** The ladder
makes the proxy the coarsest rung by construction, so the shell is no longer *needed* — but it is still
the cheapest possible representation of a whole planet's silhouette from another star, and it is driven
by the same authoritative height function, so it is derived-from rather than substituted-for and remains
legal. *Recommendation:* **do not build it.** One representation fewer is worth more than the saving, the
proxy already exists and already streams, and every extra representation is another thing the edit
pyramid has to be reconciled against. Reserve nothing; if the proxy reads badly from interplanetary
distance, a displaced proxy sphere is a later, purely cosmetic addition that constrains nothing.
*Blocks.* The height field's form — much less than before, since the ladder already requires the height
function to be evaluable at any octave count, which is the same property the shell wanted.
*Cost of deferring.* Now low. It was the highest-cost open item in the section; it is not any more.

**24. Where does the mesher come from?** *(§5, decision 5-A.)*
*Options.* (A1) Write our own from the published bit expressions — three hundred to eight hundred lines
plus a coverage suite and a determinism fixture. (A2) Depend on the maintained crate. (A3) Vendor it
(permissive licence, attribute). (A4) or (A5) Depend on either of two others.
*Recommendation.* **(A1), with (A3) acceptable if the first slice must move faster.** Every off-the-shelf
option assumes full axis-aligned cubes and would be forked at the first slope, the first material seam
strip and the first warped rim; one candidate has been unmaintained since 2022 with a released
correctness bug stranded on a development branch.
*Note added by Addendum 2.* Add "and the first skirt" to that list of forks. A skirt is an extra ring of
quads emitted around a chunk border with a per-chunk relief height — trivial in a mesher we own, an
outright fork in one we do not.
*Blocks.* The mesher slice, which is the second of eight rendering slices.
*Cost of deferring.* Low and reversible — the integer chunk-geometry output is the seam, so swapping the
producer behind it is contained.

**25. Where do the decorative prop meshes come from?** *(§6, decision 6-2.)*
*Options.* (A) Buy the stylised nature packs as greybox now and re-author later — about €46–200, days of
pipeline work, zero art lead time, with the risk that greybox becomes ship. (B) Commission an original
prop set — months of lead time, roughly €15–40k for sixty to eighty coherent props, full control, no
licence ambiguity. (C) Free public-domain scan-based props — zero cost and zero licence risk, but small,
incoherent sets and no nature biome set. (D) Fully procedural props from the seed.
*Recommendation.* **(A) plus (C) now, (B) scheduled, (D) for one class.** Take (A) for the terrain and
block-edit phases with a dated written re-authoring commitment and a checked-in per-pack provenance
manifest; take (C) in parallel for rocks specifically, because scan-based rocks blend into a
physically-based voxel world where stylised rocks do not; budget and schedule (B) to land before any
public build; take (D) for leaf clusters *on necessity* — a cluster's shape depends on its neighbours and
its distance from the trunk, so a fixed bought mesh structurally cannot serve it. Two licence clauses are
live: source files must never leave the team, and the assets must never be fed to any generative tool.
*Note added by Addendum 2 — two couplings to decision 39.* First, **the impostor bake consumes whichever
archetype set this row lands on**, so the licence constraints above extend to the baked atlases: a baked
impostor is a derived work of a bought mesh and the "source files never leave the team" clause reaches
it. Second, an idea worth taking whichever way this row goes, because it costs nothing and is the
cheapest quality win in the whole detail-level study: **shape variation — one authored prop asset,
per-instance procedural deformation** (scale, lean, branch phase, hue jitter) rather than N authored
variants. Ours must be **hash-derived from the cell key rather than randomised**, which makes it
deterministic and identical on every client — strictly better than the shipped precedent it comes from,
and free, because the instance already carries a cell-derived seed. It costs a few bytes per instance in
the buffer §6.7 already ships, no new assets and no new material slots, which matters against §5.3.6's
128-material / 512 MiB cap. It also compounds with impostors: one atlas still serves a varied forest.
*Blocks.* Art lead time; visual identity.
*Cost of deferring.* One-way in one direction only: shipping recognisable bought art establishes a visual
identity that is expensive to change. Buying the packs and never shipping them costs about €200.

**26. Does the server's light field carry colour?** *(§2, decision 2-A.)*
*Options.* (i) No server light field at all, so "can this plant grow" and "is it dark here" have no
answer. (ii) A single-channel light plus sky-exposure field, server-side only, never sent to the client.
(iii) Three independent colour channels.
*Recommendation.* **(ii).** ~~The binary render rule already caps how much world is drawn~~ — *that
premise is retracted with row 7; the argument survives on its own without it.* Inside the short radius
where a light field is consulted at all, a handful of real lights beats a voxel light grid on both looks
and cost, and the field's actual consumers are gameplay questions (growth, darkness) rather than
rendering. Colour triples the memory and the propagation work for no gameplay answer the single channel
does not already give. **The field is a tier-0 structure and is never coarsened** — it feeds growth and
other simulation, which decision 7's exclusion list keeps at full fidelity.
*Blocks.* The light propagation pass and the saved state layout.
*Cost of deferring.* Colour is a one-way door: adding two more channels after the mesher and the
per-block state layout are frozen is a rewrite of both.

**27. Voice and video: build, rent, or reserve and ship text only?** *(§7, decision 7-B.)*
*Options.* (A) Self-hosted forwarding servers behind our own control plane — full control of the
proximity cap and of retention, roughly 120 to 1,200 cores at a hundred thousand players, billed per
core-minute. (B) A managed vendor billed per monthly active user — cheapest to start, asymptotically more
expensive, and it hands enforcement of the proximity cap to a third party that does not know our world
geometry. (C) No voice at launch; text only, with the media handle reserved on the wire.
*Recommendation.* **(C) now, (A) later, never (B).** Reserving the handle costs a few bytes in one list
today; building a media control plane before there are players to talk to spends a phase on the wrong
phase. One talking player costs roughly four and a half times an entire world-to-world signal link, and
voice is the single largest recurring infrastructure line in the product. **Attached rider, needing its
own answer whichever option is taken: is voice recorded for after-the-fact reporting?** That is a consent
question, and adding recording after launch means re-collecting consent from the whole player base.
*Blocks.* The media handle's fields.
*Cost of deferring.* Low for the transport; genuinely one-way for the recording rider.

**28. Does the client show a preview block before the server confirms?** *(§4, decision 4-D.)*
*Options.* (D1) The protocol fixes only — a reliable message lane, an off-tick acceptance receipt,
batched multi-block commands, and the client sending the resolved target rather than the server
re-aiming. (D2) D1 plus a translucent, unlit, non-colliding preview that persists past the click and is
discarded on the server's answer. (D3) Apply the edit to the client's own world and re-mesh, reconciling
later.
*Recommendation.* **D1 now and unconditionally; measure; adopt D2 only if it still feels soft.** The
protocol fixes alone take the click-to-pixels time from roughly 250 ms down to 73–123 ms. D2 touches no
standing law — no simulation state, no collider, nothing to roll back — but it *looks* like prediction, so
it deserves a ruling rather than a quiet implementation. D3 is rejected: it directly contradicts the
no-prediction and server-does-all-maths laws, and its failure mode is the world visibly rewriting itself.
*Blocks.* The build interface.
*Cost of deferring.* Nothing is foreclosed by starting with D1, but the ruling should be on the record
before the build interface is designed around it.

**29. Does block damage heal by itself?** *(§2, decision 2-E.)*
*Options.* (i) Nothing heals — every scar is permanent until repaired. (ii) Natural terrain heals slowly,
built materials do not. (iii) Everything heals.
*Recommendation.* **(ii).** It matches the fiction and it is measured: damage drains with a time constant
of about nine minutes, so the damage table only grows without bound above a sustained 146 damaged blocks
per second in one chunk. Note that built materials never heal under any option, so the memory safeguard —
a lossless switch to a fixed-size layout plus a per-region cap with a loud refusal — is needed regardless.
*Blocks.* One derived value and one slow-tick rule.
*Cost of deferring.* None structural.

**30. Is radio interceptable?** *(§7, decision 7-G.)* The relay cannot enforce a read permission, because
it never holds the channel's declaration.
*Options.* (A) Radio is open by design; read permissions are documented as enforceable only where the
declaration lives, and confidentiality becomes a player-built mechanic through a cipher block pair, with
the relay forwarding traffic it cannot read. (B) The relay enforces read permissions, which means
replicating every net's allowlist to a node that should be a dumb forwarder, with its own fencing and
revocation across the galaxy.
*Recommendation.* **(A).** Cheaper, better fiction, and honest — (B)'s guarantee would only be as strong
as the weakest relay. Signals intelligence, direction-finding, jamming and code-breaking all become
content. The cipher block must be described to players as in-game confidentiality, not secrecy from the
operator.
*Blocks.* Whether confidentiality is a player mechanic or a platform guarantee.
*Cost of deferring.* Asymmetric: making an open channel private later is a straightforward addition;
making a private channel public later breaks every player who built around secrecy.

**31. How far does chemistry go?** *(§2, decision 2-C.)*
*Options.* (i) Rusting and weathering — one material turning into another over time — plus a corrosive
damage type. (ii) A full reacts-with web.
*Recommendation.* **(i).** A reactions web grows the balancing and testing burden as the square of the
material count for the least gameplay return of any property group in a multiplayer game.
*Blocks.* Nothing.
*Cost of deferring.* None — purely additive, and a reactions table can land years later without touching
anything saved to disk.

**32. Is hiding in grass ever a mechanic?** *(§6, decision 6-5.)*
*Options.* Yes — the server must be able to sample how concealed a player is, which under the recommended
authority model is one call per player per tick, proportional to players rather than blades. No —
decoration stays purely cosmetic and a modified client that declines to draw grass gains a small unfair
advantage.
*Recommendation.* **Decide now, but the retrofit is genuinely cheap** provided decision 10 takes the safe
side, which this design already does. The real irreversible choice is the *placement* of the evaluator,
not the mechanic. *One clause the ladder adds:* if the answer is yes, the concealment sample is evaluated
**at tier 0 on the server, never from whatever tier a client happens to be drawing** — otherwise two
players at different distances would see different terrain *facts*, which decision 7's exclusion list
forbids.
*Blocks.* Nothing, if decision 10 is answered as recommended.
*Cost of deferring.* Almost none.

**33. Do decorative props ever become carryable items?** *(§6, decision 6-6.)*
*Options.* Yes — which moves bought-asset usage adjacent to a prohibited clause and moves a placed prop
across the promotion boundary, since a player-placed prop is authoritative state that must persist and
therefore becomes a real block. No — props remain world dressing placed by the generator.
*Recommendation.* **No for the first release.** Placeable decoration is a legitimate later feature and is
cleanly expressible as promoted blocks, needing no change to anything designed here. If the answer becomes
yes, obtain written confirmation from the asset vendor before any of their meshes becomes the placeable one.
*Blocks.* Licence exposure only.
*Cost of deferring.* Low; sequencing matters more than timing.

**34. What shape is a permission grant?** *(§7, decision 7-F.)*
*Options.* (A) Plain keyed rows in the world's own permission table, with the key transferable as text —
exactly what the roadmap already names, no new library, and it covers every scenario in this document
including the station-autopilot handshake. (B) An attenuable token library, which adds one capability the
simple form cannot express: handing someone a permission they can narrow further before passing it on,
without contacting the issuer.
*Recommendation.* **(A) now, with one reserved optional field in the permission row so (B) is a pure
addition rather than a migration.**
*Blocks.* The grants table's schema.
*Cost of deferring.* Low if the reserved field ships; a durable-table change if it does not.

**35. Which cryptographic tag stamps a cross-world message batch?** *(§7, decision 7-D.)*
*Options.* (A) The keyed hash already used elsewhere in the workspace and already named in the phase
deliverables — no new library, about a seventh of one percent of a tick. (B) A faster modern hash that is
not currently a dependency of any crate here — about a twenty-fifth of one percent of a tick.
*Recommendation.* **(A).** The measured 367-fold gap that rules out per-message public-key signatures says
nothing about the choice between these two at per-batch rates, where both are noise. (B) buys roughly one
tenth of one percent of a tick and costs a new dependency plus a contradiction with a written deliverable.
The tag is the same width either way, so (B) remains a one-line swap.
*Blocks.* Nothing.
*Cost of deferring.* Low. It is escalated only because adopting a new library is never an engineering call
here.
