per-chunk decorated-cell table with span writes and a bulk-rebuild path on the task pool; the expiring
growth log and the unbounded-lifetime override set as **two named new persisted record types**; grow-in
driven by the client's interpolated authoritative tick; the prop tier; and leaf materials declaring in
their own definition that they are not drawn as cubes, with overhanging clusters drawn instead.
*Added by Addendum 2 — the no-pop machinery must also cover distance falloff, and the reason is
empirical.* The most-reported complaint about the shipped title studied for this section is not tier
crossings at all — it is clutter and grass appearing a few metres in front of a walking player, bad
enough that the studio shipped a separate graphics option partly because of it. **So §6.5's edit-reactivity
ramp must also be the distance ramp, and the ramp must be wide**; a short density ramp pops exactly as
visibly as a mesh swap. The pop-detector gate correspondingly must include a **forward-walk traverse at
eye height**, not only a flyover — that is the case the reference title visibly failed.
*Done when:* the edit-latency gate holds (a bounded number of write ranges and bytes per edit), the bulk
path triggers on a crater and never blocks the main thread, both new record types survive a hard kill
and a re-shard, and the walking pop gate passes.

#### P6b — world simulation *(pending decision 13)*

**P6b.1 — The shared propagation engine and the slow-tick scheduler.** *Size: L.*
*Lands:* one monomorphic attenuating flood over the six-neighbour graph with separate increase and
decrease queues and a per-tick cell budget that carries over, expressed as data rows for light, sky
exposure, structural support, heat, radiation and signal strength; the sampling scheduler whose cost is
proportional to loaded sections and independent of world content; and the boundary assertion that every
attenuation table reaches zero at a world boundary, so a fire on a docked ship cannot become a
distributed-systems problem. **All of it is tier-0 machinery and never sees a coarse chunk**, by
decision 7's exclusion list.
*Done when:* the flood benchmark's ball sizes match the closed form exactly and the boundary assertion is
a harness test rather than a review item.

**P6b.2 — The twelve mechanics.** *Size: XL.*
*Lands:* light, sky exposure, structural support (with the rule that generated blocks are unconditionally
anchored and the check runs only within thirty-two blocks of a player's edit), falling blocks merged into
single rigid bodies, fire, fluids, pressure and rooms, growth, weathering, freezing, explosions and
radiation; the three catch-up classes with their persisted inputs; and the gravity capability on the shard
profile with the support model selected by the capability *value*, never by a shard kind.
*Done when:* the four gravity-dependent mechanics pass their own identical fixture on **two
gravity-bearing profiles** — a spherical planet and a flat spin station — while the gravity-free subset
passes the ordinary planet-and-ship fixture. Four unbounded worst cases (explosions, collapse, mass
falling-block conversion and spall cascades) all sit behind deferred budgeted queues, never inline in the
edit path.
*One coupling to name:* every mechanic that changes a block writes through the edit path, so **every
mechanic also updates the pyramid** — which is free, because it goes through the same walk-up with the
same early exit and the same one-storage-block-per-rung cost, and which is why the pyramid must exist
before this phase rather than after it.

#### P8 — ships

**P8.1 — Construction realms and the weld.** *Size: L.*
*Lands:* minting a construction world from a crafted, quota'd anchor item rather than from an untethered
block placement; adjacency joining an existing construction rather than minting a third; the deliberate
weld as a one-time durable transfer of one world's whole edit set into another through the existing
transfer machinery; and abandonment reaping as an ordinary owner-authority operation at spin-up, never as
a background writer. **A weld also merges two pyramids** — and under the one update rule that is *not* an
entry-wise merge of two entry sets, which could never produce a correct dominant substance or fill: it is
**the same walk-up re-run over the merged delta set** for every coarse cell either side touched, which
needs no new machinery. It must be in the weld's transaction, or the welded structure's distant
appearance is stale until something touches it.
*Done when:* a welded structure keeps every edit across a hard kill and a re-shard, **and its pyramid
recomputed from the merged deltas is byte-identical to the one the weld produced**.

**P8.2 — Ship-on-terrain contact.** *Size: M.*
*Lands:* the planet owning the contact, with the hull entering the planet's physics world as a ghost
collider through the existing machinery and the resulting pose shipped back as the ship world's authored
placement. **Tier 0 on both sides, by the collision rule.**
*Done when:* a ship lands, rests and takes off without either world's private physics being visible to
the other.

**P8.3 — Kinematic articulation.** *Size: L.*
*Lands:* articulation computed rather than solved — each actuator's scalar state from its transfer
function, the child sub-assembly's pose as an exact analytic rigid offset, colliders moved as
kinematic-position bodies, reaction applied analytically; contacts disabled between a parent and its own
articulated child with the commanded motion refused by a discrete shape-cast instead; lock-implies-merge;
build-time cycle detection; and the cap of 512 actuators per assembly, derived from the honest byte
arithmetic of the entity state blob rather than asserted.
*Done when:* an articulated machine crosses a world boundary **as one entity**, with its actuator states
as quantised scalars in its blob, and reassembles identically.

**P8.4 — The top rungs and the hand-off to the realm proxy.** *Size: M.* *(Was: "The far-field planet
shell, L, conditional on decision 23". **Reduced and de-conditioned** — the ladder covers the band the
shell existed for, so what remains is the join at the top, not a second representation.)*
*Lands:* the continuity check between the coarsest resident chunk tier and the realm proxy — the proxy
becomes the next rung rather than a different kind of thing, so it is the same crossfade with the same
band; and the demand-loop coupling that keeps the proxy resident as the guaranteed no-hole fallback while
coarse tiers stream in behind it.
*Done when:* a warp approach shows a body growing continuously from a dot, through the proxy, into the
body's **face-covering rung** (`tier_depth − 1` — rung 12 on the starter body, 18 on an Earth-sized one)
and down to tier 0, with the pop detector silent at every join.

> **[N2] Corrected.** ~~"through the proxy into tier 7 and down to tier 0"~~ **struck.** Rung 7 as the
> hand-off point is option **G3**, which register row 1 *rejects* for failing the seamless law — so this
> acceptance test, which exists to certify precisely this join, was certifying the option the register
> turns down. The hand-off rung is per body and derived (`tier_depth − 1`), never a literal. If row 1
> comes back G2 or G3 instead, this done-when changes with it — it must cite the row, not a number.

#### P9 — functional blocks and signals

**P9.1 — The signal bus core.** *Size: XL.*
*Lands:* the interned channel table with double buffering and compiled subscriber lists; the two lanes
behind one message arm with a versioned envelope and per-body classification; the three routing planes,
each with a bounded radius, and the inverted index at each parent; the channel declaration with its
validated liveness invariant (an exported latest-wins channel must declare a republish period at least
twice as fast as its consumer's deadline, or holding the throttle down cuts the engines); the interest
set whose lifetime is bound to the existing demand ledger rather than to a second timer; the tiered
authentication with one truncated tag per bundle per destination per tick; the bounded replay window with
eviction and refusal; the retained-port table; and the uniform one-tick propagation delay written down
*before* any block behaviour is authored.
*Done when:* the load gate holds (ten thousand functional blocks at realistic churn inside the per-tick
delivery budget); the "no listener, no traffic" assertion passes; the "no traffic without a heartbeat gap"
assertion passes; and the interest-set and replay-window memory assertions hold.
*Run-anywhere fixture:* a switch toggling a lamp through two combinators, on a planet profile and a ship
profile, plus an anti-vacuity assertion that no signal code reads the geometry capability.
*One assertion the ladder adds:* **no signal, functional block or behaviour may read a chunk's tier.** A
beacon must not stop blinking because you flew away; its housing may coarsen, its behaviour may not. This
is the anti-vacuity assertion's twin and costs one grep-shaped test.

**P9.2 — The shipping block set and arbitration.** *Size: L.*
*Lands:* the twenty-seven blocks that ship against machinery this design defines — twelve logic, eight
interface, four communications, three door — six kernels with their closed parameter sub-enums and
**zero per-block behaviour functions**; arbitration as a per-port field with its two validated
cross-products; the durable grants table with the station-autopilot handshake; and the probe budget with
its deterministic round-robin deferral and its declared sort key, so a sensor's contact list is ordered
by entity identifier rather than by a physics data structure's internal layout.
*Done when:* adding a block is one manifest row and zero behaviour code, verified by a loop over the
static table; the probe budget assertion holds; and the pilot-versus-autopilot preemption is a priority
ordering with no branch anywhere asking "is this a pilot".

**P9.3 — The block cover.** *Size: L.*
*Lands:* the cover as an optional per-face attachment in the parent block's configuration blob, never a
block kind; the closed widget registry; server-side composition into a bounded draw-command list with
static per-widget caps refused at configuration time; one instanced world-space pass with one signed-
distance glyph atlas baked at build time and hashed in continuous integration; the legibility-derived
angular threshold; and the aggregate per-client byte budget filled in descending angular size. *The
legibility threshold is the same angular-size rule as tier selection, one level down again — a panel too
small to read emits no draw list, which is parameter falloff, not substitution.*
*Done when:* the panel scale test passes — five hundred covers, 128 sessions, inside the per-client byte
budget and the shard tick allowance, in one or two draw calls, **and a session receives no draw list for
a panel it is not authorised for.**

**P9.4 — The relay plane.** *Size: L.*
*Lands:* rendezvous hashing over the fence-versioned relay set with the dual-read migration window;
light-lag held at the routing node in a hierarchical timing wheel; the refusal-with-hysteresis for
latest-wins channels beyond the light budget; the offline mailbox for accounts and the deliberate
asymmetry that machines do not get one.
*Done when:* a relay joining or leaving remaps only a small fraction of nets and no standing radio net
sees an outage.

### 8.4 Benchmarks and gates this design owes

Every number below is a promise. An unasserted budget is an assumption. **Nine rows are added by the
detail-level ladder (marked ✦), one is retired as measured, and one — mesher throughput — is promoted
because the noise benchmark it used to sit behind has run.**

| Gate | The number it must hold | First runs |
|---|---|---|
| ~~**Noise throughput**~~ **✅ MEASURED** | ~~Publishes ns/evaluation for five shapes; derives the maximum flight speed~~ **Done: 12.19 ns per evaluation, 0.885 ms per 62³ surface chunk, Apple M4 Pro, one core. Generation risk closed. The flight-speed derivation moves to the two rows below.** | S0.0 — **complete** |
| **Mesher throughput — PROMOTED** | Typical tier-0 chunk ≤ 120 µs; adversarial checkerboard ≤ 45 ms; **plus a per-tier curve over EVERY legal rung of the fixture body (0 … `tier_depth − 1`; 0–12 on the starter world) — and this curve, not the noise constant, is what derives the maximum sustainable flight speed** (one-way door 42). ~~"tier 0 through tier 7"~~ struck **[N3]**: the curve tunes a one-way gameplay door and stopped five rungs short of the ladder it gates, on the same page as the byte-identity gate whose whole point is that one tier proves nothing about its neighbours | P4.2 |
| ✦ **Residency and upload under motion** | Columns per second sustained at flight speed through generate + mesh + **upload**, against the resident-byte cap; the governor of decision 38 holds the cap without visible tier oscillation | P4.10 |
| ✦ **Coarse generation is cheaper** | A tier-L chunk costs strictly less than a tier-0 chunk, monotonically in L — the proof that octave-dropping is real and not decorative | P4.1 |
| ✦ **Tier count under load** | **≤ 7,500 resident chunks INCLUDING crossfade residency, measured WHILE MOVING**, at the shipped `crossfade_band_fraction`, and inside the stated memory budget. Steady state is 6,821; the crossfade multiplier is 1.078 at f = 0.15 (7,353) and 1.101 at f = 0.2 (7,510). **This gate is what BOUNDS `crossfade_band_fraction`, not the reverse: the shipped default is 0.15 because 0.2 does not pass.** A residency gate that excludes the transient peak is not a residency gate *(corrected: the earlier "~7,000" failed by construction)* | P4.10 |
| ✦ **No pop** | The pop detector sees no discontinuity at any tier crossing — **at flight speed AND on a forward walk at eye height**, the second being the case the reference title visibly failed | P4.10 / P6.6 |
| ✦ **Coarse envelope (property test)** | The tier-L height at any point lies within the tier-0 height's min/max over its coarse cell, over random seeds and random coarse cells — the obligation that **fixes the SIGN**, i.e. proves the crack can only open downward. **It is paired with, not a duplicate of, §3.5.6's `terrain_tier_agreement`**, which bounds the MAGNITUDE at \|h(dir,L) − h(dir,0)\| < 4·k_rough·2^L. A skirt needs both; either alone leaves a hole in the argument | P4.1 |
| ✦ **Shadow double-cast** | No tier boundary shows double-darkening or acne during a crossfade. **Closed BY CONSTRUCTION via the start-up assertion `shadow_max_distance ≤ (1 − crossfade_band_fraction) × R₀`, re-asserted whenever the residency governor moves `px_per_cell`.** The engine does **not** apply the visibility-range dither in the shadow pass, so this is a known defect to be closed rather than discovered. **The negative control at 900 m MUST show the acne band, or the gate is not testing anything** | P4.11 |
| ✦ **Collision is tier-0 only** | An assertion, not a test: the collider builder refuses a non-zero tier | P5.2 |
| ✦ **Edit survival across tiers** | A dug tunnel and a built tower are visible at *every* tier boundary; the fly-away / fly-back run shows zero disappearance and zero pop | P6.1 |
| ✦ **Pyramid equals its deltas** | The pyramid recomputed from the delta log is byte-identical to the incrementally maintained one, after an edit storm and after a hard kill | P6.1 |
| **Terrain byte-identity** | Identical 128-bit digest across three targets at two optimisation levels, over ~64 chunk keys spanning all faces, edges, corners, band floor and ceiling, a water column and both hemispheres — **with the digest set indexed by `(seed, chunk key, tier)` and the cross-build diff covering EVERY legal tier of the fixture body** *(corrected from "two coarse tiers": `h(dir, L)` is a different function per L, so a tier that passes proves nothing about its neighbours)* | P4.1 |
| **Client-server generator parity** | The client crate and the sim crate produce equal digests for the same chunk list | P4.1 |
| **Texture-coordinate precision** | Bit-identical coordinates for the same block at the world origin and at a billion metres | P4.3 |
| **Upload budget** | One click at a chunk corner ≤ 4 MB; total video memory ≤ 3.0 GiB asserted at start-up | P4.3 |
| **Shader tap budget** | Worst shipping configuration ≤ 32 taps at tier 0, asserted from a shader-variant compile check; **≈ 2 taps at tier ≥ 4**; three effect combinations forbidden at build time | P4.4 |
| **Crumbling-edge golden table** | 10,000 corner configurations including a cube-face-seam block and all eight cube corners; the exhaustive 256-configuration containment and amplitude proof; **and a tier-2 chunk byte-identical with the crumble path on and off** | P4.5 |
| **Merge-ratio regression** | Constructed materials exactly unchanged; natural surfaces inside the stated retained-win band | P4.5 |
| **Decoration golden vectors** | 4,096 inputs to byte-exact instance records, in the pre-merge gate | P4.7 |
| **Decoration field golden** | A fixed block field plus growth log plus seed, evaluated at five ticks, hashed | P4.7 |
| **Decoration cross-implementation parity** | Software-adapter diff pre-merge; **real-hardware diff on each shipped backend, scheduled, with a named owner** — the software run cannot catch backend code-generation divergence and saying so is the point | P4.7 / scheduled |
| **Decoration frame time** | **p99 ≤ 1.90 ms** on the declared reference tier, over 300 frames with timestamp queries *(§6.10 revised its own contract from 2.80 ms and returned 0.90 ms to the frame table, naming §5's ladder as the claimant; the gate follows the design)* | P4.7 |
| **Collider chunk-seam** | A character walked across a chunk boundary at twenty sampled offsets receives no vertical impulse | P5.2 |
| **Collider residency** | ≤ 27 MB per dynamic-body cluster, including the co-located-sessions density case | P5.2 |
| **Collider determinism** | Construction from the block field bit-identical across binaries (the solver need not be) | P5.2 |
| **Click to pixels** | Protocol half 73–123 ms; render half echo-to-pixels ≤ 33 ms with zero main-thread stall | P6.1 / P6.3 |
| **Edit fan-out** | Proportional to observers-with-that-chunk-resident × dirty chunks, measured against the density baseline | P6.1 |
| **Pyramid walk-up cost** *(was "Pyramid write cost — ≤ 8 entry writes per edit, no disk read on the edit path"; that gate was unpassable against the update rule it gated)* | **≤ 1 entry write and ≤ 1 pyramid storage-block read per rung per touched coarse cell** — a rung-L parent's eight children always lie in ONE rung-(L−1) storage block because the chunk edge of 62 cells is even. **Zero reads of the edit log, zero reads of any tier-0 delta**; a miss resolves through the GENERATOR, not through disk. All writes ride the log's own write transaction. p99 ≤ (rungs − 1) × 8 × 5 × 12.19 ns — **5.85 µs at thirteen rungs, 9.75 µs at twenty-one** — and ≤ 1 % of the click-to-pixels budget; the early-exit depth distribution is reported | P6.1 |
| **Damage resolution** | Nanoseconds per hit, constant-time spread asserted; a million hits per second sustained | P6.2 |
| **Sparse-table promotion crossover** | The measured crossover matches the computed one, driving a chunk from empty to full | P6.2 |
| **Damage replication** | ≤ one message per session per tick — about 7 % of the measured worst-case peak at 128 sessions | P6.2 |
| **Shaped-lane ceiling** | Under 2 MB per chunk by construction; ≤ 0.4 ms for a three-thousand-shaped-cell chunk | P6.3 |
| **Merge-barrier worst case** | The adversarial checkerboard wall inside its stated bound, degrading to per-cell quads rather than to a server cost | P6.3 |
| **Decoration edit latency** | p99 recompute plus write ≤ 0.15 ms; ≤ 9 write ranges totalling ≤ 216 bytes per edit | P6.6 |
| **Decoration bulk edit** | A ten-metre crater and a hull destruction in one batch trigger the bulk path on the task pool; main thread never exceeds its budget | P6.6 |
| **Propagation kernel** | Cells per millisecond per field row; the taxicab ball sizes match the closed form exactly; 64 concurrent floods against the per-tick budget | P6b.1 |
| **Simulation-cost accumulator** | Constant time per edit; a fifty-thousand-block ship fully rebuilt | P6b.2 / P8 |
| **Signal delivery** | ~0.5 ns per delivery; ten thousand functional blocks at realistic churn inside a one-million-delivery per-tick budget (1 % of a tick) | P9.1 |
| **Interest-set memory** | ~14.5 MB across 27,000 live worlds; ~1.3 MB at a thousand-child node | P9.1 |
| **Replay-window memory** | Bounded by the declared entry cap with eviction-and-refuse, not by an attacker's patience | P9.1 |
| **Probe budget** | 64 probes per tick per world, ≤ 0.64 ms — 1.3 % of a tick on top of the signal pass | P9.2 |
| **Panel scale** | 500 covers, 128 sessions: inside the per-client byte budget and the shard tick allowance, one or two draw calls, **and no draw list delivered to an unauthorised session** | P9.3 |
| **Coverage** | Tier-A 100 % region and branch, with each new Tier-A crate added to the coverage list **in the commit that creates it** | Every slice |
| **Run-anywhere** | Named per slice above; the still-owed re-anchor-forcing variant discharges at P6.1 | Per slice |

**Where the next benchmark slot should go, and why it is not lighting.** The one shipped AAA title with
published measurements comparable to our ambitions runs per-pixel ray-traced diffuse global illumination
across a 200 km² open world for 3–4 fps on PC, with the CPU barely stressed; its frame goes to crowds,
battles and **streaming-heavy transitions**, and its most-criticised flaw traces to a texture-memory
target enforced by uniformly aggressive detail reduction. That reorders our own risk register the same
way §5.3.6 already argued: **the lighting ambitions are not what will sink the frame; residency and
upload under motion is.** Hence the ✦ residency row above, and hence decision 38's governor.

### 8.6 Cross-section consistency report

**Nine genuine disagreements** — the original six between the six sections, plus three the detail-level
ladder exposes — **and five smaller mismatches.** Each is stated plainly with an adjudication. Nothing
here is papered over. Items 1–6 are unchanged in substance; only item 1 gains a clause.

**1. The saved block record — three sections give three different answers.** §3 sizes it at eight bytes
and raises it as its own decision; §4 rules "keep five bytes" and says §3's decision should be struck;
§6 says six bytes; §2 specifies exactly five with a particular layout; §5 states in passing that "§3 and
§4 independently settle the record at eight bytes", which is wrong about §4 on both the width and the
identity model; §7 restates §3's eight bytes as settled. **Adjudication:** this is decision 2 and it is
the register's second row. §4's argument is *specifically* against independent substance and shape
fields, not against width — it wins on the identity model and loses on the width. §2 and §4 additionally
contradict each other on the sixth bit: §2 spends it on a generated-versus-placed marker and encodes
mirroring as a shape; §4 spends it on a mirror flag and keeps a total mirror map anyway. Both are
load-bearing: without the placed marker the structural system collapses every natural cave roof, and
without the mirror flag symmetry building punches holes. At five bytes you can have one, not both — which
is the decisive argument for widening. §6's separate state byte is *largely already answered* by §2's
existing sparse side table, which carries exactly the bits decoration wants; the remaining question is
whether decoration can afford a sparse join instead of a record field, and since it already scans the
chunk to build its per-cell table, it can. **Recommended synthesis: eight bytes — eighteen bits of cell
index, sixteen of block identity, six of orientation including the mirror flag, one generated-versus-
placed marker, eight of material-interpreted state, fifteen reserved and rejected on decode if non-zero.**
Addendum 1 §B.4 offers the defensible alternative: five bytes closes if the two upstream verdicts stand.
**Clause added by the ladder:** the edit pyramid is **not** a candidate for the reserved bits. It has a
different key, a different lifetime and a different write rate; it is decision 37's own table. Widening
the placement log to carry derived summary data would break exactly the discipline §2 defends.

**2. Who owns the physics-library question.** §2 says rapier is a committed roadmap deliverable so this
is not an adoption question; §4 and §7 say neither library is in the lockfile and adoption is the owner's
call. **Adjudication:** both are right about different things. The roadmap does name the physics engine as
a phase deliverable, but a roadmap line is not the owner's consent for the *collision* library's new
sparse voxel shape, which is what both sections actually escalate. Merged into decision 16 with two parts,
and the two sections agree on everything that matters — the spike, and routing every shape through an
opaque project-owned identifier so the answer stays reversible.

**3. The shape row is specified twice, incompatibly.** §2's version stores volume in millionths of a cubic
metre, one coverage rasterisation, a millidegree walkable slope, and three authored face masks. §4's
version stores volume as an exact whole number over a lattice fine enough to represent any shape on a
thirty-second grid, two rasterisations (conservative for the occluder, liberal for the occludee, so the
only possible error is under-culling and therefore overdraw, never a hole), slope as an exact rational,
and one *derived* face mask replacing all three. **Adjudication: §4's row supersedes.** §2's volume field
cannot express one third, one sixth, two thirds or five sixths — four of the twenty-three catalogue
entries — and §2's millidegree slope field was proven to be a tripwire wired to nothing on a warped grid,
because the same wedge presents anything from 43.5 to 56.1 degrees across one planet. §2's substance row
is unaffected. One consequence must be carried through: §2's mass derivation must be restated on §4's
lattice, and §4's ruling that **a cell is the unit of matter** — one block yields one unit and weighs one
nominal cell's worth wherever it was mined — stands, because it removes a two-and-a-half-times
position-dependent mining exploit that would be invisible to players and durable in a scarcity-driven
economy.

**4. Where the crumbling-edge function lives, and how many new crates exist.** §5 places it in a new
mesher crate; §6 says that is no longer viable once decoration consumes it and proposes a third small
crate; §4 argues against creating a new crate at all. Between them the sections create four new crates.
**Adjudication: two new crates, not four, and the function lives in the core crate.** The displacement is
a pure function of a corner identity, an occupancy byte and a material amplitude table — it is domain data
manipulation and belongs beside the corner-identity operation it already depends on, where both the mesher
and the decoration evaluator reach it without either depending on the other. The static shape, substance
and function tables also stay in the core crate, per §4. That leaves exactly one new crate — the mesher
and decoration evaluator together, Tier-A, added to the coverage list in the commit that creates it — with
the sim-to-decoration dependency edge expressed as a module boundary and enforced by the same check §6
specifies. **Naming hazard to fix on the way in:** the cube-sphere mapping curve and the edge displacement
are two different things and §3 and §5 both call theirs a "warp". **The ladder adds no crate:** skirts go
in the mesher, the pyramid goes in the block store beside the deltas, and the count-to-shape table goes in
core because it must be identical on server and client.

**5. Decoration's rule key assumes a record layout nobody adopted.** §6 keys its lookup on a ten-bit
material and a twelve-bit geometry identifier packed in the record — the research pool's split, which
neither §2 nor §4 adopts. **Adjudication:** re-derive the key against the combined identity number,
resolving substance and shape through the block-type table rather than reading packed record bits, and
re-derive the sixteen-entry shape class as a projection of the shape identifier. Same table, same cost,
correct inputs.

**6. Decoration adds a render-model field to a block definition that does not exist.** §6 wants leaf
materials to declare they are not drawn as cubes. **Adjudication:** that is a flag bit on §4's shape row
plus a foliage shape family — §4's flag byte has room — not a new enum on a new struct. §6's underlying
point is correct and important: the mesher must consult the *authoritative* block definition for this, not
a cosmetic table, or the render mesh becomes a function of a client-facing layer.

**7. NEW — three sections and one addendum state a hard drawn-radius cap. It no longer exists.**
§3.7 gives "the honest answer about the draw radius"; §5.9 is built around "the no-LOD collision"; and
Addendum 1 §C.4 states the finding in bold — *"the binding constraint is the drawn radius, not the planet
radius; roughly 700 m to 1 km of fully meshed terrain is what one-metre blocks with no detail tiers can
afford."* **Adjudication: all three are correct conditional on a clause that has been retracted — "with
no detail tiers".** With the ladder, resident chunk count is logarithmic in view distance, so there is no
drawn-radius cap at all; what is capped is the **resident chunk budget**, which is a different quantity
with a different governor (decision 38). Every occurrence must be restated in those terms rather than
deleted, because a reader who remembers "we cap the draw distance near a kilometre" needs to learn that it
changed and why. The specific replacement sentences: §3.7 — the client holds a *tiered* set whose count is
bounded by the byte cap, not a disc bounded by a radius; §5.9 — retitled from "the no-LOD collision" to
the tier ladder, which is where the ladder's client half is specified; Addendum 1 §C.4 — dissolved, with
its flight table (79,277 chunks at 100 m altitude, 7.9 million at 10 km) replaced by ~5,000 and ~6,000.

**8. NEW — three sections each invented a private detail carve-out; they collapse into one ladder.**
§5.8/§6.5 gives the ambient-occlusion slab a "short radius beyond which the term is simply absent"; §6.2
builds a two-tier decoration scheme with its own distances; §5.9 proposes an analytic displaced-sphere
shell as a second representation of the terrain. **Each was a level-of-detail system built while the rule
said there were none**, which is precisely the accumulation failure the original row 7 predicted.
**Adjudication: one ladder, three rungs of it.** The occlusion slab is resident at tiers 0–1 and absent
above (D-SHP-5, restated). Decoration's tiers become density falloff parameterised by the chunk's own
tier, with an optional impostor rung (decision 39) — no second distance system. The analytic shell is
**not built** (decision 23): the ladder covers its band and the realm proxy is the rung above it. The
general rule this establishes and the design should state once: **a subsystem may not invent its own
distance ladder; it consumes the chunk's tier.**

**9. NEW — Addendum 2 says the material feature ladder is "trivially permitted". It is required.**
§C.8 lists distance-blended detail-normal scales and mipmaps among four things that "dissolve and need no
further ruling". **Adjudication: mipmaps are indeed mandatory-and-settled, but the feature ladder is not
optional and must be specified.** At tier 5 a chunk spans 62 × 32 = 1,984 m while the detail tile's world
period stays 4 m, so the tile repeats 496 times across one chunk and hardware mip selection returns its
average colour — the "everything turns to mush at distance" failure. The fix is to fade the detail tile
out and a larger macro layer in, drop the normal map, drop parallax and drop the two-material seam blend,
**all keyed on `ChunkHeader.detail_tier` as a per-draw uniform** — not on per-pixel camera distance, which
would disagree with the per-entity dither band *inside* the band. It also extends the addendum's own
argument from the generator to the shader: tap count falls from ~8 at tier 0 to ~2 at tier ≥ 4, so coarse
tiers get cheaper per pixel as well as per triangle. Without it the ladder looks *worse* than no ladder.

**Five smaller mismatches, resolved in one line each.**

- **The geometry seam's operation count.** §3 declares six operations; §4 adds two; §5 adds one. All three
  count from §3's six. The seam has **nine** operations and they must all land in slice S0.1, or the
  retrofit re-plumbs both the mesher and the collider. *Amended:* all nine now take the tier as a
  parameter, and the exhaustive gate runs at more than one tier.
- **The occupancy threshold for ambient occlusion** is stated in two different volume units, one of which
  no longer exists. Use §4's exact cell-fraction lattice.
- **The frame-space method decoration needs** is written against the address type §3 deletes. It takes
  §3's sector-carrying address instead — and, worth stating because it strengthens §6's own case, §3's
  addressing is *already* anchor-invariant, so §6's headline risk (a routine world re-centring re-rolling
  every meadow on the planet) is removed by the addressing choice rather than by the method. Keep the
  method as the typed guarantee.
- **Four separate tuning structs** now exist (block store, render, decoration, signal), against the
  no-magic-numbers rule's "one config struct". The rule's operative reading, already set by the existing
  transport and transfer tuning precedent, is **one struct per subsystem, never an inline literal**. Name
  all four in one place so the set stays reviewable. *Amended:* the ladder adds **five fields to the
  render struct and no fifth struct** — pixels-per-cell target, pixels-per-cell ceiling, resident byte
  cap, governor hysteresis and crossfade band fraction. *With one rider, because a field consumed by more
  than one subsystem is how two copies of it end up disagreeing:* `crossfade_band_fraction` is **one**
  field on the render struct, **read** and never re-declared, by the tier dither bands, the ambient-
  occlusion strength ramp, the prop impostor band and the shadow-distance derivation. The rim-warp fade is
  *not* on it — it has its own on/off pair — and decoration's plateau fractions are a different concept
  (where falloff begins, not where two rungs blend), so both survive alongside it.
- **NEW — Addendum 2 cites a wire field that is not a terrain tier.** §A claims the wire "already carries
  a `coarsen_level: u8` precision ladder". It carries a *pose*-precision hop counter on
  `OccupantInterest` (`intershard.rs:659`), and line 303 reserves the WHAT lane as a **concept**. The
  architecture did anticipate the lane; it did not reserve a field. Correct the citation, and plant the
  request-side `tier: u8` in S0.4 while it is free (door 45, D-WLD-9).

### 8.7 Critical path — if you do only three things next

*This list has been rewritten twice. The original three were: answer register rows 1–7; run the noise
benchmark; land the four plant slices. **The noise benchmark has run** (12.19 ns per evaluation, 0.885 ms
per surface chunk — generation risk closed), and **row 7 has been answered** by the owner's retraction of
the detail-level ban. Two of the three original items are discharged. These are the three that replace
them.*

**One. Freeze the three formats, in one session: rows 1, 2 and 37 — the grid family (now including the
ladder's top rung and therefore the chunk key's tier-field width), the saved block record, and the
edit-pyramid entry.** They are one dependent chain and they share one deadline, because all three are
written into the first world that is ever saved and none of them can be changed afterwards without a
migration over every planet, ship, station and blueprint that has ever been edited. Row 3 (the warp curve)
rides along with row 1 and takes minutes once row 1 is settled. **Row 37 is the one that is new and the
one most likely to be underestimated**, because it looks like an implementation detail and is not: it is
permanent, derived delta data, and its five sub-questions — what an entry holds, how the fill is spent on
a shape, how storage blocks are keyed, the tier-0-only write invariant, and what happens when the derived
data disagrees with its source — decide whether a player's dug tunnel still exists when they look back at
it from a hilltop. Rows 4, 5 and 7 no longer belong in this session: two are per-body data and one is
answered.

**Two. Land the plant slices — the geometry seam, the block registry with the full catalogue declared,
the render seam widening, and the wire-and-transport slice — before a single line of generator or mesher
code.** Unchanged in substance and now carrying four ladder items that are free today and are protocol or
key migrations tomorrow: the chunk address's **five** detail-tier bits (three is not enough for a large
planet viewed from altitude, and four is not enough for an Earth-sized one — **58 of 64 bits used, six to
spare**); the geometry seam's nine operations taking the tier as a parameter; the render seam's
`detail_tier` byte becoming a **used** per-draw uniform plus the two crossfade margins; and the
**requested-tier byte on the chunk and block-edit request lane, together with the tier descriptor on its
delta payload**, neither of which exists in any form today — the field Addendum 2 believed was already
reserved is a pose hop counter on a different message. Each is cheap for the same reason as before: there is currently exactly
one producer, one consumer or one caller. The render seam widening should still land *alone*, because its
throwaway synthetic tests are the mesher's future acceptance fixtures — written once, used twice.

**Three. Measure the mesher and the residency path under motion — the two terms that are now the
unmeasured ones.** The noise benchmark closed generation as a risk; it did not close the frame. The
maximum sustainable flight speed (one-way door 42, a *gameplay* door because ship performance is tuned
around it) no longer derives from noise cost — it derives from how many chunk columns per second the
mesher can produce and the graphics card can accept while the resident-byte cap is held. Three numbers
are owed and none is hard to get: the mesher's per-tier cost curve (which is also the proof that
octave-dropping is a saving rather than a decoration), the sustained columns-per-second through generate
plus mesh plus upload at flight speed, and the resident-chunk count of a 100 km view **while moving**,
with the crossfade band resident. That last one is where the fade-direction rule earns its place — coarse
fades in early, fine dies at its own range, +10 % peak residency instead of +40 % — and it is the
difference between the gate passing and failing at the only moment it matters. The wider calibration
finding from the one comparable shipped title points the same way: its frame goes to streaming
transitions, not to lighting.

## Appendix A — Measured: terrain-noise throughput

**Run 2026-08-03.** Discharges §8.7's benchmark item and §8.4's first row — the one unmeasured constant
in the design, which the repository's own earlier analysis flagged as an assumption
(`scripts/snowflow_technique_analysis.md` assumed 30 ns per evaluation and warned the horizon fill might
be anywhere from 4 to 40 seconds of one core).

**Method.** A standalone binary, no workspace dependency added, written to the design's own generation
rules so the measurement is of the *shippable* path: scalar `f64` only, the repository's landed
`SplitMix64` avalanche as the integer lattice hash (§3.5's rule 8 — no second hash), a quintic-polynomial
fade, gradients from a constant table, and **no transcendental function anywhere**. Apple M4 Pro,
`rustc 1.94.1`, `opt-level=3`, fat LTO, one codegen unit, single core, steady state after warm-up,
`black_box` on every accumulator. Source: `scripts/noisebench/` (its own workspace root, so
`cargo check --workspace` never sees it).

### A.1 Primitives

| Operation | Cost |
|---|---|
| Integer lattice hash, one corner | **1.39 ns** |
| One 3D gradient-noise evaluation (8 hashes, 8 dot products, 7 interpolations) | **12.19 ns** |
| Fractal sum, 4 octaves (the cave/density field) | **45.50 ns** |
| Fractal sum, 6 octaves (the surface height field) | **66.45 ns** |

The single evaluation is **2.5× cheaper than the 30 ns the earlier analysis assumed**, which removes the
pessimistic end of its 4-to-40-second range outright.

### A.2 Per-chunk cost, three strategies

| Strategy | Per 62³ chunk |
|---|---|
| A — 3D density at every cell, 4 octaves (naive) | **10.15 ms** |
| B — height field per column + fill by comparison + caves per cell over a third of the volume | **4.16 ms** |
| **C — height field + fill + caves on a coarse lattice, sampled every 4th cell, interpolated** | **0.885 ms** |
| (a chunk the conservative band test resolves as uniform rock or uniform air) | **0.252 ms** |

The height field is never the cost: 3,844 columns at 6 octaves is 0.252 ms, and filling all 238,328
cells by comparison against it is 0.037 ms. **The three-dimensional cave field is the entire problem** —
3.87 of strategy B's 4.16 ms.

### A.3 The lever that decides it

Caves are low-frequency features; sampling them once per cell is oversampling by construction. Sampling
the field on a coarser lattice and interpolating between samples stays bit-deterministic here because a
power-of-two step makes every interpolation weight exactly representable.

| Sample every | Samples per chunk | Cost, 4 octaves, full chunk | Speed-up |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 cell | 262,144 | 11.63 ms | 0.3× |
| 2 cells | 35,937 | 1.95 ms | 2.0× |
| **4 cells** | **4,913** | **0.625 ms** | **6.2×** |
| 8 cells | 729 | 0.420 ms | 9.2× |

Step 4 is the recommendation: 6.2× cheaper than per-cell, and it still resolves a cave mouth to within
four metres, which at one-metre cells is the scale caves are authored at. Step 8 buys a further 33 % and
starts to round tunnel walls visibly. Octave count is the weaker lever — 4 to 3 octaves saves 24 % and
costs a visible layer of detail.

### A.4 What it meant then, and what the ladder changed

At the starter body's radius the ground horizon at eye height is **741 m**, holding **449 chunk
columns** — which independently reproduces §3.7's figure from a different direction, a useful cross-check
on the radius arithmetic.

| | Strategy A | Strategy B | **Strategy C** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fill the whole horizon (1,348 chunks), one core | 13.7 s | 5.61 s | **1.19 s** |
| Fill the whole horizon, eight cores | 1.71 s | 0.70 s | **0.15 s** |

> **⚠ SUPERSEDED IN PART by Addendum 2.** This appendix's flight table was computed against a
> **single-detail** world, where visible chunk count grows with the *square* of view distance. Under the
> detail ladder it grows with the *logarithm*, so those figures are now an upper bound of historical
> interest rather than a budget. The per-chunk costs in A.1–A.3 are unaffected and remain the pinned
> numbers — and coarse rungs are cheaper still, because a rung drops octaves it cannot resolve.

### A.5 The three conclusions

1. **The phase-invalidation risk is closed.** Client-side generation ahead of a moving player is
   comfortably affordable. **Under the ladder this is no longer even close** — a 100 km view is ~6,800
   chunks, and coarse rungs cost less than tier-0 ones.
2. **§3.5's generation strategy gains a required rule, not an optimisation.** *The three-dimensional
   density field is evaluated on a lattice coarsened by a power-of-two step — 4 by default, carried as a
   field in the generation tuning struct, never an inline literal — and interpolated to cells.* Written
   per-cell the design is 11.5× more expensive. This belongs in the generator's first slice: retrofitting
   it changes generated terrain and therefore invalidates every stored edit, so it sits inside the same
   one-way door as the curve and the radius.
3. **The benchmark becomes a regression gate,** not a one-off: a tier-0 surface chunk must stay at or
   under 1.20 ms on the reference machine, and §8.4's promoted mesher gate now carries the per-rung curve
   beside it. It is cheap, dependency-free, and it is the tripwire for somebody later adding an octave, a
   second noise field or a transcendental call without noticing the cost.

**One caveat, stated plainly.** These figures are for a hand-written Perlin-style gradient noise, which
is what the determinism rules force us toward and roughly what a vendored implementation would cost. If
the noise-source decision (register row 8) lands on an external crate instead, this benchmark must be
re-run against it before the number is trusted.
